# Thymosin Beta-4
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/thymosin-beta-4
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: tb-500 tb500 tb4 thymosin beta-4 full, Tβ4, TMSB4X (gene)
2. Origin: Made by the body
3. Sequence: SDKPDMAEIEKFDKSKLKKTETQEKNPLPSKETIEQEKQAGES (43 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: Investigational; the eye program is furthest along. Injectable use is unapproved and WADA-banned (S2).

## Summary
5. Thymosin beta-4 is a protein made by nearly every cell that holds actin ready to rebuild the cell's scaffolding. It is investigated for wound healing, heart repair and eye-surface disease, with reliable repair in animal studies. Human eye trials disappointed, and grey-market TB-500 is often this full molecule, used for tendon and muscle injury recovery.
6. Punch line: The full repair protein behind TB-500. Weekly shots for tendon and muscle injuries; slower, whole-body healing.
7. Used for: Injury and soft tissue repair

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Tissue repair: Keeps cells ready to rebuild
9. Inflammatory signaling: Lowers inflammation signals
10. Cellular protection: Helps heart cells survive in mice
11. Pain & sensory: Less injury pain reported
12. Heart & vessels (backed only by animal or user reports): Heart repair in mice
13. Bone & cartilage (backed only by animal or user reports): Joint recovery reported
14. Immunity (backed only by animal or user reports): Immune signalling studied in animals

## How it works
15. Holds actin ready for cell rebuilding · G-actin sequestering · role Tissue repair
   Inside nearly every cell, Tβ4 binds single actin units (G-actin) and keeps them in reserve. When a cell has to move or reshape, that stock is released to build new filaments fast. This is its best-established job, shown in biochemistry and cell work.
16. Moves repair cells into wounds · Cell migration · role Tissue repair
   Outside cells, Tβ4 promotes migration of endothelial and skin cells, the ones that line vessels and close wounds. Repair cells reach damaged tissue faster, so wounds close sooner. This is reliable in animal wound and cornea models, but eye drop trials in people missed their main endpoints.
17. Grows new blood vessels · Angiogenesis · role Tissue repair
   Tβ4 promotes angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels into healing tissue. Better blood supply brings oxygen and repair cells to the injury. This is shown in animal wound and heart models.
18. Lowers inflammatory signals · NF-κB, TNF-α down · role Inflammatory signaling
   Tβ4 lowers NF-κB activation and TNF-α, central drivers of inflammation. A calmer injury site can heal with less secondary damage. This is shown in cell and animal studies.
19. Helps heart muscle survive injury, in animals · ILK, Akt survival · role Heart & vessels
   In heart injury models, Tβ4 activates ILK (integrin-linked kinase) and Akt, survival signals inside heart muscle cells. More cells survive the injury. This is shown in animals, not in people.
20. Releases an anti-scarring fragment · Ac-SDKP cleavage · role Cellular protection
   The front end of Tβ4 can be cut to release Ac-SDKP, a tetrapeptide that limits fibrosis. This adds an anti-scarring effect to the repair process. The seven-residue TB-500 fragment sold on the grey market lacks this end.
21. Mechanism overview: Tβ4 is a 43 amino acid protein, the main G-actin sequestering molecule in cells. By holding actin monomers, it controls how quickly cells can remodel their cytoskeleton and migrate. Outside cells it promotes endothelial and skin cell migration and angiogenesis, and lowers NF-κB and TNF-α signalling. In heart injury models it activates ILK and Akt, improving heart muscle cell survival. Its N-terminus is cleaved to release Ac-SDKP, an anti-scarring tetrapeptide. Together these explain the reliable wound, cornea and heart repair in animals.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
22. Typical: 2–2.5 mg · 2–3× weekly · cycle load 4–6 wk → maint. 4–8 wk · route Sub-Q (reported)
23. Half-life: ~4 hours
24. Dose note: Top reported Sub-Q is about 10 mg a week (5 mg twice weekly) for severe injury. Much bigger numbers online are hospital IV trials, not injections people run.
25. Most people take: Load: 2 to 2.5 mg, 2 to 3 times a week for 4 to 6 weeks. Maintenance: 0.75 to 2 mg, 1 to 2 times a week for 4 to 8 weeks.
26. Some load higher, up to 5 mg twice a week.
27. Loading (common): 2–2.5 mg · 2× weekly (4–5 mg/wk) · 4–6 wk · Sub-Q · for injury, recovery [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4] (reported)
28. Maintenance: 2 mg · 1× weekly or every 2 wk · 6–12 wk · Sub-Q · for post-loading [S2] [S5] [S4] (reported)
29. Aggressive: 5 mg · 2× weekly (10 mg/wk), taper · until healed · Sub-Q · for severe injury [S6] [S7] [S1] (reported)

## What people report
30. Grey-market 'TB-500' is often actually this full-length molecule; reported for injury recovery like the fragment.
31. Liked / worked: Reliable wound and corneal healing in animals
32. Liked / worked: IV dosing tolerated in volunteers
33. What worked: Reliable wound and corneal healing in animals; human eye results so far are mixed.
34. Went wrong / did not work: SEER-1 stopped early, missed significance
35. Went wrong / did not work: SEER-3 missed its main endpoint
36. Went wrong / did not work: Dry-eye trials missed
37. Went wrong / did not work: Heart and broad repair unconfirmed in people
38. What went wrong: The big systemic human promise (heart, broad repair) has not been confirmed in large trials; most injectable use rides on animal data.
39. Most reported: Grey-market 'TB-500' often this full molecule
40. Most reported: Injury recovery, like the fragment

## What has been tested
41. Heart & vessels: Heart repair after injury (animal)
42. Tissue repair: Wound healing (animal)
43. Tissue repair: Corneal healing (animal)
44. Cellular protection: IV safety, healthy volunteers (human)
45. Tissue repair: Neurotrophic keratopathy, eye drops (trial)
46. Tissue repair: Dry eye, eye drops (trial)
47. Strong animal data for heart, wound and corneal repair. Human trials of the full molecule: IV safety studies in healthy volunteers (Ruff 2010), and RGN-259 eye drops in Phase 3 for neurotrophic keratopathy: SEER-1 was stopped early and missed significance, SEER-3 missed its main endpoint in 2025, and SEER-2 results are due late 2026. Dry-eye trials also missed.
48. What it helps: Animal studies show reliable wound, corneal and heart repair. IV dosing was tolerated in healthy volunteers. Human eye trials disappointed: SEER-1 in neurotrophic keratopathy stopped early without significance, SEER-3 missed its main endpoint, and dry eye trials missed. Grey-market TB-500 is often this full molecule, used by people for tendon and muscle injury recovery.
49. Trial: active · Phase 3 · neurotrophic keratitis eye drops (RGN-259) · NCT05555589 · ReGenTree / HLB Therapeutics. SEER-2 finished its last patient visit in August 2026 with topline results due November 2026. (checked 2026-10-23) [S8] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
50. People with active or recent cancer: Tβ4 drives new blood vessels and cell migration; high levels track with tumour spread. (reported)
51. Drug-tested athletes: Thymosin beta-4 and TB-500 are named on the WADA list; doping cases exist. (verified)
52. People with proliferative retinopathy or vascular malformations: Pro-angiogenic peptides could feed abnormal vessel growth. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
53. BPC-157: BPC-157 works on growth signalling and blood flow at the injury, while Tβ4 moves repair cells in and supplies the actin they rebuild with. People stack them for tendon and muscle injuries and they are sold pre-mixed as BPC-157 + TB-500 and in several wider blends, but the pair has not been tested together in people.
54. KPV: Tβ4 handles cell movement, vessel growth and actin supply for repair, while KPV turns down inflammation inside gut and immune cells. They are sold pre-mixed in KLOW and Tβ4 + BPC + KPV. The pair has not been tested together in people.
55. Cartalax: Cartalax is claimed by the Khavinson group to tune connective tissue genes in cartilage, while Tβ4 brings repair cells and new vessels. They are sold pre-mixed as Cartalax + Tβ4 + BPC-157 for joints. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
56. Named for the thymus, where it was found in 1981, though nearly every cell makes it and platelets carry the most. Its job is holding actin, the cell's scaffolding, ready to rebuild. Its start carries a natural acetyl cap.
57. First studied for: Wound healing, heart repair and eye-surface disease.
58. Name story: 'Beta' means it sat in the near-neutral charge band of calf-thymus fraction 5, not that it is related to the alpha thymosins. 'TB-500' is just market shorthand for 'thymosin beta'; strictly it names the 17–23 fragment. [S9] (verified)
59. 1981: Found in the thymus; later seen in nearly every cell
60. 2000s: Strong animal data for heart, wound and corneal repair
61. 2010: IV safety study in healthy volunteers
62. 2025: Eye-drop Phase 3s miss; SEER-1 stopped early, SEER-3 missed
63. Today: Investigational eye drug, SEER-2 due late 2026; injectable use WADA-banned

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Two different molecules, one market name [lab]
64. This is the thing to settle before anything else, because almost every confused claim about this compound starts here. The full protein is 43 residues. The material nominated and sold as TB-500 is a seven-residue fragment, residues 17 to 23, carrying an acetyl group on its front end. Reviewing them for the US compounding list, the FDA stated plainly that TB-500 and thymosin beta-4 are not the same substance [1] (verified).
65. That has a practical consequence that cuts against the usual reassurance. People often say grey-market TB-500 is "actually the full molecule, which is better studied". Sometimes it is. But the two have different evidence bases, different stability, different molecular weights and different regulatory records, and a label naming one while containing the other is a mislabelling either way. The free base fragment is listed at 889.01 g/mol under one CAS number, the acetate at 949.1 under another, and the nomination's own stated identifier matched neither of them [1] (verified).
66. The identity confusion was not limited to buyers. In the nomination the agency reviewed, the substance named was the free base while the submitted certificate of analysis was for the acetate salt, listing the acetate's CAS number, formula and molecular weight [1]. Like the other peptides in this group, TB-500 is a common name rather than an approved generic name, which the agency flagged as a patient safety risk because there is no reference standard to test a batch against [1] (verified).

### What was actually nominated, and what the paperwork showed [lab]
67. The nominated product was a 3 mg per millilitre lyophilised powder for subcutaneous and intramuscular injection, for wound healing [1] (verified). That is the specific claim the agency evaluated, not recovery, not tendon repair.
68. For the free base, no certificate of analysis was submitted at all. A publicly available certificate tested appearance, identity by mass spectrometry and HPLC, and peptide purity, and did not test assay, impurities, bacterial endotoxins or aggregates [1]. For the acetate, the supplied certificate was more thorough, covering appearance, solubility, amino acid composition, water, acetate content, impurity limits of 2.0% total and 1.0% for the largest single impurity, and purity, but it did not report identification, assay, aggregates or bacterial endotoxins [1] (verified).
69. As with the other peptides in this review round, the impurity limits leave impurities of unknown identity, and the agency's concern is that unidentified impurities and aggregation can drive immune responses to an injected peptide. It judged injectable routes to pose a significant immunogenicity risk on that basis, with no immunogenicity studies available either way [1] (verified). Both forms were concluded to be not physically and chemically well characterised.
70. Storage is cold: below minus 20 degrees Celsius for the free base, below minus 15 for the acetate [1].

### Mechanism, and which molecule each step was shown with [mixed]
71. The actin story belongs to the full protein. Holding actin monomers in reserve is what sets how fast a cell can rearrange its own scaffolding and crawl, which is the common root of the wound, cornea and heart findings. Everything downstream of that is a consequence of cells being able to move and survive, not of a receptor being switched on.
72. The heart survival step came from a 2004 paper in Nature working in mouse cardiac tissue and cells, which reported that the full protein activates integrin-linked kinase and promotes cardiac cell migration and survival after injury [2] (verified, animals and cells). This is the most cited mechanistic result in the field and it was done with the 43-residue protein.
73. Here is where the fragment's own record gets uncomfortable. The wound-healing data most often invoked for TB-500 came from a 2003 study using the non-acetylated seven-residue sequence applied topically to aged mice. The agency's position is that this cannot be extrapolated to the acetylated injected fragment, because it differs in both the molecule and the route [1] (verified).
74. And when the fragment itself was tested directly, in a 2024 in vitro fibroblast scratch assay, TB-500 free base at 50 micrograms per millilitre did not significantly promote wound closure. A metabolite, the N-acetylated five-residue fragment, showed a small but statistically significant effect at the same concentration [1] (verified, cells). A negative result in a simple assay at a high concentration is not the end of the question, but it is the only direct test of the marketed fragment's core claim, and it did not support it.
75. Pharmacokinetics for the fragment amount to one animal study in a different species: horses given 10 mg subcutaneously reached plasma peaks of 0.05 and 0.08 nanograms per millilitre [1]. There is no intramuscular pharmacokinetic data, and none in humans, for either the fragment or by any route [1] (verified).

### The human record for the full protein [people]
76. Systemic human exposure exists, and it was well tolerated. A Phase 1 programme on an injectable formulation of the full protein ran a double-blind, placebo-controlled single ascending intravenous dose stage in 40 healthy volunteers and a 14-day dosing stage in a further 40, reporting no adverse events judged related to the drug [3] (verified). Doses and pharmacokinetics were not reported in the public announcement, which is a real limitation when that study is cited as the safety basis for injected use.
77. A separate first-in-human randomised, double-blind single- and multiple-dose Phase 1 study of recombinant human thymosin beta-4 in healthy volunteers has been published [4] (reported). Together these establish that intravenous dosing of the full protein has been tolerated in small, short, monitored settings. They do not establish anything about subcutaneous dosing of a seven-residue fragment over weeks, which is the actual pattern of use.
78. For the fragment, the agency found no clinical studies, no human exposure data and no human pharmacokinetic data by any route [1]. Its adverse event database returned nothing, and a separate complaint system returned two cases involving a blended fragment-and-BPC-157 product with no safety assessment attached [1] (verified). There is no established human dose for the fragment, and no study from which one could be derived.
79. The eye programme is where the full protein has been tested properly, and it is the most informative part of the record precisely because it is rigorous. The third pivotal trial in neurotrophic keratitis completed its last patient visit in August 2026 and entered data cleaning and analysis, run across 50 sites, 41 in the United States and 9 across Italy, Spain and Poland, with topline results aimed for November 2026 [5,6] (reported). Given that the earlier pivotal trials in this programme did not deliver a clear win, this readout is the single most consequential pending result for the molecule, in either form.

### Safety: an absence rather than a finding [lab]
80. For the fragment, the toxicology section of the record is empty. No acute toxicity studies, no repeat-dose studies, no genotoxicity studies, no developmental or reproductive studies and no carcinogenicity studies were submitted or identified for either the free base or the acetate [1] (verified).
81. That is a different situation from a compound that has been tested and raised concerns. It means the ordinary questions, what dose causes harm, what organ is affected first, whether it damages DNA, whether it affects pregnancy, whether it causes tumours, have not been asked of this molecule at all. The agency noted the absence of carcinogenicity data without drawing a conclusion from it [1] (verified).
82. The widely repeated line that this peptide has an excellent safety profile with no reported side effects is, read against the record, a statement about the absence of studies and of surveillance reports rather than about the presence of safety data. Both readings produce the same sentence; only one of them is informative.
83. One consideration specific to the biology is worth stating carefully. A molecule whose job is to make cells migrate and survive is, in principle, acting on capabilities that matter in tumour spread as well as in repair. No study has examined this for either form (speculated). It is an argument from mechanism, not an observation.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
84. The agency proposed not adding either the free base or the acetate to the 503A compounding bulks list. Its reasons were, in order: neither substance is well characterised; there is no history of use in compounding; there is no evidence of effectiveness for wound healing; there is no human safety data; injectable routes carry immunogenicity risk; and approved wound therapies already exist [1] (verified).
85. The advisory committee recommended adding it anyway, voting 8 to 6 with one abstention on 23 July 2026, for wound healing [7,8]. The same committee recommended BPC-157 and KPV by the same margin, against the same staff opposition [8,9].
86. That recommendation is advisory and changes nothing by itself. Adding the substance requires formal notice-and-comment rulemaking, which has not begun and carries no deadline [7] (verified). The interim path under consideration is an "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides", sent to the White House budget office for review on 14 October 2026 and unpublished as of mid-October, with its covered substances and conditions not public [7] (verified). It would be enforcement discretion rather than approval, and could be withdrawn without rulemaking.
87. In sport, injectable use of either form is prohibited under the peptide hormones and growth factors class. That is a straightforward position and has not changed.

### Open questions [mixed]
88. Does the acetylated seven-residue fragment do anything? The one direct test of it against its own nominated indication was negative, and the positive wound data belongs to a different molecule applied a different way. This is the field's central unexamined assumption.
89. If the fragment works through a metabolite, as the 2024 assay faintly suggested, then dose, timing and route logic all change, and none of the existing conventions were built on that premise.
90. What is in the vial, the fragment or the full protein? There is no routine identity testing that distinguishes them in grey-market supply, and the two are regulated and evidenced separately.
91. Does the full protein work in the eye? The November 2026 readout will largely answer this, and it is the only well-powered test of the molecule in humans anywhere.
92. Does intravenous tolerability in 80 monitored volunteers over 14 days say anything about repeated subcutaneous dosing over months? Nothing in the record connects the two.
93. Everything about long-term safety, in both forms. There is no toxicology at all for the fragment, which makes this less an open question than an unopened one.

# BPC-157
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/bpc-157
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: bepecin, PL 14736, PL-10, PLD-116, Body Protection Compound 157
2. Origin: Fragment of a natural protein
3. Sequence: GEPPPGKPADDAGLV (15 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: Unapproved everywhere. FDA placed it in 503A Category 2 in 2023, then moved it to 'previously in Category 2' by April 2026 after the nomination was withdrawn; staff proposed not adding it; the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8-6 in July 2026 to recommend adding it, with no proposed rule as of early October 2026. WADA lists it S0, banned in and out of competition.

## Summary
5. BPC-157 is a 15-amino-acid chain based on a protective fragment of human gastric juice, now treated as a stable synthetic peptide. People use it for tendon, ligament and gut repair. Animal work is strong, human data are small, and it is unapproved and WADA-banned; users report help with elbow, shoulder and knee pain, often paired with TB-500.
6. Punch line: The Wolverine peptide. Most used for tendon, joint and gut healing, injected near the injury, often with TB-500.

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Tissue repair: Faster tendon and ligament healing in rats
8. Digestive & gut: Protects the stomach and gut lining
9. Inflammatory signaling: Calms injury inflammation
10. Pain & sensory: Less joint and tendon pain reported
11. Heart & vessels (backed only by animal or user reports): Grows new blood vessels
12. Neural protection (backed only by animal or user reports): Nerve protection in rats
13. Bone & cartilage (backed only by animal or user reports): Bone and tendon-to-bone repair in rats

## How it works
14. Grows new blood vessels into injured tissue · VEGFR2, Akt, eNOS · role Tissue repair
   In rat models BPC-157 raises VEGFR2, a receptor for blood vessel growth signals, and activates Akt and eNOS downstream. Cell and rat studies show more vessel formation and faster blood flow recovery, without more VEGF itself. No receptor for BPC-157 has been identified.
15. Moves repair cells into the wound · FAK, paxillin · role Tissue repair
   BPC-157 activates FAK and paxillin, proteins that anchor cells and steer their movement. Fibroblasts, the cells that lay down new tissue, then migrate into the injury faster. This comes from rat and cell work, mostly from one research group.
16. Makes tendon cells more responsive to growth hormone · GH receptor up · role Tissue repair
   In fibroblasts from rat Achilles tendon, BPC-157 raised growth hormone receptor levels. Treated cells then grew more and activated JAK2 when growth hormone was added. It does not act like growth hormone; it makes tendon cells respond more to what is present. Shown only in rat cells.
17. Shields gut lining from NSAID damage, in rats · Gastric cytoprotection · role Digestive & gut
   BPC-157 protects the stomach and gut lining from damage caused by NSAIDs, a property called gastric cytoprotection. In rats this means fewer lesions and better healing of colitis and surgical gut joins. Human gut data are limited to a small enema trial in ulcerative colitis.
18. Lowers inflammatory signals in injury models · TNF-α, IL-6 down · role Inflammatory signaling
   In injury models BPC-157 lowers the inflammatory messengers TNF-α and IL-6. Less of these signals means a calmer injury site during repair. This is shown in animals, but the studies lack clear dose-response relationships, which weakens the mechanism case.
19. Steadies nitric oxide signalling · NO system · role Heart & vessels
   In isolated rat arteries and human endothelial cells, BPC-157 activated Src and eNOS and freed eNOS from caveolin-1, raising nitric oxide output. The vessels relaxed, mostly through their lining. This is shown in cells and isolated tissue, not in people.
20. Mechanism overview: BPC-157 is a stable 15 amino acid peptide from a fragment of a gastric juice protein. No receptor has been identified, and most mechanism data come from one Zagreb group. In rat models it upregulates VEGFR2 and activates Akt and eNOS, driving new vessel growth into injured tendon, ligament and muscle. It activates FAK and paxillin, helping fibroblasts migrate into the wound, and increases growth hormone receptors on tendon cells, making them more responsive to GH. It also steadies nitric oxide signalling, lowers TNF-α and IL-6, and protects the gut lining from NSAID damage.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
21. Typical: 250–500 mcg · 1–2× daily · cycle 4–8 weeks · route Sub-Q, oral (logged)
22. Half-life: ~15 min (rat, IV)
23. Dose note: No reports of 10 mg injected, once or twice a day. The reported top is about 2 mg a day (1 mg twice daily). 10 mg figures come from single IV infusions in a small safety study, vial sizes, and rat doses in mg/kg read as flat doses.
24. Most people take: 250 to 500 mcg per injection, once or twice a day
25. Courses mostly 4 to 8 weeks. Oral use shows no clear pattern.
26. Common: 250–500 mcg · 1–2× daily · 4–8 wk · Sub-Q · for general repair, tendon/joint [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4] [S5] (reported)
27. Higher / injury: 500 mcg 2× daily (≈1 mg/day) · 2× daily, ~12 h apart · 4–6 wk · Sub-Q near injury · for active injury [S1] [S3] [S4] (reported)
28. Aggressive: 1 mg 2× daily (2 mg/day) · 2× daily · short courses · Sub-Q; or oral 1 mg 2× daily · for stubborn injury, heavy users; oral gut use [S2] [S6] (reported)
29. Logged: 0.2 to 0.4 mg, most logged per injection, 138 of 246 entries
30. Logged: 250 and 500 mcg, tie as the most common fixed dose, 11 accounts

## What people report
31. 98% favorable, 128 user logs
32. 1,245 Reddit reports; recovery 326, pain 256
33. 73% better, 30 of 41 clear outcomes
34. Most consistent signal is musculoskeletal: elbow, shoulder, knee, post-surgery. Typical reported dose 250-500 mcg SC once or twice daily, 4-8 week courses. Sleep, gut and mood shifts reported both ways. Commonly stacked with TB-500.
35. Liked / worked: Faster tendon and ligament healing in rats
36. Liked / worked: Gut lining protected in rats
37. Liked / worked: 11 of 12 knee patients improved in a small series
38. What worked: In animals, faster tendon-to-bone and ligament healing, protected gut lining, and healing at sites away from the injection. In people, the aggregators lean strongly positive: PeptIQ logs 98% favorable across 128 user logs, and SelfAssay's 1,245 Reddit reports are led by recovery (326) and pain (256). Of ~50 forum accounts read directly, about 73% of clear outcomes were better; injected accounts that named a dose and site were nearly all positive (a success-reporting bias).
39. Went wrong / did not work: Oral use: split results, many no-change reports
40. Went wrong / did not work: No large human efficacy trial yet
41. What went wrong: Oral is the weak route: split results, several no-change reports from people who tried capsules or bottles. Human efficacy is essentially unproven outside the small knee series. SelfAssay logs anhedonia (42), a vague 'high-risk' tag (33), anxiety, insomnia and nausea; a few accounts stopped over itching, mood dips or chest pain (one ER visit called it anxiety).
42. Most reported: Elbow, shoulder, knee and post-surgery recovery
43. Most reported: Gut calmer for some
44. Most reported: Sleep and mood shifts both ways
45. Most reported: Often paired with TB-500

## What has been tested
46. Tissue repair: Achilles and ligament tears (rat)
47. Muscle & performance: Crushed and torn muscle (rat)
48. Digestive & gut: Colitis and gut joins after surgery (rat)
49. Digestive & gut: Ulcerative colitis, enema (trial)
50. Pain & sensory: Knee pain, injected into the joint (human)
51. Organ function: Bladder pain, 12 women (human)
52. Animal studies are extensive and almost all from one group: rat Achilles and medial-collateral-ligament tears, muscle crush, colitis, and gut-join (anastomosis) healing. Human data are thin. PL 14736, the enema form, ran a Phase I in 32 healthy volunteers and a Phase II in 53 people with ulcerative colitis (published only as a 2005 abstract). An oral Phase I was cancelled in 2016. A small retrospective knee series (Lee 2021, ~12 people, 4 mg into the joint) reported 11 of 12 improved. A bladder pilot in 12 women and a 2-person IV pilot reported no adverse events. A hamstring Phase 2 (NCT07437547, SC daily 14 days vs placebo) is recruiting.
53. What it helps: Animal work is strong: faster Achilles and ligament healing, muscle repair and gut lining protection in rats. Human data are small: 11 of 12 knee pain patients improved after joint injection, and an enema form was trialled in ulcerative colitis. User reports centre on elbow, shoulder and knee tendon pain and recovery after surgery, often paired with TB-500. Oral use for gut symptoms gives split results.
54. Trial: active · Phase 1 · recovery after rotator cuff surgery · NCT07803250 · University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences. First US placebo controlled BPC-157 trial, not yet recruiting; the only earlier registered trial (2015) was cancelled. (checked 2026-10-23) [S7] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
55. People with active or recent cancer: Raises VEGFR2 signalling and new vessel growth in animal work; tumours use the same pathway. (inferred)
56. Drug-tested athletes: Banned since 2022 under S0 (non-approved substances); positives have led to bans. (verified)
57. People with proliferative retinopathy or vascular malformations: Pro-angiogenic peptides could feed abnormal vessel growth. (inferred)
58. People with known peptide or injection allergies: FDA reviewers flagged immunogenicity and impurity risk; no human safety dataset exists. (reported)

## Synergies (paired with)
59. TB-500 frag 17–23: BPC-157 drives vessel growth and growth hormone sensitivity at the injury, while the TB-500 fragment is meant to help repair cells crawl in through actin binding. People stack them for tendon and soft tissue injuries, but the fragment's own data are thin and the pair has not been tested together.
60. GHK-Cu: BPC-157 brings blood supply and repair cell movement, while GHK-Cu delivers copper for collagen cross-linking and remodels scar matrix. They are sold pre-mixed as GHK-Cu + BPC-157 and inside the GLOW and KLOW blends, but the pairing is user logic, not trial data.
61. KPV: BPC-157 protects and repairs the gut lining, while KPV calms inflammation inside gut and immune cells by blocking NF-κB. People pair them for colitis and gut flares, and they come pre-mixed in KLOW and Tβ4 + BPC + KPV. The pair has not been tested together.
62. NAD+: BPC-157 acts on local tissue repair, while NAD+ supplies the coenzyme that cell energy and DNA repair enzymes run on. People add NAD+ as a general recovery and energy layer alongside an injury protocol. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
63. Somatropin (HGH): BPC-157 raises growth hormone receptors on tendon cells in rat work, and somatropin supplies the growth hormone itself, which drives IGF-1 and collagen synthesis. The logic is a more receptive tissue meeting more signal. The pair has not been tested together.
64. MOTS-c: BPC-157 targets the injured tissue, while MOTS-c works on whole-body metabolism through AMPK, the cell's energy sensor, in mice. People combine them for recovery alongside training and fat loss goals. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
65. Ipamorelin: Ipamorelin triggers growth hormone pulses through the ghrelin receptor, while BPC-157 makes tendon cells more responsive to growth hormone in rat cells. People pair them for injury recovery and sleep. The pair itself has not been tested together.
66. Retatrutide: These serve different goals: retatrutide drives weight loss through GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors, while BPC-157 is used for tendon and gut repair. People on a weight protocol sometimes run BPC-157 for an injury or gut complaint at the same time. There is no data on the combination.
67. ARA-290: ARA-290 acts on the innate repair receptor to calm nerve inflammation and regrow small nerve fibres in small trials, while BPC-157 supports blood supply and repair in injured tissue. People pair them for injuries with a nerve pain side. The pair has not been tested together.
68. Cartalax: Cartalax is a short peptide claimed by the Khavinson group to tune connective tissue genes in cartilage, while BPC-157 brings vessel growth and repair cell movement. They are sold pre-mixed as Cartalax + Tβ4 + BPC-157 for joints, but the pairing is user logic, not trial data.
69. PEA: PEA is usually added to BPC-157 for pain and inflammation, while BPC-157 works on tissue repair itself. This library holds no data on PEA yet, so the logic is cautious, and the pair has not been tested together.
70. Thymosin Beta-4: BPC-157 works on growth signalling and blood flow at the injury, while Tβ4 moves repair cells in and supplies the actin they rebuild with. People stack them for tendon and muscle injuries and they are sold pre-mixed as BPC-157 + TB-500 and in several wider blends, but the pair has not been tested together in people.

## Where it comes from
71. BPC stands for Body Protection Compound. A Zagreb team led by Predrag Sikiric reported the 15-amino-acid chain in the early 1990s, isolated from a protective fragment of human gastric juice. The parent protein it is cut from has never been published, so BPC-157 is treated as a stable synthetic peptide rather than a known natural one.
72. First studied for: Studied first for the gut: protecting the stomach lining and healing ulcers, which is where the stomach-juice origin and the name come from. The tendon, ligament and muscle uses came later, almost entirely from rat work.
73. Name story: BPC means Body Protection Compound. The '157' is never explained; it is not the residue count, which is 15. Gym slang calls it the 'Wolverine' peptide. [S8] (verified)
74. Early 1990s: Found in human stomach juice in Zagreb; studied for ulcers
75. 2000s to 2010s: Rat work spreads to tendon, ligament, muscle and gut healing
76. 2005: Enema form tested in ulcerative colitis, Phase II
77. 2016: Oral Phase I cancelled without results
78. Today: The best-known recovery peptide; FDA panel backed compounding in 2026

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where it came from, and what is still missing from that story [lab]
79. The compound has been described in the published literature since 1993, out of a single laboratory in Zagreb [1,2]. The part of the origin story that never arrived is the parent protein. A fragment is, by definition, cut from something larger, but the protein it was supposedly cut from has never been identified in print. That means the usual chain of evidence for a natural peptide, find the protein, find the cleavage, show the body makes the fragment on purpose, was never completed (verified). In practice it is treated as a synthetic 15-residue peptide whose sequence happens to have been written down in 1993.
80. The naming problem is not cosmetic. BPC-157 is a common name, not an approved generic name, and the FDA flagged inconsistent naming as a safety risk in its own right, because without a reference standard there is nothing to check a batch against [2]. There are also two different substances sharing the name: the free base (CAS 137525-51-0) and the acetate salt (CAS 216441-37-1). When two compounding pharmacies nominated it for the US compounding list, they themselves were inconsistent about which of the two they meant, so the agency ended up evaluating both separately [2] (verified).
81. Earlier development ran under other names, PL-10, PLD-116, PL 14736 and Bepecin, through a Croatian pharmaceutical programme [1] (verified). Those names matter when reading old trial records, because the human work was done on a rectal formulation under those codes, not on anything resembling what circulates now.

### What is actually in a vial, as far as anyone has documented [lab]
82. This is the least discussed and most practically important part of the record. Reviewing the certificates of analysis submitted with the US nominations, the FDA found: no certificate at all for the free base; for the acetate, one certificate reporting 97.8% purity with related substances at 1.1% maximum individual and 2.2% total, and a second reporting only a purity figure of 98.34% [2]. In both cases the impurities were not identified, only counted. Neither certificate included endotoxin testing, bioburden, residual solvent or aggregate testing [2] (verified).
83. Those gaps are the reason the agency concluded the substance is not well characterised, and they feed directly into its immunogenicity concern. Solid-phase peptide synthesis can leave peptide-related impurities and aggregates behind, and aggregates are a known trigger for immune responses to peptide drugs. No immunogenicity studies of this compound exist, so the risk could not be ruled out either way [2] (verified). For a 15-residue peptide given by injection or nasal spray, the agency considered that risk significant rather than theoretical.
84. Stability is tighter than most handling assumes. The lyophilised powder is recommended for storage below minus 18 degrees Celsius, and once reconstituted the solution is documented as stable for only two to three weeks at refrigerator temperature [2] (verified). Nothing in the record supports the longer shelf lives often quoted.
85. Independent batch testing exists outside the official record and is worth reading for what it shows about spread rather than for any single verdict. One public testing service tracks 149 vendors for this compound; its default standard scores purity, dose accuracy and label quality together, and a representative vendor record shows 11 tests with 7 passing and 4 failing, including one result with a fill-volume deviation of +30% [3] (reported). The same service offers endotoxin testing but does not publish those results, so sterility and endotoxin remain the least visible part of product quality.

### Mechanism, one step at a time, with the model each step came from [mixed]
86. No receptor has been identified, which shapes everything below. What exists is a set of signalling observations, mostly from two groups, each tied to a specific preparation.
87. Step one, vessel growth. In a 2017 study from a Taiwanese group, the compound raised VEGFR2 at both mRNA and protein level in endothelial cells, increased vessel density in the chick chorioallantoic membrane assay and in endothelial tube formation, and sped blood-flow recovery in rat hind-limb ischaemia measured by laser Doppler [4]. The informative detail is what did not change: VEGF-A itself was not increased [4]. So the proposal is not more growth factor but a more responsive receptor. The same work showed the receptor being pulled into the cell, and that blocking endocytosis with dynasore abolished both the downstream signalling and the extra tube formation [4] (verified, in cells and rats).
88. Step two, how that receptor gets switched on without its usual ligand. The same group's 2020 follow-up worked in isolated rat aortic rings and human umbilical vein endothelial cells. Relaxation was concentration-dependent and reached about 48% in rings with intact endothelium but only about 19% with the endothelium stripped away, so the effect runs through the vessel lining rather than the muscle [5]. Blocking nitric oxide cut relaxation from about 38% to 10 to 12%. In cells, phosphorylation of Src, caveolin-1 and eNOS all rose, a Src inhibitor blunted them, and the binding between eNOS and caveolin-1 fell to about half of control, which is the step that frees the enzyme to make nitric oxide [5]. Nitric oxide signal rose about 1.35-fold (verified, in cells and isolated tissue).
89. Step three, tendon cells specifically. In fibroblasts taken from rat Achilles tendon, a gene expression screen put the growth hormone receptor among the most strongly upregulated genes after treatment, confirmed at mRNA and protein level, dose- and time-dependently. Adding growth hormone to treated cells then raised proliferation and activated JAK2, the receptor's normal downstream kinase [6] (verified, in rat cells). The proposal is sensitisation: the peptide does not act like growth hormone, it makes the cell listen harder to whatever growth hormone is present.
90. What that chain does not include is a dose-response relationship. Reviewing the rodent pharmacology across colonic fistula, NSAID-lesion and liver-injury models, the FDA's assessment was that the studies lacked established dose-response relationships and mechanistic understanding [2] (verified). That is the weakest joint in the mechanism story: effects are reported across a very wide dose span without the orderly increase that normally distinguishes a drug effect from an artefact.

### What the body does with it [animals]
91. One proper pharmacokinetic programme exists, published in 2022 by a group at Air Force Medical University in Xi'an, funded by Chinese national and provincial science foundations [7]. It is the source for nearly every number quoted elsewhere, so it is worth knowing what it actually did.
92. Rats received 20 micrograms per kilogram intravenously and 20, 100 or 500 micrograms per kilogram intramuscularly, plus a seven-day repeat arm and a tritium-labelled arm. Dogs received 6 micrograms per kilogram intravenously and 6, 30 or 150 intramuscularly, plus a seven-day repeat arm [7]. Elimination half-life was under 30 minutes in both species, and the FDA's reading of the data put it at 15.2 minutes in rats and 5.3 minutes in dogs [2,7]. Kinetics were linear across the tested range.
93. Bioavailability after intramuscular injection was about 14 to 19% in rats but 45 to 51% in dogs [7] (verified). That three-fold species gap is rarely mentioned and makes any confident extrapolation to humans unwise.
94. Distribution in rats peaked around one hour, highest in kidney, then liver, stomach wall, spleen and thymus; intestine, lung and skin tracked plasma; gonads, heart and skeletal muscle sat lower; brain and body fat were lowest, which suggests little crosses into the brain [7]. Over 72 hours, recovery was 15.9% in urine, 9.1% in bile, 2.3% in faeces, with about 54% still in the carcass [7]. The peptide breaks down quickly to smaller fragments and then to free amino acids that enter ordinary metabolism, with proline the main one [7] (verified).
95. No human pharmacokinetic data exist for oral, subcutaneous, nasal or transdermal use. In the rectal studies where plasma was measured at all, levels were undetectable or mostly below the limit of quantification [2] (verified). So there is no human exposure figure to anchor anything to.
96. For anyone subject to testing: metabolites are detectable in urine for four to five days by mass spectrometry, at limits of detection well below the threshold used for peptides in sport [8] (verified).

### The human record, in full, because it is short [people]
97. A 2025 systematic review in a peer-reviewed orthopaedic journal screened the literature and found 36 studies: 35 preclinical and one clinical [8]. That ratio is the single most honest summary of the evidence base.
98. One controlled trial exists. Reported only as a 2005 meeting abstract, it randomised 53 people with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis one-to-one to a daily 80 mg enema or placebo for two weeks; 46 completed, with three withdrawals for adverse events on drug and two on placebo. Mean disease activity index change was minus 3.2 (95% CI minus 5.58 to minus 0.82) on drug against minus 1.6 (95% CI minus 3.86 to 0.67) on placebo, and the reported between-group difference was 1.6 with a confidence interval from minus 4.84 to 1.62, which crosses zero [2]. Reviewing it, the FDA found the abstract inadequate: no endpoint definition, no inclusion criteria, no statistical methods [2] (verified). This is the trial that gets cited as human evidence of benefit. It did not show one.
99. Everything else is uncontrolled. A 2021 retrospective chart review from a private wellness clinic in Orlando enrolled 17 people with varied chronic knee pain and reached 16 by telephone; 12 received the peptide alone, of whom 11 reported improvement, and 4 received it with thymosin beta-4, of whom 3 did. Follow-up was a phone survey administered by a college student volunteer, all outcomes were self-reported with no objective testing, only 4 of 16 had a knee MRI, and patients paid out of pocket [9] (verified). The authors declared no conflicts and reported no adverse events.
100. A 2024 case series gave 12 women with interstitial cystitis a single 10 mg intravesical injection during cystoscopy after they had failed standard therapy; 10 reported complete symptom resolution and 2 reported about 80% improvement, with no adverse events and no dropouts [10] (reported). Uncontrolled, self-reported, single-arm.
101. The remaining human exposure is small and mostly safety-oriented: a rectal enema up to 2 mg/kg daily for eight days in 24 healthy subjects, and an intravenous sequence of 10 mg then 20 mg in 2 healthy subjects [2]. No serious adverse events were reported in any of these, but the FDA noted the monitoring was unclear and the studies small and short [2]. A Phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetic trial registered in Mexico in 2015 for 42 healthy volunteers has never posted results and was reportedly withdrawn from submission in 2016 [2,8] (verified).
102. Put plainly: there is no established human dose. Nothing in the record establishes an effective dose, a dose-response relationship, or a safe long-term dose by any route people actually use. Every figure in circulation is either an animal dose converted by body weight, a single-procedure dose from one of the uncontrolled series above, or a community convention.

### Two trials that could change this, and how to read them [people]
103. A Phase 2 trial in acute hamstring strain is recruiting: randomised, placebo-controlled, quadruple-blind, one-to-one, 120 participants aged 18 to 45, daily subcutaneous dosing for 14 days against matching placebo, both arms on standardised rehabilitation, with assessments at days 3, 7, 14, 28 and 56 and recurrence follow-up three months after return to play. The co-primary endpoints are time to unrestricted sport and change in MRI-assessed injury volume at day 14 [11] (verified). That is a real design, and MRI volume is a hard endpoint.
104. One caveat belongs with it. Trial registration is self-submitted and is not peer review. The sponsor's peptide studies share a single site and identical listed start and primary completion dates across a cluster of records, and one record in that cluster carries "Mock Study" in its registered title [12] (reported). That is not evidence of wrongdoing by anyone, and it is not a reason to dismiss the trial. It is a reason to treat the registration as an announcement rather than a result, and to wait for reported data.
105. A Phase 1 trial at a US university medical centre is registered for recovery after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair: randomised, parallel, quadruple-masked, self-administered daily subcutaneous dosing for 90 days after surgery, against both matched saline and a no-treatment arm, with isometric shoulder strength by handheld dynamometer at baseline, 12 weeks and 5 months as the primary outcome. Enrolment is listed as 30 in the structured field and twenty in the plain-language summary; listed start is January 2027 [12,13] (verified). Neither trial has results. Until one does, the human efficacy question stays open.

### Safety: what has been looked at, and the shape of what has not [mixed]
106. Acute animal toxicity is reassuring as far as it goes. No lethal or toxic dose has been identified. Single intramuscular dosing gave no-observed-adverse-effect levels of 20 mg/kg in rats and 10 mg/kg in dogs, and gross and histological examination of major organs found no changes over six weeks in rats and dogs [2,8]. The genotoxicity battery was negative: Ames at 5 to 2000 micrograms per plate, chromosomal aberration in CHL cells at 100 to 400 micrograms per millilitre, and a mouse micronucleus assay at 25 to 100 mg/kg intramuscularly [2]. A rat teratogenicity study gave a no-effect level of 4 mg/kg [2] (verified).
107. The 28-day repeat-dose study is where the picture gets more textured. Rats received 0.2, 1.0 or 4.0 mg/kg daily and dogs 0.1, 0.5 or 2.0 mg/kg daily, all intramuscular [2,14]. Clotting time moved in opposite directions in the two species: shortened in rats, prolonged in dogs [2]. Rats showed raised ALT, glucose and triglycerides, and significant changes in mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration, platelet indices and red cell distribution width; the histopathology for that study was not included in the published manuscript [2]. In dogs, serum creatinine fell significantly in females at the top dose and in males at the middle dose and above [2] (verified). None of this is alarming on its own. It is also not a clean bill of health, and it is the opposite of the "no side effects in any study" claim that circulates.
108. The absences matter more than any finding. There are no carcinogenicity studies. There are no repeat-dose studies longer than 28 days, in any species. There are no acute or repeat-dose studies by the routes people actually use, oral, subcutaneous, nasal or transdermal. There are no peri- or post-natal developmental studies [2] (verified).
109. Human adverse event reporting is thin and hard to attribute. Three reports reached the FDA's surveillance system, all involving injectable products: injection-site redness and swelling in someone also injecting thymosin, shortness of breath with minimal detail, and hyperpigmentation with darkening of the gums that recurred on re-exposure to a combination product labelled for research purposes only. None could be attributed to this peptide alone [2] (verified).
110. Two theoretical concerns deserve to be named as theoretical. First, a mechanism that works by promoting new vessel growth is, in principle, a mechanism that could support tumour growth; no study has tested this, and one cancer-cachexia study found no significant effect on tumour size [1] (speculated). Second, an independent review noted that proline, the main metabolite, can generate reactive oxygen species through proline oxidase, and that sustained excess nitric oxide has its own downstream problems [1] (speculated). Both are reasoned arguments from known biology, not observations.

### Who produced the evidence, and why that is part of the evidence [lab]
111. Most of the animal literature traces to one group in Zagreb across three decades [1,2]. That is not an accusation; founding groups often dominate early literature on a compound they discovered. It does mean the usual safeguard of independent replication is largely absent, and that reading five papers does not necessarily mean reading five independent assessments.
112. The useful development is that independent groups have now entered. The angiogenesis and vasomotor mechanism work came from a Taiwanese university group with no connection to the original laboratory [4,5]. The pharmacokinetics came from a Chinese military medical university [7]. A 2025 literature and patent review came from an independent Polish academic group, and it drew the cancer and metabolite concerns above, which the original group then contested in a published comment-and-reply exchange in the same journal [1] (verified). Disagreement in print is a sign of a field becoming normal.
113. Independent does not mean disinterested. The authors of the 2025 orthopaedic systematic review disclosed relationships with several orthopaedic device companies, and the review itself contains internal inconsistencies in its study counts between text and tables [8] (verified). Worth knowing when quoting its numbers.
114. The patent landscape is scattered across many unrelated private parties, covering uses from acute respiratory distress to scar dressings to a sublingual combination with semaglutide [1]. No single company holds a development programme that would plausibly fund the trials needed for approval, which is part of why the evidence has stayed where it is.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
115. No approved product exists in any country, and the substance appears in no major pharmacopoeia [2] (verified).
116. The US picture changed twice in 2026 and is easy to misread. In April, the FDA removed twelve peptide bulk substances from the compounding Category 2 list, effective 22 April 2026. That happened because the original nominators withdrew their nominations, not because the agency revised a safety judgement [15]. Removal from Category 2 did not place the substance in Category 1 or on the approved bulks list, so it sits in a gap: still an unapproved new drug, without even the Category 1 enforcement-discretion policy to rely on [15] (verified).
117. In July, the agency's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee met on the 23rd and 24th and voted 8 to 6 with one abstention to recommend adding it to the 503A bulks list, for ulcerative colitis, the indication the agency had reviewed [16,17]. The agency's own scientists had recommended against, finding the evaluation criteria weighed against both the free base and the acetate [2]. Their stated difficulty was identity before efficacy: these peptides have no universally accepted chemical definition, which makes evaluation very hard [16]. The committee also recommended KPV and TB-500 by the same margin [17].
118. What that vote is not: approval, a finding of benefit, or permission to compound. It is advisory. Adding a substance to the bulks list requires formal notice-and-comment rulemaking, which the agency has not begun and faces no deadline to begin; one attorney quoted at the time estimated eight to twelve months before pharmacies would have unambiguous authority [16,18] (verified).
119. The live development is an interim route. On 14 October 2026, the agency and its department sent an "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" to the White House budget office for regulatory review. As of mid-October it had not been issued or published, and its terms, including which peptides it covers and what conditions attach, are not public [18] (verified). The expected shape is enforcement discretion for prescription compounding by state-licensed 503A pharmacies, possibly with route restrictions, patient disclosures and adverse-event reporting attached, and it could be withdrawn without rulemaking [18] (reported). Pressure runs both ways: a drug-safety organisation filed a citizen petition in October 2026 asking the agency to stop compounding of untested peptides [19] (reported).
120. Elsewhere: prohibited in sport at all times under the non-approved substances class [2,20]. On the US Department of Defense prohibited ingredients list, so service members are told to avoid it by any route [20]. Not a controlled substance under US drug scheduling, which is why it is sold as a research chemical with not-for-human-consumption labelling [8,20]. A New Zealand committee proposed prescription classification in May 2023 [2]. The agency has separately cautioned against compounded products containing it, citing safety risks and possible contamination with other substances [20] (verified).

### Open questions [mixed]
121. What protein is it a fragment of? Until that is published, the claim that this is a natural human peptide rests on a 1993 assertion rather than a demonstrated biosynthetic pathway.
122. Is there a receptor? Every mechanism above is a downstream signalling observation. Without a binding target, there is no way to predict tissue selectivity, no structure-activity work, and no rational basis for dose.
123. Does any of it survive a controlled human trial? The hamstring trial's MRI endpoint is the first design capable of answering that for soft tissue. One negative result there would matter a great deal.
124. Why does the species gap in bioavailability exist, and which way do humans fall? Three-fold between rats and dogs, with no human data, is a wide gap to guess across.
125. What happens past 28 days? The entire long-term safety question is unexamined, in any species, by any route. That is the single largest hole, given that reported use runs in multi-week courses.
126. Does the pro-angiogenic mechanism carry an oncological risk? Unstudied. It cannot be ruled in or out from current data.
127. Is the material people obtain the material in the studies? Given unidentified impurities, absent endotoxin and aggregate testing, and a documented spread in independent batch results, this is arguably the most answerable open question, and the one most within reach of better testing rather than better trials.

# TB-500 frag 17–23
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/tb-500-frag-17-23
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: TB-500 (strict sense), Ac-LKKTETQ, Tβ4 (17-23)
2. Origin: Fragment of a natural protein
3. Sequence: LKKTETQ (7 amino acids). Acetylated start (Ac-), not shown
4. Legal and approval status: Unapproved everywhere and banned in sport at all times. FDA 503A Category 2 in 2023, removed April 2026 after the nomination was withdrawn; the July 2026 advisory committee gave a favorable non-binding recommendation; no final rule found. WADA S2.3 (growth factors), prohibited at all times, no exemption. Australia/New Zealand treat it as a prescription medicine.

## Summary
5. TB-500 fragment 17-23 is a synthetic seven-amino-acid peptide copying the actin-binding region of thymosin beta-4, meant to carry its repair action in a smaller molecule. People use it for tendon, wound and soft-tissue recovery, often stacked with BPC-157. There is no human trial of the fragment, and many vials are actually full thymosin beta-4, so reports mix molecules; it is banned in sport at all times.
6. Punch line: The strict TB-500: seven-residue repair core of thymosin beta-4. Weekly shots, usually stacked with daily BPC-157.

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Tissue repair: Moves repair cells into wounds
8. Inflammatory signaling: Lowers inflammation signals
9. Cellular protection: Helps cells survive injury
10. Pain & sensory: Less injury pain reported
11. Heart & vessels (backed only by animal or user reports): Heart repair seen with the full protein
12. Bone & cartilage (backed only by animal or user reports): Joint and bone recovery reported
13. Immunity (backed only by animal or user reports): Immune balance in animal work

## How it works
14. Holds actin so cells can crawl into wounds · G-actin binding · role Tissue repair
   The fragment carries the LKKTETQ motif that lets thymosin beta-4 bind single actin units (G-actin) and hold them in reserve. With that reserve, cells can rebuild their skeleton fast and crawl into a wound. This is shown for the full protein; the one direct cell test of the fragment found no significant wound closure.
15. Grows new vessels at the injury · Angiogenesis · role Tissue repair
   In the full thymosin beta-4 protein, this region promotes angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels into healing tissue. Better blood supply carries oxygen and repair cells to the injury. This is shown in animals with the full protein, not with the fragment.
16. Lowers inflammatory signals · TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6 down · role Inflammatory signaling
   With full thymosin beta-4, animal studies show lower TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6, the main inflammatory messengers at an injury. A calmer site can heal with less ongoing damage. Whether the seven-residue fragment does the same has not been tested.
17. Data mostly from the full 43-mer, assumed shared · Thymosin beta-4 · role Cellular protection
   Nearly all the evidence comes from the full 43 amino acid thymosin beta-4, and the fragment is assumed to share it. It lacks the other domains, including the end that releases anti-scarring Ac-SDKP, and regulators state the two are different substances. No human trial of the fragment exists.
18. Mechanism overview: The 17 to 23 fragment (LKKTETQ) is the actin-binding motif of thymosin beta-4. It binds monomeric G-actin and holds it in reserve, letting cells rapidly rebuild their cytoskeleton and crawl into a wound. Most data come from the full 43 amino acid Tβ4, where this region drives cell migration and new vessel growth, and TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6 fall. The fragment is assumed to carry these repair effects, but it lacks the other domains, including the anti-scarring Ac-SDKP end.

PeptIQ's favorable rate is far lower than BPC-157's (38%), with headache (70) and fatigue (65) logged often, and users describe a flu-like reaction. No human efficacy data for the fragment.
41. Most reported: Weekly mg dosing, unlike BPC-157's daily mcg

## What has been tested
45. Tissue repair: Wound and tendon repair, full Tβ4 (animal)
46. Heart & vessels: Heart cell survival after injury (mouse)
47. Inflammatory signaling: Inflammatory cytokines (animal)
48. Cellular protection: Full Tβ4 safety, 40 volunteers IV (human)
49. Tissue repair: Rotator cuff, elbow, knee recovery (users)
50. Almost all mechanism and outcome data come from full-length thymosin beta-4, not the 7-mer, which is assumed to share them. In animals: G-actin binding that keeps cells mobile, faster cell migration into wounds, new vessel growth, lower TNF-alpha/IL-1beta/IL-6, and a heart-cell survival signal (Bock-Marquette 2004, Nature). Full-length human trials exist for safety (Ruff 2010, 40 volunteers IV, no dose-limiting toxicity) and for eye disease (RGN-259 drops). No controlled human trial of the TB-500 fragment itself exists.
51. What it helps: There is no human trial of the fragment. Animal work, mostly with full Tβ4, shows wound and tendon repair and heart cell survival. In forum accounts, 79% of clear outcomes were better, most often for rotator cuff, elbow, pec and knee injuries and post-surgery recovery. Many vials are actually full Tβ4, so reports mix molecules. Users often stack it with BPC-157.
52. Trial: none. The 17 to 23 fragment sold as TB-500 has never been tested in humans; trials used full thymosin beta-4. (checked 2026-10-23) [S8] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
53. Drug-tested athletes: TB-500 is named on the WADA list as a thymosin beta-4 derivative. (verified)
54. People with active or recent cancer: The actin-binding 17-23 region is the part that drives cell migration, a step in tumour spread. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
55. BPC-157: The fragment is meant to help repair cells move in through actin binding, while BPC-157 drives vessel growth and makes tendon cells more responsive to growth hormone in rat work. People stack them for tendon and soft tissue injuries. The pair has not been tested together.
56. GHK-Cu: The fragment targets cell movement into the wound, while GHK-Cu delivers copper for collagen building and scar remodelling. People pair them to approach skin and wound repair from two angles. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
57. KPV: KPV calms inflammation inside gut and immune cells by blocking NF-κB, while the fragment is used for tissue repair. People combine them when an injury or gut issue has a strong inflammatory side. The pair has not been tested together.
58. NAD+: NAD+ supports cell energy and DNA repair enzymes, while the fragment is used for local tissue repair. People add NAD+ as a general recovery layer. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
59. Somatropin (HGH): Somatropin raises IGF-1 and supports collagen synthesis and lean mass, while the fragment is used to move repair cells into injured tissue. People pair them for injury recovery and body composition. The pair has not been tested together.
60. MK-677: MK-677 raises growth hormone and IGF-1 through the ghrelin receptor and deepens sleep, while the fragment is used for local repair. People pair them for recovery. MK-677 also raises hunger, and the pairing is user logic, not trial data.
61. MOTS-c: MOTS-c works on whole-body metabolism through AMPK in mice, while the fragment is used for tissue repair. People combine them in training and recovery stacks. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
62. Ipamorelin: Ipamorelin triggers growth hormone pulses while sparing cortisol and prolactin, while the fragment is used to support repair at the injury. People stack them for recovery and sleep. The pair has not been tested together.
63. IGF-1 LR3: IGF-1 LR3 drives protein building and muscle stem cell growth through the IGF-1 receptor, while the fragment is used for cell movement into injured tissue. People pair them for muscle injury recovery. IGF-1 LR3 can drop blood sugar, and the pair has not been tested together.
64. Retatrutide: These serve different goals: retatrutide drives weight loss through GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors, while the fragment is used for injury repair. People on a weight protocol sometimes run it for an injury at the same time. There is no data on the combination.
65. Collagen: Collagen is usually taken to supply building material for tendon and skin, while the fragment is used to help repair cells reach the injury. This library holds no data on collagen yet, and the pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
66. A synthetic, acetylated 7-amino-acid peptide (Ac-LKKTETQ) copying the actin-binding region, positions 17-23, of thymosin beta-4, a 43-amino-acid protein made in most human cells. It first surfaced as a designer doping agent in racehorses; equine detection methods were published in 2012.
67. First studied for: Meant to carry thymosin beta-4's repair and anti-inflammatory action in a smaller, cheaper molecule, mainly for soft-tissue and tendon injury.
68. Name story: Strictly speaking this is the original TB-500: the doping literature uses that name for this fragment, not for full thymosin beta-4. 'TB-500' is a trade code, not a medical name. [S9] (verified)
69. 1980s to 1990s: Thymosin beta-4 mapped; its actin-binding stretch is positions 17 to 23
70. 2004: Full-length Tβ4 protects heart cells in mice (Nature)
71. 2012: Found in racehorses; equine doping tests published
72. 2023 to 2026: FDA Category 2, then removed; July 2026 panel favourable
73. Today: The weekly recovery shot, usually paired with BPC-157

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What was actually nominated, and under which name [lab]
74. In 2026 US regulators evaluated this fragment for the compounding list, and the paperwork is instructive. The nominated product was a 3 mg per millilitre lyophilised powder for subcutaneous and intramuscular injection, for wound healing [1] (verified). Not tendon repair, not recovery, not injury. Wound healing is the single claim that was formally assessed.
75. The nomination described the active entity as the LKKTETQ site within the parent protein, and regulators evaluated two substances under the name: a free base at 889.01 g/mol under one CAS number, and an acetate salt at 949.1 under another [1]. The nomination's own stated alternate identifier matched neither of them [1] (verified). The named substance was the free base while the submitted certificate of analysis was for the acetate, listing the acetate's CAS number, formula and molecular weight.
76. Regulators noted that this is a common name rather than an approved generic name, and treated the inconsistent naming as a patient safety issue in itself: with no reference standard, there is nothing against which a batch can be checked [1] (verified). The doping literature's use of the name for this fragment, rather than for the full protein, is the older and more precise usage, but it is not a regulatory identity.

### What the certificates do and do not cover [lab]
77. For the free base, no certificate of analysis was submitted with the nomination. A publicly available one tested appearance, identity by mass spectrometry and HPLC, and peptide purity, and did not test assay, impurities, bacterial endotoxins or aggregates [1] (verified).
78. For the acetate, the certificate was more complete: appearance, solubility, amino acid composition, water content, acetate content, impurity limits of 2.0% total and 1.0% for the largest single impurity, and purity. It did not report identification, assay, aggregates or bacterial endotoxins [1] (verified).
79. The impurity limits are the quiet problem. A limit caps how much unidentified material is present without saying what it is. Regulators' concern is that unidentified peptide-related impurities and aggregates are a known driver of immune responses to injected peptides, and they judged injectable routes to carry significant immunogenicity risk on that basis, with no immunogenicity studies available for either form [1] (verified). Both were concluded to be not physically and chemically well characterised.
80. Storage is colder than most handling assumes: below minus 20 degrees Celsius for the free base, below minus 15 for the acetate [1].

### What a seven-residue fragment can and cannot inherit [cells]
81. The inheritance argument is that this stretch is the actin-binding motif, so it should carry the parent protein's repair effects. There is a specific reason to be careful with that reasoning, and it is not the one usually given.
82. The front end of this fragment carries an acetyl group. The wound-healing data most often invoked for it came from a 2003 study that used the non-acetylated seven-residue sequence, applied topically, in aged mice. Regulators' position is that this cannot be extrapolated to the acetylated injected form, because both the molecule and the route differ [1] (verified). So the foundational positive result is for a chemically different peptide delivered a different way.
83. That matters more than it sounds. Acetylation changes charge at the front end of a very short peptide, and in a seven-residue molecule the front end is a large fraction of the whole. It is not a cosmetic modification.
84. Regulators also stated plainly that this fragment and the 43-residue parent protein are not the same substance [1] (verified). The practical consequence runs in both directions: data from the parent cannot be assumed to transfer down, and a vial containing the parent under this name does not contain what the label says.

### The one direct test of the marketed molecule [cells]
85. This is the most important and least circulated finding about this compound.
86. In a 2024 in vitro fibroblast scratch assay, the free base at 50 micrograms per millilitre did not significantly promote wound closure. A metabolite, the N-acetylated five-residue fragment, showed a small but statistically significant effect at the same concentration [1] (verified, cells).
87. A single negative assay does not settle a question. But this is the only direct test of the marketed fragment against its own nominated indication, it used a high concentration, and it did not support the claim. The accompanying observation that a shorter breakdown product did something is more interesting than the negative itself: if activity sits with a metabolite rather than the administered peptide, then the whole logic of what to give and when changes (inferred).
88. Set against that, there is no cell or animal study showing the acetylated fragment reproducing the parent protein's wound, cornea or heart results. The assumption of shared activity has not been tested and, where tested at all, was not confirmed.

### What the body does with it [animals]
89. Pharmacokinetics amount to one study in a species nobody is dosing. Horses given 10 mg subcutaneously reached plasma peaks of 0.05 and 0.08 nanograms per millilitre [1] (verified). There is no intramuscular pharmacokinetic data for either form, and none in humans by any route [1].
90. Those plasma figures are strikingly low for a 10 mg dose, which is consistent with a short peptide being cleared and broken down fast. It also means there is no exposure number from any species to anchor a human expectation to, and nothing to connect a given amount injected to a concentration at a tendon.
91. The detection side is better developed than the therapeutic side, because the compound's first scientific attention came from drug testing rather than from medicine. That asymmetry is worth noticing: the methods for proving someone used it are more mature than the methods for showing it works.

### Safety: unopened rather than open [lab]
92. No acute toxicity studies, no repeat-dose studies, no genotoxicity studies, no developmental or reproductive studies and no carcinogenicity studies were submitted or identified for either form [1] (verified).
93. So the standard questions have not been asked: what dose causes harm, which organ is affected first, what happens over months, whether it damages DNA, whether it affects pregnancy, whether it causes tumours. Regulators noted the absence of carcinogenicity data without drawing a conclusion from it [1].
94. Human surveillance is similarly empty. The adverse event database returned nothing for this substance. A separate complaint system returned two cases involving a blended product combining it with another repair peptide, with no safety assessment attached, and causality could not be assigned to either component [1] (verified). That is a direct cost of blending, not a finding about this molecule.
95. The commonly repeated claim of an excellent safety profile with no reported side effects is, against this record, a statement about absent studies and absent surveillance. The reported pattern of headache and flu-like fatigue in community use has no counterpart anywhere in the formal literature and no mechanism has been investigated for it (reported).

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
96. Regulators proposed not adding either form to the 503A compounding bulks list, citing poor characterisation, no history of use in compounding, no evidence of effectiveness for wound healing, no human safety data, immunogenicity risk, and the existence of approved wound therapies [1] (verified).
97. The advisory committee recommended adding it anyway, voting 8 to 6 with one abstention on 23 July 2026, for wound healing [2,3]. Agency staff had recommended against all seven peptides considered that week.
98. That recommendation is advisory. Addition requires formal notice-and-comment rulemaking, which has not begun and carries no deadline [2] (verified). An "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" went to the White House budget office on 14 October 2026 and was unpublished as of mid-October, with its covered substances and conditions not public [2]. Removal from the do-not-compound category in April 2026 followed withdrawn nominations rather than a revised safety finding, and left the substance outside any recognised category rather than cleared [4] (verified).

### Open questions [mixed]
99. Does the acetylated fragment do anything at all? The one direct test against its own nominated indication was negative, and the positive wound data belongs to a chemically different peptide applied topically. This is the field's central unexamined assumption, and it is testable cheaply.
100. If activity sits with a metabolite, what follows? The 2024 assay's only positive result was for a breakdown product, which would change the logic of what is worth administering.
101. Which molecule is in the vial? Regulators state the fragment and the parent protein are different substances, and no routine identity test in grey-market supply distinguishes them, so pooled user reports describe a mixture of molecules.
102. What exposure does any dose produce in a human? One horse study is the entire pharmacokinetic record.
103. Everything about toxicology. There is none, in any species, by any route, which makes long-term safety an unopened question rather than an open one.
104. Why the divergence between forum reports and app-logged favourability? Both populations are self-selected, and the gap may be as much about which molecule people actually received as about effect.
