# GHK-Cu
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/ghk-cu
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: copper tripeptide-1, prezatide copper, prezatide copper acetate, copper peptide, tripeptide-copper complex
2. Origin: Fragment of a natural protein
3. Sequence: GHK (3 amino acids). Bound to one copper ion; weight shown is GHK alone
4. Legal and approval status: Not an approved drug anywhere. In the US the non-injectable form sits in FDA 503A Category 1 'under evaluation' (except injectable routes); the injectable nomination was withdrawn in April 2026. A compounding advisory meeting is due before end of February 2027. WADA does not name it.

## Summary
5. GHK-Cu is the copper complex of the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine, carried naturally in human blood; the copper turns it blue. It is used for skin repair, collagen, wound healing and hair, with plasma levels falling with age as the anti-aging hook. Controlled studies show faster diabetic ulcer closure and thicker skin with topical forms, while injected use has never been studied in humans.
6. Punch line: Blue copper peptide that fades with age. Applied or injected for collagen, firmer skin, wound healing and hair.

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Skin & aesthetics: Builds collagen, firmer skin
8. Tissue repair: Faster wound closure
9. Inflammatory signaling: Calms redness and swelling
10. Hair: Hair regrowth reported
11. Cellular protection (backed only by animal or user reports): Delivers copper to antioxidant enzymes
12. Organ function (backed only by animal or user reports): Lung repair in mice
13. Cognition (backed only by animal or user reports): Memory in older mice

## How it works
14. Carries copper to tissue that is rebuilding · Cu(II) delivery · role Tissue repair
   GHK, a tripeptide found in human plasma, binds copper (Cu(II)) tightly and delivers it to tissue. Copper-dependent enzymes such as lysyl oxidase then cross-link new collagen and elastin into strong fibres. Plasma GHK falls with age, though the commonly quoted figures lack a clear primary source.
15. Turns up collagen and elastin making · Fibroblast signalling · role Skin & aesthetics
   In fibroblasts, the cells that make skin and connective tissue, GHK-Cu raises collagen, elastin and glycosaminoglycan synthesis. Small topical human studies report thicker skin and shallower wrinkles, including 40 women over 8 weeks. Injected use has not been studied in people.
16. Remodels scar and wound matrix · MMP and TIMP balance · role Tissue repair
   GHK-Cu shifts the balance between MMPs, enzymes that break down matrix, and TIMPs, their inhibitors. This lets old scar tissue be cleared while new matrix is laid down. A randomised topical trial in diabetic ulcers showed faster closure than vehicle.
17. Enlarges hair follicles in lab studies · Dermal papilla cells · role Hair
   In lab studies GHK-Cu enlarges dermal papilla cells, the signalling cells at the base of each hair follicle. Larger papillae are linked to thicker hair growth. This is cell data only; hair regrowth in people comes from user reports.
18. Lowers inflammatory signals in cell studies · TNF-α, IL-6 down · role Inflammatory signaling
   In cell studies GHK-Cu lowers TNF-α and IL-6, two key inflammatory messengers. Less inflammatory signalling fits calmer healing and less redness. User reports of less redness match this, but it has not been tested as an anti-inflammatory in human trials.
19. Shifts many genes toward repair, in cell data · Gene expression · role Cellular protection
   Gene expression data suggest GHK-Cu shifts many genes toward repair and away from damage. These are broad cell data, mainly from one group; about 35% of the primary literature carries Pickart or Margolina as an author. Treat the scope as claimed, not confirmed.
20. Mechanism overview: GHK is a tripeptide in human plasma that binds copper tightly and declines with age. As GHK-Cu it delivers copper to tissue, where copper-dependent enzymes such as lysyl oxidase cross-link collagen and elastin. In fibroblasts it raises collagen, elastin and glycosaminoglycan synthesis, and shifts the balance between MMPs and their inhibitors, the TIMPs, which remodels scar and wound matrix. Cell work shows lower TNF-α and IL-6 and enlarged hair follicle papilla cells. Broad gene expression shifts toward repair are claimed, mainly by one group.

40. Went wrong / did not work: Some topical users saw no change
41. What went wrong: Injection is unstudied and the most common source of trouble: burning and stinging at the site (worse at high concentration), welts, bruising, skin sloughing, and a few people who threw out vials. Several topical users saw no change or more fine lines. The gene-expression 'resetting' and longevity claims rest on cell and animal data only.
42. Most reported: Smoother skin, less redness
43. Most reported: Some hair regrowth
44. Most reported: Topical users steadier, injectors louder
45. Most reported: Injection sting eases with dilution

## What has been tested
46. Tissue repair: Diabetic foot ulcers, gel (trial)
47. Skin & aesthetics: Facial skin, 40 women, 8 weeks (trial)
48. Skin & aesthetics: Skin thickness and wrinkles (human)
49. Tissue repair: Wounds in rabbits and rats (animal)
50. Organ function: Lung fibrosis (mouse)
51. Cognition: Memory in old mice (mouse)
52. Hair: Hair regrowth (users)
53. Human evidence is topical only. A randomised diabetic-ulcer trial (Mulder 1994) showed far faster closure than vehicle. Small facial studies (Leyden 2002; Badenhorst 2016, 40 women, 8 weeks double-blind) reported thicker skin and reduced wrinkle depth, beating vehicle and Matrixyl. Animal work covers rabbit and rat wounds, lung fibrosis and mouse cognition. No human study of injected GHK-Cu exists, and no therapeutic trial is registered; a 2026 review noted about 35% of the primary literature carries Pickart or his colleague Margolina as an author.
54. What it helps: Controlled studies show faster diabetic foot ulcer closure with a gel, and thicker skin with shallower wrinkles in small trials, including 40 women over 8 weeks. Injected use has never been studied in humans. In forums, 71% of clear outcomes were better, mostly smoother skin, less redness and some hair regrowth. Topical users report steadier results; injectors report louder effects with burning at the site.
55. Trial: unclear · Phase 2 · skin wound healing gel · NCT07437586 · Hudson Biotech. Recruiting, but the sponsor is an obscure firm that also lists gray market peptide trials, one titled a mock study. Treat with caution until another sponsor or a result appears. (checked 2026-10-23) [S6] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
56. Wilson's disease or copper overload: Each dose delivers copper; people who cannot clear copper accumulate it in liver and brain. (inferred)
57. People with cholestatic liver disease: Copper leaves the body through bile; PBC, PSC and bile duct blockage raise body copper. (inferred)
58. High-dose zinc users or copper-allergic people: Zinc and copper compete; injected copper can cause local reactions in metal-sensitive skin. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
59. BPC-157: GHK-Cu builds and remodels collagen, while BPC-157 brings new blood vessels and repair cells to the injury. They are sold pre-mixed as GHK-Cu + BPC-157 and inside GLOW and KLOW, but the pairing is user logic, not trial data.
60. TB-500 frag 17–23: GHK-Cu supplies copper for collagen building and scar remodelling, while the TB-500 fragment is used to help repair cells crawl into the wound. People pair them for skin and wound repair. The pair has not been tested together.
61. KPV: GHK-Cu rebuilds skin matrix, while KPV calms inflammation by blocking NF-κB inside cells. People pair them for red, irritated or eczema-prone skin, and they are sold pre-mixed as GHK-Cu + KPV and in KLOW. There is no combination study.
62. Retatrutide: Retatrutide drives weight loss, while GHK-Cu is used for skin quality and collagen. Some users add GHK-Cu to support skin during fast weight loss. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
63. MOTS-c: MOTS-c works on metabolism and energy through AMPK in mice, while GHK-Cu works on skin and connective tissue repair. People combine them in longevity stacks covering two separate systems. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
64. NAD+: NAD+ supports cell energy and DNA repair enzymes, while GHK-Cu targets collagen and skin repair. Both are used for ageing, so people stack them to cover cell energy and skin structure. The pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
65. The copper(II) complex of the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine, isolated from human plasma by Loren Pickart in 1973 and sequenced in 1977. The copper turns it blue. Plasma levels fall from about 200 ng/mL at age 20 to about 80 ng/mL at 60, which is the hook for the anti-aging claims.
66. First studied for: Pickart noticed young blood plasma made old liver tissue behave younger, and traced it to this copper carrier. First developed as a wound-healing agent (ProCyte's Iamin gel), later as a skincare and hair ingredient (copper tripeptide-1).
67. Name story: Gly-His-Lys holding a copper ion. Cosmetic labels call it "copper tripeptide-1"; the official drug name is prezatide copper. [S7] (verified)
68. 1973: Isolated from human plasma by Loren Pickart; sequenced 1977
69. 1980s to 1990s: Wound gel developed; diabetic ulcer trial in 1994
70. 2000s: Becomes copper tripeptide-1 in skincare and hair products
71. 2026: Injectable FDA nomination withdrawn; topical still under review
72. Today: Skin and hair peptide, topical and injected

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### The experiment underneath the claim [cells]
73. The origin story is usually told as "young blood made old tissue act young", which is true but skips the actual design, and the design is what sets the limits of the claim. The work grew out of studies of fibrinogen, a clotting protein that rises with age. Liver tissue from patients aged 60 to 80 showed elevated fibrinogen production. When liver cells from those older patients were incubated in blood from younger people, they behaved almost like younger tissue [1] (verified).
74. So the original observation was about a liver cell's protein output in culture, not about skin, not about collagen, and not about an organism getting younger. The peptide was isolated from human plasma albumin and reported in Nature in 1973 (Pickart and Thaler, 243:85-87), and the sequence was identified four years later in Experientia (Schlesinger, Pickart and Thaler, 1977, 33:324-325) [1] (verified). Everything since has been an extension from that starting point to tissues it was not originally studied in.
75. The widely quoted figures for plasma levels declining with age, roughly 200 nanograms per millilitre at 20 against 80 at 60, circulate without a clear primary citation attached to them in the reference literature [1] (reported). They may well be right. They are also the load-bearing premise of the entire replacement rationale, and that premise is less well sourced than its popularity suggests.

### Why bound copper behaves differently from loose copper [lab]
76. This is the most chemically solid part of the record and the part that gets least attention. Free copper ions are reactive in a way that damages tissue: they cycle between oxidation states and generate reactive species. A 1981 study in the Biochemical Journal (Lau and Sarkar) showed that when copper is held by this tripeptide, that redox activity is effectively silenced [1] (verified, in vitro).
77. That is the real argument for the complex over a copper salt. It is not that the peptide delivers more copper, it is that it delivers copper in a form that does not do damage on the way. The binding geometry has been determined independently by X-ray crystallography, electron paramagnetic resonance and nuclear magnetic resonance (Hureau et al., Chemistry, 2011) [1] (verified), so this is structural chemistry rather than inference.
78. The practical reading: the copper chemistry is well understood, and it is the best-established thing about this molecule. The biology built on top of it is considerably softer.

### What the cell studies measured, and the direction nobody quotes [cells]
79. The fibroblast work is real and reasonably old. Collagen synthesis in cultured skin fibroblasts was reported in FEBS Letters in 1988 (Maquart et al.); sulfated glycosaminoglycan synthesis in Life Sciences in 1992 (Wegrowski et al.); matrix metalloproteinase-2 expression in fibroblast cultures in Life Sciences in 2000 (Siméon et al.), with decorin reported by the same group [1] (reported, cells). These are the primary sources for almost every claim about collagen and matrix.
80. Here is the part that rarely survives the trip into marketing copy. The molecule stimulates both the matrix-degrading enzymes and their inhibitors. The reference literature draws the obvious conclusion from that and says it should therefore be used with caution [1] (verified). Simultaneously pushing breakdown and the brake on breakdown is coherent as a remodelling signal, where old matrix has to come out before new matrix goes in. It is also not the same thing as "builds collagen", and in a tissue that is not actively repairing, net remodelling is not obviously a benefit.
81. A note on how to read these: cell-culture concentrations in this literature are often in the nanomolar range, applied directly to fibroblasts in a dish. Nothing in that design speaks to what concentration reaches a fibroblast in living skin through any route.

### The gene-expression claim, traced to its source [cells]
82. The "resets thousands of genes toward repair" framing has one main scientific parent, and it is worth reading accurately because what it found is more interesting and less flattering than the summary.
83. A 2012 study in Genome Medicine profiled gene expression in lung tissue from eight regions each of six patients with severe emphysema plus two donor lungs, 64 regions in total, and matched the expression patterns to emphysema severity measured histologically. The resulting signature was then queried against a drug-expression database to find compounds whose effects ran opposite to it. This tripeptide came out of that screen [2] (verified).
84. Then they tested it. In distal lung fibroblasts from former smokers with emphysema, the peptide at 10 nanomolar did three things: it changed where integrin-beta-1 sat in the cell and reorganised actin into contractile filaments; it restored collagen gel contraction, which is impaired in these cells, back toward the level seen in former smokers without the disease; and under second-harmonic imaging the treated cells remodelled collagen into fibrils more effectively [2] (verified, human cells).
85. The detail that reframes everything: the paper reports that these effects resembled activation of the TGF-beta pathway, and that the peptide acted like TGF-beta-1 in these assays [2] (verified). TGF-beta is the central pro-fibrotic signal in the body. So the mechanism behind the lung finding is not a gentle rejuvenation programme, it is engagement of a fibrosis-adjacent pathway that happens to be useful when the problem is tissue that has lost its ability to contract and remodel. That is a genuinely promising finding for a specific repair deficit. It is a poor argument for continuous use in healthy tissue (inferred).

### The animal wound work [animals]
86. Wound healing has been reported across rats, rabbits, mice and pigs, much of it in veterinary journals: Veterinary Dermatology in 2006 and 2008 (Cangul et al.; Gul et al.), Veterinary Surgery in 2003 (Canapp et al.), and Life Sciences in 2007 in diabetic rats (Arul et al.) [1] (reported, animals).
87. The most quotable single number comes from a rat ischaemic skin flap model, where wound area fell 64.5% against 28.2% in controls [1] (reported). Ischaemic flaps and diabetic rats share a feature worth noticing: both are models of impaired healing. The pattern across this literature is that effects show up most clearly where repair is already failing, which is consistent with the lung finding above and inconsistent with a general-purpose enhancement story.

### The human record, including the trial that failed [people]
88. The published positive human evidence is topical and small: controlled facial studies reporting firming and reduced wrinkle depth, which the reference literature itself characterises as having relatively small sample sizes and short durations [1] (verified). That is a fair description and not a dismissal; small short trials are how cosmetic ingredients are normally assessed.
89. What is almost entirely missing from the popular account is that this molecule had a proper pivotal programme, and it did not succeed. Under the name Iamin Gel, a Washington-state company ran two Phase III trials in diabetic plantar foot ulcers, enrolling 511 patients across 30 medical centres, testing 0.5% and 2% formulations against placebo [3,4]. The result, announced in October, was that the drug was no better than placebo [4] (verified). The company's share price fell 68% on the day [4].
90. That matters for how the earlier positive ulcer trial should be read. A smaller randomised trial reporting faster closure, followed by a 511-patient multi-centre pivotal programme finding no difference against placebo, is the classic pattern of an early signal that did not replicate at scale. The pivotal result is the more informative of the two, because it was larger, controlled, multi-centre and designed to be decisive. No approved product followed.
91. For the injected route, there is still no human study of any kind, and no therapeutic trial registered. That has not changed, and it is the route with the thinnest evidence and the loudest claims.

### The route with no regulatory file [lab]
92. There is an asymmetry worth knowing when comparing this compound to its stack-mates. For BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV, the US agency published detailed assessments in 2026 covering identity, certificates of analysis, impurities, endotoxin and aggregate testing, toxicology and immunogenicity. For injectable copper tripeptide, no such document exists yet, because its advisory review was deferred to a later meeting [5,6] (verified).
93. So the honest statement is not that injected use has been assessed and cleared, nor that it has been assessed and faulted. It has not been assessed. The questions the agency asked of the other three, what exactly is in the vial, what the unidentified impurities are, whether aggregates are present, whether endotoxin is tested, whether an injected peptide-metal complex raises immunogenicity concerns, have not yet been asked in public of this one.
94. The additional variable here, absent from the other three, is the metal. An injected copper complex raises questions a plain peptide does not: how much copper is delivered, what happens to it after the peptide is degraded, and what repeated dosing does to copper handling. Nothing in the available record addresses this (verified as absent).

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
95. The sequence in 2026 was messier than the summaries suggest, and the detail matters because it changes what is permitted. On 22 April 2026, non-injectable copper tripeptide was removed from Category 1 as part of a bulk withdrawal action affecting twelve peptide substances, which happened because nominators withdrew rather than because of any safety finding. On 5 May 2026 the nominator clarified that it had intended to withdraw only the injectable-route nomination, and the topical form was restored to Category 1, where it sits under temporary compounding enforcement discretion [5] (verified).
96. The injectable route was left unclassified: not in Category 1, not in Category 2, not on the approved bulks list [5] (verified). Legal commentary on that gap advises against compounding it while it persists.
97. Injectable copper tripeptide is scheduled for review at a second advisory committee meeting expected before the end of February 2027, alongside four other peptides, with no date set as of mid-October 2026 [5,6] (reported). That meeting is the next real decision point.
98. Cosmetic topical use is a separate world and continues unaffected, since the ingredient is a long-established cosmetic additive rather than a drug in that context.

### Open questions [mixed]
99. Why did the pivotal ulcer programme fail where the smaller trial succeeded? Dose, formulation, wound selection and trial size are all candidates, and nobody has published a post-mortem. Until someone does, the honest reading is that topical healing benefit did not replicate at scale.
100. Is the TGF-beta-like action a feature or a warning? It explains the lung and wound results and it is also the pathway behind fibrosis. The answer probably depends entirely on whether the tissue is damaged or healthy, which is exactly the distinction continuous cosmetic use erases.
101. What does the plasma-decline figure actually rest on? The replacement rationale depends on it and its primary source is hard to pin down.
102. What happens to the copper after injection, and does repeated dosing shift copper handling? Unstudied, and unique to this compound among the common repair peptides.
103. Does simultaneous stimulation of matrix-degrading enzymes and their inhibitors net out positively in skin that is not injured? The reference literature's own caution suggests this is not settled.
104. Does injected use do anything a topical does not? With no human study of the injected route at all, this remains a claim rather than a finding, despite being the form most discussed.

# KPV
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/kpv
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: alpha-MSH (11-13), Lys-Pro-Val, tripeptide KPV, L-lysyl-L-prolyl-L-valine
2. Origin: Fragment of a natural protein
3. Sequence: KPV (3 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: US: not approved. Removed from FDA Category 2 in April 2026; the July 2026 advisory panel voted 8-6-1 for compounding, no rule yet. Australia, EU, UK: no approved product, sale needs a medicine licence. WADA: not named, falls under S0.

## Summary
5. KPV is the tripeptide Lys-Pro-Val, the last three amino acids of alpha-MSH, keeping its anti-inflammatory action without the tanning. It is studied for gut inflammation such as colitis and for inflamed skin. Evidence is animal and user-reported, with no human trial, but users rate gut benefits highest and report calmer colitis, eczema, psoriasis and rosacea, usually within 3 to 14 days.
6. Punch line: The anti-inflammatory tail of alpha-MSH, minus the tanning. Often blended with BPC-157 and GHK-Cu.

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Inflammatory signaling: Switches off inflammation signals
8. Tissue repair: Helps the gut lining close
9. Digestive & gut: Calms colitis in mice
10. Immunity: Steadies overreacting immune cells
11. Organ function (backed only by animal or user reports): Studied for skin and lung

## How it works
12. Calms inflammation without tanning · Alpha-MSH 11 to 13 · role Inflammatory signaling
   KPV is the last three amino acids (Lys-Pro-Val, positions 11 to 13) of alpha-MSH, a melanocortin hormone. It keeps much of alpha-MSH's anti-inflammatory action but not the skin-darkening effect. This is shown in cell studies and mouse colitis models; no human trial exists.
13. Gets into gut and immune cells · PepT1 transporter · role Digestive & gut
   KPV enters gut lining and immune cells through PepT1, a transporter that normally carries small peptides from digested food. PepT1 becomes more active in the inflamed colon, so uptake is highest where inflammation is. This is why oral use is common, though it is shown only in cells and mice.
14. Blocks a key inflammation switch inside cells · NF-κB down · role Inflammatory signaling
   Inside the cell, KPV blocks activation of NF-κB, the master switch for inflammatory genes. Output of inflammatory cytokines falls as a result. This is shown in human gut, immune and skin cell lines and in mice.
15. Works even without the tanning receptor · MC1R independent · role Immunity
   Its anti-inflammatory effect persists in mice lacking a working MC1R, the receptor alpha-MSH uses for pigment. So KPV acts inside the cell rather than through melanocortin signalling. This is what separates it from tanning peptides.
16. Eases colitis and helps colon lining heal, in mice · Colitis models · role Tissue repair
   In mouse models of colitis (DSS and TNBS), KPV eased inflammation and helped the colon lining heal, including as oral nanoparticles aimed at the colon. These are the core outcome data. No human trial exists or is registered.
17. Mechanism overview: KPV is the C-terminal tripeptide (Lys-Pro-Val) of alpha-MSH, positions 11 to 13. It carries much of alpha-MSH's anti-inflammatory action without the tanning effect. It enters gut epithelial and immune cells through the PepT1 transporter, which is upregulated in the inflamed colon. Inside the cell it blocks NF-κB activation, lowering inflammatory cytokine output. The effect persists without the MC1R receptor, so it does not depend on melanocortin signalling. In mouse colitis models this calms inflammation and helps the colon lining heal.

## What has been tested
45. Digestive & gut: Colitis, DSS and TNBS models (mouse)
46. Digestive & gut: Oral nanoparticles to the colon (mouse)
47. Inflammatory signaling: Gut, immune and skin cell lines (cell)
48. Skin & aesthetics: Eczema, psoriasis, rosacea (users)

It is taken into gut and immune cells by the PepT1 transporter, which gets more active when the colon is inflamed, which is why oral use is common. No human trial exists and none is registered.

## Who shouldn't take it
53. People with IBD on biologics or immunosuppressants: KPV damps NF-kB signalling; stacking it onto immune drugs is untested. (inferred)
54. People fighting an active infection: Blunting inflammation can blunt the response clearing the infection. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
55. BPC-157: KPV calms inflammation inside gut and immune cells, while BPC-157 protects and repairs the gut lining. People pair them for colitis and gut flares, and they are sold pre-mixed in KLOW and Tβ4 + BPC + KPV. The pair has not been tested together in people.
56. GHK-Cu: KPV damps inflammation through NF-κB, while GHK-Cu rebuilds collagen and remodels skin matrix. People pair them for eczema, rosacea and irritated skin, and they are sold pre-mixed as GHK-Cu + KPV and in KLOW. There is no combination study.
57. TB-500 frag 17–23: KPV calms inflammation, while the TB-500 fragment is used to help repair cells move into injured tissue. People combine them when an injury has a strong inflammatory side. The pair has not been tested together.
58. Thymosin Alpha-1: Thymosin Alpha-1 activates T-cells and antiviral defences, while KPV turns down inflammatory signalling. People pair them to support immune function while calming overactive inflammation. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
59. LL-37: LL-37 kills bacteria and breaks up biofilms, while KPV calms the inflammation that infection drives. People pair them for gut and skin issues with a microbial side. LL-37 can itself drive skin inflammation, and the pair has not been tested together.
60. Larazotide: Larazotide tightens the seals between gut lining cells through the zonulin pathway, while KPV calms inflammation inside those cells. People pair them for leaky gut and celiac-type symptoms from two angles. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
61. Thymosin Beta-4: Tβ4 moves repair cells into damaged tissue and grows new vessels, while KPV turns down NF-κB inflammation. They are sold pre-mixed in KLOW and Tβ4 + BPC + KPV for repair with less inflammation. The pair has not been tested together in people.

## Where it comes from
62. The tripeptide Lys-Pro-Val, the last three amino acids (residues 11-13) of alpha-MSH, the hormone that tans skin. KPV keeps the calming, anti-inflammatory part and leaves the tanning behind.
63. First studied for: Studied as the anti-inflammatory core of alpha-MSH, aimed mostly at the gut (colitis) and inflamed skin.
64. Name story: One-letter code for Lys-Pro-Val (lysine got K because L was taken by leucine). [S5] (verified)
65. 1980s to 1990s: Identified as the calming tail, residues 11 to 13, of alpha-MSH
66. 2000s: Colitis work in mice, including mice without MC1R
67. 2010s: Oral nanoparticles aimed at the colon
68. 2026: Removed from FDA Category 2; July panel voted 8 to 6 for compounding
69. Today: Gut and skin calming peptide, oral or injected

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What was actually nominated, and for what [lab]
70. When a compounding pharmacy asked US regulators to allow this tripeptide onto the 503A list, the request was for a 0.1% cream or gel, applied topically, for wound healing and inflammatory skin conditions such as psoriasis and eczema [1] (verified). The nomination was later withdrawn, and the agency carried on evaluating both the free base and the acetate salt on its own initiative.
71. That detail is worth holding onto, because the official evidence review is about a skin cream. It is not about injection, not about oral capsules and not about the gut, even though the agency noted that online marketing promotes injectable, oral, topical and nasal forms for a long list of conditions including colitis and Crohn's disease [1] (verified). The gap between what was formally assessed and what circulates is wider here than for any other peptide in this group.
72. Both salts share a single CAS number in most public references, which sounds convenient and is actually a problem: it means the paperwork does not reliably distinguish them. The free base is 342.43 g/mol, the acetate 402.5 [1]. In the nomination the agency reviewed, the certificate of analysis was titled for the acetate while listing the free base's molecular formula [1] (verified). Like its stack-mates, KPV is a common name rather than an approved generic name, which the agency flagged as a safety risk in itself.

### The citation audit [lab]
73. This is the most clarifying single fact in the record, and it comes from the agency simply reading the sources it was given. The nomination cited nine references in support of effectiveness. Eight were animal studies of alpha-MSH derivatives. One was a study in human cadaver skin. None of the nine tested this tripeptide in a living human [1] (verified).
74. Reviewing the wider literature itself, the agency found no clinical evidence for either nominated indication, and noted that approved therapies exist for both [1]. It also found no published human studies of compounded products containing it, and no record of any outsourcing facility compounding it between January 2017 and June 2025 [1] (verified). So the claim of established practical use does not hold up either.
75. A fair summary: the evidence for this molecule is a well-constructed argument from a parent hormone's biology, supported by animal and cell work, with nothing human attached to it at any point.

### Mechanism, step by step, and where each step was shown [cells]
76. Step one, getting in. The proposed route into cells is the PepT1 transporter, a di- and tripeptide carrier. This was shown in human intestinal epithelial cell lines, specifically Caco2-BBE and HT29-CL.19A, and in Jurkat T cells [1,2] (verified, cells). The appeal of this mechanism is that the transporter is more active in inflamed intestine, so the molecule would concentrate where it is needed. That logic is sound and it is also why oral use became the common route.
77. Step two, what happens inside. The proposed actions are inhibition of NF-kappa-B activation and interference with interleukin-1-beta signalling [1] (verified as proposed). NF-kappa-B is the master switch for inflammatory gene expression, so blocking its activation is a coherent explanation for broad calming effects across tissues.
78. What is missing from this chain is any quantitative anchor. There is no measured binding affinity to a target, no demonstrated dose-response in a living animal tied to tissue concentration, and no pharmacokinetic data at all, in any species, by any route [1] (verified). The mechanism is a plausible route and a plausible destination with no measurements of the journey.

### The receptor question, answered more sharply than usual [cells]
79. The familiar framing is that this fragment keeps alpha-MSH's calming action without the tanning, and works without the tanning receptor. The agency's review puts it more strongly than that, and the stronger version is more interesting.
80. Tested directly, the tripeptide did not displace alpha-MSH from its binding site, and it did not raise cyclic AMP in macrophages expressing the MC1R receptor. The agency's conclusion was that melanocortin receptors are unlikely to be its targets at all [1] (verified, cells).
81. So this is not a selective melanocortin agonist that skips the pigment effect. It is a fragment of a hormone that appears to work through a different mechanism entirely, probably intracellular, reached by a peptide transporter rather than a surface receptor. That reframes the whole family resemblance: the alpha-MSH lineage explains where the sequence came from, not how it acts (inferred).
82. It also means the usual reassurance, that this is just a well-understood hormone's active core, does not hold. The hormone's receptor pharmacology does not transfer to it.

### The colitis work, in detail [animals]
83. The animal result that built this molecule's reputation is a 2008 study in Inflammatory Bowel Diseases, and it is genuinely striking. It used two independent colitis models: chemical colitis induced by 2.5% dextran sodium sulfate in drinking water for six days, and an immune-driven model created by transferring CD45RBhi T cells [3] (verified).
84. In the chemical model, treated mice recovered earlier and regained more body weight, with fewer inflammatory infiltrates and lower colonic myeloperoxidase activity, which is a direct measure of neutrophil infiltration rather than a subjective score. In the transfer model, treated mice recovered, regained weight and showed less histological inflammation [3].
85. The decisive arm used mice with a non-functional MC1R receptor. In those animals, treatment rescued every treated mouse from death during chemical colitis [3] (verified). That is the experiment behind the receptor-independence claim, and it is a strong design: if the effect survives removal of the proposed receptor, the receptor is not required.
86. Two limits on reading it. The published abstract does not state the dose, schedule or route, so the study cannot be used to derive any dosing logic [3]. And both models are acute chemical or immune injury in mice, which is the standard proxy for inflammatory bowel disease and has a long history of producing results that did not carry into human trials (verified).

### Human data, and what that means for dose [people]
87. There are no human studies of this tripeptide, for any indication, by any route. The agency found no human products, no clinical studies and no human pharmacokinetic data [1] (verified). Its adverse event database and its complaint system together returned no reports through 3 December 2025 [1].
88. That absence of adverse event reports is sometimes read as evidence of safety. It is better read as evidence of absent surveillance: an unapproved substance bought as a research chemical and self-administered does not generate the reports that an approved drug does, and nobody is collecting them.
89. There is no established human dose, and no study from which one could be derived. Every number in circulation originates from community convention or from converting animal doses, and the underlying animal studies frequently do not publish the doses they used in retrievable form. This is a case where the usual practice of citing "reported" ranges has nothing underneath it at the research end.
90. One route-specific finding deserves attention, because it cuts against the nominated form. The tripeptide did not permeate human cadaver skin well. Penetration increased in vitro when iontophoresis or microneedle abrasion was applied [1] (verified). So the one form that was formally nominated, a plain topical cream, faces a delivery problem that the nomination's own supporting science identified.

### Chemistry and product reality [lab]
91. For the free base, no certificate of analysis accompanied the nomination. Publicly available certificates report only purity, with no impurity limits, no aggregate testing and no microbial testing [1]. For the acetate, the certificate reported total impurities of 0.9% against a 2.0% limit and a largest single impurity of 0.24% against a 1.0% limit, which is good, but gave no impurity identities, no aggregate data and no microbial testing [1] (verified).
92. The agency concluded that neither form is well characterised, and that there is insufficient data to conclude that immunogenicity and aggregation risks are absent [1] (verified).
93. Two chemistry details with practical consequences. The salts differ sharply in solubility: the free base dissolves to about 0.70 mg per millilitre in water, the acetate to about 5 mg per millilitre [1]. A product made with one and handled as though it were the other will not behave as expected. And storage differs: the free base is reported stable for up to three years at minus 20 degrees Celsius, while the acetate's stated storage is ordinary refrigeration at 2 to 8 degrees [1].
94. Under forced degradation the acetate breaks down to a cyclised product, Lys-Pro diketopiperazine [1] (verified). Cyclisation of a proline-containing peptide is a known and predictable degradation route, and it means a degraded vial does not simply contain less of the peptide, it contains something else.

### Safety: unexamined rather than reassuring [lab]
95. No acute toxicity studies, no repeat-dose studies, no genotoxicity studies, no developmental or reproductive studies and no carcinogenicity studies were submitted or identified for either form [1] (verified). No pharmacokinetic or toxicokinetic studies exist either.
96. So the standard questions have not been asked. What dose causes harm, which organ is affected first, what happens over months, whether it affects DNA or pregnancy: all unexamined.
97. The reported pattern of early reactions in community use, headaches and flu-like feelings sometimes at low exposures, with people who have mast-cell problems reacting at the smallest amounts, has no counterpart anywhere in the formal record, and no mechanism has been investigated for it (reported). Given a proposed mechanism that acts on inflammatory signalling and an entry route through a transporter that immune cells express, an immune-mediated reaction is not implausible, but nothing has tested it (speculated).
98. The agency's overall position was that there is no human safety data and the risks are unknown [1]. That is a precise statement and worth preferring over any confident claim in either direction.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
99. The agency's own staff proposed not adding either form to the 503A bulks list, for four stated reasons: neither substance is well characterised, the extent of compounding use is unknown, there is no evidence of effectiveness in humans, and there is no human safety data with risks unknown [1] (verified).
100. The advisory committee recommended adding it anyway, voting 8 to 6 with one abstention on 23 July 2026, for wound healing and inflammatory conditions [2,4]. Staff had found that the evidence weighed against it, noting that none of the studies they located involved humans [5].
101. As with the others, that recommendation is advisory and alters nothing by itself. Addition requires formal notice-and-comment rulemaking, which has not started and has no deadline [4] (verified). An "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" went to the White House budget office on 14 October 2026 and was unpublished as of mid-October, with its covered substances and conditions not public [4]. Removal from the do-not-compound category in April 2026 happened because nominations were withdrawn, not because of a revised safety judgement, and left the substance outside any recognised category [6] (verified).
102. In sport, it is not named on the prohibited list, which places it under the catch-all class for non-approved substances rather than outside the rules.

### Open questions [mixed]
103. If melanocortin receptors are not the target, what is? Without an identified target there is no basis for predicting selectivity, no structure-activity work and no rational dose.
104. Does anything reach the intended tissue? With zero pharmacokinetic data in any species and poor permeation through human skin, the delivery question is unanswered for every route in use.
105. Do the mouse colitis results mean anything for human inflammatory bowel disease? This model has a long record of promising results that did not translate, and no human trial has ever been attempted here, let alone registered.
106. What explains the early reactions people report at very low exposures? Nothing in the formal record addresses this, and it is the most common practical complaint.
107. Which salt is in a given product, and was it handled accordingly? Shared CAS numbers, a seven-fold solubility difference and different storage requirements make this genuinely ambiguous.
108. Everything about long-term safety. There is no toxicology of any kind, which makes this unopened rather than open.

# Retatrutide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/retatrutide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: reta ly3437943 triple agonist glp-3, LY-3437943
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: YAQGTFTSDYSILLDKKAQAAFIEYLLEGGPSSGAPPPS (39 amino acids). Positions 2 and 20 are Aib and 13 is α-methyl-leucine, shown as A and L; fat chain on K17 and amide end not shown
4. Legal and approval status: Not approved anywhere. Phase 3 has read out; no approval yet. Sold only grey-market as a research chemical.

## Summary
5. Retatrutide is Eli Lilly's investigational lab-designed peptide that activates three gut-hormone receptors at once: GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. It is aimed at obesity, type 2 diabetes and liver fat, by quieting hunger and burning more energy. Phase 3 trial data show very large weight loss, and grey-market users report strong appetite suppression, but it is not approved and nausea and GI upset are the main drawbacks.
6. Punch line: Triple-agonist weekly shot. Hits GLP-1, GIP and glucagon; trials saw over a quarter of body weight lost.
7. Used for: Weight loss

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Appetite & satiety: Strong appetite control
9. Fat metabolism: Glucagon arm burns fat
10. Glucose & insulin: Lowers blood sugar and A1c
11. Reward & urges: Fewer cravings reported
12. Sleep & rhythms (backed only by animal or user reports): Studied in sleep apnea
13. Pain & sensory (backed only by animal or user reports): Less knee pain in a trial
14. Cognition (backed only by animal or user reports): Users report less food noise

## How it works
15. Quiets hunger in the brain · GLP-1 receptor · role Appetite & satiety
   Retatrutide activates the GLP-1 receptor in the hypothalamus and brainstem, the brain's appetite centres. That cuts hunger and slows stomach emptying, so meals end sooner. In human trials this drives large weight loss, along with the nausea and vomiting that rose with dose.
16. Boosts insulin after meals · GIP receptor · role Glucose & insulin
   At the GIP receptor it boosts insulin release when blood sugar is high after meals, and it acts on fat tissue. This helps lower glucose without causing lows on its own. In human trials A1c fell, and it is being tested separately in type 2 diabetes.
17. Burns more energy and liver fat · Glucagon receptor · role Fat metabolism
   The glucagon receptor arm is the distinctive part. It raises energy expenditure and drives fat burning in the liver, which is why liver fat drops so sharply in trials. Glucagon activity can also raise resting heart rate, a signal reported in earlier trial work.
18. Dampens food cravings and reward · Mesolimbic GLP-1R · role Reward & urges
   GLP-1 receptors in the brain's mesolimbic reward circuit also respond, lowering the pull of high-reward food. Users report fewer cravings, not only less hunger. The reward effect is drawn from GLP-1 biology in animals and people, rather than measured directly for this drug.
19. Mechanism overview: Retatrutide is a single peptide that activates three receptors: GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. GLP-1 receptor activation in the hypothalamus and brainstem cuts hunger and food reward, and slows stomach emptying. GIP receptor activation enhances glucose-dependent insulin release and acts on fat tissue. The glucagon arm is the distinctive part: it raises energy expenditure and drives fat oxidation in the liver, which is why liver fat drops so sharply. A fatty acid side chain binds albumin, allowing once-weekly dosing.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
20. Typical: 2–12 mg · once weekly · cycle ongoing, titrated · route Sub-Q (verified)
21. Half-life: ~6 days
22. Dose note: No label. 12 mg weekly is the trial ceiling.
23. Common: 4–8 mg · 1× weekly · ongoing, after slow titration · Sub-Q · for most grey-market users; stop short of 12 mg [S1] [S2] (reported)
24. Microdose / low: 0.5–2 mg/wk · 1× weekly, or split 0.5 mg every other day · 12–24 wk start, or ongoing for 'longevity' · Sub-Q · for new users, tolerance testing, longevity crowd [S2] [S3] [S4] (reported)
25. Trial max: 9–12 mg · 1× weekly · after 16 wk titration (2→4→6→9→12) · Sub-Q · for users copying the Phase 2/3 escalation [S5] [S1] (reported)

## What people report
26. Grey-market use mirrors the trials: steady weekly dosing, strong appetite suppression, GI upset on titration. Early users report the fat-loss and appetite effect first.
27. Liked / worked: 28.3% weight loss at 80 weeks vs 2.2% on placebo
28. Liked / worked: Weight still falling at 80 weeks
29. Liked / worked: Lower liver fat, blood pressure and A1c
30. What worked: In trials, the largest weight loss of any single drug so far, still rising at 80 weeks, with falls in liver fat, blood pressure and A1c.
31. Went wrong / did not work: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea drive dropouts
32. Went wrong / did not work: Heart rate rise under watch
33. Went wrong / did not work: No approval; all human data are trial data
34. What went wrong: GI side effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) are the main dropout driver, as with the whole class; heart-rate rise is watched. Not approved, so all human data are trial data.
35. Most reported: Strong appetite suppression
36. Most reported: Fat loss felt first
37. Most reported: GI upset during titration
38. Most reported: Steady weekly dosing, mirroring trials

## What has been tested
39. Fat metabolism: Obesity, 48 weeks (trial)
40. Fat metabolism: Obesity, 80 weeks, TRIUMPH-1 (trial)
41. Pain & sensory: Obesity with knee osteoarthritis (trial)
42. Glucose & insulin: Type 2 diabetes, TRANSCEND-T2D (trial)
43. Organ function: Liver fat (trial)
44. Phase 2 obesity trial: about 24% weight loss at 48 weeks on the top dose. Phase 3 began reading out in late 2025: TRIUMPH-4 (obesity with knee osteoarthritis, Dec 2025, reported) and TRIUMPH-1 (obesity, May 2026: 28.3% weight loss at 80 weeks on 12 mg, against 2.2% on placebo). Diabetes is tested in a separate program, TRANSCEND-T2D.
45. What it helps: Trial data only. In obesity, TRIUMPH-1 showed 28.3% weight loss at 80 weeks against 2.2% on placebo, and weight was still falling. Trials also show lower liver fat, blood pressure and A1c, and it is being tested in type 2 diabetes and in obesity with knee osteoarthritis. Grey-market users report strong appetite suppression and fat loss felt first, with nausea and GI upset during titration.
46. Trial: active · Phase 3 · obesity, type 2 diabetes, fatty liver · NCT07165028 · Eli Lilly. Eleven open trials as of October 2026, including a head to head against tirzepatide (TRIUMPH-5) and a recruiting fatty liver outcomes trial. (checked 2026-10-23) [S6] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
47. Personal or family history of MTC or MEN2: GLP-1 receptor agonists cause C-cell tumours in rodents; trials exclude these people. (inferred)
48. People relying on the contraceptive pill: Contains GIP agonism like tirzepatide, whose label warns pill absorption drops after starts and dose increases. (inferred)
49. People with arrhythmia or a fast resting pulse: The glucagon arm raised resting heart rate in trials, peaking around week 24. (reported)
50. Anyone booked for surgery, endoscopy or sedation: Very slow stomach emptying raises the risk of inhaling stomach contents under anaesthesia. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
51. BPC-157: Retatrutide drives weight and liver fat loss, while BPC-157 is used for tendon and gut repair. Some users add BPC-157 hoping to ease GI upset during dose increases, based on gut protection seen in rats. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
52. TB-500 frag 17–23: Retatrutide works on appetite and metabolism, while the TB-500 fragment is taken for tissue repair and recovery. People combine them while training through a fat loss phase. The goals are separate, and the pair has not been tested together.
53. GHK-Cu: Retatrutide drives fast fat loss, while GHK-Cu is used to support collagen and skin repair. People pair them hoping to limit loose skin during large weight loss. That use is plausible but untested, and the pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
54. Eli Lilly's investigational chain (LY3437943) that hits three gut-hormone receptors at once: GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. Still in trials, but its structure is published.
55. First studied for: Built for obesity and type 2 diabetes, with liver fat and metabolic disease close behind.
56. Name story: Lilly's LY3437943 hits three receptors: GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon, hence the "triple G" nickname. "GLP-3" is street slang only; no hormone called GLP-3 exists. [S7] (inferred)
57. 2023: Phase 2 obesity trial: about 24% weight loss at 48 weeks
58. Dec 2025: Phase 3 begins reading out, TRIUMPH-4 in knee arthritis (reported)
59. May 2026: TRIUMPH-1: 28.3% weight loss at 80 weeks on 12 mg
60. Today: Unapproved triple agonist with the biggest trial weight loss yet; grey-market only

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What the pivotal trial actually measured [people]
61. TRIUMPH-1 randomised 2,339 adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, and without diabetes, one-to-one-to-one-to-one across three doses and placebo, dosed weekly for 80 weeks [1] (verified). A pre-specified extension carried 532 participants with a starting body mass index of 35 or above out to 104 weeks.
62. The primary measure was percent body weight change at 80 weeks. Results ran 19.0% at the low dose, 25.9% at the middle dose and 28.3% at the top dose, against 2.2% on placebo [1]. In the extension, the top dose reached 30.3% at 104 weeks, and participants switched from placebo onto drug reached 19.2% [1] (verified).
63. Two secondary measures are more informative than the headline. Waist circumference fell 16.3, 21.8 and 24.1 centimetres across the three doses against 3.6 on placebo, which matters because waist tracks visceral fat more closely than total weight does [1]. And the proportion losing at least 30% of starting body weight was 15.3%, 37.9% and 45.3% against 0.5% on placebo [1] (verified). That last figure is the one that moved clinical conversation, because losing 30% of body weight was previously the territory of surgery.
64. What the trial did not measure: it was not a cardiovascular outcome trial, it excluded diabetes, and at 80 weeks weight was still falling, so the plateau has not been located.

### The dose-response is the real finding, in both directions [people]
65. A clean dose-response is what separates a drug effect from noise, and this one is clean. Weight loss, waist reduction and the proportion hitting large thresholds all rose in order across the three doses [1].
66. Tolerability moved in the same order. Discontinuation for adverse events ran 4.1%, 6.9% and 11.3% across the three doses against 4.9% on placebo [1] (verified). So at the top dose, roughly one in nine participants stopped because of side effects, and the placebo rate tells you some of that would have happened anyway.
67. The gastrointestinal pattern scaled too: nausea 28.6%, 38.4% and 42.4% against 14.8% on placebo; vomiting 10.6%, 22.8% and 25.3% against 4.8% [1] (verified).
68. Read together, those two gradients are the practical substance of the trial. The top dose bought roughly 9 percentage points more weight loss than the low dose and roughly tripled the chance of stopping. That is a genuine trade-off rather than a free gain, and it is the kind of detail that disappears when a compound is described by its best number alone.

### One signal that is not in the class playbook [people]
69. Dysesthesia, meaning altered or unpleasant skin sensation, appeared in 5.1%, 12.3% and 12.5% of the three dose groups against 0.9% on placebo [1] (verified). That is a roughly thirteen-fold difference from placebo at the higher doses, with a dose relationship.
70. This is worth flagging because it is not a familiar feature of the established incretin drugs, so it is plausibly tied to the third receptor arm rather than to the shared mechanism (inferred). The trial sponsor described these events as generally mild to moderate, with most resolving during treatment [1] (reported).
71. Heart rate is the other arm-specific question. Glucagon receptor activation raises energy expenditure, and it also raises resting heart rate; Phase 2 work reported an increase of roughly 3 to 5 beats per minute [2] (reported). The pivotal release did not report heart rate figures [1], which is a gap rather than a reassurance.
72. Neither point argues against the compound. Both argue that a third receptor means a third side-effect profile, and that the class-wide intuitions people carry over from older drugs will be incomplete here.

### The other three trials, and what a hazard ratio of 0.82 does and does not show [people]
73. All four Phase 3 trials had reported topline results by October 2026 [2] (reported).
74. In obesity with type 2 diabetes, results reported in July 2026 showed up to 20.8% weight loss with HbA1c falling by as much as 1.6 percentage points [2]. Weight loss is reliably smaller in diabetes across this whole drug class, so the gap from the non-diabetes trial is expected rather than disappointing.
75. In obesity with knee osteoarthritis, results reported in December 2025 showed 28.7% weight loss at 68 weeks alongside significant improvement in knee pain [2] (reported).
76. The cardiovascular trial, in people with a body mass index of 35 or above and established cardiovascular disease, reported up to 22.6% weight loss and a pre-specified composite cardiovascular hazard ratio of 0.82 against placebo [2] (reported). That number deserves careful handling. A hazard ratio of 0.82 points in the right direction, but a pre-specified analysis inside a weight-loss trial is not the same as a dedicated, adequately powered cardiovascular outcome trial, and nothing in the topline establishes that it crossed a significance threshold with a trial designed to test it. Treat it as encouraging and not as established (inferred).

### Where approval stands, and why that matters here more than usual [people]
77. As of October 2026 the compound was not approved anywhere, and no marketing application had been submitted. The developer has indicated an intent to file in the first quarter of 2027, after completing manufacturing data, with any decision following well after that [2] (reported).
78. That timeline creates a situation worth naming plainly. The efficacy evidence here is unusually strong for an unapproved compound: four Phase 3 trials, thousands of participants, a clean dose-response, publication in a major journal [1]. The manufacturing and quality evidence for anything circulating outside that programme is entirely separate from it, and none of the trial data speaks to what is in an unapproved vial.
79. For every other compound in this catalog, weak trial evidence and uncertain product quality travel together. Here they come apart: the molecule has been tested properly, and the supply has not. Those are two different questions and conflating them in either direction produces a wrong conclusion (inferred).

### Open questions [mixed]
80. Where does weight loss plateau? It was still falling at 80 weeks and reached 30.3% by 104 weeks in the extension, so the ceiling has not been observed.
81. What happens on stopping? No published data address regain after this compound specifically, and the class pattern suggests it should be expected.
82. Is the dysesthesia signal durable, dose-limiting or mechanistic? It is dose-related and roughly thirteen-fold over placebo, and its cause has not been established.
83. What does the glucagon arm do to the heart over years? Resting heart rate rose in Phase 2 and the pivotal release did not report it. A long cardiovascular trial is the only way to settle this.
84. Does the cardiovascular signal hold up in a trial built to test it? A pre-specified composite inside a weight trial is a reason to run that trial, not a substitute for it.
85. How much muscle comes off at 28 to 30% total weight loss? Body composition is the obvious question at this magnitude of loss and is not in the topline reporting.
