# KLOW
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/klow
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: KLOW blend, KLOW stack, KLOW 80, GLOW + KPV, GHK-Cu + BPC-157 + TB-500 + KPV
2. Origin: Blend of 4 peptides
3. Legal and approval status: Not approved anywhere. US: BPC-157, TB-500, KPV and injectable GHK-Cu left FDA Category 2 in April 2026 when nominations were withdrawn; non-injectable GHK-Cu sits in Category 1; the July 2026 panel voted for BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV compounding, no rule yet. WADA: BPC-157 and TB-500 banned at all times; KPV under S0.

## Summary
4. KLOW combines GHK-Cu (a copper skin peptide), BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV, the anti-inflammatory tail of alpha-MSH. It is used for skin, repair and gut inflammation: GHK-Cu signals collagen, BPC-157 and thymosin beta-4 support healing, and KPV calms inflammation inside cells. Evidence comes from the separate components and user reports of calmer gut and skin. No study of the blend exists, and GHK-Cu can cause itching welts.
5. Punch line: GLOW plus KPV. Copper peptide for skin, BPC-157 and TB-500 for repair, KPV to calm gut inflammation.
6. Used for: Skin, gut and inflammation, plus repair

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Skin & aesthetics: Copper peptide for collagen; KPV calms inflamed skin
8. Inflammatory signaling: KPV switches off NF-κB inside cells
9. Tissue repair: BPC-157 and TB-500 for wound and tendon repair
10. Digestive & gut: KPV and BPC-157 aimed at gut lining and colitis
11. Hair (backed only by animal or user reports): Hair and nail gains reported
12. Immunity (backed only by animal or user reports): KPV steadies mast cells and immune cells
13. Pain & sensory (backed only by animal or user reports): Joint comfort reported

## How it works
14. Signals skin to build collagen · GHK-Cu: copper delivery · role Skin & aesthetics
   GHK-Cu binds copper and carries it into tissue that is rebuilding, where it signals fibroblasts, the skin's collagen-making cells. That shifts the balance toward new collagen and elastin and matrix remodelling. The best data are topical skin studies in people; injected use is not studied in humans.
15. Blocks a key inflammation switch inside gut and immune cells · KPV: PepT1 uptake, NF-κB down · role Inflammatory signaling
   KPV, the last three amino acids of alpha-MSH, enters gut and immune cells through PepT1, a peptide transporter. Inside, it blocks activation of NF-κB, a master switch for inflammatory genes, without needing the tanning receptor. Colitis improved in mouse studies; there are no human data.
16. Helps blood vessels grow into damage · BPC-157: VEGFR2, eNOS · role Tissue repair
   BPC-157 acts on VEGFR2 and eNOS, the receptor and enzyme that drive new blood vessel growth and nitric oxide release. Better blood supply brings oxygen and repair cells into damaged tendon, muscle or gut. This is shown in rat injury models, not in human trials.
17. Moves repair cells into wounds · Tβ4: G-actin sequestering · role Tissue repair
   Thymosin beta-4 binds single actin units (G-actin) and holds them in reserve. When a repair cell needs to move, that stock is released to build filaments fast, so cells migrate into the wound. Shown in cell and animal work; human wound trials used the full protein.
18. Protects the gut lining · BPC-157 and KPV, colitis models · role Digestive & gut
   BPC-157 protects the stomach and gut lining from damage, and KPV calms inflammation in the colon wall. In mouse and rat colitis models, the lining healed faster with each one alone. The two have never been tested together for gut effects.
19. Mechanism overview: KLOW keeps GLOW's logic (GHK-Cu for matrix and collagen gene expression, BPC-157 for angiogenesis, thymosin beta-4 for actin-driven migration) and adds KPV, alpha-MSH 11 to 13. KPV enters gut and immune cells through PepT1 and blocks NF-κB activation independent of MC1R. Chemically KPV is the quietest addition: no histidine, methionine or asparagine, so no copper binding or oxidation hot spot. The 5:1:1:1 ratio puts GHK-Cu at 62.5% of the powder; how the four behave together in liquid has not been studied.

## What is inside the blend
20. GHK-Cu: 50 mg · Collagen, skin remodelling, hair
21. BPC-157: 10 mg · Blood vessel growth, gut lining
22. TB-500 (Thymosin Beta-4): 10 mg · Cell migration into wounds
23. KPV: 10 mg · Gut, mast cell and skin inflammation
24. Most common ratio: GHK-Cu 50 · BPC-157 10 · TB-500 10 · KPV 10 = 80 mg (22 of 22 listings (11 state the split, 11 sell 80 mg))
25. Other ratio seen: KLOW + Snap-8 = 115 mg (1 listing (different product))
26. Version Common retail: GHK-Cu 50 · BPC-157 10 · TB-500 10 · KPV 10 = 80 mg
27. Why GHK-Cu is in it: Skin and collagen signal; hair and nails
28. Why BPC-157 is in it: Angiogenesis and gut protection
29. Why TB-500 is in it: Cell migration; human wound trial data (full Tβ4)
30. Why KPV is in it: Targeted anti-inflammatory for gut and skin; the reason to pick KLOW over GLOW
31. Mixing chemistry: KPV has no histidine, methionine or asparagine, so it adds no copper or oxidation risk.
32. Mixing chemistry: Same copper rules as GLOW: keep vitamin C and glutathione out; blue is normal, green or brown is not.
33. Mixing chemistry: COAs show GHK-Cu overfill up to about 20%, which shifts the ratio toward copper.
34. Mixing chemistry: One KLOW COA failed its own purity and content specs yet stated 'complies'. Read the numbers, not the verdict.
35. Mixing chemistry: Ask for mg of each of the four by LC-MS or HPLC, not one purity figure.
36. Self-mixing: Building KLOW from four vials stacks four overfill errors and four salt pHs, including acidic BPC-157 acetate into the copper; buying GLOW and a separate KPV vial is the simpler split.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
37. Typical: 10–15 units (80 mg in 3 mL) · 1× daily · cycle 4–12 weeks · route Sub-Q (reported)
38. Half-life: per component
39. Most people take: No standard dose. Most land BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV near 330 to 500 mcg each: 10 to 15 units of an 80 mg vial in 3 mL. Guides disagree widely, from 200 to 500 mcg of total blend to 6 mg.

## What people report
40. Sub-Q once daily. Common draw is 10 to 15 units of an 80 mg vial in 3 mL (about 1.7 to 2.5 mg GHK-Cu and 330 to 500 mcg each of BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV). Guides range from 200 mcg of total blend to a titration up to 22.5 units (6 mg). Courses 4 to 12 weeks, then 2 to 4 weeks off.
41. Liked / worked: Gut, bloating and rosacea calmer in user reports
42. Liked / worked: 9 of 15 classifiable Finnrick tests passed
43. Liked / worked: Powder COAs near label for all four
44. What worked: Users report calmer gut and bloating, rosacea and eczema settling, better skin, and recovery benefits; KPV users often notice change within days 3 to 14. KLOW has the most independent tests of the three skin blends: 9 of 15 classifiable Finnrick tests passed (May to Sep 2026).
45. Went wrong / did not work: Never tested as a blend
46. Went wrong / did not work: Burning welts from the copper share
47. Went wrong / did not work: Dose guides differ by 10 times or more
48. What went wrong: No controlled data; reports are anecdotes, one self-described as n of 1. The GHK-Cu share causes burning welts and itching for some, lasting 24 hours. Nausea (attributed to BPC-157), first-week tiredness, headache and a faint blue-green tint at the site are reported. One unnamed-lab KLOW COA failed its own specs yet said 'complies'.
49. Most reported: Gut and skin calming within days to weeks
50. Most reported: Nausea and first-week tiredness
51. Most reported: Faint blue-green tint at the site
52. Most reported: 4 to 12 week courses

## What has been tested
53. Digestive & gut: KPV in DSS and TNBS colitis (mouse)
54. Skin & aesthetics: GHK-Cu topical skin studies (human)
55. Tissue repair: BPC-157 and Tβ4 tissue repair (rat)
56. Skin & aesthetics: Rosacea, eczema, bloating (users)
57. Never tested as a blend; one aggregator states no preclinical or clinical study examines the four together. Component evidence: KPV in mouse colitis, GHK-Cu in skin studies, BPC-157 and thymosin beta-4 in animal repair. Powder COAs from two labs (Jul to Aug 2026) show each component close to label, with GHK-Cu up to 120%.
58. What it helps: Evidence is component-level and user-reported. KPV eases colitis in mice; GHK-Cu has skin data; BPC-157 and thymosin beta-4 have animal repair data. No study of the blend exists. Users report calmer gut, skin and rosacea plus recovery benefits, often within the first 2 weeks.

## Who shouldn't take it
59. Wilson's disease or copper overload: Each dose delivers copper; people who cannot clear copper accumulate it in liver and brain. (inferred)
60. People with active or recent cancer: Raises VEGFR2 signalling and new vessel growth in animal work; tumours use the same pathway. (inferred)
61. Drug-tested athletes: TB-500 is named on the WADA list as a thymosin beta-4 derivative. (verified)
62. People with IBD on biologics or immunosuppressants: KPV damps NF-kB signalling; stacking it onto immune drugs is untested. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
63. GHK-Cu: GHK-Cu is already the largest part of KLOW by mass, so adding more mainly raises the skin and collagen share. People do it to push the skin side. The extra dosing has not been studied.
64. KPV: KPV is already in KLOW. Adding standalone KPV raises the gut and skin anti-inflammatory share over the repair parts, which some users want for colitis-type symptoms. KPV has mouse data only, and the pairing is user logic, not trial data.
65. BPC-157: BPC-157 is already in KLOW. Extra BPC-157 tilts the blend toward gut protection and blood vessel growth for injury repair. No study tests the blend with added BPC-157, so the pairing is user logic.
66. Thymosin Beta-4: Thymosin beta-4 is already in KLOW. Extra Tβ4 brings the cell migration share closer to standalone use for injury repair. A 2026 rat Achilles study found BPC-157 plus Tβ4 no better than either alone.
67. Larazotide: Larazotide tightens the seals between gut lining cells through the zonulin pathway, while KLOW's KPV and BPC-157 calm inflammation and protect the lining. People pair them for leaky gut symptoms. The pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
68. GLOW plus KPV: GHK-Cu 50 mg, BPC-157 10 mg, TB-500 10 mg and KPV 10 mg, 80 mg total, a 5:1:1:1 ratio. KPV is the anti-inflammatory three-residue tail of alpha-MSH. On the common retail version TB-500 is full thymosin beta-4.
69. First studied for: A 2025 to 2026 extension of GLOW, adding KPV for gut, mast cell and skin inflammation. Pitched for people with gut issues, rosacea or chronic inflammation on top of skin and repair goals.
70. Name story: Read as GLOW with a K for the added KPV. No source states who coined it. [S1] (inferred)
71. 1973: GHK-Cu found in human plasma
72. 2000s: KPV calms colitis in mice
73. 2024 to 2025: GLOW sold as 50+10+10 mg
74. 2025 to 2026: KLOW adds KPV 10 mg, 80 mg total
75. Apr 2026: All four components leave or sit outside FDA Category 2
76. May to Sep 2026: 19 Finnrick tests; 9 of 15 classifiable pass

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What "never tested as a blend" actually means [mixed]
77. The phrase gets used as a mild caveat. It carries more than that, and it is worth unpacking into the three separate things that have not been examined.
78. First, pharmacology. Nobody has measured whether the four do the same things together that they do apart. Two of them act partly through the same pathway, nitric oxide signalling in the case of the gastric peptide, and matrix remodelling in the case of the copper tripeptide, so additive, redundant and opposing outcomes are all possible and none has been tested (verified as absent).
79. Second, chemistry in solution. The four sit in one vial, dissolved together, for the life of that vial. No stability study of the combination exists. What is known is that each component has its own documented degradation behaviour and its own storage requirement, and those requirements do not match (see below).
80. Third, safety attribution. Each injected component separately drew the same concern from US regulators in 2026: that peptide-related impurities and aggregates can drive immune responses, and that no immunogenicity studies exist for any of them [1,2,3] (verified). Combining four peptides in one solution multiplies the impurity and aggregate surface without adding any data about it (inferred).
81. None of that says the blend is dangerous. It says the blend is, in evidence terms, a fifth product with no file of its own.

### The four components do not have comparable evidence [mixed]
82. A blend tends to inherit the reputation of its best-regarded ingredient. Read component by component, the evidence here is not just thin, it is unevenly thin in ways that matter.
83. The copper tripeptide has the most human data of the four, and the most discouraging large result. Its pivotal programme in diabetic foot ulcers enrolled 511 patients across 30 centres at two strengths against placebo, and the drug was no better than placebo [4,5] (verified). Its positive human evidence is topical, small and short. The injected route, which is what a blend uses, has never been studied in humans at all.
84. The gastric peptide has exactly one controlled human trial, reported as a 2005 meeting abstract: 53 people with ulcerative colitis, a daily 80 mg enema against placebo for two weeks, with a between-group difference whose confidence interval crossed zero. Regulators found the abstract inadequate for lacking endpoint definitions, inclusion criteria and statistics [1] (verified). Everything else human is uncontrolled.
85. The thymosin fragment is the weakest of the four and the one most often assumed strongest. Regulators found no clinical studies, no human exposure data and no human pharmacokinetic data by any route, and no toxicology studies of any kind: no acute, no repeat-dose, no genotoxicity, no reproductive, no carcinogenicity [2] (verified). When the marketed fragment was tested directly in a fibroblast wound-closure assay at 50 micrograms per millilitre, it did not significantly promote closure [2].
86. The tripeptide from alpha-MSH has no human studies, no pharmacokinetic data in any species and no toxicology studies [3]. Its nomination cited nine references, eight animal studies of related compounds and one cadaver-skin study, none testing it in a living human [3] (verified). It was nominated only as a 0.1% topical cream, not for injection.
87. So the blend combines one component with a failed pivotal trial, one with a single inadequate and non-significant controlled trial, and two with no human data whatsoever.

### The identity problem, multiplied by four [lab]
88. Each of these substances exists in at least two forms, a free base and an acetate salt, with different molecular weights and, in two cases, different solubility and storage requirements. For each one, regulators found that nominators had been inconsistent about which form they meant, in some cases submitting a certificate of analysis for one form under the name of the other [1,2,3] (verified). None of the four has an approved generic name, so there is no reference standard to test a batch against, which regulators flagged as a patient safety issue in its own right.
89. One mismatch is specific to this blend and worth stating plainly. Regulators stated that the marketed seven-residue fragment and the full 43-residue protein are not the same substance [2] (verified). Retail versions of this blend commonly contain the full protein under the fragment's name. That is not a minor labelling quirk: it means the vial contains a molecule with a different evidence base, different stability and a different regulatory record from the one on the label, and that the component list cannot be used to look up what is actually present.
90. Independent batch testing of the blend is better than for most, and still mixed. Across one public testing service's classifiable results from May to September 2026, 9 of 15 passed. Powder certificates from two laboratories in July and August 2026 showed each component near its label figure, with the copper tripeptide running as high as 120% of label. One certificate from an unnamed laboratory failed its own stated specifications while recording the conclusion "complies" (verified, as logged in the card record).
91. The copper component being the one that runs over label is the least convenient result, since it is the largest share of the powder by a wide margin and the component carrying a metal.

### The chemistry one vial has to satisfy at once [lab]
92. This is where documented facts about the separate components say something concrete about the combination.
93. Storage requirements conflict. The gastric peptide's lyophilised powder is recommended below minus 18 degrees Celsius, with reconstituted solution documented as stable only two to three weeks refrigerated [1]. The thymosin fragment is stored below minus 20 as free base and below minus 15 as acetate [2]. The alpha-MSH tripeptide is reported stable up to three years at minus 20 as free base, while its acetate's stated storage is ordinary refrigeration at 2 to 8 degrees [3] (verified). A single blended vial can only be stored one way, so at least one component is being held outside its documented condition, and after reconstitution the shortest-lived component sets the real shelf life of the whole vial (inferred).
94. Solubility sets a constraint that can be checked with arithmetic. At the common composition, 10 mg of the alpha-MSH tripeptide in a 3 mL reconstitution is about 3.3 mg per millilitre. The documented water solubility of its free base is about 0.70 mg per millilitre; its acetate dissolves to about 5 mg per millilitre [3]. On those figures the free base could not fully dissolve at that concentration and the acetate could, which means a blend that reconstitutes clearly at 3 mL is almost certainly built on the acetate salt (inferred, assuming the cited water-solubility figures carry over into the blended solution).
95. Degradation is predictable for at least one component: under forced conditions the alpha-MSH tripeptide acetate cyclises to a diketopiperazine [3] (verified). A degraded vial therefore does not simply contain less of that component, it contains a different molecule, and nothing in the record describes what that does alongside three other peptides and a copper complex.
96. The copper itself is the variable with no file. An injected copper complex raises questions a plain peptide does not: how much copper is delivered, where it goes once the peptide is degraded, and what repeated dosing does to copper handling. Nothing in the available record addresses this for the single agent, let alone in a mixture (verified as absent).

### What a blend costs you in information [mixed]
97. There is a practical argument for blends, which is convenience, and a practical cost, which is attribution. Both deserve stating honestly.
98. If something improves, four components could be responsible, and the two with no human data at all are as likely candidates as the two with some. If something goes wrong, the same ambiguity applies in reverse. The reported adverse effects of this blend map neatly onto single components, stinging and welts to the copper share, nausea to the gastric peptide, with first-week tiredness and headache unattributed (reported), which suggests the ingredients are not masking each other, but it also means nobody using the blend learns which component they actually respond to.
99. That matters more here than it would for a fixed-dose approved combination, because the ratio is fixed by the vendor rather than by evidence. At the common composition the copper tripeptide is roughly five parts to one of each other component, which makes this, in mass terms, mostly a copper peptide product with three additions. Nothing in the literature establishes that this ratio is the right one for any purpose; no study of any ratio exists (verified as absent).
100. A regulator's framing of the general problem fits here: for each of these substances individually, the agency's difficulty was identity before efficacy, because these peptides lack a universally accepted chemical definition, which makes evaluation very hard [6]. A four-component mixture of four such substances inherits all four of those problems simultaneously.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
101. No approved product contains this combination anywhere, and the four components sit in three different regulatory positions, which is unusual and makes blanket statements wrong.
102. The gastric peptide, the thymosin fragment and the alpha-MSH tripeptide were each removed from the US do-not-compound category in April 2026, because nominations were withdrawn rather than because of any revised safety finding, which left them outside any recognised category rather than cleared [7] (verified). On 23 July 2026 the advisory committee recommended all three for the 503A bulks list by 8 to 6 with one abstention each, against the agency's own staff, who had proposed not adding any of them [1,2,3,8]. Those recommendations are advisory, require formal rulemaking that has not begun, and carry no deadline [9].
103. The copper tripeptide is in a different position again. Its non-injectable form was restored to Category 1 on 5 May 2026 after a nominator clarified it had meant to withdraw only the injectable nomination, and it sits there under temporary enforcement discretion. The injectable route was left unclassified, and has not yet been reviewed by the committee at all; that review is expected before the end of February 2027 [7,9] (verified).
104. So an injectable blend of all four draws on three substances recommended but not yet permitted, plus one whose injectable form has never been assessed. An "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" went to the White House budget office on 14 October 2026 and was unpublished as of mid-October, with its covered substances and conditions not public [9] (verified). Until it appears, nobody can say whether a blend of this kind would fall inside it.
105. In sport, two of the four are prohibited at all times, and the other two fall under catch-all provisions rather than outside the rules.

### Open questions [mixed]
106. Does the combination do anything the components do not? No study of any kind has addressed this, which makes the central premise of the product untested.
107. Which salt forms are present, and does the vial contain the fragment or the full protein? Regulators state those are different substances. Without identity testing that distinguishes them, the label cannot answer this.
108. What is the real shelf life after reconstitution? The components' documented stability windows differ and the shortest one governs, but nobody has measured the mixture.
109. What happens to the copper over repeated dosing? Unstudied for the single agent and unexamined in combination, and it is the largest component by mass.
110. Why is the copper component the one that runs over label in independent testing, and is that a weighing, a filling or a measurement artefact? This is answerable by testing.
111. If a user responds, to what? The fixed ratio and four simultaneous components make individual attribution impossible by design, which is the quiet cost of every blend.
112. Would a blend fall within the interim compounding policy once published? Unknowable until it is published, and the four components' differing positions make it genuinely uncertain.

# Semaglutide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/semaglutide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus, NN9535, NNC 0113-0217
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain
3. Sequence: HAEGTFTSDVSSYLEGQAAKEFIAWLVRGRG (31 amino acids). Position 2 is Aib, shown as A; fatty acid chain on K20 not shown
4. Shown with an FDA approved badge
5. Legal and approval status: FDA-approved (Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy), plus an oral Wegovy pill for obesity approved in December 2025 (reported). Widely approved worldwide. The grey-market vials in this catalog are not the approved product. WADA does not ban it.

## Summary
6. Semaglutide is Novo Nordisk's lab-modified GLP-1 analogue, with two amino acid swaps and a fatty-acid tail that stretch the natural two-minute hormone into a once-weekly drug. It is approved for type 2 diabetes and obesity, working mainly by suppressing appetite. Trials show about 15% weight loss and fewer heart attacks and strokes in some patients; users report GI upset, muscle loss without resistance training and regain after stopping.
7. Punch line: Ozempic and Wegovy. The weekly GLP-1 shot that quiets food noise; about 15% weight loss, fewer heart attacks.
8. Used for: Weight loss, type 2 diabetes

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
9. Appetite & satiety: Quiets hunger and food noise
10. Glucose & insulin: Lowers blood sugar
11. Heart & vessels: Fewer heart attacks and strokes
12. Reward & urges: Fewer cravings, including alcohol
13. Organ function (backed only by animal or user reports): Protects the kidneys
14. Mood (backed only by animal or user reports): Mood shifts reported

## How it works
15. Quiets hunger in the brain · GLP-1 receptor · role Appetite & satiety
   Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors in the hypothalamus and brainstem, the brain's appetite centres. Hunger falls and fullness comes sooner, so people eat less. This is the main way weight falls, confirmed in the large STEP trials with about 15% weight loss in obesity.
16. Slows stomach emptying · GLP-1 receptor, gut · role Appetite & satiety
   Through GLP-1 receptors in the gut and its nerve signalling, semaglutide slows how fast the stomach empties. Food sits longer, fullness lasts, and sugar reaches the blood more gradually. This also drives the nausea and GI upset common during dose increases.
17. Raises insulin and cuts glucagon when glucose is high · GLP-1R, beta and alpha cells · role Glucose & insulin
   On pancreatic beta cells it boosts insulin, and on alpha cells it cuts glucagon, but only when glucose is high. Blood sugar falls with little risk of hypoglycemia on its own. The SUSTAIN trials confirmed better glucose control in type 2 diabetes.
18. Fatty tail rides albumin for weekly dosing · Albumin binding · role Glucose & insulin
   A C18 fatty diacid chain lets semaglutide bind albumin, the main blood protein, which shields it from clearance. A swap at position 8 also blocks the enzyme DPP-4. Together these stretch its action to a full week.
19. Cuts heart attack and stroke risk in trials · CV outcomes, SELECT · role Heart & vessels
   In SELECT, adults with obesity and established heart disease but no diabetes had 20% fewer heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths than on placebo. All three outcomes moved the same way. The result applies to that population, not to healthy people.
20. Dampens reward-driven cravings · Mesolimbic GLP-1R · role Reward & urges
   GLP-1 receptors in mesolimbic reward circuits, the brain's craving system, turn down the pull of food reward when activated. Users report fewer cravings. The circuit detail comes mainly from animal studies; in people it shows up as reported changes in craving.
21. Mechanism overview: Semaglutide is a GLP-1 analogue with 94 percent sequence match to the native hormone. Two changes make it last a week: a swap at position 8 blocks DPP-4, and a C18 fatty diacid chain binds albumin, slowing clearance. It activates GLP-1 receptors in the hypothalamus and brainstem to cut hunger, in mesolimbic circuits to dampen food reward, in the gut to slow emptying, and on beta and alpha cells to raise insulin and cut glucagon only when glucose is high. Weight falls mostly through eating less.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
22. Typical: 0.25–2.4 mg (HD 7.2 mg) · once weekly · cycle Ongoing · route Sub-Q (verified)
23. Half-life: ~7 days
24. Dose note: Label maximum is 2.4 mg weekly, 7.2 mg for the high-dose version approved in 2026.
25. Standard: 1–2.4 mg · 1× weekly · ongoing; 0.25 mg start, step up every 4 wk · Sub-Q · for most patients and compounded users; many hold at 1–1.7 mg [S1] [S2] (reported)
26. Microdose: 0.125–0.5 mg · 1× weekly or split 2× weekly; some every 2–4 wk for maintenance · ongoing · Sub-Q · for low-side-effect weight maintenance, 'longevity' [S1] [S2] [S3] (reported)
27. High (label HD): 7.2 mg · 1× weekly · after ≥4 wk tolerating 2.4 mg · Sub-Q · for obesity needing more loss (Wegovy HD) [S4] (reported)

## What people report
28. Grey-market and compounded use is enormous. Users report strong appetite suppression, GI upset on titration, and the same regain when they stop.
29. Liked / worked: About 15% weight loss in obesity trials
30. Liked / worked: Better glucose control
31. Liked / worked: Fewer heart attacks and strokes without diabetes
32. What worked: Roughly 15% body-weight loss in the obesity trials, better glucose control, and fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with obesity and heart disease (SELECT), the first time shown in people without diabetes. Liraglutide proved a heart benefit in diabetes earlier.
33. Went wrong / did not work: Nausea, vomiting, constipation
34. Went wrong / did not work: Rare pancreatitis and gallbladder issues
35. Went wrong / did not work: Muscle loss without resistance training
36. Went wrong / did not work: Weight regain on stopping
37. What went wrong: Nausea, vomiting, constipation; rare pancreatitis and gallbladder issues; muscle loss without resistance training; weight regain on stopping. A boxed warning covers thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents.
38. Most reported: Strong appetite suppression
39. Most reported: GI upset on titration
40. Most reported: Regain after stopping
41. Most reported: Rodent thyroid tumor warning widely noted

## What has been tested
42. Fat metabolism: Obesity, STEP program (trial)
43. Glucose & insulin: Type 2 diabetes, SUSTAIN (trial)
44. Heart & vessels: Heart events in obesity, SELECT (trial)
45. Among the most heavily trialled peptides in existence: large cardiovascular-outcome and weight trials (STEP, SUSTAIN, SELECT). SELECT showed a reduction in major cardiovascular events in people with obesity and established heart disease.
46. What it helps: STEP trials showed about 15% weight loss in obesity, and SUSTAIN showed better glucose control in type 2 diabetes. SELECT showed fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with obesity and heart disease without diabetes. Users report strong appetite suppression and fewer cravings. GI upset on titration, muscle loss without resistance training and regain after stopping are common themes.
47. Trial: active · Phase 3 · fatty liver disease (MASH) outcomes · NCT04822181 · Novo Nordisk. Approved as Ozempic, Wegovy and Rybelsus, with dozens of trials still open from liver disease to addiction. (checked 2026-10-23) [S5] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
48. Personal or family history of MTC or MEN2: Causes thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents; boxed warning and contraindication on the label. (verified)
49. Anyone booked for surgery, endoscopy or sedation: Food can stay in the stomach for days and be inhaled into the lungs under anaesthesia. (verified)
50. People with diabetic retinopathy: Fast glucose drops worsened retinopathy in the SUSTAIN-6 trial; the label flags it. (verified)
51. People with optic nerve disease or one good eye: EMA lists sudden optic nerve stroke (NAION) as a very rare side effect. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
52. Cagrilintide: Semaglutide works through the GLP-1 receptor, while cagrilintide adds the amylin signal for fullness and slower stomach emptying from the brainstem. The two hormones normally act together after meals. The pair has been tested together in obesity trials, where cagrilintide adds to semaglutide's weight effect.

## Where it comes from
53. Novo Nordisk's GLP-1 analogue: two amino acid swaps and a fatty-acid tail that rides albumin, stretching the two-minute natural hormone into a once-weekly drug. It began as a diabetes medicine; the weight loss became the headline.
54. First studied for: Type 2 diabetes (Ozempic/Rybelsus), then obesity (Wegovy).
55. Name story: The "-glutide" ending is the INN stem for GLP-1 analogues. Novo built it in 2012 as a longer-acting liraglutide. [S6] (verified)
56. 2017: Approved for type 2 diabetes as Ozempic
57. 2021: Approved for obesity as Wegovy
58. 2023: SELECT: fewer heart attacks and strokes in obesity
59. Dec 2025: Oral Wegovy pill approved for obesity (reported)
60. Today: The default weight-loss drug; huge compounded and grey-market use

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What the cardiovascular trial actually measured [people]
61. This is the trial that changed the drug's standing, so it is worth knowing its shape rather than its headline. It enrolled 17,604 adults across 41 countries, aged 45 or older, with a body mass index of 27 or above, with established cardiovascular disease and no history of diabetes. They received 2.4 mg once weekly by injection or placebo, added on top of standard care, for up to five years [1] (verified).
62. The endpoint was a composite: first occurrence of cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack or non-fatal stroke. There were 1,270 first events across the trial, and the drug was associated with a statistically significant 20% reduction, with all three components of the composite contributing to the effect [1] (verified).
63. Two things follow that are often lost. First, a composite endpoint with all components moving in the same direction is a stronger result than a composite carried by one soft component, so this is a genuinely robust finding. Second, the comparison was against placebo on top of standard cardiovascular care, in people who already had heart disease. It is not a result about healthy people, and it was not designed to be.
64. The population also explains the most common misreading. This was a trial in people with obesity or overweight and established cardiovascular disease, deliberately excluding diabetes, because the question was whether the benefit existed outside diabetes. It did. That does not extend to people without cardiovascular disease, in whom the absolute benefit would be much smaller even if the relative effect were identical (inferred).

### The gap between the trials and how it is actually used [people]
65. The trial programme tested a specific thing: a stepped titration to a defined maintenance dose, taken continuously, in defined populations, with weight or cardiovascular events as the measured outcome. A large share of current use does not resemble that.
66. Sub-label dosing for appetite control, metabolic tidiness or longevity has no trial behind it. There is no study measuring outcomes at a fraction of the maintenance dose, no study of intermittent or every-few-weeks schedules, and no study in people without obesity or diabetes. The absence is not a hint that it does not work; it is simply unmeasured territory, and the honest label for it is unstudied rather than reported (verified as absent).
67. The long half-life, around a week, has a consequence that matters more at the edges of use than in the middle. Changes take weeks to express fully and weeks to wash out, so self-adjusting dose on the basis of how a given week felt is working with a signal that lags the input substantially (inferred). The trials sidestepped this by using fixed four-week titration steps.
68. The ceiling moved in March 2026, when a higher-dose 7.2 mg weekly version was approved for obesity in the US [2] (verified). Worth noting the direction of travel: the approved range has been extending upward on trial evidence, while a good deal of community practice has been moving downward on no evidence at all. Both trends are real and they are not in conversation with each other.

### Product reality: where this one differs from every other peptide here [people]
69. Unlike the repair peptides, an approved, characterised version of this molecule exists. That makes the grey-market and compounded supply a different kind of problem: not an unstudied substance, but a studied substance of uncertain identity, concentration and sterility, used without the labelling and titration support the evidence was generated with.
70. The documented failure mode is dosing error, and it is specific. Regulators described reports of patients receiving 5 to 20 times the intended dose from multi-dose vials; clinicians miscalculating when converting milligrams to units or millilitres, including one prescription written for 20 units instead of 2, which delivered ten times the intended dose to three patients; a patient who received no clear instructions from a telemedicine prescriber, searched online and took five times the intended dose; a clinician who recalculated his own dose and gave himself ten times the intended amount; and patients supplied with syringes far larger than the prescribed volume [3] (verified). Reported consequences included gastrointestinal effects, fainting, dehydration, headache, gallstones and acute pancreatitis, with some hospitalisations [3].
71. That list is worth reading closely because none of those events are pharmacology. They are unit-conversion and packaging failures, and they are the predictable result of separating a titrated microgram-scale injectable from the pen that doses it.
72. A 2025 analysis covering 2018 to 2024 linked compounded versions of this drug class to a higher rate of adverse effects than the non-compounded products, and it was cited in the US advisory debate on peptide compounding as a caution about pharmacy standards [4] (reported). Enforcement has followed the same line: warning letters went to online peptide vendors in August 2026, and to a compounder over its products in this class and its telehealth prescribing practices in September 2026 [5] (verified).
73. The practical reading for anyone comparing sources: with this molecule, the concentration stated on a vial and the volume in a syringe are where the risk lives, far more than the molecule itself.

### The generic wave, and why it changes the picture [people]
74. The patent position began unwinding in several large markets during 2026, and this is the development most likely to reshape grey-market demand.
75. In India, a generic launched around March 2026. In the US, a first tentative generic approval was granted in April 2026. In Canada, generics of the diabetes product were approved on 29 April 2026 and launched in mid-May, Apotex on 14 May and a second company two days later, both as pre-filled pens for type 2 diabetes in adults, making Canada the first G7 market with a generic version on pharmacy shelves. In China, a marketing application for a generic of the obesity product was accepted for review in February 2026. Health Canada was reviewing at least four further submissions [6] (verified).
76. Why an encyclopedia entry should care: the main driver of grey-market use of this molecule has been price and access, not the absence of an approved option. Characterised, pen-delivered generics at generic prices remove much of that rationale in the markets where they land. The dosing-error failure mode described above is almost entirely a property of vial-and-syringe supply, and it largely disappears with a pen (inferred).
77. The uneven part is that approvals so far are mostly for the diabetes indication and the diabetes dose range, not the obesity product, so access for weight management remains patchier than the headlines imply [6] (verified).

### Open questions [mixed]
78. What happens below the tested dose range? Sub-label dosing is now widespread and has never been measured for any outcome, including the appetite effect people are actually chasing.
79. Who benefits cardiovascularly outside the trial population? The 20% relative reduction was measured in people with established heart disease. The absolute benefit in lower-risk people is unknown and would necessarily be smaller.
80. What does very long-term use look like? The pivotal cardiovascular trial ran up to five years, which is long by trial standards and short relative to a treatment many people expect to continue indefinitely.
81. Does the muscle-loss question have a dose-dependent answer? It is well recognised as a risk and poorly quantified across the dose range, and it interacts with the sub-label dosing question above.
82. Will generic availability actually displace grey-market vials, or will price simply fall on both sides? The dosing-error evidence suggests the public-health answer hinges on delivery format rather than on the molecule.
83. For compounded and grey-market supply specifically: what is the real distribution of concentration accuracy? The adverse-event signal points at it, and unlike most questions on this page, it is answerable by testing rather than by trials.

# BPC-157 + TB-500
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/bpc-157-tb-500
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Wolverine stack, Wolverine blend, BPC/TB, BPC-157 + Tβ4, BPC-157 + Thymosin Beta-4, TB-500 + BPC-157
2. Origin: Blend of 2 peptides
3. Legal and approval status: Not approved anywhere as a drug or as a combination. US: BPC-157 and TB-500 left FDA 503A Category 2 in April 2026 when nominations were withdrawn; the July 2026 advisory panel voted in favour of compounding, no rule yet. Australia: both Schedule 4, prescription only. WADA: both banned at all times.

## Summary
4. This blend combines BPC-157, a 15-residue peptide from a gastric juice protein, with TB-500, usually full thymosin beta-4, in one vial sold as the Wolverine stack. People pair them for tendon, joint and post-surgery recovery, since one is thought to grow blood vessels and the other to help cells move into wounds. The one combined rat study found no extra benefit from pairing.
5. Punch line: The Wolverine stack in one vial. BPC-157 grows blood vessels, TB-500 moves repair cells; the default injury stack.
6. Used for: Tendon, ligament, joint and post-surgery recovery

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Tissue repair: Two different routes to tendon and wound healing
8. Inflammatory signaling: Lowers inflammation around injury
9. Pain & sensory: Joint and tendon pain eases for many users
10. Digestive & gut: BPC-157 side protects gut lining in rats
11. Muscle & performance (backed only by animal or user reports): Used for muscle tears and training recovery
12. Heart & vessels (backed only by animal or user reports): Both studied for heart tissue in animals
13. Bone & cartilage (backed only by animal or user reports): Studied for bone and fracture healing in rats

## How it works
14. Grows new blood vessels into injured tissue · BPC-157: VEGFR2, eNOS · role Tissue repair
   BPC-157 switches on the VEGFR2 receptor and the eNOS enzyme, which together drive new blood vessel growth. More vessels bring oxygen and repair cells into poorly supplied tissue like tendon. This is shown in rat injury models, while TB-500 adds a separate cell-migration route.
15. Shields gut lining, in rats · BPC-157: cytoprotection · role Digestive & gut
   BPC-157 protects the gut lining, a property called cytoprotection, and shields it from damage such as NSAID injury in rats. This is where the peptide was first studied. Its gut role adds a second use to the blend, but human data for it are thin.
16. Helps cells move into the wound by managing actin · Tβ4: G-actin sequestering · role Tissue repair
   Thymosin beta-4 binds single actin units (G-actin) and keeps them ready, so repair cells can build their internal scaffold and crawl into the wound. In the 2026 rat Achilles study, TB-500 alone improved tendon strength. The combination added nothing measurable over either alone.
17. Calms inflammatory signalling · Tβ4: NF-κB down · role Inflammatory signaling
   Thymosin beta-4 lowers NF-κB, the main switch for inflammatory genes. Less inflammation lets repair proceed with less tissue damage. This is shown in animal and cell work, with BPC-157 adding its own anti-inflammatory effect in injury models.
18. Mechanism overview: BPC-157 drives angiogenesis through VEGFR2, Akt and eNOS, activates FAK and paxillin for fibroblast migration, and upregulates growth hormone receptor on tendon fibroblasts. Thymosin beta-4 sequesters G-actin, promoting cell migration, and lowers NF-κB driven inflammation; its 17 to 23 region carries the actin binding. The rationale for pairing is two partly separate repair routes. The 2026 rat Achilles study suggests they may converge downstream, since combining added nothing measurable. On paper the two prefer different pH in solution: BPC-157 about 6.5 to 8.5, thymosin beta-4 about 5.5 to 6.

## What is inside the blend
19. BPC-157: 10 mg · Blood vessel growth and gut lining protection
20. TB-500 (Thymosin Beta-4): 10 mg · Cell migration into wounds via actin
21. Most common ratio: BPC-157 10 · TB-500 10 = 20 mg (14 of 16 listings (8 state the split, 6 sell a 20 mg 1:1 vial))
22. Other ratio seen: BPC-157 5 · TB-500 5 = 10 mg (7 listings (usually sold alongside the 20 mg))
23. Other ratio seen: BPC-157 30 · TB-500 30 = 60 mg (1 listing)
24. Other ratio seen: 30 mg total, split not stated = 30 mg (1 listing)
25. Version Common retail: BPC-157 5 · TB-500 5 = 10 mg
26. Version Common retail: BPC-157 10 · TB-500 10 = 20 mg
27. Version Common retail: BPC-157 30 · TB-500 30 = 60 mg
28. Why BPC-157 is in it: Angiogenesis and gut protection; most user data of any repair peptide
29. Why TB-500 is in it: Cell migration and actin handling; the only one with human wound trials (full Tβ4)
30. Mixing chemistry: Different pH comfort zones on paper: BPC-157 about 6.5 to 8.5, full thymosin beta-4 about 5.5 to 6.
31. Mixing chemistry: Full Tβ4 has a methionine that oxidises; the 7-residue fragment does not. Check which form is in the vial.
32. Mixing chemistry: No copper or histidine issue between these two.
33. Mixing chemistry: Some COAs give purity as area% only, which cannot confirm the 1:1 ratio. Ask for mg of each.
34. Mixing chemistry: One blend COA lists mannitol as filler.
35. Self-mixing: Mixing two vials yourself sets each at its own salt pH, stacks two overfill errors into the ratio and adds needle passes; drawing both into one syringe right before injecting avoids long liquid contact.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
36. Typical: 0.5–1 mg blend · 1× daily · cycle 6–12 weeks · route Sub-Q (reported)
37. Half-life: per component
38. Most people take: 0.5 to 1 mg of a 1:1 blend daily, which is 250 to 500 mcg each of BPC-157 and TB-500. On a 20 mg vial in 2 mL that is 5 to 10 units. People size it to the BPC-157 dose; the TB-500 share ends up far below standalone TB-500 loading (2 to 5 mg twice a week).

## What people report
39. Sub-Q daily, usually 0.5 to 1 mg of the blend (250 to 500 mcg of each). Courses 6 to 12 weeks, 2 to 4 weeks off. Some inject near the injury. People who want the higher weekly TB-500 doses (2 to 5 mg twice a week) run separate vials instead, because a 1:1 daily blend gives far less TB-500 per week.
40. Liked / worked: Tendon stronger with TB-500 in the combo rat study
41. Liked / worked: Default injury stack; pain eases in about 2 weeks
42. Liked / worked: Some recorded improvement in US medical notes
43. What worked: Users describe it as the default stack for tendon, ligament, joint and post-surgery recovery, with pain easing in about 2 weeks and the clearest changes at 3 to 6 weeks. A September 2026 analysis of US medical records found BPC-157 users (often on this pair) mostly started for pain, sports injury or gut symptoms, with some notes recording improvement.
44. Went wrong / did not work: Combining gave no added benefit in rats
45. Went wrong / did not work: 0 of 8 classifiable Finnrick blend tests passed
46. Went wrong / did not work: Some stopped for mood, skin or gut effects
47. What went wrong: The rat study found no extra benefit from combining. In that records analysis responses were noted for only a third of patients, and some stopped for neuropsychiatric, skin or gut side effects. Independent testing is poor: of 8 classifiable Finnrick tests of the blend (May to Sep 2026), none passed its purity standard. Reported side effects: tiredness or head pressure in the first weeks, headache, nausea, dizziness, injection site redness.
48. Most reported: Tendon, joint and post-surgery recovery
49. Most reported: Daily 250 to 500 mcg of each
50. Most reported: Tired or heavy-headed in the first weeks
51. Most reported: Separate vials for heavier TB-500 loading

## What has been tested
52. Tissue repair: Achilles transection, BPC-157 + TB-500 together (rat)
53. Tissue repair: Tendon, ligament and muscle injury, each alone (rat)
54. Pain & sensory: Knee pain, BPC-157 injected, 16 patients (human)
55. Tissue repair: Wounds and dry eye, full Tβ4 (trial)
56. Only one study has tested the pair together: a 2026 rat Achilles transection study (8 rats per group, 4 weeks). TB-500 alone improved tendon strength and histology scores; the combination improved one histology score but gave no added benefit over either peptide alone. Everything else is component research: BPC-157 in rats plus a 16-patient knee series, thymosin beta-4 in rats and in human wound and eye trials.
57. What it helps: Evidence is animal and user-reported. Each peptide alone speeds tendon and wound healing in rats; full thymosin beta-4 has human trials in wounds and dry eye. The one combined study, in rats, showed no extra benefit from pairing. Users rate it highly for tendon, joint and post-surgery recovery, usually within 2 to 6 weeks.

## Who shouldn't take it
58. People with active or recent cancer: Raises VEGFR2 signalling and new vessel growth in animal work; tumours use the same pathway. (inferred)
59. Drug-tested athletes: Banned since 2022 under S0 (non-approved substances); positives have led to bans. (verified)
60. People with proliferative retinopathy or vascular malformations: Pro-angiogenic peptides could feed abnormal vessel growth. (inferred)
61. People with known peptide or injection allergies: FDA reviewers flagged immunogenicity and impurity risk; no human safety dataset exists. (reported)

## Synergies (paired with)
62. GHK-Cu: GHK-Cu brings copper and collagen remodelling for skin and scar, while the BPC-157 and TB-500 pair covers deeper vessel growth and cell migration. Adding all three is sold as GLOW. No study has tested this stack, so the pairing is user logic, not trial data.
63. KPV: KPV blocks NF-κB inside gut and immune cells, while the blend works on vessel growth and cell migration. People add it for inflamed injuries or gut flares alongside repair. The combination has not been tested.
64. TB-500 frag 17–23: The 17 to 23 fragment carries the actin-binding region of thymosin beta-4, which the blend already contains in full. Adding it doubles up on the same mechanism. There is no data showing extra benefit, and the pair has not been tested together.
65. Thymosin Beta-4: This blend already contains thymosin beta-4 as TB-500, so adding more just raises that half's share. People do it when they want more cell migration and anti-inflammatory action. No study supports extra benefit.
66. BPC-157: This blend already contains BPC-157, so adding more raises the vessel growth and gut-protection half. In the only controlled tendon study, BPC-157 alone did not reach significance on strength. There is no data showing extra benefit from the added dose.

## Where it comes from
67. A two-peptide vial pairing BPC-157, a 15-residue peptide from a gastric juice protein, with TB-500. On the common retail version TB-500 means full 43-residue thymosin beta-4, not the 7-residue fragment. Sold 1:1 as 5+5, 10+10 or 30+30 mg.
68. First studied for: Assembled by the research-peptide market as an all-round injury stack. No company or trial designed it.
69. Name story: Sold as the Wolverine stack, after the X-Men character who heals from anything. A marketing name, not a scientific one. [S1] (verified)
70. 1981: Thymosin beta-4 isolated from calf thymus
71. Early 1990s: BPC-157 reported from gastric juice in Zagreb
72. 2010s to 2020s: Paired by users and sold premixed as the Wolverine stack
73. Apr 2026: Both removed from FDA Category 2 after nominations withdrawn
74. Jul 2026: FDA panel votes for compounding; same year a rat study finds no added benefit from combining
75. Sep 2026: US records study: new BPC-157 users up 33-fold since 2020

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### The one study that tested the pair, read properly [animals]
76. A 2026 study in a Turkish orthopaedic journal is the only published work to test these two together, and because it is the entire direct evidence base for the blend it is worth reading in full rather than by its conclusion [1].
77. Thirty-two male Sprague-Dawley rats, about 330 grams, were randomised into four groups of eight: vehicle, one peptide, the other peptide, and both. Each animal had a standardised full transection of the right Achilles tendon with a Kessler repair on day zero. Dosing began on day one and ran for 30 days, all by intraperitoneal injection: the gastric peptide at 10 micrograms per kilogram per day, the thymosin component at 60 micrograms per kilogram per day [1] (verified). Within each group of eight, four tendons went to mechanical testing and four to histology.
78. Maximum load to failure: vehicle 26.91 newtons, gastric peptide alone 37.16, thymosin alone 37.41, the combination 34.54 [1]. The overall test was significant, and the only surviving pairwise comparison after correction was the thymosin component against vehicle [1] (verified).
79. On histology, the Bonar total improved significantly only for the thymosin component against vehicle. The Movin total improved significantly for the thymosin component and for the combination, but not for the gastric peptide alone [1] (verified).
80. The authors state the result directly: combining the two conferred no additional benefit over either agent alone. They set out three candidate explanations, overlapping downstream pathways, a ceiling effect, or doses that were not optimal for a tendon model, and tested none of them [1] (verified).

### Three things in that study that cut against the usual framing [animals]
81. First, the gastric peptide alone did not reach significance on the mechanical measure, the one that speaks to whether a tendon can take load [1]. In a product whose reputation rests largely on that component, the single controlled tendon experiment did not confirm it, while the component usually treated as the junior partner did.
82. Second, the combination's mechanical result was numerically below both single agents, 34.54 against 37.16 and 37.41 [1]. With four tendons per group this is well within noise and should not be read as interference. It is, equally, the opposite of the additive pattern the pairing is sold on, and it is the only direct observation anyone has (verified, with the caveat stated).
83. Third, a collagen finding that reads as positive may not be. Type III collagen was higher with the thymosin component, and the authors explicitly cautioned that elevated type III should not be assumed favourable, because type III is characteristic of early repair rather than mature tendon [1] (verified). More early-repair collagen at four weeks could mean faster healing or could mean healing that has not matured.
84. The authors' own limitations are extensive and worth respecting: a single four-week timepoint so later maturation was not assessed, healthy young male rats only, no functional testing, no molecular or pharmacokinetic work, a thymosin dose not optimised for tendon, histology subsets of four with no a priori power calculation, no blinding of surgery or dosing, and mechanics limited to maximum load with no stiffness or cross-sectional area [1]. They describe the work as exploratory and hypothesis-generating. That is the correct reading, and it is also the strongest direct evidence this blend has.

### The route the study used is not the route people use [animals]
85. Dosing was intraperitoneal, into the abdominal cavity [1]. That is standard practice in rodent work and it is not comparable to subcutaneous injection in a person: absorption, first-pass exposure through the portal circulation and peak concentration all differ.
86. This matters for the blend specifically because the pairing's rationale is systemic repair signalling reaching an injured tendon. A study that delivers both peptides into the peritoneum of a rat tells you something about systemic effect in that species and nothing about what reaches a human tendon (inferred).
87. It also compounds a gap already present for both components separately: neither has human pharmacokinetic data by the routes in use. For the gastric peptide, regulators found no human pharmacokinetics by any proposed route, and in the human studies where plasma was measured it was undetectable or mostly below the limit of quantification [2]. For the thymosin fragment, there is no human pharmacokinetic data at all, and the only animal data is a single horse study [3] (verified). So there is no exposure figure for either component to connect a dose to a tissue.

### Which molecule is the second component [lab]
88. Regulators stated in 2026 that the seven-residue fragment and the 43-residue parent protein are not the same substance [3] (verified). On the common retail version of this blend the second component is the full protein, under the fragment's trade name.
89. That single fact breaks the chain of inference the product relies on in both directions. The animal study above used material called by the fragment's name; the wound and eye data people cite belongs to the full protein; and the formal regulatory assessment of effectiveness and safety was carried out on the fragment [1,3]. These are three different molecules' worth of evidence being pooled under one label.
90. Neither component has an approved generic name, and for each one regulators found nominators had been inconsistent about whether they meant a free base or an acetate salt, in at least one case submitting a certificate for one form under the name of the other [2,3] (verified). A two-component vial inherits both identity problems at once.
91. Independent batch testing of the blend is the weakest of the blends tracked: across eight classifiable results from May to September 2026, none passed the testing service's purity standard (reported, as logged in the card record and not re-verified in this pass).

### What combining adds, and what it costs [mixed]
92. In evidence terms, combining adds nothing measurable. The one study designed to detect an additive effect did not find one [1]. No study has tested any other ratio, any other route, or any other timepoint.
93. What combining costs is attribution, and there is a concrete illustration of that cost in the regulatory record. Both components' adverse-event reviews turned up cases involving blended products where causality could not be assigned to either ingredient: a report of injection-site redness and swelling in someone also injecting the thymosin component, and a report of hyperpigmentation with gum darkening that recurred on re-exposure to a two-peptide product [2,3] (verified). Each of those is an observation that a single-agent vial would have made interpretable and a blend made permanently ambiguous.
94. The same applies to benefit. A person who improves on a blend has learned that the blend did something, not which half, and therefore cannot narrow what to continue. Given that the one controlled experiment found the two components performing comparably alone and no better together, that lost information has a real cost (inferred).
95. There is one piece of human safety data touching either component, and it is very small: an uncontrolled pilot infusing the gastric peptide intravenously in two healthy adults at up to 20 mg, reporting no measurable change in cardiac, liver, kidney or thyroid markers and no adverse effects [4] (reported). Two people, no control, no efficacy endpoint.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
96. No approved product contains either component, and none contains the combination. Both left the US do-not-compound category in April 2026 because nominations were withdrawn, not because of a revised safety finding, which left them outside any recognised category rather than cleared [5] (verified).
97. On 23 July 2026 the advisory committee recommended both for the 503A bulks list, each by 8 to 6 with one abstention, against agency staff who had proposed adding neither [2,3,6]. Staff had assessed the gastric peptide for ulcerative colitis and the thymosin fragment for wound healing, and found the evidence weighed against both.
98. Those recommendations are advisory and change nothing by themselves: addition requires formal notice-and-comment rulemaking, which has not begun and has no deadline [7] (verified). An "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" went to the White House budget office on 14 October 2026 and was unpublished as of mid-October, with its covered substances and conditions not public [7].
99. Nothing in any of this addresses combinations. A substance being eligible for compounding individually would not make a premixed two-peptide injectable an assessed product (inferred).
100. In sport, both components are prohibited at all times.

### Open questions [mixed]
101. Does any ratio or schedule produce an additive effect? The single experiment tested one ratio, one route, one duration, and found none. The question is open rather than answered.
102. Would the result hold at twelve weeks instead of four? Tendon maturation continues well past the single timepoint used, and the authors name this as their main limitation.
103. Why did the component with the larger reputation fail to reach significance on load to failure? Dose, route, or genuine absence of effect in this model are all live explanations.
104. Is elevated early-repair collagen good? The study's own authors declined to assume so, and nobody has followed the tissue out to maturity.
105. Which thymosin molecule is in a given vial, and does it matter? Regulators say the two are different substances; no routine identity test distinguishes them in grey-market supply.
106. What reaches an injured tendon in a person? No human pharmacokinetic data exists for either component by any route in use.
107. Why does independent purity testing of this blend fail more often than for the single agents? Testing could answer this; it needs no trial.

# Tirzepatide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/tirzepatide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: LY3298176, Mounjaro, Zepbound
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: YAEGTFTSDYSIALDKIAQKAFVQWLIAGGPSSGAPPPS (39 amino acids). Positions 2 and 13 are Aib, shown as A; fatty acid chain on K20 and amide end not shown
4. Shown with an FDA approved badge
5. Legal and approval status: FDA-approved (Mounjaro, Zepbound) and widely approved. Catalog vials are not the approved product. Not WADA-banned.

## Summary
6. Tirzepatide is Eli Lilly's lab-designed dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist, a single chain that works both receptors. It is used for type 2 diabetes, obesity and obstructive sleep apnea. Trials show 20 to 22% weight loss at the top dose, and users often report a stronger effect than semaglutide, with similar GI issues and regain after stopping.
7. Punch line: Mounjaro and Zepbound. Weekly GIP plus GLP-1 shot; about 20% weight loss at top dose, beyond semaglutide.
8. Used for: Weight loss, diabetes, sleep apnoea

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
9. Appetite & satiety: Strong appetite control
10. Glucose & insulin: Lowers blood sugar and A1c
11. Sleep & rhythms: Approved for sleep apnea
12. Pain & sensory: Joint pain studied
13. Heart & vessels (backed only by animal or user reports): Heart outcomes under study
14. Reward & urges (backed only by animal or user reports): Fewer cravings reported

## How it works
15. Boosts insulin when glucose is high · GIP and GLP-1 receptors · role Glucose & insulin
   Tirzepatide activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors on pancreatic beta cells, with stronger action at GIP. Both boost insulin only when glucose is high. The SURPASS trials showed strong A1c reductions in type 2 diabetes.
16. Quiets hunger, slows the stomach · GLP-1 receptor · role Appetite & satiety
   Through the GLP-1 receptor it cuts hunger in the brain's appetite centres and slows stomach emptying. People eat less and feel full longer. SURMOUNT showed 20 to 22% weight loss at the top dose, and a head-to-head trial beat semaglutide on weight.
17. Improves how fat tissue stores and burns fat · GIP receptor, adipose · role Fat metabolism
   GIP receptors on fat tissue improve how fat cells store fat and release it for burning. This adds a second route to the GLP-1 effect and helps explain the larger weight loss. The weight results are human; how much this fat tissue effect contributes is less clear.
18. Eases sleep apnoea through weight loss · OSA, FDA label 2024 · role Sleep & rhythms
   Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is driven heavily by excess weight around the airway. Tirzepatide improved OSA in a dedicated trial, and the FDA added it to the label in 2024. The benefit comes through weight loss, not a direct action on the airway.
19. Dampens food reward and cravings · Central GLP-1R, GIPR · role Reward & urges
   Both GLP-1 and GIP receptors sit in brain reward circuits that drive cravings. Activating them dampens the pull of food reward. Users report fewer cravings, often more than on semaglutide; the circuit detail comes mainly from animal work.
20. Fatty tail rides albumin for weekly dosing · C20 diacid, albumin · role Glucose & insulin
   A C20 fatty diacid chain binds albumin, the main blood protein, which slows clearance and keeps the peptide circulating for days. This allows once-weekly dosing. It is the same strategy semaglutide uses, with a slightly longer fatty chain.
21. Mechanism overview: Tirzepatide is a single 39 amino acid peptide that activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors, with stronger action at GIP. GLP-1 receptor signalling cuts hunger, slows the stomach and boosts insulin when glucose is high. GIP receptor signalling adds insulin release and acts on fat tissue to improve how it stores and burns fat. Both act on brain reward circuits that drive cravings. A C20 fatty diacid binds albumin for weekly dosing. The dual action explains why it outperforms semaglutide on weight and A1c.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
22. Typical: 2.5–15 mg · once weekly · cycle Similar to sema · route Sub-Q (verified)
23. Half-life: ~5 days
24. Dose note: Label maximum 15 mg weekly. About three in four real-world users stay under 10 mg.
25. Most people take: 2.5mg/week → titrate to 5-15mg/week · Similar to sema. 3-6 months continuous, reassess.
26. Common: 5–10 mg · 1× weekly · ongoing; 2.5 mg start, +2.5 mg every 4 wk · Sub-Q · for most real-world users stop below 10 mg [S1] [S2] (reported)
27. Label max: 12.5–15 mg · 1× weekly (some split 2×) · ongoing, ≥20 wk to reach · Sub-Q · for full escalation, higher BMI or diabetes [S3] [S2] (reported)
28. Microdose: 0.25–1.25 mg · 1× weekly, or 2.5 mg/wk split 2–3× · ongoing; one public case 12 wk · Sub-Q · for longevity and maintenance crowd [S4] [S5] [S6] (reported)

## What people report
29. Heavily used grey-market and compounded. Users report stronger effect than semaglutide for many, with the same GI titration issues.
30. Liked / worked: About 20 to 22% weight loss at top dose
31. Liked / worked: Strong A1c reduction
32. Liked / worked: Sleep apnea improved
33. What worked: Around 20-22% body-weight loss at the top dose, strong A1c reduction, and improvement in sleep apnea, which is why the catalog stripe carries Sleep.
34. Went wrong / did not work: Class GI side effects
35. Went wrong / did not work: Rodent thyroid tumor warning applies
36. Went wrong / did not work: Regain on stopping
37. What went wrong: Same GI side-effect profile as the class; the rodent thyroid-tumor warning applies; regain on stopping.
38. Most reported: Stronger than semaglutide for many
39. Most reported: Same GI issues on titration

## What has been tested
40. Glucose & insulin: Type 2 diabetes, SURPASS (trial)
41. Fat metabolism: Obesity, SURMOUNT (trial)
42. Sleep & rhythms: Obstructive sleep apnea (trial)
43. The SURPASS (diabetes) and SURMOUNT (obesity) programs; SURMOUNT reported some of the largest weight loss of any approved drug, and a trial in obstructive sleep apnea led to an added indication.
44. What it helps: SURMOUNT trials showed 20 to 22% weight loss at the top dose in obesity. SURPASS showed strong A1c reductions in type 2 diabetes. It also improved obstructive sleep apnea, which is now on its label. Users report a stronger effect than semaglutide for many, with the same GI issues on titration and regain after stopping.
45. Trial: active · Phase 3 · obesity heart and death outcomes · NCT05556512 · Eli Lilly. Approved as Mounjaro and Zepbound; SURMOUNT-MMO is testing whether it cuts deaths and heart events. (checked 2026-10-23) [S7] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
46. People relying on the contraceptive pill: Slower gastric emptying lowers pill absorption; label advises backup contraception for 4 weeks after start and each dose step. (verified)
47. Personal or family history of MTC or MEN2: Causes thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents; boxed warning and contraindication on the label. (verified)
48. Anyone booked for surgery, endoscopy or sedation: Food can stay in the stomach for days and be inhaled into the lungs under anaesthesia. (verified)
49. People with diabetic retinopathy: Label flags diabetic retinopathy complications in people with a history of it. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
50. AOD-9604: Tirzepatide cuts appetite and improves glucose handling, while AOD-9604, a growth hormone fragment, is claimed to boost fat breakdown without affecting blood sugar. People add it hoping for extra fat loss. AOD-9604's fat claims rest mainly on rodent data, and the pair has not been tested together.
51. L-Carnitine: Tirzepatide lowers food intake, while L-carnitine shuttles fatty acids into mitochondria for burning. People pair them to support fat use and training energy during weight loss. Muscle uptake of carnitine needs insulin, and the pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
52. Eli Lilly's dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist: one chain works two receptors. The first of its kind, approved in 2022.
53. First studied for: Type 2 diabetes (Mounjaro), then obesity (Zepbound).
54. Name story: Built on the GIP hormone's backbone with GLP-1 activity added, so its name skips the '-glutide' ending of semaglutide and liraglutide. Lilly's code was LY3298176; dual incretins like it get nicknamed 'twincretins'. [S8] (inferred)
55. 2022: First dual GIP/GLP-1 drug, approved for diabetes as Mounjaro
56. 2023: Approved for obesity as Zepbound
57. 2024: Sleep apnea added as an indication
58. Today: Top approved weight-loss drug; heavy compounded and grey-market use

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### The head-to-head trial, because this is the only pair in the class directly compared [people]
59. Most drug comparisons are inferred by lining up separate trials, which is unreliable because populations and designs differ. Here there is a real head-to-head, and it is the most useful single piece of evidence about this compound.
60. SURMOUNT-5 randomised 751 adults one-to-one, in the US and Puerto Rico, to maximum tolerated doses of either drug, for 72 weeks, with both groups receiving diet and activity counselling. Participants had obesity, or overweight with at least one of hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea or cardiovascular disease, and no diabetes [1] (verified).
61. Average weight loss at 72 weeks was 20.2% against 13.7%, a 47% greater relative reduction [1]. The threshold figures matter more for a decision: at least 20% of body weight lost by 48.4% against 27.3%, and at least 25% lost by 31.6% against 16.1% [1] (verified). Waist circumference fell 18.4 centimetres against 13.0.
62. Two design caveats belong with those numbers. The trial was open-label, meaning everyone knew which drug they were taking, which can influence reported outcomes and adherence. And it was not powered to compare safety and tolerability, so the discontinuation figures, 6.1% against 8.0%, are descriptive rather than a finding [1] (verified).
63. The honest summary: on weight, superiority is established in a direct comparison. On everything else, the trial was not built to adjudicate.

### What the sleep apnoea trials measured, and why it was a stronger result than the weight data [people]
64. The sleep apnoea programme deserves attention because it used a hard, machine-measured endpoint rather than a scale reading.
65. Two parallel 52-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials enrolled 469 adults with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnoea and obesity: one in people unable or unwilling to use positive airway pressure therapy, the other in people already using it [2] (verified).
66. The apnoea-hypopnoea index, the count of breathing interruptions per hour, fell by 27.4 events per hour against 4.8 on placebo in the first trial, and by 30.4 against 6.0 in the second [2]. Weight loss was about 18% and 20% respectively, and systolic blood pressure fell 9.6 and 7.6 points [2] (verified).
67. That is a large effect on an objective measure, in both the treated and untreated-by-device populations, and it is the basis for the sleep indication. It also illustrates something general about this drug class: the downstream benefits of substantial weight loss are often easier to demonstrate cleanly than weight loss itself, because they are measured by instruments rather than reported.

### The cardiovascular trial, and the result people get backwards [people]
68. This is the most misreported trial in the compound's record, so the design matters.
69. SURPASS-CVOT randomised 13,165 adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, 6,586 to this drug titrated up to 15 mg weekly and 6,579 to dulaglutide 1.5 mg weekly, with median follow-up around four years [3] (verified). Mean age 64, mean HbA1c 8%, mean diabetes duration 15 years.
70. Critically, the comparator was not placebo. It was another drug in the same family already shown to reduce cardiovascular events. The trial was designed to test non-inferiority, with a margin of 1.05 [3].
71. The composite of cardiovascular death, heart attack or stroke occurred in 12% against 13%, hazard ratio 0.92. Non-inferiority was met. Superiority was not: the superiority test did not reach significance [3] (verified).
72. So the correct reading is that this drug is at least as protective as an established comparator, in a population already on good cardiovascular care, and was not shown to be better. Headlines describing it as beating the comparator on cardiovascular protection overstate a non-significant trend. Headlines describing it as failing a cardiovascular trial understate a met non-inferiority endpoint against an active drug, which is a harder bar than placebo (verified). The authors noted the absence of a placebo group, limited global diversity and some between-group imbalances as limitations [3].

### Where the approved product and the catalog vial diverge [people]
73. This molecule has been tested about as thoroughly as a metabolic drug can be: diabetes and obesity programmes, a sleep apnoea programme, a four-year cardiovascular outcome trial in over 13,000 people, and a direct head-to-head [1,2,3]. The evidence question is largely settled. The supply question is entirely separate and untouched by any of it.
74. The documented failure mode across this drug class in non-pen supply is dosing error rather than pharmacology. Regulators described reports of patients receiving five to twenty times the intended dose from multi-dose vials, clinicians miscalculating conversions between milligrams, units and millilitres, and patients supplied with syringes far larger than the prescribed volume, with consequences including dehydration, gallstones and acute pancreatitis [4] (verified). None of those events are properties of the drug.
75. Enforcement has tracked the same problem: warning letters went to online peptide vendors in August 2026 and to a compounder over products in this class and its telehealth prescribing practices in September 2026 [5] (verified).
76. The useful distinction for anyone comparing sources: with this compound the molecule is well characterised and the container is not. That is the inverse of the situation for the repair peptides in this catalog, and it calls for a different kind of caution (inferred).

### Open questions [mixed]
77. Does the cardiovascular benefit extend beyond diabetes with established disease? The four-year trial was run in that specific population against an active comparator, and says nothing directly about lower-risk people.
78. Would a placebo-controlled cardiovascular trial have shown superiority? Non-inferiority against an effective drug leaves the absolute size of the benefit unquantified.
79. How much of the sleep apnoea effect is weight loss and how much is anything else? The trials were not designed to separate those, and the distinction matters for whether the benefit persists if weight returns.
80. What does the head-to-head weight advantage mean for an individual? A 6.5 percentage point average difference in an open-label trial does not predict which drug suits a given person, and tolerability was not formally compared.
81. What happens to body composition at 20% or more weight loss, and does resistance training change the answer? Widely discussed, poorly quantified across doses.
82. For grey-market and compounded supply specifically: what is the real distribution of concentration accuracy? The adverse-event pattern points squarely at this, and it is answerable by testing rather than by trials.
