# Cagrilintide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/cagrilintide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: cagri amylin cagrisema, AM833, NN9838, GLXC-26801, CagriSema (with semaglutide)
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain
3. Sequence: KCNTATCATQRLAEFLRHSSNNFGPILPPTNVGSNTP (37 amino acids). Fatty acid chain on the N end, a bridge joining the two C, amide end; none shown
4. Legal and approval status: Not approved. Novo Nordisk filed CagriSema with the FDA in December 2025; no decision yet.

## Summary
5. Cagrilintide is Novo Nordisk's lab-modified, once-weekly version of amylin, the fullness hormone released alongside insulin. It is used mainly for obesity, signalling fullness in the brainstem and slowing stomach emptying, and it is paired with semaglutide as CagriSema. It is not approved, and grey-market users mostly run it in a semaglutide stack; GI side effects are common and CagriSema fell short of tirzepatide in one head-to-head trial.
6. Punch line: Weekly long-acting amylin, the fullness hormone. Paired with semaglutide as CagriSema: about 23% weight lost.
7. Used for: Weight loss, often with semaglutide

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Appetite & satiety: Amylin signal for fullness
9. Glucose & insulin: Slows sugar after meals
10. Reward & urges: Curbs urge to eat

## How it works
11. Signals fullness in the brainstem · Amylin receptors · role Appetite & satiety
   Cagrilintide activates amylin receptors, which are calcitonin receptors paired with RAMP proteins, in the area postrema and brainstem. These sites signal fullness, so meals end sooner. Alone it produced weight loss in obesity trials in people.
12. Slows stomach emptying · Amylin receptors · role Appetite & satiety
   Amylin receptor activation also slows the rate the stomach empties into the gut. Food stays longer, which adds to fullness and softens blood sugar spikes after meals. The same effect drives the high nausea and vomiting rates seen in human trials.
13. Holds back glucagon after meals · AMY receptors, alpha cells · role Glucose & insulin
   Amylin normally holds back glucagon release from the pancreatic alpha cells after meals. Cagrilintide mimics this, so the liver releases less glucose when it is not needed. This mirrors the role of the natural amylin co-released with insulin.
14. Adds to GLP-1 effect when paired · With semaglutide · role Appetite & satiety
   Amylin reaches satiety circuits partly distinct from those of GLP-1, so the two add up. Paired with semaglutide as CagriSema, REDEFINE 1 reached 22.7% weight loss at 68 weeks in people. That trial did not isolate how much cagrilintide itself contributed.
15. Dampens food reward signalling · Hindbrain, mesolimbic · role Reward & urges
   Amylin signalling in the hindbrain feeds into mesolimbic reward pathways that drive food seeking. Lowering that signal reduces the drive to eat for pleasure as well as hunger. This reward effect comes mainly from animal studies of amylin, not direct human measurement.
16. Mechanism overview: Cagrilintide is a long-acting analogue of amylin, the hormone co-released with insulin. It activates amylin receptors, which are calcitonin receptors paired with RAMP proteins, and the calcitonin receptor itself. In the area postrema and brainstem these receptors signal fullness, so meals end sooner. It also slows gastric emptying and suppresses glucagon after meals. Because amylin acts on circuits partly distinct from GLP-1, the two add together: paired with semaglutide it gives more weight loss than either alone. A fatty acid chain binds albumin for once-weekly dosing.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
17. Typical: 1–4.5 mg · once weekly · cycle Continuous, similar to sema · route Sub-Q (reported)
18. Half-life: ~7 days
19. Most people take: 1-2.5mg/week → titrate to 2.5-4.5mg/week · Continuous, similar to sema.
20. Common: 1.7–2.4 mg · 1× weekly · after 16 wk titration (0.25→0.5→1→1.7→2.4) · Sub-Q · for stack with reta or sema, copying REDEFINE [S1] [S2] (reported)
21. Low add-on: 0.25–1 mg/wk · 1× weekly, or 0.25 mg 2–3× weekly · ongoing · Sub-Q · for appetite add-on to a GLP-1; mood-sensitive users [S3] [S4] (reported)
22. Trial top: 4.5 mg · 1× weekly · 26 wk (Phase 2) · Sub-Q · for monotherapy users chasing trial max [S2] [S4] (reported)

## What people report
23. Grey-market use is usually as part of a sema+cagri stack.
24. Liked / worked: Solid weight loss on its own
25. Liked / worked: Additive with semaglutide
26. Liked / worked: 22.7% weight loss at 68 weeks as CagriSema
27. What worked: Solid weight loss alone and additive with semaglutide; amylin slows gastric emptying and curbs intake.
28. Went wrong / did not work: GI side effects
29. Went wrong / did not work: Weaker alone than dual agonists
30. Went wrong / did not work: Missed matching tirzepatide head to head (reported)
31. What went wrong: GI side effects; weaker alone than the dual agonists; CagriSema fell short of tirzepatide in a direct comparison.
32. Most reported: Mostly used in a sema plus cagri stack

## What has been tested
33. Fat metabolism: Obesity, alone (trial)
34. Fat metabolism: Obesity with semaglutide, REDEFINE 1 (trial)
35. Fat metabolism: CagriSema vs tirzepatide, REDEFINE 4 (trial)
36. Phase 2 on its own, and Phase 3 as CagriSema (with semaglutide): REDEFINE 1 gave 22.7% weight loss at 68 weeks; REDEFINE 4 missed its goal of matching tirzepatide head to head (reported).
37. What it helps: Trial data. Alone, it produced solid weight loss in obesity. Combined with semaglutide as CagriSema, REDEFINE 1 reached 22.7% weight loss at 68 weeks. Against tirzepatide head to head in REDEFINE 4, it reportedly fell short. Grey-market users mostly run it in a semaglutide plus cagrilintide stack for appetite and weight, with the usual GI side effects.
38. Trial: active · Phase 3 · obesity, cagrilintide alone · NCT07220642 · Novo Nordisk. Now in its own Phase 3 program as a standalone drug after showing 11.8% weight loss on its own in REDEFINE 1. (checked 2026-10-23) [S5] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
39. Insulin or sulfonylurea users: Amylin analogues add to insulin; pramlintide carries a boxed warning for severe low blood sugar. (inferred)
40. People with gastroparesis or severe slow digestion: Amylin slows the stomach further; pramlintide is contraindicated in gastroparesis. (inferred)
41. Anyone booked for surgery, endoscopy or sedation: Delayed gastric emptying raises aspiration risk under anaesthesia. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
42. Semaglutide: Semaglutide cuts hunger through the GLP-1 receptor, while cagrilintide adds fullness through amylin circuits that are partly separate. Together as CagriSema they gave more weight loss than either typically does alone. This pair has been tested in human trials, though it missed matching tirzepatide head to head.

## Where it comes from
43. Novo Nordisk rebuilt amylin, the fullness hormone the pancreas releases alongside insulin, into a once-weekly form.
44. First studied for: Obesity, mainly as the amylin half of the CagriSema combination.
45. Name story: The '-lintide' ending echoes pramlintide, the first amylin drug. 'CagriSema' is simply cagrilintide plus semaglutide in one shot. [S6] (verified)
46. 2020s: Once-weekly amylin analogue tested alone in Phase 2
47. 2025: REDEFINE 1: CagriSema gives 22.7% weight loss at 68 weeks
48. Dec 2025: CagriSema filed with the FDA
49. Today: Mainly seen as the amylin half of CagriSema; not approved

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What the pivotal trial measured, and what it did not include [people]
50. REDEFINE 1 randomised 3,417 adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one related condition, and without type 2 diabetes, to the combination product or placebo, dosed weekly for 68 weeks under double-blind conditions [1] (verified).
51. Weight reduction at 68 weeks was 22.7% against 2.3% on placebo under the estimand that assumes adherence, and 20.4% against 3.0% under the estimand that counts everyone regardless of adherence [1]. That gap between the two figures, roughly 2 percentage points, is the cost of real-world adherence and is usually the more honest number to carry forward.
52. The detail that matters for reading this compound on its own: the published pivotal release reports the combination against placebo and does not report separate single-agent arms for the amylin analogue alone or the established incretin alone [1] (verified). So the trial establishes what the pair does. It does not quantify, in that trial, how much the amylin half contributed.
53. That is the central evidence problem for this entry. This compound is nearly always studied and used as half of a pair, and the pivotal evidence is for the pair. Its solo Phase 2 work exists but is far smaller, and no large trial has isolated its independent contribution at the doses used in combination (verified as absent).
54. Tolerability: gastrointestinal events in 79.6% against 39.9% on placebo, with nausea 55% against 12.6%, constipation 30.7% against 11.6% and vomiting 26.1% against 4.1%. Discontinuation for adverse events was 6% against 3.7% [1] (verified). A nausea rate above half is high for this class.

### The head-to-head that did not go as expected [people]
55. REDEFINE 4 compared the combination directly against the leading dual-receptor drug: 809 adults with obesity and at least one related condition, no diabetes, 84 weeks, open-label [2] (reported).
56. Weight loss came in at 20.2% against 23.6% under the treatment-regimen estimand, and 23.0% against 25.5% under the efficacy estimand. Non-inferiority was not demonstrated [2] (reported). Since non-inferiority failed, no superiority test for the comparator was formally reported, so the correct statement is that the combination did not prove itself as good as the comparator, rather than that the comparator was proven better.
57. The timing is worth noting for anyone tracking the regulatory story. The marketing application was filed in December 2025, before these head-to-head results were released in February 2026, and the filing rests on the placebo-controlled trials rather than on the comparison [2] (reported).
58. This is a useful corrective to a common assumption. Adding a second mechanism does not automatically beat a well-optimised dual-receptor molecule. Two targets chosen well can outperform two targets combined, and the arithmetic of mechanisms is not additive in practice (inferred).

### Why the amylin pathway is a reasonable bet anyway [mixed]
59. The pharmacological case for this target does not rest on the head-to-head result, and it is worth separating the two.
60. Amylin signalling reaches satiety circuits in the hindbrain that are partly distinct from the incretin circuits, which is the mechanistic basis for expecting additive effects rather than overlapping ones. In the placebo-controlled trial, the pair did produce more weight loss than the established incretin alone achieves in its own trials, which is consistent with genuine addition even though cross-trial comparison is weak evidence (inferred).
61. There is also a precedent with a cautionary edge. The first amylin-based drug reached approval years earlier for use alongside insulin, and it carries a boxed warning for severe hypoglycaemia in that setting and is contraindicated in gastroparesis (verified, as reflected in the card's cautions). That history is the best available guide to what this receptor family does when pushed, and it points at the stomach and at glucose control rather than at anything exotic.
62. The practical consequence of the mechanism is that gastric emptying slows, and the pivotal trial's nausea and vomiting rates are consistent with that. For a compound whose action is partly to make meals end sooner, gastrointestinal effects are not a side issue; they are the mechanism being felt (inferred).

### Where approval stands, October 2026 [people]
63. The combination product's marketing application was filed in December 2025 and, as of late October 2026, had not been approved. The developer guided toward a decision in the final quarter of 2026, with no public decision date identified [2] (reported).
64. The single agent is not separately filed or approved anywhere. Anyone encountering it outside a trial is encountering an unapproved compound whose pivotal evidence belongs to a two-drug product it was studied inside (verified).
65. That has a specific consequence for interpretation. Reported effects from combination use cannot be attributed to this compound, and the trial that would settle its independent contribution at combination doses has not been run (inferred).

### Open questions [mixed]
66. What does this compound do on its own at the doses used in the combination? The pivotal programme did not isolate it, which leaves its independent effect size genuinely unknown.
67. Why did the head-to-head fail non-inferiority when the placebo-controlled result looked so strong? Population, open-label design, titration and dose optimisation are all candidates, and none has been established.
68. Does the amylin pathway add anything that matters beyond weight, such as a different pattern of regain or a different effect on muscle? Untested.
69. How does a nausea rate above half interact with long-term adherence? The two estimands in the pivotal trial already show adherence costing about 2 percentage points of effect over 68 weeks.
70. Does the insulin interaction seen with the earlier amylin drug carry over? The mechanism suggests caution with glucose-lowering treatment, and no trial has characterised it for this molecule.
71. If approved, does the combination earn a place against an already-superior single molecule? That is now a commercial and clinical question rather than a pharmacological one.

# MOTS-c
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/mots-c
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: MOTSc, mitochondrial ORF of the 12S rRNA-c
2. Origin: Made by the body
3. Sequence: MRWQEMGYIFYPRKLR (16 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: Unapproved research chemical. The July 2026 FDA compounding advisory panel recommended it; the vote is non-binding and needs a rule before it takes effect.

## Summary
5. MOTS-c is a peptide encoded in the mitochondria's own DNA, which in mice behaves like exercise in a molecule by acting on AMPK. It is studied for metabolic health, insulin sensitivity and endurance. Evidence is mainly mouse, with no human trial of MOTS-c itself; users report energy, endurance and fat loss, often stacking it with 5-Amino-1MQ and NAD+.
6. Punch line: Exercise in a molecule, encoded in mitochondrial DNA. Mouse data on endurance and fat; often stacked with NAD+.
7. Used for: Energy, endurance, fat loss

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Cellular energy: Exercise-like signal in cells
9. Glucose & insulin: Better sugar handling in mice
10. Fat metabolism: Resists weight gain in mice
11. Drive & mental stamina: More endurance reported
12. Muscle & performance (backed only by animal or user reports): Older mice ran farther
13. Immunity (backed only by animal or user reports): Immune balance in mice
14. Pain & sensory (backed only by animal or user reports): Less soreness reported

## How it works
15. Mimics the metabolic effect of exercise · AMPK activation · role Cellular energy
   MOTS-c activates AMPK, the cell's main energy sensor, indirectly. Once on, AMPK pushes cells toward glucose uptake and fat burning, the same shift exercise produces. This is shown in mice and cells, largely from one lab, and no receptor has been identified.
16. Moves to the nucleus under stress · Stress-response genes · role Cellular energy
   Under metabolic stress, MOTS-c moves from the mitochondria into the nucleus and regulates stress-response genes. This makes it a message from the mitochondria to the rest of the cell. It is shown in cell studies and was a key part of the original discovery.
17. Improves muscle glucose uptake, in mice · Folate cycle, AICAR · role Glucose & insulin
   MOTS-c inhibits the folate cycle and the purine pathway tied to it, which builds up AICAR, a natural AMP mimic. AICAR switches on AMPK, improving muscle glucose uptake. This is shown in mice and remains the proposed model, not a settled pathway.
18. Resists diet-induced fat gain, in mice · Fat oxidation · role Fat metabolism
   In mice fed a high-fat diet, MOTS-c raised fat oxidation and limited weight gain while keeping glucose handling better. The effect fits its AMPK activation. No completed human trial of MOTS-c exists; an analogue, CB4211, finished a small early trial in fatty liver and obesity.
19. Rises with exercise, falls with age · mtDNA 12S rRNA gene · role Muscle & performance
   MOTS-c is encoded inside the mitochondrial 12S rRNA gene, part of the mitochondria's own DNA. Blood levels rise with exercise and fall with age in people. These are observational human data; they do not show that giving it reverses ageing.
20. Mechanism overview: MOTS-c is a 16 amino acid peptide encoded inside the mitochondrial 12S rRNA gene. It inhibits the folate cycle, which builds up AICAR, an AMP mimic that activates AMPK. AMPK switches cells toward glucose uptake and fat oxidation, the same shift exercise produces. Under metabolic stress MOTS-c moves into the nucleus and regulates stress-response genes. Blood levels rise with exercise and fall with age. Most mechanism work comes from one lab and mouse models.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
21. Typical: 5–10 mg · 1–3× weekly · cycle 4-8 weeks on, 4-8 weeks off · route Sub-Q (reported)
22. Half-life: Unknown
23. Most people take: 5-10mg 1-3x/week SC · 4-8 weeks on, 4-8 weeks off.
24. Common: 5 mg · every 5 days (×4) or 2–3× weekly · 20 days to 6 wk, then long break · Sub-Q · for energy, metabolic [S1] [S2] [S3] (reported)
25. Low daily: 0.5–2 mg · 1× daily · not stated · Sub-Q · for starters, sleep-sensitive users [S1] [S3] (reported)
26. High: 10 mg/wk or 5 mg 3×/wk · 1× weekly, or 3× weekly · 4–10 wk (60–100 mg total) · Sub-Q · for experienced users, 'max' protocols [S3] [S1] (reported)

## What people report
27. Reported for energy, endurance and fat loss, often in a 5-Amino-1MQ/NAD+ stack.
28. Liked / worked: Exercise-like metabolic gains in mice
29. Liked / worked: Resists diet-induced obesity in mice
30. Liked / worked: Human levels rise with exercise
31. What worked: In animals, exercise-like metabolic gains. Users report energy, drive and better glucose readings.
32. Went wrong / did not work: No trial of MOTS-c itself
33. Went wrong / did not work: Anti-aging case rests on animal data
34. What went wrong: No human efficacy data; the anti-aging framing rests on animal and association data.
35. Most reported: Energy, endurance and fat loss
36. Most reported: Better glucose readings
37. Most reported: Often stacked with 5-Amino-1MQ and NAD+

## What has been tested
38. Glucose & insulin: Glucose handling (mouse)
39. Cellular energy: Running endurance (mouse)
40. Fat metabolism: Diet-induced obesity (mouse)
41. Organ function: Fatty liver, analogue CB4211 (trial)
42. Aging & senescence: Blood levels with age and exercise (human)
43. Mouse studies: better glucose handling, more endurance, resistance to diet-induced obesity. Human levels fall with age and rise with exercise. No completed trial of MOTS-c itself; an analogue (CB4211) finished a small Phase 1a/1b in fatty liver and obesity in 2021.
44. What it helps: Evidence is mainly mouse: better glucose handling, longer running endurance and resistance to diet-induced obesity. In people, blood levels rise with exercise, and an analogue, CB4211, entered a fatty liver trial. MOTS-c itself has no human trial. Users report energy, endurance, fat loss and better glucose readings, often stacking it with 5-Amino-1MQ and NAD+.
45. Trial: unclear · Phase 2 · insulin sensitivity in prediabetes · NCT07505745 · Hudson Biotech. First placebo controlled MOTS-c trial (120 people, 12 weeks), but run by an obscure sponsor whose other listings include a mock study. Treat with caution until another sponsor or a result appears. (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
46. Insulin or sulfonylurea users: Raises insulin sensitivity via AMPK; adding it to glucose-lowering drugs can drop sugar too far. (inferred)
47. Drug-tested athletes: WADA S4.4 bans AMPK activators as metabolic modulators; MOTS-c works through AMPK. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
48. 5-Amino-1MQ: MOTS-c activates AMPK for fat burning and glucose uptake, while 5-Amino-1MQ blocks the fat cell enzyme NNMT, which spares NAD. People stack them for fat loss, and they are sold pre-mixed as NAD+ + MOTS-c + 5-Amino-1MQ. Both rest on mouse data, and the combination is untested.
49. NAD+: MOTS-c pushes cells toward fuel use through AMPK, while NAD+ is the coenzyme that energy metabolism and sirtuins run on. They are sold pre-mixed as NAD+ + MOTS-c + 5-Amino-1MQ for energy and metabolic ageing. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
50. BPC-157: MOTS-c works on whole-body metabolism and endurance in mice, while BPC-157 targets tendon and tissue repair in rats. People combine them in training stacks for performance plus recovery. The pair has not been tested together.
51. TB-500 frag 17–23: MOTS-c works on energy and endurance through AMPK, while the TB-500 fragment is used for injury repair. People run them together in training and recovery stacks. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
52. GHK-Cu: MOTS-c targets metabolism and energy, while GHK-Cu targets collagen and skin repair. People combine them in longevity stacks covering two separate systems. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
53. Found in 2015 by Changhan Lee in Pinchas Cohen's USC lab, hiding inside the mitochondria's own DNA in a ribosome gene. In mice it behaves like exercise in a molecule, acting on AMPK and metabolic stress pathways.
54. First studied for: Studied for metabolic health, insulin sensitivity and exercise capacity.
55. Name story: MOTS-c = Mitochondrial Open reading frame of the Twelve S rRNA, type c. It is coded inside mitochondrial DNA, hidden within the 12S rRNA gene. [S5] (verified)
56. 2015: Found at USC, encoded in mitochondrial DNA
57. 2021: Analogue CB4211 finishes small Phase 1a/1b in fatty liver
58. Jul 2026: FDA compounding panel recommends it; non-binding
59. Today: Exercise-in-a-molecule peptide; still unapproved

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Why the discovery was interesting, independent of whether the compound works [lab]
60. The 2015 paper that introduced this peptide made a claim about biology that was more startling than any claim about therapy: that the mitochondrial genome, long treated as a small set of genes for respiratory-chain components, also encodes short signalling peptides that act on the rest of the cell [1] (verified).
61. That reframes the mitochondrion from a power plant taking orders to a compartment that sends messages outward. The idea has held up well enough to generate a field, and it is the main reason this molecule attracts serious researchers rather than only enthusiasts.
62. The mechanism proposed in that paper is worth stating precisely, because the popular version compresses it into something simpler. The peptide was proposed to act on the folate-dependent one-carbon pool and to inhibit the de novo purine synthesis pathway tethered to it. Blocking that pathway causes an intermediate to accumulate, and that intermediate is itself a potent activator of the cell's main energy sensor. So the energy-sensor activation is proposed to be indirect, a downstream consequence of a metabolic bottleneck, not a direct binding event [1] (verified as the paper's proposed model).
63. The 2015 paper presents this as a proposed model in its own figure legend [1]. It is a hypothesis with supporting data, not a settled pathway, and no receptor has been identified.

### Why a short peptide encoded inside a ribosomal RNA gene is contested [lab]
64. There is a genuine scientific argument here that rarely surfaces in consumer material, and it is worth understanding because it bears on how seriously to take the biology.
65. The reading frame sits inside a gene whose product is a structural RNA, in a genome that uses a different genetic code from the nucleus and has its own translation machinery. For the peptide to be a real signalling molecule, a short open reading frame inside that RNA gene has to be translated, and the product has to leave the organelle and act elsewhere. Each of those steps is plausible and each has been questioned (verified that the mechanism is proposed rather than established).
66. This is not a reason to dismiss the molecule. Synthetic peptide given to an animal can have effects whether or not the body makes it the same way. It is a reason to treat the framing of this compound as a natural hormone that declines with age as the least secure part of the story, because that framing depends on the endogenous biology being exactly as proposed (inferred).
67. The observed associations, that circulating levels rise with exercise and fall with age, are correlations in human samples. They do not establish that supplying the peptide reproduces what exercise does, and the gap between an exercise-associated molecule and an exercise substitute is the whole question (inferred).

### What was actually measured in animals [animals]
68. The animal work targets skeletal muscle and metabolic handling, and the effects reported are metabolic rather than structural: better glucose handling, resistance to diet-induced obesity, greater running endurance (verified as the literature's consistent findings, in mice).
69. What is missing from the animal literature is the thing that would make the exercise analogy real. Exercise produces cardiovascular remodelling, mitochondrial biogenesis, bone loading, and effects on mood and sleep. The animal data here speak to glucose and fat handling and to endurance capacity, which is a subset (inferred).
70. There is also a dose-response and exposure gap shared with most peptides in this catalog. No pharmacokinetic data in any species was identified in the regulatory review, so there is no way to connect an injected amount to a tissue concentration, and the animal doses cannot be translated (verified as absent in the regulatory record [2]).

### The human record, and the analogue that was tested instead [people]
71. No completed trial of this peptide itself exists. The closest human evidence belongs to a different molecule: a modified analogue developed by a company, which completed a small early-phase study in fatty liver disease and obesity around 2021 (verified as the card records; details of that programme were not retrievable in this pass).
72. An analogue is a different compound. A developer modifies a natural sequence precisely because the natural one has properties, usually stability or exposure, that make it unsuitable as a drug. So the existence of an analogue programme is simultaneously evidence that the target interested a drug developer and evidence that the unmodified peptide was not considered the right molecule to develop (inferred).
73. There is no human efficacy data for the peptide, no human safety dataset, and no established human dose. Every circulating figure derives from community convention or from converting mouse doses (verified as absent).
74. The reported user experience, energy, drive and improved glucose readings, is the pattern one would expect from a compound acting on the cell's energy sensor, and it is also the pattern one would expect from almost any intervention undertaken deliberately by someone paying attention to their metabolic numbers. Self-reported energy is the least specific endpoint in this entire field (inferred).

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
75. In the July 2026 advisory round, agency staff proposed that neither the free base nor the acetate be added to the 503A compounding bulks list, applying the four standard criteria of characterisation, safety, effectiveness and history of compounding use [2] (verified). The original nomination had been withdrawn, and the agency proceeded anyway.
76. The committee recommended it regardless, by 7 to 5 with two abstentions on 23 July 2026, for obesity and osteoporosis, the indications the agency had reviewed [3] (verified). That margin is narrower and the abstentions more numerous than for the repair peptides considered the same week.
77. As with the others, the recommendation is advisory and changes nothing by itself. Addition requires formal notice-and-comment rulemaking, not begun and with no deadline [4] (verified). An interim enforcement-discretion policy covering certain peptides went to the White House budget office on 14 October 2026 and was unpublished as of mid-October, with its covered substances not public [4].
78. In sport, the position follows from the mechanism rather than from a named listing: metabolic modulators acting on the cell's main energy sensor fall within a prohibited class, so a compound whose entire proposed mechanism is activation of that sensor sits inside it (inferred).

### Open questions [mixed]
79. Is the peptide genuinely translated and secreted in humans, or is the therapeutic effect of synthetic peptide unrelated to an endogenous signalling system? The replacement framing depends entirely on the former.
80. Is energy-sensor activation really downstream of a purine-synthesis bottleneck? That is the proposed model in the original paper and remains a model.
81. Does anything reach muscle after injection? With no pharmacokinetic data in any species, this is unanswered for every route in use.
82. Why did development proceed with a modified analogue rather than the natural sequence? The answer would say a lot about the unmodified peptide's drug-likeness.
83. Do exercise-associated levels mean anything causal? Falling with age and rising with exercise is consistent with the peptide being a marker of mitochondrial activity rather than a driver of it.
84. What is the toxicology? None was identified in the regulatory review, so long-term safety is unopened rather than open.
85. Does it do anything measurable in a human? A small, short, placebo-controlled trial with glucose handling as the endpoint would settle more than another decade of mouse work.

# GLOW
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/glow
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: GLOW blend, GLOW stack, GLOW 70, GHK-Cu + BPC-157 + TB-500
2. Origin: Blend of 3 peptides
3. Legal and approval status: Not approved anywhere. US: BPC-157, TB-500 and injectable GHK-Cu left FDA Category 2 in April 2026 when nominations were withdrawn; non-injectable GHK-Cu sits in Category 1; the July 2026 panel voted for BPC-157 and TB-500 compounding, no rule yet. WADA: BPC-157 and TB-500 banned at all times.

## Summary
4. GLOW is a three-peptide vial combining the copper peptide GHK-Cu with BPC-157 and TB-500 (usually full thymosin beta-4) in a 5:1:1 ratio. People combine the collagen-building skin peptide with the two Wolverine stack repair peptides for skin quality and healing. No study of the blend exists, and the copper share causes stinging and redness at the injection site.
5. Punch line: GHK-Cu plus the Wolverine repair pair, 5:1:1. Copper for skin texture and scars, the pair for healing.
6. Used for: Skin quality, collagen, wound and injury repair

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Skin & aesthetics: Copper peptide aimed at collagen and skin quality
8. Tissue repair: BPC-157 and TB-500 cover wound and tendon repair
9. Inflammatory signaling: All three lower inflammation in models
10. Hair: Hair and nail gains reported, GHK-Cu side
11. Pain & sensory (backed only by animal or user reports): Joint comfort reported
12. Digestive & gut (backed only by animal or user reports): BPC-157 side, gut lining in rats

## How it works
13. Signals skin to build collagen and remodel · GHK-Cu: copper delivery, gene expression · role Skin & aesthetics
   GHK-Cu delivers copper to tissue and shifts gene expression toward collagen, elastin and glycosaminoglycan synthesis and remodelling. It is the only skin and collagen signal in the vial. Its support is cell, animal and small topical human skin studies, not injection.
14. Helps blood vessels grow into damage · BPC-157: VEGFR2, eNOS · role Tissue repair
   BPC-157 activates VEGFR2 and eNOS to grow new blood vessels into damaged tissue. Better blood supply brings oxygen and repair cells to slow-healing sites like tendon. This is shown in rat injury models.
15. Moves repair cells into wounds · Tβ4: G-actin sequestering · role Tissue repair
   Thymosin beta-4 binds G-actin so repair cells can build their scaffold and crawl into wounds. Full Tβ4 has human wound trials. In the 2026 rat study, TB-500 alone helped tendon strength but adding BPC-157 gave no extra benefit.
16. Damps inflammation · GHK-Cu and Tβ4: NF-κB down · role Inflammatory signaling
   GHK-Cu and thymosin beta-4 both lower NF-κB, the main switch for inflammatory genes. Less inflammation lets repair proceed with less tissue damage. This is shown in cell and animal studies, and no study has checked how the three interact.
17. Mechanism overview: GHK-Cu delivers copper to tissue and shifts gene expression toward collagen, elastin and glycosaminoglycan synthesis and remodelling; it binds Cu(II) very tightly at neutral pH and more weakly as pH drops. BPC-157 adds angiogenesis (VEGFR2, Akt, eNOS) and fibroblast migration; thymosin beta-4 adds actin-driven cell migration and NF-κB suppression. The intended split is GHK-Cu for skin matrix, the other two for deeper tissue repair. No study has checked for interaction, and the 2026 rat study found the BPC-157 and TB-500 pair added nothing over either alone.

## What is inside the blend
18. GHK-Cu: 50 mg · Collagen, skin remodelling, hair
19. BPC-157: 10 mg · Blood vessel growth, gut lining
20. TB-500 (Thymosin Beta-4): 10 mg · Cell migration into wounds
21. Most common ratio: GHK-Cu 50 · BPC-157 10 · TB-500 10 = 70 mg (18 of 25 listings (7 state the split, 11 sell 70 mg))
22. Other ratio seen: GHK-Cu 35 · TB-500 10 · BPC-157 5 = 50 mg (3 listings)
23. Other ratio seen: GHK-Cu 30 · BPC-157 10 · TB-500 10 = 50 mg (1 listing (slug), 2 more 50 mg with no split)
24. Other ratio seen: 30 mg and 60 mg totals, split not stated = 30 / 60 mg (2 listings)
25. Version Common retail: GHK-Cu 50 · BPC-157 10 · TB-500 10 = 70 mg
26. Why GHK-Cu is in it: The only skin and collagen signal in the vial; hair and nail effects
27. Why BPC-157 is in it: Angiogenesis and gut protection
28. Why TB-500 is in it: Cell migration; human wound trial data (full Tβ4)
29. Mixing chemistry: GHK-Cu holds its copper tightly near neutral pH; acidic BPC-157 acetate liquid can weaken that grip.
30. Mixing chemistry: Copper plus a reducing agent (vitamin C, glutathione) oxidises peptides: never add them to the vial.
31. Mixing chemistry: Blue is normal. A shift to green, teal or brown suggests the copper has come off (reported, thresholds unverified).
32. Mixing chemistry: Release COAs show drift: BPC-157 at 117% of label in one, totals 94% in another.
33. Mixing chemistry: Stability after mixing is only claimed by sellers and affiliates, from 21 days to 3 months; nothing independent.
34. Self-mixing: Self-mixing puts an acidic BPC-157 acetate solution into the copper vial and pushes pH toward where GHK-Cu starts losing copper; separate vials or same-syringe draws avoid that.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
35. Typical: 10–15 units (70 mg in 3 mL) · 1× daily or 5×/week · cycle 8–12 weeks · route Sub-Q (reported)
36. Half-life: per component
37. Most people take: No standard dose. Most size it to land BPC-157 near 330 to 500 mcg: 10 to 15 units of a 70 mg vial mixed with 3 mL, which also delivers 1.7 to 2.5 mg GHK-Cu. One aggregator lists only 200 to 500 mcg of total blend, about a tenth of that.

## What people report
38. Sub-Q daily or 5 days a week. Common draw is 10 to 15 units of a 70 mg vial in 3 mL (about 1.7 to 2.5 mg GHK-Cu and 330 to 500 mcg each of BPC-157 and TB-500). Courses 8 to 12 weeks, then a break or 2 to 3 shots a week. If it irritates, people halve to 5 units for 1 to 2 weeks.
39. Liked / worked: Smoother skin and softer lines reported by weeks 4 to 6
40. Liked / worked: Faster wound and scab healing reported
41. Liked / worked: COAs show components near label
42. What worked: Users report better skin texture, hydration and smaller fine lines from weeks 4 to 6, faster scab and wound healing, joint comfort and stronger nails and hair. Guides describe early dewiness in week 1 and clearer change by weeks 5 to 8.
43. Went wrong / did not work: Never tested as a blend
44. Went wrong / did not work: Burning welts and itching from the copper share
45. Went wrong / did not work: Timelines come from affiliate guides without counts
46. What went wrong: No controlled data at all; the timelines come from affiliate guides without counts. The copper share stings: users describe burning welts lasting a day and intense itching, not fixed by changing needle length or angle. Redness at the site for 30 to 60 minutes is common. Finnrick: 1 of 2 classifiable GLOW tests passed (Jul to Sep 2026).
47. Most reported: Skin texture, hydration, scars
48. Most reported: Hair and nail gains
49. Most reported: Sting and redness at the site
50. Most reported: Breaks after 8 to 12 weeks

## What has been tested
51. Skin & aesthetics: GHK-Cu topical skin studies (human)
52. Tissue repair: GHK-Cu wound healing (animal)
53. Tissue repair: BPC-157 tendon and gut healing (rat)
54. Tissue repair: Tβ4 wound trials (trial)
55. Skin & aesthetics: Texture, fine lines, scars (users)
56. The blend has never been tested in animals or people. Component evidence: GHK-Cu in cell, animal and small topical skin studies; BPC-157 in rats and one uncontrolled knee series; thymosin beta-4 in rats and human wound trials. Lab work exists only on the powder: release COAs show components near label, with drift (BPC-157 +17% in one).
57. What it helps: Evidence is component-level and user-reported. GHK-Cu has cell, animal and small topical human skin data; BPC-157 and thymosin beta-4 have animal repair data and, for full Tβ4, human wound trials. No study of the blend exists. Users report better skin texture, faster healing and joint comfort over 4 to 8 weeks.

## Who shouldn't take it
58. Wilson's disease or copper overload: Each dose delivers copper; people who cannot clear copper accumulate it in liver and brain. (inferred)
59. People with active or recent cancer: Raises VEGFR2 signalling and new vessel growth in animal work; tumours use the same pathway. (inferred)
60. Drug-tested athletes: TB-500 is named on the WADA list as a thymosin beta-4 derivative. (verified)
61. People with cholestatic liver disease: Copper leaves the body through bile; PBC, PSC and bile duct blockage raise body copper. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
62. KPV: KPV adds a direct NF-κB block in gut and immune cells, stronger than the anti-inflammatory side of GLOW. Adding it turns GLOW into the KLOW stack. That combination has not been tested in animals or people.
63. GHK-Cu: GLOW already contains GHK-Cu, so adding more raises the skin and collagen share and the copper load. People do this for skin-first goals. There is no data on extra benefit.
64. BPC-157: GLOW already contains BPC-157, so adding more raises the vessel growth and gut-protection share. In the only controlled tendon study, BPC-157 alone did not reach significance on strength. There is no data on extra benefit.
65. Thymosin Beta-4: GLOW already contains thymosin beta-4 as TB-500, so adding more raises the cell-migration share. It was the stronger half in the one rat tendon study. There is no data on extra benefit from the added dose.

## Where it comes from
66. A three-peptide vial: GHK-Cu 50 mg, BPC-157 10 mg and TB-500 10 mg, 70 mg total, a 5:1:1 ratio. GHK-Cu, the copper peptide, makes up about 71% of the powder. On the common retail version TB-500 is full thymosin beta-4.
67. First studied for: Put together by the research-peptide market around 2024 to 2025 as a skin and repair blend: the collagen copper peptide plus the two Wolverine stack peptides. Popularised by newsletters and wellness clinics.
68. Name story: No source explains the name. It most likely refers to the skin glow it is marketed for, and it became the template for KLOW (GLOW plus KPV). [S1] (inferred)
69. 1973: GHK-Cu found in human plasma by Loren Pickart
70. 2010s to 2020s: BPC-157 and TB-500 paired as the Wolverine stack
71. 2024 to 2025: GLOW sold as a 50+10+10 mg vial for skin and repair
72. Apr 2026: BPC-157, TB-500 and injectable GHK-Cu leave FDA Category 2
73. Jun to Sep 2026: Lab COAs and Finnrick tests of GLOW published

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What combining these three adds in evidence terms [mixed]
74. Nothing has been measured. The blend has never been tested in an animal or a person, and no study of any three-component ratio exists (verified as absent).
75. What has been tested is two of the three, together, in one experiment. A 2026 rat Achilles transection study ran four groups of eight: vehicle, the gastric peptide alone, the thymosin component alone, and both, dosed intraperitoneally for 30 days after a Kessler repair [1]. The authors hypothesised an additive benefit and found none, stating that combining the two conferred no additional benefit over either agent alone [1] (verified).
76. Two details from that study bear on this blend specifically. On load to failure, the gastric peptide alone did not reach significance against vehicle, while the thymosin component alone did [1]. And the combination's mechanical result sat numerically below both single agents, which with four tendons per group is within noise but is the opposite of the pattern the pairing is sold on [1].
77. So the deeper two-thirds of this product rests on one exploratory experiment that looked for addition and did not find it. The authors offered overlapping downstream pathways, a ceiling effect, or non-optimal dosing as explanations, and tested none [1] (verified).
78. The copper component was not in that study. Its interaction with either of the others has never been examined in any system.

### The three components do not have comparable evidence [mixed]
79. A blend inherits the reputation of its best-regarded ingredient. Read separately, the three sit at very different places.
80. The copper tripeptide has the most human data and the most discouraging large result: a pivotal programme in diabetic foot ulcers enrolling 511 patients across 30 centres at two strengths against placebo found the drug no better than placebo [2,3] (verified). Its positive human evidence is topical, small and short. The injected route, which is what a blend uses, has never been studied in humans.
81. The gastric peptide has one controlled human trial, a 2005 meeting abstract in ulcerative colitis whose between-group confidence interval crossed zero, and which regulators judged inadequate for lacking endpoint definitions, inclusion criteria and statistics [4] (verified).
82. The thymosin component is the thinnest and the most often assumed strongest. Regulators found no clinical studies, no human exposure data, no human pharmacokinetic data by any route, and no toxicology studies of any kind for the marketed fragment [5] (verified). When that fragment was tested directly in a fibroblast wound-closure assay at 50 micrograms per millilitre, it did not significantly promote closure [5].
83. On the common retail version the thymosin component is the full 43-residue protein rather than the fragment. Regulators stated in 2026 that these are not the same substance [5] (verified), so the component list cannot be used to look up which evidence applies.

### The chemistry three components have to satisfy at once [lab]
84. This is where documented facts about the separate components say something concrete about the mixture, and it is the most practically useful part of this entry.
85. The components prefer different acidity. The copper tripeptide binds its copper ion very tightly at neutral pH and more weakly as pH falls, while the two repair peptides have different preferred ranges from each other, one toward neutral-to-slightly-alkaline and one toward mildly acidic (as the card records). A single solution sits at one pH. It therefore cannot sit at all three optima, and whichever compromise is struck, at least one component is held outside its preferred range (inferred).
86. The specific concern that follows is copper. If the solution is held toward the acidic end to suit the peptide that prefers it, the copper complex's binding is weaker there, which is the condition under which copper is less fully held (inferred). The reason bound copper is tolerable in the first place is that complexation silences its reactivity; a documented 1981 study showed that redox activity is effectively silenced when the metal is held by this tripeptide (verified, in vitro, as indexed in the copper peptide reference literature). Weaker binding is therefore the one chemical variable in this product with a clear mechanism for harm, and no study has measured free copper in any multi-peptide blend (verified as absent).
87. Storage requirements also conflict. The gastric peptide's lyophilised powder is recommended below minus 18 degrees Celsius, with reconstituted solution documented as stable only two to three weeks refrigerated [4]. The thymosin fragment is stored below minus 20 as free base and below minus 15 as acetate [5]. A single vial can only be stored one way, and after reconstitution the shortest-lived component sets the real shelf life of the whole product (inferred).
88. Release certificates on the powder show components near label with drift, including the gastric peptide running about 17% over in one batch, and independent testing is thin: one of two classifiable results passed between July and September 2026 (reported, as logged in the card record and not re-verified in this pass).

### What the copper share means that the other components do not [lab]
89. At the common composition the copper tripeptide is about five parts to one of each other component, which makes this, in mass terms, mostly a copper peptide product with two additions. Nothing in the literature establishes that this ratio is right for any purpose, because no ratio has been studied (verified as absent).
90. An injected copper complex raises questions a plain peptide does not: how much copper is delivered per dose, where it goes once the peptide is degraded, and what repeated dosing does to copper handling over weeks. Nothing in the available record addresses this for the single agent, let alone in a mixture (verified as absent).
91. There is also a regulatory asymmetry that bears on this. For the gastric peptide and the thymosin fragment, regulators published detailed 2026 assessments covering identity, certificates, impurities, endotoxin, aggregates, toxicology and immunogenicity [4,5]. For injectable copper tripeptide, no such document exists, because its advisory review was deferred to a later meeting [6] (verified). So the component making up most of the mass is the one with no published agency assessment of what is in it.
92. The stinging and welts users describe at injection sites are attributed to the copper share and are consistent with a reactive metal complex meeting tissue (reported). They are also the clearest signal in the whole product that something is happening locally that nobody has characterised.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
93. No approved product contains this combination anywhere, and the three components sit in three different regulatory positions.
94. The gastric peptide and the thymosin fragment left the US do-not-compound category in April 2026 because nominations were withdrawn, not because of a revised safety finding, leaving them outside any recognised category rather than cleared [6] (verified). On 23 July 2026 the advisory committee recommended both for the 503A bulks list, each by 8 to 6 with one abstention, against agency staff who had proposed adding neither [4,5,7].
95. The copper tripeptide is placed differently again. Its non-injectable form was restored to Category 1 on 5 May 2026 after a nominator clarified it had meant to withdraw only the injectable nomination, and it sits there under temporary enforcement discretion. The injectable route was left unclassified and has not been reviewed by the committee at all; that review is expected before the end of February 2027 [6] (verified).
96. So an injectable blend of all three draws on two substances recommended but not yet permitted, plus one whose injectable form has never been assessed. Addition to the list requires formal rulemaking, which has not begun [8]. An interim enforcement-discretion policy went to the White House budget office on 14 October 2026 and was unpublished as of mid-October, with its covered substances and conditions not public [8] (verified). Nothing in any of this addresses premixed combinations.
97. In sport, two of the three are prohibited at all times.

### Open questions [mixed]
98. Does any three-way combination add anything? The only pairwise test among these components looked for addition and found none, and the copper component has never been combined with either in a study.
99. How tightly is the copper held in a multi-peptide solution at whatever pH the product sits at, and is any of it free? This is the single most consequential unmeasured variable, and it is answerable by analytical chemistry rather than by a trial.
100. What happens to delivered copper over a multi-week course? Unstudied for the single agent and unexamined in combination, in the component that makes up most of the mass.
101. What is the real shelf life after reconstitution? The components' documented stability windows differ and the shortest governs, but nobody has measured the mixture.
102. Which thymosin molecule is present? Regulators say the fragment and the full protein are different substances, and no routine identity test distinguishes them in grey-market supply.
103. If a user responds, to what? Three simultaneous components at a vendor-fixed ratio make attribution impossible by design.
104. Why does the copper component sting, and is the local reaction telling us something about the chemistry? Nobody has looked.

# SS-31
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/ss-31
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: elamipretide, Forzinity, Bendavia, MTP-131
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: RYKF (4 amino acids). D-Arg shown as R; Dmt (dimethyl tyrosine) shown as Y; amide end
4. Shown with an FDA approved badge
5. Legal and approval status: Elamipretide (Forzinity) received FDA accelerated approval for Barth syndrome on 19 September 2025. Every other use is unapproved, and grey-market SS-31 is not the approved product.

## Summary
6. SS-31 (elamipretide) is a synthetic four-amino-acid peptide that concentrates in the inner mitochondrial membrane by binding cardiolipin, stabilizing the machinery that makes cellular energy. It is aimed at mitochondrial disease and heart failure, and received FDA accelerated approval for Barth syndrome in 2025. Other trials were mixed or missed their endpoint, and grey-market users report energy and recovery, with injection-site reactions.
7. Punch line: Elamipretide. Binds the inner mitochondrial membrane to steady energy output; FDA approved for Barth syndrome.
8. Used for: Barth syndrome; mito energy

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
9. Cellular energy: Steadies the energy machinery
10. Cellular protection: Protects mitochondria from damage
11. Muscle & performance: Approved for Barth muscle weakness
12. Drive & mental stamina: More stamina reported
13. Cognition (backed only by animal or user reports): Clearer head reported
14. Heart & vessels (backed only by animal or user reports): Studied in heart failure

## How it works
15. Sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane · Cardiolipin binding · role Cellular energy
   SS-31 (elamipretide) is a small peptide that crosses cell membranes and concentrates in the inner mitochondrial membrane. There it binds cardiolipin, a fat that anchors and organises the energy-making machinery. This targeting is well shown in cell and animal studies.
16. Steadies the energy-making machinery · Electron transport chain · role Cellular energy
   By stabilising cardiolipin, SS-31 keeps the folds of the inner membrane (cristae) intact and the electron transport chain complexes working together. Electron flow is more efficient and ATP output rises. This is shown in models of heart, kidney and muscle.
17. Cuts mitochondrial oxidative stress · ROS down · role Cellular protection
   More efficient electron flow means fewer electrons leak out to form reactive oxygen species, the damaging by-products of energy production. Lower oxidative stress protects mitochondria and the cells around them. This is shown in animal and cell studies.
18. Improves muscle strength in Barth syndrome · FDA approval 2025 · role Muscle & performance
   Barth syndrome is caused by defective cardiolipin, which makes it the clearest target. The FDA gave accelerated approval in 2025 for muscle strength, but the randomised phase of the 12-person trial missed its endpoints; gains appeared only in a long open-label extension. A confirmatory trial is required.
19. Protects heart cells in injury models · Cardiac mitochondria · role Heart & vessels
   In heart injury models SS-31 protects cardiac mitochondria and limits cell damage. Animal results for heart and kidney are strong. Human heart failure trials gave mixed results, so the animal benefit has not clearly carried over.
20. Mechanism overview: SS-31, elamipretide, is a tetrapeptide of alternating aromatic and basic residues that crosses cell membranes and concentrates in the inner mitochondrial membrane. There it binds cardiolipin, the phospholipid that anchors and organises the electron transport chain complexes. Stabilising cardiolipin keeps cristae intact and electron flow efficient, raising ATP output and cutting the electron leak that forms reactive oxygen species. Barth syndrome is a disease of defective cardiolipin, which makes it the clearest target. In models it protects heart, kidney and muscle mitochondria.

## Synergies (paired with)
48. Humanin: SS-31 protects the energy machinery inside mitochondria, while humanin, a peptide made by mitochondria, blocks cell-death signals and improves insulin sensitivity in rodents. People pair them for mitochondrial ageing from two angles. The pair has not been tested together.
49. MOTS-c: SS-31 keeps the mitochondrial membrane and energy chain intact, while MOTS-c, another mitochondrial signal, shifts metabolism through AMPK in mice. People stack them for energy and metabolic ageing. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

Some users pair them for energy during weight loss. There is no data on the combination, and tesofensine raises heart rate.

## Where it comes from
51. A synthetic 4-amino-acid peptide (elamipretide/MTP-131) that concentrates in the inner mitochondrial membrane by binding cardiolipin, stabilizing the machinery that makes cellular energy.
52. First studied for: Mitochondrial diseases and heart failure, by protecting energy production in damaged tissue.
53. Name story: SS stands for Szeto–Schiller: Hazel Szeto (Cornell) and Peter Schiller (IRCM Montreal), who designed the series. It became elamipretide and in September 2025 Forzinity, the first FDA-approved Barth syndrome drug. [S8] (verified)
54. 2000s: Mitochondria-targeted peptide; strong animal heart and kidney data
55. 2010s to 2020s: Trials in heart failure, myopathy, dry AMD; myopathy Phase 3 misses
56. Sep 2025: Accelerated FDA approval for Barth syndrome as Forzinity
57. Today: Niche approved drug; grey-market energy and recovery peptide

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What the approval was actually based on, which is not what it sounds like [people]
58. This is the most important thing to understand about this compound, and the summary version gets it backwards.
59. The pivotal trial, TAZPOWER, enrolled 12 males with genetically confirmed Barth syndrome in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design: six to drug and six to placebo for 12 weeks, a four-week washout, then crossover [1] (verified). The primary endpoints were six-minute walk distance and a total fatigue score.
60. In that randomised phase, there was no statistically significant difference in walk distance, no difference in fatigue score, and no improvement in knee extensor strength [1] (verified). The controlled portion of the pivotal trial missed everything it set out to measure.
61. The approval rests on what came afterward: a 168-week open-label extension, in which all participants received drug. Knee extensor strength first appeared to improve at week 36 but was not sustained. By week 168, all subjects showed significant improvement, with a median change of 63 newtons [1] (verified). Accelerated approval followed in September 2025 for improving muscle strength in patients weighing at least 30 kilograms, at 40 mg subcutaneously once daily, with a required post-approval randomised placebo-controlled confirmatory trial [1].
62. So the evidence is: twelve people, a failed randomised phase, and a benefit visible only in an uncontrolled extension after more than three years of continuous treatment. The agency accepted that for an ultra-rare fatal disease with no other treatment, which is a defensible regulatory judgement. It is not a demonstration that the molecule reliably improves muscle strength (verified).

### Why an open-label extension after three years is weak evidence, and why it was accepted anyway [people]
63. In an open-label extension everyone knows they are on drug, there is no comparison group, and the people still enrolled at week 168 are the ones who chose to stay. Each of those independently biases toward an apparent benefit. Natural history also runs in the background: a measure taken repeatedly over three years in a dozen young people will move for reasons unrelated to treatment (inferred).
64. The strength signal's own shape is a caution. It appeared at week 36, then was not sustained, then was present at week 168 [1]. A genuine pharmacological effect usually does not vanish and return; a noisy measure in a tiny sample does exactly that.
65. What makes the approval reasonable despite all that is the disease. Barth syndrome is a rare genetic disorder of cardiolipin, the specific phospholipid this molecule binds, and there was no approved treatment. Accelerated approval exists for precisely this situation: accept weaker evidence of a surrogate benefit, require a proper trial afterwards. The confirmatory trial is mandated and has not reported [1] (verified).
66. The practical consequence for anyone reading the approval as validation of the molecule's broader promise: it is the narrowest possible approval, in the one disease where the target is the known defect, on the weakest evidence the pathway permits.

### The broader programme, and what it failed to show [people]
67. This molecule has been tested in considerably more than its approved indication, and the pattern of those results is the most informative thing about it.
68. A Phase 3 trial in primary mitochondrial myopathy missed its main endpoint. Heart failure work produced mixed results. Dry age-related macular degeneration has been trialled (verified, as the card records). Extensive animal work shows protection of heart, kidney and muscle mitochondria.
69. That shape, strong and consistent preclinical protection followed by a failed Phase 3 in the most obvious human indication, is one of the most common patterns in drug development and usually means one of three things: the animal models do not capture the human disease, the exposure achieved in people is insufficient at the target, or the endpoint cannot detect the effect size present (inferred). None of those has been established here.
70. The mechanism remains the compound's strongest asset. Binding cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane is a specific, structurally grounded proposal, and it explains why Barth syndrome, a disease of defective cardiolipin, is the clearest target. It also implies the opposite of a general-purpose benefit: the clearer the mechanism, the narrower the population in whom it should matter (inferred).

### What the label says about handling the drug, and why that is relevant outside the label [people]
71. Because an approved version exists, there is a characterised safety and handling profile here that no other unapproved peptide in this catalog has. It is worth reading for what it reveals.
72. Dose is 40 mg subcutaneously once daily, with a reduction to 20 mg daily in severe renal impairment, meaning estimated filtration below 30 and not on dialysis [1] (verified). That renal adjustment tells you the compound is cleared by the kidneys and that exposure rises when they are impaired.
73. The most common adverse events are injection-site reactions, specifically redness, induration, itching and pain. In the open-label extension, 2 of 10 participants discontinued because of injection-site reactions [1] (verified). For a daily subcutaneous injection, that is a meaningful discontinuation driver rather than a nuisance.
74. Warnings include hypersensitivity reactions, including serious allergic reactions. The formulation is not approved for neonates because it contains benzyl alcohol [1] (verified).
75. The label also makes an unusual statement about time course: measurable benefit was observed only after more than three years of treatment, and long-term use is needed [1]. That is a direct consequence of the evidence base described above, and it is irreconcilable with the way the compound is discussed as a short-course energy intervention (inferred).
76. Grey-market material is not the approved product, and the approved product's characterisation does not transfer to it (verified).

### Open questions [mixed]
77. Does the confirmatory trial replicate the strength benefit? That trial is required and has not reported, and it is the single result that would convert an accelerated approval into an established one.
78. Why did the randomised phase fail while the extension succeeded? Sample size, duration, measure choice and open-label bias are all candidates, and distinguishing them matters for every other indication.
79. Why did the large mitochondrial myopathy Phase 3 miss? Without an answer, there is no rational basis for expecting benefit in any other mitochondrial condition.
80. Does the mechanism predict benefit outside cardiolipin-defect disease? Binding cardiolipin is specific, which argues for a narrow population rather than a broad one.
81. What exposure does the approved daily dose achieve at the inner mitochondrial membrane, and is that the step the failed trials fell at? Not publicly established.
82. Does anything in the approval support the energy and recovery uses it is bought for? Nothing in the record addresses healthy people, short courses, or any outcome resembling those claims.
83. What happens over years in people without the disease? The only long-duration human data comes from twelve patients with a specific genetic defect.

# Tesamorelin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/tesamorelin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: TH9507, Egrifta, Egrifta SV, Egrifta WR, tesamorelin acetate
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain
3. Sequence: YADAIFTNSYRKVLGQLSARKLLQDIMSRQQGESNQERGARARL (44 amino acids). Hexenoyl group on the start, amide end
4. Shown with an FDA approved badge
5. Legal and approval status: FDA-approved (Egrifta) for HIV lipodystrophy; other uses are off-label/grey-market. WADA-banned.

## Summary
6. Tesamorelin is a stabilized GHRH analogue, sold as Egrifta, engineered to resist breakdown and last longer than sermorelin. It is FDA-approved to reduce visceral belly fat in HIV lipodystrophy, and small trials show lower liver fat and, in one RCT, better memory in older adults. Belly fat returns after stopping and blood sugar can rise; users treat it as the most evidence-backed GHRH analogue.
7. Punch line: Egrifta. A sturdier GHRH that raises your own growth hormone; the only one approved to cut belly fat.
8. Used for: Visceral fat loss (HIV label)

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
9. Endocrine & growth: Raises the body's own GH
10. Fat metabolism: Cuts belly fat around organs
11. Organ function: Less liver fat
12. Sleep & rhythms: Better sleep reported
13. Cognition (backed only by animal or user reports): Memory studied in older adults
14. Inflammatory signaling (backed only by animal or user reports): Lower inflammation markers

## How it works
15. Prompts the pituitary to release GH · GHRH receptor · role Endocrine & growth
   Tesamorelin binds pituitary GHRH receptors and triggers GH release in pulses, so the body's feedback control stays intact. IGF-1 rises as a result. Phase 3 human trials confirmed the GH and IGF-1 rise alongside its fat effects.
16. Stabilised to resist breakdown · Modified GHRH 1-44 · role Endocrine & growth
   It is the full 44 amino acid GHRH with a small chemical cap on the front end that shields it from DPP-4, the enzyme that cuts natural GHRH. This extends its action enough for once-daily use, the form tested in human trials.
17. Cuts deep belly (visceral) fat · GH-driven lipolysis · role Fat metabolism
   GH strongly drives lipolysis, the release of stored fat, and deep belly (visceral) fat is unusually GH-sensitive. In phase 3 trials in HIV lipodystrophy, imaging showed clear visceral fat loss against placebo. The fat returns after stopping.
18. Lowers liver fat in trials · Hepatic fat fraction · role Organ function
   The same GH-driven fat release lowers fat stored in the liver. In a randomised trial in people with HIV and fatty liver, liver fat fell more than on placebo, and fewer treated people showed fibrosis progression. The trial was small, so it is a strong signal, not settled.
19. Improved memory in older adults in one RCT · GHRH, brain GABA up · role Cognition
   In one randomised trial in older adults, GHRH treatment improved memory and raised brain levels of GABA, the main calming messenger. The result is small and has not been replicated, so treat it as early human evidence.
20. Mechanism overview: Tesamorelin is the full 44 amino acid GHRH with a trans-3-hexenoyl group on the N-terminus, which protects it from DPP-4 and extends its action. It binds pituitary GHRH receptors and stimulates pulsatile GH release, raising IGF-1 while feedback control stays intact. GH released this way strongly drives lipolysis in visceral fat, which is metabolically active and GH-sensitive. Liver fat falls by the same route. In one trial in older adults it raised brain GABA levels alongside memory gains.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
21. Typical: 1–2 mg · daily · cycle 6-12 months continuous · route Sub-Q (verified)
22. Half-life: ~26 minutes
23. Most people take: 1-2mg/day SC · 6-12 months continuous. FDA studies ran 26-52 weeks.
24. Common: 1 mg · daily, pre-bed · 12–16 wk · Sub-Q · for general VAT loss, women, lean users [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4] (reported)
25. Label / higher: 2 mg · daily · 26–52 wk · Sub-Q · for serious visceral or liver fat; trial dose [S5] [S6] [S7] (verified)
26. Aggressive: 3–4 mg · daily · 8–16 wk · Sub-Q · for upper community, research supply [S3] (reported)

## What people report
27. Reported for belly-fat loss, sleep and recovery; the most 'evidence-backed' of the GHRH analogues.
28. Liked / worked: Clear visceral fat reduction
29. Liked / worked: Raises IGF-1
30. Liked / worked: Small liver fat and cognitive signals

37. Most reported: Sleep and recovery

## What has been tested
38. Fat metabolism: HIV lipodystrophy (trial)
39. Organ function: Fatty liver (trial)
40. Cognition: Cognition in aging (trial)
41. Phase 3 trials in HIV-associated lipodystrophy showed significant visceral-fat reduction; later studied for fatty liver and cognition in aging.
42. What it helps: Approved for excess visceral belly fat in HIV lipodystrophy, where trials showed clear reductions. Small trials show lower liver fat in fatty liver disease and, in one RCT, better memory in older adults. Belly fat returns after stopping, and blood sugar can rise. Users report belly fat loss, sleep and recovery, and treat it as the most evidence-backed GHRH analogue.
43. Trial: active · Phase 2 · physical function and frailty in HIV · NCT06554717 · Massachusetts General Hospital. Approved as Egrifta for HIV belly fat, now being tested with exercise against frailty through 2028. (checked 2026-10-23) [S8] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
44. Pituitary tumour, pituitary surgery or brain radiation: Label contraindication: needs an intact hypothalamic-pituitary axis. (verified)
45. People with active or recent cancer: Raises IGF-1; label contraindicates active malignancy. (verified)
46. People with prediabetes or poorly controlled diabetes: Raises blood glucose and HbA1c; label requires monitoring and warns about glucose intolerance. (verified)
47. People allergic to mannitol: Mannitol is an excipient; label contraindicates hypersensitivity. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
48. Ipamorelin: Tesamorelin drives GH through the GHRH receptor and ipamorelin adds a cleaner ghrelin-receptor pulse, aiming for more GH than either alone. Sold pre-mixed as Tesamorelin + Ipamorelin and in a three-way blend, but the pair has not been tested together in trials.
49. CJC-1295 no DAC: Both are GHRH analogues on the same receptor, so they overlap more than they complement. They appear together in the pre-mixed Tesamorelin + Ipamorelin + CJC-1295 no DAC, where ipamorelin adds the second pathway. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
50. GHRP-2: Tesamorelin brings trial-backed GHRH drive, and GHRP-2 adds a strong ghrelin-receptor pulse at the cost of hunger, cortisol and prolactin. People pair them for a bigger GH response. The pair itself has not been tested together.
51. GHRP-6: GHRP-6 adds a ghrelin-receptor pulse and strong appetite on top of tesamorelin's GHRH drive. That hunger works against tesamorelin's main use, fat loss, so it suits bulking more than cutting. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
52. Hexarelin: Hexarelin adds the strongest ghrelin-receptor push to tesamorelin's GHRH drive, but its effect fades with repeated use and it raises cortisol and prolactin more. Used for short blocks. The pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
53. A stabilized GHRH analogue (Egrifta), engineered to resist breakdown and last longer than sermorelin.
54. First studied for: Reducing the visceral belly fat (lipodystrophy) that builds up in people on HIV therapy.
55. Name story: The full 44-residue GHRH, the whole hormone sermorelin trims to 29, with a small trans-3-hexenoic acid cap on its front end. Canadian developer Theratechnologies coded it TH9507; '-relin' marks the INN growth-hormone-release family. [S9] (verified)
56. 2010: Approved as Egrifta for HIV-linked belly fat
57. 2010s: Studied in fatty liver and cognition in aging
58. Today: Best-evidenced GHRH analogue; off-label for belly fat

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What the pivotal trial measured, with the numbers that matter [people]
59. This is the best-evidenced compound in the growth-hormone-releasing family, so the pivotal trial is worth reading in detail rather than by its conclusion.
60. It enrolled 412 people with HIV and abdominal fat accumulation across 43 sites, 86% men, randomised two-to-one to 2 mg daily subcutaneously or placebo for 26 weeks [1] (verified).
61. Visceral adipose tissue, measured by imaging rather than reported, fell 15.2% on drug while rising 5.0% on placebo [1]. Insulin-like growth factor 1 rose 81%, about 109 nanograms per millilitre, against a 5% fall on placebo. Triglycerides fell 50 milligrams per decilitre against a 9 milligram rise [1] (verified).
62. The measure to notice is the first one. Visceral fat assessed by imaging is an objective endpoint, and a 20 percentage point separation from placebo on it is a solid result. This is the reason the compound carries more credibility than the rest of its family: the effect was demonstrated on an instrument, not a questionnaire.
63. Glucose is the honest complication. There were no significant differences between groups in fasting glucose, two-hour glucose or insulin in this trial [1] (verified). That is a better result than the mechanism predicts, and it sits alongside the label's requirement to monitor glucose. The resolution is that growth hormone raises glucose reliably enough to warrant monitoring, while a 26-week trial in this population did not detect a group difference (inferred).

### The immunogenicity finding nobody quotes [people]
64. Antibodies to the drug appeared in 48.6% of treated participants against 2.7% on placebo, and six patients developed urticaria [1] (verified).
65. Nearly half of treated people mounting an antibody response is a striking number, and it is the single most useful data point in this catalog for thinking about injected peptides generally. Regulators repeatedly flag immunogenicity as an unquantified risk for unapproved injected peptides, noting that aggregates and unidentified impurities can drive immune responses and that no studies exist to settle it. Here is a well-characterised, properly manufactured, approved 44-residue peptide, studied in a controlled trial, and the answer was: about half (verified).
66. That reframes the concern. The question for unapproved peptides is not whether an injected peptide can provoke an antibody response. It evidently can, even when the product is clean. The open question is what those antibodies do, and for this compound the trial found no loss of effect attributable to them, which is reassuring for it specifically and says nothing about any other molecule (inferred).
67. Discontinuation for adverse events was 12.1% on drug against 2.9% on placebo, and treatment-related adverse events ran 53.8% against 36.5% [1] (verified). Overall and serious adverse event rates did not differ significantly. So the tolerability cost is real and mostly non-serious.

### Where it has been tested beyond its approval, and what those trials found [people]
68. Two further randomised trials are more interesting than the approval, because they tested whether the visceral-fat mechanism translates into organ-level benefit.
69. A liver trial randomised 61 people with HIV and a hepatic fat fraction above 5% to 2 mg daily or placebo for 12 months, followed by a six-month open-label phase [2] (verified). Liver fat fell by 4.1 percentage points more than placebo, a 37% relative reduction. Steatosis resolved, meaning fat fraction fell below 5%, in 35% of treated participants against 4% on placebo. Fibrosis progressed in 2 treated participants against 9 on placebo [2] (verified).
70. That fibrosis result is the most clinically meaningful number associated with this compound. Fibrosis progression is what turns fatty liver into liver disease, and a reduction in it is a harder outcome than a fat percentage. The trial was small and the comparison was a secondary one, so it is a strong signal rather than a settled finding (inferred).
71. The liver trial also found no effect on fasting glucose, no overall effect on ALT or lipids, with ALT falling only in those whose levels were elevated at baseline, and a significant reduction in C-reactive protein [2] (verified).
72. A separate randomised trial in older adults reported better memory performance alongside a rise in brain GABA levels (reported, as the card records). That result is small, single and has not been replicated, and cognition trials in ageing have a poor record of replication generally (inferred).

### Why the mechanism predicts the shape of the benefit, including its limits [mixed]
73. The compound does not supply growth hormone. It stimulates the pituitary to release it in pulses, which leaves the body's feedback control intact. That design decision explains most of what follows.
74. Pulsatile release under intact feedback is why this compound does not produce the acromegalic effects of supraphysiological growth hormone, and why its effects are modest rather than dramatic. The ceiling is set by how much the pituitary will release, not by how much is injected (inferred).
75. It also explains the tissue selectivity. Visceral fat is unusually growth-hormone-sensitive and metabolically active, which is why it responds while other fat depots respond less, and why liver fat falls by the same route [1,2] (inferred from the mechanism and consistent with both trials).
76. The same logic sets the limits. An intact pituitary is required, which is why the label contraindicates pituitary tumour, pituitary surgery and brain radiation. Raised growth hormone signalling means raised insulin-like growth factor 1, which is why active malignancy is contraindicated. And growth hormone opposes insulin, which is why glucose monitoring is required (verified via the label positions the card records).
77. Visceral fat returns after stopping, which the mechanism also predicts: nothing about pulsed stimulation changes the set point that produced the fat in the first place (inferred).

### Open questions [mixed]
78. Does the fibrosis result replicate? Two progressions against nine in a 61-person trial is the most clinically important number here and the one most in need of a larger confirmation.
79. Does any of this transfer outside HIV-associated fat accumulation? Both randomised trials were run in that population, which has a specific pattern of fat distribution and metabolic disturbance.
80. What happens to glucose over years rather than months? Two trials found no group difference while the label requires monitoring, which means the question is unresolved rather than answered.
81. What do the antibodies do over long-term use? Nearly half of treated participants developed them in 26 weeks, with no detected loss of effect in that window.
82. Is the cognition signal real? One small randomised trial, unreplicated, in a field where unreplicated cognition results are the norm.
83. What is the right comparison for off-label use? The approved evidence is for a daily injection in a specific disease, and nothing in the record addresses intermittent use in healthy people for body composition.
84. Does the visceral-fat benefit matter if it reverses on stopping? That is a question about indefinite treatment, and no trial has run long enough to answer it.
