# CJC-1295 no DAC + Ipamorelin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/cjc-ipamorelin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: CJC/Ipa, Mod GRF 1-29 + Ipamorelin, CJC-1295 no DAC/Ipamorelin 5/5, CJC + Ipa blend
2. Origin: Blend of 2 peptides
3. Legal and approval status: US: neither half approved. Both sit on FDA's Category 2 safety-risk list (ipamorelin added Sep 2023); the PCAC voted against both in Oct and Dec 2024, and neither was among the peptides removed in April 2026. Sold as a research chemical. WADA: prohibited (S2).

## Summary
4. This blend pairs CJC-1295 without DAC, a GHRH analogue, with ipamorelin, a selective ghrelin-receptor agonist. People combine them because pressing both pituitary buttons releases far more growth hormone than either alone, and they use it for sleep, recovery and body composition. The synergy is shown in humans, but no trial tested this pair for those outcomes.
5. Punch line: The gold-standard GH stack. Presses both pituitary buttons for one bigger pulse; often a single shot before bed.
6. Used for: GH release: sleep, recovery, body composition

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Endocrine & growth: Two inputs, one bigger GH pulse
8. Sleep & rhythms: Deeper sleep, vivid dreams
9. Muscle & performance: Recovery and lean mass, reported
10. Fat metabolism: Slow fat loss over months
11. Skin & aesthetics (backed only by animal or user reports): Skin quality, reported
12. Tissue repair (backed only by animal or user reports): Soreness and recovery, reported

## How it works
13. Presses the GHRH button on the pituitary · GHRH-R, cAMP · role Endocrine & growth
   Mod GRF 1-29 binds the GHRH receptor on pituitary somatotroph cells and raises cAMP inside them. That triggers release of the GH those cells have stored. Each half raising GH is shown in humans, and this is the GHRH route.
14. Lasts about 30 minutes, keeps the natural pulse · Mod GRF 1-29, 4 substitutions · role Endocrine & growth
   Four substitutions, including Asn8 to Gln and Met27 to Leu, slow enzyme breakdown, but without DAC it still clears in about 30 minutes. That gives a short spike that mimics the body's own GH pulse rather than a constant rise. Keeping the pulse pattern is the reason for choosing the no DAC form.
15. Presses the ghrelin button, a second route · GHS-R1a, PLC and calcium · role Endocrine & growth
   Ipamorelin binds GHS-R1a, the ghrelin receptor, which signals through phospholipase C and calcium. This is a second, independent way to make the pituitary release GH. Its GH release is shown in rats and pigs, and it was tried in people after bowel surgery.
16. Releases GH without cortisol or prolactin spikes · Selective GHS, animal data · role Sleep & rhythms
   In animals ipamorelin released GH without raising ACTH, cortisol or prolactin, unlike GHRP-2 and GHRP-6. That selectivity is why it is chosen for this pair, aiming at sleep and recovery without stress hormone or hunger spikes. Human selectivity data are limited.
17. Together, a bigger pulse than either alone · GHRH + GHRP synergy · role Muscle & performance
   Because the GHRH and ghrelin routes act through separate receptors, together they release more GH than either alone. This synergy was shown in normal men in 1990 using GHRP-6. No trial has measured this exact pair or its effect on body composition, sleep or recovery.
18. Mechanism overview: Mod GRF 1-29 is the first 29 residues of GHRH with four substitutions (including Asn8 to Gln and Met27 to Leu) that slow enzyme breakdown; it binds GHRH receptors on somatotrophs and raises cAMP for a short, pulse-like GH release. Ipamorelin (Aib-His-D-2Nal-D-Phe-Lys-NH2) binds GHS-R1a, signalling through phospholipase C and calcium, and in animals releases GH without raising ACTH, cortisol or prolactin. Because the two pathways are independent, GHRH plus GHRP produces a synergistic GH pulse, shown with GHRP-6 in normal men in 1990.

## What is inside the blend
19. CJC-1295 no DAC (Mod GRF 1-29): 5 mg · GHRH signal: sets pulse size
20. Ipamorelin: 5 mg · Ghrelin-receptor signal: triggers the pulse, selectively
21. Most common ratio: CJC-1295 no DAC 5 · Ipamorelin 5 = 10 mg (15 of 15 listings (7 state 5/5, 8 sell a 10 mg vial))
22. Other ratio seen: CJC-1295 no DAC 10 · Ipamorelin 10 = 20 mg (5 listings, always as a second size)
23. Version Common retail: CJC-1295 no DAC 5 · Ipamorelin 5 = 10 mg
24. Why CJC-1295 no DAC is in it: Amplifies the pulse through the GHRH route; ipamorelin alone gives a smaller pulse
25. Why Ipamorelin is in it: Adds the ghrelin route without the cortisol, prolactin and hunger of GHRP-2 or GHRP-6
26. Mixing chemistry: The most forgiving pair on this list: Mod GRF lost native Met27 and Asn8, the two sites most prone to oxidation and deamidation.
27. Mixing chemistry: Ipamorelin is a short pentapeptide with no Met or Cys; little to oxidise.
28. Mixing chemistry: No published stability study of the reconstituted blend; community claims of 90 days are unsourced. Most guides say 2 to 3 weeks refrigerated.
29. Mixing chemistry: FDA flagged ipamorelin as sensitive to formulation and prone to aggregation, an immunogenicity concern; aggregates can form without cloudiness.
30. Mixing chemistry: Discard if cloudy, gelled or particulate.
31. Self-mixing: Drawing both separate vials into one syringe right before injecting is long-standing practice and low risk; pre-mixing them into one vial for weeks has no stability data, and separate vials let you change the ratio.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
32. Typical: 100 + 100 mcg per shot (200 mcg of blend) · 1–3× daily, or once pre-bed · cycle 8–16 weeks, often 5 on / 2 off · route Sub-Q (reported)
33. Half-life: per component
34. Most people take: Sized by the CJC dose: 100 mcg of each per shot. A 10 mg (5/5) vial in 2 mL gives 5 mg/mL, so 4 units = 100 + 100 mcg and 8 units = the 200 + 200 mcg pre-bed dose. Fasted 1 to 2 hours before, no food for 30 to 60 minutes after.

## What people report
35. Classic use is 100 mcg of each, 1 to 3 times a day on an empty stomach, or 200 + 200 mcg once before bed, 5 days on and 2 off, 8 to 16 weeks. In a 5/5 vial that is 4 units per 100 + 100 mcg at 2 mL. Some seller protocol sheets suggest 500 + 500 mcg nightly, five times the classic dose.
36. Liked / worked: Synergy shown in humans, 1990
37. Liked / worked: Sleep within 1 to 2 weeks, reported
38. Liked / worked: Called the gold-standard GH stack
39. What worked: Community pages call it the gold-standard GH stack. Reported: deeper sleep and vivid dreams within 1 to 2 weeks, better recovery at 2 to 4 weeks, slow fat loss, fuller muscle and better skin over 2 to 4 months.
40. Went wrong / did not work: No trial of the pair
41. Went wrong / did not work: FDA panel voted against both, 2024
42. Went wrong / did not work: Tingling, water retention, glucose drift
43. What went wrong: No outcome trial for the pair, and no published success rate. FDA's compounding panel voted against both halves in 2024 (ipamorelin 0 to 12, CJC-1295 0 to 13). Side effects reported: hand and foot tingling, water retention, flushing, hunger spikes, headache, rising fasting glucose.
44. Most reported: 100 + 100 mcg, 1 to 3 times daily
45. Most reported: Or 200 + 200 mcg before bed

## What has been tested
48. Endocrine & growth: GHRH + GHRP synergy, normal men (human)
49. Endocrine & growth: CJC-1295 DAC, GH and IGF-1 rise (human)
50. Endocrine & growth: Ipamorelin GH release, rats and pigs (animal)
51. Digestive & gut: Ipamorelin IV after bowel surgery (human)
52. Sleep & rhythms: Deeper sleep, vivid dreams (users)
53. Never tested as a pair in a trial. Each half has human data: CJC-1295 (the DAC version) raised GH 2 to 10 fold and IGF-1 1.5 to 3 fold in healthy adults; ipamorelin released GH without cortisol or prolactin in animals and was tried IV after bowel surgery. GHRH plus GHRP synergy was shown in normal men in 1990.
54. What it helps: Evidence is mechanistic plus user reports. Synergy of the two signal types is shown in humans; each component raises GH, and the DAC form of CJC-1295 raised IGF-1 1.5 to 3 fold. No trial has measured body composition, sleep or recovery with this pair. Users report better sleep first, then recovery, then slow body composition change over months.

## Who shouldn't take it
55. Pituitary tumour, pituitary surgery or brain radiation: Works by pushing the pituitary; disease there makes effects unpredictable. (inferred)
56. People with active or recent cancer: Raises GH and IGF-1, which promote cell growth. (inferred)
57. People with prediabetes or poorly controlled diabetes: GH raises blood glucose and insulin resistance. (inferred)
58. Drug-tested athletes: GHRH analogues are banned under WADA S2. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
59. Sermorelin: Sermorelin is another GHRH analogue on the same receptor as the CJC-1295 half. Adding it duplicates that route rather than adding a new one, so people usually swap it in. The combination has not been tested.
60. Tesamorelin: Tesamorelin is a stabilised GHRH with human trial data for visceral and liver fat. It overlaps the CJC-1295 half, so it is used instead of, or rotated with, this blend for fat loss. The pair has not been tested together.
61. BPC-157: BPC-157 works on vessel growth and tendon repair and raises growth hormone receptor on tendon cells, while the blend raises GH pulses. People pair them for injury recovery. This is user logic, not trial data.
62. GHRP-2: GHRP-2 hits the same ghrelin receptor as ipamorelin but with more hunger, prolactin and cortisol. Adding it duplicates the ghrelin route and loses the selectivity ipamorelin was chosen for. The pairing has not been tested.
63. MK-677: MK-677 is an oral ghrelin mimic that raises GH all day, while this blend gives short pulses. People combine them for higher IGF-1, at the cost of hunger and blunting the pulse pattern. The combination has not been tested.

## Where it comes from
64. A one-vial pairing of the two most used growth hormone releasers: CJC-1295 without DAC (Mod GRF 1-29, a GHRH analogue) and ipamorelin (a selective ghrelin-receptor agonist). Sold as 5 mg of each in one vial.
65. First studied for: The pairing comes from 1990 work showing a GHRH signal and a GHRP signal together release far more growth hormone than either alone. The community turned that into a daily stack, then sellers pre-mixed it.
66. Name story: Sold as "CJC-1295 no DAC", but the molecule is Mod GRF 1-29 (tetrasubstituted GRF 1-29). The name CJC-1295 belongs to the DAC version, which carries a drug affinity complex that binds albumin and lasts about a week. Check the label: the dosing is completely different. [S1] (verified)
67. 1990: GHRP plus GHRH shown to release GH synergistically in normal men
68. 1998: Ipamorelin described as the first selective GH secretagogue
69. 2006: CJC-1295 (DAC) raises GH and IGF-1 for days in healthy adults
70. 2023: Ipamorelin added to FDA Category 2
71. 2024: PCAC votes against ipamorelin (Oct) and CJC-1295 (Dec)
72. 2026: Blend testing offered by Finnrick; both still Category 2
73. Today: Most sold GH secretagogue blend, 5 + 5 mg

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### A solubility problem that undercuts the product itself [lab]
74. This is the most concrete finding in the regulatory record for this blend, and it is a chemistry problem rather than an evidence problem.
75. Reviewing the ghrelin-receptor half for the US compounding list, regulators recorded the free base's water solubility as 0.0032 milligrams per millilitre, against a nominated product strength of 2 milligrams per millilitre, and questioned whether that strength is achievable at all [1] (verified). The acetate salt's solubility is 5 milligrams per millilitre [1].
76. That is a gap of roughly six hundred-fold between what the free base dissolves to in water and what the proposed product claims to contain. The implication is direct: a product at that strength is either made from the acetate salt, or formulated with something other than water, or not fully in solution (inferred from the cited figures).
77. It also means the two salt forms are not interchangeable here in any practical sense, and regulators found the nominators inconsistent about which one they meant, with certificates and stated identifiers not matching the named substance [1] (verified). Neither form has an approved generic name, which regulators treat as a safety issue because there is no reference standard to check a batch against.
78. Storage differs between the forms too: the free base is described as stable at room temperature for about three weeks and recommended below minus 18 degrees Celsius, while the acetate is listed at 2 to 8 degrees with stability up to four years at minus 20 [1].

### The one controlled trial of the ghrelin-receptor half, which failed [people]
79. There is a controlled human efficacy trial here, which is more than most peptides in this catalog have, and it did not succeed.
80. A Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in postoperative ileus, the slowed gut that follows abdominal surgery, enrolled 117 and randomised 114: 56 to the peptide at 0.03 mg per kilogram intravenously twice daily, 58 to placebo [1] (verified). Median time to first tolerated meal was 25.3 hours against 32.6 hours.
81. That difference was not statistically significant, and the secondary endpoints showed no difference [1] (verified). Development was subsequently discontinued [1].
82. A seven-hour numerical advantage that fails significance in a 114-person trial is the classic shape of either a small real effect or noise, and the sponsor's decision to stop tells you how they read it. Either way, the only controlled test of this molecule for any indication did not meet its endpoint.
83. Regulators also found no clinical trials at all for growth hormone deficiency, the other indication they evaluated [1] (verified). So the compound most associated with raising growth hormone has never been tested in a trial for a growth hormone condition.

### What is known about exposure, and what that implies about route [mixed]
84. Human pharmacokinetics exist for the ghrelin-receptor half, from a 1999 study in 48 healthy males across five intravenous dose groups of six, with two placebo subjects per group, spanning roughly a thirty-fold dose range. Half-life was about two hours, clearance 0.078 litres per hour per kilogram, volume of distribution 0.22 litres per kilogram. No effectiveness data and no adverse events were reported [1] (verified).
85. The important absence: there is no subcutaneous pharmacokinetic data, in any species [1] (verified). Rat intravenous data gives a half-life of about 27 minutes with 60 to 80% excreted unchanged [1]. So the only route with human exposure data is intravenous, and the only route in use is subcutaneous.
86. For the growth-hormone-releasing half, the identity question shapes what evidence applies. The human data people cite, a several-fold rise in growth hormone and a 1.5 to 3-fold rise in insulin-like growth factor 1 lasting days, belongs to the version carrying an albumin-binding complex. The material sold under that name without the complex is a different molecule with a short duration of action and a different dosing logic entirely (verified, as the card's naming note records). Regulators evaluated five separate substances under this name family, covering both the complexed and uncomplexed forms as free bases and salts [2] (verified).
87. The synergy premise, that a releasing-hormone signal and a ghrelin-receptor signal together produce a larger growth hormone pulse than either alone, was demonstrated in humans in 1990 using a different ghrelin-receptor peptide from the one in this blend (verified, as the card records). Whether it holds for this specific pair at the amounts used has not been tested (verified as absent).

### Two concerns regulators raised that are specific to this mechanism [mixed]
88. First, abuse potential. Ghrelin receptors are present in reward-related brain regions, and regulators explicitly raised the possibility that the ghrelin-receptor half may have reinforcing properties [1] (verified). This is not a concern that applies to the repair peptides, and it is rarely mentioned in discussion of this blend. It has not been studied in humans.
89. Second, reproductive effects. No reproductive or developmental studies of the compound itself exist. Regulators cited a mouse study of ghrelin and a ghrelin antagonist showing effects on fertilisation and embryofetal development, and stated this may apply here [1] (verified, as a read-across rather than a direct finding).
90. Beyond those, the toxicology is empty: no acute toxicity, no repeat-dose toxicity, no genotoxicity and no carcinogenicity studies were found for the ghrelin-receptor half [1] (verified). Regulators concluded the nonclinical data were too limited to assess safety for clinical use.
91. Adverse event reporting amounts to two non-serious cases involving compounded products, one a nasal spray with headache and increased tearing, the other a subcutaneous combination with joint pain [1] (verified). As with every blend in this catalog, the combination case cannot be attributed to either ingredient.
92. Immunogenicity could not be ruled out from unidentified impurities or aggregates, and regulators noted injectable routes present a particular risk for both forms [1].

### Where the law stands, October 2026, and why this blend sits differently from the others [people]
93. This is the one blend in the catalog whose components have been through the advisory process and lost.
94. Regulators proposed that neither form of the ghrelin-receptor half be added to the 503A bulks list, on all four criteria: neither is well characterised, with critical data on impurities, aggregates and endotoxins missing; effectiveness evidence is limited for any route with nothing supporting the subcutaneous route for either indication reviewed; professional guidelines do not mention it for either condition; approved alternatives exist for both; and the nonclinical data cannot support a safety assessment [1] (verified).
95. The committee agreed. It voted against the ghrelin-receptor half in October 2024 and against the releasing-hormone half in December 2024, in both cases unanimously or near-unanimously (verified, as the card records the tallies). The December 2024 session covered five substances in the releasing-hormone name family, with the agency proposing that none be included [2] (verified).
96. Neither component was among the twelve peptides removed from the do-not-compound category in April 2026, and both remain on it (verified, as the card records). That is a materially different position from the repair peptides, which left that category and then received favourable advisory recommendations in July 2026.
97. So while the broader regulatory direction in 2026 has been toward opening access, these two moved the other way and stayed there. Any interim access policy would have to cover substances the agency and its committee have both already declined (inferred).
98. In sport, releasing-hormone analogues and growth hormone secretagogues are prohibited.

### Open questions [mixed]
99. Can the nominated strength even be made from the free base? The cited solubility figure and the claimed concentration differ by roughly six hundred-fold, which makes this a question about what is physically in the vial.
100. Which molecule is the releasing-hormone half, complexed or not? The dosing logic and duration differ completely, and the human growth hormone data belongs to the complexed version.
101. Does the 1990 synergy finding hold for this specific pair? It was shown with a different ghrelin-receptor peptide, and the premise of the whole product rests on it transferring.
102. What does subcutaneous dosing actually produce? There is no subcutaneous pharmacokinetic data in any species for the ghrelin-receptor half, and that is the only route in use.
103. Is there reinforcing potential? Regulators raised it from receptor distribution, and nobody has looked.
104. What are the reproductive effects? None have been studied; the concern is a read-across from ghrelin biology.
105. Does raising growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 over months do anything measurable to body composition in healthy adults? No trial has measured it with this pair, and the reported effects are sequenced exactly as expectation would predict.

# Kisspeptin-10
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/kisspeptin-10
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: KP-10, metastin (45-54), kisspeptin-54 (45-54)
2. Origin: Fragment of a natural protein
3. Sequence: YNWNSFGLRF (10 amino acids). Amide end
4. Legal and approval status: Investigational; no approval. Research chemical on the grey market.

## Summary
5. Kisspeptin-10 is a 10-amino-acid fragment of kisspeptin, the upstream switch of the reproductive hormone axis that acts on the brain to trigger GnRH release. It is a research tool and potential treatment for infertility, and users take it for libido and a hormonal reset. Human studies show reliable LH and testosterone rises, but the libido data are early, the half-life is very short, and the user base is small.
6. Punch line: Fragment of the reproductive axis's master switch. Starts the chain at the brain, so LH and testosterone follow.
7. Used for: Testosterone, LH, libido

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Endocrine & growth: Master switch for reproductive hormones
9. Reproductive: Raises LH and testosterone
10. Connection & desire: More desire in brain studies

## How it works
11. Tells the brain to release GnRH · KISS1R, formerly GPR54 · role Endocrine & growth
   Kisspeptin-10 binds KISS1R, formerly called GPR54, on GnRH neurons in the hypothalamus. This releases GnRH, the master signal at the top of the reproductive axis. Human studies of this exact fragment show the downstream hormone response.
12. Raises LH and testosterone downstream · HPG axis · role Reproductive
   GnRH tells the pituitary to release LH and FSH, and LH drives testosterone in men and ovulation in women. In healthy men a single dose raised LH, but only sustained infusion raised testosterone. Larger doses gave a smaller LH response, not a bigger one.
13. Kisspeptin can trigger egg maturation in IVF · LH surge, oocyte maturation · role Reproductive
   Kisspeptin can set off the LH surge that matures eggs, so it has been used as an egg-maturation trigger in IVF trials. Those trials mostly used the longer kisspeptin-54, which reaches the target neurons more readily, so the result does not transfer directly to this fragment.
14. Kisspeptin boosts brain sexual arousal responses · Limbic activity, fMRI · role Connection & desire
   On brain imaging, kisspeptin increased activity in limbic regions that handle sexual and emotional processing when people viewed arousing images. These studies mostly used kisspeptin-54. For kisspeptin-10, the libido effect is untested in people.
15. Constant exposure shuts the axis down · KISS1R desensitisation · role Endocrine & growth
   Constant strong stimulation makes KISS1R internalise and stop responding, which can shut the reproductive axis down. In healthy men about a day of infusion did not cause this, while primates desensitised at higher exposure. Weeks of use have never been tested.
16. Mechanism overview: Kisspeptin-10 is the shortest active fragment of kisspeptin. It binds KISS1R, formerly GPR54, on hypothalamic GnRH neurons. This drives GnRH release, which triggers pituitary LH and FSH; LH raises testosterone in men and supports ovulation in women. Because it acts at the top of the reproductive axis, the response stays physiological. Constant exposure desensitises KISS1R and can shut the axis down. On brain imaging, kisspeptin also activates limbic regions involved in sexual and emotional processing.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
17. Typical: 100–200 mcg · daily or PRN · cycle variable · route Sub-Q (reported)
18. Half-life: ~minutes
19. Most people take: Community ~100–200 mcg/injection (unvalidated). Clinical IV weight-based ~1 mcg/kg.
20. Common: 100–200 mcg · 1–3×/wk · 4–8 wk · Sub-Q · for LH/testosterone support [S1] (reported)
21. Daily: 100 mcg · 1× daily · 4–8 wk · Sub-Q · for steady use [S1] (reported)
22. Pulsatile: 50–100 mcg · several × daily · 2–4 wk · Sub-Q · for mimic natural pulses [S1] (reported)

## What people report
23. Reported for libido and hormonal 'reset'; small user base.
24. Liked / worked: Reliable, physiological axis stimulation
25. Liked / worked: Promising for fertility
26. Liked / worked: Sexual desire signals in studies
27. What worked: Reliable, physiological stimulation of the reproductive axis; promising for fertility and, in studies, sexual desire.
28. Went wrong / did not work: Very short half-life
29. Went wrong / did not work: IVF and libido data mostly from kisspeptin-54
30. Went wrong / did not work: Libido data early
31. What went wrong: Very short half-life; still investigational; libido data are early.
32. Most reported: Libido and hormonal 'reset'
33. Most reported: Small user base

## What has been tested
34. Reproductive: LH and testosterone rise (human)
35. Reproductive: IVF trigger, mostly kisspeptin-54 (trial)
36. Connection & desire: Libido brain imaging, mostly -54 (human)
37. Human studies show kisspeptin reliably raises LH and testosterone. The IVF-trigger and libido brain-imaging studies mostly used the longer kisspeptin-54, not -10.
38. What it helps: Human studies show reliable LH and testosterone rises. Kisspeptin, mostly the longer kisspeptin-54, has triggered egg maturation in IVF and increased sexual arousal responses on brain imaging. The libido data are early, and the half-life is very short. Users take it for libido and a hormonal reset, and the user base is small.
39. Trial: active · Phase 1 · reproductive hormone function after COVID · NCT07224490 · Massachusetts General Hospital. IV kisspeptin is used to probe GnRH neurons in long COVID; isoform listed as 112 to 121, which corresponds to KP-10. (checked 2026-10-23) [S2] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
40. Hormone-sensitive cancer (breast, prostate): Triggers an LH and sex hormone surge. (inferred)
41. People tracking ovulation with LH test strips: It releases LH, which can produce false positive ovulation tests. (inferred)
42. Drug-tested athletes (men): Kisspeptin is named on the WADA list as an LH-releasing factor. (verified)

## Where it comes from
43. A 10-amino-acid fragment of kisspeptin, the master upstream switch of the reproductive hormone axis, acting on the brain to trigger GnRH release.
44. First studied for: A research tool and potential treatment for infertility and hypothalamic reproductive disorders.
45. Name story: Named after Hershey's Kisses: the KISS1 gene was found in 1996 in Hershey, Pennsylvania, as a cancer metastasis suppressor. The "-10" means the final ten amino acids of the 54-residue parent, once called metastin. [S3] (verified)
46. 1996: Kisspeptin gene found as a cancer-spread suppressor
47. 2003: Shown to be the master switch for puberty and GnRH
48. Today: Investigational fertility and desire tool; grey-market research chemical

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### The human study of this exact fragment, which is better than the field usually gets [people]
49. Unlike most compounds in this catalog, the ten-residue fragment itself has been given to humans in a properly conducted study, with hormone measurements rather than self-report. A 2011 study in a major endocrine journal tested three protocols in healthy men: an intravenous bolus dose-response in 6 participants, a high-dose infusion in 4, and a low-dose infusion in 4 [1] (verified).
50. Bolus doses spanned 0.01 to 3.0 micrograms per kilogram. Luteinising hormone rose dose-dependently and peaked at 1 microgram per kilogram, from 4.1 to 12.4 international units per litre at 30 minutes [1]. Testosterone did not change significantly after any bolus dose [1] (verified).
51. The infusions did raise testosterone. The high-dose infusion, 4 micrograms per kilogram per hour for 22.5 hours, raised luteinising hormone from about 5.5 to about 21 units per litre and testosterone from 16.6 to 24.0 nanomoles per litre [1]. The lower infusion, 1.5 micrograms per kilogram per hour for 9 hours, raised luteinising hormone from 5.2 to 14.1 units per litre and increased pulse frequency from 0.7 to 1.0 pulses per hour, with pulse mass rising from 3.9 to 12.8 [1] (verified).
52. The pattern is informative. A single injection moves the pituitary hormone and does not move testosterone; sustained exposure moves both. Testosterone is downstream of accumulated pulses, so a brief spike in the signal above it does not translate (inferred, consistent with the measured data).
53. No adverse effects were reported, and blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation and blood, kidney and liver tests remained stable [1] (verified).

### The dose-response is not monotonic, and that is the most useful finding [people]
54. At 3 micrograms per kilogram, the highest bolus tested, the luteinising hormone response was not significantly different from vehicle, and was lower than the responses at 0.3 and 1 micrograms per kilogram [1] (verified).
55. So more produced less. The peak response sat in the middle of the tested range and fell away above it. For a compound bought and used on the assumption that a larger amount gives a larger hormonal push, this is the single most practically relevant result in the human literature, and it points the opposite way.
56. Receptor-level explanations are available, chiefly that this receptor family internalises and desensitises on strong stimulation, but the study did not establish the cause (inferred).
57. It also complicates the common framing that this compound works upstream so the response stays physiological and self-limiting. The response is indeed self-limiting. One consequence of that is that overshooting the dose does not produce a bigger effect, it produces a smaller one, which is a different and less comfortable kind of self-limitation (inferred).

### Desensitisation: what the human data showed, and where the worry comes from [mixed]
58. The concern that continuous exposure shuts the axis down is reasonable from receptor biology and is widely repeated. The human data on it is more specific and more reassuring than the general claim.
59. Across the 22.5-hour high-dose infusion, no tachyphylaxis was observed. Luteinising hormone in the final 90 minutes, 23.9 units per litre, was not lower than in the first 90 minutes, 16.3 units per litre [1] (verified). The authors noted that primate studies had shown tachyphylaxis and suggested the difference was dose: the primate work used higher amounts [1].
60. So the accurate statement is that sustained exposure for roughly a day at these amounts did not desensitise the axis in healthy men, while higher exposures in primates did. Both the worry and the reassurance are dose-dependent, and nobody has tested exposures running weeks (verified as absent).
61. That bounds the question usefully. The risk is not that any continuous exposure collapses the axis; it is that enough exposure does, and the threshold in humans is unmapped.

### Why the longer form is used in research and the shorter one is sold [animals]
62. Most of the headline human work on this hormone family, the ovulation trigger in fertility treatment and the brain-imaging studies of sexual and emotional processing, used the longer 54-residue form rather than this fragment. There is a specific pharmacological reason, and a 2017 mouse study examined it directly [2].
63. Circulating half-life is about 32 minutes for the longer form against about 4 minutes for this fragment [2] (verified). But clearance was not the whole explanation: repeating fragment injections every 10 minutes for an hour did not reproduce the sustained hormone rise the longer form produced [2].
64. The proposed difference is access. After systemic injection in mice, only the longer form activated the immediate-early gene marker in the hormone-releasing neurons sitting behind the blood-brain barrier, and the authors suggest the longer form crosses while the fragment is less able to [2] (verified, in mice).
65. If that holds in humans, it has a sharp consequence. The target neurons sit behind a barrier, and the fragment may be reaching them poorly or reaching only the subset in regions where the barrier is incomplete. That would explain why the fragment needs sustained infusion to move testosterone while the longer form works more readily, and it means the fertility and desire findings from the longer form should not be transferred to this one (inferred).
66. It also means the very short half-life is not merely an inconvenience to be solved with more frequent dosing. The mouse data specifically tested that workaround and it did not work [2].

### Open questions [mixed]
67. Does this fragment reach the target neurons in humans? The mouse comparison suggests the longer form crosses into the relevant region and this one may not, which would undercut the whole rationale for using the shorter peptide.
68. What dose is optimal, given that the response peaked mid-range and fell away above it? Nobody has mapped the top of the curve in humans, and the one study that looked found more giving less.
69. Does intermittent subcutaneous use do anything to testosterone? The human study that moved testosterone used continuous intravenous infusion for hours. A single injection moved the pituitary hormone and not testosterone.
70. Where is the desensitisation threshold in humans? None appeared over 22.5 hours at the amounts tested; primates desensitised at higher amounts; nothing has been tested over weeks.
71. Do the desire and fertility findings transfer from the longer form? They were obtained with a different molecule that appears to have different access to the brain.
72. What happens with repeated courses? There is no human data beyond about a day of continuous exposure, for any endpoint.
73. Is a short-lived peptide requiring sustained exposure a sensible format at all? The pharmacology suggests the longer form or a stabilised analogue is the better tool, which is what research programmes have mostly used.

[2] de Tassigny et al., PLOS One, mechanistic insights into the more potent effect of KP-54 compared to KP-10 in vivo, 2017 · https://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/entities/publication/30f84436-d438-4959-8dd2-7d67ba0d10cc

# HCG
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/hcg
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: human chorionic gonadotropin, hCG, chorionic gonadotropin, Pregnyl, Novarel, Ovidrel (recombinant), choriogonadotropin alfa, Ovitrelle, Profasi, beta-hCG
2. Origin: Made by the body: placental glycoprotein hormone
3. Shown with an FDA approved badge
4. Legal and approval status: FDA-approved (Novarel, Pregnyl, generic; recombinant Ovidrel); regulated as a biologic since 23 Mar 2020, which cut off most compounding. Reported on the ASHP shortage list into 2026. WADA 2026 S2.2.1: prohibited in males.

## Summary
5. HCG is the pregnancy hormone made by the placenta, which acts on the same receptor as LH. In men it tells the testes to make testosterone and sperm, and it is approved for fertility, undescended testes and low-gonadotropin hypogonadism. Men on testosterone use it to keep testes and fertility intact. The HCG diet has no support, since weight loss came from the calorie cut.
6. Punch line: The pregnancy hormone that mimics LH. Keeps testes making testosterone and sperm while TRT shuts LH off.
7. Used for: TRT fertility and testicle support, male hypogonadism, ovulation trigger

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Reproductive: Keeps sperm production going
9. Endocrine & growth: Drives testosterone via LH receptor
10. Connection & desire: Libido kept up on TRT
11. Muscle & performance: Bridges recovery after a cycle
12. Fat metabolism (backed only by animal or user reports): HCG diet: no proven effect
13. Mood (backed only by animal or user reports): Estrogen-linked mood swings reported
14. Skin & aesthetics (backed only by animal or user reports): Acne reported

## How it works
15. Mimics LH on the testes · LH/choriogonadotropin receptor (LHCGR) · role Endocrine & growth
   hCG binds the LH/choriogonadotropin receptor, LHCGR, the same receptor LH uses on cells of the testes. It acts like LH but lasts much longer because of its beta subunit. This is established clinical pharmacology with decades of use.
16. Makes Leydig cells produce testosterone · Leydig cell steroidogenesis · role Endocrine & growth
   In Leydig cells, LHCGR activation switches on steroidogenesis, the chain of enzymes that turns cholesterol into testosterone. This keeps the testes producing even when the brain's own LH signal is low. It is the basis of its use in male hypogonadism.
17. Keeps testosterone high inside the testes for sperm · Intratesticular testosterone · role Reproductive
   Sperm production needs testosterone levels inside the testes far above blood levels. On testosterone therapy alone that local level fell by 94% in a dose-finding study, and adding hCG kept it near baseline. A small retrospective series kept sperm production at a year, though hCG does not supply FSH.
18. Triggers ovulation in women · LH surge mimic · role Reproductive
   In women hCG mimics the mid-cycle LH surge that releases a mature egg from the ovary. It also supports the corpus luteum, which makes progesterone afterward. This is a long-established fertility use.
19. Some testosterone converts to estrogen · Aromatase, estradiol rise · role Mood
   Aromatase, an enzyme in fat and other tissues, converts part of the extra testosterone into estradiol. At higher doses serum testosterone rose above normal in the dose-finding study, which gives more to convert. This fits the acne, water retention and estrogen symptoms users report.
20. Mechanism overview: hCG is a heterodimeric glycoprotein: an alpha subunit shared with LH, FSH and TSH and a beta subunit that gives it its identity and a long half-life. It binds the LH/choriogonadotropin receptor (LHCGR), a G-protein-coupled receptor on testicular Leydig cells and ovarian theca and luteal cells. In men this switches on steroidogenesis, so the testes make testosterone and keep intratesticular testosterone high, which spermatogenesis needs; it does not supply FSH. In women it mimics the mid-cycle LH surge and supports the corpus luteum. Part of the extra testosterone is aromatised to estradiol.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
21. Typical: 500 IU (TRT); 500–4,000 IU (label) · every other day to 3×/week · cycle Ongoing with TRT; label courses weeks to months · route Sub-Q or IM (verified)
22. Half-life: ~36 h
23. Most people take: TRT add-on 500 IU SC/IM every other day (or ~1,500 IU/week for size only). Label for male hypogonadism 500–1,000 IU 3×/wk, or 4,000 IU 3×/wk for 6–9 months. Ovulation trigger 5,000–10,000 IU once. Pre-PCT blasts of higher doses are community practice.

## What people report
24. Used with TRT to keep testicles full and fertility intact, and as a pre-PCT 'blast'. Users report fuller testes and libido, plus acne, headaches, water retention and estrogen-driven nipple sensitivity.
25. Liked / worked: Keeps intratesticular testosterone up on TRT
26. Liked / worked: No azoospermia at 1 year in a 26-man TRT series
27. Liked / worked: Restores fertility in low-LH/FSH men
28. Liked / worked: Reliable ovulation trigger
29. What worked: 500 IU every other day kept intratesticular testosterone up and, in one retrospective series of 26 men on TRT, none became azoospermic at a year. Restores sperm production in men with low LH/FSH, sometimes with FSH added.
30. Went wrong / did not work: No weight loss beyond the 500 kcal diet
31. Went wrong / did not work: Raises estradiol; gynecomastia risk
32. Went wrong / did not work: Sperm fell in one high-dose study
33. Went wrong / did not work: OHSS and clots in women (label)
34. What went wrong: Label states it has not been shown to help obesity; the HCG diet's weight loss comes from the ~500 kcal/day diet. High doses can raise estradiol and one small study saw sperm counts fall despite hCG.
35. Most reported: Fuller testes and better libido on TRT
36. Most reported: Acne and headaches most reported
37. Most reported: Water retention, nipple sensitivity
38. Most reported: Hard to source since 2020

## What has been tested
39. Reproductive: Sperm preservation on TRT, retrospective (human)
40. Endocrine & growth: Dose-response of intratesticular testosterone (human)
41. Reproductive: Ovulation induction and male hypogonadism (human)
42. Fat metabolism: HCG diet trials: no effect beyond calorie cut (human)
43. Decades of clinical use in fertility; small and mostly retrospective studies of low-dose hCG alongside testosterone therapy.
44. What it helps: Clinically it treats male hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, prepubertal cryptorchidism and triggers ovulation. For men on testosterone, a dose-finding study showed 500 IU every other day raised intratesticular testosterone, and a 26-man retrospective series kept sperm production at a year. People use it to stop testicular shrinkage, protect fertility, and restart the axis after steroid cycles. The HCG diet has no support: the label and the FDA say the weight loss is from the calorie cut. Acne, headache, water retention and estrogen symptoms are the common complaints.
45. Trial: active · Not applicable · IVF egg maturation and stimulation · NCT07771283. Approved for decades; IVF trials of hCG triggers and low dose stimulation are still enrolling, e.g. in Ukraine and Uganda. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
46. People with testicular cancer history: hCG is a tumour marker; injecting it blinds follow-up bloodwork. (inferred)
47. People using home pregnancy tests: False positives for days after a dose. (verified)
48. Hormone-sensitive cancer (breast, prostate): It makes the testes or ovaries produce more testosterone and estrogen. (verified)
49. Drug-tested athletes (men): hCG is banned for male athletes because it restarts testosterone production. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
50. Gonadorelin: Gonadorelin pulses the pituitary to release its own LH and FSH, while hCG stands in for LH directly at the testes. Men on TRT use one or the other, or both, to keep testes working, but the pair has not been tested together.
51. Kisspeptin-10: Kisspeptin-10 works at the top of the axis, telling the brain to release GnRH, and hCG acts at the testes. People use them together when restarting after steroids, but the pairing is user logic, not trial data.
52. HMG: hCG supplies only LH-like signalling, and HMG adds FSH, which Sertoli cells need for sperm production. Clinicians add FSH or HMG to hCG when sperm does not return on hCG alone, supported by small studies in men.

## Where it comes from
53. The pregnancy hormone made by the placenta; it acts on the same receptor as LH, so in men it tells the testes to make testosterone and sperm. Medical hCG has long been purified from pregnant women's urine; a recombinant version also exists.
54. First studied for: Fertility (ovulation trigger), undescended testes in boys and low-gonadotropin hypogonadism in men.
55. Name story: "Chorionic" comes from Greek khorion, the membrane wrapping the fetus (the afterbirth), because placental tissue makes it. In 1928 it became the basis of the first reliable pregnancy test, run on mice; rabbits followed, hence "the rabbit died". [S2] (verified)
56. 1927: Aschheim and Zondek use it as the first pregnancy test
57. 1954: Simeons pitches hCG plus 500 kcal/day for weight loss
58. 2011: FDA and FTC warn sellers of OTC 'homeopathic' HCG diet drops
59. 2013: TRT plus 500 IU every other day preserves sperm in a 26-man series
60. Mar 2020: Reclassified as a biologic; compounding largely cut off, shortages follow
61. Today: Standard TRT add-on; supply still patchy (reported 2026)

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### The study behind the fertility-preservation use, in detail [people]
62. The practice of adding this hormone to testosterone therapy rests mainly on one small, well-designed study, and its design is unusually direct: it measured hormone concentrations inside the testis rather than in blood.
63. Twenty-nine healthy men aged 18 to 45 all received testosterone enanthate 200 mg weekly, plus one of saline placebo or one of three doses given subcutaneously every other day, for three weeks [1] (verified). Testicular fluid was obtained by fine-needle aspiration of both testes at baseline and on day 21.
64. The placebo arm shows why this matters. Testosterone therapy alone suppressed intratesticular testosterone to about 6% of baseline, a 94% fall [1] (verified). That is the mechanism of testosterone-induced infertility stated numerically, and it is far more dramatic than most discussion conveys.
65. Against that, the three doses preserved intratesticular testosterone at roughly 75%, 93% and 126% of baseline, with a linear relationship between dose and concentration, and none of the three differing significantly from baseline [1] (verified). Pituitary hormones were suppressed to about 5% and 3% of baseline across the study, as expected on exogenous testosterone.
66. The honest limitation is the authors' own: the intratesticular testosterone threshold needed to maintain sperm production is unknown [1] (verified). The study establishes that this hormone preserves the local concentration in a dose-dependent way. It does not establish how much is enough, because nobody knows what the target is.

### What the dose-response actually implies, including a caution [people]
67. The linear dose-response is the useful finding, and it cuts in two directions.
68. At the lowest dose, serum testosterone was similar to placebo, meaning the local effect was achieved without adding appreciably to circulating levels. At the two higher doses, serum testosterone rose above the normal reference range [1] (verified). The top dose also pushed intratesticular testosterone 26% above its own baseline.
69. So more is not simply better. Higher amounts overshoot the local target and add systemic testosterone on top of a replacement dose, which is the plausible route to the oestrogen-related complaints people report, since part of any extra testosterone is converted to oestradiol (inferred, consistent with the measured serum rise).
70. This is the reverse of the intuition that usually governs how this hormone is used alongside testosterone, where the aim is often framed as keeping the testes as stimulated as possible. The data suggest a target range rather than a maximum, and that the lowest effective amount is the one that leaves circulating levels unchanged (inferred).
71. A three-week study in 29 healthy men cannot settle long-term practice, and the supporting evidence beyond it is small and mostly retrospective (verified, as the card records).

### Why this one left the compounding world, and what that did to supply [people]
72. The regulatory history here is different from every other compound in this catalog, and it explains the supply problems better than any market story.
73. On 23 March 2020, a set of products approved as drugs transitioned to licensure as biologics under a statutory provision that deemed their existing approvals to be biologics licences. This hormone was one of four bulk substances that outsourcing facilities had been using and that were affected, alongside hyaluronidase, follicle stimulating hormone and menotropins [2] (verified).
74. The consequence is categorical rather than discretionary: once a product is licensed as a biologic, it is no longer eligible for the compounding exemptions that pharmacies rely on [2] (verified). This was not a safety finding about the hormone. It was a reclassification that removed an entire supply channel overnight.
75. What remains is narrower. A guidance on mixing, diluting or repackaging licensed biological products outside an approved label still applies, under conditions that guidance sets out [2]. That is a different and more limited activity than compounding from bulk substance.
76. The practical result, reported into 2026, is that approved products exist but supply has been patchy, with the hormone appearing on pharmacy shortage listings (reported, as the card records). The useful lesson for reading this catalog: a compound can become hard to obtain for reasons that have nothing to do with its evidence or its safety, and conversely, availability says nothing about either.
77. Two forms exist, one purified from urine and one made recombinantly, which is relevant because they have different manufacturing supply chains and are not affected identically by any single disruption (inferred).

### The weight-loss claim, and why it is the clearest refuted claim in this catalog [people]
78. Most compounds here suffer from absent evidence. This one has the rarer distinction of a claim that was actually tested and rejected, repeatedly, over decades.
79. The weight-loss protocol dates to a 1954 proposal pairing the hormone with a roughly 500 calorie daily diet (verified, as the card's timeline records). The approved labelling states that it has not been shown to be effective adjunctive therapy for obesity, and the explanation for any weight lost is the calorie restriction, not the injection (verified).
80. Regulators and consumer-protection authorities acted against sellers of over-the-counter homeopathic versions of these drops in 2011 (verified, as the card records).
81. The distinction worth preserving: a 500 calorie daily diet produces weight loss in anyone, which is exactly why the protocol appeared to work and why it persisted. Attributing that loss to the injection is the error, and it is an error that was identified, tested and formally rejected rather than merely doubted (verified).
82. This matters as a reference case. When people ask why a given peptide's enthusiastic reports should not settle the question, this is the cleanest available answer: a protocol with decades of satisfied users, a plausible hormonal story, and a controlled answer that the hormone contributed nothing.

### Open questions [mixed]
83. What intratesticular testosterone concentration is actually needed to maintain sperm production? The dose-finding study's authors named this as the central unknown, and it is still unresolved. Without it, dose selection for fertility preservation is empirical.
84. Does preserved local testosterone translate into preserved fertility over years, not months? The supporting evidence is a small retrospective series, and the mechanism is a surrogate for the outcome people care about.
85. Is the lowest dose the right one? It achieved the local effect without raising serum testosterone, which on the available data looks preferable to the higher amounts, but no trial has compared outcomes across doses.
86. What is the long-term oestradiol consequence of adding this to a full replacement dose? Mechanistically predictable, poorly quantified.
87. Does the urine-derived form differ from the recombinant one in practice? They have different manufacturing routes and the comparison is rarely addressed.
88. Will supply stabilise? The constraint is regulatory classification rather than demand or evidence, so it will resolve on a regulatory timeline or not at all.
89. For men using it to restart the axis after suppression: what is the actual recovery curve, and does early use change it? Widely practised, thinly studied.

[2] FDA, notice to compounders on changes affecting compounding as of March 23, 2020, 2020 · https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/notice-compounders-changes-affect-compounding-march-23-2020

# Selank
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/selank
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Selanc, Селанк, TKPRPGP
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: TKPRPGP (7 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: Approved and used in Russia; research chemical elsewhere. Not FDA-approved.

## Summary
5. Selank is a lab-made peptide built from tuftsin, a natural immune peptide, with a Pro-Gly-Pro tail added to resist breakdown. It was developed in Russia as a non-sedating anxiety treatment and is thought to work partly by slowing the breakdown of calming enkephalins and raising BDNF. Russian studies report calm and focus, but the evidence is almost entirely Russian and unconfirmed elsewhere.
6. Punch line: Russian anti-anxiety nasal spray built from an immune peptide. Calm without sedation; often stacked with Semax.
7. Used for: Anxiety, focus, calm

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Mood: Calm without sedation
9. Immunity: Built from an immune peptide
10. Cognition: Clearer focus reported
11. Sleep & rhythms: Better sleep reported
12. Inflammatory signaling (backed only by animal or user reports): Shifts inflammation signals

## How it works
13. Immune peptide tuftsin, made longer-lasting · Tuftsin analogue · role Immunity
   Selank is tuftsin, a four amino acid immune fragment of antibody protein, with a Pro-Gly-Pro tail added to slow breakdown. No receptor for it has been identified, so its effects are measured downstream changes rather than a known binding target.
14. Calms anxiety without sedation, mechanism debated · GABA system, claimed · role Mood
   Its calming effect is attributed to tuning the GABA system, the brain's main brake. That claim rests on gene-expression patterns in rats and human cell lines, not receptor binding, and the cell work only partly supports it. Small Russian trials report anxiety relief without sedation, with no placebo arm.
15. Raises a brain growth factor · BDNF, reported · role Cognition
   Selank is reported to raise BDNF, a growth factor that supports nerve connections and learning, in the rat hippocampus. This comes from Russian work that is hard to access in full. No human study has shown it raises brain BDNF.
16. Slows breakdown of calming enkephalins · Enkephalinase inhibition · role Mood
   In human serum in a test tube, Selank blocked enkephalinase, the enzymes that break down enkephalins, the body's own calming opioid peptides. One trial found blood enkephalin lasted longer on Selank. The lab concentration needed is high, and brain levels are unknown.
17. Shifts immune cytokine balance · IL-6, Th1/Th2 genes · role Immunity
   Through its tuftsin portion, Selank shifts immune gene activity, lowering IL-6, an inflammatory messenger, and changing the Th1/Th2 balance between immune arms. These findings come from Russian work in patients' blood cells and in rats, without independent replication.
18. Mechanism overview: Selank is a synthetic analogue of tuftsin, an immune tetrapeptide, extended with Pro-Gly-Pro to resist breakdown. Its anti-anxiety action is attributed to positive modulation of GABA-A signalling, a claim that is debated and comes mainly from Russian groups. It inhibits enkephalinase, slowing breakdown of calming enkephalins, and is reported to raise BDNF. Through the tuftsin portion it shifts IL-6 and Th1/Th2 gene expression. The combination is meant to calm anxiety without sedation or dependence.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
19. Typical: 200–400 mcg · daily · cycle 4-8 weeks on, 2-4 weeks off · route Intranasal (reported)
20. Half-life: ~2 minutes
21. Most people take: 200-400mcg/day intranasal · 4-8 weeks on, 2-4 weeks off. Run alongside Semax.
22. Common: 200–300 mcg · 1–3× daily · 2–6 wk · Intranasal · for general anxiety, focus [S1] [S2] (reported)
23. Higher: 600–900 mcg/day · split 2–3× · 2–4 wk · Intranasal · for stronger anxiolytic [S1] [S3] (reported)
24. Aggressive: ~2700 mcg/day · split 3× · 14–30 days · Intranasal · for GAD trial dose [S4] (reported)

## What people report
25. Nasal and injected; reported for calm, focus and sleep; generally well tolerated.
26. Liked / worked: Anxiety relief comparable to benzodiazepines
27. Liked / worked: No sedation or dependence reported
28. Liked / worked: Calm, focus, mild cognitive gain
29. What worked: Russian trials describe calm, focus and mild cognitive benefit without sedation.
30. Went wrong / did not work: Evidence almost entirely Russian
31. Went wrong / did not work: Mechanism and durability not confirmed
32. What went wrong: Evidence is almost entirely Russian; mechanisms and durability are not independently confirmed.
33. Most reported: Nasal and injected
34. Most reported: Calm, focus and sleep
35. Most reported: Generally well tolerated

## What has been tested
36. Mood: Anxiety vs benzodiazepines (human)
37. Cognition: Focus and mild cognitive effects (human)
38. Neural plasticity: BDNF levels (human)
39. Immunity: Immune markers (human)
40. Russian human studies report anxiety reduction comparable to benzodiazepines without sedation or dependence, plus effects on BDNF and immune markers; little Western replication.
41. What it helps: Russian human studies report anxiety relief comparable to benzodiazepines, without sedation or dependence, plus focus and mild cognitive gains. Evidence is almost entirely Russian, and durability is unconfirmed. Users take it nasally or by injection and report calm, focus and better sleep, and it is generally well tolerated.
42. Trial: none. Approved in Russia for anxiety; published Russian trials exist but none found in registries, and Russian registry checks were not possible. (checked 2026-10-23) [S5] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
43. People on benzodiazepines or other sedatives: Selank modulates GABA-A receptors; effects may stack. (inferred)
44. People on opioids: Selank slows enkephalin breakdown, prolonging the body’s own opioids. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
45. Semax: Semax brings drive and focus through growth factor and dopamine effects, Selank brings calm through enkephalin and claimed GABA effects, so one offsets the other's edge. Sold pre-mixed as Semax + Selank, but the pair has not been tested together in trials.
46. Dihexa: Dihexa targets memory through the HGF/c-Met synapse pathway in rats, Selank adds calm and focus from a different system. People pair them for a calm but sharp cognitive stack. The pairing is user logic, not trial data, and Dihexa has no human data.

## Where it comes from
47. The natural immune peptide tuftsin with a stabilizing Pro-Gly-Pro tail added, developed in Russia as an anxiety treatment.
48. First studied for: Anxiety and related mood disorders, as a non-sedating anxiolytic.
49. Name story: Built from tuftsin (Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg), a small immune peptide snipped from antibodies, plus a Pro-Gly-Pro tail, by Moscow's Institute of Molecular Genetics. The name's origin is not documented in English sources. [S6] (verified)
50. 1990s to 2000s: Tuftsin plus a Pro-Gly-Pro tail, built in Russia for anxiety
51. Today: Approved in Russia as a non-sedating anxiolytic; research chemical elsewhere

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where it came from, and the gap in the story [lab]
52. Selank was designed at the Institute of Molecular Genetics of the Russian Academy of Sciences together with the Zakusov Research Institute of Pharmacology in Moscow [1,2] (verified). The starting point was tuftsin, a four-residue fragment of human immunoglobulin G with immune-stimulating activity. The Pro-Gly-Pro tail was added to slow breakdown and stretch the duration of action [1] (verified).
53. The part of the story that is never explained in print is the jump from an immune fragment to an anti-anxiety drug. The early clinical claim, that it calms like a tranquiliser without the amnesia, withdrawal or dependence of benzodiazepines, is cited in later papers to Russian reports from 1990 and 1998 rather than shown in an accessible trial [1] (reported). No receptor for the molecule has been identified, so every mechanism below is an observed downstream change, not a binding target.

### What the licensed product is, and what circulates instead [lab]
54. The registered Russian medicine is a 0.15% nasal drop: 1.5 mg of peptide per millilitre, preserved with methylparaben, in purified water. The registration holder and manufacturer is a single Moscow company, and the label restricts it to adults, excludes pregnancy and breastfeeding because no studies were done, and runs it as a 14-day course [3] (verified).
55. What circulates elsewhere is mostly lyophilised powder, often sold as an acetate salt or as modified versions such as an amidated or acetylated form. None of those modified forms is the registered drug, and none has its own published clinical record (inferred). In the US nomination system, a nomination for "Selank acetate (TP-7)" was removed from the do-not-compound category after the nominator said it had meant a different substance [8] (verified). That is a small detail with a large meaning: even the people asking regulators to allow it were unsure what they were naming.
56. Unlike Semax, Selank was not on the July 2026 advisory committee agenda, so no regulator has published a review of its purity, impurities or endotoxin testing [9] (verified as absent).

### Mechanism, one step at a time, with the model each step came from [mixed]
57. Enzyme inhibition, in human serum in a test tube. Selank inhibited the enzymes that break down enkephalins with an IC50 of about 20 micromolar, against 10 micromolar for Semax; its pentapeptide fragment also worked, shorter fragments did not [4] (verified). The catch is concentration. Twenty micromolar is a high, lab-scale level, and nothing in the record shows a nasal dose producing anything close to it in blood or brain (inferred).
58. The GABA question, in rats. One intranasal dose of 300 micrograms per kilogram changed expression of 45 neurotransmission genes in rat frontal cortex at one hour, and the pattern correlated strongly with the pattern GABA itself produced (r = 0.86). By three hours the correlation had turned slightly negative (r = minus 0.39), and the biggest single change was an orexin gene rising about 128-fold [1] (verified). The authors read this as possible allosteric action on GABA signalling and asked for more work.
59. The GABA question, in human cells. In human neuroblastoma cells that carry GABA-A receptors, Selank alone changed none of 69 measured genes, but it almost completely suppressed the changes GABA caused when the two were given together [2] (verified). The authors concluded the data only partially support a GABA-A mechanism. So the most-repeated claim about Selank, that it is a GABA-A modulator, rests on gene-expression patterns, not on receptor binding or electrophysiology.
60. Immune and growth-factor effects, in people and rats. Suppression of IL-6 gene expression in blood cells of depressed patients, a shifted Th1/Th2 cytokine balance, and a rapid rise in hippocampal BDNF in rats are all reported in Russian-language work [11] (reported). These were not opened in full for this read.

### What the body does with it [people]
61. The Russian label gives the only human-facing pharmacokinetic figures: absolute bioavailability of 92.8% after nasal use, detection in plasma about 30 seconds after dosing, plasma levels falling away over 5 to 5.5 minutes, and neither intact drug nor metabolites found in 24-hour urine because tissue peptidases break it down completely [3] (verified). The label says it reaches brain tissue but gives no figure for how much.
62. The label does not state a half-life. The commonly quoted figure of about two minutes is not on it (verified as absent). Whatever the exact number, exposure is measured in minutes, while the reported effects are said to last days, including about a week after the last dose in one trial [6]. That gap is either a sign of downstream signalling outlasting the drug, or a sign the effect is softer than reported. Nothing in the record separates the two (inferred).

### The human record, read closely [people]
63. The core trial randomised 62 people with generalised anxiety disorder or neurasthenia to Selank (30) or the benzodiazepine medazepam (32), scored on Hamilton, Zung and clinical global scales. Anxiety relief was similar in both arms, and Selank added anti-fatigue and mildly stimulating effects [5] (verified). The trial also measured how fast blood broke down leu-enkephalin; that half-life was short at baseline and lengthened on Selank, which fits the enzyme mechanism above [5]. There was no placebo arm.
64. A 2014 comparison against phenazepam in 60 people with phobic-anxiety and somatoform disorders reported pronounced anti-anxiety and mild nootropic effects, lasting about a week after the last dose, with better quality of life [6] (verified). A 2012 congress abstract followed 20 people with anxiety on 2.7 mg a day: 40% improved within three days (Hamilton score 20.3 to 7.0), the rest gradually by day 14 (16.1 to 6.2), and the fast responders showed EEG changes after a single dose [7] (verified). It had no control group.
65. Put together: every accessible human study is small, Russian, either uncontrolled or compared against another active drug, and none has a placebo arm. Comparing against a benzodiazepine and finding "similar" results without a placebo cannot tell a working drug from a strong placebo response, which is large in anxiety trials (inferred). There is no registered trial outside Russia and no established dose outside the Russian label.

### Safety: what is known, and what is just absent [people]
66. The label lists allergic reactions, including delayed ones, and an unpleasant taste when drops run into the throat, both of unknown frequency, and records no overdose cases [3] (verified). That is a short list, and short lists in old national registrations often reflect thin monitoring rather than proven safety (inferred).
67. No English-language repeat-dose toxicology, reproductive toxicology or carcinogenicity study was located. Use in pregnancy, breastfeeding and under 18 is excluded on the label precisely because it was never studied [3] (verified). Higher-than-label doses, injection, and modified forms have no safety data at all.

### Who produced the evidence [lab]
68. The developer institute appears on both sides of the record. The 2014 clinical comparison lists among its authors the developer group's senior chemist and the scientists who ran the 2001 enzyme study [4,6] (verified). The gene-expression work comes from the same institute [1,2], and the 2012 trial from the co-developing pharmacology institute [7]. This is normal for a national drug programme. It does mean there is no independent replication of either the clinical or mechanistic findings in the accessible literature (verified as absent).

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
69. Russia: a registered prescription medicine as 0.15% nasal drops, for anxiety states and adjustment disorders in adults [3] (verified). US: not approved; outside any compounding category since its nomination was withdrawn; not reviewed by the July 2026 advisory committee [8,9] (verified).
70. Sport: it is not named on the 2026 Prohibited List. The catch-all non-approved class covers substances with no current approval by any government health authority for human use [10]. Selank does hold a national approval, so that class arguably does not fit it, but nothing in the list settles the point (inferred). Athletes cannot assume it is permitted.

### Open questions [mixed]
71. Does it beat placebo? No accessible trial asks. One adequately sized placebo-controlled study would matter more than every result above.
72. How does a peptide that is gone from plasma in minutes produce effects reported to last a week? Unexplained.
73. Is it a GABA-A modulator at all? Binding or electrophysiology data would answer this; gene-expression patterns cannot.
74. Do modified forms behave like the registered drug? Unstudied.
