# Semax
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/semax
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Семакс, (Pro8,Gly9,Pro10)ACTH(4-10), H-Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro-OH
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: MEHFPGP (7 amino acids)
4. Shown with an FDA approved badge
5. Legal and approval status: Registered and used in Russia; research chemical elsewhere. The July 2026 FDA compounding advisory panel recommended it; non-binding, no rule yet.

## Summary
6. Semax is a seven-amino-acid lab-made peptide based on a piece of ACTH, with a stabilizing Pro-Gly-Pro tail and without the hormone's stress effects. It is used in Russia after stroke, and people elsewhere take it nasally for focus, motivation and mental clarity, with BDNF and monoamine changes proposed as the mechanism. Evidence is overwhelmingly Russian and not confirmed to Western standards.
7. Punch line: Russian stroke medicine built on a piece of ACTH, minus the stress. A nasal spray that raises BDNF.
8. Used for: Focus, memory, drive

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
9. Cognition: Focus and attention
10. Neural plasticity: Raises BDNF, a nerve growth signal
11. Neural protection: Used after stroke in Russia
12. Drive & mental stamina: More motivation reported
13. Pain & sensory (backed only by animal or user reports): Pain relief studied
14. Mood (backed only by animal or user reports): Brighter mood reported

## How it works
15. A piece of ACTH without the hormone action · ACTH(4-7) fragment · role Cognition
   Semax is ACTH(4-7), a small piece of the stress hormone ACTH, with a Pro-Gly-Pro tail for stability. It keeps the brain activity of this fragment but does not trigger cortisol release. Its precise mechanism is described as unknown even in the Russian literature.
16. Raises brain growth factors · BDNF, TrkB, reported · role Neural plasticity
   Semax is reported to raise BDNF and its receptor TrkB in the hippocampus and cortex. BDNF supports nerve connections, learning and neuron survival. This comes mainly from Russian rodent work, with minimal Western replication.
17. Claimed melanocortin signalling · MC receptors, claimed · role Cognition
   Because its sequence matches part of alpha-MSH, Semax is claimed to act on melanocortin receptors in the brain. Direct binding has not been established, so this remains a claim rather than a known mechanism.
18. Used for stroke in Russia; protects neurons in rats · Ischaemia gene expression · role Neural protection
   In rat stroke models, Semax shifts gene activity in damaged brain tissue toward protection and repair. Russia registers a stronger form for acute ischaemic stroke, and Russian trials report better recovery, but these have not been confirmed to Western standards.
19. Raises dopamine and serotonin turnover, in rodents · Monoamine release · role Drive & mental stamina
   In rodents, Semax increases the turnover of dopamine and serotonin, messengers tied to motivation, attention and mood. This fits the drive and focus users report, but it has not been measured in people.
20. Mechanism overview: Semax is ACTH 4-7 (Met-Glu-His-Phe) extended with Pro-Gly-Pro for stability. It keeps the neuroactive properties of this ACTH fragment without stimulating cortisol. It is reported to raise BDNF and its receptor TrkB in the hippocampus and cortex, supporting plasticity and neuron survival. In rodents it increases dopamine and serotonin turnover, and in rat stroke models it shifts gene expression toward protection and repair. Melanocortin receptor action is claimed but unestablished. Most data come from Russian groups.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
21. Typical: 200–600 mcg · daily · cycle 4-8 weeks on, 2-4 weeks off · route Intranasal (reported)
22. Half-life: ~20 minutes
23. Most people take: 200-600mcg/day intranasal (split between nostrils) · 4-8 weeks on, 2-4 weeks off.
24. Common: 200–600 mcg · 1–2× daily · 10–14 days on, 7–14 off · Intranasal (0.1%) · for nootropic focus [S1] [S2] (reported)
25. Higher: 600–1000 mcg/day · split 2–3× · short trials, ≤2 wk · Intranasal (0.1%) · for experienced users [S1] [S2] (reported)
26. Label max / stroke: 6–20 mg/day · 3–5× daily · 10 days · Intranasal (1%) · for acute ischemic stroke only [S3] (verified)

## What people report
27. Nasal; reported for focus, motivation and mental clarity; among the most-used nootropic peptides.
28. Liked / worked: Russian trials: benefit after stroke
29. Liked / worked: Cognitive and attention gains reported
30. Liked / worked: Raised BDNF
31. What worked: Russian trials describe cognitive and neuroprotective benefit, especially after stroke.
32. Went wrong / did not work: Evidence overwhelmingly Russian
33. Went wrong / did not work: Not confirmed to Western standards
34. What went wrong: Evidence is overwhelmingly Russian and not independently confirmed to Western standards.
35. Most reported: Nasal
36. Most reported: Focus, motivation, mental clarity
37. Most reported: One of the most-used nootropic peptides

## What has been tested
38. Neural protection: Stroke recovery (human)
39. Cognition: Memory and attention (human)
40. Neural plasticity: BDNF levels (human)
41. Russian human studies report benefit in stroke, cognition and attention, and raised BDNF. Western replication is minimal.
42. What it helps: Russian trials report better recovery after stroke, improved memory and attention, and raised BDNF, and Russia uses it clinically for stroke. Evidence is overwhelmingly Russian and unconfirmed to Western standards. Users take it nasally for focus, motivation and mental clarity; it is one of the most-used nootropic peptides.
43. Trial: none. Approved in Russia for stroke; Russian studies are published but none found in international registries, and the Russian registry was unverifiable. (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
44. People with a history of seizures: Russian prescribing info lists convulsive disorders as a contraindication. (reported)
45. People with acute psychosis or severe anxiety: Raises dopamine and serotonin turnover; Russian label excludes acute psychotic states. (reported)

## Synergies (paired with)
46. Selank: Semax brings drive and focus through BDNF and dopamine, Selank brings calm through enkephalin and claimed GABA effects, so Selank softens Semax's edge. Sold pre-mixed as Semax + Selank, but the pair has not been tested together in trials.
47. Dihexa: Semax works on BDNF and monoamines, Dihexa on HGF/c-Met synapse building, two growth signals aimed at memory and focus. People stack them for cognition. The pairing is user logic, not trial data, and Dihexa has only rat data.

## Where it comes from
48. A seven-amino-acid peptide: a piece of ACTH (residues 4-7) plus a stabilizing Pro-Gly-Pro tail, developed in Russia as a neuroprotective nootropic.
49. First studied for: Stroke recovery and cognitive enhancement; used in Russian emergency medicine for stroke.
50. Name story: Reportedly a Russian acronym for 'SEMь AminoKiSlot', seven amino acids. It is the ACTH(4–7) start, MEHF, with a Pro-Gly-Pro tail added in place of the hormone's own residues 8–10. [S5] (reported)
51. 1980s to 1990s: ACTH(4-7) plus Pro-Gly-Pro, built in Russia; used in stroke care
52. Jul 2026: FDA compounding panel recommended it; non-binding, no rule yet
53. Today: Registered in Russia; among the most-used nootropic peptides

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where it came from [lab]
54. Semax was built in Moscow from the ACTH(4-7) fragment, Met-Glu-His-Phe, which matches part of alpha-MSH, with a Pro-Gly-Pro tail for stability [5] (verified). It was first described in the literature in 1991 and placed on Russia's list of vital and essential drugs on 7 December 2011 [3] (verified). It has a real national drug history, which sets it apart from most compounds in this library.
55. What that history does not include is a defined mechanism. Even the licensing country's literature describes the mechanism as unknown [3] (reported). The Russian label itself sells the compound in two very different strengths for two different jobs: 0.1% for cognitive and neurological indications, and 1% for acute ischaemic stroke only [2] (verified).

### What is actually in a vial [lab]
56. The registered product is nasal drops with methylparaben as preservative, in 3 mL bottles [2] (verified). What US nominators proposed instead was injection or nasal spray at 7.5 mg or 1 mg per millilitre [1] (verified).
57. The FDA's July 2026 review found the naming unreliable: certificates titled "semax acetate" carried the identifiers of the free base. The acetate certificates listed identity, purity and water, and allowed single unidentified impurities of up to 1% or 2%, but none reported aggregates, bioburden or endotoxin [1] (verified). Both forms were judged not well characterised.
58. Solubility is a concrete problem. The free base dissolves in water to about 2 mg/mL and in phosphate buffer to about 10 mg/mL [1] (verified). A 7.5 mg/mL product would therefore need buffer or the salt form, since plain water would not hold it (inferred). Lyophilised powder is quoted as stable four years at minus 20 degrees, but reconstituted solution only 2 to 7 days in the fridge [1] (verified), far shorter than most handling assumes.
59. No nasal spray device information, meaning container, closure or pump, was supplied, which the agency flagged as a strong concern for a nasal product [1] (verified).

### Mechanism, one step at a time, with the model each step came from [mixed]
60. Melanocortin receptors, in cells and animals. Semax competitively blocked alpha-MSH at MC4 and MC5 receptors and did not block MC3 [3] (reported). So the receptor action, where it exists, looks like antagonism or partial agonism rather than switching receptors on.
61. Enzymes, in human serum. Semax inhibited enkephalin-degrading enzymes with an IC50 of about 10 micromolar [4] (verified), a concentration well above anything nasal dosing is shown to reach (inferred).
62. Stroke, in rats. A single nasal dose of 250 micrograms per kilogram after photothrombotic stroke gave infarcts about 20% smaller at day 8, and intraperitoneal dosing reduced neuronal damage after carotid occlusion [1] (verified). Transcriptome work after ischaemia shows inflammatory genes turned down and neurotransmission genes turned up, and the Pro-Gly-Pro tail alone does not reproduce it, so the ACTH part matters [5] (verified).
63. Blood clotting, in rats. This is the least-known part of the profile. Nasal 1 mg/kg a day for five days raised fibrinolytic activity, another group found a hypocoagulation profile, and platelet aggregation fell about 35%. The breakdown product Pro-Gly-Pro was itself anticoagulant [1] (verified). No dose-response was examined.
64. Dopamine, in mice. Semax potentiated amphetamine-induced dopamine release in the striatum, which the FDA called concerning for abuse potential; no abuse or reinforcement study exists [1] (verified).

### What the body does with it [mixed]
65. The label states nasal uptake of up to 60 to 70%, arrival in the brain within about 4 minutes, rapid breakdown in blood and urinary excretion, with active fragments, and an effect lasting 20 to 24 hours after one dose [2] (verified). No half-life is given.
66. The rat numbers put the brain claim in proportion. After intravenous dosing, peak brain level was about 0.005% of the dose; after nasal dosing, about 0.072% at 2 minutes, with brain-to-blood ratios of 0.24 and 0.67 [1] (verified). Nasal delivery does favour the brain, but the amount arriving is a tiny fraction of what is given. The main metabolite is Pro-Gly-Pro [1].
67. No human pharmacokinetic study exists for any route, and no subcutaneous data exist in any species [1] (verified). So injection, the route many people now use, has no exposure data behind it.

### The human record [people]
68. The stroke use is the oldest claim. A 2018 Russian study of patients at different stages of ischaemic stroke is cited for faster and greater recovery of neurological function [5,6] (reported). The full paper was not opened for this read.
69. The FDA found only two usable references for the three uses it reviewed. One 2002 meeting abstract in chronic ischaemic brain disease gave clotting labs without full results and no functional outcome [1]. The other, from 1996, was open-label and uncontrolled. In 12 people with migraine, a single nasal dose cut a pain-sensitivity score from 78% to 32%, and 4 of 12 reported the headache stopping within two hours. In 16 people with typical trigeminal neuralgia, nothing changed. In 9 with dental nerve pain, 6 resolved, but attack frequency and duration did not fall, and the authors concluded Semax has no analgesic activity by itself [1] (verified).
70. Across the safety literature, roughly 33 to 47 healthy adults, 69 adults with medical conditions and 451 children with depression or tics have been exposed, all nasally. Three of the sources were meeting abstracts, one reported no adverse events, and the rest did not discuss them [1] (verified). There is no established human dose outside the Russian label.

### Safety: what has been looked at, and what has not [mixed]
71. Absent: acute toxicity, repeat-dose toxicity, reproductive toxicity and two-year carcinogenicity studies [1] (verified). The one cancer-related study gave 3 mg/kg intraperitoneally to female mice that already had mammary tumours; tumours ended smaller (7.4 against 15.0 cubic centimetres) and lifespan longer, but with one dose, one sex and under three months it cannot assess cancer risk [1] (verified).
72. The label contraindicates Semax in pregnancy, breastfeeding, acute psychosis, anxiety disorders and a history of seizures [2] (verified). That anxiety line matters, because Semax is often sold paired with an anti-anxiety peptide for people who feel overstimulated.
73. The FDA's adverse event system held one report: a consumer who bought 0.1% nasal drops online reported eye pain and burning, hospitalisation, and pain still unresolved a year later [1] (verified). The antithrombotic animal data raise a bleeding question for anyone on blood thinners or facing surgery; it has not been studied in people (inferred).

### Who produced the evidence [lab]
74. Almost all of it comes from the Moscow institutes that developed the drug and their clinical partners [1,5] (verified). That is typical for a national medicine, and the work is not trivial: there are transcriptome and proteome studies in rat stroke models. What is missing is any independent replication outside Russia, and any trial built to current standards with a placebo arm and pre-registered endpoints (verified as absent in the FDA review).

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
75. Russia: a registered medicine on the essential drugs list [2,3] (verified). US: listed in the do-not-compound category as of 2024 [11], then reviewed by the FDA, whose staff concluded the criteria weighed against both forms [1]. On 24 July 2026 the advisory committee nonetheless voted 8 to 5 with one abstention to recommend it, for cerebral ischaemia, migraine and trigeminal neuralgia [7,8] (verified). The vote is advisory, and a bulks-list listing still needs rulemaking.
76. An interim access policy for compounding certain peptides went to White House regulatory review on 14 October 2026; it had not been issued and the peptides it covers are not public [9] (verified).
77. Sport: not named on the 2026 Prohibited List. The catch-all class covers substances with no current government approval anywhere [10]; Semax is approved in Russia, so that class arguably does not fit, but the list does not settle it (inferred).

### Open questions [mixed]
78. Does it help stroke recovery in a placebo-controlled trial? This is the most answerable question and the one with the oldest claim.
79. What do the antithrombotic effects mean in people? Unstudied, and relevant to anyone bleeding-prone.
80. Does the dopamine potentiation carry abuse risk? No study exists.
81. What happens with injection, and with long-term use? No exposure or toxicity data exist for either.

# Pinealon
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/pinealon
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: EDR, EDR peptide, Glu-Asp-Arg
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: EDR (3 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: Not an approved drug anywhere; sold as a Khavinson bioregulator.

## Summary
5. Pinealon is a lab-made tripeptide (Glu-Asp-Arg) from the Khavinson bioregulator tradition, aimed at the brain. It is used for cognition, sleep and longevity, and is claimed to protect neurons by regulating genes and reducing oxidative stress. The evidence is Russian cell and rat work with no independent trials, and detailed first-hand reports are few.
6. Punch line: Khavinson bioregulator tripeptide for the brain. Claimed to shield neurons; evidence is Russian cell and rat work.
7. Used for: Cognition, sleep, brain aging

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Cognition: Memory support in old animals
9. Neural protection: Protects neurons from stress
10. Sleep & rhythms: Deeper sleep reported
11. Mood: Calmer mood reported
12. Cellular protection (backed only by animal or user reports): Antioxidant action in cells
13. Drive & mental stamina (backed only by animal or user reports): More energy reported
14. DNA & telomeres (backed only by animal or user reports): Claimed to tune genes

## How it works
15. Claimed to protect neurons via gene control · Khavinson group · role Neural protection
   The Khavinson group claims short peptides like Pinealon (Glu-Asp-Arg) enter the cell nucleus and bind DNA, adjusting gene activity in nerve tissue. No receptor is known, and the gene-control evidence is largely computer modelling. No independent lab has confirmed it.
16. Claimed to cut oxidative stress in neurons · ROS down, claimed · role Cellular protection
   In rat neuron cultures, Pinealon lowered reactive oxygen species, the damaging free radicals produced under stress, and reduced cell death after toxic insults. These are cell findings from the originating group only.
17. Claimed to aid memory under stress, in rats · Cognition, claimed · role Cognition
   Rat studies from the same group claim better memory and learning under stress after Pinealon. The work has not been repeated elsewhere, and there are no controlled human trials of cognition.
18. Claimed to support melatonin making · Pineal, claimed · role Sleep & rhythms
   Pinealon is linked by name and claim to the pineal gland, which makes melatonin. Supporting melatonin production is asserted in Russian reports, but no study cleanly shows it in people. Treat it as an unverified claim.
19. Mechanism overview: Pinealon is the tripeptide Glu-Asp-Arg from the Khavinson group in St Petersburg. The group claims short peptides like this enter the nucleus and bind DNA, adjusting gene expression in specific tissues. For Pinealon, the claimed effects are lower reactive oxygen species and less cell death in neurons under stress, better memory in stressed rats, and support for melatonin synthesis. No receptor is known, and no independent lab has confirmed the mechanism.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
20. Typical: 1–2 mg · once daily, AM · cycle 10–20 days, 2–4×/yr · route Sub-Q (reported)
21. Half-life: short
22. Dose note: Doses run from 100 mcg to 20 mg, about 100–200× apart. The mg figures likely carry capsule sizes over to injection.
23. Most people take: Most guides: 1 mg a day, some 2 mg, Sub-Q in the morning for 10 to 20 days. Guides range from 100–300 mcg up to 5–10 mg; there is no tested human injection dose.
24. Research doses are far lower: the patent used 1 to 10 mcg IM a day for 10 days. Oral capsules run 100 to 200 mcg twice a day for 20 to 30 days.
25. Common injected: 1–2 mg · 1× daily AM · 10–20 days, 2–3×/yr · Sub-Q · for biohackers [S1] [S2] (reported)
26. Study / microdose: 100–300 mcg · 1–2× daily · 10–30 days · Oral capsule or Sub-Q · for study dose, cautious users [S3] [S4] [S5] (reported)
27. High / oral mg: 5–20 mg · 1× daily · 10–30 days · Oral or Sub-Q · for oral capsule users, aggressive SC [S5] [S4] (reported)

## What people report
28. Reported for cognition and sleep; longevity interest.
29. Liked / worked: Russian reports of cognitive protection
30. Liked / worked: Russian reports of better sleep
31. What worked: Russian reports of cognitive protection and sleep benefit.
32. Went wrong / did not work: No independent trials

## What has been tested
38. Neural protection: Nerve cell protection (animal)
39. DNA & telomeres: Gene-regulating effects (cell)
40. Russian animal and cell studies claim neuroprotection and gene-regulating effects; no independent trials.
41. What it helps: Evidence is Russian cell and animal work. Rat studies claim neuron protection and better memory under stress, and Russian reports describe cognitive protection and better sleep. No independent trials exist. Users take it for cognition, sleep and longevity, and detailed first-hand reports are few.
42. Trial: none. No registered human trial of this tripeptide exists. Khavinson bioregulator studied only in unregistered Russian clinical reports; no registry trial found in ClinicalTrials.gov, EU CTR, ISRCTN or ChiCTR, Russian registry unverifiable. (checked 2026-10-23) [S6] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
43. People with active or recent cancer: Marketed as gene-regulating and proliferative; effect on tumours untested. (inferred)
44. People on sleep or melatonin medicines: Pineal bioregulators are claimed to raise melatonin; stacking is untested. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
45. Epitalon: Both come from the Khavinson bioregulator family, Pinealon aimed at neurons and Epitalon at the pineal gland and ageing, so users run them as a brain and sleep course. Neither has independent trials, and the pair has not been tested together.
46. DSIP: DSIP is taken for sleep onset and Pinealon for claimed neuron protection and melatonin support, aiming at sleep from two angles. Both rest on weak evidence. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
47. NA Semax Amidate: The Semax analogue adds drive and claimed BDNF support, Pinealon adds claimed neuron protection. They are sold pre-mixed in Semax + Selank + PE-22-28 + Pinealon, but that blend and the pair have not been tested together.
48. NA Selank Amidate: The Selank analogue adds calm and focus, Pinealon adds claimed neuron protection and sleep support. Both appear in the pre-mixed Semax + Selank + PE-22-28 + Pinealon. The combination has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
49. A tripeptide (Glu-Asp-Arg) Khavinson bioregulator aimed at the brain, from pineal/neural peptide research.
50. First studied for: Neuroprotection and cognitive support in aging, in the Russian program.
51. Name story: Named for the pineal gland, in Khavinson's habit of naming bioregulators after their target organ. It is just three amino acids, Glu-Asp-Arg (EDR). [S7] (inferred)
52. 1990s to 2000s: Glu-Asp-Arg tripeptide from Khavinson pineal and neural research
53. Today: A brain-aimed bioregulator with longevity interest

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where it came from, and what kind of evidence that implies [lab]
54. Pinealon is the tripeptide Glu-Asp-Arg, also written EDR, one of a family of short "bioregulator" peptides from the St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and the Pavlov Institute group around Vladimir Khavinson [2,4] (verified). Unlike a fragment cut from a known hormone, it was designed to stand for a tissue: the logic is that tiny peptides carry tissue-specific signals into cells. That logic is the group's own hypothesis, not an established principle of biology (inferred).
55. The literature is almost entirely Russian-language or from the originating group, and the English record mostly consists of reviews that summarise that work rather than new primary data [2,4] (verified).

### Mechanism, one step at a time, with the model each step came from [mixed]
56. Free radicals, in cells. In rat cerebellar neurons, EDR reduced reactive oxygen species triggered by ouabain, homocysteine and hydrogen peroxide, delayed homocysteine-driven ERK1/2 activation from about 2.5 to about 20 minutes, and lowered lipid hydroperoxides; similar effects were reported in activated neutrophils [1,2] (reported).
57. Gene control, mostly on a computer. The headline claim that EDR binds DNA and adjusts genes rests on molecular modelling: two predicted binding motifs, a search that found matching motifs in the promoters of two metabolic genes (PPARA and PPARG) and in a serotonin-synthesis gene, and an assumption that the peptide reaches the nucleus [2] (verified). A separate older study reported short fluorescent peptides entering HeLa cell nuclei and binding DNA in a test tube [6] (reported), but the 2021 EDR review itself presents no uptake or nuclear-localisation data for EDR [2] (verified). Prediction, not demonstration.
58. Brain function, in rats. Reported findings include normalised CNS function in offspring of mothers with high homocysteine, lower brain caspase-3 and better maze learning after hypoxia in old and young rats, and raised antioxidant enzymes in hypoxia-sensitive animals [2,4] (reported). Most are cited secondhand in reviews.
59. Human neurons in a dish. The most modern study converted skin cells from three women aged 61 to 68 into neurons and gave EDR at 10 micrograms per millilitre for 10 days. Oxidative DNA damage fell 23% (p = 0.057, so borderline), primary processes rose 28% and total dendrite length 46%, while mitochondrial activity, lysosomes and two ageing markers did not change [3] (verified). Three donors, one concentration, a lab dish.

### What the body does with it [lab]
60. There is no published pharmacokinetic data for Pinealon in any species (verified as absent in the sources reviewed). Free tripeptides are generally broken down quickly by blood and gut peptidases, so how much of an injected or swallowed dose reaches a neuron intact is unknown (inferred). The product is sold both as oral capsules and as injectable powder, with no study comparing what either route delivers.

### The human record [people]
61. The 2021 review by the originating group describes oral EDR added to standard therapy in 72 patients with the after-effects of traumatic brain injury, reporting better memory, fewer and milder headaches and better work performance, and a second group with fewer errors on an attention test and a higher EEG alpha index [2] (reported). Neither design, control group nor blinding is described. Memory improvement in elderly patients is claimed in the abstract without detail.
62. No randomised, placebo-controlled trial of Pinealon has been located, no trial is registered, and no study outside the originating network exists. There is no established human dose (verified as absent in the sources reviewed).

### Safety, and the shape of what is missing [mixed]
63. No toxicology of any kind, acute, repeat-dose, reproductive or carcinogenicity, has been located, and no adverse-event series exists (verified as absent in the sources reviewed). The claimed mechanism, a peptide that enters the nucleus and changes gene expression, is precisely the kind of action that would normally demand long-term safety work; that it has none is the main gap (inferred).
64. A practical point: the human reports used oral capsules, while much current use is injection of lyophilised powder. Injected material raises sterility, endotoxin and impurity questions that have never been addressed for this peptide (inferred).

### Status and open questions [mixed]
65. Not an approved drug anywhere. Not on any US compounding list reviewed for this read, and not among the peptides at the July 2026 advisory committee. In sport it is not named, and as a substance with no government approval for therapeutic use it falls in the catch-all non-approved class [5] (inferred).
66. Open questions: does EDR reach the nucleus of a living neuron? Does any effect survive a placebo-controlled trial? Is any oral dose absorbed intact? And does an independent lab reproduce even the antioxidant cell findings? Each is answerable, and none has been answered.

# Retatrutide + Cagrilintide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/reta-cagri
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Reta/Cagri, Reta + Cagri blend, retatrutide/cagrilintide 12.5/2.5
2. Origin: Blend of 2 peptides
3. Legal and approval status: Neither part is approved anywhere. FDA says both cannot be compounded under federal law; retatrutide sellers drew warning letters (Sep 2025, Mar 2026, Aug 2026). Lilly plans to file retatrutide in Q1 2027; a CagriSema decision is expected Q4 2026. WADA: not named, falls under S0.

## Summary
4. This blend pairs retatrutide, Lilly's triple GLP-1, GIP and glucagon agonist, with cagrilintide, Novo's long-acting amylin analogue. Users combine them for weight loss, since the amylin side adds a second fullness route and quiets cravings retatrutide leaves behind. Both drugs have large human trials, but the pair has only a rat study. Stacked nausea and constipation are the main complaints.
5. Punch line: Triple agonist plus amylin. Cagrilintide adds a second fullness route, quieting cravings retatrutide leaves behind.
6. Used for: Weight loss, appetite and cravings

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Appetite & satiety: Two satiety routes: incretin and amylin
8. Fat metabolism: Glucagon side raises fat burning
9. Glucose & insulin: Lowers glucose and A1c
10. Reward & urges: Quiets cravings and food noise
11. Pain & sensory (backed only by animal or user reports): Knee pain eased in a retatrutide OA trial

## How it works
12. Hits three appetite and metabolism receptors · GLP-1R, GIPR, glucagon receptor agonist · role Appetite & satiety
   Retatrutide is one molecule that switches on three receptors: GLP-1 and GIP, the gut hormone receptors that cut hunger and lift insulin, plus the glucagon receptor. Together they drive large weight loss. Phase 2 and TRIUMPH-1 human trials show this for retatrutide alone.
13. Glucagon arm raises energy use and liver fat burning · Glucagon receptor · role Fat metabolism
   The glucagon receptor arm raises energy use and makes the liver burn more of its stored fat. This adds to weight loss from eating less, and is the main thing retatrutide has that semaglutide lacks. Shown in human trials of retatrutide alone.
14. Long-acting amylin copy: fuller sooner, slower stomach · Amylin and calcitonin receptors (DACRA) · role Appetite & satiety
   Cagrilintide is a long-acting copy of amylin that also activates calcitonin receptors. It makes people full sooner and slows stomach emptying, through a route separate from GLP-1. Human trials show weight loss alone and more when combined with semaglutide.
15. Acts on brain reward and craving circuits · Area postrema, hindbrain amylin signalling · role Reward & urges
   Amylin acts in the area postrema, a hindbrain zone outside the blood-brain barrier, to cut meal size and dampen reward-driven eating. This is why users report fewer cravings. Shown in human cagrilintide trials; the craving effect on this pair is user-reported.
16. Mechanism overview: Retatrutide is a single acylated peptide agonist at GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors; the glucagon arm raises energy expenditure and hepatic fat oxidation on top of incretin-driven satiety. Cagrilintide is a lipidated, long-acting amylin analogue that also activates calcitonin receptors (a dual amylin and calcitonin receptor agonist). Amylin signals through the area postrema and hindbrain to slow gastric emptying, reduce meal size and dampen reward-driven eating, a route separate from GLP-1, which is why amylin plus incretin pairs add weight loss in trials of cagrilintide with semaglutide.

## What is inside the blend
17. Retatrutide: 12.5 mg · Triple incretin plus glucagon: the main weight-loss driver
18. Cagrilintide: 2.5 mg · Amylin route: fullness, slower stomach, fewer cravings
19. Most common ratio: Retatrutide 12.5 · Cagrilintide 2.5 = 15 mg (7 of 8 listings)
20. Other ratio seen: Retatrutide 25 · Cagrilintide 5 = 30 mg (1 listing (second size))
21. Other ratio seen: Retatrutide 10 · Cagrilintide 2.5 = 12.5 mg (1 listing)
22. Version Common retail: Retatrutide 12.5 · Cagrilintide 2.5 = 15 mg
23. Version Larger vial: Retatrutide 20 · Cagrilintide 4 = 24 mg
24. Version Other seller splits: Retatrutide 10 · Cagrilintide 2 (also 10 + 2.5, 8 + 2) = 12 mg
25. Why Retatrutide is in it: Adds the glucagon arm and the strongest incretin signal; cagrilintide alone loses far less weight
26. Why Cagrilintide is in it: Adds the amylin route for meal size and cravings, which incretins leave partly untouched
27. Mixing chemistry: The CagriSema maker states cagrilintide and semaglutide cannot share one formulation: cagrilintide needs about pH 4, semaglutide about pH 7.4; their pen keeps them in two chambers.
28. Mixing chemistry: The licensed amylin drug pramlintide (pH 4) carries a label rule never to mix it with insulin, for the same reason.
29. Mixing chemistry: Retatrutide's own formulation pH is not public; as an acylated incretin like semaglutide it is likely soluble only near neutral pH, so a shared liquid is a compromise for at least one part.
30. Mixing chemistry: Cagrilintide is surface-reactive and forms high-molecular-weight aggregates in storage; dissolve by swirling, never shaking.
31. Mixing chemistry: A slight off-white tint is described as normal in blend vials; haze, particles or gel mean discard.
32. Self-mixing: Mixing the two reconstituted vials into one is the case most at odds with the licensed formulations (pH 4 vs neutral); same-day injections in separate syringes at separate sites is what most guides describe, and separate vials allow independent titration.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
33. Typical: 1–4 mg retatrutide + 0.2–0.8 mg cagrilintide · 1× weekly · cycle Ongoing, after slow titration · route Sub-Q (reported)
34. Half-life: per component
35. Most people take: Sized by the retatrutide dose. 12.5/2.5 vial in 2.5 mL (5 mg/mL reta, 1 mg/mL cagri): 20 units = 1 + 0.2 mg, 40 units = 2 + 0.4 mg, 80 units = 4 + 0.8 mg. Steps held at least 4 weeks; step back if GI effects are heavy.

## What people report
36. Weekly, Sub-Q. Common route: retatrutide alone first, then add cagrilintide once stable. On a 12.5/2.5 vial in 2.5 mL, 20 units = 1 mg reta + 0.2 mg cagri; 40 units = 2 + 0.4. Many use separate vials through titration and switch to the blend at maintenance. Reported ratios range from 5:1 down to 1:1 for heavy cravings.
37. Liked / worked: Each part has large human trials
38. Liked / worked: Pair beat either alone in rats, 2026
39. Liked / worked: Users report fewer cravings at lower reta doses
40. What worked: Users and guides report the cagrilintide side quieting cravings and emotional eating that persist on retatrutide, at lower retatrutide doses. Most community protocols stay around 2 to 4 mg retatrutide weekly with 0.4 to 0.8 mg cagrilintide.
41. Went wrong / did not work: No human trial of the pair
42. Went wrong / did not work: Stacked nausea, vomiting, constipation
43. Went wrong / did not work: Fixed ratio blocks separate titration
44. What went wrong: Stacked GI effects are the main complaint: nausea, vomiting, constipation, worst while titrating. Retatrutide adds dose-related skin tingling (dysesthesia, 5 to 21% in trials) and a higher heart rate; cagrilintide adds injection-site reactions (17% vs 3%) and anti-drug antibodies in about half of users. A fixed vial cannot titrate the two separately.
45. Most reported: Reta first, cagri added once stable
46. Most reported: 1 to 4 mg reta + 0.2 to 0.8 mg cagri weekly
47. Most reported: Separate vials to titrate, blend at maintenance
48. Most reported: Hold each step 4 weeks

## What has been tested
49. Fat metabolism: Retatrutide, phase 2 and TRIUMPH-1 (human)
50. Appetite & satiety: Cagrilintide alone, REDEFINE 1 (human)
51. Appetite & satiety: Retatrutide + cagrilintide, obese rats (animal)
52. Reward & urges: Cravings and food noise (users)
53. No human trial of the pair as of Oct 2026; one 2026 rat study reported more weight loss with the pair than either alone. Separately: retatrutide 12 mg weekly gave 24.2% loss at 48 weeks (phase 2) and 28.3% at 80 weeks (TRIUMPH-1); cagrilintide 2.4 mg alone gave 11.8% at 68 weeks (REDEFINE 1), 22.7% with semaglutide.
54. What it helps: Both halves have large human trials; the pair has only a rat study. Expect the GI profile of both, likely heavier during titration. Users report the amylin side mainly helps cravings and emotional eating, and lets them hold a lower retatrutide dose.

## Who shouldn't take it
55. Personal or family history of MTC or MEN2: GLP-1 receptor agonists cause C-cell tumours in rodents; trials exclude these people. (inferred)
56. Insulin or sulfonylurea users: Amylin analogues add to insulin; pramlintide carries a boxed warning for severe low blood sugar. (inferred)
57. People relying on the contraceptive pill: Contains GIP agonism like tirzepatide, whose label warns pill absorption drops after starts and dose increases. (inferred)
58. People with gastroparesis or severe slow digestion: Amylin slows the stomach further; pramlintide is contraindicated in gastroparesis. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
59. Semaglutide: Semaglutide is the GLP-1 drug cagrilintide was trialled with, giving 22.7% weight loss in REDEFINE 1. Adding it to retatrutide doubles up GLP-1 receptor action. That overlap has not been tested together.
60. Tirzepatide: Tirzepatide shares the GLP-1 and GIP receptors with retatrutide, so stacking them doubles up the same targets rather than adding a new one. People sometimes switch between them. The combination has not been tested.
61. Eloralintide: Eloralintide is another long-acting amylin drug, acting on the same fullness receptors as cagrilintide. Adding it doubles up the amylin side rather than adding a new route. The pairing has not been tested.
62. Amylin: Amylin here refers to pramlintide, the short-acting mealtime amylin drug. It overlaps with cagrilintide's amylin action. Stacking both duplicates one route, and the pairing has not been tested together.
63. 5-Amino-1MQ: 5-Amino-1MQ blocks the NNMT enzyme in fat cells, a different target from the appetite receptors here, and shrank fat cells in obese mice. People add it for fat loss. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
64. Lilly's triple agonist retatrutide (GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors) pre-mixed with Novo's long-acting amylin analogue cagrilintide. Most sold at a fixed 5 to 1 ratio, usually 12.5 + 2.5 mg per vial.
65. First studied for: A grey-market copy of the CagriSema idea (amylin plus an incretin), using the strongest incretin in development instead of semaglutide. Users add the amylin side for cravings and food noise that retatrutide leaves behind.
66. 2021: Cagrilintide alone: 10.8% weight loss at 26 weeks, phase 2
67. 2023: Retatrutide phase 2: 24.2% at 48 weeks
68. 2025: REDEFINE 1: CagriSema 22.7% at 68 weeks
69. May 2026: TRIUMPH-1 topline: retatrutide 28.3% at 80 weeks
70. 2026: Rat study: pair beats either alone
71. Today: Sold pre-mixed 5:1, mainly 12.5 + 2.5 mg

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What has and has not been studied as a pair [mixed]
72. No human trial of retatrutide with cagrilintide has been located, and none is registered in the sources reviewed (verified as absent). The evidence people lean on is a different pairing: cagrilintide with semaglutide. In REDEFINE 1, 3,417 adults took the combination, either drug alone or placebo for 68 weeks; adherent participants lost 22.7% on the combination, 16.1% on semaglutide, 11.8% on cagrilintide alone and 2.3% on placebo [4,5] (verified). Gastrointestinal effects hit 80% on the combination against 40% on placebo [4].
73. That result does not transfer automatically. Semaglutide acts on one receptor; retatrutide acts on three and already produces far larger losses on its own, so there is less room left for a second drug to add, and the glucagon arm brings effects semaglutide does not have (inferred). The single 2026 rodent paper located for this read tested retatrutide alone, about 25% lower body weight than obese controls over four weeks, not the pair [9] (verified). A rodent study of the pair itself could not be traced.

### Each component, one level deeper than the headline [people]
74. Retatrutide. The phase 2 trial enrolled 338 adults for 48 weeks; at 12 mg weight fell 24.2% against 2.1% on placebo [1] (verified). Heart rate rose with dose, peaking around week 24 and easing afterwards; cardiac arrhythmia adverse events reached 14% in some dose groups against 2% on placebo, mostly mild [1] (verified). TRIUMPH-1, 2,339 adults over 80 weeks, gave 28.3% at 12 mg on treatment and 25.0% by intention to treat, against 2.2% and 3.9% on placebo [2] (verified). At 12 mg, 11.3% stopped for adverse events, and a skin-sensation disturbance called dysesthesia appeared in 12.5% against 0.9% [2] (verified), a signal the older incretin drugs did not show.
75. Cagrilintide. Its phase 2 trial randomised 706 adults for 26 weeks; weight fell 10.8% at 4.5 mg against 9.0% on liraglutide and 3.0% on placebo [3] (verified). Injection-site reactions rose with dose to 43%. Anti-drug antibodies appeared in 46 to 73% of participants by week 26, increasing with dose and time; most cross-reacted with the body's own amylin, few were neutralising, and they did not appear to blunt weight loss [3] (verified).

### The antibody finding and what it means for a vial [mixed]
76. That cagrilintide provokes antibodies in most people, even as a pharmaceutical-grade product in a controlled trial, is the most under-discussed fact in this pairing (verified for the trial product). Antibodies that cross-react with native amylin are, in principle, antibodies against one of the body's own hormones. In the trial they were mostly non-neutralising and harmless over 26 weeks [3].
77. Material outside that supply chain adds unknown impurities and aggregates, which are the usual drivers of immune responses to peptides (inferred). A second peptide in the same solution adds its own (inferred). Nobody has measured antibody rates with research-grade cagrilintide, or with either peptide sharing a vial.

### The fixed ratio and the titration problem [mixed]
78. The common 5 to 1 mass ratio lines up roughly with the top trial doses of each, about 12 mg of retatrutide and 2.4 mg of cagrilintide (inferred from [2,4]). The trials, though, escalated each drug on its own schedule: retatrutide from 2 mg, stepping every four weeks [2]. In a blend, every step moves both at once, so the dose of the more nauseating component cannot be held while the other is raised (inferred).
79. Side effects stack on overlapping routes. At 12 mg, retatrutide's nausea rate was 42.4% against 14.8% on placebo [2]; cagrilintide alone gave nausea in 20 to 47% [3] (verified for each alone). Their sum in one person is unmeasured.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
80. The FDA states plainly that retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law, because neither is part of an approved drug or has been found safe and effective for any condition [6] (verified). It has sent warning letters to telehealth companies marketing retatrutide, to ingredient distributors selling it to compounders, and to outsourcing facilities repackaging it [6] (verified). In August 2026 the developer filed six lawsuits against sellers and reported more than 200 referrals to regulators and prosecutors [7] (verified).
81. Sport: neither is named on the 2026 Prohibited List, but with no government approval both fall in the catch-all non-approved class, prohibited at all times [8] (inferred application, verified wording). If a cagrilintide product is approved, that would change for that component (inferred).

### Open questions [mixed]
82. Does adding amylin to a triple agonist add meaningful weight loss, or mostly side effects? Untested in people.
83. Does the pair push heart rate or arrhythmia further than retatrutide alone? Unknown.
84. What are antibody rates with research-grade material? Unmeasured.
85. Is there an interaction between dysesthesia and the amylin route? Nobody has looked.

# Epitalon
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/epitalon
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Epithalon, Epithalone, AEDG peptide, Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: AEDG (4 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: Not an approved drug. The July 2026 FDA compounding advisory panel recommended it; non-binding, no rule yet.

## Summary
5. Epitalon is a synthetic four-amino-acid peptide designed from epithalamin, a pineal gland extract, in Khavinson's lab. It is the best-known longevity peptide, claimed to activate telomerase and restore melatonin rhythm, and users inject it in short cycles and report better sleep. The telomerase and lifespan claims rest on one research tradition and are not independently confirmed.
6. Punch line: The best-known longevity peptide, from a pineal extract. Short cycles for sleep; telomerase claims stay unproven.
7. Used for: Longevity, sleep

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Aging & senescence: Claimed telomerase activation
9. Sleep & rhythms: Restores melatonin rhythm
10. DNA & telomeres: Telomere claims from cell work
11. Mood: Calmer mood reported
12. Neural plasticity (backed only by animal or user reports): Brain cell studies
13. Pain & sensory (backed only by animal or user reports): Less aches reported
14. Cognition (backed only by animal or user reports): Clearer head reported

## How it works
15. Claimed to switch on telomerase · Telomerase, claimed · role Aging & senescence
   The Khavinson group claims Epitalon switches on telomerase, the enzyme that rebuilds telomeres, the protective caps on chromosome ends. This would let cells divide more times before ageing. It comes almost entirely from one group and has not been independently confirmed.
16. Claimed to lengthen telomeres in human cells · Telomere length, claimed · role DNA & telomeres
   In human cell cultures the same group reports telomeres lengthened after Epitalon. This is cell data only. The FDA's 2026 review found no human study of the synthetic peptide showing this in the body.
17. Claimed to restore melatonin rhythm · Pineal gland, claimed · role Sleep & rhythms
   Russian reports describe restored night-time melatonin rhythm and better sleep in older people. Many of these human results, including the mortality cohorts, used epithalamin, a crude pineal extract, not the synthetic tetrapeptide sold today.
18. Claimed to reopen silenced genes in aged cells · Chromatin, claimed · role DNA & telomeres
   In aged cells, chromatin, the packaging around DNA, becomes condensed and silences genes. The group claims Epitalon loosens it and reactivates those genes. This is cell work from the originating group without outside replication.
19. Mechanism overview: Epitalon is the tetrapeptide Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly, a synthetic version of a claimed active part of epithalamin, a pineal gland extract. The Khavinson group claims it activates telomerase and lengthens telomeres in human cell cultures, restores night-time melatonin rhythms in older people, and reopens condensed chromatin in aged cells, reactivating silenced genes. If true, this would slow replicative aging and restore circadian signalling. These claims come almost entirely from one group, and telomerase activation has not been independently confirmed.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
20. Typical: 5–10 mg · daily · cycle 10-20 day protocol, 2x/year · route Sub-Q (reported)
21. Half-life: ~2 hours
22. Dose note: The 5–10 mg figure traces to epithalamin, an older pineal extract given 10 mg every 3 days. One analysis puts the human-equivalent dose of synthetic epitalon near 200 mcg a day.
23. Most people take: Injectable 5–10 mg/day ×10–20 days is most common; peptide-db lists 100–500 mcg (sources conflict ~10×).
24. Common: 1–5 mg · 1× daily · 10–20 days, 2–3×/yr · Sub-Q · for general anti-aging [S1] [S2] (reported)
25. Higher: 5–10 mg · 1× daily · 10–20 days, 1–2×/yr · Sub-Q · for telomere protocol [S3] [S4] [S5] (reported)
26. Aggressive: 50–100 mg · 1× daily · 10–20 days · Sublingual · for oral/sublingual users [S3] (reported)

## What people report
27. Injected in short cycles; reported for sleep and a general 'reset'; the best-known longevity peptide.
28. Liked / worked: Melatonin rhythm restored in Russian reports
29. Liked / worked: Better sleep reported
30. Liked / worked: Lower mortality claimed, controversially
31. What worked: Russian reports of restored melatonin rhythm, better sleep, and (controversially) longevity markers.
32. Went wrong / did not work: Telomerase claims not independently confirmed
33. Went wrong / did not work: Lifespan claims rest on one research group
34. What went wrong: The telomerase and lifespan claims are not independently confirmed; the evidence rests on one research tradition.
35. Most reported: Injected in short cycles
36. Most reported: Sleep and a general reset
37. Most reported: The best-known longevity peptide

## What has been tested
38. Aging & senescence: Mortality in elderly cohorts (human)
39. DNA & telomeres: Telomerase activation (cell)
40. Sleep & rhythms: Melatonin rhythm (human)
41. Russian studies, including multi-year human cohorts, claim lower mortality and telomerase activation in cell work; almost no independent Western replication.
42. What it helps: Russian reports describe restored melatonin rhythm and better sleep in older people, and claim lower mortality in elderly cohorts, a controversial result resting on one group. Telomerase activation is cell data only. Users inject it in short cycles and report better sleep and a general reset; it is the best-known longevity peptide.
43. Trial: none. A July 2026 review states no registered clinical studies of Epitalon exist; older human data come from Khavinson group reports from the 2000s. Khavinson bioregulator studied only in unregistered Russian clinical reports; no registry trial found in ClinicalTrials.gov, EU CTR, ISRCTN or ChiCTR, Russian registry unverifiable. (checked 2026-10-23) [S6] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
44. People with active or recent cancer: Activates telomerase in cell studies; most cancers rely on telomerase to keep dividing. (inferred)
45. People on melatonin or sedatives: Raised melatonin output in aged monkeys; effects may add up. (reported)

## Synergies (paired with)
46. Thymalin: Thymalin targets the ageing immune system through T and B cells, Epitalon targets the pineal gland and telomeres, and both come from the same Russian bioregulator programme. Users run them as a combined longevity course. The pair has not been tested together.
47. Pinealon: Both are Khavinson bioregulators, Epitalon for pineal rhythm and ageing, Pinealon for claimed neuron protection, so users run them together for sleep and brain ageing. Neither has independent trials. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
48. DSIP: Epitalon is used for claimed melatonin rhythm and DSIP for deeper sleep, approaching sleep from two angles. Both have weak, inconsistent evidence. The pair itself has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
49. A synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly) designed from epithalamin, a peptide extract of the pineal gland, in Khavinson's lab; the flagship longevity peptide of the Russian school.
50. First studied for: Slowing aging, by (claimed) telomerase activation and pineal/melatonin normalization.
51. Name story: A synthetic four-residue stand-in (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly, hence "AEDG") for Epithalamin, a crude extract of the pineal gland, which sits in the brain region called the epithalamus. Khavinson's St Petersburg lab designed it from the extract's amino acid makeup. [S7] (verified)
52. 1980s to 1990s: Designed from epithalamin, a pineal extract, in Khavinson's lab
53. 2000s: Multi-year Russian human cohorts on aging and mortality
54. Jul 2026: FDA compounding panel recommended it; non-binding, no rule yet
55. Today: The best-known longevity peptide

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where it came from, and the substitution hidden in the story [lab]
56. Epithalamin, a crude polypeptide extract of cattle pineal gland, appears in accessible research from 1973. Epitalon, the four-residue Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly, was later synthesised from the extract's amino acid makeup, and its presence in human pineal extract was first reported only in 2017 [2] (verified).
57. That order matters more than any single study. The most quoted human results, the multi-year mortality cohorts, were done with the extract, not with the synthetic tetrapeptide sold today [4,5] (verified). Treating them as evidence for Epitalon assumes the four residues are the whole active ingredient of a crude extract. That has never been shown (inferred). When the FDA reviewed Epitalon in 2026, it found no human cohort or mortality study of the synthetic peptide at all [1] (verified).

### What is actually in a vial [lab]
58. The FDA found that one nominator's certificate listed a molecular formula matching neither the free base nor the acetate, and another submitted an acetate certificate under free-base identifiers [1] (verified). The acetate certificate that did exist reported 99.5% purity with total impurities up to 2% and single impurities up to 1%, none identified, and no bioburden, endotoxin or aggregate testing [1] (verified). No certificate at all was submitted for the free base.
59. Water solubility of the free base is limited, and the agency doubted that a 3 mg/mL product could be made in water [1]. Reconstituted solution is reported stable 2 to 7 days at 4 degrees [1] (verified).
60. Two identity traps are specific to this peptide. Eight stereoisomers are possible and only the all-L form has been studied, and market products have been checked by mass spectrometry to separate genuine material from the swapped-sequence isomer EADG [2] (verified). Products are sold as acetate or trifluoroacetate salts, which differ in weight and in what else ends up in the vial [2].

### Mechanism, one step at a time, with the model each step came from [mixed]
61. Telomerase, in the originating group's cells. Human fetal lung fibroblasts given 50 ng/mL for four days showed higher telomerase expression and activity and longer telomeres, and treated cultures kept dividing past passage 44 while controls stopped at 34 [1,2] (reported).
62. Telomerase, in an independent lab. A 2025 London university study is the first outside replication and is more complicated than either side tends to quote. In normal fibroblasts and mammary epithelial cells, three weeks at 1 microgram per millilitre raised telomerase activity about 4-fold and 26-fold and lengthened telomeres; four days did nothing. In two breast cancer lines, telomeres also lengthened, but telomerase activity did not rise; instead the alternative, telomerase-independent lengthening pathway (ALT) rose about 10-fold and 3-fold [3] (verified). The authors suggested this supports safe use in healthy people, a claim their experiments did not test [3].
63. Melatonin, in monkeys. Older rhesus monkeys given 2 micrograms per kilogram intramuscularly for 10 days had evening melatonin more than 4-fold higher and evening cortisol about 30% lower; younger monkeys showed no melatonin change [1] (verified). Yet in isolated rat pineal tissue, Epitalon at up to 100 micromolar did not increase melatonin release [1] (verified), so whatever raises melatonin probably does not act on the gland directly.
64. Chromatin, in cells. Decondensation of heterochromatin in lymphocytes from donors aged 76 to 80 is reported from the same group [5] (reported).

### What the body does with it [animals]
65. There is no pharmacokinetic data, including half-life, for either form in any species, people included [1] (verified). The only distribution work gave a fluorescent label to pregnant rabbits; signal appeared in liver, lungs and gut at one hour and weakly in brain, and the agency noted it does not prove the signal was the peptide [1]. The commonly quoted two-hour half-life has no source in the regulatory record (verified as absent).

### The human record [people]
66. For the synthetic peptide, the one randomised placebo-controlled study enrolled 75 women aged 40 to 50, gave about 0.5 mg a day under the tongue for 20 days, and found urinary melatonin metabolite about 1.6 to 1.7-fold higher plus changes in clock gene expression [1,2] (verified). Blinding was not specified, no sleep outcome was measured, and the reported mood improvement (83% against 25%) came without a described method [1]. A retinitis pigmentosa series of 162 patients used 5 micrograms per eye by injection beside the eyeball for 10 days [2] (reported).
67. For the extract, the cohorts are larger and older. A study of 266 people over 60 reported 1.6 to 1.8-fold lower mortality over six years, and up to 4.1-fold with the thymic extract added and yearly courses [5] (reported). A comparison of 39 elderly coronary patients on six courses of epithalamin over three years against 40 on standard therapy reported preserved endurance, normalised melatonin rhythm and lower mortality [4] (verified). The paper's own title says pituitary gland and 15-year follow-up while the abstract describes a pineal peptide over three years [4], which is the kind of inconsistency that should lower confidence.
68. No trial in insomnia, the use reviewed in 2026, has ever been run, and no trial has used injection under the skin [1] (verified). There is no established human dose for the synthetic peptide.

### Safety: what has been looked at, and what has not [mixed]
69. Absent: acute toxicity, repeat-dose toxicity, reproductive toxicity and two-year carcinogenicity [1] (verified). The mouse tumour and lifespan studies used females only, one fixed dose, and at most about 22 weeks of exposure, which the agency said cannot assess cancer risk [1]. No adverse event reports reached the FDA or its food complaint system [1].
70. The cancer question is the honest centre of this compound. A drug designed to lengthen telomeres pushes in the direction that unusually long telomeres point to in population studies, where they are linked to several cancers, which the agency named as an unresolved concern [1] (verified). The independent 2025 data add a specific wrinkle: in cancer cells it switched on a different lengthening pathway [3]. Neither finding shows harm; together they explain why long-term safety data are not optional here (inferred).

### Who produced the evidence [lab]
71. Nearly all pharmacology and every human study come from one St Petersburg group and its partners, much of it in Russian and not verified by the FDA [1,2] (verified). The 2025 review that catalogued this work came from an independent Warsaw pharmacy faculty with no external funding, and it lists inconsistent reporting, very low or non-monotonic doses and unreplicated 1990s data among the limitations [2] (verified). The 2025 telomere replication is genuinely independent [3]. That makes two outside groups engaging seriously, which is more than most compounds of this kind have.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
72. Not an approved drug anywhere, with no EMA-authorised product and no approval in the major European markets or Canada and Australia [1] (verified). In 2024 it sat in the US do-not-compound category [10]. On 24 July 2026 the advisory committee recommended adding it to the bulks list for insomnia, against staff advice [1,6]. The count is reported as 7 to 4 with one abstention by one trade summary and 7 to 5 by a law firm [6,7] (reported); either way it is advisory and needs rulemaking. An interim access policy for certain peptides went to White House review on 14 October 2026, with covered peptides not public [8] (verified).
73. Sport: not named, but with no government approval it falls in the catch-all non-approved class, prohibited at all times [9] (inferred application, verified wording).

### Open questions [mixed]
74. Is the synthetic tetrapeptide the active ingredient of the extract that produced the cohort results? Never tested.
75. What happens to telomeres and cancer risk over years of courses? Unstudied in any species past about five months.
76. Does it improve sleep, measured as sleep? No trial has looked.
77. What reaches the blood after injection or under the tongue, and for how long? No data exist.

# DSIP
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/dsip
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: emideltide, delta-sleep-inducing peptide, Deltaran (DSIP product)
2. Origin: Made by the body
3. Sequence: WAGGDASGE (9 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: Research chemical. The July 2026 FDA compounding advisory panel voted against it.

## Summary
5. DSIP, or Delta Sleep-Inducing Peptide, is a small peptide linked to deep sleep. People inject it before bed for deeper sleep, and it is claimed to dampen stress hormones, though its mechanism is unknown. No gene or receptor for it has ever been found, and the old, small human studies gave inconsistent results.
6. Punch line: Named for deep delta sleep, injected before bed. No gene or receptor ever found; results vary widely.
7. Used for: Sleep

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Sleep & rhythms: Named for deep delta sleep
9. Pain & sensory: Pain relief in old studies
10. Neural protection: Stress protection in animals
11. Reward & urges: Withdrawal studied
12. Endocrine & growth (backed only by animal or user reports): Lowers stress hormones

## How it works
13. Unknown; no gene or receptor ever found · Unidentified · role Sleep & rhythms
   DSIP was isolated from the blood of sleeping rabbits in 1977, but no gene, precursor protein or receptor has ever been found. Its mechanism is unknown, and it may not even be a true mammalian hormone. Everything below rests on effects, not a target.
14. Claimed to promote deep sleep in early studies · Slow-wave EEG, claimed · role Sleep & rhythms
   Early human studies, all given into a vein, claimed more slow-wave, or delta, sleep. Results grew weaker as trials became better designed, and no study has tested it by injection under the skin, the way users take it.
15. Claimed to ease opioid and alcohol withdrawal · Opioid system, claimed · role Reward & urges
   Early studies claimed DSIP eased opioid and alcohol withdrawal, possibly through the body's opioid systems. These were small, older studies with inconsistent results, and the link to opioid receptors was never established.
16. Claimed to dampen stress hormones · ACTH, cortisol, claimed · role Endocrine & growth
   DSIP was claimed to blunt release of ACTH and cortisol, the main stress hormones. Findings were inconsistent across studies and remain unexplained, so this is a historical claim rather than an established effect.
17. Mechanism overview: DSIP, delta sleep-inducing peptide, is a nine amino acid peptide first isolated in 1977 from the blood of sleeping rabbits. No gene or specific receptor has ever been identified, so its mechanism is unknown. Early studies claimed it increases slow-wave delta sleep, dampens ACTH and cortisol stress responses, and eases opioid and alcohol withdrawal, possibly through opioid systems. These effects were inconsistent across studies and remain unexplained.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
18. Typical: 100–200 mcg · as needed · cycle 2-4 weeks, or as needed · route Sub-Q (reported)
19. Half-life: ~7 minutes
20. Most people take: 100-200mcg before bed SC · 2-4 weeks, or as needed. No strict cycling required.
21. Common: 100–250 mcg · 1× nightly, or 3×/wk · 2–8 wk · Sub-Q · for sleep [S1] [S2] (reported)
22. Higher: 300–500 mcg · 1× pre-bed · 2–4 wk · Sub-Q · for poor responders [S3] [S1] (reported)
23. Study: ~25 nmol/kg (~1.5 mg/70 kg) · single or short series · short · IV · for trial reference [S4] (reported)

## What people report
24. Injected before bed; reported for sleep, highly variable.
25. Liked / worked: Some early reports of better sleep
26. Liked / worked: Some stress-hormone effects
27. What worked: Some early reports of improved sleep and stress-hormone effects.
28. Went wrong / did not work: Old, small, inconsistent studies
29. Went wrong / did not work: No mechanism to explain it
30. What went wrong: Evidence is old, small and inconsistent, with no known gene or receptor to explain it.
31. Most reported: Injected before bed
32. Most reported: Reported for sleep
33. Most reported: Highly variable results

## What has been tested
34. Sleep & rhythms: Deep delta-wave sleep (human)
35. Pain & sensory: Chronic pain (human)
36. Endocrine & growth: Stress hormones (human)
37. Small, old human studies on sleep, chronic pain and stress hormones gave mixed results; interest faded for lack of a clear mechanism or gene.
38. What it helps: Small, old human studies gave some reports of deeper delta-wave sleep, effects on stress hormones and use in chronic pain, with inconsistent results. Users inject it before bed for sleep and describe highly variable outcomes. With no known mechanism, there is little to explain why it works for some people and not others.
39. Trial: none. Human sleep and withdrawal studies date to the 1980s and 1990s; no registered trial found, and the Russian product Deltaran has no registry trial on record. (checked 2026-10-23) [S5] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
40. People on opioids or sedatives: DSIP interacts with opioid systems in animal studies; stacking is untested. (inferred)
41. People with narcolepsy or sleep apnea: Unpredictable sedation on top of disordered breathing or sleep. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
42. Pinealon: DSIP is taken for sleep onset and Pinealon for claimed melatonin support and neuron protection, aiming at sleep from two angles. Both rest on weak evidence. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
43. Epitalon: Epitalon is used for claimed melatonin rhythm, DSIP for deeper sleep, so users pair them in sleep and ageing courses. Both have weak and inconsistent evidence. The pair has not been tested together.
44. Magnesium glycinate: Magnesium glycinate is a common sleep supplement, and magnesium plays a role in calming nerve signalling. Users add it to DSIP as a low-risk sleep base. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
45. Delta Sleep-Inducing Peptide, found in 1977 in the blood of rabbits put to sleep by brain stimulation. The oddity: no gene for it has ever been found.
46. First studied for: Promoting deep (delta-wave) sleep.
47. Name story: Delta Sleep-Inducing Peptide: named in 1974 by a Swiss team that pulled it from the brain blood of rabbits kept in induced sleep, and credited it with bringing on delta, or slow-wave, EEG sleep. [S6] (verified)
48. 1977: Found in blood of rabbits put to sleep by brain stimulation
49. 1980s: Small human studies on sleep, pain and stress hormones
50. Jul 2026: FDA compounding panel voted against it
51. Today: A sleep peptide curiosity; still no gene or receptor found

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where it came from, and the origin that never resolved [animals]
52. A Swiss group isolated the nonapeptide Trp-Ala-Gly-Gly-Asp-Ala-Ser-Gly-Glu from the cerebral venous blood of rabbits held in electrically induced sleep, with the defining papers dated 1977 [2] (verified). Its regulatory name is emideltide [1].
53. Half a century later, no gene, precursor protein or receptor has been found, and its site of synthesis is unknown [2] (reported). A database search lines the sequence up with a hypothetical protein from a soil bacterium, which raises the possibility, unproven, that what was isolated was not a mammalian hormone at all [2] (speculated). DSIP-like material has been measured in the hypothalamus, pituitary, gut, breast milk and blood, but immunoreactivity is not the same as proof of an endogenous peptide (inferred).

### What is actually in a vial [lab]
54. One certificate submitted to the FDA listed the formula C35H57N13O14S2, which the agency said corresponds to no form of emideltide; another tested for acetic acid but carried free-base identifiers [1] (verified). Neither form's certificate set impurity limits, and none reported endotoxin, bioburden or aggregates [1].
55. Solubility is a real constraint. The free base dissolves in water at about 0.5 mg/mL, so the proposed 1 mg/mL injection may not be achievable with it; the acetate dissolves at about 10 mg/mL in buffer [1] (verified). Supplier guidance recommends a carrier protein for long-term storage and warns against freeze-thaw [1].

### What the body does with it [mixed]
56. In vitro half-life is about 15 minutes, set by an aminopeptidase-like enzyme [2] (reported). It may circulate partly bound to carrier proteins, but that has not been confirmed. Human plasma levels of DSIP-like material are reported to fall at sleep onset, the opposite of what a sleep-inducing signal might predict, and levels in depression are reported both higher and lower by different studies [2] (reported).
57. No pharmacokinetic study by subcutaneous injection exists in people, and the FDA found no human trial by that route at all [1] (verified).

### The human record, which got weaker as it got better designed [people]
58. Every human trial gave DSIP intravenously, at 25 to 35 nanomoles per kilogram [1] (verified). The pattern across them is worth seeing whole.
59. The early, smaller or externally controlled studies looked positive. In 6 middle-aged insomniacs in a crossover, sleep improved from the second to the sixth hour after a slight arousal in the first. In 14 people given seven nightly injections, sleep latency fell from 58.4 to 27.6 minutes and total sleep rose from 313 to 385 minutes, but against an externally matched group, not a true placebo [1] (verified).
60. The properly placebo-controlled studies did not hold up. In 16 insomniacs over three nights, there was no significant objective difference against placebo, and the authors called the benefit little. In 6 severe insomniacs in a randomised crossover, there was no significant difference from placebo or baseline [1] (verified).
61. Narcolepsy rests on one 35-year-old man: sleep attacks fell from six to three, better with morning dosing [1]. In withdrawal, an uncontrolled study of 60 opioid users reported a good decrease in signs in 40 of those assessed, with anxiety and insomnia returning 24 to 72 hours later; a later open study of 7 saw withdrawal scores fall from 34.4 to 17.8 after the first injection, but only 2 finished and 2 needed another sleep drug [1] (verified). The authors of that later study called effectiveness an open question.
62. There is no established human dose by any route people use now.

### Safety and quality concerns [mixed]
63. What the trials recorded: transient arousal in the first hour, delayed effects on sleep 13 to 22 hours later, and rebound anxiety and insomnia after withdrawal treatment stopped [1] (verified). Long-term safety has never been studied [2].
64. The agency's main concern was not toxicity but identity and immunogenicity: an injectable peptide with unidentified impurities and no aggregate data, given repeatedly [1] (verified). A Russian preparation, Deltaran, is reported to have extended maximum lifespan in ageing mice by about 24% [2] (reported), but no human safety record follows from that.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
65. Not a registered drug in any country searched, and in no major pharmacopoeia [1] (verified). Listed in the US do-not-compound category in 2024 [6]. On 24 July 2026 the advisory committee voted 6 in favour, 7 against, with one abstention, for opioid withdrawal, chronic insomnia and narcolepsy, making it the only one of seven peptides that day not recommended [3,4] (verified). FDA staff had also recommended against [1].
66. Sport: not named, but with no government approval it falls within the catch-all non-approved class, prohibited at all times [5] (inferred application, verified wording).

### Open questions [mixed]
67. Is it a mammalian peptide? Without a gene or precursor, the question from 1977 is still open.
68. Does it do anything under the skin? The route in use today has never been tested in a human trial.
69. Why did effects shrink as controls improved? The honest reading is that the early signal was mostly expectation and night-to-night variation, but a larger modern trial would settle it (inferred).
