# Semax + Selank
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/semax-selank
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Semax/Selank 20 mg, Semax/Selank 10 mg, Russian nootropic stack, Selank-Semax nasal spray
2. Origin: Blend of 2 peptides
3. Legal and approval status: Russia: both approved medicines (Semax on the national essential drug list since 2011). US: not approved; Semax removed from FDA Category 2 on 15 Apr 2026 and won an 8-5-1 PCAC vote in July 2026; Selank was not on that list. WADA: neither named; S0 applies.

## Summary
4. Semax + Selank combines two Russian heptapeptides: Semax, an ACTH(4-10) analogue, and Selank, a tuftsin analogue. People stack them for calm, focused thinking, with Semax raising BDNF and alertness and Selank slowing the breakdown of calming peptides. Each has Russian clinical data, but the pair has only one rat study and user reports. A fixed blend stops you adjusting each one, and Semax late in the day can disrupt sleep.
5. Punch line: The Russian nootropic stack, usually a morning nasal spray. Semax drives focus, Selank removes the jitter.
6. Used for: Focus with calm

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Cognition: Semax raises BDNF in animal brain
8. Mood: Selank calms anxiety (Russian trials)
9. Drive & mental stamina: Semax activating, dopamine-linked
10. Neural protection: Semax used after stroke in Russia
11. Sleep & rhythms (backed only by animal or user reports): Late Semax disrupts sleep
12. Immunity (backed only by animal or user reports): Selank shifts cytokine balance

## How it works
13. Raises brain growth factor · BDNF and TrkB up in hippocampus · role Cognition
   Semax raises BDNF, a growth factor for nerve cells, and its receptor TrkB in the hippocampus, the memory centre. More BDNF signalling favours learning, new connections and nerve cell survival after injury. This is shown in animal studies; Russian clinical use covers stroke recovery and cognition.
14. Lifts alertness · Dopamine and serotonin modulation · role Drive & mental stamina
   Semax adjusts dopamine and serotonin activity, the brain chemicals for drive and mood. That gives the activating, alert side of the pair. The neurotransmitter effects come from animal studies; Russian clinical data cover Semax, but Western replication is limited.
15. Slows breakdown of calming peptides · Enkephalinase inhibition · role Mood
   Both peptides slow enkephalinase, the enzymes that break down enkephalins, the body's own calming opioid peptides. In human serum in a test tube, both blocked these enzymes. Whether two blockers of the same enzymes add up has never been measured.
16. Shifts immune signalling · IL-6 and T-helper cytokine balance · role Immunity
   Selank shifts immune messengers, including IL-6 and the T-helper cytokine balance. It was developed from tuftsin, an immune peptide. A 2022 rat social-stress study of the pair reported restored immune responses; there are no human data for this effect.
17. Mechanism overview: Semax (Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro) is ACTH(4-10) with a Pro-Gly-Pro tail for stability; in animals it raises hippocampal BDNF and TrkB and modulates dopamine and serotonin. Selank (Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg-Pro-Gly-Pro) extends tuftsin with the same tail; it inhibits enkephalin-degrading enzymes, shifts IL-6 and T-helper cytokine balance and alters serotonin metabolism. Both share enkephalinase inhibition; Semax leans activating, Selank anxiolytic.

## What is inside the blend
18. Semax: 10 mg · Focus, alertness, BDNF
19. Selank: 10 mg · Calm, anxiety relief
20. Most common ratio: Semax 10 · Selank 10 = 20 mg (12 of 13 listings)
21. Other ratio seen: Semax 5 · Selank 5 = 10 mg (1 listing)
22. Other ratio seen: N-Acetyl Semax 10 · N-Acetyl Selank 10 = 20 mg (1 listing (within the 12, acetylated form))
23. Version Most listings: Semax 10 · Selank 10 = 20 mg
24. Version Smaller vial: Semax 5 · Selank 5 = 10 mg
25. Version High-Selank vial (one seller): Selank 30 · Semax 10 = 40 mg
26. Version Nasal spray: Semax 50 mcg · Selank 50 mcg per spray = 11 mg / 110 sprays
27. Why Semax is in it: The activating, focus side; Selank alone can feel sedating
28. Why Selank is in it: Takes the edge off Semax's stimulation and anxiety
29. Mixing chemistry: Semax carries Met and His, so it is the one that oxidises; keep the vial cold and dark (guides say wrap in foil).
30. Mixing chemistry: Selank (TKPRPGP) has no Met, His or Asn and is chemically quiet.
31. Mixing chemistry: Both end in Pro-Gly-Pro, added for resistance to breakdown; similar size and charge suggests they share a vial comfortably.
32. Mixing chemistry: Nasal sprays are liquid from the start; formulation and preservative are rarely disclosed.
33. Mixing chemistry: Avoid freeze-thaw cycles.
34. Self-mixing: Separate vials or sprays let you titrate each and take Selank alone at night; most guides prefer this, and the two-spray format is the more common purchase.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
35. Typical: 250–300 mcg of each · 1–2× daily, mornings · cycle 2–4 weeks on, then break · route Nasal, Sub-Q (reported)
36. Half-life: per component
37. Most people take: About 300 mcg of each, 1:1. A 10 + 10 mg vial in 4 mL: 10 units gives 250 mcg of each (a 5 + 5 mg vial in 2 mL gives the same). Combined sprays run about 50 mcg of each per spray.

## What people report
38. Nasal or Sub-Q, mornings. Common: about 300 mcg of each, 1:1. Selank often started alone for a week before Semax is added. Cycles 2 to 4 weeks on, then a break.
39. Liked / worked: Both approved medicines in Russia
40. Liked / worked: Users report focus without jitter
41. Liked / worked: Selank matched medazepam in a 62-patient anxiety trial
42. What worked: Users report clearer thinking, calm sustained focus, steadier mood and better stress handling; one writer says Semax alone feels anxious in meetings while the pair suits collaborative work. Aggregator scores: Semax 7.1, Selank 6.8 out of 10.
43. Went wrong / did not work: No human trial of the pair
44. Went wrong / did not work: Fixed ratio blocks separate titration
45. Went wrong / did not work: Semax late in the day hurts sleep
46. What went wrong: Semax: overstimulation, headache, sleep problems if dosed after about 2 pm, nasal irritation. Selank: drowsiness, appetite increase, emotional flattening at higher doses. A fixed blend stops you titrating each one; guides suggest running each alone first.
47. Most reported: About 300 mcg of each, mornings
48. Most reported: Selank first, Semax added later
49. Most reported: Nasal spray most common

## What has been tested
50. Each has Russian clinical studies (Selank: a 62-patient anxiety trial against medazepam). Together: a 2022 rat study gave both in a social-stress model and reported restored immune responses. No human trial of the pair.
51. What it helps: Each has Russian clinical data: Semax for stroke recovery and cognition, Selank for generalised anxiety (62 patients vs medazepam). The pair has one rat social-stress study and user reports of calm focus. Western replication is limited.

## Who shouldn't take it
52. People with a history of seizures: Russian prescribing info lists convulsive disorders as a contraindication. (reported)
53. People on benzodiazepines or other sedatives: Selank modulates GABA-A receptors; effects may stack. (inferred)
54. People with acute psychosis or severe anxiety: Raises dopamine and serotonin turnover; Russian label excludes acute psychotic states. (reported)
55. People on opioids: Selank slows enkephalin breakdown, prolonging the body’s own opioids. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
56. NA Semax Amidate: NA Semax Amidate is Semax capped at both ends to last longer, assumed to act like Semax. Adding it doubles the focus side of the pair. No study tests the capped form or the stack.
57. NA Selank Amidate: NA Selank Amidate is Selank capped at both ends for longer action, assumed to act like Selank. Adding it strengthens the calm side. The capped form has no trial data, and the stack has not been tested.
58. Pinealon: Pinealon is a Khavinson bioregulator studied for neuron protection under oxidative stress and sleep rhythm, adding a protection angle to focus and calm. A four-peptide blend pairs it with capped Semax and Selank, but the combination has not been tested.
59. PE-22-28: PE-22-28 blocks the TREK-1 potassium channel, a mood route neither Semax nor Selank uses, with antidepressant-like effects in mice. People add it for mood. The pairing has not been tested together.
60. Cerebrolysin: Cerebrolysin is a pig brain peptide mix with nerve growth factor-like activity and stroke and dementia trial data, overlapping Semax's BDNF effect. People stack them for brain recovery. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
61. Two Russian heptapeptides in one vial or spray: Semax, an ACTH(4-10) analogue for focus, and Selank, a tuftsin analogue for calm.
62. First studied for: Each was developed and approved in Russia for clinical use (Semax for stroke and cognition, Selank for anxiety). Paired by users as a focused-but-calm stack.
63. 1980s to 1990s: Semax developed from ACTH(4-10) in Moscow
64. 2000s: Selank developed from tuftsin; approved in Russia for anxiety
65. 2011: Semax added to Russia's essential drug list
66. 2022: Rat study tests both in social stress
67. Apr 2026: Semax removed from FDA Category 2
68. Today: Sold mostly as 10 + 10 mg vials (5 + 5 smaller) and 1:1 nasal sprays

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Was the pair ever studied together? [mixed]
69. Not as a combination in people. No human trial of the two given together has been located, and no registered trial exists (verified as absent in the sources reviewed). The two come from the same Moscow institute and often appear in the same papers, but side by side rather than together: in rats with Parkinson-like damage, for example, each peptide was tested on its own, neither changed motor activity, and only Selank reduced anxiety [4] (verified).
70. The one direct head-to-head measurement is biochemical. In human serum in a test tube, both inhibited enkephalin-degrading enzymes, Semax at an IC50 of about 10 micromolar and Selank at about 20 [3] (verified). Whether two inhibitors of the same enzymes add, overlap or simply saturate the same target has never been measured (inferred).

### The two licensed labels pull against each other [people]
71. This is the most concrete fact about the pairing, and it rarely gets mentioned. The Russian Semax label lists anxiety disorders, acute psychosis and a history of seizures among its contraindications [1] (verified). The Russian Selank label exists for anxiety states and adjustment disorders [2] (verified).
72. The usual reason for pairing them, Selank to take the edge off Semax's stimulation, therefore runs into Semax's own label: in its country of approval it is not meant for people with an anxiety disorder at all (verified that the contraindication exists; what it means for the pair is inferred). Someone who feels anxious on Semax is, by that label, someone the drug was not meant for, and adding a second peptide is a workaround nobody has tested.

### Licensed products versus the blended vial [lab]
73. Both registered medicines are separate nasal drops from the same Russian manufacturer, each preserved with methylparaben: Semax at 0.1% or 1%, Selank at 0.15% [1,2] (verified). No licensed product combines them (inferred, none located).
74. The solubility arithmetic is worth doing. A 10 + 10 mg vial in 4 mL holds 2.5 mg/mL of each. The documented water solubility of Semax free base is about 2 mg/mL, rising to about 10 mg/mL in phosphate buffer [5] (verified). On those figures, free-base Semax would sit just above its limit in plain water, so a vial that dissolves cleanly is most likely using the salt form or a buffered diluent (inferred, assuming the figures carry over into the mixture).
75. Shelf life is set by the shorter-lived part. Reconstituted Semax is quoted as stable only 2 to 7 days in the fridge [5] (verified), and no comparable figure has been published for Selank. A mixed vial used over weeks is outside any documented stability window (inferred).

### Two peptides that are both gone in minutes [mixed]
76. Selank's label gives 92.8% nasal bioavailability, plasma detection at about 30 seconds and levels falling away over 5 to 5.5 minutes [2] (verified). Semax's label gives up to 60 to 70% nasal uptake and arrival in the brain within about 4 minutes, while claiming an effect lasting 20 to 24 hours [1] (verified). In rats, peak brain Semax after nasal dosing was about 0.072% of the dose [5].
77. Both are cleared by the same tissue peptidases, and both inhibit enkephalin-degrading peptidases. Whether either slows the other's breakdown, lengthening exposure in a way neither label describes, is a plausible question that has never been asked (speculated). By injection, which many blends assume, neither has any human exposure data [5] (verified for Semax).

### The evidence is uneven between the two [people]
78. Semax has had a full regulatory review. The FDA found two usable clinical references for its proposed uses, both small and uncontrolled; in the pain study the authors themselves concluded Semax has no analgesic activity by itself [5] (verified). Its rodent profile includes antithrombotic effects and potentiation of amphetamine-induced dopamine release, both unstudied in people [5].
79. Selank has no regulatory review in English. Its accessible human record is a handful of small Russian trials, compared against benzodiazepines or uncontrolled, none with a placebo arm (reported; see the Selank entry). So one half of the blend has been examined and found thin, and the other half has not been examined.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
80. Semax: recommended for the US bulks list by the advisory committee on 24 July 2026, 8 to 5 with one abstention, against FDA staff advice; still needs rulemaking [5,6] (verified). Selank: not reviewed; its acetate nomination was removed from the do-not-compound category earlier because the nominator meant a different substance [7] (verified). An interim access policy for certain peptides went to White House review on 14 October 2026, peptides not yet named [8] (verified). A blend therefore pairs one substance recommended but not yet permitted with one sitting outside every category (inferred).
81. Sport: neither is named on the 2026 list. Both hold Russian approvals, which arguably takes them outside the catch-all non-approved class [9], but the list does not address them and athletes cannot assume either is allowed (inferred).

### Open questions [mixed]
82. Does the pair do anything either does not do alone? Untested in any species as a combination.
83. Should someone who gets anxious on Semax be taking it at all? Its own label says not, and that question deserves an answer before a second peptide is added.
84. How long does a mixed vial stay potent? Unmeasured, with one component documented at days.
85. Do the two change each other's breakdown? A simple plasma study could answer it.

# Thymosin Alpha-1
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/thymosin-alpha-1
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: thymalfasin, Zadaxin, Timosina, Tα1
2. Origin: Fragment of a natural protein
3. Sequence: SDAAVDTSSEITTKDLKEKKEVVEEAEN (28 amino acids). Acetylated start, not shown
4. Shown with an FDA approved badge
5. Legal and approval status: Approved in about 35 countries (China and Italy among them) as Zadaxin; not FDA-approved.

## Summary
6. Thymosin Alpha-1 is a 28-amino-acid peptide from the thymus that tunes the immune response, especially T-cells and dendritic cells. It is approved in about 35 countries as Zadaxin, including for hepatitis B, and is used as an immune adjuvant, with users reporting immune resilience. It is not FDA-approved, and trials in melanoma, COVID-19 and sepsis were inconclusive or mixed.
7. Punch line: Thymus peptide that trains T cells. Approved as Zadaxin in about 35 countries, including for hepatitis B.
8. Used for: Immune support, chronic infection

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
9. Immunity: Trains T cells and immune response
10. Inflammatory signaling: Balances inflammation
11. Aging & senescence: Supports the aging immune system
12. Organ function: Used in hepatitis
13. Neural protection (backed only by animal or user reports): Studied for nerves
14. Cancer biology (backed only by animal or user reports): Added to cancer treatment abroad

## How it works
15. Matures and activates T-cells · T-cell maturation · role Immunity
   Thymosin alpha-1, a natural peptide from the thymus, helps young T-cells mature and become active. T-cells are the immune cells that target infected and abnormal cells. This underpins its approval as thymalfasin in many countries outside the US.
16. Primes dendritic cells · TLR2, TLR9 · role Immunity
   It acts at TLR2 and TLR9, sensors on dendritic cells that normally detect germs, and switches on MyD88 signalling. That primes dendritic cells, the scouts that show threats to T-cells, strengthening the immune response. This comes from cell and animal work.
17. Boosts antiviral interferon and NK activity · IFN-α/γ, NK cells · role Immunity
   Through this priming it raises interferon alpha and gamma, key antiviral messengers, and increases natural killer (NK) cell activity. This supports antiviral and antitumour defence, shown in lab studies and reflected in its use as a vaccine and chemotherapy adjuvant.
18. Rebalances inflammation in sepsis trials · Cytokine balance · role Inflammatory signaling
   In hyperinflammation it rebalances cytokines, the immune signalling molecules, rather than simply boosting them. This is why it was tested in sepsis. Human trials gave mixed results, and a large sepsis trial reportedly showed no survival gain.
19. Helps clear hepatitis B; approved outside the US · HBV, immune adjuvant · role Organ function
   By strengthening T-cell and interferon responses it helps the body clear hepatitis B virus. Phase 3 use led to approval for chronic hepatitis B in many countries, though US trials were not definitive.
20. Mechanism overview: Thymosin alpha-1 is a 28 amino acid peptide first isolated from thymus tissue. It acts as an agonist at TLR2 and TLR9 on dendritic cells and other immune cells, triggering MyD88 signalling. That primes dendritic cells, promotes T-cell maturation and raises interferon alpha and gamma and NK cell activity, strengthening antiviral and antitumour defence. It also rebalances cytokines during hyperinflammation, which is why it was studied in sepsis. It is approved as thymalfasin in many countries.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
21. Typical: 1.6 mg · twice weekly · cycle 4-week cycles, 2-4x/year · route Sub-Q (verified)
22. Half-life: ~2 hours
23. Most people take: 1.6mg 2x/week SC · 4-week cycles, 2-4x/year. Some chronic conditions use continuous.
24. Label / common: 1.6 mg · 2× weekly · 8–12 wk (hep B 26 wk) · Sub-Q · for immune support; label dose [S1] [S2] (reported)
25. Acute: 1.6 mg · daily 3–14 days, then 2× weekly; ICU q12h × 7 d · 2–4 wk · Sub-Q · for acute illness; sepsis trial [S1] [S2] (reported)
26. High: 3–6.4 mg · 2–3× weekly · 4–8 wk · Sub-Q · for aggressive immune cycles [S2] (reported)

## What people report
27. Reported for immune resilience and recovery; among the more evidence-backed immune peptides.
28. Liked / worked: Approved and widely used for hepatitis abroad
29. Liked / worked: Used as an immune adjuvant
30. What worked: Approved and used widely abroad for hepatitis and as an immune adjuvant.
31. Went wrong / did not work: US hepatitis and melanoma trials not definitive
32. Went wrong / did not work: COVID studies small and mixed
33. Went wrong / did not work: Large sepsis trial: no survival gain (reported)
34. What went wrong: Never FDA-approved; US hepatitis and melanoma trials were not definitive; COVID studies were small and mixed, and a large sepsis trial reported no survival benefit (reported).
35. Most reported: Immune resilience and recovery
36. Most reported: Among the better-backed immune peptides

## What has been tested
37. Immunity: Hepatitis B and C (trial)
38. Cancer biology: Chemotherapy adjuvant (trial)
39. Immunity: Sepsis (trial)
40. Immunity: COVID-19 (trial)
41. Immunity: Vaccine adjuvant (human)
42. Approved in many countries (not the US): Phase 3 use in hepatitis B and C, as a chemotherapy adjuvant, and studied in sepsis and COVID-19.
43. What it helps: Approved in many countries outside the US for hepatitis B and used as an immune adjuvant with vaccines and chemotherapy. US hepatitis and melanoma trials were not definitive, COVID-19 studies were small and mixed, and a large sepsis trial reportedly showed no survival gain. Users report it for immune resilience and recovery; it is among the better-backed immune peptides.
44. Trial: active · Phase 2 · low lymphocyte counts in blood cancer patients · NCT06584006 · The First Affiliated Hospital of Xiamen University. Approved as Zadaxin in China and dozens of other countries, and still heavily trialled in China, from sepsis to boosting cancer immunotherapy. (checked 2026-10-23) [S3] (verified)

## Who shouldn't take it
45. Transplant recipients on anti-rejection drugs: Boosts T-cell activity, working against anti-rejection drugs; excluded in label info. (reported)
46. People with autoimmune disease: Stimulating T cells can flare autoimmunity. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
47. KPV: Thymosin alpha-1 strengthens antiviral and T-cell defence, while KPV calms inflammation through NF-κB, mostly shown in mice. People pair them to support immunity while damping excess inflammation. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
48. A 28-amino-acid peptide from the thymus (Zadaxin), a tuner of the immune response, especially T-cells and dendritic cells.
49. First studied for: Supporting immune responses in infection and cancer, and as a vaccine adjuvant.
50. Name story: 'Alpha' is about electric charge, not structure: Goldstein's group sorted calf-thymus 'fraction 5' peptides by isoelectric point (alpha acidic, beta near-neutral, gamma basic). This was the first acidic one, sequenced in 1977; the synthetic drug is thymalfasin. [S4] (verified)
51. 1970s: Isolated from the thymus as an immune tuner
52. 1990s to 2000s: Approved abroad as Zadaxin for hepatitis and as an adjuvant
53. 2020s: Small, mixed COVID studies; large sepsis trial no survival gain (reported)
54. Today: Approved in about 35 countries; not FDA-approved

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where it came from, and why it is different from most peptides here [lab]
55. Thymosin alpha-1 is a 28-residue peptide first isolated from a calf thymus extract; the drug version, thymalfasin, is synthetic [6] (verified). It is a natural human peptide: healthy adults carry about 0.1 to 1 ng/mL in serum, highest in the thymus [1] (verified).
56. What sets it apart is that a licensed, manufacturer-controlled product exists. Zadaxin is supplied as a 1.6 mg vial for subcutaneous injection, made in Italy, with a licence holder in Singapore and indications in chronic hepatitis B and, with interferon, hepatitis C [7] (verified). Its approvals span Asia-Pacific, Latin America, Eastern Europe and the Middle East, plus Italy as a flu vaccine adjuvant for immunocompromised people, India for hepatitis B, and an EMA orphan designation in liver cancer [1] (reported; the FDA could not verify the manufacturer's full country list).

### What is actually in a vial, licensed versus not [lab]
57. The licensed product is reconstituted with its own 1 mL of sterile water just before use, and the label is clear it is subcutaneous only, not intravenous [7] (verified).
58. Material outside that channel is a different question. Reviewing the US nomination, the FDA found free base and acetate confused in the paperwork, certificates without impurity, aggregate, bioburden or endotoxin data, and doubted that the proposed 3 mg/mL could be reached given limited water solubility; the highest concentration it found used clinically was 2 mg/mL [1,2] (verified). The research-grade powder does not inherit the licensed product's quality record (inferred).

### Mechanism, one step at a time, with the model each step came from [mixed]
59. Dendritic cells, in cells and mice. In dendritic cells exposed to the fungus Aspergillus, the peptide drove maturation and IL-12 production through p38 MAPK and NF-kappaB, dependent on MyD88 and Toll-like receptor signalling; in mice it strengthened Th1 antifungal immunity and protected highly susceptible transplant recipients from aspergillosis [5] (verified). This is the study most often cited for the TLR mechanism, and it is a fungal infection model.
60. T cells and cytokines, in people. Clinical and lab work summarised for hepatitis B describes effects on T-cell development, higher interferon-gamma and IL-2, and more NK cell killing [6] (reported).
61. Vaccines, in mice. Anti-tetanus antibodies were about 25 to 35% higher in young mice given the peptide, but there was no boost with a pneumococcal vaccine [1] (verified). The adjuvant effect is real in some settings and absent in others.

### What the body does with it [people]
62. After 1.6 to 2.2 mg under the skin in healthy volunteers, peak levels were 32.6 to 78.9 ng/mL at 0.67 to 2 hours, half-life was 1.8 to 2.6 hours, and five daily doses did not accumulate [1] (verified). Levels return near baseline within about a day.
63. Set against the endogenous range, one standard dose raises blood levels roughly 30 to several hundred times above normal for a few hours (inferred from the two ranges). The twice-weekly schedule therefore produces pulses, not a steady state, and the immune effects are presumed to outlast the drug.

### The human record, where size changes the answer [people]
64. Hepatitis B is the indication that built its reputation. Seven randomised trials of 1.6 mg twice weekly for six months reported a significantly higher sustained response than no treatment, with a peculiar timing: benefit was not obvious on treatment and complete virological response rose gradually after it stopped [6] (reported). These trials predate today's antivirals.
65. Sepsis is where the record turned. A 2025 meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials, all from China, found lower 28-day mortality overall (odds ratio 0.73), but the benefit came from the six lower-quality trials (odds ratio 0.41, 359 patients); the five higher-quality trials showed no significant effect (0.82, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.03), and the test for publication bias was positive [4] (verified).
66. The largest trial settles most of that. TESTS randomised 1,106 adults with sepsis at 22 Chinese centres to 1.6 mg every 12 hours or placebo for seven days. Day-28 mortality was 23.4% against 24.1%, hazard ratio 0.99 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.27); 90-day mortality was also no different [3] (verified). Exploratory subgroups pointed both ways, worse under 60 (hazard ratio 1.67) and better with diabetes (0.58), neither surviving correction for multiple testing [3].
67. In the US it was trialled in cancer from the early 1980s; a phase 1 escalation in 14 patients reached 9.6 mg/m2 without a dose-limiting toxicity [1] (verified). More than 4,400 trial subjects are cited across infections, cancers and vaccines [1], but no US approval followed.

### Safety: a real record, with real limits [mixed]
68. Of all the peptides in this library, this one has the most human safety data. In TESTS, adverse events (66.4% against 67.6%) and serious adverse events (26.8% against 29.3%) matched placebo [3] (verified). The manufacturer reports over 17 million doses given with infrequent, mild adverse experiences, an estimate from manufacturer-affiliated authors [1] (reported). Injection-site redness and discomfort are the common complaint [1].
69. The licensed label contraindicates it in people being deliberately immunosuppressed, such as transplant recipients, unless benefit clearly outweighs risk, because it is designed to stimulate immunity [7] (verified). Anyone with an autoimmune condition faces the same logic, though that has not been formally studied (inferred).
70. The gaps: no carcinogenicity study, and the acute and 13-week toxicology the manufacturer reports (no signals up to 20 mg/kg once, or 6 mg/kg a day) was never provided to the FDA as data [1] (verified). The FDA's adverse event system held one report, in a hepatitis C patient also on peginterferon [1].

### Who produced the evidence [people]
71. The licence holder co-funded TESTS, and several authors reported grants or consulting fees from it [3] (verified). That trial is also the one that found no effect, which counts in favour of its credibility. The sepsis meta-analysis found that the positive signal sat in small single-centre trials [4], a familiar pattern for industry-adjacent fields.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
72. Not FDA-approved; no NDA has been approved, though four US orphan designations exist [1,2] (verified). It left the do-not-compound category when its nominator withdrew [8], and at the December 2024 advisory committee the members voted 17 to 4 against adding either form to the bulks list, the acetate vote citing a lack of convincing effectiveness data [2] (verified). It was not part of the 2026 peptide votes.
73. Sport: not named on the 2026 Prohibited List [9]. Because it is approved in several countries, the catch-all non-approved class does not obviously apply (inferred). Thymosin beta-4 and its fragments are a different molecule and are explicitly banned [9] (verified).

### Open questions [mixed]
74. Does it help hepatitis B on top of modern antivirals? The original trials compared it to nothing.
75. Is there any group in sepsis that benefits? TESTS hints at subgroups but cannot prove one.
76. Is research-grade powder equivalent to the licensed product? Unknown without impurity and endotoxin testing.
77. What does repeated immune stimulation do over years in healthy people? Unstudied.

# Orforglipron
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/orforglipron
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Foundayo, LY3502970, OWL833, LY-3502970
2. Origin: Not a peptide: small molecule
3. Shown with an FDA approved badge
4. Legal and approval status: FDA-approved as Foundayo for chronic weight management on 1 Apr 2026; type 2 diabetes submission pending at FDA. UK approval Aug 2026 (reported); EMA CHMP positive opinion for obesity and T2D on 16 Oct 2026, EU decision pending. Not compoundable; WADA does not ban GLP-1 agonists.

## Summary
5. Orforglipron is a small-molecule, non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist taken as a pill. It quiets hunger, slows the stomach and raises insulin when glucose is high, and it is FDA-approved for chronic weight management. It causes less weight loss than injectable semaglutide or tirzepatide, GI effects are common, and it cannot be compounded.
6. Punch line: Non-peptide GLP-1 pill. No fasting rules; milder than shots, often used to keep weight off after them.
7. Used for: Weight loss, type 2 diabetes

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Appetite & satiety: Quiets hunger, in pill form
9. Glucose & insulin: Beat oral semaglutide on HbA1c
10. Fat metabolism: About 12% weight loss
11. Reward & urges: GLP-1 craving dampening (class)
12. Heart & vessels (backed only by animal or user reports): CV safety shown in ACHIEVE-4
13. Digestive & gut (backed only by animal or user reports): Nausea, constipation common

## How it works
14. Switches on the GLP-1 receptor from a pill · Non-peptide GLP-1R agonist · role Appetite & satiety
   Orforglipron is a small molecule, not a peptide, that sits in a pocket of the GLP-1 receptor different from where the natural hormone binds. It still switches the receptor on, leaning toward G-protein signalling. Because it survives digestion it works as a daily pill, as shown in Phase 3 trials in people.
15. Quiets hunger and slows the stomach · GLP-1R, hypothalamus and gut · role Appetite & satiety
   Through GLP-1 receptors in the hypothalamus and brainstem it lowers hunger, and in the gut it slows stomach emptying. People eat less without trying to. In ATTAIN-1 this produced clear weight loss against placebo over 72 weeks in adults without diabetes.
16. Raises insulin when glucose is high · GLP-1R, beta cells · role Glucose & insulin
   On pancreatic beta cells it raises insulin release only when glucose is high, the standard GLP-1 effect. That lowers blood sugar with little risk of lows on its own. In the ACHIEVE trials HbA1c fell further than on oral semaglutide in people with type 2 diabetes.
17. Cleared by the liver over ~1.5 days · CYP3A4 metabolism · role Glucose & insulin
   The liver breaks it down mainly through the enzyme CYP3A4, and most leaves in the faeces. A half-life of one to two days suits daily dosing. The practical cost is drug interactions: strong CYP3A4 blockers raise its levels and strong inducers cut them, a new issue for this class.
18. Dampens food reward (class effect) · Mesolimbic GLP-1R · role Reward & urges
   GLP-1 receptors in the brain's reward circuit, the mesolimbic system, damp the pull of food and other rewards. This is a class effect seen with injectable GLP-1 drugs and in animal work. It has not been measured for orforglipron specifically, so it is inferred from the class.
19. Mechanism overview: Orforglipron is a non-peptide small molecule that binds the GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) and activates it like the native hormone, but survives digestion and absorbs without the fasting rules oral semaglutide needs. It acts in the hypothalamus and brainstem to cut hunger, in the gut to slow emptying, and on pancreatic beta cells to raise insulin only when glucose is high. It is cleared by the liver through CYP3A4 with a half-life of about one to two days, which suits daily dosing.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
20. Typical: 0.8–17.2 mg tablet · once daily · cycle Ongoing; step up every 30+ days · route Oral (verified)
21. Half-life: 29–49 hours
22. Most people take: Oral tablet daily, any time, with or without food: 0.8 → 2.5 → 5.5 mg, then 9, 14.5 or 17.2 mg. Trial capsules were 1–36 mg (36 mg capsule = 17.2 mg tablet).

## What people report
23. Mostly anticipatory chatter before approval; since launch, users note oral convenience and GI upset. It cannot be compounded, so cheap copies are research-chemical powders.
24. Liked / worked: 12.4% weight loss on top dose
25. Liked / worked: Beat oral semaglutide on HbA1c and weight
26. Liked / worked: No food or water timing rules
27. Liked / worked: CV safety supported
28. What worked: 12.4% weight loss on the top dose at 72 weeks (ATTAIN-1); in diabetes it beat oral semaglutide on HbA1c (−2.2% vs −1.4%) and weight (9.2% vs 5.3%). ACHIEVE-4 supported cardiovascular safety.
29. Went wrong / did not work: Less weight loss than injectables
30. Went wrong / did not work: Nausea, constipation, diarrhea, vomiting
31. Went wrong / did not work: ~10% quit on top dose
32. Went wrong / did not work: Boxed thyroid tumor warning
33. What went wrong: Less weight loss than injectable semaglutide or tirzepatide; GI effects in most users and about 10% quitting on the top dose. Boxed thyroid C-cell tumor warning like the class.
34. Most reported: Oral convenience praised
35. Most reported: GI upset on titration
36. Most reported: Used to maintain weight after injectables
37. Most reported: Cannot be compounded

## What has been tested
38. Fat metabolism: Obesity, ATTAIN-1 and -2 (human)
39. Glucose & insulin: Type 2 diabetes, ACHIEVE program (human)
40. Heart & vessels: CV safety vs insulin glargine, ACHIEVE-4 (human)
41. Phase 3 ATTAIN (obesity) and ACHIEVE (type 2 diabetes) programs, including head-to-heads against oral semaglutide and dapagliflozin and a cardiovascular safety trial against insulin glargine (ACHIEVE-4).
42. What it helps: ATTAIN-1 showed 12.4% weight loss on the top dose at 72 weeks, and the ACHIEVE program showed HbA1c and weight beating oral semaglutide and dapagliflozin in type 2 diabetes. ACHIEVE-4 supported cardiovascular safety. People use it to avoid injections or to hold weight after stopping an injectable. GI effects and lower peak weight loss than injectables are the trade-offs.
43. Trial: active · Phase 3 · peripheral artery disease · NCT07223593 · Eli Lilly. FDA approved as Foundayo on 1 April 2026, the first oral non peptide GLP-1 pill; Lilly is still recruiting Phase 3 trials in new uses. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (verified)

## Who shouldn't take it
44. Personal or family history of MTC or MEN2: GLP-1 agonist class carries the C-cell tumour warning. (reported)
45. Anyone booked for surgery, endoscopy or sedation: Slows stomach emptying; aspiration risk under anaesthesia. (reported)
46. People relying on the contraceptive pill: Delayed gastric emptying can lower pill absorption. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
47. Tirzepatide: Tirzepatide is a weekly injection hitting GIP and GLP-1 receptors with larger weight loss; orforglipron is a daily pill on GLP-1 alone. People use the pill to hold weight after stopping the injection rather than together. Taking both at once has not been tested.
48. Semaglutide: Both act on the same GLP-1 receptor, semaglutide as a peptide injection or tablet and orforglipron as a small-molecule pill. They duplicate each other, so the logic is switching, not stacking. ACHIEVE-3 compared them head to head, but no trial tested them together.

## Where it comes from
49. A small-molecule GLP-1 agonist discovered by Chugai and licensed to Lilly in 2018: a pill that hits the GLP-1 receptor without being a peptide, so no injection and no fasting rules.
50. First studied for: Obesity (approved), then type 2 diabetes.
51. Name story: Discovered by Chugai in Japan and licensed to Lilly in 2018. The "-glipron" ending is shared by other non-peptide GLP-1 pills (danuglipron, lotiglipron), not the "-glutide" of injectable peptides. US approval came April 2026 as Foundayo. [S2] (inferred)
52. 2018: Lilly licenses it from Chugai
53. Aug 2025: ATTAIN-1: 12.4% weight loss at 72 weeks
54. Feb 2026: ACHIEVE-3 beats oral semaglutide in T2D
55. Apr 2026: FDA approves Foundayo for obesity
56. Oct 2026: EMA committee backs it for obesity and T2D

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Not a peptide, and why that changes everything downstream [lab]
57. Orforglipron is a small molecule, not a peptide, which is why it survives the gut. A 2020 cryo-EM structure of the human GLP-1 receptor bound to it (then coded LY3502970) shows it sitting in a pocket in the upper part of the receptor, touching the extracellular domain and several helices, rather than where the natural hormone binds [1] (verified).
58. Two consequences follow from that binding mode. It is a partial agonist biased toward G-protein signalling over beta-arrestin recruitment, which may matter for tolerability and receptor desensitisation, though that link is not proven in people [1] (verified for the bias; inferred for its meaning). And it depends on a tryptophan found only in primate receptors, so it barely acts on rodent receptors [1] (verified).

### What that species quirk did to the safety file [animals]
59. Injectable GLP-1 drugs carry a boxed warning because they caused thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents. Orforglipron produced no tumours in a two-year rat study or a 26-week transgenic mouse study, but the label explains why that is not reassurance: the drug is not pharmacologically active in rats or mice [2] (verified). The tumour test could not have shown a receptor-driven effect. The label keeps the class boxed warning and the contraindication in medullary thyroid cancer and MEN 2, with human relevance undetermined [2] (verified).
60. This is an unusual position for an approved drug: the standard rodent safety model was blind to its main mechanism, so long-term human surveillance carries more of the weight than usual (inferred). Developmental studies used monkeys and rabbits; rabbit malformations appeared only at about 14 times clinical exposure [2] (verified).

### What the body does with it [people]
61. Bioavailability is about 77% at the 0.8 mg dose, peak levels come 4 to 8 hours after a dose, half-life is about 29 to 49 hours, and about 87% leaves in faeces, under 1% in urine; metabolism runs mainly through the liver enzyme CYP3A4 [2] (verified). Food has no clinically relevant effect at approved strengths [2].
62. That CYP3A4 dependence is the practical part. Clarithromycin raised exposure about 3.5-fold, so with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors the maximum dose is 9 mg; carbamazepine cut exposure 82% and efavirenz 61%, so strong inducers are to be avoided [2] (verified). It also raised simvastatin acid exposure 2 to 2.5-fold, capping simvastatin at 20 mg, and the label asks for a non-oral or backup contraceptive for 30 days after starting and after every dose step [2] (verified). These interactions are a new problem for the class: injectable peptides largely avoid them (inferred).

### The human record [people]
63. Obesity. ATTAIN-1 randomised 3,127 adults without diabetes for 72 weeks. Mean weight change was minus 7.5%, 8.4% and 11.2% at the three trial doses against minus 2.1% on placebo; at the top dose 55% lost at least 10% and 19% at least 20% [3] (verified). Discontinuation for adverse events was 5 to 10% against 3% [3]. On treatment, the figure rises to about 12.4% [7].
64. Early type 2 diabetes. ACHIEVE-1 gave it alone to 559 people for 40 weeks; HbA1c fell about 1.2 to 1.5 points from a baseline of 8.0%, against 0.4 on placebo [4] (reported, from a trade summary of the paper).
65. Head to head. ACHIEVE-3 compared it with oral semaglutide in 1,698 people on metformin for 52 weeks, open-label. At the top doses HbA1c fell 2.2 against 1.4 points and weight 9.2% against 5.3%, but discontinuation for adverse events was roughly double, 9.7% against 4.9% [5] (verified). Better effect, worse tolerability, both real.
66. Heart. ACHIEVE-4 randomised 2,749 people with type 2 diabetes and raised cardiovascular risk against insulin glargine, open-label. Major cardiovascular events had a hazard ratio of 0.84 (95% CI 0.59 to 1.20), meeting the non-inferiority margin of 1.8 but not showing superiority [6] (verified). All-cause death was lower (hazard ratio 0.43), but that analysis was not protected against chance across multiple tests [6], so it is a signal, not a finding. A dedicated outcomes trial in obesity is ongoing [6].

### Side effects in numbers [people]
67. From the label, at the 5.5, 9 and 17.2 mg tablets against placebo: nausea 26, 34 and 35% against 10%; vomiting 13, 21 and 24% against 4%; constipation 20, 27 and 24% against 9%; diarrhoea 21, 23 and 25% against 11%. Overall, 8% stopped for adverse reactions against 3%, mostly gastrointestinal [2] (verified).
68. Class warnings apply: pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, kidney injury from dehydration, hypoglycaemia with insulin or sulfonylureas, worsening diabetic retinopathy, and aspiration risk under anaesthesia [2] (verified).

### Who produced the evidence [people]
69. Discovered by a Japanese company and licensed in 2018 to the current US developer (reported), which ran and reported every phase 3 trial cited here [3,5,6] (verified). The trials are large, registered and published in major journals, which is a different tier of evidence from anything else in this library. Some of the most quoted figures, such as ACHIEVE-4's mortality result and the on-treatment weight figure, come first from company releases, so the peer-reviewed versions are the ones to check (inferred).

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
70. US: approved on 1 April 2026 for chronic weight management, label revised July 2026 [2,7] (verified). EU: the CHMP adopted a positive opinion at its 12 to 15 October 2026 meeting for weight management and type 2 diabetes; the European Commission decision follows [8] (verified).
71. Sport: GLP-1 agonists are not named anywhere on the 2026 Prohibited List, and as an approved drug it falls outside the catch-all non-approved class [9] (verified for the list contents; inferred for its application).

### Open questions [mixed]
72. Is the thyroid warning relevant to a drug rodents cannot respond to? Only human follow-up can say.
73. Does the mortality signal in ACHIEVE-4 hold in a trial designed to test it?
74. How much of the tolerability gap against oral semaglutide is dose escalation speed, and how much is the molecule?
75. What happens to weight after stopping a daily pill, compared with weekly injections? Not yet reported.

# Oxytocin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/oxytocin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Pitocin, Syntocinon, Induxin
2. Origin: Made by the body
3. Sequence: CYIQNCPLG (9 amino acids). Ring closed by a bridge between the two C; amide end
4. Shown with an FDA approved badge
5. Legal and approval status: FDA-approved (Pitocin) for obstetrics. Intranasal/social use is off-label/compounded.

## Summary
6. Oxytocin is a nine-amino-acid hormone made by the body and released from the posterior pituitary, driving labour, milk letdown and social bonding. Its proven, FDA-approved use is obstetric, as Pitocin for inducing labour and controlling bleeding. Users take it nasally or sublingually for mood and closeness, but intranasal trials in autism and social anxiety are largely mixed or negative.
7. Punch line: The bonding hormone. Proven for labour and milk letdown; taken nasally for closeness, with variable effects.
8. Used for: Mood, closeness and libido

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
9. Connection & desire: Closeness and bonding
10. Reproductive: Starts labour and milk letdown
11. Endocrine & growth: Pituitary hormone
12. Mood: Calm and trust studied
13. Tissue repair (backed only by animal or user reports): Wound healing studied

## How it works
14. Contracts the uterus during labour · Myometrial OXTR, Gq/Ca2+ · role Reproductive
   Oxytocin binds OXTR on uterine muscle, a Gq-coupled receptor that raises calcium inside the cell and makes it contract. This is its proven, long-approved use, given by injection in hospital to start labour and control bleeding after birth.
15. Lets milk down during breastfeeding · Myoepithelial OXTR · role Reproductive
   In the breast, oxytocin binds OXTR on myoepithelial cells that wrap the milk glands and squeezes them, pushing milk out. A licensed nasal spray once existed for this let-down reflex but was discontinued for commercial reasons.
16. Released from the pituitary as a hormone · Posterior pituitary · role Endocrine & growth
   Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus and released into blood from the posterior pituitary in response to birth, suckling and touch. Released this way it acts on distant tissues. This is textbook endocrine physiology.
17. Shapes bonding and social behaviour · Central OXTR, amygdala · role Mood
   Inside the brain, OXTR in the amygdala and reward circuits shapes trust, bonding and how much attention social cues get. Animal work is strong. Intranasal trials in autism and social anxiety are largely mixed or negative, and how much nasal oxytocin reaches the brain is debated.
18. Surges at orgasm, adds to closeness · Hypothalamic OT neurons · role Connection & desire
   Hypothalamic oxytocin neurons fire around orgasm, and blood oxytocin rises at that moment in people. This is thought to add to feelings of closeness afterwards. Whether taking it nasally boosts libido is not established.
19. Speeds wound healing in animal studies · Anti-inflammatory OXTR · role Tissue repair
   Acting through OXTR on immune and skin cells, oxytocin dampens inflammation. In animal studies this speeds wound healing. There is no human evidence for this use.
20. Mechanism overview: Oxytocin is a nine-amino-acid hormone made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. It binds OXTR, a Gq-coupled receptor that raises intracellular calcium. In the uterus that contracts smooth muscle during labour. In the breast it squeezes myoepithelial cells to let milk down. Inside the brain, OXTR in the amygdala and reward circuits shapes trust, bonding and social salience, and oxytocin neurons fire at orgasm, adding to closeness. Animal work also shows anti-inflammatory effects that speed wound healing.

21. Typical: 10–40 IU · as needed · cycle As needed · route Intranasal (reported)
22. Half-life: ~3-5 minutes IV
23. Most people take: 10-40iu intranasal (20iu = ~1 spray each nostril) · As needed. No cycling.
24. Common: 18–24 IU · as needed, 45–75 min before · as needed · Intranasal · for social, intimacy [S1] [S2] (reported)
25. Low daily: 10–20 IU · 1× daily · ongoing · Intranasal · for mood, bonding [S2] [S3] (reported)
26. Higher: 40 IU · as needed · short-term · Intranasal · for top of studied range [S1] [S4] (reported)

34. Most reported: Nasal or sublingual

36. Most reported: Variable effects

## What has been tested
37. Reproductive: Labor induction, bleeding (human)
38. Mood: Autism, intranasal (trial)
39. Mood: Social anxiety (trial)
40. Connection & desire: Bonding and closeness (human)
41. Long-approved for obstetric use. Intranasal oxytocin has been studied widely for autism, social anxiety and bonding, with inconsistent results.
42. What it helps: Its proven uses are obstetric: inducing labour and controlling bleeding after birth. Intranasal trials in autism and social anxiety produced some signals but are largely mixed or negative, and how much nasal dosing reaches the brain is debated. Users take it nasally or sublingually for mood, closeness and libido, with variable effects.
43. Trial: active · Phase 2 · stress in dementia caregivers (nasal spray) · NCT06364228 · University of Nebraska. Approved for labour induction; dozens of nasal spray trials are running for stress, autism, social behaviour and sexual wellbeing. (checked 2026-10-23) [S5] (verified)

## Who shouldn't take it
44. People prone to low sodium (diuretics, SSRIs, marathoners): Oxytocin acts like antidiuretic hormone and can cause water intoxication. (verified)
45. People with borderline personality or attachment anxiety: Intranasal oxytocin reduced trust and cooperation in some of these people. (reported)
46. Anyone who could be pregnant: It contracts the uterus; that is its approved use. (verified)

## Where it comes from
47. The nine-amino-acid 'bonding' hormone of the posterior pituitary, driving uterine contraction, milk letdown, and social attachment.
48. First studied for: Inducing labor and controlling postpartum bleeding (Pitocin).
49. Name story: From Greek oxys (swift) + tokos (childbirth): "quick birth", after Henry Dale found in 1906 that it contracts the uterus. In 1953 du Vigneaud made it the first peptide hormone ever synthesized, winning the 1955 Nobel. [S6] (verified)
50. 1953: First peptide hormone sequenced and synthesized
51. 1950s: Approved as Pitocin for labor and postpartum bleeding
52. 2000s to 2010s: Intranasal trials in autism, social anxiety and bonding
53. Today: An obstetric staple; social use is off-label

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Two drugs with one name [people]
54. Oxytocin as an approved medicine is an injection given in hospital to start or strengthen labour and control bleeding after birth. Oxytocin as people use it socially is a nasal spray taken for closeness, calm or sex. They share a molecule and almost nothing else: different route, different dose logic, different evidence and a different regulatory status (inferred from the sources below).
55. The licensed injection is standardised in units, not milligrams: 10 USP units per millilitre, with 0.5% chlorobutanol as preservative, buffered to pH 3.5, for intravenous infusion or intramuscular injection [1] (verified). A unit is a measure of biological activity, so units and micrograms do not convert cleanly from one product to another (inferred).

### What happened to the nasal spray [people]
56. A licensed nasal oxytocin did exist in the US. Syntocinon Nasal Spray was approved in 1960 to help milk let-down after birth, and was discontinued in 1997 for commercial reasons [6] (verified). A 2013 licence deal aimed to bring it back for lactation and to trial it in schizophrenia and autism [6] (verified); no relaunch is evident in the current record (inferred). So nasal oxytocin bought in the US today is, in practice, a compounded or imported product, not a licensed one (inferred).

### What the body does with it [mixed]
57. In blood, oxytocin lasts minutes: a plasma half-life of about 1 to 6 minutes, shorter in late pregnancy, cleared by kidney and liver [1] (verified). It also has a built-in antidiuretic effect; with long infusions this has caused water intoxication with seizures, coma and maternal death [1] (verified). That risk belongs to high-dose infusion, not a nasal puff, but it shows the hormone is not only about bonding.
58. The central question for nasal use is whether it reaches the brain. In monkeys, labelled oxytocin given nasally, not intravenously, appeared two hours later in brain regions along the olfactory and trigeminal nerve routes, including the striatum and orbitofrontal cortex [4] (verified). In people, the evidence is thinner: in measured studies, the share of a nasal dose recovered in cerebrospinal fluid is on the order of 0.001% [5] (reported). Some does get in. How much, and whether it is enough to matter, is still argued (inferred).

### The human record on trust and bonding [people]
59. The idea of oxytocin as a trust hormone rests largely on a 2005 study in which 58 investors given nasal oxytocin trusted more in an economic game, at a one-tailed p of 0.029, with no effect on the other side of the exchange or on risk-taking [2] (verified).
60. A 2015 critical review found six conceptual replications, none of which reliably reproduced it; one found the reverse in women. Pooling seven studies and 481 people gave an effect size of 0.077, not significant, and that was with inclusion rules chosen to favour the hypothesis [2] (verified). Detecting even the upper plausible effect would need more than 400 participants, about the total of every trust study combined at the time [2].
61. The newer reading is that oxytocin raises the salience of social cues, good and bad, rather than making people more trusting or warmer across the board [8] (reported). That fits why effects vary so much by person and context (inferred).

### The largest clinical test [people]
62. In autism, a 24-week trial randomised 290 children and adolescents aged 3 to 17 to nasal oxytocin, targeting 48 IU a day, or placebo. Social withdrawal scores and cognitive measures did not differ between groups, and adverse events were similar [3] (verified). It is the largest trial of nasal oxytocin in autism, and it was clearly negative.
63. Sexual and intimacy uses have no comparably sized trial in the record reviewed for this entry (verified as absent in the sources reviewed). There is no established dose for social or sexual use.

### Safety, and what has not been studied [people]
64. The injection label's adverse effects are obstetric and serious: uterine hyperstimulation and rupture, arrhythmia, hypertensive episodes, anaphylaxis and fetal distress [1] (verified). The label also states it is not indicated for elective induction of labour, because benefit against risk was never established [1] (verified).
65. For nasal social use, the large autism trial found adverse events no different from placebo over 24 weeks [3]. Long-term daily nasal use in adults, and use in pregnancy outside obstetric care, are unstudied (verified as absent in the sources reviewed). Because it acts on the uterus, pregnancy is the obvious line not to cross (inferred).

### Who produced the evidence [people]
66. The early social-neuroscience literature was built on small samples and flexible analyses, and later work points to publication bias in the field [2,8] (reported). The autism trial was the first test at a size able to give a clear answer [3]. The pattern, strong small early results followed by weak large ones, is the same one seen with many compounds here (inferred).

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
67. US: approved as an injection for obstetric use; nasal and social use is off-label, typically through compounding [1,6] (verified for the approval; inferred for current supply). Sport: oxytocin is not named on the 2026 Prohibited List and, as an approved medicine, does not fall in the catch-all non-approved class [7] (verified for the list contents; inferred for its application).

### Open questions [mixed]
68. How much of a nasal dose reaches the human brain, and does it act there or through the body? Still unresolved.
69. Is there a group that reliably benefits socially? The autism trial says not in that population; others are untested at scale.
70. What does daily use for months do? No long-term adult data exist.

# Vitamin B12
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/vitamin-b12
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: cobalamin, cyanocobalamin, methylcobalamin, hydroxocobalamin, B12 shot, mecobalamin (INN for methylcobalamin), cobamamide (adenosylcobalamin), extrinsic factor
2. Origin: Not a peptide: cobalt-containing vitamin
3. Shown with an FDA approved badge
4. Legal and approval status: Cyanocobalamin injection is FDA-approved (Rx, 1,000 mcg/mL); hydroxocobalamin is approved too. Injectable methylcobalamin has no FDA-approved product and is compounded; final 503A bulk status not confirmed. Not on the WADA list.

## Summary
5. Vitamin B12 is a cobalt-centred vitamin, not a peptide, needed to make red blood cells, myelin and DNA. Injections are approved for pernicious anaemia and other deficiency, and are also popular as an energy shot in wellness and weight-loss clinics. Benefit is mostly seen in people who were low, and acne flares are the most common complaint.
6. Punch line: Cobalt vitamin for blood, nerves and DNA. The clinic energy shot; real lift mostly if you're low.
7. Used for: Deficiency, energy, weight-loss clinic add-on

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Cellular energy: Fixes deficiency fatigue
9. Neural protection: Protects nerves and myelin
10. Cognition: Clears deficiency brain fog
11. Mood: Low B12 linked to low mood
12. Skin & aesthetics (backed only by animal or user reports): Acne flares reported
13. Sleep & rhythms (backed only by animal or user reports): Methyl form tied to sleep rhythm

## How it works
14. Helps make red blood cells and DNA · Methionine synthase, folate cycle · role Cellular energy
   As methylcobalamin, B12 is the cofactor for methionine synthase, which keeps folate moving through the DNA-making cycle. Without it, dividing cells in bone marrow cannot copy DNA properly and red cells come out large and few. Correcting this fixes deficiency anaemia in people.
15. Keeps nerve insulation healthy · Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, myelin · role Neural protection
   As adenosylcobalamin, B12 runs methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in mitochondria, a step needed for healthy fat handling in myelin, the insulation around nerves. Deficiency damages nerves and spinal cord. Treating it early stops neuropathy from progressing in people, while late damage can stay.
16. Lowers homocysteine · Homocysteine to methionine · role Cognition
   Methionine synthase also turns homocysteine back into methionine. Low B12 lets homocysteine build up in blood, which is a marker of deficiency and linked to vascular and brain risk. Giving B12 lowers homocysteine, mainly in people who were low.
17. Feeds skin bacteria porphyrins · C. acnes porphyrin output · role Skin & aesthetics
   Skin bacteria called C. acnes take up B12 and shift their metabolism toward making porphyrins, molecules that trigger inflammation in follicles. That explains acne-like flares after injections. The evidence is case reports and lab work on the bacteria.
18. Mechanism overview: Cobalamin is a corrinoid ring around a cobalt atom. In cells it works as two cofactors: methylcobalamin for methionine synthase, which recycles homocysteine to methionine and keeps folate moving through DNA synthesis, and adenosylcobalamin for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in mitochondria, which matters for myelin. Cyanocobalamin and hydroxocobalamin are converted to both forms in the body. Absorption from the gut needs intrinsic factor, which injections bypass.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
19. Typical: 1,000 mcg (1 mg) community; 100 mcg (label) · weekly (community); label loading then monthly · cycle Ongoing · route IM or deep Sub-Q (not IV) (verified)
20. Half-life: Most of large doses excreted in 48 h; stores last months
21. Most people take: Label for pernicious anaemia: 100 mcg IM/deep SC daily for 6–7 days, then alternate days, then every 3–4 days, then 100 mcg monthly for life. Common practice is 1,000 mcg weekly to monthly. High-dose oral (1–2 mg/day) and nasal gel are alternatives.

## What people report
22. Weekly shots for energy and in weight-loss clinics, often compounded with GLP-1s. People report an energy lift (mostly those who were low), red-tinged urine with hydroxocobalamin, and acne on the face and back.
23. Liked / worked: Reverses deficiency anaemia
24. Liked / worked: Halts early deficiency nerve damage
25. Liked / worked: Bypasses absorption problems
26. What worked: Reverses deficiency anaemia and can halt nerve damage when caught early. Injections bypass the intrinsic-factor problem of pernicious anaemia, metformin users and gut surgery.
27. Went wrong / did not work: No energy boost if levels are normal
28. Went wrong / did not work: 50–98% of a big dose lost in urine
29. Went wrong / did not work: Acne flares
30. Went wrong / did not work: Rare anaphylaxis, low potassium early in severe anaemia
31. What went wrong: No proven energy or weight benefit when B12 levels are already normal. Most of a large injected dose leaves in the urine within 48 h. Acne flares, rare anaphylaxis, and low potassium when treating severe anaemia.
32. Most reported: Energy lift, mostly if low
33. Most reported: Acne on face and back
34. Most reported: Methyl form preferred for 'MTHFR' (no proof)
35. Most reported: Common in GLP-1 clinic blends

## What has been tested
36. Cellular energy: Pernicious anaemia and deficiency (human)
37. Neural protection: Deficiency neuropathy (human)
38. Skin & aesthetics: Acneiform eruption case reports (human)
39. Decades of clinical use for deficiency; large vitamin trials found no harm at 0.4–1 mg/day.
40. What it helps: Injections treat pernicious anaemia, malabsorption after gut surgery and deficiency from metformin, acid blockers, veganism or age, fixing anaemia and stopping early nerve damage. NIH notes no proven difference between oral forms; methylcobalamin superiority is a marketing claim. People take weekly shots for energy and focus, often in weight-loss clinics; benefit is mostly in those who were low. Acne flares are the most common complaint.
41. Trial: active · Phase 4 · B12 deficiency. Approved and cheap, so academic trials of oral versus injected or sublingual B12 run continuously, though one example checked had already completed. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
42. People with Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy: Cyanocobalamin can speed optic nerve damage. (verified)
43. People with cobalt allergy: Cobalt sits at the centre of the B12 molecule; the label contraindicates use. (verified)
44. People with very low potassium: Treating deficiency can drop potassium fast. (verified)
45. People prone to acne or rosacea: High-dose B12 linked to acne flares. (reported)

## Synergies (paired with)
46. Semaglutide: Semaglutide drives weight loss through the GLP-1 receptor, while B12 is added in weight-loss clinics for energy and to cover lower intake while eating less. Benefit is mostly in people who are low. The pairing is clinic practice, not trial data.
47. Tirzepatide: Tirzepatide brings large weight loss through GIP and GLP-1 receptors, while B12 is a common clinic add-on for energy and to guard against deficiency during reduced eating. Gain is mainly for people who were low. The pair has not been tested together.
48. NAD+: NAD+ is used as a cell energy coenzyme, while B12 supports red cells and nerves. Both are sold as energy shots, often given together. The pairing is user and clinic logic, and the combination has not been tested.
49. Glutathione: Glutathione is an antioxidant used for skin brightening, while B12 covers red cells, nerves and energy in deficient people. They are often given together in drip and injection clinics. The combination is clinic practice, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
50. A cobalt-centred vitamin needed to make red blood cells, myelin and DNA. Cyanocobalamin is the stable pharmacy form; methylcobalamin is an active form sold mainly through compounders.
51. First studied for: Pernicious anaemia and other B12 malabsorption.
52. Name story: Cobalamin is named for the cobalt atom at its core. The cyanide in cyanocobalamin is a purification accident: it latched on during charcoal clean-up in the 1948 isolation, and that form stayed the commercial 'vitamin B12'. [S2] (verified)
53. 1926: Raw liver diet rescues pernicious anaemia (inferred date)
54. 1948: Vitamin B12 isolated (inferred date)
55. 2021: Compounding panel votes to keep methylcobalamin available
56. 2023: Case report: B12 injections trigger acne
57. Today: Ubiquitous clinic shot, often blended with GLP-1s

# Ipamorelin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/ipamorelin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: NNC 26-0161, NNC-26-0161
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: AHAFK (5 amino acids). Aib shown as A, D-2-naphthylalanine shown as A, D-Phe shown as F; amide end. Weight is approximate
4. Legal and approval status: Unapproved research chemical. WADA-banned.

## Summary
5. Ipamorelin is a synthetic pentapeptide that mimics ghrelin to release growth hormone cleanly, without the hunger, cortisol or prolactin spikes of older GHRPs. People use it for sleep, recovery and fat loss, almost always stacked with CJC-1295. Human studies confirm a clean GH rise, but benefits beyond that are inferred from GH physiology, it failed a bowel recovery trial, and it is WADA-banned.
6. Punch line: The clean GH releaser: mimics ghrelin without hunger, cortisol or prolactin spikes. Nearly always paired with CJC.
7. Used for: GH release, recovery, sleep

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Endocrine & growth: Releases GH without cortisol spikes
9. Sleep & rhythms: Deeper sleep reported
10. Muscle & performance: Recovery and lean mass reported
11. Pain & sensory: Less soreness reported
12. Bone & cartilage (backed only by animal or user reports): Bone growth in rats
13. Skin & aesthetics (backed only by animal or user reports): Better skin reported

## How it works
14. Mimics ghrelin to trigger a GH pulse · Ghrelin receptor, GHSR-1a · role Endocrine & growth
   Ipamorelin binds the ghrelin receptor (GHSR-1a) on GH-making cells of the pituitary and in the hypothalamus. This sets off a GH pulse, amplifies the brain's own GHRH signal and blunts somatostatin, the brake on GH. Human studies confirm a clean GH rise.
15. Spares cortisol, prolactin and hunger · Selective GHS · role Endocrine & growth
   Older ghrelin mimics such as GHRP-2 and GHRP-6 also push out cortisol and prolactin and drive hunger. Ipamorelin is a selective secretagogue, so at standard use it barely moves those. In human studies this shows up as a GH rise with few side effects.
16. Raises IGF-1 downstream of GH · GH, liver IGF-1 · role Muscle & performance
   Each GH pulse signals the liver to make IGF-1, the hormone that carries most of GH's effects on muscle, fat and bone. Ipamorelin's benefits for lean mass are inferred from this GH and IGF-1 physiology, not from outcome trials in people.
17. Increases bone mineral content, in rats · GH, IGF-1 on bone · role Bone & cartilage
   GH and IGF-1 drive bone-building cells and bone growth. In rat studies ipamorelin raised bone mineral content, consistent with that route. No human study has shown a bone benefit, so this remains an animal finding.
18. Claimed to deepen sleep via night GH pulses · Slow-wave sleep, claimed · role Sleep & rhythms
   Most of the day's GH is released in pulses during deep, slow-wave sleep. Users claim that adding night-time GH pulses deepens sleep, but no trial has measured sleep on ipamorelin. Treat this as user report built on GH physiology.
19. Mechanism overview: Ipamorelin is a pentapeptide that activates the ghrelin receptor GHSR-1a on pituitary somatotrophs and in the hypothalamus. This triggers a GH pulse and amplifies GHRH while blunting somatostatin. It is selective: unlike GHRP-2 and GHRP-6, it barely raises cortisol, prolactin or hunger at standard doses. Each GH pulse drives liver IGF-1, which carries the downstream effects on lean mass, fat and bone. Pairing with a GHRH analogue such as CJC-1295 gives a larger pulse than either alone, because the two act on separate receptors.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
20. Typical: 100–300 mcg · daily · cycle 8-12 weeks on, 4 weeks off · route Sub-Q (reported)
21. Half-life: ~2 hours
22. Most people take: 100-300mcg before bed SC (empty stomach) · 8-12 weeks on, 4 weeks off. Can run longer.
23. Common: 200–300 mcg · 1–2× daily · 8–12 wk, 5 on/2 off · Sub-Q · for general GH support, sleep [S1] (reported)
24. Stacked: 100–200 mcg + equal CJC no DAC · 2–3× daily · 8–16 wk · Sub-Q · for GHRH stack [S1] [S2] (reported)
25. Higher: 200–300 mcg · 3× daily (AM fasted, post-WO, bed) · 12–16 wk · Sub-Q · for recomp, bodybuilding [S1] [S3] (reported)

## What people report
26. Perhaps the most popular GH-optimization peptide; reported for sleep, recovery, fat loss. Commonly stacked with CJC-1295.
27. Liked / worked: Clean GH rise with few side effects
28. Liked / worked: Strong synergy with CJC-1295
29. What worked: Raises GH with a clean side-effect profile; strong synergy with CJC-1295.
30. Went wrong / did not work: Post-surgery gut trials: no better than placebo
31. Went wrong / did not work: No large efficacy trials; benefits inferred from GH
32. Went wrong / did not work: Modest effect alone
33. What went wrong: No large efficacy trials; benefits inferred from GH; effect modest alone.
34. Most reported: Sleep, recovery and fat loss
35. Most reported: Usually stacked with CJC-1295

## What has been tested
36. Endocrine & growth: GH release (human)
37. Digestive & gut: Recovery after bowel surgery (trial)
38. Endocrine & growth: GH release (animal)
39. Early human and animal studies showed clean GH release. Phase 2 trials for gut recovery after surgery found no benefit over placebo, and that development stopped.
40. What it helps: Human studies confirm a clean GH rise with few side effects. Rat studies showed more bone mineral content. Trials in bowel recovery after surgery found no benefit over placebo. Users report better sleep, recovery and fat loss, almost always stacking it with CJC-1295. Benefits beyond GH release are inferred from GH physiology rather than outcome trials.
41. Trial: none. Last trials 2008 to 2011 for gut recovery after surgery, which failed; never tested in humans since. (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
42. People with active or recent cancer: Raises GH and IGF-1, which promote cell growth. (inferred)
43. People with prediabetes or poorly controlled diabetes: GH raises blood glucose and insulin resistance. (inferred)
44. Drug-tested athletes: GH secretagogues are banned under WADA S2. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
45. CJC-1295 no DAC: CJC-1295 no DAC works on the GHRH receptor, ipamorelin on the ghrelin receptor, so the two hit separate switches and give a larger GH pulse together. This is the classic GH stack, sold pre-mixed as CJC-1295 no DAC + Ipamorelin, but the pair has not been tested together in people.
46. CJC-1295 with DAC: The DAC version keeps GHRH tone raised for days, while ipamorelin adds sharp ghrelin-receptor pulses on top. People pair them for a higher baseline plus pulses. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
47. Sermorelin: Sermorelin is a short-acting GHRH that keeps natural pulses, and ipamorelin adds a ghrelin-receptor push from a second route. Together they aim for a bigger but still pulsatile GH release. The pair itself has not been tested together.
48. Tesamorelin: Tesamorelin brings the best human evidence in this family, for visceral and liver fat, and ipamorelin adds a separate ghrelin-receptor GH pulse. They are sold pre-mixed as Tesamorelin + Ipamorelin, but the combination has not been studied in trials.
49. BPC-157: BPC-157 targets local repair, blood vessel growth and tendon cell GH receptors, while ipamorelin raises the GH that those cells respond to. People pair them for injury recovery. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
50. TB-500 frag 17–23: The fragment is used for wound and tendon repair through actin and vessel growth, mostly on data from full Tβ4, while ipamorelin adds a systemic GH and IGF-1 lift. People stack them for recovery. The pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
51. A synthetic pentapeptide ghrelin-mimetic (GH secretagogue) designed to release GH cleanly, without the hunger, cortisol or prolactin spikes of older GHRPs.
52. First studied for: A selective GH-releasing agent for research and GH-optimization.
53. Name story: Novo Nordisk's NNC 26-0161, billed in its 1998 debut paper as "the first selective growth hormone secretagogue": it raises GH without the cortisol and prolactin bumps of GHRP-6 and GHRP-2. [S5] (verified)
54. 1998: Designed as a clean GH releaser without hunger, cortisol or prolactin spikes
55. 2000s: Phase 2 trials for gut recovery after surgery; no benefit, dropped
56. Today: The most popular GH-optimization peptide; unapproved, WADA-banned
