# Tesamorelin + Ipamorelin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/tesa-ipamorelin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Tesa/Ipa, Tesa-IPA, Tesamorelin/Ipamorelin 5/5, Tesamorelin/Ipamorelin 10/3
2. Origin: Blend of 2 peptides
3. Legal and approval status: Tesamorelin: FDA-approved only as Egrifta for HIV lipodystrophy (EGRIFTA WR approved Mar 2025); compounded copies drew an FDA warning letter in Aug 2026. Ipamorelin: FDA Category 2, PCAC voted 0 to 12 against in Oct 2024. The blend is not approved anywhere. WADA: both prohibited (S2).

## Summary
4. This blend pairs tesamorelin, the only FDA-approved GHRH analogue, with ipamorelin, a selective ghrelin-receptor agonist. People use it to aim tesamorelin's belly-fat effect at a bigger growth hormone pulse through two routes. Tesamorelin alone cut visceral fat about 20% over 26 weeks in HIV lipodystrophy trials, but nothing is known about the pair. Users report fat loss over months, deeper sleep early, and water retention and joint stiffness.
5. Punch line: Approved belly-fat GHRH plus ipamorelin's second GH route. One nightly shot; the pricier cousin of CJC/Ipa.
6. Used for: Visceral fat loss, GH release, sleep

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Endocrine & growth: GHRH plus ghrelin route, bigger GH pulse
8. Fat metabolism: Tesamorelin's belly-fat effect
9. Sleep & rhythms: Deeper sleep from the ipamorelin side
10. Muscle & performance: Lean mass and recovery, reported
11. Skin & aesthetics (backed only by animal or user reports): Skin quality, reported
12. Organ function (backed only by animal or user reports): Liver fat, from tesamorelin data

## How it works
13. Full-length GHRH copy, stabilised at the front end · GHRH 1-44 with trans-3-hexenoyl cap · role Endocrine & growth
   Tesamorelin is the full 44 amino acid GHRH with a trans-3-hexenoyl cap that protects it from DPP-4 breakdown. It binds GHRH receptors in the pituitary and raises cAMP, prompting the body to release its own growth hormone. Shown in human trials.
14. Shrinks belly fat in trials · Visceral adipose tissue down · role Fat metabolism
   In phase 3 trials in people with HIV lipodystrophy, tesamorelin shrank visceral fat, the fat around the organs, by about 20% over 26 weeks while IGF-1 rose. Glucose and insulin did not change significantly in that trial. The data are from tesamorelin alone.
15. Presses the ghrelin button, a second route · GHS-R1a agonist · role Endocrine & growth
   Ipamorelin activates GHS-R1a, the ghrelin receptor, which signals through phospholipase C and calcium rather than cAMP. This gives a second, independent push on GH release. The effect is shown in animals; human trial data are limited.
16. Releases GH without cortisol or prolactin spikes · Selective GHS, animal data · role Sleep & rhythms
   Ipamorelin releases GH without raising cortisol or prolactin, unlike older GHRPs. That selectivity is shown in rats and pigs. Users report deeper sleep and vivid dreams early on, which fits GH pulses at night but is user-reported.
17. Together, a bigger pulse than either alone · GHRH + GHRP synergy · role Muscle & performance
   Because GHRH acts through cAMP and ipamorelin through calcium, the two routes add up to a larger GH pulse than either alone. This GHRH plus GHRP synergy is shown in healthy men. The tesamorelin and ipamorelin pair itself has not been tested.
18. Mechanism overview: Tesamorelin is human GHRH 1-44 with a trans-3-hexenoyl group on the N-terminus, which protects it from DPP-4 cleavage; it binds GHRH receptors and raises cAMP in somatotrophs. Ipamorelin binds GHS-R1a and signals through phospholipase C and calcium, releasing GH selectively in animals. The independent routes make GHRH plus GHRP synergistic. Tesamorelin keeps native Met27 and Asn8, so in solution it is more prone to oxidation and deamidation than Mod GRF 1-29.

## What is inside the blend
19. Tesamorelin: 10 mg · GHRH signal with trial data for visceral fat
20. Ipamorelin: 3 mg · Ghrelin-receptor signal: triggers the pulse, selectively
21. Most common ratio: Tesamorelin 10 · Ipamorelin 3 = 13 mg (6 of 13 listings)
22. Other ratio seen: Tesamorelin 5 · Ipamorelin 5 = 10 mg (3 listings)
23. Other ratio seen: Tesamorelin 10 · Ipamorelin 5 = 15 mg (2 listings)
24. Other ratio seen: Tesamorelin 12 · Ipamorelin 3 = 15 mg (2 listings)
25. Other ratio seen: Tesamorelin 8 · Ipamorelin 2 = 10 mg (1 listing)
26. Other ratio seen: Tesamorelin 20 · Ipamorelin 5 = 25 mg (1 listing)
27. Other ratio seen: Tesamorelin 6 · Ipamorelin 2 = 8 mg (1 listing)
28. Version Common retail, tesamorelin-heavy: Tesamorelin 10 · Ipamorelin 3 = 13 mg
29. Version Common retail, balanced: Tesamorelin 5 · Ipamorelin 5 = 10 mg
30. Why Tesamorelin is in it: The only GHRH analogue with phase 3 visceral-fat data
31. Why Ipamorelin is in it: Adds the ghrelin route, multiplying the pulse without cortisol or prolactin
32. Mixing chemistry: Tesamorelin keeps native Met27 and Asn8, the sites most prone to oxidation and deamidation; Mod GRF had them removed.
33. Mixing chemistry: The licensed maker's first version (Egrifta SV) had to be used immediately after mixing; it took a reformulation (EGRIFTA WR, 2025) with its own excipients to hold a vial for one week.
34. Mixing chemistry: Grey-market blends claim 4 to 6 weeks refrigerated; no published data supports that for tesamorelin in BAC water.
35. Mixing chemistry: At 44 amino acids tesamorelin has more structure for benzyl alcohol to disturb than short peptides.
36. Mixing chemistry: Discard if cloudy, gelled or particulate.
37. Self-mixing: Drawing tesamorelin and ipamorelin into one syringe right before injecting is the better-supported route; separate vials also let you fix the ratio (most guides want more ipamorelin than the 10/3 vial gives) and use the tesamorelin vial fast.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
38. Typical: 0.5–1 mg tesamorelin equivalent · 1× daily, pre-bed · cycle 8–12 weeks on, 4–8 off · route Sub-Q (reported)
39. Half-life: per component
40. Most people take: Sized by the tesamorelin dose. 10/3 vial in 2 mL (5 mg/mL tesa, 1.5 mg/mL ipa): 10 units = 0.5 mg + 150 mcg, 20 units = 1 mg + 300 mcg. 5/5 vial in 2 mL: 10 units = 250 + 250 mcg. Fasted, before bed.

## What people report
41. 10 + 3 vial in 2 mL: 20 units = 1 mg tesamorelin + 300 mcg ipamorelin, once nightly, fasted, 5 on 2 off, 8 to 12 weeks. 5 + 5 vial: 200 to 400 mcg of blend nightly. Seller sheets push 2 mg tesamorelin (the label dose) + 600 mcg ipamorelin. Some add a morning dose in weeks 4 to 8.
42. Liked / worked: Tesamorelin cut visceral fat ~20% in trials
43. Liked / worked: Synergy shown in humans, 1990
44. Liked / worked: Sleep within 1 to 2 weeks, reported
45. What worked: Users and guides report the tesamorelin pattern: visceral fat and waist down over 2 to 3 months, plus deeper sleep and vivid dreams from the ipamorelin side within 1 to 2 weeks. Community pages list it as niche, mainly because tesamorelin is expensive.
46. Went wrong / did not work: No trial of the pair
47. Went wrong / did not work: Glucose intolerance risk from tesamorelin
48. Went wrong / did not work: Water retention, joint stiffness, tingling
49. What went wrong: No blend trial, no success rates published. Early water retention, flushing, vivid dreams; joint stiffness and slight night hunger by weeks 3 to 4; tingling and carpal tunnel signs; tesamorelin raises glucose intolerance and diabetes risk in its own label data.
50. Most reported: 10/3: 20 units at 2 mL, nightly

## What has been tested
54. Fat metabolism: Tesamorelin, HIV visceral fat, phase 3 (human)
55. Endocrine & growth: GHRH + GHRP synergy, normal men (human)
56. Endocrine & growth: Ipamorelin GH release, rats and pigs (animal)
57. Sleep & rhythms: Deeper sleep, vivid dreams (users)
58. Never tested as a pair. Tesamorelin alone has phase 3 trials: 2 mg daily for 26 weeks cut visceral fat about 20% (27.8 cm²) in people with HIV lipodystrophy, with IGF-1 up 80%. Ipamorelin alone has animal selectivity data. GHRH plus GHRP synergy is shown in men.
59. What it helps: Strongest evidence of the GH blends for fat: tesamorelin alone cut visceral fat about 20% over 26 weeks in HIV lipodystrophy trials, with IGF-1 up 80% and no significant change in glucose or insulin in that trial. Nothing is known about the pair. Users report fat loss over months and better sleep early.

## Who shouldn't take it
60. Pituitary tumour, pituitary surgery or brain radiation: Label contraindication: needs an intact hypothalamic-pituitary axis. (verified)
61. People with active or recent cancer: Raises GH and IGF-1, which promote cell growth. (inferred)
62. People with prediabetes or poorly controlled diabetes: GH raises blood glucose and insulin resistance. (inferred)
63. Drug-tested athletes: GH secretagogues are banned under WADA S2. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
64. CJC-1295 no DAC: CJC-1295 no DAC is a second GHRH copy on the same receptor as tesamorelin. Adding it gives overlap, not new synergy, as in the triple blend. The combination has not been tested.
65. Sermorelin: Sermorelin is another GHRH copy on the same receptor as tesamorelin. Adding it duplicates the GHRH side rather than adding a route. The pairing has not been tested together.
66. MK-677: MK-677 is an oral ghrelin mimic on the same receptor as ipamorelin, raising GH all day rather than in pulses. People add it for sleep and lean mass. It raises hunger, and the pairing has not been tested.
67. AOD-9604: AOD-9604 is a growth hormone fragment aimed at fat breakdown without GH receptor action, with rodent data only. People add it for fat loss. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
68. Tesamorelin, the only FDA-approved GHRH analogue (Egrifta), pre-mixed with ipamorelin, a selective ghrelin-receptor agonist. Sold in two splits: 5 + 5 mg (balanced) and 10 + 3 mg (tesamorelin-heavy).
69. First studied for: Built by the community to aim tesamorelin's proven belly-fat effect at a bigger growth hormone pulse, using the same GHRH plus GHRP synergy behind CJC/Ipa.
70. 1990: GHRP plus GHRH synergy shown in normal men
71. 1998: Ipamorelin described as the first selective GH secretagogue
72. 2007: Tesamorelin 2 mg daily cuts visceral fat ~20% in HIV trial
73. 2010: FDA approves tesamorelin (Egrifta)
74. 2024: PCAC votes against ipamorelin
75. 2025: EGRIFTA WR approved: reconstitute weekly, not daily
76. Today: Sold pre-mixed as 5/5 and 10/3

# CJC-1295 no DAC
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/cjc-1295-no-dac
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Modified GRF (1-29), Mod GRF 1-29, tetrasubstituted GRF(1-29)
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain
3. Sequence: YADAIFTQSYRKVLAQLSARKLLQDILSR (29 amino acids). Position 2 is D-Ala; amide end
4. Legal and approval status: Unapproved research chemical. WADA-banned.

## Summary
5. CJC-1295 no DAC, also called modified GRF 1-29, is a GHRH analogue engineered for stability that stays short-acting without the DAC tail. People use it to raise GH in natural pulses, usually paired with a GHRP such as ipamorelin, for sleep, recovery and body composition. No human study exists for this exact molecule, so effects are inferred, though it is a very common grey-market GH peptide.
6. Punch line: Mod GRF 1-29. Sturdier GHRH without the DAC tail; short-acting, so GH rises in natural pulses.
7. Used for: GH release, often with ipamorelin

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Endocrine & growth: Raises natural GH pulses
9. Sleep & rhythms: Deeper sleep reported

## How it works
10. Prompts the pituitary to release GH · GHRH receptor · role Endocrine & growth
   CJC-1295 no DAC binds the GHRH receptor on pituitary GH cells, which raises cAMP inside the cell and releases stored GH. This is the same switch the body's own GHRH uses. No human study of this exact molecule exists, so the effect is inferred from related GHRH data.
11. Resists breakdown, still short-acting · Modified GRF 1-29 · role Endocrine & growth
   It is the active first 29 amino acids of GHRH with four swaps that resist DPP-4, the enzyme that quickly cuts natural GHRH. That makes it more stable, but it still clears within about half an hour, so it amplifies a pulse rather than holding GH up all day.
12. Amplifies GH pulses when paired with a GHRP · GHRH and GHS synergy · role Endocrine & growth
   GHRH opens the GH gate while ghrelin mimics such as ipamorelin push from a second receptor and blunt somatostatin. Acting together, the two pathways produce a much larger pulse than either alone. This synergy is well shown for GHRH plus secretagogues, but extrapolated for this molecule.
13. GHRH signalling deepens slow-wave sleep · Slow-wave sleep · role Sleep & rhythms
   GHRH signalling in the hypothalamus promotes deep, slow-wave sleep, and GH is mostly released during that stage. A GHRH analogue is expected to support it. This rests on GHRH physiology and user reports, with no sleep study of this exact peptide.
14. Mechanism overview: CJC-1295 without DAC, also called modified GRF 1-29, is the first 29 amino acids of GHRH, its active core, with four substitutions that resist DPP-4 cleavage and improve stability. It binds GHRH receptors on pituitary somatotrophs, raising cAMP and triggering GH release. Its half-life is about 30 minutes, so it amplifies a pulse rather than raising GH continuously, preserving the natural pattern. Combined with a ghrelin mimetic such as ipamorelin, the two pathways synergise into a much larger pulse. GHRH tone also deepens slow-wave sleep.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
15. Typical: 100–300 mcg · daily · cycle 8–12 weeks on, 4 off · route Sub-Q (reported)
16. Half-life: ~30 minutes
17. Most people take: 100mcg combined with 100-300mcg Ipamorelin before bed · Same as Ipamorelin.
18. Common: 100 mcg (+100 mcg ipa) · 2–3× daily · 8–16 wk · Sub-Q · for 'saturation' stack [S1] (reported)
19. Pre-bed: 200 mcg (+200 mcg ipa) · 1× nightly, 5 on/2 off · 12+ wk · Sub-Q · for convenience, sleep [S1] [S2] (reported)
20. Clinic top: 500 mcg (+500 mcg ipa) · 1× nightly, 5 on/2 off · 3 mo, 2 mo off · Sub-Q · for one clinic's month-3 maintenance [S3] (reported)

## What people report
21. One of the most common grey-market GH-optimization peptides; reported for sleep, recovery, body composition.
22. Liked / worked: Reported to raise GH pulses
23. Liked / worked: Reported synergy with ipamorelin
24. What worked: Reported to raise GH pulses, especially with ipamorelin.
25. Went wrong / did not work: No human study of this exact molecule
26. Went wrong / did not work: Short action, frequent dosing
27. Went wrong / did not work: No outcome trials
28. What went wrong: Short action needs frequent dosing; no outcome trials; benefits inferred from GH itself.
29. Most reported: Sleep and recovery
30. Most reported: Body composition

## What has been tested
31. Endocrine & growth: GH release, inferred from DAC data (users)
32. No published human study of this exact molecule; the human data belong to the DAC version. Its effects, including the synergy with ipamorelin, are extrapolated.
33. What it helps: No human study exists for this exact molecule; GH release is inferred from related GHRH data and user experience. Users report bigger GH pulses, especially with ipamorelin, along with better sleep, recovery and body composition. It is one of the most common grey-market GH peptides. There are no outcome trials.
34. Trial: none. Mod GRF 1 to 29 has no registered human trial; only the DAC version was tested (2005 to 2006) before development stopped. (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
35. Pituitary tumour, pituitary surgery or brain radiation: Works by pushing the pituitary; disease there makes effects unpredictable. (inferred)
36. People with active or recent cancer: Raises GH and IGF-1, which promote cell growth. (inferred)
37. Drug-tested athletes: GHRH analogues are banned under WADA S2. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
38. Ipamorelin: CJC-1295 no DAC opens the GHRH gate and ipamorelin pushes through the ghrelin receptor with few side effects, so the pulse is larger than either alone. Sold pre-mixed as CJC-1295 no DAC + Ipamorelin, but the pair has not been tested together in people.
39. GHRP-2: GHRP-2 gives a strong ghrelin-receptor GH pulse and CJC-1295 no DAC adds GHRH drive from the other side. People pair them for a bigger pulse and accept more hunger, cortisol and prolactin. The pairing is user logic, not trial data for this molecule.
40. GHRP-6: GHRP-6 adds a ghrelin-receptor pulse and strong hunger, CJC-1295 no DAC adds GHRH drive. People pair them when bulking and eating more is the goal. The pair itself has not been tested together.
41. Hexarelin: Hexarelin is the strongest ghrelin mimic but fades with repeated use, and CJC-1295 no DAC adds GHRH drive to amplify its pulse. Used for short, hard GH blocks. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
42. Tesamorelin: Both act on the GHRH receptor, so they overlap rather than complement each other. They appear together in the pre-mixed Tesamorelin + Ipamorelin + CJC-1295 no DAC, where ipamorelin supplies the second pathway. The pair alone has not been tested.

## Where it comes from
43. A GHRH analogue (also called modified GRF 1-29 or CJC-1295 without the Drug Affinity Complex), engineered for stability but still short-acting without the DAC tail.
44. First studied for: Studied to raise GH in natural pulses, usually paired with a GHRP.
45. Name story: Properly called Modified GRF (1-29): the first 29 amino acids of growth hormone-releasing hormone with four swaps for stability. Selling it as 'CJC-1295' is a mislabel; the CJC code belongs to the DAC version, and even papers have confused the two. [S5] (verified)
46. 2000s: Stabilised GRF 1-29, also called modified GRF 1-29
47. Today: Top grey-market GH-pulse peptide, usually with ipamorelin; WADA-banned

# Collagen peptides
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/collagen-peptides
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: hydrolysed collagen, hydrolyzed collagen, collagen hydrolysate, gelatin hydrolysate, bioactive collagen peptides, marine collagen, bovine collagen, porcine collagen, Pro-Hyp, Hyp-Gly
2. Origin: Digest of a natural protein: collagen from cow hide, pig skin, fish skin or scales, cut with enzymes
3. Legal and approval status: Sold worldwide as a food ingredient and dietary supplement; gelatin is GRAS in the US. Not a medicine anywhere.

## Summary
4. Collagen peptides are short protein fragments made by enzyme-cutting collagen, usually from cow hide, pig skin or fish skin. People take them for skin, joints, tendon and bone, since fragments like Pro-Hyp reach the blood intact and may prompt skin and cartilage cells to build matrix. Pooled trials show modest gains in skin hydration, but a 2025 meta-analysis found no skin benefit in independent or high-quality trials.
5. Punch line: Enzyme-cut collagen from cow, pig or fish, a daily scoop. Pro-Hyp fragments reach the blood intact.
6. Used for: Skin hydration and elasticity, joint pain, tendon and bone

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Skin & aesthetics: Hydration and elasticity in pooled trials
8. Bone & cartilage: Bone density after menopause, one trial
9. Tissue repair: Tendon size and pain with training
10. Pain & sensory: Knee arthritis pain, modestly
11. Muscle & performance (backed only by animal or user reports): More lean mass with strength training
12. Hair (backed only by animal or user reports): Users report stronger nails and hair
13. Digestive & gut (backed only by animal or user reports): Users report gut comfort

## How it works
14. Digestion cuts it into short fragments and free amino acids · Digestion · role Digestive & gut
   In the gut, protease enzymes cut collagen peptides into free amino acids and short chains. Most of the dose ends up as ordinary amino acids, the same fate as any dietary protein. Only a small fraction survives as intact fragments, and that fraction is where the specific claims rest.
15. Pro-Hyp and Hyp-Gly reach the blood intact · Hydroxyproline dipeptides · role Skin & aesthetics
   Dipeptides containing hydroxyproline, chiefly Pro-Hyp and Hyp-Gly, resist digestion and appear in blood within one to two hours in human feeding studies. After four weeks of daily intake the share of Hyp-Gly rose while Pro-Hyp stayed most abundant. These are the closest thing collagen has to an active ingredient.
16. Fragments prompt skin fibroblasts to make collagen and hyaluronan · Fibroblast signal, cell studies · role Skin & aesthetics
   In cell studies, these fragments signal skin fibroblasts, the cells that build the dermis, to divide and make hyaluronan and collagen. Pooled human trials show modest gains in skin hydration and elasticity, but independent and high quality trials found no benefit.
17. Supplies glycine, proline and hydroxyproline for new collagen · Building blocks · role Tissue repair
   The freed amino acids supply glycine, proline and hydroxyproline, the raw materials collagen is built from. Whether this beats an equal dose of other protein is largely untested. In eight men, vitamin C enriched gelatin before skipping roughly doubled a collagen synthesis marker.
18. May push cartilage and bone cells toward building matrix · Chondrocyte and osteoblast signal · role Bone & cartilage
   In cell studies, collagen fragments push chondrocytes and osteoblasts, the cartilage and bone building cells, toward making matrix. Human trials are small: knee arthritis pain fell modestly in high risk of bias trials, and one industry linked year long trial reported higher spine and hip density after menopause.
19. Mechanism overview: Collagen peptides are collagen cut by enzymes into a mixture of fragments, mostly a few to a few dozen amino acids long. There is no single chain: like Cerebrolysin, the product is defined by its source and process. After a dose, most is broken down to free amino acids, but hydroxyproline-containing dipeptides, chiefly Pro-Hyp and Hyp-Gly, resist digestion and appear in blood within an hour or two. In cell studies these fragments prompt skin fibroblasts to divide and make hyaluronan, and cartilage and bone cells to build matrix. The rest supplies glycine, proline and hydroxyproline, the raw material of new collagen.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
20. Typical: 2.5–10 g · once daily · cycle 8–12 weeks, then ongoing · route Oral (verified)
21. Half-life: Pro-Hyp peaks in blood at 1–2 h, gone by ~12 h
22. Most people take: Trials use 2.5–5 g a day for skin, 5 g for bone and tendon, about 10 g for knee arthritis and 15 g with strength training for muscle. Any time of day; tendon studies give it with vitamin C about an hour before loading.
23. Skin: 2.5–5 g · 1× daily · 8–12 wk · Oral · for skin hydration, elasticity [S1] [S2] (verified)
24. Bone and tendon: 5 g · 1× daily · 3–12 mo · Oral · for bone after menopause, tendon with training [S3] [S4] [S5] (verified)
25. Joints: 10 g · 1× daily · 12–24 wk · Oral · for knee arthritis pain [S6] (verified)
26. Muscle: 15 g · 1× daily · 12 wk · Oral · for with strength training, older men [S7] (verified)

## What people report
27. A daily scoop in coffee or water; people report stronger nails, better skin and less joint ache.
28. Liked / worked: Modest skin hydration and elasticity gains in pooled trials
29. Liked / worked: Modest knee pain relief
30. Liked / worked: Bone density, tendon size and lean mass gains in single trials
31. What worked: Pooled trials show modest gains in skin hydration and elasticity and modest knee pain relief; single trials report bone density, tendon size and lean mass gains.
32. Went wrong / did not work: Wrinkles: no reliable effect
33. Went wrong / did not work: No skin benefit in independent, high-quality trials
34. Went wrong / did not work: Most trials small and industry-funded
35. What went wrong: Wrinkles do not reliably improve. In a 2025 meta-analysis, trials without industry funding and high-quality trials showed no skin benefit.
36. Most reported: Daily scoop in coffee or water
37. Most reported: Nails, hair, skin
38. Most reported: Less joint ache

## What has been tested
39. Skin & aesthetics: Skin hydration and elasticity (trial)
40. Pain & sensory: Knee arthritis pain (trial)
41. Bone & cartilage: Bone density after menopause (trial)
42. Tissue repair: Achilles and patellar tendon (trial)
43. Muscle & performance: Lean mass with strength training (trial)
44. Dozens of small randomised trials, mostly 2.5 to 15 g a day for 8 weeks to a year: skin hydration and elasticity, knee arthritis pain, bone density after menopause, tendon and muscle with training.
45. What it helps: Pooled randomised trials show modest improvements in skin hydration and elasticity, but wrinkles do not reliably improve, and a 2025 meta-analysis found no skin benefit in independent or high-quality trials. Knee arthritis pain falls modestly in small, high-risk-of-bias trials. Single industry-linked trials report higher bone density after menopause, larger tendons and more lean mass with training.
46. Trial: active · Supplement trial · telomeres, inflammation and strength over 24 weeks · NCT07456449 · University of Vienna. One of many ongoing collagen trials; this one is co-sponsored by an industry collagen research institute. (checked 2026-10-24) [S8] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
47. People with fish allergy (marine collagen): Fish collagen is a registered fish allergen; one in five fish-allergic patients in one study had IgE to it, some with a negative standard fish test. Jellyfish and shellfish-sourced powders exist too. (verified)
48. People with alpha-gal syndrome: Bovine and porcine collagen carry the alpha-gal sugar from tick-bite meat allergy; reactions by mouth are uncommon but can be delayed and severe. (reported)
49. Kidney stone formers: Collagen is rich in hydroxyproline, which the body partly turns into oxalate; 5–10 g gelatin loads raised urinary oxalate and glycolate. (verified)
50. People with histamine intolerance: Bone broth and some collagen powders are reported to trigger flushing or headaches; slow-cooked and fermented sources can carry more histamine. Thin data. (reported)
51. Anyone counting it as their protein: It has no tryptophan and little leucine, so it is not a complete protein; matters on low-protein or kidney diets where every gram is budgeted. (verified)
52. People avoiding pork or beef: Most powders are bovine or porcine and labels often just say collagen. (verified)
53. Pregnant or breastfeeding: No supplement-dose trials; heavy metals found in some powders matter more here. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
54. Vitamin C: Vitamin C is the cofactor the enzymes need to finish new collagen, while collagen peptides supply the raw amino acids and signalling dipeptides. In eight men, vitamin C enriched gelatin before exercise roughly doubled a collagen synthesis marker, but larger trials of the pair are lacking.
55. GHK-Cu: GHK-Cu signals fibroblasts to make collagen and elastin and remodels the matrix, while collagen peptides supply building blocks and fragments that prompt fibroblasts in cell studies. People pair them for skin from the signal and supply sides, but the pair has not been tested together.
56. BPC-157: BPC-157 grows blood vessels and moves repair cells into injured tissue in animals, while collagen peptides supply the amino acids new tendon needs and grew tendons in small training trials. People stack them for tendon recovery, but the pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
57. Gelatin, boiled-down collagen, has been eaten for centuries. Enzyme-cut collagen hydrolysate became a commercial ingredient in the late 20th century; in 2005 a Japanese team showed short collagen fragments such as Pro-Hyp reach human blood intact.
58. First studied for: A by-product of the meat and gelatin industry, sold first for joints and bone, later as a skin supplement.
59. Name story: Collagen comes from the Greek kolla, glue, plus -gen, producing: boiling hide and bone made glue. Hydrolysate means split with water and enzymes into short pieces; peptides is the marketing name for the same thing. [S9] (reported)
60. 2005: Pro-Hyp found in human blood after eating collagen hydrolysate
61. 2014: 2.5 g a day lifts skin elasticity in an 8-week trial
62. 2018: 5 g a day raises spine and hip bone density in a one-year trial
63. 2025: Meta-analysis: no skin benefit in independent, high-quality trials
64. Today: A cheap daily supplement; modest, contested benefits

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What is in the scoop [lab]
65. Collagen peptides are not one peptide. They are collagen, mostly type I from cow hide, pig skin or fish skin and scales, boiled to gelatin and then cut with enzymes into a mixture of fragments [11] (verified). Like Cerebrolysin, the product is defined by its source and its process rather than by a sequence, so two brands with the same label can differ in fragment size, source animal and the share of small peptides (inferred).
66. What matters biologically is the small fraction that survives digestion. In 2005 researchers fed volunteers gelatin hydrolysate and found prolyl-hydroxyproline (Pro-Hyp) as the dominant collagen peptide in blood, peaking within one to two hours, with smaller amounts of Ala-Hyp, Pro-Hyp-Gly and others [11] (verified). After four weeks of daily intake the blood profile shifted, with a rising share of hydroxyprolyl-glycine (Hyp-Gly), while Pro-Hyp stayed the most abundant [12] (verified). These two dipeptides are the closest thing collagen has to an active ingredient.

### The skin evidence, and the funding problem [people]
67. Early trials of specific peptides were positive: 2.5 g or 5 g a day for eight weeks improved skin elasticity against placebo in 69 women, with hydration trending better but not significant [4] (verified). Pooled analyses since then report modest gains in hydration and elasticity [3] (reported), and an updated 2026 meta-analysis put the effects at standardised mean differences of about 0.44 for hydration and 0.62 for elasticity, with no reliable effect on wrinkles and signs of publication bias [2] (reported).
68. The 2025 meta-analysis of 23 trials and 1,474 people cut the other way. Pooled, collagen looked effective; split by funding, trials without industry money showed no benefit, and high-quality trials showed no effect on hydration, elasticity or wrinkles [1] (reported). Industry groups disputed how funding and quality were classified [1] (reported). The honest reading is a small effect at best, measured mostly by instruments on the skin surface, in short trials, from a field where most studies are commercially linked (inferred).

### Joints, bone, tendon and muscle [people]
69. Knee osteoarthritis: a 2023 meta-analysis of four trials and 507 patients found less pain on collagen peptides (standardised mean difference about −0.58), but every trial was rated high risk of bias and the result was heterogeneous [5] (verified).
70. Bone: in a one-year trial of 102 postmenopausal women with low bone density, 5 g a day raised spine and femoral neck density against placebo, with a rise in a bone formation marker [6] (reported; summarised by the manufacturer, single trial).
71. Tendon: with calf strengthening, 5 g a day sped recovery in 20 people with Achilles tendinopathy in a crossover trial [7] (verified), and in young men doing heavy training, 5 g a day grew the patellar tendon more than placebo without changing stiffness or strength [8] (verified). In eight men, 15 g of vitamin C enriched gelatin an hour before skipping roughly doubled a collagen synthesis marker [9] (verified).
72. Muscle: older men on 15 g a day plus resistance training gained more lean mass than training alone over 12 weeks [10] (reported). Collagen is a poor protein for muscle on paper, so the result is surprising and has not been widely replicated (inferred).

### Safety, quality and who should think twice [mixed]
73. Side effects in trials are rare and mild: fullness, a taste, mild stomach upset (reported across trials). The real issues are source and quality. Hydroxyproline, abundant in collagen, is partly converted to oxalate; in a controlled feeding study gelatin raised urinary oxalate by 43% and glycolate fivefold, and 5 to 10 g loads moved them while 1 to 2 g did not [13] (verified). That matters for calcium oxalate stone formers.
74. Allergy depends on the animal. Fish collagen is a registered fish allergen, and some fish-allergic patients react to it without reacting to the usual fish test [14] (verified). Bovine and porcine collagen carry alpha-gal, the sugar behind tick-bite meat allergy [15] (reported).
75. Heavy metals: a non-profit test of 30 collagen products found measurable lead in 37% and cadmium in 17%, with 4 of 30 over its limits; industry called the report sensational and not peer reviewed [16] (reported). Look for third-party testing and a named source animal (inferred).

### Open questions [mixed]
76. Does the benefit come from specific dipeptides, or from protein and glycine any food could supply? Few trials compare collagen with an equal dose of another protein.
77. Why do independent trials of skin outcomes look null while sponsored ones look positive?
78. Do bone density gains hold and reduce fractures? No fracture trial exists.
79. What dose matters? Skin trials found no clear dose-response, and duration seemed to matter more [2] (reported).

# MIC + B12
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/mic-b12
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: MIC B12, Lipo-B, Lipo B12, lipotropic B12 shot, MICC, LC120, LC216
2. Origin: Blend: amino acids + vitamin (lipotropic injection)
3. Legal and approval status: US: not FDA-approved as a combination; made by 503A compounding pharmacies on prescription. Cyanocobalamin injection alone is approved for B12 deficiency. Grey-market LC120 and LC216 vials are sold for research use. Not on the WADA list.

## Summary
4. MIC + B12 is the classic lipotropic injection, combining methionine, inositol and choline with vitamin B12. Clinics sell it as a weekly fat-burning and energy shot, on the idea that the trio helps the liver move fat out. B12 clearly helps people who are deficient, but no trial shows meaningful weight loss from the shot, and extra B12 does nothing measurable at normal levels.
5. Punch line: The classic lipotropic shot: methionine, inositol and choline with B12. A weekly diet companion; fat loss unproven.
6. Used for: Energy and fat-loss support during a diet

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Fat metabolism: MIC trio claimed to move fat out of the liver
8. Cellular energy: B12 for red cells and fuel use
9. Organ function: Choline and methionine for the liver
10. Neural protection: B12 keeps nerves healthy
11. Skin & aesthetics (backed only by animal or user reports): High B12 can cause acne-like breakouts

## How it works
12. Lets the liver package and export fat · Choline → phosphatidylcholine, VLDL · role Organ function
   Choline becomes phosphatidylcholine, which the liver needs to package fat into VLDL particles for export. Without enough choline, fat builds up in the liver, shown in animals and people. Extra choline helps when intake is low; there is no evidence it moves more fat on a normal diet.
13. Methyl donor for the liver · Methionine → SAM · role Organ function
   Methionine is converted to SAM, the main methyl donor. SAM drives the PEMT pathway, a second route to phosphatidylcholine, so it supports liver fat export too. These lipotropic effects are shown mainly in animals on deficient diets.
14. Lipid and insulin signalling · Inositol, phosphoinositides · role Fat metabolism
   Inositol is the building block of phosphoinositides, signalling lipids that relay insulin's message inside cells. That links it to sugar and fat handling. Its best human evidence is oral use in polycystic ovary syndrome, not injected use for fat loss.
15. Needed for red cells and nerves · B12: methionine synthase, methylmalonyl-CoA mutase · role Cellular energy
   B12 is a cofactor for methionine synthase, which recycles homocysteine into methionine and keeps DNA and red cell production going, and for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in odd-chain fat breakdown. Injections clearly correct deficiency in human trials; extra B12 adds little when levels are normal.
16. Protects nerves when B12 is low · Myelin maintenance · role Neural protection
   B12 is needed to maintain myelin, the insulating layer around nerves. When B12 runs low, nerves can be damaged, causing numbness and weakness. Treating deficiency protects nerves in people; there is no evidence of extra nerve benefit when levels are already normal.
17. Mechanism overview: Methionine, inositol and choline are classed as lipotropes, nutrients that prevent or reverse hepatic fat accumulation. Choline is required for phosphatidylcholine synthesis and VLDL secretion; methionine supplies S-adenosylmethionine for the PEMT pathway, which also makes phosphatidylcholine. Inositol is a phosphoinositide precursor involved in insulin signalling. Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for methionine synthase, which regenerates methionine from homocysteine, and for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in odd-chain fat metabolism. The pairing is biochemically coherent, but lipotropic effects are shown mainly in deficient animals, and no controlled human trial measures fat loss from the combined injection.

## What is inside the blend
18. Methionine: 25 mg per mL · Methyl donor for liver fat handling
19. Inositol: 50 mg per mL · Insulin and lipid signalling
20. Choline: 50 mg per mL · Lets the liver export fat
21. Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin): 1 mg per mL · Energy and nerves; the only part with approved use
22. Most common ratio: Methionine 25 · Inositol 50 · Choline 50 · B12 1 = 126 mg/mL (3 of 6 pharmacy/clinic formulas (+1 guide))
23. Other ratio seen: Methionine 25 · Inositol 50 · Choline 50 · B12 0.33 ("MICC") = ~125 mg/mL (2 pharmacies)
24. Other ratio seen: Methionine 25 · Choline 50 · B12 1, no inositol (Lipo-B) = 76 mg/mL (1 pharmacy)
25. Version Common pharmacy: Methionine 25 · Inositol 50 · Choline 50 · B12 1 = 126 mg/mL
26. Version LC120: Methionine 15 · Choline 50 · L-Carnitine 50 · Dexpanthenol 5 = 120 mg/mL
27. Version LC216 (Lipo-B): L-Carnitine 20 · Arginine 20 · Methionine 25 · Inositol 50 · Choline 50 · B6 25 · B5 25 · B12 1 = 216 mg/mL
28. Why Methionine is in it: Methyl groups for the liver
29. Why Inositol is in it: Insulin and lipid signalling
30. Why Choline is in it: Liver fat export
31. Why Vitamin B12 is in it: Energy and nerves when B12 is low
32. Mixing chemistry: Ready-made liquid in a multi-dose vial; nothing to reconstitute.
33. Mixing chemistry: B12 is red and light-sensitive; keep the vial in its box.
34. Mixing chemistry: Cyanocobalamin is the usual B12; some clinics swap methylcobalamin, which is less stable to light.
35. Mixing chemistry: LC120 has no B12 at all despite the 'Lipo' label: it is a carnitine formula.
36. Mixing chemistry: Don't use if cloudy or particles appear.
37. Self-mixing: Not mixed by the user; it comes ready. Some people draw it with a separate B12 or Lipo-C vial in one syringe, which adds needle passes and untested contact.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
38. Typical: 1 mL (≈1 mg B12) · 1× weekly (some 2×) · cycle 4–12 weeks · route IM (reported)
39. Half-life: per component
40. Most people take: 1 mL intramuscular once a week is the usual clinic dose, sometimes twice a week in supervised weight-loss programs, reassessed every 4 to 8 weeks. LC120 and LC216 vials are dosed the same way, 1 mL at a time.

## What people report
41. 1 to 2 mL IM once a week, some twice, over 4 to 12 weeks. Reports: injection-site soreness, nausea, mild stomach upset, headache, a metallic taste at higher methionine doses, acne-like breakouts from B12. Often paired with a GLP-1 or phentermine program.
42. Liked / worked: Fixes low B12 and its tiredness
43. Liked / worked: Weekly shot helps diet adherence
44. Liked / worked: Cheap and widely compounded
45. What worked: People with low B12 feel more energy, and that is real. Clinics report weekly shots help adherence during a diet.
46. Went wrong / did not work: No trial shows weight loss from the shot
47. Went wrong / did not work: B12 adds nothing if levels are normal
48. Went wrong / did not work: Oral B12 works as well for levels
49. What went wrong: No good trial shows meaningful weight loss from the shot. Reviews say weight change on it comes from diet and exercise. Extra B12 does nothing measurable when levels are already normal.
50. Most reported: 1 mL IM weekly
51. Most reported: Sore site, nausea, headache
52. Most reported: Acne-like breakouts from B12
53. Most reported: Paired with GLP-1 programs

## What has been tested
54. Cellular energy: B12 injection for deficiency (human)
55. Organ function: Choline and fatty liver (animal)
56. Fat metabolism: MIC + B12 for weight loss (none)
57. No controlled trial of MIC + B12 as a product. B12 injections are approved for deficiency. Choline and methionine have lipotropic (liver fat) effects mostly in animals; a Cochrane review found oral 1,000 mcg B12 raises blood levels as well as injections.
58. What it helps: B12 injections clearly help people who are deficient. The MIC trio's fat-moving effects are shown in deficient animals, not in people on a normal diet. No trial measures weight loss from MIC + B12, and guides credit any loss to diet.

## Who shouldn't take it
59. People with homocystinuria or high homocysteine: Methionine is the direct precursor of homocysteine. (inferred)
60. People with Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy: Cyanocobalamin can speed optic nerve damage. (verified)
61. People with cobalt allergy: Cobalt sits at the centre of the B12 molecule; the label contraindicates use. (verified)
62. People with very low potassium: Treating deficiency can drop potassium fast. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
63. Lipo-C: Lipo-C shares choline and methionine with MIC + B12 and adds carnitine and B1 and B5 for fuel use. People combine or alternate them during diets. Neither has a weight loss trial, and the pair has not been tested together.
64. Vitamin B12: Standalone B12 just raises the B12 dose already in MIC + B12. It matters only if someone is deficient, where injections clearly work. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
65. L-Carnitine: L-carnitine adds the fat shuttle into mitochondria, which MIC + B12 lacks, with small weight loss effects in oral trials. Clinics pair them for fat loss support. The pair has not been tested together.
66. Semaglutide: Semaglutide does the main weight loss work through the GLP-1 receptor, with large human trials. MIC + B12 is added for liver fat handling and B12 while eating less. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
67. Tirzepatide: Tirzepatide drives weight loss through GIP and GLP-1 receptors, with large human trials. MIC + B12 is added as a nutrient layer during the deficit. The pair has not been tested together.
68. Glutathione: Glutathione is the main cellular antioxidant and is used for skin brightening. Clinics bundle it with MIC + B12 in wellness injection menus. The two work on different systems, and the pairing has not been tested.
69. NAD+: NAD+ carries electrons for energy production and feeds repair enzymes, while MIC + B12 supports liver fat export and B12 status. Clinics pair them for energy. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
70. The classic 'lipotropic' shot: methionine, inositol and choline (MIC) with vitamin B12. The common formula per mL is methionine 25, inositol 50, choline 50 mg and B12 1 mg (1,000 mcg). Grey-market 'LC' vials add carnitine and more B vitamins.
71. First studied for: A weight-loss clinic and med-spa staple in the US since at least the 2000s, sold as a weekly 'fat-burning' energy shot.
72. Name story: MIC is the initials of methionine, inositol and choline; B12 is the vitamin added. 'Lipo-B' is the same shot, named for lipotropic plus B12. 'LC' codes like LC120 and LC216 give total mg per mL. [S1] (reported)
73. 1930s: Choline found to stop fatty liver in animals: the 'lipotropic' idea
74. 1948: Vitamin B12 isolated
75. 2000s: MIC + B12 shots spread through US weight-loss clinics (inferred)
76. 2018: Cochrane: oral and injected B12 raise levels about equally
77. Today: Compounded MIC + B12; grey-market LC120 and LC216

# Sermorelin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/sermorelin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Geref, Gerel, GRF 1-29, GHRH(1-29)NH2, sermorelin acetate
2. Origin: Fragment of a natural protein
3. Sequence: YADAIFTNSYRKVLGQLSARKLLQDIMSR (29 amino acids). Amide end
4. Legal and approval status: Previously FDA-approved, now discontinued as a product; compounded and grey-market use continues. WADA-banned.

## Summary
5. Sermorelin is a fragment of growth-hormone-releasing hormone, the first 29 amino acids and its active core, which prompts the pituitary to release its own GH in natural pulses. It was used for pituitary function testing and childhood GH deficiency, and users take it for sleep, recovery and body composition, often with a GHRP. Effects are smaller and slower than injected GH and need a working pituitary.
6. Punch line: The first 29 amino acids of GHRH. Gets the pituitary pulsing its own GH; gentler than injecting GH.
7. Used for: GH support, sleep, recovery

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Endocrine & growth: Prompts the pituitary to release GH
9. Cognition: Clearer head reported
10. Muscle & performance: Recovery reported
11. Sleep & rhythms: Deeper sleep reported
12. Mood (backed only by animal or user reports): Steadier mood reported

## How it works
13. Prompts the pituitary to release its own GH · GHRH receptor · role Endocrine & growth
   Sermorelin is GHRH 1-29, the shortest fully active piece of the body's GH-releasing hormone. It binds GHRH receptors on pituitary GH cells, raises cAMP and releases the pituitary's own stored GH. Human studies show it reliably raises GH, and it was used to test pituitary function.
14. Keeps natural GH pulses · Pituitary feedback intact · role Endocrine & growth
   Because it works upstream of GH, somatostatin and IGF-1 feedback still regulate the response. GH comes out in natural pulses rather than a flat high, which limits overshoot. The trade-off is that it needs a working pituitary to do anything.
15. Raises IGF-1 and lean mass modestly · GH, IGF-1 · role Muscle & performance
   Each GH pulse drives the liver to make IGF-1, which supports muscle and lean mass. Human studies show GH and IGF-1 rise, but gains are smaller and slower than with injected GH. It was used in childhood GH deficiency trials.
16. GHRH signalling deepens slow-wave sleep · Slow-wave sleep · role Sleep & rhythms
   GHRH signalling in the hypothalamus promotes deep, slow-wave sleep, the stage when most GH is released. This is established GHRH physiology. Users report better sleep on sermorelin, though sleep has not been its trial endpoint.
17. GHRH improved cognition in older adults, one RCT · GHRH, IGF-1 · role Cognition
   In one randomised trial in older adults, GHRH treatment improved cognitive scores, probably through GH and IGF-1 effects on the brain. It is a single trial, so treat it as an early human signal rather than proof.
18. Mechanism overview: Sermorelin is GHRH 1-29, the shortest fully active fragment of growth hormone releasing hormone. It binds GHRH receptors on pituitary somatotrophs, raises cAMP and triggers GH release. Because it acts upstream, somatostatin and IGF-1 feedback still regulate the response, so GH rises in natural pulses rather than as a flat high. GH then drives liver IGF-1, modestly lifting lean mass. Its half-life is minutes, so it needs frequent dosing. GHRH signalling also deepens slow-wave sleep.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
19. Typical: 200–500 mcg · daily · cycle 3-6 months continuous · route Sub-Q (reported)
20. Half-life: ~12 minutes
21. Most people take: 200-500mcg before bed SC · 3-6 months continuous. Some run indefinitely.
22. Common: 200–300 mcg · nightly · 3–6 mo · Sub-Q · for general, sleep [S1] [S2] (reported)
23. Clinic: 300–500 mcg · nightly · 6–12 mo · Sub-Q · for age 45+, titrated on IGF-1 [S3] [S2] (reported)
24. Compounded high: 500–1000 mcg · nightly, or 2–3×/wk · 6–12 mo · Sub-Q · for compounding-pharmacy protocols [S1] (reported)

## What people report
25. Popular grey-market 'GH optimization'; reported for sleep, recovery and body composition, often with a GHRP.
26. Liked / worked: Reliably raises GH and IGF-1
27. Liked / worked: Gentler than injected GH
28. What worked: Reliably raises GH and IGF-1 by working through the body's own pulse control, which keeps it gentler than injected GH.
29. Went wrong / did not work: Smaller, slower effect than GH
30. Went wrong / did not work: Needs a working pituitary
31. Went wrong / did not work: Short half-life, frequent dosing
32. What went wrong: Effect is smaller and slower than direct GH; needs an intact pituitary; short half-life means frequent dosing.
33. Most reported: Sleep, recovery, body composition
34. Most reported: Often paired with a GHRP

## What has been tested
35. Endocrine & growth: Pituitary function test (human)
36. Endocrine & growth: Childhood GH deficiency (trial)
37. Used clinically for decades as a GH-deficiency diagnostic and therapy; it was FDA-approved (as Geref) before being discontinued for commercial reasons, not safety.
38. What it helps: Human studies show it reliably raises GH and IGF-1, and it was used for pituitary function testing and in childhood GH deficiency. Effects are smaller and slower than injected GH and need a working pituitary. One RCT of GHRH in older adults showed improved cognition. Users report better sleep, recovery and body composition, often pairing it with a GHRP.
39. Trial: none. Approved as Geref in 1997 and pulled in 2008 for commercial reasons; no recent registered trial found (search incomplete). (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
40. People with untreated hypothyroidism: Prescribing info required thyroid correction first; low thyroid blunts response. (reported)
41. People with active or recent cancer: Raises GH and IGF-1, which promote cell growth. (inferred)
42. Drug-tested athletes: GHRH analogues are banned under WADA S2. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
43. Ipamorelin: Sermorelin drives GH through the GHRH receptor and ipamorelin adds a clean ghrelin-receptor pulse, so the two pathways give a bigger but still natural GH release. People use it as an alternative to the CJC stack. The pair has not been tested together.
44. GHRP-2: GHRP-2 adds a strong ghrelin-receptor push to sermorelin's GHRH drive, so pulses are larger. The cost is more hunger, cortisol and prolactin than with ipamorelin. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
45. GHRP-6: GHRP-6 adds a ghrelin-receptor pulse and strong hunger to sermorelin's GHRH drive. People pair them when gaining weight and appetite is part of the goal. The pair itself has not been tested together.
46. Hexarelin: Hexarelin is the strongest ghrelin mimic and sermorelin adds GHRH drive, giving a large pulse. Hexarelin fades with repeat use and raises cortisol and prolactin more, so it suits short blocks. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
47. A fragment of growth-hormone-releasing hormone (the first 29 amino acids, the active core), which prompts the pituitary to release its own GH in natural pulses.
48. First studied for: A diagnostic test of pituitary function and a treatment for childhood GH deficiency.
49. Name story: The first 29 of growth hormone-releasing hormone's 44 amino acids, hence the old lab name GRF 1–29. '-relin' is the INN stem for hormone-release-stimulating peptides. FDA-approved as Geref, then dropped in 2008 for business reasons, not safety. [S5] (verified)
50. 1997: Approved as Geref for childhood GH deficiency and testing
51. 2008: Discontinued for commercial, not safety, reasons
52. Today: Compounded GH-optimisation peptide; WADA-banned

# Dihexa
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/dihexa
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: PNB-0408, N-hexanoic-Tyr-Ile-(6) aminohexanoic amide, N-hexanoic-Tyr-Ile-(6)-aminohexanoic amide, fosgonimeton (prodrug)
2. Origin: Lab-designed from angiotensin IV
3. Sequence: YI (2 amino acids). Hexanoyl cap on Tyr, then Ile and a 6-aminohexanoic amide tail; a modified dipeptide
4. Legal and approval status: Not approved; FDA nomination for compounding withdrawn; on the April 2026 list moved off FDA Category 2 (as of Oct 2026).

## Summary
5. Dihexa is a small modified dipeptide built from angiotensin IV at Washington State University. It boosts a growth factor signal (HGF and c-Met) that builds synapses, and was developed as an oral drug lead for Alzheimer's. Evidence is rat and cell work, no human study exists, and users report headaches and anxiety.
6. Punch line: Oral Alzheimer's lead built from angiotensin that grows new synapses. Rat data only; headaches are common.
7. Used for: Memory, focus

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Cognition: Memory restored in rats
9. Neural plasticity: New synapses in cells
10. Neural protection: Studied for dementia
11. Drive & mental stamina: Sharper focus reported
12. Cancer biology (backed only by animal or user reports): Activates a tumour growth pathway

## How it works
13. Boosts a growth factor signal that builds synapses · HGF / c-Met potentiation · role Neural plasticity
   Dihexa, a modified piece of angiotensin IV, boosts signalling by hepatocyte growth factor, HGF, through its receptor c-Met. In neurons this pathway grows dendritic spines, the contact points for synapses. This is shown in cell studies.
14. Helps HGF pair up and switch on its receptor · HGF dimerisation · role Neural plasticity
   HGF needs to pair up, or dimerise, before it can switch on c-Met. Dihexa binds HGF and helps those pairs form, so a small amount of HGF signals more strongly. This is the proposed mechanism from lab work by its developers.
15. Restores memory in impaired rats · Morris water maze, scopolamine model · role Cognition
   In rats with memory impaired by scopolamine, Dihexa restored performance in the Morris water maze, a standard memory test. The proposed basis is new synapse growth. No human study exists, and a related compound, fosgonimeton, failed its Alzheimer's trial.
16. Same pathway drives many cancers · c-Met overexpression in tumours · role Cancer biology
   HGF and c-Met signalling is overactive in many tumours, where it drives growth and spread. Boosting the same pathway carries a theoretical cancer and metastasis risk. No carcinogenicity study has been done, so the risk is untested.
17. Mechanism overview: Dihexa is a capped, modified dipeptide derived from angiotensin IV. It binds hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) and helps it form the dimers that switch on its receptor, c-Met. In neurons, HGF/c-Met signalling grows dendritic spines and new synapses, which is the proposed basis for memory rescue in rats. The same HGF/c-Met pathway is overactive in many tumours, so stronger signalling carries a theoretical cancer and metastasis risk; no carcinogenicity study exists.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
18. Typical: 5–10 mg · once daily · cycle 4–8 weeks · route Oral or transdermal (reported)
19. Half-life: unknown in humans
20. Most people take: No human dose studied. Community 5–10 mg/day oral; injectable 2–5 mg reported less often.

25. Went wrong / did not work: No human trials

27. Went wrong / did not work: BDNF comparison never made in the paper

## Where it comes from

# L-Carnitine
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/l-carnitine
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: levocarnitine, Carnitor, LC120, LC216, LC526, Lipo-C, Lipo-B, vitamin BT, Carnitene, (R)-3-hydroxy-4-(trimethylazaniumyl)butanoate
2. Origin: Not a peptide: amino-acid-derived small molecule
3. Shown with an FDA approved badge
4. Legal and approval status: FDA-approved as levocarnitine injection (Carnitor and generics) for deficiency only; 'LC' blends are unapproved research mixes. WADA: not prohibited, but IV infusions over 100 mL per 12 h are (2026 M2.2).

## Summary
5. L-Carnitine is not a peptide but a small molecule the body makes from lysine and methionine to carry fatty acids into mitochondria. Injectable levocarnitine is approved only for deficiency, yet people inject it, alone or in lipotropic blends, for fat loss and training energy. Fat-loss results are mixed, muscle uptake needs insulin, and the injection stings.
6. Punch line: The fat shuttle. Carries fatty acids into mitochondria; injected alone or in lipo blends, mixed results, stings.
7. Used for: Fat loss, training energy, carnitine deficiency

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Fat metabolism: Ferries fat into mitochondria
9. Cellular energy: Fuels mitochondrial fat burning
10. Muscle & performance: Spares glycogen in training
11. Organ function: Replaces losses in dialysis
12. Reproductive (backed only by animal or user reports): Sperm motility in oral trials
13. Glucose & insulin (backed only by animal or user reports): Insulin sensitivity claims

## How it works
14. Shuttles fatty acids into mitochondria · CPT1/CPT2 carnitine shuttle · role Fat metabolism
   CPT1 attaches long-chain fatty acids to carnitine so they can cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, and CPT2 releases them inside for beta-oxidation. Without carnitine, long-chain fat cannot reach the place it is burned. This is textbook biochemistry, and replacement is approved for carnitine deficiency.
15. Clears excess acyl groups from cells · Acylcarnitine export · role Cellular energy
   Carnitine takes up excess acyl groups, such as acetyl groups, and exports them from the cell as acylcarnitines. That frees coenzyme A for other energy reactions. In inborn errors and dialysis, this clears build-up that can harm cells.
16. Spares muscle glycogen at easy pace · PDC flux, glycogen sparing · role Muscle & performance
   During exercise, carnitine buffers surplus acetyl groups, easing the pyruvate dehydrogenase bottleneck that limits carbohydrate use. Muscle then uses its glycogen stores more efficiently at easy pace. A 24-week human study with carbohydrate raised muscle carnitine and improved cycling output.
17. Muscle uptake needs insulin · OCTN2 transporter, insulin-stimulated · role Glucose & insulin
   Muscle takes carnitine in through the OCTN2 transporter, and insulin stimulates that uptake. This is why the human study that raised muscle carnitine paired it with carbohydrate. Without an insulin rise, little extra reaches muscle.
18. Mechanism overview: L-carnitine (levocarnitine) is a quaternary ammonium compound made from lysine and methionine. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT1) attaches long-chain fatty acids to it so they can cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, where CPT2 releases them for beta-oxidation. It also buffers excess acetyl groups as acetylcarnitine, freeing coenzyme A and easing the pyruvate dehydrogenase bottleneck during exercise. Muscle takes it up through the OCTN2 transporter, which is stimulated by insulin.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
19. Typical: 50–200 mg/day (community); 10–20 mg/kg (label, dialysis) · daily or pre-workout; blends 1 mL 2–3×/week · cycle 8–16 weeks or ongoing · route Sub-Q or IM; IV clinically (reported)
20. Half-life: ~17 h (IV, terminal)
21. Most people take: Community SC/IM 50–200 mg daily or 100–200 mg pre-workout. Lipotropic blends (LC120, LC216, LC526) 1 mL 2–3×/week. Clinical IV 10–20 mg/kg after dialysis or 50 mg/kg in metabolic crisis. Oral 1–2 g/day with carbs is the studied athlete route.

## What people report
22. Injected SC or IM, often in lipotropic 'LC' blends or alongside GLP-1s, for fat loss and gym energy. People report injection sting, more energy in training, and a fishy smell at high doses; fat-loss reports are mixed.
23. Liked / worked: ~1.3 kg extra weight loss (oral meta-analysis)
24. Liked / worked: Muscle carnitine up 21% with carbs
25. Liked / worked: Treats deficiency in dialysis
26. What worked: Oral carnitine trials averaged about 1.3 kg extra weight loss. Six months of oral carnitine with carbs raised muscle carnitine ~21% and improved a 30-minute cycling test.
27. Went wrong / did not work: Small, inconsistent fat-loss effect
28. Went wrong / did not work: Muscle won't load without insulin
29. Went wrong / did not work: Seizures, nausea, odour (label)
30. Went wrong / did not work: Rare anaphylaxis
31. What went wrong: Muscle uptake needs insulin, so a shot alone may not load muscle. Label lists seizures, nausea, body odour and rare anaphylaxis.
32. Most reported: Injection sting, especially IM
33. Most reported: More energy in workouts
34. Most reported: Fishy body odour at high doses
35. Most reported: Mixed fat-loss results

## What has been tested
36. Fat metabolism: Weight loss, oral RCT meta-analysis (human)
37. Muscle & performance: Muscle fuel and cycling output, oral (human)
38. Organ function: Carnitine deficiency in dialysis (human)
39. Reproductive: Sperm motility, oral (human)
40. Approved for deficiency states; oral weight-loss RCTs pooled in meta-analyses; muscle-fuel studies in athletes.
41. What it helps: Its approved use is replacing carnitine in inborn errors and dialysis. Oral RCTs pooled in 2016 showed about 1.3 kg more weight loss than control. A 24-week study with carbohydrate raised muscle carnitine and improved cycling output. People inject it, alone or in lipotropic blends, for fat loss and training energy; fat-loss results are mixed and the injection stings.
42. Trial: active · Phase 4 · critically ill liver patients · NCT07642076 · Beni-Suef University. Approved for carnitine deficiency; still being tested as an add on in ICU liver patients in Egypt. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (verified)

## Who shouldn't take it
43. People on levothyroxine or with hypothyroidism: Carnitine blocks thyroid hormone entry into cells. (reported)
44. People with seizure disorders: The Carnitor label reports seizures in people with and without prior seizures. (verified)
45. People with heart disease or high TMAO: Gut bacteria turn carnitine into TMAO, linked to atherosclerosis. (reported)
46. People on warfarin: Case reports show carnitine raising INR and bleeding risk on warfarin. (reported)

## Synergies (paired with)
47. Semaglutide: Semaglutide cuts food intake, and L-carnitine supports moving fat into mitochondria to be burned. People pair them for fat loss and energy while eating less, but the pair has not been tested together.
48. Tirzepatide: Tirzepatide reduces intake and improves how fat tissue handles fat, and L-carnitine supports fat burning in muscle. The pairing is user logic for fat loss, not trial data.
49. 5-Amino-1MQ: 5-Amino-1MQ blocks the NNMT enzyme in fat cells, which shrank fat cells in obese mice, and L-carnitine shuttles fat into mitochondria. They are often stacked for fat loss, but the pair has not been tested together.
50. MOTS-c: MOTS-c mimics exercise through AMPK and improves fuel use in mice, and L-carnitine provides the shuttle that moves fat to be burned. Users pair them for training energy and fat loss, but the pairing is user logic, not trial data.
51. NAD+: NAD+ carries electrons for energy production, while L-carnitine delivers fatty acids into mitochondria to be burned. People pair them for energy and recovery as two steps of the same process, but the pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
52. A small molecule the body makes from lysine and methionine that ferries fatty acids into mitochondria to be burned. Injectable versions are sold alone or as 'LC' lipotropic blends with methionine, choline and B vitamins.
53. First studied for: Carnitine deficiency from inborn errors and in dialysis patients (Carnitor).
54. Name story: From Latin caro, carnis: flesh. It was first pulled from meat extract in 1905. Decades later it was briefly dubbed "vitamin BT" after mealworms (Tenebrio) turned out to need it in their diet. [S2] (verified)
55. 1950s: Carnitine's role in fatty-acid transport worked out (inferred date)
56. 1985–1992: Carnitor approved, oral then IV (dates inferred)
57. 2011: Muscle loading shown to need carbs and insulin
58. 2016: Meta-analysis: ~1.3 kg extra weight loss
59. Today: Sold as LC120, LC216, LC526 lipotropic blends

# LL-37
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/ll-37
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: FALL-39 (original name), cathelicidin, hCAP-18 (precursor protein), CAMP (gene)
2. Origin: Fragment of a natural protein
3. Sequence: LLGDFFRKSKEKIGKEFKRIVQRIKDFLRNLVPRTES (37 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: Research chemical, no approval. On the FDA compounding advisory agenda for a meeting due before end of February 2027.

## Summary
5. LL-37 is the only human cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide, a 37-residue chain that is part of innate immunity. It is studied as a natural antibiotic and wound-healing agent because it kills bacteria, breaks up biofilms and speeds wound closure in models. Its strongest results are in cells and animals, and too much of it is linked to rosacea and psoriasis, so injected use is unstudied.
6. Punch line: The body's only cathelicidin, a natural antibiotic. Kills bacteria and breaks biofilms in models; excess inflames.
7. Used for: Immune support, infections

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Immunity: Natural antibiotic peptide
9. Inflammatory signaling: Too much drives inflammation
10. Tissue repair: Helps wounds close
11. Organ function: Defends skin, lungs and gut

## How it works
12. Punches holes in bacterial membranes · Membrane disruption · role Immunity
   LL-37 is a positively charged spiral peptide that slots into the negatively charged membranes of bacteria and tears them open. Human cell membranes carry less negative charge, which gives it some selectivity. Broad killing is shown in cell and animal work.
13. Calls in and tunes immune cells · FPR2, TLR signalling · role Immunity
   LL-37 also signals to the host. Through FPR2, a receptor on immune cells, it calls in neutrophils and other cells, and it tunes TLR signalling, the germ-sensing system. These effects come mostly from cell and animal studies.
14. Speeds wound closure · Keratinocyte migration · role Tissue repair
   LL-37 drives keratinocytes, the main skin cells, to migrate across a wound and close it. Faster wound closure is shown in animal models, and early human wound studies exist but are limited.
15. Neutralises bacterial endotoxin · LPS binding · role Inflammatory signaling
   LL-37 binds LPS, the endotoxin on the outer wall of some bacteria, so it cannot trigger TLR4 and set off a strong inflammatory reaction. This dampening is shown in cell and animal work.
16. Breaks up bacterial biofilms · Biofilm disruption · role Immunity
   Biofilms are sticky colonies that shield bacteria from antibiotics and immune attack. LL-37 breaks them up in lab models. This is cell and animal evidence, and it has not been shown for injected use in people.
17. Drives skin inflammation in psoriasis · Self-DNA, pDC activation · role Inflammatory signaling
   LL-37 binds the body's own DNA released from damaged cells, which lets plasmacytoid dendritic cells sense it and pour out interferon. In people, excess LL-37 is tied to psoriasis and rosacea. This is the clearest human finding about it.
18. Mechanism overview: LL-37 is the only human cathelicidin, cut from its precursor hCAP18 by proteases in skin and neutrophils. Its positive, amphipathic helix inserts into negatively charged bacterial membranes and tears them open, and it binds bacterial LPS so endotoxin cannot trigger TLR4. It also signals to the host. Through FPR2 it recruits immune cells, and it drives keratinocyte migration to close wounds. The same activity has a cost. LL-37 complexes with self-DNA, pushing plasmacytoid dendritic cells to make interferon, which feeds psoriasis and rosacea.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
19. Typical: 100–200 mcg · daily, 5 days/wk · cycle 2–4 weeks · route Sub-Q (reported)
20. Half-life: very short
21. Dose note: In the leg-ulcer trial the lowest strength worked best and the highest did no better than placebo.
22. Most people take: SC 100–200 mcg/day, 5 days a week. Topical 0.5 mg/mL for wounds. Anecdotal.
23. Common: 100–200 mcg · daily, 5 on/2 off · 8–12 wk · Sub-Q · for immune support [S1] [S2] (reported)
24. Titration / low: 50 mcg → up · daily, +50 mcg weekly · 8–16 wk · Sub-Q · for sensitive users, Lyme/biofilm [S1] [S2] (reported)
25. Acute: 200–400 mcg · daily · 2–4 wk · Sub-Q · for active infection [S1] [S2] (reported)

## What people report
26. Reported for chronic infection and gut/immune issues; enthusiast use, variable results.
27. Liked / worked: Broad antimicrobial activity in models
28. Liked / worked: Wound healing in models
29. Liked / worked: Real innate-immune importance
30. What worked: Broad antimicrobial and wound-healing activity in models; genuine innate-immune importance.
31. Went wrong / did not work: Too much drives inflammation, rosacea, psoriasis
32. Went wrong / did not work: Injected human use unstudied
33. What went wrong: It is a double-edged peptide: too much drives inflammation (rosacea, psoriasis links); injectable human use is unstudied and could provoke inflammation.
34. Most reported: Chronic infection, gut and immune issues
35. Most reported: Variable results

## What has been tested
36. Immunity: Direct antimicrobial action (cell)
37. Tissue repair: Wound healing (animal)
38. Inflammatory signaling: Rosacea and psoriasis links (human)
39. Tissue repair: Early wound and infection studies (human)
40. Extensive cell and animal work: direct antimicrobial action, wound healing, immune modulation; a role in some skin diseases (rosacea) where it is over-expressed. Early human wound and infection studies exist.
41. What it helps: Its strongest results are in cells and animals: broad killing of bacteria, biofilm breakup and faster wound closure in models. Human data link it to skin disease more than treatment, with excess LL-37 tied to rosacea and psoriasis. Early human wound and infection studies exist. Injected use is unstudied, and user reports centre on chronic infection, gut and immune problems, with mixed results.
42. Trial: none · Phase 2 · venous leg ulcers and diabetic foot ulcers. Last trials were a Swedish Phase 2b for leg ulcers (ropocamptide, 2022) and an Indonesian diabetic foot ulcer cream study published 2023; nothing active now. (checked 2026-10-23) [S3] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
43. People with psoriasis, lupus or rosacea: LL-37 is overexpressed in these and helps drive them by activating immune cells against DNA. (reported)
44. People with active or recent cancer: Promotes growth of ovarian, breast and lung tumours in lab studies. (reported)

## Synergies (paired with)
45. KPV: LL-37 attacks bacteria and biofilms while also stirring immune signalling, and KPV calms inflammation through NF-κB, mostly in mouse colitis models. People pair them for gut and chronic infection problems. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
46. The only human cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide, a 37-residue chain that starts with two leucines, part of innate immunity, active against bacteria and in wound healing.
47. First studied for: Studied as a natural antibiotic and wound-healing/immune-modulating agent.
48. Name story: Named by its first two residues (Leu-Leu) and its length, 37. It was first reported in 1995 as FALL-39, a guessed 39-residue form; a year later the real peptide turned out two amino acids shorter and got renamed. [S4] (verified)
49. 1995: Identified as the only human cathelicidin
50. 2000s: Wound, infection and skin-disease roles mapped
51. Today: Research chemical; on FDA compounding agenda before end of Feb 2027

# MT-2
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/mt-2
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Melanotan II, MT-II, Melanotan-2, Ac-Nle-c[Asp-His-D-Phe-Arg-Trp-Lys]-NH2
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: LDHFRWK (7 amino acids). Ring-closed (cyclic); Nle shown as L, D-Phe shown as F; acetylated start, amide end
4. Legal and approval status: Never approved; flagged by regulators as unsafe/illegal to sell. On the FDA PCAC agenda (Melanotan II). Grey-market only.

## Summary
5. MT-2 is Melanotan II, a synthetic cyclic analogue of alpha-MSH that switches on melanocortin receptors broadly. People inject it mainly for sunless tanning, and it also raises libido and cuts appetite. It is unapproved and sold on the grey market, with common nausea and reports of darkened moles and a melanoma concern.
6. Punch line: The Barbie drug. Injected for a sunless tan; also lifts libido, cuts appetite, darkens moles. Nausea is common.
7. Used for: Tanning without much sun; libido

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Tanning: Darkens skin without sun
9. Skin & aesthetics: Darker moles and freckles
10. Connection & desire: Raises arousal
11. Appetite & satiety: Lowers appetite

## How it works
12. Darkens skin by switching on pigment cells · MC1R, eumelanin · role Tanning
   Melanotan II activates MC1R on melanocytes, the pigment cells in skin. This raises cAMP inside the cell and shifts output toward eumelanin, the dark brown pigment. Human studies show reliable tanning with little or no sun.
13. Darkens moles and freckles too · Melanocyte MC1R · role Skin & aesthetics
   The same MC1R activation reaches every melanocyte, including those in moles and freckles, which darken too. Users also report new pigmented spots, and case reports have raised a melanoma concern that remains unresolved.
14. Triggers arousal and erections · Central MC3R, MC4R · role Connection & desire
   Melanotan II crosses into the brain, where it activates MC3R and MC4R in the hypothalamus. These receptors drive sexual arousal, and early human studies confirmed spontaneous erections in men. The broad receptor activity also brings nausea and flushing.
15. Cuts appetite · Hypothalamic MC4R · role Appetite & satiety
   MC4R in the hypothalamus is a central appetite brake. Activating it cuts hunger, and human studies show a drop in appetite on melanotan II. Nausea likely adds to the effect.
16. Mechanism overview: Melanotan II is a cyclic alpha-MSH analogue that hits several melanocortin receptors at once. At MC1R on melanocytes it raises cAMP and switches pigment output toward dark eumelanin, which tans skin and also darkens moles and freckles. It crosses into the brain, where MC4R and MC3R activation in the hypothalamus drives sexual arousal and spontaneous erections and cuts appetite. That lack of selectivity explains both its appeal and its nausea, flushing and pigment changes.

18. Half-life: ~33 hours

## Where it comes from
48. Melanotan II, a synthetic cyclic analogue of alpha-MSH that activates melanocortin receptors broadly, driving tanning, appetite suppression and erections.
49. First studied for: Developed at the University of Arizona as a sunless-tanning agent; the erection effect spun off into PT-141.
50. Name story: Melanotan II, the Arizona tanning project's second analog. It reportedly got a new career when one of the scientists accidentally injected himself with double the dose and had an eight-hour erection, which led to PT-141. [S6] (reported)
51. 1980s to 1990s: Built at University of Arizona as a sunless tanning agent
52. 1990s: Erection effect spun off into PT-141
53. 2000s to 2010s: Drug development dropped; regulators warn against sales
54. Today: Grey-market tanning peptide; on the FDA PCAC agenda
