# Tβ4 + BPC + KPV
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/tb4-bpc-kpv
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Tri-HealMax, Tri-Heal Max, Coremend, Tβ4 + BPC-157 + KPV, Tβ4 + KPV + BPC-157, TB-500 + BPC-157 + KPV, CORE blend
2. Origin: Blend of 3 peptides
3. Legal and approval status: Not approved anywhere as a drug or as a combination. US: BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV left FDA 503A Category 2 in April 2026 when nominations were withdrawn; the July 2026 advisory panel voted in favour of compounding all three, no rule yet. Australia: BPC-157 and TB-500 Schedule 4. WADA: BPC-157 and TB-500 banned at all times; KPV under S0.

## Summary
4. This blend adds KPV to the so-called Wolverine pair of thymosin beta-4 (Tβ4) and BPC-157, sold as Tri-HealMax or Coremend. It is used for injury recovery and inflammation, with BPC-157 and Tβ4 supporting repair and KPV damping NF-κB inflammation. Evidence is by component, mostly in rats and mice, and the one combination study found no extra benefit. Users report better recovery and calmer gut, while others see little.
5. Punch line: The Wolverine pair plus KPV. Tβ4 and BPC-157 rebuild tissue while KPV damps the inflammation around it.
6. Used for: Injury repair with inflammation control

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Tissue repair: BPC-157 and Tβ4 for tendon, muscle and wound repair
8. Inflammatory signaling: KPV and Tβ4 lower NF-κB signalling
9. Digestive & gut: KPV and BPC-157 aimed at gut lining
10. Pain & sensory: Soreness and injury pain ease in reports
11. Immunity (backed only by animal or user reports): KPV steadies immune cells
12. Muscle & performance (backed only by animal or user reports): Used for muscle tears and training recovery

## How it works
13. Moves repair cells into wounds · Tβ4: G-actin sequestering · role Tissue repair
   Thymosin beta-4 binds single actin units (G-actin) and holds them in reserve. When a repair cell needs to move, the stock is released to build filaments fast, so cells migrate into the wound. Shown in cell and animal work; human wound and eye trials used the full protein.
14. Helps blood vessels grow into damage · BPC-157: VEGFR2, eNOS · role Tissue repair
   BPC-157 acts on VEGFR2 and eNOS, the receptor and enzyme that drive new blood vessel growth and nitric oxide release. Better blood supply carries oxygen and repair cells into damaged tissue. This is shown in rat injury models, not human trials.
15. Blocks a key inflammation switch inside cells · KPV: PepT1 uptake, NF-κB down · role Inflammatory signaling
   KPV, the last three amino acids of alpha-MSH, enters gut and immune cells through PepT1, a peptide transporter. Inside, it blocks NF-κB, a master switch for inflammatory genes. This damps inflammation at the injury or gut wall, shown in mice only.
16. Protects gut lining · BPC-157 and KPV, colitis models · role Digestive & gut
   BPC-157 shields the stomach and gut lining from damage, and KPV calms inflammation in the colon wall. Each one helped the lining heal in rodent colitis models. The two have not been tested together for gut effects.
17. Mechanism overview: Thymosin beta-4 sequesters G-actin to drive cell migration and lowers NF-κB signalling; BPC-157 adds VEGFR2, Akt and eNOS driven angiogenesis and FAK and paxillin fibroblast migration; KPV, alpha-MSH 11 to 13, enters cells via PepT1 and blocks NF-κB. Tri-HealMax weights Tβ4 at 2.5 times the others, which brings a daily dose closer to standalone Tβ4 use than a 1:1 stack; Coremend is even. KPV is chemically quiet; full Tβ4 carries an oxidisable methionine.

## What is inside the blend
18. Tβ4 (TB-500): 25 mg · Cell migration into wounds; the main share
19. BPC-157: 10 mg · Blood vessel growth, gut lining
20. KPV: 10 mg · Anti-inflammatory, gut and immune cells
21. Most common ratio: TB-500 25 · BPC-157 10 · KPV 10 = 45 mg (6 of 11 listings)
22. Other ratio seen: TB-500 10 · BPC-157 10 · KPV 10 = 30 mg (4 listings)
23. Other ratio seen: BPC-157 15 · TB-500 15 · KPV 15 (compounded, 3 mg/mL x 5 mL) = 45 mg (1 listing)
24. Version Tri-HealMax: Tβ4 25 · BPC-157 10 · KPV 10 = 45 mg
25. Version Coremend: TB-500 10 · KPV 10 · BPC-157 10 = 30 mg
26. Why Tβ4 is in it: Actin-driven cell migration; human wound trial data
27. Why BPC-157 is in it: Angiogenesis and gut protection
28. Why KPV is in it: Targeted NF-κB damping for gut and skin inflammation
29. Mixing chemistry: Same pH split as the Wolverine pair: BPC-157 about 6.5 to 8.5, full Tβ4 about 5.5 to 6.
30. Mixing chemistry: KPV adds no histidine, methionine or asparagine, so no new reactive site.
31. Mixing chemistry: Full Tβ4 at 25 mg brings more oxidisable methionine than a 1:1 vial; keep it cold and dark.
32. Mixing chemistry: No copper in this blend, so the GLOW and KLOW colour checks do not apply.
33. Mixing chemistry: No public COA for either ratio found; ask for mg of each.
34. Self-mixing: Self-mixing lets you pick the Tβ4 share, but adds three salt pHs and three overfill errors; drawing from separate vials into one syringe keeps liquid contact short.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
35. Typical: No standard dose · 1× daily · cycle 4–6 weeks · route Sub-Q (reported)
36. Half-life: per component
37. Most people take: No standard dose. Most size it to BPC-157 at 250 to 500 mcg: 7.5 to 15 units of a 45 mg Tri-HealMax vial in 3 mL (that also gives 0.6 to 1.25 mg Tβ4), or 7.5 to 15 units of a 30 mg Coremend vial in 3 mL. One aggregator lists only 200 to 500 mcg of total blend.

## What people report
38. Sub-Q once daily. One aggregator lists 200 to 500 mcg of total blend; people who size to BPC-157 at 250 to 500 mcg take far more, about 7 to 15 units of either vial in 3 mL. Some inject near the injury in the first 2 weeks, then drop to 1 to 2 shots a week. Courses 4 to 6 weeks, 2 to 4 off.
39. Liked / worked: Recovery and soreness better in user reports
40. Liked / worked: Gut comfort reported
41. Liked / worked: Higher Tβ4 share than 1:1 stacks
42. What worked: Users of the stack describe better recovery, less soreness, calmer gut and faster return to training. Guides expect anti-inflammatory effects in the first days and tissue repair over 2 to 4 weeks.
43. Went wrong / did not work: Never tested as a blend
44. Went wrong / did not work: No lab test of either ratio found
45. Went wrong / did not work: Some report minimal results
46. What went wrong: Others report minimal results or doubt product quality. No independent lab test or COA of either ratio was found. Expected side effects follow the components: injection site redness, mild tiredness, headache; KPV can cause flu-like feelings at low doses in sensitive users.
47. Most reported: Injury and training recovery
48. Most reported: Daily, near the injury early on
49. Most reported: Two ratios, very different Tβ4 dose
50. Most reported: 4 to 6 week courses

## What has been tested
51. Tissue repair: Achilles, BPC-157 + TB-500 together (rat)
52. Digestive & gut: KPV colitis (mouse)
53. Tissue repair: Tβ4 wound and eye trials (trial)
54. Tissue repair: Recovery and soreness (users)
55. Never tested as a blend; the aggregator page states no published study of the three together. The only combination data is the 2026 rat Achilles study of BPC-157 plus TB-500, which found no added benefit. KPV evidence is mouse colitis; thymosin beta-4 has human wound and eye trials.
56. What it helps: Evidence is component-level and user-reported. Each repair peptide helps tendon and wound healing in rats; full Tβ4 has human wound trials; KPV eases colitis in mice. The only combination study, BPC-157 plus TB-500 in rats, found no extra benefit. Users report better recovery and gut comfort, with others seeing little.

## Who shouldn't take it
57. People with active or recent cancer: Tβ4 drives new blood vessels and cell migration; high levels track with tumour spread. (reported)
58. People with IBD on biologics or immunosuppressants: KPV damps NF-kB signalling; stacking it onto immune drugs is untested. (inferred)
59. Drug-tested athletes: Thymosin beta-4 and TB-500 are named on the WADA list; doping cases exist. (verified)
60. People fighting an active infection: Blunting inflammation can blunt the response clearing the infection. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
61. BPC-157: BPC-157 is already in this blend. Extra BPC-157 tilts it toward blood vessel growth and gut protection. In the 2026 rat Achilles study, BPC-157 plus Tβ4 did no better than either alone.
62. Thymosin Beta-4: Thymosin beta-4 is already in this blend, weighted heaviest in some versions. Extra Tβ4 raises the cell migration share. Tβ4 alone outperformed vehicle in the 2026 rat Achilles study, while the BPC-157 plus Tβ4 pair added nothing.
63. KPV: KPV is already in this blend. Extra KPV raises the anti-inflammatory share for gut and skin. KPV has mouse colitis data only, and the pairing is user logic, not trial data.
64. GHK-Cu: GHK-Cu adds copper delivery and collagen signalling for skin and matrix repair, which this blend lacks. Adding it turns the stack into KLOW. The four together have not been tested.

## Where it comes from
65. The Wolverine pair plus KPV, sold in two ratios: Tri-HealMax, Tβ4 25 + BPC-157 10 + KPV 10 = 45 mg (2.5:1:1, heavy on thymosin beta-4), and Coremend, 10 + 10 + 10 = 30 mg. A similar 10+10+10 kit is sold elsewhere as a CORE blend.
66. First studied for: Assembled by the research-peptide market as an injury stack with an anti-inflammatory third peptide: BPC-157 and Tβ4 for repair, KPV to damp inflammation and, users say, take the sting out.
67. Name story: Tri-HealMax: three healing peptides, with Max likely pointing to the larger thymosin beta-4 share. Coremend is a product name for the even 10+10+10 version. Neither name is explained by its makers. [S1] (inferred)
68. 1981: Thymosin beta-4 isolated
69. Early 1990s: BPC-157 reported in Zagreb
70. 2000s: KPV calms colitis in mice
71. 2020s: Sold premixed as Tri-HealMax 25+10+10 and Coremend 10+10+10
72. 2026: All three leave FDA Category 2; rat study finds BPC-157 + TB-500 add nothing together

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Two of the three were finally tested together, and the combination lost [animals]
73. For once a blend's central premise has been examined, at least in part. A 2026 study in a peer-reviewed orthopaedic surgery journal took 32 male Sprague-Dawley rats, cut the Achilles tendon fully and repaired it with a Kessler technique, then split them into four groups of eight: vehicle, BPC-157 at 10 micrograms per kilogram daily, thymosin beta-4 at 60 micrograms per kilogram daily, and both together, all intraperitoneal, from the first day after surgery for 30 days [1] (verified, in animals).
74. Maximum load to failure at four weeks, reported as medians, was 26.91 newtons for vehicle, 37.16 for BPC-157, 37.41 for thymosin beta-4, and 34.54 for the combination [1] (verified). Only thymosin beta-4 against vehicle survived correction for multiple comparisons, adjusted p=0.0406, with BPC-157 against vehicle at adjusted p=0.389 [1].
75. Read the combination column again. It is not just that two plus two failed to make four; the combination arm sat numerically below both single agents on the mechanical endpoint. On the histological scores the pattern repeated: thymosin beta-4 differed from control on both total scores, the combination differed from control on one, BPC-157 on neither, and there were no significant differences among the treatment groups at all [1] (verified).
76. The authors' conclusion is the sentence that matters here: combined treatment did not confer additional benefits compared with either agent alone [1] (verified). They offered overlapping downstream pathways, a ceiling effect and suboptimal dosing as possible explanations and labelled all three speculative, since no molecular or pharmacokinetic analyses were done [1].
77. The study's own limits are stated plainly and are worth carrying: a single four-week time point, healthy young male rats, no functional testing, histology subgroups of only four tendons per group with no power calculation, no blinding of surgery or dosing, and biomechanics limited to peak load without stiffness or energy to failure [1] (verified). It received no financial support and declared no conflicts [1]. So this is not a definitive negative. It is the only direct test of the combination in existence, and it points the opposite way to the product's premise.
78. Note also what it did not test: the third component. No study of any kind has examined KPV alongside the other two (verified as absent).

### The three components have very unequal, and unevenly thin, evidence [mixed]
79. A blend inherits the reputation of its best-regarded ingredient. Component by component, that reputation does not survive contact with the regulatory reviews of 2026.
80. BPC-157 has exactly one controlled human trial, reported only as a 2005 meeting abstract in ulcerative colitis, whose between-group difference had a confidence interval crossing zero, and which the FDA found inadequate for lacking endpoint definitions, inclusion criteria and statistical methods [2] (verified, as recorded in this library's component entry). Everything else human is uncontrolled.
81. Thymosin beta-4 is the component most often assumed strongest and is the weakest on paper for the marketed fragment. The FDA found no clinical studies, no human exposure data and no human pharmacokinetic data by any route for the nominated substance, and no toxicology studies of any kind: no acute, no repeat-dose, no genotoxicity, no reproductive, no carcinogenicity [3] (verified, as recorded in this library's component entry).
82. KPV has no human studies, no pharmacokinetic data in any species and no toxicology studies. Its nomination cited nine references, eight animal studies of related compounds and one cadaver-skin study, none testing it in a living person, and it was nominated as a 0.1% topical cream rather than for injection [4] (verified, as recorded in this library's component entry).
83. So the blend combines one component with a single inadequate and non-significant controlled trial and two with no human data whatsoever, one of which was never proposed for injection at all.

### The identity problem, and the one mismatch specific to this vial [lab]
84. None of the three has an approved generic name, so there is no reference standard to test a batch against, which regulators flagged as a patient safety issue in its own right. Each exists as both a free base and an acetate salt with different molecular weights, and in each case nominators were inconsistent about which form they meant [2,3,4] (verified, as recorded in this library's component entries).
85. One mismatch belongs specifically to any blend containing thymosin beta-4. Regulators stated that the marketed seven-residue fragment and the full 43-residue protein are not the same substance [3] (verified). Products in this family commonly contain the full protein under the fragment's name, or the reverse. That is not a labelling quirk: the two molecules have different evidence, different stability and different regulatory records, so the ingredient list cannot be used to look up what is actually present.
86. It also changes the chemistry of the vial. The full protein carries an oxidisable methionine; the short fragment does not. A vial built on full protein at the larger share is therefore the most oxidation-sensitive version of this blend, which is why light and cold storage matter more here than in a fragment-based mix (inferred).
87. KPV is the chemically quiet one: no histidine, methionine or asparagine, so it adds no new reactive site to the solution (verified as a structural observation). The pH preferences of the components do not match, with the gastric peptide's range sitting above the full protein's, so a single blended solution cannot be optimal for both (inferred).
88. No public certificate of analysis for either common ratio was found in this review (verified as absent), which leaves the mass of each component in a given vial unverifiable from outside.

### The ratio is a product decision, not a finding [mixed]
89. At the leading composition the thymosin share is two and a half times each of the others, so by mass this is predominantly a thymosin product with two additions. The even version is a different product in everything but name.
90. Nothing in the literature establishes that either ratio is right for any purpose, because no study of any ratio exists (verified as absent). The one combination study used doses in a six-to-one ratio favouring thymosin by weight, closer to the weighted vial than to the even one, and found no added benefit at that ratio [1]. That is a single data point, at one dose pair, in one species, against one injury.
91. The practical consequence of a fixed ratio is attribution. If something improves, three components could be responsible, and the two with no human data are as plausible as the one with a single inadequate trial. If something goes wrong, the ambiguity runs the same way. Nobody using a fixed blend learns which component they respond to, which is the quiet cost of every blend and is sharper here because the rat study suggests the components may not even be additive (inferred).
92. There is a real argument on the other side, which is convenience: one reconstitution, one injection, one vial to store. That is a genuine benefit and it is a handling benefit, not a pharmacological one.

### Safety, as an absence rather than a finding [mixed]
93. The three components drew the same concern from US regulators in 2026: peptide-related impurities and aggregates from synthesis can drive immune responses, and no immunogenicity studies exist for any of them [2,3,4] (verified, as recorded in this library's component entries). Dissolving three peptides in one vial multiplies the impurity and aggregate surface without adding any data about it (inferred).
94. Beyond immunogenicity, the absences are the story. For the thymosin fragment and for KPV there is no toxicology at all, of any kind, in any species [3,4]. For BPC-157 there are no repeat-dose studies longer than 28 days in any species, and none by the routes people actually use [2]. A combination cannot be safer than the sum of what has not been studied about its parts.
95. Nothing here says the blend is dangerous. It says that in evidence terms the blend is a fourth product with no file of its own, and that its three parts between them have one inadequate controlled human trial and no toxicology for two of the three.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
96. No approved product contains this combination anywhere, and no approved product contains any of the three components as a single agent.
97. The US sequence in 2026 is easy to misread. On 15 April 2026 the FDA said it would remove twelve peptides from the do-not-compound Category 2 within seven days, because the original nominations had been withdrawn; the agency was explicit that lifting that designation did not make any peptide eligible for compounding, and it simultaneously scheduled advisory committee review [5] (verified). On 29 June the agency's own staff urged that none of the seven peptides under review be added to the 503A bulks list, citing poorly characterised substances, limited or absent human data and immunogenicity risk; the same day a reconstituted advisory committee was announced, with roughly half its members reported to have ties to peptide businesses or clinics [5] (verified).
98. At the meeting on 23 and 24 July 2026 the committee recommended six peptides for addition, including all three components of this blend, each passing 8 to 6 with one abstention, and declined one [5] (verified). Those recommendations are advisory only. The agency must still decide whether to accept them, publish a proposed rule, take comments and issue a final rule, with no statutory deadline; for scale, a 2016 proposed rule on ten bulk substances was not finalised until 2019 [5] (verified).
99. The live development is an interim route. An Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides went to the White House budget office on 14 October 2026 and had not been issued as of mid-October. Its expected shape is temporary enforcement discretion for state-licensed 503A pharmacies compounding for individual patients on prescription; it would approve nothing, would not cover research-use-only, supplement or outsourcing-facility channels, could be restricted by route, and could be narrowed or withdrawn without rulemaking [5] (reported). Until it is published, nobody can say whether a three-peptide blend would fall inside it.
100. In sport, BPC-157 is named explicitly on the 2026 Prohibited List and thymosin beta-4 and its derivatives are named under peptide hormones and growth factors, both prohibited at all times; KPV is not named and falls under the catch-all class for substances without approval for human use [6] (verified for the two named, inferred for the third).

### Open questions [mixed]
101. Does the combination do anything the components do not? The one direct test, in two of the three, found no added benefit and a numerically lower peak load than either alone [1]. That needs repeating at other doses and time points before it is treated as settled, in either direction.
102. Why would two repair peptides fail to add? Overlapping downstream pathways and a ceiling effect are the obvious candidates, and the study that raised them could not test either [1].
103. What has KPV got to do with tendon repair? It was nominated as a topical cream, has no injectable human data, and has never been studied alongside the other two [4].
104. Does the vial contain the fragment or the full protein? Regulators say they are different substances [3], and no public certificate of analysis for either common ratio was found.
105. What is the real shelf life after reconstitution for a three-peptide solution whose components have different pH preferences and one of which oxidises? Unmeasured for the mixture.
106. Would a blend fall inside the interim compounding policy once published? Unknowable until it appears, and a mixture is exactly the case such a policy may not address [5].

# Liraglutide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/liraglutide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Victoza, Saxenda, Xultophy (with insulin degludec), NN2211, lira
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain
3. Sequence: HAEGTFTSDVSSYLEGQAAKEFIAWLVRGRG (31 amino acids). GLP-1(7-37) with K34R; C16 palmitic acid on K26 via a glutamic acid spacer (not shown)
4. Shown with an FDA approved badge
5. Legal and approval status: FDA-approved (Victoza 2010, Saxenda 2014) with generics: first generic Victoza Dec 2024 (Hikma), first generic Saxenda Aug 2025 (Teva), more since (e.g. Biocon Feb 2026). Approved worldwide. Grey-market vials are not the approved product. WADA does not ban it.

## Summary
6. Liraglutide is Novo Nordisk's first long-acting GLP-1 analogue, a modified hormone with a fatty-acid tail that binds albumin. It is an approved drug for type 2 diabetes (Victoza) and obesity (Saxenda), quieting hunger, slowing stomach emptying and raising insulin. The SCALE trial showed about 8 kg average loss over 56 weeks. It is weaker than later weekly drugs, needs daily injections, and carries a boxed warning for rodent thyroid tumors.
7. Punch line: The original daily GLP-1, sold as Saxenda and Victoza. Now generic, the budget pick; weaker than weekly shots.
8. Used for: Weight loss, type 2 diabetes

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
9. Appetite & satiety: Cuts hunger, slows stomach
10. Glucose & insulin: Lowers blood sugar
11. Heart & vessels: Fewer CV deaths (LEADER)
12. Fat metabolism: About 5–8% weight loss
13. Neural protection (backed only by animal or user reports): Studied in Alzheimer's, mixed

## How it works
14. Quiets hunger in the brain · GLP-1 receptor, hypothalamus · role Appetite & satiety
   Liraglutide activates GLP-1 receptors in the hypothalamus and brainstem, the regions that set hunger and fullness. People feel full sooner and think about food less. In the large SCALE human trials this produced steady, moderate weight loss over a year.
15. Slows stomach emptying · GLP-1 receptor, gut · role Appetite & satiety
   GLP-1 receptors along the gut and its nerves slow the rate the stomach empties into the intestine. Food stays longer, which adds to fullness and flattens the rise in blood sugar after meals. It is also behind the early nausea users report.
16. Raises insulin and cuts glucagon when glucose is high · GLP-1R, beta and alpha cells · role Glucose & insulin
   On pancreatic beta cells it raises insulin, and on alpha cells it cuts glucagon, but only when blood glucose is high. That glucose dependence is why low blood sugar is uncommon on its own. In LEADER, severe hypoglycaemia was actually less frequent on drug than placebo.
17. Fatty tail rides albumin · C16 acylation, albumin binding · role Glucose & insulin
   A C16 fatty acid attached through a small spacer makes the molecule cluster under the skin and grip albumin in the blood. This slows absorption and shields it from the DPP-4 enzyme and kidney clearance. A half-life of minutes becomes about 13 hours, enough for daily dosing.
18. Lowers CV event risk in diabetes · CV outcomes, LEADER · role Heart & vessels
   In the LEADER human trial in high-risk type 2 diabetes, fewer people on liraglutide had a heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death than on placebo. Cardiovascular and overall deaths also fell. The benefit was shown in people with diabetes and existing risk, not in healthy users.
19. Mechanism overview: Liraglutide is GLP-1(7-37) with lysine 34 swapped for arginine and a C16 palmitic acid attached to lysine 26 through a glutamic acid spacer. The fatty acid makes it self-associate under the skin and bind albumin, which slows absorption and shields it from DPP-4 and kidney clearance, giving a half-life of about 13 hours. It activates GLP-1 receptors in the hypothalamus and brainstem to cut hunger, in the gut to slow emptying, and on beta and alpha cells to raise insulin and cut glucagon only when glucose is high.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
20. Typical: 0.6–1.8 mg (diabetes); 3 mg (obesity) · once daily · cycle Ongoing · route Sub-Q (verified)
21. Half-life: ~13 hours
22. Dose note: Label maximum is 3 mg daily for weight and 1.8 mg for diabetes.
23. Most people take: Label: start 0.6 mg daily, add 0.6 mg each week to 3 mg for obesity (Saxenda) or 1.2–1.8 mg for diabetes (Victoza). Stop Saxenda if under 4% loss by week 16. Users often hold 1.2–1.8 mg for weight.
24. Obesity (label): 3 mg · 1× daily · ongoing; 0.6 mg start, +0.6 mg weekly · Sub-Q · for Saxenda and generic users; adults and teens 12+ [S1] (verified)
25. Diabetes (label): 1.2–1.8 mg · 1× daily · ongoing; 0.6 mg for 1 wk first · Sub-Q · for Victoza; adults and children 10+ [S2] [S3] (verified)
26. Low maintenance: 1.2–1.8 mg · 1× daily · ongoing · Sub-Q · for users wanting fewer side effects and lower cost [S4] (reported)

## What people report
27. Now cheap as a generic, so used as a budget GLP-1, often held at 1.2–1.8 mg. Users report nausea in the first weeks and 5–10% loss, consistent with trials.
28. Liked / worked: 8.4 kg vs 2.8 kg loss at 56 weeks (SCALE)
29. Liked / worked: 13% fewer major CV events in diabetes
30. Liked / worked: Lower CV and all-cause death in LEADER
31. Liked / worked: Now generic and cheap
32. What worked: About 8 kg average loss versus 2.8 kg on placebo at 56 weeks (SCALE); fewer heart attacks, strokes and CV deaths in high-risk diabetes (LEADER, HR 0.87). Weaker than semaglutide and tirzepatide.
33. Went wrong / did not work: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
34. Went wrong / did not work: Gallbladder disease, rare pancreatitis
35. Went wrong / did not work: Higher resting heart rate
36. Went wrong / did not work: Weight regain on stopping
37. Went wrong / did not work: Daily injections
38. What went wrong: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea; gallbladder disease and rare pancreatitis; raised resting heart rate; regain on stopping. Boxed warning for rodent thyroid C-cell tumors. Daily injections.
39. Most reported: Nausea in the first 2–4 weeks
40. Most reported: 5–10% weight loss
41. Most reported: Many stay at 1.2–1.8 mg
42. Most reported: Used as a budget GLP-1

## What has been tested
43. Fat metabolism: Obesity, SCALE program (human)
44. Glucose & insulin: Type 2 diabetes, LEAD program (human)
45. Heart & vessels: CV outcomes, LEADER (human)
46. Neural protection: Alzheimer's and Parkinson's pilot trials (human)
47. Large programs: LEADER cardiovascular outcome trial (9,340 people, 3.8 years) and the SCALE obesity trials (SCALE Obesity, 3,731 people, 56 weeks), plus pediatric trials.
48. What it helps: SCALE showed about 8 kg average loss versus 2.8 kg on placebo over 56 weeks at 3 mg, and LEADER showed fewer heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths in high-risk type 2 diabetes. It is weaker than the weekly drugs that followed, but generics made it the cheapest GLP-1 option. Users report nausea early and modest, steady loss; daily injections are the main complaint.
49. Trial: active · Phase 1 · stomach emptying before surgery · NCT07225816 · Novo Nordisk. Approved since 2010 and now generic; Novo is still recruiting a study on leftover stomach food in GLP-1 users before anesthesia. (checked 2026-10-23) [S5] (verified)

## Who shouldn't take it
50. Personal or family history of MTC or MEN2: Causes thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents; boxed warning and contraindication on the label. (verified)
51. Anyone booked for surgery, endoscopy or sedation: Food can stay in the stomach for days and be inhaled into the lungs under anaesthesia. (verified)
52. People with depression or suicidal thoughts: Saxenda label: avoid with history of suicide attempts or active suicidal ideation. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
53. Semaglutide: Both act on the same GLP-1 receptor, so they are alternatives more than a stack. Semaglutide is weekly and gave far more weight loss in the head-to-head STEP 8 trial. People switch from one to the other; combining them has not been tested.
54. Metformin: Metformin lowers sugar output from the liver, while liraglutide works on insulin, glucagon and appetite. They are commonly used together in type 2 diabetes and many LEADER participants took both. The add-on use is clinical routine, though this library has no separate data on the pair.

## Where it comes from
55. Novo Nordisk's first long-acting GLP-1 analogue, developed under Lotte Bjerre Knudsen: one amino-acid swap plus a fatty-acid tail that binds albumin, stretching minutes into about 13 hours. The parent of semaglutide.
56. First studied for: Type 2 diabetes (Victoza, US 2010), then obesity at 3 mg (Saxenda).
57. Name story: The -glutide ending is the INN stem for GLP-1 analogues; 'lira' has no published meaning. Novo's team under Lotte Bjerre Knudsen made it by adding a fatty acid and spacer to GLP-1 so it would bind albumin. [S6] (inferred)
58. 2009–2010: Approved for type 2 diabetes in the EU and US (Victoza)
59. Dec 2014: Approved for obesity at 3 mg (Saxenda)
60. 2016–2017: LEADER: fewer CV deaths; CV indication added 2017
61. 2019–2020: Pediatric approvals (T2D 10+, obesity 12+)
62. Dec 2024 – Aug 2025: First US generics of Victoza, then Saxenda
63. Today: Overtaken by semaglutide and tirzepatide; the low-cost option

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Why this one has a different kind of evidence file [people]
64. Almost everything else in this library is held up by animal work and inference. Liraglutide is the opposite case: it has been through full regulatory review twice, carries a boxed warning, and has a cardiovascular outcome trial with nearly ten thousand participants. The useful work here is not defending it, it is reading its own trials closely, because the gap between what they measured and how it is used is wide.
65. The weight programme was a set of 56-week placebo-controlled trials. In the largest, 3,731 adults with overweight or obesity and a weight-related condition, the placebo-subtracted weight change was minus 5.4% (95% CI minus 5.8 to minus 4.95, p<0.0001). In 846 adults who also had type 2 diabetes it was minus 4.0% (95% CI minus 4.8 to minus 3.1), and in a 422-person maintenance trial minus 6.1% (95% CI minus 7.5 to minus 4.6) [1] (verified). The odds of losing at least 10% of body weight were roughly four to seven times placebo depending on the trial [1].
66. Note which population those numbers come from: people with a weight-related condition, enrolled with a lifestyle programme, in trials that lasted just over a year. The commonly quoted 8% figure is total weight change including the placebo arm's own loss; the drug's contribution is the placebo-subtracted figure above (inferred from the trial reporting).

### The cardiovascular trial, read as a trial rather than a headline [people]
67. LEADER randomised 9,340 adults with type 2 diabetes to liraglutide or placebo and followed them a median of 3.8 years [2] (verified). The population was deliberately high-risk: 72.4% already had cardiovascular disease, 81.3% had cardiovascular disease or chronic kidney disease stage 3 or worse, mean HbA1c was 8.7% and mean diabetes duration 12.8 years [2].
68. The composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack and non-fatal stroke occurred in 13.0% on drug against 14.9% on placebo, hazard ratio 0.87 (95% CI 0.78 to 0.97), superiority p=0.01 [2]. Cardiovascular death fell from 6.0% to 4.7%, hazard ratio 0.78 (0.66 to 0.93), p=0.007, and death from any cause from 9.6% to 8.2%, hazard ratio 0.85 (0.74 to 0.97), p=0.02 [2]. A kidney composite fell from 7.2% to 5.7%, hazard ratio 0.78 (0.67 to 0.92), p=0.003 [2] (verified). Stroke alone did not reach significance, hazard ratio 0.89 (0.72 to 1.11), p=0.30 [2].
69. The number needed to treat is the honest translation: 66 people treated for three years to prevent one primary outcome event, and 98 to prevent one death [2] (verified). The HbA1c difference was 0.40 percentage points and the weight difference 2.3 kilograms at 36 months [2], so this is not a trial where the benefit can be attributed to large weight loss.
70. Two limits travel with it. The population was high-risk, so the result does not transfer to a healthy person using the drug cosmetically, and the trial itself says so. And exploratory outcomes were not corrected for multiple comparisons [2] (verified). The trial was funded by the manufacturer with NIH grant support [2].

### What the safety file actually contains [people]
71. The boxed warning is about rodent tumours, and its wording is careful in a way that is worth reading rather than paraphrasing: liraglutide causes dose-dependent and treatment-duration-dependent thyroid C-cell tumours at clinically relevant exposures in both sexes of rats and mice, and whether it does so in humans is unknown, because the human relevance of those rodent tumours has not been determined. It is contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, and routine calcitonin monitoring or thyroid ultrasound is described as of uncertain value for early detection [3] (verified). In LEADER, there were no cases of medullary thyroid carcinoma on drug and one on placebo [2].
72. In LEADER the imbalances that did appear were elsewhere. Acute gallstone disease occurred in 3.1% on drug against 1.9% on placebo, p<0.001 [2] (verified), and the label notes gallbladder disease was more common than placebo even after accounting for weight loss [3]. Acute pancreatitis was slightly less frequent on drug, 18 cases against 23, p=0.44 [2], which is the opposite of the common assumption. Pancreatic cancer went the other way, 13 cases against 5, p=0.06 [2] (verified) a difference that did not reach significance and has never been resolved.
73. Severe hypoglycaemia was less frequent on drug, 2.4% against 3.3% [2], which reflects the glucose-dependent mechanism, though the label still warns about the combination with sulfonylureas or insulin [3].
74. Resting heart rate rises by about 2 to 3 beats per minute on average, and the label says to stop if the increase is sustained [3] (verified). Severe gastrointestinal reactions occurred in 4.8% against 1.4% on placebo [3]. Suicidal ideation was reported in 0.3% (9 of 3,384) on drug against 0.1% (2 of 1,941) on placebo, with one attempt in an adult and one death by suicide in a 125-patient paediatric trial; the label states there is insufficient information to establish a causal relationship, and advises against use with prior attempts or active ideation [3] (verified). Post-marketing acute kidney injury has followed dehydration from vomiting and diarrhoea [3]. Because it slows stomach emptying, there are rare aspiration reports under anaesthesia or deep sedation [3].
75. Discontinuation for adverse events in LEADER was 9.5% against 7.3%, p<0.001 [2]; in the weight trials 6.4% stopped for gastrointestinal problems alone, with nausea in 40% and vomiting in 15% [1] (verified).

### The head-to-head that explains why it lost its market [people]
76. One trial compared it directly with weekly semaglutide, and it is the single most informative study for anyone choosing between them. STEP 8 randomised 338 adults 3:1:3:1 across semaglutide 2.4 mg, placebo, liraglutide 3.0 mg and placebo, at 19 US sites, for 68 weeks [4] (verified).
77. At 68 weeks, mean weight change was minus 15.8% on semaglutide, minus 6.4% on liraglutide and minus 1.9% on pooled placebo. At least 10% loss was reached by 70.9%, 25.6% and 15.4%; at least 15% by 55.6%, 12.0% and 6.4%; at least 20% by 38.5%, 6.0% and 2.6% [4] (verified).
78. Tolerability split in an interesting direction. Gastrointestinal events were almost identical, 84.1% on semaglutide against 82.7% on liraglutide, but discontinuation for adverse events was 3.2% against 12.6% [4] (verified). The daily injection was not better tolerated despite the smaller effect; four times as many people stopped it.
79. Two caveats belong with this. The comparison between the two active drugs was open-label, since randomisation to semaglutide or liraglutide was not masked, and only each drug against its own placebo was blinded [4] (verified). And the trial was funded by the company that makes both, with several authors employed by or financially tied to it, including one who had advised on liraglutide's own development [4] (verified). The result is still the best direct evidence available, and it is consistent with what happened commercially.

### Product reality, and why the generics change the question [mixed]
80. This is one of the few entries where a legitimate, characterised product exists and is now cheap. US generic versions of the diabetes presentation arrived in December 2024 and of the weight presentation in August 2025, with more since (verified as stated in the card's own sourcing; manufacturer announcement pages were used rather than a regulatory database, which could not be opened for this review).
81. That matters because the usual argument for grey-market material, that the approved product is unaffordable or unavailable, is weakest here. A generic pen is a known quantity: a defined salt, a defined concentration, a sterile filled device, a lot number, and a recall mechanism. A vial of powder sold for research carries none of those, and nothing about the molecule being well studied transfers to a batch nobody has tested (inferred).
82. The molecule itself is unusually robust compared with most peptides in this library: a C16 fatty acid on lysine 26 through a glutamic acid spacer makes it self-associate under the skin and bind albumin, which is what turns a GLP-1 half-life of minutes into about 13 hours [3]. That same self-association is why concentration, pH and excipients are not cosmetic details in a formulation.

### Where the law stands, and open questions [mixed]
83. Approved in the US and widely internationally, for type 2 diabetes and separately for weight management, with paediatric indications and a cardiovascular risk-reduction indication added on the strength of LEADER [2,3] (verified). It is not named on the 2026 WADA Prohibited List, and as a government-approved medicine it does not fall into the catch-all class for non-approved substances either, so on the published text it is not prohibited in sport [5] (inferred from the class definitions).
84. Does the cardiovascular benefit exist in people without diabetes or established disease? LEADER answered the high-risk question only, and nobody has run the low-risk version.
85. What was the pancreatic cancer imbalance? Thirteen cases against five, p=0.06, in a 3.8-year trial is the kind of signal that is neither dismissible nor interpretable without longer follow-up [2].
86. Does the rodent thyroid tumour mechanism apply to humans? The label says the relevance is undetermined, and a decade and a half of use has not settled it.
87. What happens after stopping? The weight trials ran about a year on treatment, and durability is the question the whole class still answers poorly.
88. Why does a drug with a quarter of the effect get stopped four times as often? STEP 8 found that pattern and did not explain it; daily injection burden and slower titration tolerance are both plausible and untested (speculated).

# PE-22-28
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/pe-22-28
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: spadin analog, Mini-spadin, GVSWGLR, Gly-Val-Ser-Trp-Gly-Leu-Arg, sortilin propeptide (22-28)
2. Origin: Lab-shortened fragment of a natural propeptide
3. Sequence: GVSWGLR (7 amino acids). 7-residue analog of spadin, itself cut from the sortilin propeptide
4. Legal and approval status: Not approved anywhere; preclinical research compound; not on any FDA list (as of Oct 2026).

## Summary
5. PE-22-28 is a 7-amino-acid shortened version of spadin, a natural peptide that blocks the TREK-1 potassium channel in neurons. It was designed in France as a fast-acting antidepressant lead, and users take it for mood, motivation and focus. All evidence is from mice and cells, showing antidepressant effects within four days, and no human trial exists.
6. Punch line: Shortened spadin built as a fast antidepressant. Blocks TREK-1 in neurons; mice lifted within four days.
7. Used for: Mood, motivation, focus

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Mood: Antidepressant effect in mice
9. Neural plasticity: New hippocampal neurons in mice
10. Cognition: Focus and clarity reported
11. Neural protection: Neuron survival under stress
12. Drive & mental stamina (backed only by animal or user reports): More motivation reported
13. Sleep & rhythms (backed only by animal or user reports): Sleep changes reported

## How it works
14. Blocks a potassium channel that keeps neurons quiet · TREK-1 (KCNK2) inhibitor · role Mood
   PE-22-28 blocks TREK-1 (KCNK2), a two-pore potassium channel that leaks potassium out of neurons and keeps them hard to fire. Removing that leak makes neurons easier to activate. The idea rests on mice bred without TREK-1, which resisted depression-like behaviour.
15. Lets serotonin neurons fire more · 5-HT neuron excitability up · role Mood
   With TREK-1 blocked, serotonin neurons in the dorsal raphe of the brainstem fire more readily. More serotonin signalling is the shared end point of most antidepressants. In mice PE-22-28 acted as an antidepressant within four days, but no human study exists.
16. Grows new neurons in the memory centre · Hippocampal neurogenesis, BDNF · role Neural plasticity
   Four days of dosing raised markers of new neuron formation in the hippocampus of mice, and raised PSD-95, a synapse scaffold protein, in cultured neurons. Conventional antidepressants take weeks to do this in mice. How large or durable the effect is remains unknown.
17. Strong and selective in the dish · IC50 ~0.1 nM; no TREK-2, TRAAK, hERG effect · role Neural protection
   In human TREK-1 channels expressed in cultured cells, PE-22-28 blocked half the current at about 0.12 nanomolar, roughly 400 times stronger than spadin. It left TREK-2, TRAAK, TRESK, TASK-1 and the cardiac hERG channel untouched. That is a clean but small panel, and it says nothing about brain levels.
18. Mechanism overview: PE-22-28 is a seven-residue analog of spadin, the peptide released when sortilin's propeptide is cleaved. It blocks TREK-1 (KCNK2), a two-pore potassium channel that dampens neuron firing; TREK-1 knockout mice are resistant to depression. Blocking it raises the excitability of serotonin neurons in the dorsal raphe and, in mice, drives hippocampal neurogenesis within days. In cell tests it was about 400 times more potent than spadin and did not touch related channels or the cardiac hERG channel.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
19. Typical: 50–200 mcg · once daily · cycle 4–8 weeks · route Sub-Q or intranasal (reported)
20. Half-life: ~23 h claimed
21. Most people take: No human dose studied. Community 50–200 mcg/day Sub-Q or intranasal, 4–8 week runs.

Users take it for mood, motivation and focus, usually alone or inside cognitive blends with Semax, Selank and Pinealon.

## Who shouldn't take it
39. People with a history of seizures: Blocks TREK-1; TREK-1 loss makes mice seizure-prone. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
41. NA Semax Amidate: NA Semax Amidate is assumed to raise BDNF and dopamine turnover, while PE-22-28 lifts serotonin neuron firing through TREK-1. People pair them for mood plus drive, and they are sold pre-mixed as Semax + Selank + PE-22-28 + Pinealon. The combination has not been tested.
42. NA Selank Amidate: NA Selank Amidate is used for calm without sedation, while PE-22-28 targets low mood through serotonin neurons. The pairing aims at mood and anxiety from two angles, and they are sold pre-mixed as Semax + Selank + PE-22-28 + Pinealon. It is user logic, not trial data.
43. Pinealon: Pinealon is claimed to protect neurons and support sleep, while PE-22-28 works on mood through TREK-1. People add it for a broader brain-aging angle, and they are sold pre-mixed as Semax + Selank + PE-22-28 + Pinealon. The blend itself has never been tested.
44. Semax: Semax is reported to raise BDNF and dopamine and serotonin turnover in rodents, while PE-22-28 drives serotonin neuron firing and fast neurogenesis in mice. People stack them for mood, focus and motivation. Both rest on animal work, and the pair has not been tested together.
45. Selank: Selank is used for anxiety and slows breakdown of calming enkephalins, while PE-22-28 targets low mood and motivation. The stack covers anxious and flat mood from separate mechanisms. This is user logic, not trial data, and the pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
46. A 7-amino-acid shortened version of spadin, a natural peptide that blocks the TREK-1 potassium channel in neurons.
47. First studied for: Designed in France (Mazella/Borsotto group) as a fast-acting antidepressant lead.
48. Name story: PE is the propeptide cut off sortilin; the numbers are residues 22-28 of it. Spadin covers residues 12-28, so PE-22-28 is simply spadin's last seven amino acids, the "mini-spadin". [S2] (inferred)
49. 2006: Spadin found as the TREK-1-blocking piece of the sortilin propeptide
50. 2017: PE-22-28 published: shorter, stronger, longer-lasting in mice
51. 2020s: Picked up by nootropic users and sold as a research peptide
52. Today: Inside IllumiNeuro-type cognitive blends; still mouse-only

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where it came from, and who is behind every result [lab]
53. The story starts with a receptor protein rather than a drug. Sortilin, also called neurotensin receptor 3, is made with a short leading piece, a propeptide, that is cut off as the protein matures. In 2010 a group at the Institute of Molecular and Cellular Pharmacology near Nice showed that a 17-residue stretch of that propeptide, which they named spadin, blocked the TREK-1 potassium channel and behaved like an antidepressant in mice [1] (verified). The idea behind it came from the same group's 2006 finding that mice lacking TREK-1 entirely were resistant to depression-like behaviour across several tests [2] (verified).
54. PE-22-28 came next, in 2017. The group watched spadin break down in mouse blood, saw that almost all of it was gone within 30 minutes, and designed a shorter seven-residue peptide, GVSWGLR, based on the fragments that survived [3] (verified). The product sold today is that seven-residue molecule.
55. What is missing from the story is a second laboratory. Every primary result on spadin and its short analogues found in this review traces to the same French academic network, funded by national research agencies, with authors declaring no commercial conflicts [3] (verified). One of the authors held an industrial doctoral fellowship of the French CIFRE type, which by design pairs a student with a company, but no company is named as a developer (reported). Independent replication, which is the normal check on a single group's findings, has not appeared in print as far as could be found (inferred from searches; PubMed itself was not reachable for this review).

### What the two famous numbers actually mean [cells]
56. Two figures travel with this peptide: a potency about 400 times higher than spadin, and a roughly 23-hour half-life. Both come from the 2017 paper, and both say less than they appear to.
57. The potency is real but specific. In human TREK-1 channels expressed in cultured kidney cells and measured by patch clamp, the concentration that blocked half the current was 0.12 nanomolar for PE-22-28 against 40 to 60 nanomolar for spadin [3] (verified, in cells). That is a measure of how tightly it acts on one channel in a dish. It says nothing about how much reaches the brain after an injection or a nasal spray.
58. The 23 hours is not a half-life. No one has measured the peptide in blood or tissue over time. What the paper measured was how long the behavioural effect in mice lasted after one dose, and it reported half-effect times of 14, 17, 21 and 23 hours across four analogues, against about 6 hours for spadin [3] (verified). The 23-hour figure belongs to a modified analogue, not necessarily to the plain sequence in a vial. There is no pharmacokinetic data for PE-22-28 in any species: no absorption, distribution, clearance or brain penetration figures (verified as absent).
59. The mouse doses are worth knowing for scale, not as guidance. Behavioural effects were seen at 3 to 4 micrograms per kilogram by intraperitoneal injection, and in one four-day arm at 1 milligram per kilogram by stomach tube [3] (verified). The paper's own figure caption and main text disagree on one of those doses. There is no established human dose, and no study has tried to derive one.

### Mechanism, one step at a time, with the model each step came from [mixed]
60. Step one, the target. TREK-1 is a background potassium channel: when it is open, potassium leaks out and the neuron is harder to fire. Mice bred without it showed less despair-like behaviour, and their serotonin neurons in the brainstem fired more [2] (verified, in animals). That knockout result is the whole rationale. It shows that removing the channel from birth changes behaviour; it does not by itself show that blocking it in an adult does the same thing safely.
61. Step two, selectivity. At 100 nanomolar, roughly a thousand times its blocking concentration, PE-22-28 did not change currents through the closest relatives TREK-2 and TRAAK, nor through TRESK or TASK-1. At 10 micromolar the analogues did not change the cardiac hERG current, the channel most often behind drug-induced rhythm problems [3] (verified, in cells). That is a clean panel for five channels. It is not a broad screen, and no receptor or enzyme panel was reported.
62. Step three, behaviour. In male C57BL/6J mice, single doses shortened immobility in the forced swim test, and four days of dosing shortened the delay to eat in a novel environment, a test that usually needs weeks of a conventional antidepressant [3] (verified, in animals). Only male mice of one strain were used.
63. Step four, new neurons and synapses. Four days of dosing increased markers of new neuron formation in the hippocampus, and in cultured mouse cortical neurons the analogues raised PSD-95, a scaffold protein of excitatory synapses [3] (verified, in animals and cells). The speed is the interesting part, since conventional antidepressants take weeks to do this in mice. The size and durability of the effect beyond the short window studied is unknown.

### Safety: the channel does other jobs [animals]
64. There are no toxicology studies of PE-22-28: no acute, no repeat-dose, no genotoxicity, no reproductive studies, in any species (verified as absent from the primary paper and the patent). The patent text describes the peptides as lacking side effects, but reports no measured toxicity to back that [4] (verified).
65. The more important point is biological. TREK-1 is not a depression switch; it is part of how neurons protect themselves. In the group's own 2004 work, mice lacking TREK-1 were more vulnerable to seizures and to brain damage from reduced blood flow, and less sensitive to some general anaesthetics [5] (verified, in animals). A drug that blocks the channel is, in principle, pushing in the same direction as that knockout. The 2017 paper cites earlier spadin work reporting no harmful effects on pain, ischaemia or the heart, and states the authors could expect the analogues to behave similarly [3]; that is an expectation for this molecule, not a test of it (reported).
66. So the honest summary is not that it looked safe, but that the specific questions its own biology raises, seizure threshold, stroke outcome and interaction with anaesthesia, have not been asked of this peptide (inferred).

### Product reality and the human record [people]
67. There is no human study of any kind: no trial, no case series, no pharmacokinetic measurement (verified as absent from the literature found; trial registries could not be opened directly for this review). Intranasal use, which is common in practice, has never been tested in any species. The patent lists intravenous, intraperitoneal and oral routes as possibilities, and its examples used injection into the abdomen of mice only [4] (verified).
68. The patent family is also a reminder that the molecule in commerce is not the one the inventors chose to protect. The US claims cover an alanine-substituted version, AVSWGLR, and its biotinylated form, not the native GVSWGLR sequence [4] (verified). In the 2017 paper that modified version gave the strongest neurogenesis signal [3]. The commercial product is therefore the unprotected, cheaper-to-copy sibling of the lead candidate (inferred).
69. A seven-residue peptide containing tryptophan is vulnerable to oxidation and light, and spadin itself was shown to be cut apart in blood within half an hour [3]. No stability data for the short analogue in solution, in a vial or in a nasal spray has been published (verified as absent).

### Where the law stands, and open questions [mixed]
70. Not approved anywhere, not in any registered clinical programme found, and not nominated for or reviewed under the US compounding lists (verified as of October 2026). It is not named on the 2026 WADA Prohibited List, which means it falls under the catch-all S0 class for pharmacological substances with no government approval for human use, prohibited at all times [6] (inferred from the class wording).
71. Does blocking TREK-1 in an adult human change mood at all? No blocker of this channel has been tested in people for mood.
72. How much reaches the brain, by any route? Without a single pharmacokinetic measurement, the dose question cannot even be framed.
73. Does it lower seizure threshold or worsen stroke outcome? The knockout biology says those are the right questions; nobody has asked them of this molecule.
74. Does anyone outside the original group get the same results? One independent replication of the four-day neurogenesis and behavioural effects would change the weight of the whole file.

# PT-141

## Identity
1. Also called: bremelanotide, Vyleesi
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: LDHFRWK (7 amino acids). Ring-closed (cyclic); Nle shown as L, D-Phe shown as F; acetylated start
4. Shown with an FDA approved badge

## Summary
6. PT-141 is bremelanotide, a cyclic melanocortin peptide spun off from Melanotan II that keeps the arousal effect without strong tanning. It raises sexual desire through brain melanocortin pathways rather than blood flow, and is FDA-approved as Vyleesi for low desire in premenopausal women. Trial effects were modest, nausea is common, and male and grey-market use is off-label.
7. Punch line: Melanotan II's spin-off, approved as Vyleesi. Raises desire through the brain, not blood flow; nausea is common.
8. Used for: Low sexual desire, both sexes

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
9. Connection & desire: Raises desire through the brain
10. Tanning: Some skin darkening

## How it works
11. Raises desire through the brain, not blood flow · MC4R, MC3R · role Connection & desire
   Bremelanotide activates MC4R and MC3R in the brain, especially in the medial preoptic area, a hub for sexual desire. It works centrally rather than on blood flow, so it can act where PDE5 drugs do nothing. Phase 3 human trials in women led to approval.
12. Lifts dopamine in desire centres · MPOA dopamine release · role Connection & desire
   Activating these receptors raises dopamine release in the medial preoptic area, the circuit that drives sexual motivation. This step comes from animal work. In people it shows up as modest gains in desire in phase 3 trials, with nausea common.
13. Can darken skin and gums with repeat use · MC1R · role Tanning
   Bremelanotide still activates MC1R on pigment cells, a leftover from its parent melanotan II. With repeated dosing this can darken skin and gums, a known effect listed for the approved drug.
14. Briefly raises blood pressure after a dose · Sympathetic MC4R tone · role Heart & vessels
   MC4R activation raises sympathetic nerve tone, which briefly lifts blood pressure after a dose. Blood pressure concerns halted an earlier nasal programme, and the approved injection carries a blood pressure warning.
15. Mechanism overview: Bremelanotide is a cyclic peptide derived from Melanotan II, tuned to keep the arousal effect with less tanning. It activates MC4R and MC3R in the brain, especially in the medial preoptic area, where it raises dopamine release in circuits that drive sexual desire. Because it works centrally rather than on penile or clitoral blood flow, it can act where PDE5 drugs do nothing. Sympathetic MC4R tone briefly raises blood pressure, and residual MC1R activity darkens skin and gums with repeat dosing.

## Where it comes from
42. Bremelanotide, a cyclic melanocortin peptide spun off from Melanotan II, keeping the sexual-arousal effect without the strong tanning.
43. First studied for: Low sexual desire, acting on the brain's melanocortin pathways rather than on blood flow.
44. Name story: "PT" reportedly stands for Palatin Technologies, which developed it. It is essentially Melanotan II with the C-terminal amide swapped for an acid, and was approved in 2019 as Vyleesi. [S4] (reported)
45. 1990s to 2000s: Bremelanotide spun off from Melanotan II for arousal
46. 2019: FDA approves Vyleesi for low desire in premenopausal women
47. Today: Approved for female HSDD; used off-label by men

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### The part of the origin story that explains the side effects [lab]
48. Bremelanotide is not a designed-from-scratch molecule. It is the active breakdown product of melanotan II, differing from it by one chemical group: where melanotan II ends in an amide, this ends in an acid [1] (verified). Palatin stopped work on melanotan II in 2000 and carried the metabolite forward instead [1].
49. That lineage matters because the parent was a tanning peptide, and the family it belongs to acts on all the melanocortin receptors except the one that drives cortisol. Bremelanotide is described as a non-selective agonist across MC1, MC3, MC4 and MC5, acting mainly at MC3 and MC4 [1] (verified). The arousal effect and the pigment effect are not two separate things that happen to coexist; they are two receptors in one family being hit by one molecule. Nothing about the design removed the pigment arm, it was reduced relative to the parent.
50. The development path is also the clearest safety signal in the file, and it is usually left out. A nasal spray was taken into mid-stage trials in both women and men, including four trials in erectile dysfunction. The FDA halted that programme in 2007 over blood pressure increases, the commercial partner ended its agreement, and the nasal formulation was abandoned in 2008 [1] (verified). The injection that was eventually approved in June 2019 exists because the nasal route failed on cardiovascular grounds, not because injection was preferred.

### What the approved trials actually measured, and what they found [people]
51. Two identical 24-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials supported approval, with 635 women on drug and 632 on placebo, followed by a 52-week open-label extension [2] (verified).
52. There were two co-primary endpoints, both questionnaires. On the desire domain of the Female Sexual Function Index, the change from baseline was +0.5 against +0.2 on placebo in the first trial and +0.6 against +0.2 in the second. On the single question measuring distress about low desire, the change was minus 0.7 against minus 0.4 in both [2] (verified). The p-values are small, the differences are not: roughly a third of a point on one scale and three tenths on another, against placebo.
53. The endpoint that is easiest for a non-specialist to interpret was negative. The number of satisfying sexual events did not differ from placebo, with p-values of 0.76 and 0.70 [2] (verified). So the approved claim rests on self-reported desire and distress, not on a change in what actually happened.
54. The dropout figures belong next to the efficacy figures. Premature discontinuation during the blinded period was 40% against 13% on placebo in the first trial and 39% against 25% in the second, and 18% of women on drug stopped specifically for adverse reactions against 2% on placebo [2] (verified). A treatment that four in ten participants stop inside six months is being described accurately only when that is said out loud.

### The tolerability profile in plain numbers [people]
55. Nausea affected 40% of women on drug against 1.3% on placebo, usually starting within an hour and lasting about two hours. It was heaviest on the first dose, 21%, and fell to around 3% with later doses. Thirteen percent needed anti-sickness medication and 8% stopped treatment because of it [2] (verified). Flushing reached 20.3% against 0.3%, headache 11.3% against 1.9%, vomiting 4.8%, and injection-site reactions 13.2% against 8.4% [2].
56. Pigment change is the effect most often treated as cosmetic trivia, and the label's own numbers argue otherwise. Focal darkening of the face, gums and breasts occurred in 1% with as-needed use, but in a study using daily dosing 38% developed it, with a further 14% developing new changes on continued use. Risk was higher with darker skin and with frequent dosing, and resolution was not confirmed in everyone [2] (verified). Frequent or daily use is exactly the pattern reported outside the label, and it is the pattern associated with the pigment change that may not reverse (inferred).
57. One case of acute hepatitis occurred in the open-label extension and the drug's role could not be definitively excluded, though liver test outliers were not imbalanced in the blinded trials [2] (verified).

### The cardiovascular arm, measured rather than described [people]
58. Every dose raises blood pressure and lowers heart rate, typically resolving within 12 hours [2] (verified). In a 127-patient ambulatory monitoring study the mean daytime rise was 1.9 mmHg systolic and 1.7 mmHg diastolic, with a peak mean systolic rise of 2.8 mmHg and a mean heart rate fall of 0.5 beats per minute [2] (verified).
59. Those averages look small, and the label's response to them is not small: it is contraindicated in uncontrolled high blood pressure and in known cardiovascular disease, not recommended in people at high cardiovascular risk, and requires cardiovascular risk assessment before starting and periodically afterwards [2] (verified). The averages are averages; the regulator priced in the individuals at the tail, and the 2007 halt of the nasal programme shows what the tail can look like with higher systemic exposure [1].
60. This is the one section where off-label male use diverges sharply from the evidence base. The trials that generated every number above enrolled premenopausal women. No approved indication, and no completed late-stage programme, exists for men; the male trials in erectile dysfunction were part of the nasal programme the FDA stopped [1] (verified). The cardiovascular screening the label requires has no counterpart when the compound is obtained outside that system (inferred).

### What the body does with it, including the interactions nobody expects [people]
61. Subcutaneous bioavailability is essentially complete, around 100%. Peak concentration averages 72.8 nanograms per millilitre at a median of about one hour, plasma protein binding is 21%, volume of distribution about 25 litres, clearance about 6.5 litres per hour, and terminal half-life about 2.7 hours. It is broken down by hydrolysis of the ring's amide bonds, with about 65% of a radiolabelled dose recovered in urine and 23% in faeces [2] (verified).
62. Impairment matters more than the short half-life suggests. Exposure rose 1.2-fold in mild, 1.5-fold in moderate and 2-fold in severe kidney impairment, and 1.2-fold in mild and 1.7-fold in moderate liver impairment, with severe liver impairment never studied [2] (verified).
63. The interaction section is the part most likely to catch someone out, because it has nothing to do with sexual medicine. The drug slows stomach emptying, so it can reduce absorption of swallowed medicines. The label says to avoid oral naltrexone products used for alcohol or opioid dependence, because naltrexone exposure may be significantly reduced, and to avoid oral drugs that depend on reaching a threshold concentration, such as antibiotics; it also flags drugs needed to act fast, such as indomethacin [2] (verified).
64. Use is not recommended in pregnancy, with contraception advised. Human data are limited to a handful of outcomes in the trials. In animals, fetal harm appeared in dogs at exposures at least 16 times the maximum human dose and developmental delays in mice at roughly 125 times [2] (verified).

### Who owns it now, and where the law stands [mixed]
65. The commercial history is a string of partners handing it on: King Pharmaceuticals in 2004 and out after the 2007 halt, Gedeon Richter for Europe in 2014 and terminated in 2016, AMAG for North America in 2017, approval in 2019 [1] (verified). Palatin then sold the product outright to Cosette Pharmaceuticals in 2023 in a deal worth up to $171 million [3] (verified). Four partners and an outright sale inside twenty years is a commercial signal, not a scientific one, but it tells you how the owners read the market.
66. It is approved in the United States for premenopausal women with acquired, generalised hypoactive sexual desire disorder, with the label explicitly excluding postmenopausal women, men, and use to enhance performance [2] (verified). It is not approved in Europe or the UK [1] (verified as of the source; EMA pages could not be opened directly for this review).
67. For sport: bremelanotide is not named on the 2026 Prohibited List, and because it holds government approval for human therapeutic use it does not fall into the catch-all class for non-approved substances either, so on the published text it is not prohibited [4] (inferred from the class definitions). That is a different position from most compounds in this library and should not be generalised to melanotan II.

### Open questions [mixed]
68. Is a third of a point on a desire questionnaire, with no change in satisfying events, a difference people can feel? The approval says the endpoint was met; it does not settle what the effect is worth, and the 40% dropout rate suggests many participants answered that question for themselves.
69. Does the pigment change reverse? The label says resolution was not confirmed in all patients, and the highest rates came from daily dosing [2]. Nobody has followed frequent users long enough to answer it.
70. What does repeated use do in men, at the doses actually used? The entire safety dataset is female, the male programme was stopped on blood pressure grounds, and no one has repeated it [1].
71. Why does the brain effect need a molecule that also hits pigment and vascular receptors? A genuinely MC4-selective agonist would answer whether the side effects are separable from the effect.
72. How much of the reported benefit is anticipation? With an as-needed drug taken before a planned event, a short-onset side effect profile that is obvious to the user makes effective blinding difficult, which the 40% versus 13% dropout gap hints at (inferred).
