# Survodutide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/survodutide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: BI 456906
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain
3. Sequence: HAQGTFTSDYSKYLDERAAKDFIKWLESA (29 amino acids). Position 2 is Ac4c (aminocyclobutane carboxylic acid), shown as A; Glucagon-based chain; K24 carries a C18 diacid via gGlu and Gly-Ser linker; C-terminal amide
4. Legal and approval status: Investigational as of 22 Oct 2026: Phase 3 SYNCHRONIZE-1 and -2 read out (Apr and Oct 2026), CVOT results expected late 2026, LIVERAGE MASH trials ongoing; FDA Breakthrough (MASH) but no filing announced. Not approved anywhere; WADA S0 (non-approved substance) applies (inferred).

## Summary
5. Survodutide is Boehringer Ingelheim's weekly dual agonist of the glucagon and GLP-1 receptors, licensed from Zealand Pharma. It cuts appetite while telling the liver to burn fat, so interest centres on obesity and fatty liver (MASH). Phase 3 trials showed up to 16.6% weight loss, but GI side effects drove dropouts, and it is not yet approved.
6. Punch line: Weekly glucagon and GLP-1 dual aimed squarely at fatty liver. Phase 3 reached about 16.6% weight loss.
7. Used for: Weight loss, liver fat, MASH

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Fat metabolism: Burns fat, shrinks visceral fat
9. Organ function: Clears liver fat, MASH resolution
10. Appetite & satiety: Cuts hunger via GLP-1
11. Glucose & insulin: Lowers HbA1c in diabetes
12. Cellular energy (backed only by animal or user reports): Glucagon raises energy burn
13. Digestive & gut (backed only by animal or user reports): Nausea and vomiting on titration

## How it works
14. Quiets hunger and slows the stomach · GLP-1 receptor · role Appetite & satiety
   Survodutide activates the GLP-1 receptor in the brain and gut. That lowers hunger and slows stomach emptying, so people eat less. The resulting weight loss has been shown in the Phase 3 SYNCHRONIZE trials in people.
15. Tells the liver to burn stored fat · Glucagon receptor, hepatic · role Organ function
   Its glucagon receptor arm acts mainly on liver cells and tells them to burn stored fat. In a 48-week biopsy trial in MASH, liver fat and liver inflammation fell far more than on placebo. Fibrosis, the endpoint tied to liver outcomes, moved much less.
16. Raises energy spending · Glucagon receptor · role Cellular energy
   Glucagon receptor signalling raises resting energy use, a known effect of the hormone. That is the reason a glucagon arm was added on purpose. In people this step is inferred from receptor pharmacology, since trials measured weight and liver fat, not energy spending directly.
17. Lowers glucose despite glucagon arm · GLP-1R insulin effect · role Glucose & insulin
   Glucagon alone would raise blood glucose, but the GLP-1 arm boosts insulin when glucose is high and overrides that pull. In SYNCHRONIZE-2, HbA1c fell clearly against placebo in people with type 2 diabetes. So the glucagon arm does not undo glucose control at trial doses.
18. Fatty tail rides albumin for weekly dosing · C18 diacid acylation · role Fat metabolism
   A C18 fatty diacid binds albumin, the main carrier protein in blood, which slows clearance. An Ac4c swap at position 2 protects it from the DPP-4 enzyme. Together they allow once-weekly injections.
19. Mechanism overview: Survodutide is a 29-residue glucagon-derived peptide with an Ac4c swap at position 2 for DPP-4 resistance and a C18 fatty diacid that binds albumin for weekly dosing. It activates both the glucagon receptor (GCGR) and the GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) at sub-nanomolar potency. The GLP-1 arm cuts hunger in the brain, slows stomach emptying and boosts glucose-dependent insulin. The glucagon arm acts mainly on the liver, raising fat oxidation and energy expenditure, which is why liver fat drops further than weight loss alone would predict.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
20. Typical: 0.6–6.0 mg (trial) · once weekly · cycle Ongoing; slow titration over ~20 weeks · route Sub-Q (verified)
21. Half-life: ~6–7 days (est.)
22. Most people take: Trial only: weekly Sub-Q, stepped up from 0.6 mg to 3.6 or 6.0 mg maintenance in Phase 3. No oral form.

## What people report
23. Few genuine first-hand reports; grey-market interest centres on liver fat and comparison with retatrutide.
24. Liked / worked: Up to 16.6% weight loss at 76 weeks
25. Liked / worked: Visceral and liver fat fall preferentially
26. Liked / worked: HbA1c down up to 1.21% in T2D
27. Liked / worked: MASH resolution in Phase 2
28. What worked: Up to 16.6% weight loss at 76 weeks without diabetes (SYNCHRONIZE-1) and up to 13.1% with diabetes (SYNCHRONIZE-2); MRI showed visceral and liver fat falling preferentially. Phase 2 MASH resolution in 47% vs 14% on placebo.
29. Went wrong / did not work: 18% quit for GI effects in SYNCHRONIZE-2
30. Went wrong / did not work: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation
31. Went wrong / did not work: Small heart-rate rise
32. Went wrong / did not work: Weight regain after stopping (Phase 2)
33. What went wrong: GI side effects drove 18% to quit vs 1.2% on placebo in SYNCHRONIZE-2, mostly during a rigid dose escalation. Small heart-rate rise and transient lipase/amylase increases.
34. Most reported: Interest for liver fat over pure weight loss
35. Most reported: Compared unfavourably with retatrutide on raw weight loss
36. Most reported: Few genuine first-hand reports

## What has been tested
37. Fat metabolism: Obesity, SYNCHRONIZE-1 (human)
38. Glucose & insulin: Obesity with T2D, SYNCHRONIZE-2 (human)
39. Organ function: MASH with fibrosis, Phase 2 and LIVERAGE (human)
40. Phase 2 in obesity (COURAGE) and MASH, then the Phase 3 SYNCHRONIZE program in obesity with and without type 2 diabetes, plus LIVERAGE trials in MASH and cirrhosis.
41. What it helps: Phase 3 SYNCHRONIZE-1 showed up to 16.6% weight loss at 76 weeks in obesity, and SYNCHRONIZE-2 up to 13.1% in obesity with type 2 diabetes, with HbA1c and waist falling. Phase 2 MASH data showed resolution in nearly half of patients, earning FDA Breakthrough status. GI side effects and dropout are the main weakness. People look at it mostly for fatty liver and visceral fat.
42. Trial: active · Phase 3 · obesity and heart safety · NCT06077864 · Boehringer Ingelheim. Phase 3 SYNCHRONIZE readouts arrived in 2026 and new trials (SYNCHRONIZE-START, type 2 diabetes) are still enrolling. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
43. Personal or family history of MTC or MEN2: Causes thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents; boxed warning and contraindication on the label. (inferred)
44. Anyone booked for surgery, endoscopy or sedation: Food can stay in the stomach for days and be inhaled into the lungs under anaesthesia. (inferred)
45. People with arrhythmia or a fast resting pulse: Glucagon component raised heart rate in trials. (reported)

## Synergies (paired with)
46. Cagrilintide: Cagrilintide adds amylin fullness signalling in the brainstem, while survodutide brings GLP-1 appetite control plus a liver-directed glucagon arm. People pair them to stack appetite routes while keeping the liver-fat effect. The pair itself has not been tested together.
47. MOTS-c: MOTS-c activates AMPK and mimics exercise on muscle glucose uptake in mice, while survodutide drives weight and liver fat loss in human trials. People add it hoping to protect metabolic fitness during weight loss. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
48. Boehringer Ingelheim's weekly glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonist, licensed from Zealand Pharma: a glucagon backbone tuned to also hit the GLP-1 receptor, with a C18 fatty tail for weekly dosing.
49. First studied for: Obesity and MASH (fatty liver disease with inflammation and fibrosis).
50. Name story: Co-invented by Zealand Pharma and Boehringer Ingelheim (code BI 456906). Its chain opens almost exactly like glucagon, not GLP-1. Fellow glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonists cotadutide, mazdutide and pemvidutide share the same '-dutide' ending. [S2] (inferred)
51. 2011: Zealand Pharma and Boehringer partner on glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonists
52. 2023: Phase 2 COURAGE: ~15% weight loss at 46 weeks; Phase 3 starts
53. Sep 2024: FDA Breakthrough Therapy for MASH
54. Apr 2026: SYNCHRONIZE-1: up to 16.6% weight loss at 76 weeks
55. Oct 2026: SYNCHRONIZE-2: up to 13.1% in T2D; 18% quit for GI effects

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Why a glucagon arm was added on purpose [lab]
56. Glucagon is the hormone that raises blood sugar, so putting a glucagon agonist in a diabetes drug looks like a contradiction. The logic is that glucagon does two other things as well: it tells the liver to burn stored fat, and it raises resting energy expenditure. Pair it with a GLP-1 agonist strong enough to override the glucose-raising effect, and in principle you get GLP-1 appetite suppression plus a liver-directed fat-burning signal that GLP-1 alone does not have (verified as the stated design rationale).
57. That is the mechanistic bet, and the trials below are what it bought. The clearest evidence it is a real second mechanism rather than marketing is the liver data: liver fat fell much further than the weight loss alone would predict, and histology changed in a 48-week biopsy trial [1] (verified, in people).
58. The cost of the bet shows up in the tolerability columns of every trial, and in the fact that the glucagon arm has no long-term human safety precedent. No glucagon receptor agonist has ever been approved for chronic use in people (inferred).

### The liver trial, which is the most interesting dataset [people]
59. A 48-week phase 2 trial randomised 293 adults with biopsy-confirmed MASH to 2.4, 4.8 or 6.0 mg weekly or placebo, with biopsies at the end [1] (verified).
60. Histological improvement in MASH without worsening fibrosis reached 47%, 62% and 43% across the three doses against 14% on placebo [1]. Fibrosis improved by at least one stage in 34%, 36% and 34% against 22% on placebo [1]. At least a 30% reduction in liver fat by MRI was reached by 63%, 67% and 57% against 14% [1] (verified).
61. Two features of that table deserve attention. First, the response was not dose-ordered: the middle dose did best on the primary endpoint and the highest dose did worst, which is what tolerability-driven dropout tends to look like rather than a clean dose-response. Second, fibrosis, the endpoint that actually predicts liver outcomes, moved much less than the inflammation and fat endpoints did, and placebo moved too. A 34% versus 22% difference on fibrosis is a far weaker result than 62% versus 14% on MASH activity, and it is the fibrosis number that matters for whether livers fail (inferred).
62. Gastrointestinal effects in that trial were heavy: nausea 66% against 23%, diarrhoea 49% against 23%, vomiting 41% against 4%, with serious adverse events similar at 8% against 7% [1] (verified).

### The two phase 3 obesity trials, and the two sets of numbers each reports [people]
63. SYNCHRONIZE-1 ran 76 weeks across 116 sites in 14 countries, randomising 725 adults with obesity, or overweight with a complication, and no diabetes, 1:1:1 to weekly 3.6 mg, 6.0 mg or placebo, all with lifestyle counselling. Mean age was 47, mean BMI 37.9, mean weight 108.8 kg [2] (verified).
64. At 76 weeks, mean weight change was minus 12% on 3.6 mg, minus 13% on 6.0 mg and minus 5% on placebo, with at least 5% loss in 73%, 72% and 46% respectively, p at or below 0.0001 for both doses [2] (verified). Note that the higher dose added almost nothing over the lower one, and that the placebo arm lost 5% on lifestyle counselling alone.
65. SYNCHRONIZE-2 enrolled 752 adults with type 2 diabetes and a BMI of at least 27, same doses, same 76 weeks [3]. Here the reporting difference matters more than the result. Under the treatment-regimen estimand, which counts everyone as randomised including those who stopped, weight change was minus 8.2% and minus 9.8% against minus 3.9% on placebo. Under the efficacy estimand, which asks what happens in people who stay on treatment, the same trial reads minus 10.4% and minus 13.1% against minus 3.1% [3] (verified). Both are correct; the first describes a treatment decision, the second describes a drug. The larger figure is the one that circulates.
66. HbA1c fell 0.9 and 0.8 percentage points against 0.2 on placebo, at least 5% weight loss was reached by 57.6% and 64.5% against 35.1%, and hsCRP, a general inflammation marker, fell about half against 17% [3] (verified). Weight loss in people with diabetes was smaller than in those without, which is the usual pattern for this class.
67. Both trials were funded by the manufacturer, published in a major journal and presented at a diabetes meeting [2,3] (verified). One caution for anyone chasing the primary sources: the trial report and its own reference list carry different DOIs for the same paper, so citation details should be checked at the journal [3] (verified as an inconsistency in the reporting).

### Tolerability, in the numbers that decide whether people stay on it [people]
68. In SYNCHRONIZE-1, gastrointestinal adverse events affected 81% on 3.6 mg and 90% on 6.0 mg against 48% on placebo, mostly mild to moderate, with no deaths [2] (verified).
69. SYNCHRONIZE-2 reported the discontinuation figure that the obesity trial's summary did not: gastrointestinal events alone caused 18% of the 3.6 mg arm and 17.9% of the 6.0 mg arm to stop, against 1.2% on placebo [3] (verified). Roughly one person in six left the trial because of side effects, at both doses. That is high for this class and consistent with the dual mechanism: the glucagon arm does not reduce nausea, and the dose that maximised liver histology in phase 2 was not the top dose.
70. Serious adverse events were 9.2% and 8.4% against 10.8% on placebo, so no excess there. There was one case of severe hypoglycaemia, in the lower-dose arm, and two major adverse cardiovascular events, both in the lower-dose arm; one case of acute pancreatitis occurred on placebo [3] (verified).
71. What has not been published is the thing the glucagon arm most warrants: a cardiovascular outcome trial. Glucagon agonism raises energy expenditure and heart rate is a known concern across this class, and the definitive trial has not reported (verified as pending; registry pages could not be opened directly for this review).

### Product reality, and what an investigational compound means here [mixed]
72. This is a molecule with no approved product anywhere, which makes its position unlike liraglutide's and unlike BPC-157's. There is no approved label, no pharmacopoeial monograph, no reference standard in general circulation, and no generic. Everything in the trials above was manufactured, filled and titrated under a sponsor's control, over a titration schedule of roughly twenty weeks [2,3].
73. A powder sold under this name is therefore not a cheaper version of a known product; there is no known product. Nothing in the evidence above transfers to a vial nobody has characterised, and a 29-residue acylated peptide with a fatty diacid tail has formulation requirements, including concentration-dependent self-association, that are part of how the trial material behaved (inferred).
74. The structural detail that makes weekly dosing possible is the same one that makes it a formulation-sensitive molecule: an aminocyclobutane carboxylic acid substitution at position 2 protects it from the DPP-4 enzyme, and a C18 fatty diacid binds albumin to slow clearance (verified as described in the card's structural sourcing).

### Where the law stands, and open questions [mixed]
75. Investigational everywhere as of October 2026. Phase 3 obesity and diabetes trials have reported, a breakthrough designation exists for the liver indication, liver outcome trials continue, and no regulatory filing has been announced [2,3] (verified). It is not named on the 2026 WADA Prohibited List; as a substance without government approval for human therapeutic use it falls in the catch-all class prohibited at all times [4] (inferred from the class wording).
76. Does the fibrosis signal hold up? The phase 2 liver trial moved inflammation strongly and fibrosis weakly, and fibrosis is the endpoint tied to real liver outcomes.
77. Is the glucagon arm safe for years? Raising energy expenditure through the glucagon receptor has no long-term human precedent, and the cardiovascular outcome data are not yet public.
78. Why does the top dose underperform? In the liver trial the middle dose won, and in the obesity trials 6.0 mg added almost nothing over 3.6 mg while worsening tolerability.
79. How much of the effect survives real-world use rather than trial conditions? With one in six stopping for gastrointestinal effects inside a supervised trial, the gap between the two estimands in SYNCHRONIZE-2 is a preview of that question [3].
80. Does it beat the dual and triple incretin drugs already approved? No head-to-head trial against tirzepatide or semaglutide has been reported, which leaves cross-trial comparison, the least reliable kind.

# Tesofensine
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/tesofensine
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: NS2330, NS-2330, Teso
2. Origin: Not a peptide: small molecule
3. Legal and approval status: Not FDA or EMA approved. Mexico: COFEPRIS committee favoured it Feb 2023, refused Nov 2024, Medix resubmitted Feb 2025; no approval found as of Oct 2026. Not named on the WADA list (may fall under S6 stimulants, inferred).

## Summary
4. Tesofensine is a Danish triple reuptake inhibitor (serotonin, noradrenaline, dopamine) from NeuroSearch, not a peptide. Originally aimed at Parkinson's and Alzheimer's, it was dropped for weak efficacy but caused weight loss, so it became an appetite-suppressant obesity drug. A 2008 Phase 2 showed about 11 to 13 kg loss in 24 weeks. Insomnia, dry mouth, faster pulse and anxiety recur, and weight returns after stopping.
5. Punch line: Failed Alzheimer's drug turned appetite killer. Oral triple reuptake inhibitor; insomnia and racing heart common.
6. Used for: Appetite and weight loss

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Appetite & satiety: Strong appetite suppression
8. Fat metabolism: About 10% weight loss
9. Drive & mental stamina: Dopamine lift, more focus
10. Cognition: Tested in Alzheimer's, failed
11. Sleep & rhythms (backed only by animal or user reports): Insomnia common
12. Heart & vessels (backed only by animal or user reports): Raises heart rate
13. Mood (backed only by animal or user reports): Anxiety and mood shifts

## How it works
14. Keeps noradrenaline, serotonin and dopamine around longer · NET, SERT, DAT reuptake inhibition · role Appetite & satiety
   Tesofensine blocks the reuptake transporters that clear noradrenaline, serotonin and dopamine from the synapse, most strongly the noradrenaline one. All three signals last longer. This brain-wide boost is the root of both its appetite effect and its side effects, from insomnia to a faster pulse.
15. Quiets hunger circuits · Lateral hypothalamus GABA neurons · role Appetite & satiety
   A 2024 animal study linked its appetite effect to silencing GABA neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, cells that drive feeding. With them quieter, animals ate less. In the human Phase 2 trial this showed up as large weight loss over 24 weeks.
16. Nudges energy burn and fat oxidation · Sympathetic tone, night-time EE · role Fat metabolism
   More noradrenaline raises sympathetic tone, the body's activating nervous system. That nudges up energy expenditure, notably at night, and fat oxidation. This adds to the appetite effect but is a smaller part of the weight loss.
17. Dopamine lift for focus and drive · DAT inhibition · role Drive & mental stamina
   Blocking the dopamine transporter lets dopamine linger in reward and focus circuits. Users report more focus and drive. How strong this is remains unclear, since two published potency datasets disagree on the dopamine transporter.
18. Raises heart rate · Noradrenergic effect · role Heart & vessels
   The same noradrenaline push speeds the heart and raises blood pressure. In human trials heart rate rose noticeably. The developer built Tesomet, a combination with the beta-blocker metoprolol, specifically to blunt this.
19. Mechanism overview: Tesofensine blocks the reuptake transporters for noradrenaline (NET), serotonin (SERT) and dopamine (DAT), strongest at NET, so all three stay longer in the synapse. In the hypothalamus this quiets hunger, and a 2024 study tied it to silencing GABA neurons in the lateral hypothalamus that drive feeding. Higher noradrenaline also nudges energy expenditure and fat oxidation, and the dopamine lift explains the focus and drive users report. The same noradrenergic push raises heart rate and blood pressure, the reason a combination with the beta-blocker metoprolol (Tesomet) was built.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
20. Typical: 0.25–0.5 mg · once daily, morning · cycle Up to 24 weeks in trials · route Oral (verified)
21. Half-life: ~220 h (~9 days); metabolite ~16 days
22. Dose note: Long half-life means steady state takes weeks; doses above 0.5 mg added side effects for little extra loss.
23. Most people take: Trials used 0.25, 0.5 or 1 mg orally once a day; 0.5 mg is the chosen dose, needs no titration. Community users take 0.25–0.5 mg in the morning to spare sleep.
24. Trial / intended: 0.5 mg · 1× daily · 24 weeks · Oral · for Phase 2 and Mexican Phase 3; expected label dose [S1] [S2] (verified)
25. Community: 0.25–0.5 mg · 1× daily, morning · weeks to months · Oral · for grey-market users [S3] (reported)
26. High (trial): 1 mg · 1× daily · 24 weeks · Oral · for Phase 2 top arm; more side effects [S1] (verified)

## What people report
27. Bought as grey-market 0.5 mg tablets; users report strong appetite loss and focus, with insomnia, dry mouth, racing heart and anxiety the common complaints.
28. Liked / worked: 11–13 kg loss in 24 weeks
29. Liked / worked: About twice sibutramine's effect
30. Liked / worked: No titration needed
31. What worked: Over 24 weeks, 0.5 mg gave 11.3 kg and 1 mg 12.8 kg weight loss vs 2.2 kg on placebo, about double what sibutramine managed.
32. Went wrong / did not work: Dry mouth, insomnia, nausea
33. Went wrong / did not work: Heart rate up about 7 bpm
34. Went wrong / did not work: Blood pressure up at 1 mg
35. Went wrong / did not work: Failed in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's
36. Went wrong / did not work: Lancet paper under expression of concern
37. What went wrong: Dry mouth, insomnia, nausea, constipation, diarrhea; higher heart rate and blood pressure at 1 mg; 13% quit for side effects vs 6% on placebo; the Lancet paper drew an expression of concern in 2013.
38. Most reported: Strong appetite loss
39. Most reported: Insomnia if taken late
40. Most reported: Racing heart, anxiety
41. Most reported: Clean focus or stimulant feel
42. Most reported: Regain after stopping

## What has been tested
43. Fat metabolism: Obesity, Phase 2 TIPO-1 (human)
44. Fat metabolism: Obesity, Mexican Phase 3 (human)
45. Cognition: Alzheimer's and Parkinson's trials (human)
46. Appetite & satiety: Hypothalamic feeding circuits (animal)
47. Pooled Parkinson's and Alzheimer's trials, the 203-person Phase 2 TIPO-1 obesity trial (Lancet 2008), an extension, a Mexican Phase 3 by Medix, and small Tesomet trials with metoprolol.
48. What it helps: The 2008 Lancet Phase 2 showed about 11 to 13 kg loss in 24 weeks at 0.5 to 1 mg against 2 kg on placebo, and a Mexican Phase 3 followed, though its results are not fully public. It failed as a dementia and Parkinson's drug. Users take it as a cheap oral appetite suppressant; insomnia, dry mouth, a faster pulse and anxiety are the recurring complaints, and weight returns after stopping.
49. Trial: none · Phase 3 · obesity · Medix. Last trials were the Mexican Phase 3 and Saniona's Prader-Willi study around 2019 to 2021; Mexico's regulator gave a favorable opinion in 2023. (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
50. People with hypertension or heart disease: Raises heart rate and blood pressure in trials. (reported)
51. People on SSRIs, SNRIs or MAOIs: Triple reuptake inhibitor; serotonin syndrome risk. (inferred)
52. People with bipolar disorder or anxiety: Dopamine and noradrenaline lift may trigger mania. (inferred)

## Where it comes from
53. A Danish triple reuptake inhibitor (serotonin, noradrenaline, dopamine) from NeuroSearch, first aimed at Parkinson's and Alzheimer's; patients lost weight, so it became an obesity pill.
54. First studied for: Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease, dropped for weak efficacy.
55. Name story: Born at Danish NeuroSearch as code NS2330 and given the INN tesofensine; the name has no published story. Rights later passed to Saniona, which licensed Mexico to Medix. [S5] (reported)
56. 1990s–2000s: NeuroSearch tests NS2330 in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's
57. 2008: Lancet Phase 2: up to 12.8 kg loss in 24 weeks
58. 2013: Lancet issues an expression of concern on the paper
59. Feb 2023: COFEPRIS committee gives favourable opinion
60. Nov 2024: Mexico withholds approval
61. Feb 2025: Medix resubmits; still pending as of Oct 2026

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### It was never meant to be a diet drug [people]
62. Tesofensine began as NS2330, a Danish candidate for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. Development for both was dropped for lack of efficacy [1] (verified). What got noticed in those trials was an adverse event: participants, especially heavier ones, kept losing weight. The obesity programme exists because of a side effect in a failed neurology drug [1].
63. That history explains the pharmacology that follows. This is a triple monoamine reuptake inhibitor built for the brain, not a gut hormone analogue, and it sits in the same pharmacological family as the appetite suppressants that were withdrawn over cardiovascular and psychiatric effects. Nothing about its chemistry is peptide-like; it belongs in this library only because it is traded alongside peptides (inferred).
64. Potency figures depend on which dataset is quoted, which is itself worth knowing. One set of inhibition values gives noradrenaline transporter 3.2 nanomolar, dopamine transporter 8.0 and serotonin transporter 11.0; a revised set gives noradrenaline 1.7, serotonin 11 and dopamine 65 [1] (verified as both reported). Those two readings tell different stories about how dopaminergic the drug is, and the difference matters for what to expect of its drive and abuse profile.

### The famous trial, and the formal cloud over it [people]
65. The 2008 phase 2 trial is the source of nearly every number quoted for this compound. Over 24 weeks, with all participants on a 300 kcal deficit diet and rising exercise, mean weight loss was 6.7 kg at 0.25 mg, 11.3 kg at 0.5 mg and 12.8 kg at 1 mg, against 2.2 kg on placebo [1] (verified). A 48-week open-label extension re-enrolled 140 completers and reported total mean loss of 13 to 14 kg in those previously on 0.5 mg [1].
66. In 2013 the journal that published it issued an expression of concern, and the detail matters more than the label. The Danish Health and Medicines Authority inspected the trial in November 2011 as part of a random selection of completed studies. At one of five sites, informed consent, which Danish rules require a medical practitioner to take, had been delegated to non-medical staff. Blinding integrity had been questioned in an earlier 2007 inspection and rebutted by the investigators. And the contract research organisation had recorded adverse events incompletely: recurring conditions such as headache, migraine, stress and depression were not reliably captured in participants who had them before enrolling [2] (verified).
67. The authority's conclusion is the sentence to carry away: the overall side-effect profile as published was not in accordance with the actual course of the trial [2] (verified). The endpoint data and serious adverse events were found to match the source records [2]. The corresponding author himself raised the concerns with the journal, agreed that under-reporting of some adverse events was the relevant finding, and drafted an erratum [2] (verified).
68. So the efficacy numbers above are probably sound, and the tolerability numbers from that trial are specifically the ones a regulator said were understated. Anyone quoting the 12.8 kg figure without that qualification is quoting half a finding.

### The pharmacokinetics are the real practical problem [people]
69. Half-life is about 220 hours, roughly nine days, with 90% oral bioavailability, hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 and renal clearance of about 15 to 20%. The main metabolite has a half-life of about 374 hours, roughly sixteen days, reaching 31 to 34% of parent exposure at steady state while contributing about 6% of the activity [1] (verified).
70. A nine-day half-life has consequences that a daily tablet hides. Steady state takes weeks, so what someone feels in the first days is not what the drug will do at plateau. A dose change takes a month or more to express itself. If an adverse effect appears, stopping does not clear it quickly; exposure decays over weeks. And any interaction that affects CYP3A4 acts on a compound that accumulates (inferred).
71. That profile is a poor match for a self-adjusted regimen of any kind, because the feedback loop between a change and its effect is longer than most people's attention to it (inferred).

### The cardiovascular arm, and the drug built to cancel it [people]
72. At 0.25 and 0.5 mg, blood pressure rose 1 to 3 mmHg and heart rate rose by up to 8 beats per minute [1] (verified). Discontinuation for adverse events in the obesity trials was 13% against 6% on placebo, with dry mouth and insomnia dose-dependent alongside headache, nausea, diarrhoea and constipation [1].
73. The clearest evidence that the developers took the cardiovascular effect seriously is that they built a second product around it: Tesomet, a fixed combination of tesofensine with the beta-blocker metoprolol, specifically intended to blunt the heart-related effects [3] (verified). A drug that needs a beta-blocker co-formulated into it is a drug with a known cardiovascular signal, by its own sponsor's design.
74. That programme ran in hypothalamic obesity and Prader-Willi syndrome, obtained orphan drug designation in 2021, and was paused in April 2022. The company stated the pause was entirely due to funding limitations and not related to safety or efficacy, alongside a restructuring that cut about 30% of staff [3] (verified, as the company's own account).
75. The psychiatric side has never been properly characterised, and the 2013 finding is the reason. Depression and stress were among the pre-existing conditions the inspectors found were not reliably recorded [2]. For a drug that raises dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin availability, mood and sleep effects are the expected risks, and the main trial's record of them was held to be incomplete (inferred).

### The regulatory record, which is a refusal and not a pending formality [people]
76. A Mexican phase 3 trial run by the licensee enrolled 372 patients and reported about 10% mean weight loss over 24 weeks, with more than half of participants losing over 10%, against a safety database of roughly 1,600 patients [4] (verified as the sponsor's account).
77. In November 2024 the regulator did not approve it. The sponsor's own statement said it appeared the decision had not been based on the full data package as submitted, and that the partner was in dialogue with the agency about a path forward [4] (verified). A resubmission followed in February 2025, and no approval has been found as of October 2026 (verified as of this review; the agency's own register could not be opened directly).
78. No approval exists in the US or EU, and no filing has been reported there. That is twenty-five years from first-in-human work to no approved product in any major market, across two therapeutic areas and two corporate owners (inferred).

### Where it sits in sport, and open questions [mixed]
79. Unlike most entries in this library, this one is named explicitly on the 2026 Prohibited List. It appears under non-specified stimulants, which is prohibited in competition rather than at all times [5] (verified). The non-specified classification matters: it removes the reduced-sanction route available for specified substances. A nine-day half-life also means in-competition prohibition is effectively a long out-of-competition constraint, since a dose taken weeks earlier is still present (inferred).
80. What is the real adverse event profile at 0.5 mg? The dataset a regulator said understated it is still the main published source.
81. Does the mood and sleep risk scale with duration? Insomnia was dose-dependent over 24 weeks, and nobody has characterised a longer course with complete psychiatric reporting.
82. Is it dopaminergic enough to matter? The two published transporter datasets disagree eightfold on the dopamine transporter, which is exactly the parameter that governs reinforcement.
83. Why has it failed to reach approval anywhere? The refusal in the one market that reviewed it has not been explained publicly beyond the sponsor's account, which is the weakest kind of source for a regulator's reasoning.
84. What happens on stopping, given the kinetics? Weight regain after discontinuation has not been characterised for this compound, and the slow washout makes the question unusual rather than routine.

# Thymalin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/thymalin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Timalin, Тималин, thymus polypeptide extract
2. Origin: Made by the body: calf thymus extract
3. Legal and approval status: Registered prescription immunostimulant in Russia (registration renewed June 2024) and sold in parts of the CIS; not FDA or EMA approved as of Oct 2026; not named on the WADA list.

## Summary
4. Thymalin is a 1974 extract of calf thymus peptides, the first of the Russian peptide bioregulators developed by Morozov and Khavinson. It is registered in Russia for immunodeficiency and severe infections, and is thought to rebalance T and B cells. Western users take it for immune aging, usually with Epitalon, but evidence comes almost entirely from the developers' own group.
5. Punch line: The first Russian bioregulator, from calf thymus. Short courses to rebuild T cells, often paired with Epitalon.
6. Used for: Immune recovery, infection, longevity courses

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Immunity: Restores T-cell numbers
8. Aging & senescence: Longevity courses, Russian data
9. Inflammatory signaling: Lower IL-6 and CRP reported
10. Tissue repair: Supports regeneration and blood making
11. Cancer biology (backed only by animal or user reports): Fewer tumours in old rodents

## How it works
12. Raises and rebalances T and B cells · T/B lymphocyte subsets · role Immunity
   Thymalin is a calf thymus extract of short peptides that acts on lymphocyte development. It raises and rebalances T and B cell subsets, the cells that run adaptive immunity. This is shown in Russian clinical use and in animals with the thymus removed, with no Western trials.
13. Boosts germ-eating cells · Phagocytosis · role Immunity
   It enhances phagocytosis, the process where white cells such as macrophages engulf and kill germs. Better phagocytosis means faster clearance of bacteria and debris. This comes from Russian animal and clinical studies of the extract.
14. Lowers inflammation markers in COVID-19 · IL-6, CRP, D-dimer · role Inflammatory signaling
   In a small single-blind Russian trial in severe COVID-19, patients on Thymalin showed falls in IL-6, CRP and D-dimer, markers of inflammation and clotting. Lymphocytes recovered faster and fewer died. It is one small trial and needs independent repeat.
15. Nudges blood stem cells toward T cells · Haematopoietic stem cell differentiation · role Tissue repair
   In culture, the extract pushes haematopoietic stem cells, the blood-forming stem cells, toward the thymocyte line that becomes T cells. That could explain T-cell recovery after thymectomy or radiation in animals. It is cell data, and the active peptides in the mix are not defined.
16. Claimed to slow immune aging · Thymic involution, claimed · role Aging & senescence
   With age the thymus shrinks and T-cell output falls, a process called thymic involution. Thymalin is claimed to slow this. The support is Khavinson's non-randomised elderly cohorts reporting lower mortality, which have major design flaws, so this remains a claim.
17. Mechanism overview: Thymalin is a lyophilised complex of low-molecular-weight peptides acid-extracted from calf thymus, standardised as 10 mg of thymus polypeptides per vial. Its best-studied pieces are the dipeptides Glu-Trp (EW, sold as Thymogen) and Lys-Glu (KE, Vilon). It raises and rebalances T and B lymphocyte subsets, enhances phagocytosis, restores T-cell counts in thymectomised animals, and in culture pushes haematopoietic stem cells toward the thymocyte line. The Khavinson group proposes its short peptides enter the nucleus and tune gene expression; this is not independently confirmed.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
18. Typical: 5–20 mg (adults) · once daily · cycle 3–10 days, 30–100 mg per course, repeat after 1–6 months · route IM (verified)
19. Half-life: Unknown
20. Most people take: Russian label: 5–20 mg IM daily for 3–10 days (prevention 5–10 mg for 3–5 days); children 1–5 mg by age. Community longevity course 10 mg IM daily for 10 days, 1–2×/yr, often with Epitalon. Sub-Q use reported.

## What people report
21. Taken in 10-day longevity courses, often with Epitalon; few detailed first-hand reports; injection-site soreness and rare allergy noted.
22. Liked / worked: Russian reports of T-cell recovery
23. Liked / worked: Fewer COVID-19 hospital deaths in one small trial
24. Liked / worked: Fewer tumours, longer life in rodents
25. What worked: Russian reports of T-cell recovery, and in severe COVID-19 hospital deaths of 19.4% vs 40.9% on placebo (n=80); fewer tumours and longer life in rodents.
26. Went wrong / did not work: No Western or independent trials
27. Went wrong / did not work: Elderly mortality data observational
28. Went wrong / did not work: Conflicting COVID-19 figures across paper versions
29. What went wrong: Evidence comes almost entirely from the developers' own group; elderly mortality claims are observational; no independent replication.
30. Most reported: 10-day courses with Epitalon
31. Most reported: Injection-site soreness
32. Most reported: Rare allergy (bovine protein)
33. Most reported: Few detailed first-hand reports

## What has been tested
34. Immunity: Lymphocyte recovery in severe COVID-19 (human)
35. Aging & senescence: Mortality in elderly cohorts (human)
36. Immunity: T-cell restoration after thymectomy or radiation (animal)
37. Cancer biology: Spontaneous tumours and lifespan (animal)
38. Tissue repair: Blood stem cell differentiation (cell)
39. Decades of Russian clinical use and studies, including a small randomised single-blind trial in severe COVID-19 and non-randomised elderly cohorts; no Western trials.
40. What it helps: Russia registers it for immunodeficiency, severe infections, poor regeneration and immune suppression after chemotherapy or radiation. A small randomised single-blind Russian trial in severe COVID-19 reported faster lymphocyte recovery and fewer deaths, and Khavinson's elderly cohorts claim lower mortality with Thymalin and Epitalon courses. Western users take it in short courses for immune aging and longevity, usually with Epitalon. Reported side effects are injection-site reactions and rare allergy.
41. Trial: none · immune aging, COVID 19 · Khavinson group. Russian studies, including a 2020 COVID report, were not registered in any international registry; Russian registry status unverifiable. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
42. Transplant recipients on anti-rejection drugs: A thymus extract that stimulates T cells, which works against anti-rejection drugs. (inferred)
43. People with beef protein allergy: It is extracted from calf thymus, so it carries beef protein. (reported)

## Synergies (paired with)
44. Epitalon: Epitalon is claimed to act on telomerase and the pineal gland, while Thymalin targets the aging immune system. They are the classic Khavinson longevity course, and the 2003 elderly cohorts tested them alone and together. Those cohorts are small and flawed, so this is not solid trial data.
45. Thymosin Alpha-1: Thymosin Alpha-1 is a defined thymic peptide that matures T cells, primes dendritic cells and has human hepatitis B data. Thymalin is a crude thymus extract aimed at the same immune recovery. People pair them for infection and immune aging, but the pair has not been tested together.
46. Thymogen: Thymogen is the Glu-Trp dipeptide, one of the named candidate actives inside Thymalin. Using both doubles up on the same Khavinson immune signal from a defined piece and the whole extract. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
47. Vilon: Vilon is the Lys-Glu dipeptide, another candidate active in Thymalin, claimed to boost thymus and spleen cell growth. People add it to the extract for a fuller immune and longevity course. Both rest on Khavinson group data, and the pair has not been tested together.
48. Thymulin: Thymulin is a zinc-dependent thymic hormone that matures T cells and lowers inflammatory cytokines in models. Thymalin covers broader lymphocyte rebalancing. People pair them to restore thymic signalling from two angles, but the pair has never been tested together.

## Where it comes from
49. Morozov and Khavinson's 1974 extract of calf thymus peptides, the first drug of the Russian 'peptide bioregulator' class.
50. First studied for: Restoring immunity in Soviet patients with immunodeficiency, infection, burns and radiation injury.
51. Name story: Calf-thymus extract isolated by Morozov and Khavinson in 1974 at the Leningrad Military Medical Academy, registered in the USSR in 1982, and the template for the bioregulator line. Not to be confused with thymulin, a single defined nonapeptide. [S2] (verified)
52. 1974: Morozov and Khavinson isolate small peptides from calf thymus
53. 1980s: Enters Soviet clinical use as an immunostimulant (reported)
54. 2002–2003: Khavinson elderly cohorts claim lower mortality with Thymalin and Epitalon
55. 2021: Small Russian COVID-19 trial reports halved hospital deaths
56. June 2024: Russian registration renewed, indefinite validity

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What is actually in the vial, and why that is the whole problem [lab]
57. Everything else in this library is a defined molecule with a sequence. This is not. It is an acid extract of calf thymus, standardised only by total weight of low-molecular-weight peptides per vial, not by any identified active component (verified as the product's own basis of standardisation).
58. That has three consequences worth stating plainly. There is no sequence to test a batch against, so identity testing in the usual sense cannot be done; the content is a mixture whose composition can shift with the source tissue and the extraction run; and the named candidate actives, the dipeptides Glu-Trp and Lys-Glu, are sold as separate products in their own right, which means the extract's effects cannot be attributed to them without measuring them (inferred).
59. It is also a bovine tissue product given by injection. Animal-derived injectables carry a category of risk that synthetic peptides do not, around viral and transmissible agent clearance, and nothing in the accessible record describes what clearance steps the extraction includes (verified as absent from sources reachable for this review). This is the single biggest gap between how the product is discussed and how any regulator outside its home market would assess it.

### The longevity study, read line by line [people]
60. The claim that this extract extends human life rests on one 2003 paper reporting two cohorts, 266 people in total, run at institutes in St Petersburg and Kiev [1]. It is worth reading closely, because it is cited far more often than it is examined.
61. In the St Petersburg arm, 94 women aged 66 to 94 in a war veterans' home were allocated by what the paper calls stratification randomisation to placebo, Thymalin, Epithalamin, or both, described as double-blind, with 10 mg intramuscularly daily for 10 days, repeated in a second year. Six-year mortality was 81.8% in the control group of 22, against 41.7% on Thymalin, 45.8% on Epithalamin, 33.3% on both, and 20.0% in a separate 20-person group dosed annually for six years [1] (verified as reported).
62. In the Kiev arm, 152 people were allocated to placebo, Thymalin or Epithalamin, with eight-year mortality of 13.6%, 6.6% and 8.5% in groups of 48, 58 and 46 [1] (verified as reported).
63. Now the arithmetic that should stop a reader. The control group in one cohort died at 81.8% over six years; the control group in the other died at 13.6% over eight. Those are not the same kind of population, and no analysis reconciles them. The treatment effect in the first cohort rests on a control arm of 22 people in a care home, where an 82% six-year mortality means a handful of deaths either way moves the percentage by double digits (inferred).
64. What the paper does not report is as important as what it does: no causes of death, no dropouts or loss to follow-up, no confidence intervals, no mapping of the six listed statistical tests to individual results, no group sizes for the 94 women, no placebo composition, no allocation concealment, no blinding description for the Kiev arm, and no funding or conflict statement [1] (verified as absent). Its own abstract and tables disagree about whether the observation ran six or eight years and whether treatment ran two or three [1].
65. None of that makes the result false. It makes it uncheckable, which is a different thing, and it is why this paper has not moved practice outside the research tradition that produced it.

### The COVID-19 trial, which is the best-designed study in the file [people]
66. A 2021 trial at a hospital in Chita, Russia, is genuinely a controlled trial and should be given its due. Eighty adults with PCR-confirmed critical COVID-19 were randomised single-blind to standard care plus 10 mg of Thymalin intramuscularly daily for 10 days, or standard care plus 2 mL of saline on the same schedule [2] (verified).
67. In-hospital mortality was 18 of 44 (40.9%) in the control arm against 7 of 36 (19.4%) on drug, p=0.039, and time from randomisation to death differed, 7.22 against 11.2 days, p=0.005 [2] (verified).
68. That is a real randomised result with a placebo arm, and it is the strongest single piece of evidence this compound has. Its limits are structural rather than suspicious: a single centre, single-blind rather than double, 80 patients total, and a mortality difference that turns on 11 deaths. In critical COVID-19 in 2020 and 2021, single-centre trials of immunomodulators repeatedly produced large effects that larger trials did not reproduce, which is the base rate this result sits inside (inferred).
69. A second 2021 report in a Russian-language clinical journal compared 38 treated patients with 50 controls and described large fold-changes in interleukin-6, lymphocyte and CD4 counts and in antibody levels at day 200. It does not describe randomisation or blinding, does not state the dose, and reports no absolute values or statistical tests in the accessible text [3] (verified as reported, with those omissions).

### Who produced the evidence [mixed]
70. This is the part a reader cannot skip. The extract was isolated in 1974 by Morozov and Khavinson; the longevity paper is by Khavinson and Morozov; the COVID-19 trial lists Khavinson among its authors alongside the institute he heads; and the broader bioregulator theory the results are interpreted through is his [1,2] (verified). The COVID-19 trial declares no conflicts of interest [2], which is formally accurate for salary and equity but sits oddly with an author's five-decade authorship of the compound itself (inferred).
71. No independent group outside that network was found to have replicated either the mortality findings or the proposed mechanism in this review. The claim that these short peptides enter the nucleus and tune gene expression is the group's own proposal and has not been independently confirmed (verified as the state of the record found).
72. That is not an accusation of bad faith. It is the same structural problem BPC-157 has: a founding group dominating the literature on its own discovery, so that reading many papers is not the same as reading many independent assessments.

### What the body does with it, and safety [mixed]
73. There is no pharmacokinetic data: no half-life, no bioavailability, no distribution, in any species (verified as absent). For a mixture rather than a molecule, conventional pharmacokinetics is not even well defined, since there is no single analyte to measure (inferred).
74. On safety, the 2003 paper states that no allergic or other side effects were seen, but that is a general claim about decades of use rather than a reported adverse-event analysis from the trials, and the paper reports no trial-specific adverse events at all [1] (verified). The COVID-19 trial's published account focuses on efficacy and immune markers [2].
75. What is absent: no genotoxicity, no carcinogenicity, no reproductive toxicology, and no long-term controlled safety data accessible in this review. The direction of the intended effect, stimulating lymphocyte populations, raises the obvious questions about autoimmunity and about use in people with lymphoproliferative disease, and neither has been studied (inferred).
76. Decades of use in one health system is a form of evidence, and it is the weakest form, because spontaneous reporting from that era and that market is not a surveillance system anyone can audit (inferred).

### Where the law stands, and open questions [mixed]
77. It is a registered prescription immunostimulant in Russia, with registration renewed in June 2024, and is sold in parts of the former Soviet sphere (verified as stated in the card's label sourcing). It is not approved by the FDA or EMA, has not been nominated for or reviewed under the US compounding lists, and is not named on the 2026 WADA Prohibited List, which leaves it in the catch-all class for substances without approval for human therapeutic use in the relevant jurisdictions, prohibited at all times [4] (inferred from the class wording, complicated by the fact that it does hold approval in one country).
78. An approval in one jurisdiction based on a national dossier is not interchangeable with approval elsewhere, particularly for an animal-derived injectable, where tissue sourcing and viral clearance documentation are the first thing other regulators ask for (inferred).
79. What is the active component? Until that is identified and measured, every mechanistic claim is about a mixture, and no batch can be compared with another.
80. Does the COVID-19 mortality result replicate? It is the one finding here that a multicentre trial could confirm or refute, and nobody has tried.
81. Can the 2003 mortality claim be reconstructed? With no causes of death, no dropouts and two control arms that behaved six-fold differently, probably not from the published record.
82. What is in the extract that is not peptide? For a tissue extract given by injection, this is a manufacturing question with a safety answer, and the accessible record does not contain it.
83. Does stimulating T-cell populations in older people carry a cost? The theory says it restores; nothing tests whether it also drives autoimmunity or affects malignancy risk.

# Lipo-C
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/lipo-c
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Lipo-C injection, lipotropic injection with carnitine, MIC + L-Carnitine, Lipo-C Fat Blaster, LC526
2. Origin: Blend: amino acids + carnitine + B vitamins (lipotropic injection)
3. Legal and approval status: US: not FDA-approved; made by 503A compounding pharmacies on prescription (levocarnitine alone is approved only for carnitine deficiency). Grey-market 'LC' vials are sold for research only. WADA: not prohibited, but IV infusions over 100 mL per 12 hours are.

## Summary
4. Lipo-C is a compounded injection of methionine, inositol and choline (the MIC trio) plus L-carnitine and B vitamins. It is used in weight-loss clinics to support fat metabolism, with carnitine carrying fat into mitochondria and choline helping the liver export fat. Only the individual parts have trial data, mainly modest weight loss from oral carnitine. Lipo-C itself has no trial, and any fat loss is usually credited to diet.
5. Punch line: The weight-loss clinic shot. MIC trio, carnitine and B vitamins push fat from the liver into mitochondria.
6. Used for: Fat loss support and training energy, usually with a diet or GLP-1

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Fat metabolism: Carnitine carries fat into mitochondria
8. Cellular energy: B vitamins and carnitine for fuel use
9. Organ function: Choline and methionine help the liver export fat
10. Muscle & performance: Used for training energy

## How it works
11. Carries fat into mitochondria to be burned · Carnitine shuttle, CPT1 · role Fat metabolism
   L-carnitine moves long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane through CPT1, the gate enzyme of the carnitine shuttle. Inside, they are burned by beta-oxidation. Oral carnitine trials in people show a small extra weight loss; injected Lipo-C has no trial.
12. Lets the liver package and export fat · Choline → phosphatidylcholine, VLDL · role Organ function
   Choline is turned into phosphatidylcholine, which the liver needs to wrap fat into VLDL particles and send it out to the blood. Choline deficiency causes fatty liver in animals and people. Extra choline helps when intake is low, not clearly when it is adequate.
13. Methyl donor for liver fat handling · Methionine → SAM · role Organ function
   Methionine is converted to SAM, the body's main methyl donor. SAM supplies methyl groups to make phosphatidylcholine by a second route and for other liver reactions. Lipotropic effects of methionine are shown mostly in rodents fed deficient diets.
14. Helps cells use fuel · Thiamine and pantothenate (B1, B5) as coenzymes · role Cellular energy
   Thiamine (B1) is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, which feeds sugar into the energy cycle, and pantothenate (B5) builds coenzyme A, which carries fats and sugars into it. Both are essential, but extra amounts help mainly when someone is deficient.
15. Mechanism overview: Lipotropic agents promote fat export from the liver. Choline is the precursor of phosphatidylcholine, required for VLDL assembly; deficiency causes fatty liver. Methionine feeds S-adenosylmethionine, which supplies methyl groups including for phosphatidylethanolamine to phosphatidylcholine conversion. Inositol participates in phosphoinositide signalling and lipid handling. L-carnitine shuttles long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane via CPT1/CPT2 for beta-oxidation; muscle uptake depends on insulin-stimulated OCTN2 transport. Thiamine and pantothenate (dexpanthenol) are cofactors for pyruvate dehydrogenase and coenzyme A. The combination is rational on paper; no controlled trial has measured its effect on fat mass.

## What is inside the blend
16. Methionine: 15 mg per mL · Methyl donor for liver fat handling
17. Inositol: 50 mg per mL · Lipid signalling; best evidence in PCOS
18. Choline chloride: 50 mg per mL · Lets the liver export fat
19. L-Carnitine: 50 mg per mL · Carries fat into mitochondria
20. Thiamine (B1): 15 mg per mL · Coenzyme for burning carbs
21. Dexpanthenol (B5): 5 mg per mL · Coenzyme A building block
22. Most common ratio: Methionine 15 · Choline chloride 50 · L-Carnitine 50 · Dexpanthenol 5 = 120 mg/mL (5 of 11 formulas (1 pharmacy + 4 research shops 'LC120'))
23. Other ratio seen: Methionine 15 · Inositol 50 · Choline 50 · L-Carnitine 50 · Thiamine 15 · Dexpanthenol 5 = 185 mg/mL (1 (dosing guide site, no seller))
24. Other ratio seen: Methionine 25 · Inositol 50 · Choline 50 · B6 25 · B5 25 · B12 1 · Arginine 15 · L-Carnitine 15 (+lidocaine) = ~206 mg/mL (1 pharmacy)
25. Other ratio seen: Methionine 12.4 · Inositol 25 · Choline 25 · B1 50 · B2 5 · B6 2 · L-Carnitine 125 = ~244 mg/mL (1 pharmacy)
26. Other ratio seen: Methionine 25 · Inositol 50 · Choline 50 · L-Carnitine 25 · B1 5 · B6 2 · B12 1 = ~158 mg/mL (1 clinic)
27. Other ratio seen: L-Carnitine 300 · Methionine 25 · Choline 50 · Inositol 50 · B6 50 · NADH 50 · B12 1 (LC526) = 526 mg/mL (2 listings)
28. Version Common pharmacy: Methionine 15 · Inositol 50 · Choline 50 · L-Carnitine 50 · Thiamine 15 · Dexpanthenol 5 = 185 mg/mL
29. Version Short pharmacy formula (LC120): Methionine 15 · Choline 50 · L-Carnitine 50 · Dexpanthenol 5 = 120 mg/mL
30. Version Fat Blaster (LC526): L-Carnitine 300 · Methionine 25 · Choline 50 · Inositol 50 · B6 50 · NADH 50 · B12 1 = 526 mg/mL
31. Why L-Carnitine is in it: The fat-burning shuttle; the only part with weight-loss trials
32. Why Choline is in it: Liver fat export
33. Why Methionine is in it: Methyl groups for the liver
34. Why Inositol is in it: Insulin and lipid signalling
35. Why B1, B5 is in it: Coenzymes for fuel use
36. Mixing chemistry: Ready-made liquid in a multi-dose vial, not a freeze-dried powder.
37. Mixing chemistry: Some versions add lidocaine, B6 or B12; check your exact formula.
38. Mixing chemistry: Protect from light; vitamins in the mix are light-sensitive.
39. Mixing chemistry: Pharmacy beyond-use date is 28 days once compounded; don't use cloudy or discoloured liquid.
40. Mixing chemistry: Formulas are not interchangeable: mg per mL ranges from 120 to 526.
41. Self-mixing: Not mixed by the user; it comes as a ready solution. Combining it with B12 or other shots in one syringe is common, but untested.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
42. Typical: 1 mL · 1–3× weekly · cycle 12 weeks on, 2 off · route IM (Sub-Q also used) (reported)
43. Half-life: per component
44. Most people take: 1 mL by intramuscular injection once or twice a week is the common clinic dose; community tiers go to three times a week or daily. One pharmacy caps it at 2 mL twice a week, short term.

## What people report
45. 1 mL IM once to three times a week, often 12 weeks on and 2 off. Reports: injection sting and nodules (worse in the belly), a fishy body smell from choline, nausea, more trips to the toilet. Stronger grey-market LC526 adds 300 mg carnitine, NADH, B6 and B12 per mL, dosed 1 mL weekly.
46. Liked / worked: Carnitine: ~1 kg extra loss in oral trials
47. Liked / worked: Choline helps clear liver fat
48. Liked / worked: Clinics report more training energy
49. What worked: Carnitine is the best-supported part, with a modest average weight loss in oral trials. Clinics report more energy in training and support during a diet; most guides say it adds little without a calorie deficit.
50. Went wrong / did not work: No trial of the blend itself
51. Went wrong / did not work: Little effect without a calorie deficit
52. Went wrong / did not work: Nodules and sting, worse in the belly
53. What went wrong: No randomised trial of Lipo-C itself. Weight change in clinics is usually credited to diet and exercise. Reviews rate evidence as weak; carnitine uptake into muscle needs insulin, so an injection alone may not load muscle.
54. Most reported: 1 mL IM, 1 to 3× a week
55. Most reported: Fishy smell from choline
56. Most reported: Nausea, more urination
57. Most reported: 12 weeks on, 2 off

## What has been tested
58. Fat metabolism: Oral carnitine, weight loss meta-analyses (human)
59. Organ function: Choline and liver fat (human)
60. Fat metabolism: Lipo-C as a whole (none)
61. The blend has never been tested as a whole. Component evidence: oral L-carnitine meta-analyses show about 1.1 to 1.3 kg extra weight loss; choline helps clear liver fat (rodents, one small human trial); methionine and inositol lipotropic effects are mostly rodent.
62. What it helps: Component evidence only. Oral carnitine averages about 1 kg extra weight loss across trials; choline supports liver fat clearance. Lipo-C itself has no trial, and guides agree any fat loss depends mostly on diet.

## Who shouldn't take it
63. People with homocystinuria or high homocysteine: Methionine is the direct precursor of homocysteine. (inferred)
64. People on levothyroxine or with hypothyroidism: Carnitine blocks thyroid hormone entry into cells. (reported)
65. People with Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy: Cyanocobalamin can speed optic nerve damage. (verified)
66. People with seizure disorders: The Carnitor label reports seizures in people with and without prior seizures. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
67. MIC + B12: MIC + B12 overlaps heavily with Lipo-C, sharing choline and methionine, and adds inositol and B12. People rotate or combine them during diets. Neither has a weight loss trial, and the pair has not been tested together.
68. L-Carnitine: Standalone L-carnitine raises the carnitine share above what Lipo-C contains. People add it for training energy and fat burning. Oral carnitine has small weight loss effects in trials; the injected pair has not been tested.
69. Vitamin B12: Vitamin B12 adds a cofactor for methionine recycling and nerve health, which Lipo-C lacks. Clinics add it for energy during a diet. B12 clearly helps people who are deficient; the pairing has not been tested.
70. Semaglutide: Semaglutide drives weight loss by cutting appetite through the GLP-1 receptor, with large human trials. Lipo-C is added for fat handling and energy while eating less. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
71. Tirzepatide: Tirzepatide does the heavy lifting on appetite and weight through GIP and GLP-1 receptors, with large human trials. Lipo-C is added for fat metabolism and energy during the deficit. The pair has not been tested together.
72. Retatrutide: Retatrutide cuts appetite and raises energy use through three receptors, with large human trials. Users add Lipo-C as a fuel and liver support layer during weight loss. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
73. AOD-9604: AOD-9604 is a growth hormone fragment aimed at fat breakdown, with rodent data only. Users stack it with Lipo-C for fat loss. The pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
74. A compounded 'lipotropic' injection: methionine, inositol and choline (the MIC trio) plus L-carnitine and B vitamins. The 'C' is for carnitine. A typical pharmacy formula per mL is methionine 15, inositol 50, choline chloride 50, L-carnitine 50, thiamine 15 and dexpanthenol 5 mg.
75. First studied for: Grew out of US weight-loss clinics and med spas in the 2000s and 2010s as a carnitine-boosted version of MIC shots; now also sold grey-market in stronger 'LC' versions.
76. Name story: 'Lipo' from lipotropic, Greek for fat-moving; 'C' for carnitine, the part that sets it apart from plain MIC or Lipo-B (B12) shots. [S1] (inferred)
77. 1950s: Carnitine's role in fat transport worked out (inferred date)
78. 2000s: Lipotropic MIC shots spread through US weight-loss clinics (inferred)
79. 2010s: Carnitine-boosted Lipo-C formulas added (inferred)
80. 2016: Meta-analysis: oral carnitine ~1.3 kg extra weight loss
81. Today: Compounded Lipo-C and grey-market LC120, LC216, LC526

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What "never tested as a blend" means here, in the maker's own words [mixed]
82. Most blends in this library have to be assessed from outside. This one is unusual: a licensed compounding pharmacy publishes its own product page, and that page says the quiet part out loud. The evidence for the product is described as largely extrapolated from the individual components' pharmacology rather than from randomised trials of the combination; safety and efficacy for the formulation have not been evaluated by the FDA; and there is no single approved dosing schedule [1] (verified).
83. That is the honest baseline. Three separate things have not been studied: whether the components do anything together that they do not do apart, whether the mixture is stable and compatible as formulated beyond its dating, and what the combination's adverse-event profile is as opposed to each ingredient's.
84. The deeper problem specific to this product is that the name is not a formula. Published recipes under this label run from about 120 to 526 mg per mL, with different components and different ratios. A study of one would not describe another. There is no plausible reading in which a trial of this product could exist, because there is no single product to trial (inferred).

### The components do not have comparable evidence, and the biggest one has the least [people]
85. L-carnitine is the only component with weight-loss trials, and they are oral. A 2016 meta-analysis in a peer-reviewed obesity journal pooled nine randomised trials judged methodologically adequate, totalling 911 adults, and found a mean difference of minus 1.33 kg (95% CI minus 2.09 to minus 0.57) and minus 0.47 kg/m2 of BMI (95% CI minus 0.88 to minus 0.05) [2] (verified).
86. Two features of that result are usually dropped. The effect is about one and a third kilograms, which is small, and meta-regression found it diminished significantly with longer supplementation, p=0.002 [2] (verified). So the best-evidenced ingredient has a small effect that fades, measured by mouth at doses typically far above what a millilitre of this blend delivers.
87. Choline deficiency causes fatty liver, and choline is genuinely required to assemble the particles the liver uses to export fat; methionine genuinely supplies methyl groups through S-adenosylmethionine; thiamine and pantothenate are genuinely coenzymes for fuel use. All of that is real biochemistry and none of it is evidence of fat loss in people who are not deficient. No trial of injected choline, methionine, inositol or dexpanthenol for fat loss was found in this review (verified as absent).
88. Inositol's best human evidence sits in polycystic ovary syndrome, not obesity, and it is oral. It is also the component most often absent from the formula altogether, including from the four-part pharmacy version [1] (verified).

### The mechanism argument has a hole where the injection goes [mixed]
89. Carnitine's job is to carry long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane. The limiting step for that in muscle is not how much carnitine is in the blood, it is how much gets into the muscle cell, which depends on the OCTN2 transporter and is stimulated by insulin. Raising plasma carnitine does not reliably raise muscle carnitine, which is why oral loading studies have generally needed carbohydrate co-ingestion to move muscle content at all (inferred from the transport biology).
90. The same logic applies to the liver components. Choline and methionine support fat export in someone short of them. In someone whose intake is adequate, adding more does not create a shortage to correct. The rationale is a deficiency-repletion argument being applied to people who have not been shown to be deficient (inferred).
91. Nothing here contradicts the biochemistry on the card. The gap is between "this molecule is required for fat oxidation" and "adding this molecule increases fat oxidation," and no human study of this product has crossed it.

### The TMAO question, and the one argument that favours injection [mixed]
92. The two largest components by mass in most versions, carnitine and choline, are also the two best-characterised dietary precursors of trimethylamine N-oxide, a metabolite associated with cardiovascular disease. This is worth laying out properly because it is the strongest safety-adjacent argument in the file and it cuts in an unexpected direction.
93. In a 2013 Nature Medicine study, gut bacteria converted dietary carnitine to trimethylamine and then TMAO: a week of oral antibiotics made labelled TMAO nearly undetectable in five omnivores, with production returning after at least three weeks off; vegans and vegetarians had much lower fasting TMAO and a markedly reduced capacity to produce it after a carnitine challenge; mice on 1.3% carnitine in drinking water had roughly double the aortic plaque area with plasma TMAO around 114 micromolar against 17, and antibiotics blocked the effect [3] (verified, in people and animals). In a clinical cohort of 2,595 patients undergoing cardiac evaluation, high carnitine predicted events after adjustment for traditional risk factors, but the association disappeared once TMAO was accounted for [3] (verified).
94. The pivotal detail for an injection is that all those challenges were oral, and the gut microbiota are the required step. The authors themselves note that parenteral administration would bypass the microbiota, and did not test it [3] (verified as their inference, not their result).
95. So the fair reading is: the TMAO pathway is a real and well-evidenced concern for swallowed carnitine and choline, and an injected route plausibly sidesteps the main generating step. That is an argument for the route, and it is untested. The product page's listing of transient fishy body odour attributed to trimethylamine [1] suggests the pathway is not entirely bypassed in practice (inferred).

### Product reality, and the parts of the label worth reading [lab]
96. This is a ready-made aqueous solution in a multi-dose vial, not a lyophilised powder, which changes the handling questions entirely. The published four-part pharmacy formula is methionine 15, choline chloride 50, L-carnitine 50 and dexpanthenol 5 mg per mL in water for injection, supplied in 10 and 30 mL multi-dose vials, for intramuscular use, with a beyond-use date of 28 days from compounding under the relevant sterile compounding standard [1] (verified).
97. Twenty-eight days is a formulation and sterility limit on a multi-dose vial, not a suggestion. Storage is specified as either room temperature or refrigerated depending on the exact formulation, protected from light in the original carton, not frozen, not shaken vigorously, and inspected for particulates or discolouration before use [1] (verified). The B vitamins in versions that contain them are light-sensitive, which is why the carton matters.
98. The contraindication list is more specific than the product's reputation suggests, and one entry is absolute: inborn errors of sulfur amino acid metabolism such as homocystinuria. Also listed are hypersensitivity to any component and severe hepatic failure. Cautions cover advanced kidney impairment or dialysis because of carnitine accumulation, active peptic ulcer disease, levodopa use, severe heart failure or arrhythmia, and pregnancy and breastfeeding [1] (verified).
99. The interaction list is the part most likely to be missed. Carnitine may potentiate warfarin, with reports of raised INR. Levodopa-carbidopa effect may be reduced. Cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil warrant monitoring for cramping or slow heart rate. Cysteine or N-acetylcysteine may alter paracetamol metabolism [1] (verified).
100. Documented adverse effects are mostly local: injection-site pain, redness and warmth, with nausea and loose stools in a minority resolving within a day or two, and the transient fishy odour. Uncommon but serious entries are immediate hypersensitivity including anaphylaxis, and delayed eosinophilic myositis, with systemic hypersensitivity cited below 0.1% in one retrospective series [1] (verified as reported by the pharmacy).
101. One honest note about the source: that page cites several commercial clinic blogs alongside its pharmacology, and two of its regulatory citations use placeholder identifiers [1] (verified). It is the best single document available for this product and it is not a peer-reviewed one.

### Where the law stands, and open questions [mixed]
102. In the US this is a 503A compounded preparation, made for an individual patient on prescription, explicitly not FDA-approved and not evaluated by the agency for safety or efficacy [1] (verified). That is a different legal position from the injectable peptides elsewhere in this library: the components are established substances with their own histories, and levocarnitine itself is approved, but only for carnitine deficiency. Research-labelled vials sold under the same name sit outside the pharmacy framework entirely.
103. In sport, no component is named on the 2026 Prohibited List. The applicable rule is the method prohibition on intravenous infusions totalling more than 100 mL per 12 hours outside hospital care, which does not bite on a one-millilitre intramuscular injection [4] (verified).
104. Does the combination do anything the components do not? The maker says this has not been tested, which makes the premise of the product unexamined rather than disputed [1].
105. Does injected carnitine reach muscle? Plasma carnitine and muscle carnitine are different things, and the transporter step is the one nobody has measured for this route.
106. Does the injected route genuinely avoid the TMAO pathway? The gut step is required for the oral effect and plausibly bypassed, but the fishy-odour reports suggest trimethylamine still appears, and nobody has measured TMAO after an injection [1,3].
107. What does a repeated methionine load do to homocysteine? Methionine is the direct precursor, and no study of this product has measured it.
108. Which formula is a given vial? Published versions range from 120 to 526 mg per mL with different components, so every number in circulation, including dose conventions, is formula-specific and usually unlabelled as such.
