# NAD+
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/nadplus
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: nad coenzyme, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, DPN+, diphosphopyridine nucleotide, coenzyme I, cozymase, NADH (reduced form)
2. Origin: Not a peptide
3. Legal and approval status: Sold as a supplement/compounded infusion; not an approved drug for anti-aging.

## Summary
4. NAD+ is a coenzyme found in every cell, central to energy metabolism and to the sirtuin and PARP repair enzymes; it is not a peptide. People take it by infusion or injection to raise cellular NAD for energy, focus and recovery, since levels fall with age. Precursor trials raise NAD safely, but clear anti-aging outcomes in humans are unproven, and fast infusions often cause flushing and chest pressure.
5. Punch line: The energy coenzyme in every cell, falling with age. Infused or injected for focus; fast drips cause flushing.
6. Used for: Energy, recovery, healthy aging

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Cellular energy: Carries electrons that make cell energy
8. DNA & telomeres: Fuel for DNA repair enzymes
9. Cognition: Users report clearer thinking
10. Drive & mental stamina: Users report more drive
11. Reward & urges (backed only by animal or user reports): Studied in addiction clinics
12. Aging & senescence (backed only by animal or user reports): Levels fall with age

## How it works
13. Carries electrons to make cell energy · Redox coenzyme · role Cellular energy
   NAD+ is a redox coenzyme. In glycolysis and the Krebs cycle it accepts electrons to become NADH, which feeds complex I of the mitochondrial chain to make ATP. This role is settled biochemistry. Whether injected or infused NAD+ raises levels inside human cells has not been shown.
14. Fuels DNA repair enzymes · PARPs · role DNA & telomeres
   PARP enzymes burn NAD+ as fuel when they repair broken DNA, tagging damaged sites so repair proteins gather there. Heavy DNA damage can drain a cell's NAD+ supply this way. The rationale for supplementing is to keep this repair work fed, but no human trial has shown that outcome.
15. Feeds the sirtuin enzymes · Sirtuins · role Aging & senescence
   Sirtuins are enzymes that use NAD+ to strip acetyl groups from proteins, which changes how genes and metabolism are regulated. Their activity depends on NAD+ supply, which is the basis of the anti-aging case. Precursor trials raise blood NAD in people, but clear functional benefits have not followed.
16. Levels fall with age and stress · CD38 consumption · role Aging & senescence
   Tissue NAD+ falls with age, partly because CD38, an enzyme on immune and other cells, breaks it down more as inflammation rises. The one human infusion study found NAD+ cleared from blood almost as fast as it went in. Levels in blood do not show what happens inside tissues.
17. Supports neuron energy and resilience · Neuronal NAD+ pools · role Cognition
   Neurons have high energy needs and depend on steady NAD+ for both ATP production and stress repair. Animal and cell work links falling neuronal NAD+ to weaker resilience. Human users report better focus, but no human study has measured brain NAD+ after direct NAD+ dosing.
18. Mechanism overview: NAD+ is a coenzyme that carries electrons. In glycolysis and the Krebs cycle it accepts electrons to become NADH, which feeds complex I of the mitochondrial chain to make ATP. It is also consumed as a substrate: PARP enzymes burn it to repair DNA, sirtuins use it to strip acetyl groups from proteins, and CD38 breaks it down, increasingly with age and inflammation. Tissue levels decline with age, so the rationale is to restore supply for energy and repair. Whether intact NAD+ enters cells directly, or is first broken into precursors, is still debated.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
19. Typical: 50–100 mg · 2–3× weekly · cycle 4-8 weeks on, 4 weeks off · route Sub-Q, IM (reported)
20. Half-life: ~3-4 hours
21. Most people take: 50-100mg 2-3x/week SC or IM · 4-8 weeks on, 4 weeks off. Some people do continuous lower doses.
22. Common: 50–100 mg · 2–3× weekly · 8–12 wk · Sub-Q · for home injectors [S1] [S2] (reported)
23. IV loading: 250–500 mg · 4–5 sessions over 2 wk, then monthly · 2 wk load · IV · for clinic drip clients [S1] [S3] (reported)
24. High IV: 500–1000 mg · weekly ×4, then monthly · ongoing · IV · for high-dose clinic protocols [S1] [S3] (reported)

## What people report
25. IV and SC; the infusion is often described as uncomfortable (flushing, chest pressure) if run fast. Reported for energy, focus and recovery.
26. Liked / worked: Precursors reliably raise NAD
27. Liked / worked: Precursors safe in trials
28. What worked: Precursor trials reliably raise NAD levels and are safe; users report energy and mental clarity.
29. Went wrong / did not work: Anti-aging outcomes unproven in humans
30. Went wrong / did not work: Direct NAD cell entry debated
31. Went wrong / did not work: Infusion thinly studied
32. What went wrong: Whether raised NAD delivers the hoped-for anti-aging and performance outcomes is unproven in humans; direct NAD's cell entry is debated.
33. Most reported: Energy, focus and recovery
34. Most reported: Fast IV: flushing and chest pressure

## What has been tested
35. Aging & senescence: NR and NMN raise blood NAD (trial)
36. Cellular energy: Direct NAD infusion (users)
37. NAD itself is poorly cell-permeable, so most rigorous human trials use the precursors NR and NMN, which reliably raise blood NAD. Direct NAD infusion is widely used but thinly studied.
38. What it helps: Precursor trials with NR and NMN reliably raise blood NAD and look safe, but clear anti-aging outcomes in humans have not appeared. Direct NAD+ infusion is thinly studied. Users report more energy, focus and faster recovery, mostly from IV or subcutaneous courses. Fast infusions commonly bring flushing and chest pressure.
39. Trial: recent · Not applicable · NAD+ injection compared with injectable nicotinamide riboside · NCT06919328 · Nutraceuticals Research Institute. The only registered trial of NAD+ itself is past its planned end (June 2025) with no update; most current trials test NR or NMN instead. (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
40. People with active or recent cancer: Tumours depend on NAD+ for growth and DNA repair. (reported)
41. People on PARP inhibitors (olaparib etc.): PARP enzymes use NAD+; extra NAD+ may work against these drugs. (inferred)
42. People with gout: Breaks down to nicotinamide and adenine; adenine feeds uric acid. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
43. 5-Amino-1MQ: 5-Amino-1MQ blocks NNMT, an enzyme that drains the NAD salvage pathway, while NAD+ adds to the supply directly. People pair them to fill the pool and slow the leak at once, and they are sold pre-mixed as NAD+ + MOTS-c + 5-Amino-1MQ. The combination has not been tested together.
44. MOTS-c: MOTS-c activates AMPK and mimics the metabolic effect of exercise in mice, while NAD+ feeds the energy and repair enzymes that metabolism runs on. People pair them for energy and fat loss, and they come pre-mixed as NAD+ + MOTS-c + 5-Amino-1MQ. The pair itself has not been tested together.
45. BPC-157: BPC-157 works locally on blood vessel growth and repair at an injury, while NAD+ is taken for general cell energy and recovery. People run them side by side in recovery protocols. The goals overlap only loosely, and the pairing is user logic, not trial data.
46. TB-500 frag 17–23: The TB-500 fragment is used to move repair cells into wounds and calm inflammation, while NAD+ is taken to support cell energy during recovery. People combine them in recovery stacks. Neither has strong human data for this use, and the pair has not been tested together.
47. GHK-Cu: GHK-Cu carries copper and turns up collagen making in skin and wounds, while NAD+ targets cell energy and repair enzymes linked to aging. People pair them in skin and healthy aging routines. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
48. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, a coenzyme in every cell, central to energy metabolism and to the sirtuin and PARP repair enzymes. Not a peptide. Levels fall with age.
49. First studied for: Given IV and by injection to raise cellular NAD for energy, recovery and anti-aging.
50. Name story: The "+" is not marketing: it marks the positive charge on a nitrogen in the oxidised form. NADH is the same molecule carrying electrons. Older textbooks call it DPN (diphosphopyridine nucleotide) or coenzyme I. [S5] (verified)
51. 1906: Coenzyme first identified in yeast fermentation
52. 2010s: NR and NMN precursor trials show blood NAD rises
53. Today: Popular IV and injected energy and anti-aging coenzyme

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Not a peptide, not a drug, and not a thing the body lets in [mixed]
54. NAD+ is a coenzyme every cell already makes and constantly recycles. That makes it unlike everything else in this library: there is no question of whether it is biologically important, and no question of whether a cell can use it. The whole question is whether putting it into the bloodstream, as a large charged dinucleotide, raises anything inside the cells that need it.
55. The honest framing is that NAD+ is not a deficiency state waiting to be corrected like iron. It is a flux: made from precursors, consumed by PARP enzymes repairing DNA, by sirtuins, and by CD38 on cell surfaces, which rises with age and inflammation (verified as the accepted biochemistry). Measuring a level tells you very little about the rate, and all the human product claims are about levels.
56. One structural point explains most of what follows. The molecule carries two phosphates and is large by cellular standards. There is no established plasma membrane transporter that brings intact NAD+ into cells in people, which is why the field works with precursors, nicotinamide riboside and nicotinamide mononucleotide, that have known entry routes (verified as the state of the field).

### The one human pharmacokinetic study, and what it found [people]
57. There is a single published human study tracking NAD+ in blood and urine during administration, and it is small: 11 healthy men aged 30 to 55, eight given 750 mg of NAD+ intravenously in saline over six hours at roughly 2 mg per minute, three given saline alone [1] (verified).
58. The central finding is the one most often skipped. Plasma NAD+ did not rise at all for the first hours; it was described as rapidly and completely removed from circulation for at least the first two hours, and only at the six-hour mark, the end of the infusion, was it about 398% above baseline [1] (verified). In other words, a slow infusion is almost entirely cleared as fast as it goes in, until the clearance routes saturate.
59. Where it went is partly visible in the metabolites: nicotinamide rose 409%, ADP-ribose 393% and methylnicotinamide 350% at six hours, with nicotinamide mononucleotide rising 472% only at eight hours [1]. Urinary NAD+ excretion rose 538% at six hours, while urinary nicotinamide did not change significantly, so intact NAD+ was appearing in urine [1] (verified). The authors attribute the disappearance to tissue uptake and to breakdown by the surface enzymes CD38, CD157 and CD203a, and state plainly that tissue uptake was not measured [1] (inferred by the authors, not demonstrated).
60. So the only human kinetic data show rapid destruction and urinary loss of a large fraction, with the rise in blood appearing only once the system is overwhelmed. Nothing in it shows that intracellular NAD+ in any tissue increased. The dose was chosen empirically from clinic practice, and the study was funded by a company running NAD+ infusion clinics, with one author a director of it and another receiving consulting fees [1] (verified).

### What raising blood NAD+ has and has not achieved in trials [people]
61. The precursors have been tested properly, which makes them the best available guide to whether the premise works. Nicotinamide riboside reliably raises measured NAD+ in blood or muscle, and the functional results have been consistently null.
62. Twenty-four adults aged 55 to 79 took 1,000 mg daily for six weeks with no significant group difference in vascular function after correction; 40 men took 2,000 mg daily for 12 weeks with no difference from placebo in metabolic outcomes, and muscle sampling from the same cohort found no mitochondrial change; 12 older men took 1,000 mg daily for 21 days with no change in how muscle mitochondria used oxygen; 30 adults took 2,000 mg daily for 12 weeks with no significant difference in walk distance or quality of life [2] (verified as reported, with trial sizes of 12 to 40 and durations of three weeks to three months).
63. That pattern, the biomarker moves and the outcome does not, is the most important fact in this entry. It is also the pattern that an injected or infused form inherits, since raising the biomarker is precisely what it is sold to do (inferred).
64. A separate and more basic gap: there is no published human study of subcutaneous or intramuscular NAD+ at all. Every human number above comes from intravenous infusion or oral precursors (verified as absent). The commonly quoted half-life figures for injected NAD+ have no human source found in this review.

### Tolerability, measured honestly for once [people]
65. The infusion experience is usually described as flushing or discomfort that passes. A 2026 retrospective review from a commercial clinic puts numbers on it, and they are not mild. Fourteen clients received 500 mg daily for four consecutive days in 500 mL of saline, six as NAD+ and eight as nicotinamide riboside [3] (verified).
66. All six NAD+ clients, six of six, reported moderate to severe abdominal cramping, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, raised heart rate, throat pain, congestion and chest pressure during the infusion, resolving when it stopped. Five of eight NR clients reported minor tingling in the tongue, jaw and arm with minor cramping [3] (verified).
67. The mechanism of the dose schedule is visible in the timing. Clients controlled their own flow rate by tolerance, and the NAD+ group slowed theirs so much that average infusion time was about 97 minutes against 37 for NR [3] (verified). The long slow drip is not a pharmacological choice; it is what the symptoms force.
68. The limits of that study are substantial and the authors state them: retrospective, 14 people, no control group, four days only, whole-blood NAD+ assays unable to detect changes, and all seven authors employed by the clinic that funded it, with the NR donated by its manufacturer [3] (verified). It is cited here not as efficacy evidence but because the symptom list is concrete and comes from the setting where this is actually used.

### Product reality [lab]
69. NAD+ is chemically unstable in ways that matter for a product. It hydrolyses in solution, is sensitive to pH and heat, and the oxidised and reduced forms are different molecules with different stability, which is why the plus sign in the name is chemistry rather than branding.
70. Because it is sold variously as a supplement ingredient, a compounded injectable and a research powder, there is no single quality framework behind a given vial. A compounded sterile injection from a licensed pharmacy carries beyond-use dating, sterility and endotoxin requirements; a research powder carries none of those, and the molecule's instability means that content at manufacture and content at use are different questions (inferred).
71. One practical consequence of the infusion data: because clearance saturates, the rate of administration changes exposure more than the nominal amount does [1]. Two vials of the same size given at different rates are not the same exposure, which makes nominal figures a poor description of what someone received (inferred).

### Where the law stands, and open questions [mixed]
72. This is a muddle rather than a position. NAD+ itself is sold as a supplement ingredient and as a compounded injectable in the US, and is not an approved drug for any anti-ageing or energy indication (verified). It has not been through the peptide compounding review process that covers the injectable peptides elsewhere in this library, because it is not a peptide.
73. The precursor side shows how fast the ground can move. In 2022 the FDA concluded that beta-nicotinamide mononucleotide cannot be marketed as a dietary supplement, on the basis that it had already been authorised for investigation as a new drug with substantial public clinical investigation, reversing its own earlier acceptance of another filing; enforcement has not followed, and the agency does not disclose the relevant authorisation date [4] (verified). Nicotinamide riboside was not affected by that decision [4].
74. In sport, NAD+ is not named on the 2026 Prohibited List. The constraint that does apply is the method prohibition on intravenous infusions totalling more than 100 mL per 12 hours outside hospital treatment, which a 500 mL drip plainly exceeds [5] (verified). Note also that the related mitochondrial peptide MOTS-c is named on the list as an AMPK activator, so metabolic agents in this neighbourhood are not uniformly outside the rules [5].
75. Does intracellular NAD+ in any human tissue rise after infusion? The one kinetic study measured plasma and urine and inferred tissue uptake without measuring it [1].
76. Why is the biomarker-to-outcome link so consistently empty? Every well-conducted precursor trial raised NAD+ and changed nothing measurable, which is either a dose, duration, population or premise problem, and nobody has distinguished which.
77. Is injecting the intact coenzyme better than giving a precursor the body has transporters for? No study has compared them on any outcome other than infusion tolerability, where the precursor was clearly easier [3].
78. What is the cost of flooding a saturable clearance system repeatedly? Methylnicotinamide rose 350% in six hours [1], which consumes methyl groups, and nothing has examined what weekly or more frequent loading does to methyl balance (speculated).

Deep read references:

[2] Compilation of nicotinamide riboside human trials (Martens 2018, Dollerup 2018 and 2020, Elhassan 2019, Wang 2022) with endpoints and sample sizes, 2026 · https://verifiedsupplementdata.com/nr/for-nad-elevation/

# Humanin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/humanin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: HN, Alzheimer's survival peptide, MT-RNR2-encoded peptide
2. Origin: Made by the body
3. Sequence: MAPRGFSCLLLLTSEIDLPVKRRA (24 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: Research chemical; no clinical program in humans.

## Summary
5. Humanin is a small natural peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA. It is studied for protecting neurons and cells from stress, and for better insulin response and healthy aging, partly by blocking cell-death signals. Evidence is cell and animal work, and no human efficacy trials exist.
6. Punch line: A peptide coded in mitochondrial DNA. Shields neurons and cells from stress; higher in long-lived families.
7. Used for: Cell protection and metabolic aging

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Cellular protection: Protects cells from stress
9. Neural protection: Shields neurons from amyloid
10. Cellular energy: Made by mitochondria
11. Aging & senescence: Higher in long-lived families
12. Glucose & insulin (backed only by animal or user reports): Better insulin response in animals
13. Organ function (backed only by animal or user reports): Organ protection studied
14. Reproductive (backed only by animal or user reports): Fertility studied

## How it works
15. Blocks cell-death signals · Bax binding · role Cellular protection
   Inside cells, humanin binds Bax, a protein that triggers apoptosis, and stops it moving to the mitochondria to punch holes there. It also binds Bid and tBid, which help Bax assemble. Blocking this cascade keeps stressed cells alive, shown in cell studies.
16. Protects neurons from amyloid · FPRL1, gp130 receptors · role Neural protection
   Outside cells, humanin acts on the receptor FPRL1 and on a receptor complex containing gp130 that switches on JAK2 and STAT3. In cell studies this protects neurons from amyloid toxicity, and it helped in Alzheimer's mouse models. Protection persisted without FPRL1, so the receptor story is incomplete.
17. Supports mitochondrial function · Mitochondria-derived peptide · role Cellular energy
   Humanin's reading frame sits in the mitochondrial ribosomal RNA gene, making it a mitochondria-derived peptide, though nuclear copies exist and the true source is unsettled. It is linked to lower oxidative stress in cell and animal work. No effect in people has been tested.
18. Improves insulin sensitivity in rodents · Hypothalamic STAT3 · role Glucose & insulin
   In the hypothalamus, humanin signals through STAT3 and improves insulin sensitivity in the body. This was shown in rats with the peptide infused directly into the brain. Much of the animal work used a far stronger analogue, HNG, rather than natural humanin.
19. Levels fall with age, higher in long-lived · Age-linked decline · role Aging & senescence
   Blood levels of humanin fall with age in humans and mice, and children of centenarians had higher levels than controls in a small cohort. That links it to healthy aging. It is association only, and no one has been given humanin in a published human study.
20. Mechanism overview: Humanin is a 21 to 24 amino acid peptide encoded inside mitochondrial DNA. Inside cells it binds Bax and stops it moving to mitochondria, blocking the apoptosis cascade. Outside cells it acts through FPRL1 and a gp130-containing receptor complex, which protects neurons from amyloid toxicity. In the hypothalamus it signals through STAT3, improving insulin sensitivity in rodents. Blood levels fall with age and run higher in long-lived people.

## Who shouldn't take it

## Synergies (paired with)
44. MOTS-c: Both are peptides encoded in mitochondrial DNA. Humanin guards cells against death signals, while MOTS-c activates AMPK and mimics exercise on metabolism, so people pair them for metabolic aging. The pair has not been tested together, and humanin has no human data at all.
45. SS-31: SS-31 binds cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane to steady energy production and cut oxidative stress, while humanin blocks cell-death signals at the mitochondria. People pair them for mitochondrial protection from two angles. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
46. Found in 2001 in the one brain region that survived in an Alzheimer's patient, and encoded in the mitochondria's own DNA. Named for its hoped-for protective power.
47. First studied for: Studied for neuroprotection and metabolic/aging resilience.
48. Name story: Found in 2001 by Ikuo Nishimoto's Tokyo lab, fished out of surviving brain tissue of an Alzheimer's patient. The name reportedly reflects hopes it could restore humanity to people with dementia. Oddly, it's encoded in mitochondrial DNA (MT-RNR2). [S4] (reported)
49. 2001: Found in surviving brain tissue of an Alzheimer's patient
50. 2000s to 2010s: Animal and cell work on neurons and metabolism
51. Today: Mitochondrial peptide of longevity interest; no human trial

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where it came from, and the part of its address nobody has settled [lab]
52. It was found in 2001 by a cell-survival screen: material from the unaffected occipital cortex of a person who had died with sporadic Alzheimer's disease was tested for genes that kept neurons alive against Alzheimer's-type insults, and one short reading frame kept surviving [1] (verified, as described in a later review). That reading frame sits inside the gene for the large ribosomal RNA of mitochondria, a stretch of DNA not expected to code for a protein at all.
53. That location creates a real puzzle. Mitochondria and the rest of the cell read slightly different genetic codes, so the same sequence gives a 21-residue peptide if translated inside mitochondria and a 24-residue one if translated in the cytoplasm. Both forms are active and the last three residues appear not to matter [1] (verified, in cells). The nuclear genome also carries several near-copies of the same sequence, remnants of mitochondrial DNA that migrated into the chromosomes long ago. Which source actually produces the peptide measured in blood, and from which tissue, has not been resolved [1] (verified as open).
54. So the familiar line, a peptide encoded by mitochondrial DNA, is the leading hypothesis rather than a settled fact. It also means two different peptide lengths share one name, and listings rarely say which is present (inferred).

### One small peptide, five reported partners [cells]
55. The card names Bax and two receptor systems. The fuller picture is that humanin has been reported to bind at least five different things, which is unusual for a peptide this size and worth sitting with.
56. Inside the cell it binds inactive Bax and prevents the shape change that sends Bax to the mitochondria; it also binds Bid and its cleaved form tBid, which normally help Bax assemble into pores; and it binds IGFBP-3, a growth-factor binding protein that can itself trigger cell death [1] (verified, in cells). Outside the cell it acts on the formyl peptide receptor FPRL1, and on a three-part cytokine-type receptor assembled from CNTFR, WSX-1 and gp130 that switches on JAK2 and STAT3 [1] (verified, in cells).
57. One detail undercuts the tidy version of this story: neuroprotection persisted when FPRL1 was knocked down, so the receptor account is incomplete [1] (verified). Many binding partners can mean a genuinely central signal, or a sticky peptide that registers activity in whatever assay it is dropped into. The literature has not separated those readings (inferred), which is one reason an effect shown in one tissue does not reliably carry to another.

### Most of the animal evidence was not collected with humanin [animals]
58. This is the single most important thing the card cannot fit, and it changes how every quoted animal result should be read. A single-residue variant, serine 14 swapped for glycine, known as S14G or HNG, is reported to be more than a thousand times more potent at protecting cells than the natural sequence [1] (verified as claimed, though the review attributes that figure to a citation that does not support it, which is worth noting). Because it is so much stronger, HNG became the workhorse of the field.
59. The consequence is that the headline mouse experiments used the analogue. In the 2020 lifespan study, middle-aged female mice received HNG at 4 milligrams per kilogram by abdominal injection twice weekly from 18 months of age for 14 months, in a survival cohort of 100 animals [2] (verified, in animals). The metabolic work in rats that produced the insulin-sensitivity finding infused peptide directly into the brain ventricles during a clamp procedure, with the effect traced to hypothalamic STAT3 [1] (verified, in animals). Neither design resembles a peripheral injection of the natural peptide, and neither tested the natural peptide.
60. Half-life is given as roughly 30 minutes [2] (reported). No proper pharmacokinetic programme exists for either form, in any species: no bioavailability, no tissue distribution, no clearance route (verified as absent).

### The longevity claim, read against its own best study [animals]
61. The 2020 paper from the USC gerontology group is the most complete test of the longevity idea, and it is more mixed than its title suggests [2].
62. In worms, extra humanin lengthened mean life from 17.7 to 19.0 days, a small but statistically significant gain, and the gain disappeared in animals lacking daf-16, the worm version of FOXO [2] (verified, in animals). So in the one species where lifespan was extended, the effect required a separate longevity pathway to work through.
63. In mice, HNG from mid-life did not significantly change lifespan [2] (verified). What it did change was body composition at 28 months, in a small subgroup of five per group: less visceral fat, more lean mass, unchanged subcutaneous fat, with significantly lower circulating IGF-I and food intake no different from controls [2]. The authors suggest the dose may have been too low or started too late. Either way, the mammalian lifespan result is negative, and it is rarely quoted that way.
64. The cost side appeared in both species. Worms overexpressing humanin were smaller, leaner and less fertile; transgenic mice were about 12% shorter, 10% lighter, and had litters 46.5% smaller at 28 days [2] (verified). The authors read this as the familiar trade-off between reproduction and longevity. It is also a reminder that this is a growth-suppressing signal, not a tonic.

### The human record, which is association only [people]
65. No person has ever been given humanin or any analogue of it in a published study. There is no clinical trial, no case series, no human pharmacokinetic measurement, and no safety dataset of any kind (verified as absent; the review itself states that pharmacokinetic and safety data for long-term use are still needed [1]).
66. The human data that exist are measurements of peptide already in people. Blood levels fall with age in humans and mice, and growth hormone or IGF-1 treatment lowers them [1] (verified). Children of centenarians in an Ashkenazi Jewish cohort had higher circulating levels than age-matched controls, with 18 offspring against 19 controls [2] (verified). In newborns, cord-blood levels tracked mitochondrial DNA copy number across 73 samples [2]. Spinal fluid levels were lower in Alzheimer's disease than in controls, in a comparison of three or four people per group depending on whether the text or the figure legend is read [2] (verified, including the inconsistency).
67. Those are the numbers behind the longevity reputation: a handful of small cohorts, measuring a natural peptide, in people who were not taking anything. A correlation between high natural levels and long-lived families does not establish that injecting the peptide reproduces whatever the correlation reflects (inferred). It is just as consistent with high levels being a marker of healthier mitochondria rather than a cause of them.

### Safety: unexamined, with one specific question that will not go away [mixed]
68. There are no toxicology studies: no acute, no repeat-dose, no genotoxicity, no reproductive, no carcinogenicity work, for either the natural peptide or the analogue (verified as absent). The 14-month mouse dosing study reported no safety outcomes beyond survival and body composition [2].
69. The question the biology raises is cancer, and it cuts both ways, which is why it stays open. A peptide whose core action is blocking programmed cell death is, in principle, doing for a tumour cell what it does for a neuron. Some authors have proposed it as an oncopeptide, pointing to upregulation of the mitochondrial 16S rRNA region in non-Hodgkin lymphoma, detection in serum from some people with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, and higher isoform messenger RNA in chemotherapy-resistant stomach tumour tissue [1] (reported). Against that, the analogue delayed tumour growth in medulloblastoma and neuroblastoma models [1] (reported). The reviewers' own conclusion was that the evidence is not conclusive [1] (verified).
70. The reproductive findings deserve to be read as safety data rather than curiosities. Smaller litters in transgenic mice and reduced reproductive output in worms are the clearest biological effects in the whole file [2]. Nothing is known about what a growth- and IGF-suppressing signal does in a person, at any exposure.

### Where the law stands, and open questions [mixed]
71. No approved product anywhere, no registered clinical programme found, and it was not among the peptides nominated for or reviewed under the US compounding lists in 2026 (verified as of October 2026). It is not named on the 2026 WADA Prohibited List, which leaves it inside the catch-all class for pharmacological substances with no government approval for human use, prohibited at all times [3] (inferred from the class wording). Note that the related mitochondrial peptide MOTS-c is named explicitly on that list as an AMPK activator [3], so the family has regulators' attention.
72. Which gene actually makes the circulating peptide, and in which tissue? Until that is answered, the claim that this is a mitochondrial hormone rests on sequence location rather than demonstrated biology.
73. Is the 21-residue or the 24-residue form the relevant molecule, and which is in a given vial? No identity testing in general circulation distinguishes them.
74. Does the natural sequence do anything the analogue does? Nearly all the potent results used the analogue, and it is more than a thousandfold stronger in cells.
75. If high natural levels mark long-lived families, is the peptide a cause or a readout? Nothing distinguishes these yet, and the mouse lifespan result argues against the simple causal reading.
76. Does blocking apoptosis for weeks at a time carry an oncological cost? Unstudied, arguable in both directions, and the one question this mechanism cannot avoid.

# Mazdutide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/mazdutide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: LY3305677, IBI362, Xinermei, 玛仕度肽 (Chinese INN)
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain
3. Sequence: HAQGTFTSDYSKYLDEKKAKEFVEWLLEGGPSSG (34 amino acids). Position 2 is Aib, shown as A; Oxyntomodulin-style chain; K20 carries a C20 diacid via AEEA-AEEA-gGlu linker; C-terminal amide
4. Legal and approval status: Approved in China (NMPA) as Xinermei for weight management (Jun 2025) and type 2 diabetes (Sep 2025); 9 mg dose under NMPA review since Nov 2025, no approval found as of 22 Oct 2026. Not FDA-approved; no US filing announced. WADA does not list it (approved in China, so S0 does not apply; inferred).

## Summary
5. Mazdutide is Lilly's dual agonist of the GLP-1 and glucagon receptors, mimicking oxyntomodulin, developed in China by Innovent. It quiets hunger and also pushes the liver to burn fat, and is approved in China for weight management and type 2 diabetes. It is not FDA-approved, GI side effects are heavy at 9 mg, and there is almost no data outside Chinese populations.
6. Punch line: GLP-1 and glucagon dual, approved in China. Seen as the cheaper retatrutide; beat semaglutide head to head.
7. Used for: Weight loss, type 2 diabetes

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Appetite & satiety: Cuts hunger like GLP-1 drugs
9. Fat metabolism: Up to ~20% weight loss
10. Glucose & insulin: Beat semaglutide on HbA1c
11. Organ function: Liver fat down 60–80%
12. Heart & vessels (backed only by animal or user reports): Heart rate rises on titration
13. Digestive & gut (backed only by animal or user reports): Vomiting and nausea at 9 mg

## How it works
14. Quiets hunger and slows the stomach · GLP-1 receptor · role Appetite & satiety
   Mazdutide switches on the GLP-1 receptor in the brainstem and hypothalamus, the same target as semaglutide. That lowers hunger and slows how fast the stomach empties, so meals feel larger for longer. The weight loss this drives has been shown in Chinese Phase 3 trials in people.
15. Pushes the liver to burn fat · Glucagon receptor · role Organ function
   The second half of the molecule activates the glucagon receptor, which sits mostly on liver cells. Glucagon tells the liver to burn stored fat instead of keeping it. In GLORY-1, liver fat fell far more than on placebo, which fits this action, though weight loss explains part of it.
16. Raises energy use · Glucagon receptor · role Fat metabolism
   Glucagon receptor signalling also raises the body's resting energy use, a known effect of the hormone. This is the reason the design adds a glucagon arm to a GLP-1 drug. The trials measured the outcomes in people, not energy expenditure directly, so this step is inferred from receptor pharmacology.
17. Raises insulin when glucose is high · GLP-1R, beta cells · role Glucose & insulin
   On pancreatic beta cells, GLP-1 receptor activation raises insulin only when blood glucose is high, which keeps the risk of lows small. This offsets the glucose-raising pull of the glucagon arm. In the DREAMS trials HbA1c fell further than on dulaglutide and semaglutide in people with type 2 diabetes.
18. Fatty tail rides albumin for weekly dosing · C20 diacid acylation · role Fat metabolism
   A C20 fatty diacid on lysine 20 binds albumin, the main carrier protein in blood. That shields the peptide from kidney clearance and breakdown, and an Aib swap at position 2 blocks the DPP-4 enzyme. Together they stretch the half-life to several days, which is what allows once-weekly injections.
19. Mechanism overview: Mazdutide is a 34-residue oxyntomodulin analogue with Aib at position 2 to block DPP-4 and a C20 fatty diacid on lysine 20 that binds albumin, giving a half-life of several days. It activates the GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) and the glucagon receptor (GCGR) with roughly balanced binding. GLP-1R action cuts appetite and slows gastric emptying and raises glucose-dependent insulin; GCGR action raises hepatic fat oxidation and energy expenditure, which shows up as large drops in liver fat.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
20. Typical: 4–6 mg (9 mg under review) · once weekly · cycle Ongoing; step up every 4 weeks · route Sub-Q (verified)
21. Half-life: ~4–6 days (reported)
22. Most people take: Weekly Sub-Q pen, 4 or 6 mg maintenance in China; GLORY-2 stepped 3 mg every 4 weeks to 9 mg. No oral form.

23. Grey-market buyers outside China treat it as a cheaper glucagon dual agonist alongside retatrutide; detailed first-hand reports are scarce.

25. Liked / worked: Up to ~20% on 9 mg at 60 weeks
26. Liked / worked: Beat semaglutide 1 mg in DREAMS-3
27. Liked / worked: Liver fat down 60–80%
28. What worked: 14.8% weight loss on 6 mg at 48 weeks (GLORY-1) and up to 18.6–20.1% on 9 mg at 60 weeks (GLORY-2); beat semaglutide 1 mg on weight (10.3% vs 6%) and HbA1c in DREAMS-3. Liver fat fell 60–80%.
29. Went wrong / did not work: Vomiting 53% on 9 mg
30. Went wrong / did not work: Heart rate up during titration
31. Went wrong / did not work: No cardiovascular-outcome data
32. Went wrong / did not work: Almost no non-Chinese data
33. What went wrong: Heavy GI load at 9 mg (vomiting 53%, nausea 47%, diarrhea 39% in GLORY-2); heart rate up ~7 bpm during titration. No cardiovascular-outcome data and almost no data outside Chinese populations.
34. Most reported: Seen as a cheaper retatrutide alternative

## What has been tested
37. Fat metabolism: Obesity, GLORY-1 and GLORY-2 (human)
38. Glucose & insulin: Type 2 diabetes, DREAMS-1 to -3 (human)
39. Organ function: Liver fat in obesity (substudies) (human)
40. A full Chinese Phase 3 program: GLORY-1 and GLORY-2 in obesity, DREAMS-1, -2 and -3 in type 2 diabetes, including head-to-head against semaglutide. Lilly runs a smaller US Phase 2.
41. What it helps: Chinese Phase 3 trials showed 12–15% weight loss at 4–6 mg and up to about 20% at 9 mg, plus better HbA1c than semaglutide 1 mg in DREAMS-3. Liver fat, waist, blood pressure, lipids and uric acid also improved. GI effects are heavy at 9 mg and heart rate rises during titration. Outside China people use it as a dual agonist for weight and fatty liver.
42. Trial: active · Phase 3 · fatty liver in obesity · NCT06884293 · Innovent Biologics. Approved in China in 2025 as Xinermei; a Phase 3 head to head against semaglutide in fatty liver is still running. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (verified)

## Who shouldn't take it
43. Personal or family history of MTC or MEN2: Causes thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents; boxed warning and contraindication on the label. (inferred)
44. Anyone booked for surgery, endoscopy or sedation: Food can stay in the stomach for days and be inhaled into the lungs under anaesthesia. (inferred)
45. People with arrhythmia or a fast resting pulse: The glucagon part of the drug pushes resting heart rate up. (reported)

## Synergies (paired with)
46. Cagrilintide: Cagrilintide adds amylin signalling, a separate fullness pathway in the brainstem, while mazdutide works through GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. People pair them to stack appetite control from two routes and keep the liver-fat effect, but the pair itself has not been tested together.
47. Tirzepatide: Both are dual incretin drugs aimed at the same goal: tirzepatide pairs GLP-1 with GIP, mazdutide pairs GLP-1 with glucagon. They overlap heavily at the GLP-1 receptor, so they are usually compared or swapped rather than stacked. The combination has not been tested.

## Where it comes from
48. Lilly's oxyntomodulin-mimicking GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist, developed in China by Innovent under licence and the first drug of its class approved anywhere.
49. First studied for: Chronic weight management and type 2 diabetes in Chinese adults.
50. Name story: Built on oxyntomodulin, a gut hormone that naturally hits both the GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. Lilly's LY3305677 was licensed to Innovent as IBI362 and approved in China in June 2025, the first GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist on the market. [S2] (verified)
51. 2019: Lilly licenses China rights to Innovent
52. Jun 2025: China approves it for weight management (Xinermei)
53. Sep 2025: China approves it for type 2 diabetes
54. Oct 2025: DREAMS-3: beats semaglutide on weight and HbA1c
55. Nov 2025: 9 mg dose filed after GLORY-2
56. Jun 2026: GLORY-2 in JAMA; 9 mg brings heavy GI effects

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where it came from, and why it reached China first [people]
57. The molecule was designed at Lilly under the code LY3305677 and built on oxyntomodulin, a gut hormone that already touches both the GLP-1 and glucagon receptors [8] (verified). Lilly then licensed the China rights to Innovent, which ran it as IBI362. That split is the key to reading the record: nearly all of the published human data, every phase 3 trial so far and the only approval come from the Chinese programme, while Lilly has run a smaller parallel set of US studies at higher doses [5,6] (verified).
58. The order of events is unusual for a drug of this class. Most incretin drugs are approved first in the US or Europe and then elsewhere. This one was approved in China in June 2025, before any US phase 3 had read out, which makes it the first marketed GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist anywhere [8] (verified). Anyone outside China using it is using a drug that has an approval, just not in their jurisdiction.

### Mechanism, and the trade the glucagon half makes [mixed]
59. The GLP-1 half does what the class is known for: less hunger, slower stomach emptying, more insulin when glucose is high. The glucagon half is the interesting one, because on its face it should push the wrong way. Glucagon raises blood glucose by releasing it from the liver. The design bet is that, paired with GLP-1, the glucose-raising effect is cancelled out while the other glucagon effects survive: more fat burned in the liver and higher energy expenditure (inferred from the receptor pharmacology; the human trials measured the outcomes, not the energy expenditure directly).
60. The outcome that best supports the bet is liver fat. In GLORY-1, among people who started with a fatty liver, liver fat fell by about 63% on 4 mg and 73% on 6 mg at 48 weeks, against an 8% rise on placebo; in those starting above 10% liver fat it fell by about 66% and 80% [1] (verified). Weight loss alone does reduce liver fat, so this cannot be credited wholly to the glucagon arm, but the size of the drop relative to the weight lost is what the glucagon hypothesis predicts (inferred).
61. The glucose side also held. In type 2 diabetes the drug lowered HbA1c more than both dulaglutide and semaglutide in head-to-head trials [3,4], which is the clearest human evidence that the glucagon component does not undo glycaemic control at these doses (verified).

### The human record, trial by trial [people]
62. Phase 2 in Chinese adults with obesity: 248 people, 3, 4.5 or 6 mg against placebo for 24 weeks. Weight fell 6.7%, 10.4% and 11.3% against 1.0% on placebo, with no treatment discontinuations for adverse events reported [7] (reported, from the sponsor's summary of the paper).
63. GLORY-1, the phase 3 that supported approval: 610 Chinese adults, 4 or 6 mg weekly against placebo for 48 weeks. Weight fell 12.1% and 14.8% against 0.5% on placebo (efficacy estimand); counting everyone randomised regardless of adherence, 11.0% and 14.0% [1] (verified). Half of the 6 mg group lost at least 15%. Baseline weight averaged 87 kg, lighter than most Western obesity trials, which matters when comparing percentages across programmes (inferred).
64. GLORY-2, the higher dose: 9 mg weekly, reached by 3 mg steps every four weeks, for 60 weeks. Weight fell 16.7% against 1.5% on placebo, and 10.7% in the subgroup with diabetes [2] (verified). That is the dose now under review in China.
65. Diabetes: DREAMS-1 enrolled 320 people on diet and exercise alone; HbA1c fell 1.58 and 2.02 points on 4 and 6 mg against 0.25 on placebo at 24 weeks [3]. DREAMS-2 enrolled 731 on metformin-based therapy against dulaglutide 1.5 mg; HbA1c fell 1.61 and 1.66 against 1.36, and weight 6.6% and 8.5% against 2.8% [3] (reported, sponsor release of the Nature papers). DREAMS-3 put 6 mg against semaglutide 1 mg in 349 people with diabetes and obesity: HbA1c down 2.03 against 1.84 points, weight down 10.3% against 6.0% at 32 weeks [4] (reported).
66. The US data are smaller and push the dose much higher. A Lilly phase 1 took 32 people to a 16 mg target over 20 weeks and reported 20 to 21% weight loss with no serious adverse events [6] (verified). The US phase 2, published in August 2026, randomised 179 people to 3 to 6, 10 or 16 mg; at 32 weeks weight fell 7.3%, 15.6% and 18.1% against 0.9% on placebo [5] (reported). So the Chinese label doses sit at the low end of what the molecule has been pushed to.

### What the body does with it [people]
67. The C20 fatty diacid binds albumin, which is what stretches dosing to once a week [8]. The phase 1 papers report human pharmacokinetics, but the full texts could not be opened for this review, so the half-life on the card stays tagged as reported rather than verified here.
68. The practically important kinetic fact is about titration, not half-life. Every programme escalates in steps of roughly four weeks, and the adverse event curves peak during those steps and fall after [2,3] (verified). The GLORY-2 heart rate data show the same shape: a mean rise peaking at about 7 beats per minute during titration and settling to about 2.6 by week 60 [2] (verified).

### Safety: what has been measured, and what the higher doses cost [people]
69. At 4 to 6 mg the profile looks like the GLP-1 class: nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting, mostly mild to moderate and concentrated in titration, no severe hypoglycaemia in the diabetes trials, and grade 1 to 2 hypoglycaemia similar to dulaglutide [1,3] (verified).
70. The higher doses change the picture. At 9 mg in GLORY-2, vomiting was reported in 53%, nausea in 47% and diarrhoea in 39% [2] (verified). In the US phase 2, discontinuation for adverse events reached 20% at 16 mg, mostly gastrointestinal [5] (reported). The pattern is consistent across both programmes: weight loss keeps rising with dose, and so does the share of people who cannot tolerate it.
71. What has not been looked at yet: no cardiovascular outcome trial has reported, no trial longer than about 60 weeks has published, and none has been run in a non-Asian population at the approved doses. The glucagon component's long-term effects on lean mass, amino acid handling and heart rhythm in humans remain open (inferred from what is absent in the published record).

### Who produced the evidence [people]
72. Every trial summarised above was sponsored by Innovent or Lilly, and several numbers here come from company releases rather than the papers themselves [3,4,7]. That is normal for a drug in development, and the main results did pass peer review at NEJM, JAMA, Nature and Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology [1,2,3,5]. No independent trial exists yet.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
73. Approved in China for chronic weight management (June 2025) and for type 2 diabetes (September 2025), at 4 and 6 mg; the 9 mg dose was filed in November 2025 and no approval had been found as of late October 2026 [2,8]. Not approved by the FDA or EMA, and no US submission has been announced.
74. In sport, GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonists are not on the WADA Prohibited List, and because the drug has a government approval in China the non-approved substances clause does not apply (inferred from the list's wording).

### Open questions [mixed]
75. Does the glucagon arm add anything beyond more weight loss? The liver fat numbers suggest it does, but no trial has compared it against a pure GLP-1 drug at matched weight loss.
76. Where is the tolerable ceiling? Chinese labels stop at 6 mg, China is reviewing 9 mg, and US studies went to 16 mg with one in five stopping.
77. Do the results hold outside China? The US phase 2 suggests yes at higher doses, but no phase 3 has run in a Western population.
78. What happens to heart rate, lean mass and cardiovascular events over years rather than months? None of these has an outcome trial yet.

# MK-677
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/mk-677
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: ibutamoren nutrobal, MK-0677, L-163,191, LUM-201, ibutamoren mesylate
2. Origin: Not a peptide
3. Legal and approval status: Not approved. Back in development as LUM-201, in a Phase 3 trial for children with growth hormone deficiency. WADA-banned (S2). Sold grey-market as a research chemical.

## Summary
4. MK-677 (ibutamoren) is an orally active small molecule, not a peptide, that mimics ghrelin to raise growth hormone and IGF-1 around the clock. Merck developed it for GH deficiency and frailty, and users take it for sleep, recovery and lean mass. It is not approved, and appetite, water retention and blood sugar rise, while a hip-fracture trial saw more heart-failure events.
5. Punch line: Oral ghrelin mimic, not a peptide. Lifts GH and IGF-1 all day; deeper sleep, bigger hunger, water retention.
6. Used for: GH/IGF-1 boost, sleep, lean mass

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Appetite & satiety: Raises hunger
8. Sleep & rhythms: Deeper sleep reported
9. Endocrine & growth: Raises GH and IGF-1 all day
10. Muscle & performance: Adds lean mass in older adults

## How it works
11. Mimics ghrelin to raise GH all day · Ghrelin receptor, GHSR-1a · role Endocrine & growth
   MK-677 is an oral small molecule that activates the ghrelin receptor GHSR-1a. In the pituitary this triggers growth hormone release, and in the hypothalamus it boosts GHRH and blunts somatostatin. Its long action pushes larger GH pulses across the day, shown in human trials.
12. Lifts IGF-1 downstream · GH/IGF-1 axis · role Endocrine & growth
   The higher growth hormone output drives the liver to make more IGF-1, which stays raised with daily dosing. Human trials reliably show IGF-1 rising to young-adult levels in older people. A trial in Alzheimer's disease showed that raising IGF-1 alone did not slow the disease.
13. Raises hunger · Hypothalamic ghrelin signal · role Appetite & satiety
   Ghrelin is the body's hunger hormone, so activating its receptor in the hypothalamus raises appetite. Users commonly report a strong increase in hunger. This is a direct effect of the target, not a side effect that can be separated from it.
14. Deepens slow-wave and REM sleep · GH pulse at night · role Sleep & rhythms
   Larger night-time GH pulses go along with deeper slow-wave sleep and more REM sleep. One small human study found both rose at the higher dose. With fourteen people in total, that evidence base is thin for the sleep reputation it carries.
15. Adds lean mass, not proven strength · GH/IGF-1 anabolic · role Muscle & performance
   Through raised GH and IGF-1, it added lean mass in a year-long trial in healthy older adults. Strength and physical function did not change in that trial. Fasting glucose rose, and a hip-fracture trial was stopped early over heart-failure events.
16. Mechanism overview: MK-677, or ibutamoren, is an oral small molecule, not a peptide, that activates the ghrelin receptor GHSR-1a. In the pituitary this triggers GH release, and in the hypothalamus it boosts GHRH and blunts somatostatin. Its long half-life raises GH pulses across the day and lifts IGF-1 with daily dosing. Ghrelin receptor activation also drives hunger. GH's anti-insulin action raises fasting glucose, and sodium retention causes water weight. Larger night-time GH pulses accompany deeper slow-wave and more REM sleep.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
17. Typical: 12.5–25 mg · daily · cycle 4-6 weeks, 4-6 weeks off · route Oral (reported)
18. Half-life: ~24 hours
19. Dose note: Every trial used 25 mg. Doses above 25 mg come from one guide; users more often drop to 10–15 mg for side effects.
20. Most people take: 12.5-25mg/day oral before bed · 4-6 weeks, 4-6 weeks off
21. Common: 25 mg · 1× daily, pre-bed · 8–16 wk · Oral · for trial-matched standard [S1] [S2] [S3] (verified)
22. Low: 10–15 mg · 1× daily · 8 wk–6 mo · Oral · for beginners, side-effect control, long runs [S2] [S4] [S5] (reported)
23. Aggressive: up to 50 mg · 1× daily · after first cycle · Oral · for bodybuilding ramp [S6] [S5] (reported)

## What people report
24. Very popular oral GH-optimizer; reported for sleep, appetite, recovery; water retention and hunger common.
25. Liked / worked: Oral and convenient
26. Liked / worked: Reliably raises GH and IGF-1
27. Liked / worked: More lean mass in older adults
28. Liked / worked: Better sleep
29. What worked: Oral, convenient, reliably raises GH/IGF-1 and lean mass and improves sleep.
30. Went wrong / did not work: Hip-fracture trial: more heart-failure events
31. Went wrong / did not work: Raises blood sugar
32. Went wrong / did not work: Hunger and water retention
33. What went wrong: Raises appetite, blood sugar and water retention; the hip-fracture trial saw more heart-failure events.
34. Most reported: Sleep, appetite and recovery

36. Most reported: Not a peptide; a small molecule

## What has been tested
37. Endocrine & growth: GH and IGF-1 levels (trial)
38. Muscle & performance: Lean mass in older adults (trial)
39. Bone & cartilage: Hip-fracture recovery (trial)
40. Endocrine & growth: Childhood GH deficiency, LUM-201 (trial)
41. Several human trials: it reliably raises GH and IGF-1 and increased lean mass in older adults. A trial in older adults recovering from hip fracture was stopped early over heart-failure events, and it raises blood sugar.
42. What it helps: Trials show reliably raised GH and IGF-1, more lean mass in older adults, and better sleep. A hip-fracture recovery trial in older adults saw more heart-failure events. The same molecule, as LUM-201, is in trials for childhood GH deficiency. Users report deeper sleep, bigger appetite and recovery, with water retention, hunger and higher blood sugar common. Strength gains were not shown.
43. Trial: active · Phase 3 · growth hormone deficiency in children · NCT06948214 · Lumos Pharma. Under the code LUM-201, the gray market ibutamoren is in a Phase 3 as an oral pill for short children. (checked 2026-10-23) [S7] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
44. People with heart failure or heart disease: A hip-fracture trial in older adults was stopped early for more heart failure. (reported)
45. People with prediabetes or poorly controlled diabetes: Raised fasting glucose and HbA1c in a 2-year trial. (reported)
46. People with active or recent cancer: Raises IGF-1 around the clock for as long as it is taken. (inferred)
47. Drug-tested athletes: Ibutamoren (MK-677) is named on the WADA banned list as a GH secretagogue. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
48. TB-500 frag 17–23: MK-677 raises growth hormone and IGF-1 body wide, while the TB-500 fragment is used locally to move repair cells into injured tissue. People pair them for injury recovery and sleep supported repair. The pair has not been tested together, and the logic comes from users.

## Where it comes from
49. Ibutamoren, an orally active small-molecule ghrelin-receptor agonist (not a peptide) that raises GH and IGF-1 around the clock.
50. First studied for: Developed by Merck for GH deficiency and for frailty/muscle wasting in the elderly.
51. Name story: MK is Merck's in-house compound prefix; the same molecule was also Merck's L-163,191. Despite living on peptide lists, it is a small molecule that mimics ghrelin, and its INN is ibutamoren. [S8] (reported)
52. 1990s: Merck builds an oral ghrelin mimic for GH deficiency and frailty
53. 2000s: Hip-fracture trial in older adults stopped over heart failure
54. Today: Popular oral GH-optimizer; in Phase 3 as LUM-201 for children; WADA-banned

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where it came from: a Merck drug that never found its indication [people]
55. Merck designed it in the mid-1990s as L-163,191, later MK-0677, with a tentative brand name of Oratrope [1] (verified). The goal was a pill that would do what growth hormone injections do for frail older people, by persuading the pituitary to release more of its own hormone rather than replacing it. That framing explains the shape of the human record: the trials were in older adults, hip fracture patients, people with Alzheimer's disease and children with short stature, not in healthy young adults.
56. Merck ran it through several indications and stopped each one, for reasons covered below. The molecule then passed through licensees and is now back in development under a new code, LUM-201, with the original company still listed as originator [2] (verified). So the compound sold as a gym product and the one in a 2026 phase 3 for children are the same molecule with very different paperwork behind them.

### Mechanism: why it raises growth hormone all day rather than in a pulse [people]
57. It binds the ghrelin receptor, the same receptor the hunger hormone uses, which is why appetite and growth hormone release travel together on this drug. Natural ghrelin is a peptide with a short life in blood. This is a small, orally absorbed molecule with a much longer one, so instead of brief spikes the receptor is pushed for most of the day [1] (verified).
58. The useful detail is the gap between drug half-life and effect. In dogs the molecule itself has an elimination half-life of about four to six hours, yet in humans IGF-1 stays elevated for up to 24 hours after a single dose [1] (verified, animal half-life; human effect duration). Human plasma half-life figures were not found in an accessible primary source for this review. What matters for interpreting the trials is that daily dosing produces a sustained IGF-1 rise, and IGF-1, not growth hormone, is what most of the downstream effects and side effects track.
59. Because it acts on the body's own pituitary, the growth hormone it produces still comes in pulses, just larger and more frequent ones; the 1990s work described amplitude rising rather than a flat plateau (inferred from the studies of the class; the Nass trial reported pulsatile secretion restored to young-adult levels [3]).

### The human record: what each trial measured and found [people]
60. Healthy older adults, the best trial. Sixty-five healthy adults aged 60 to 81 took 25 mg or placebo daily for a year. Growth hormone and IGF-1 rose to young-adult levels. Fat-free mass rose 1.1 kg on drug and fell 0.5 kg on placebo, a 1.6 kg difference [3,4] (verified). Strength and physical function did not change [4] (reported). Fasting glucose rose by about 0.3 mmol per litre and insulin sensitivity fell [3,4] (verified). This is the source of the claim that it builds lean mass, and the same paper is the source of the claim that the lean mass did not translate into function.
61. Hip fracture recovery. A Merck phase 2b randomised 123 elderly hip fracture patients to 25 mg or placebo for 24 weeks. IGF-1 rose by about 51 ng per mL over placebo. Gait speed improved slightly, stair-climbing power and other functional measures did not significantly change, and falls trended lower without reaching significance. The trial was stopped early for a safety signal of congestive heart failure in a small number of patients, and the authors called the safety profile unfavourable in that population [5] (verified).
62. Alzheimer's disease. A Merck-funded year-long trial in people with mild to moderate disease raised IGF-1 as expected and did nothing to slow progression [6,7] (verified). Coverage at the time put enrolment at 416 [7] (reported). It is the cleanest demonstration in the record that raising IGF-1 is not the same as producing a clinical benefit.
63. Sleep. One small study: eight young men on 5 mg, 25 mg and placebo for a week each, and six older adults on 2 mg then 25 mg for two weeks each. In the young group, stage IV sleep lasted about 50% longer and REM rose over 20% at the high dose; in the older group REM rose nearly 50% and REM latency fell [8] (verified). The older arm had no placebo period, and fourteen people in total is a thin base for the sleep reputation the compound has.
64. Children with growth hormone deficiency, the live programme. Phase 2 studies reportedly met their endpoints, one enrolling 104 children, and a 12-month placebo-controlled phase 3 in treatment-naive prepubertal children is recruiting, with a long-term extension planned [2] (reported).

### Safety: what the trials actually showed [people]
65. Glucose is the most consistent signal. Every longer trial in the record moved fasting glucose up and insulin sensitivity down [3,4] (verified). The mechanism is ordinary growth hormone physiology, which opposes insulin action, so this is expected rather than idiosyncratic, and it is dose- and duration-dependent rather than a rare event (inferred).
66. The heart failure signal is the one most often left out. It appeared in frail elderly patients recovering from surgery, a population prone to fluid overload, and the published abstract does not give the case count by arm [5]. It cannot be generalised to young healthy users, and it cannot be dismissed either: fluid retention is a known effect of raising growth hormone, and the drug did enough of it in that group to stop a trial (verified that the trial stopped; inferred on mechanism).
67. Appetite rises early and, in the older adult trial, settled in most people within about three months [3] (reported). Cortisol rises acutely with dosing [1] (reported).
68. What has not been studied: no trial has looked at healthy adults under 60 for more than weeks, none has examined cancer incidence despite the sustained IGF-1 rise, and none has followed users beyond about two years.

### What is actually in the bottle [lab]
69. It is a small molecule, not a peptide, so the identity and stability problems that dominate peptide products are less severe here: it is a stable salt (the mesylate) that survives being made into capsules or liquids (inferred from chemistry). The quality problem is different. Outside the LUM-201 programme there is no pharmaceutical-grade supply, so every grey-market product is a research chemical with whatever purity and dose accuracy its maker provides. No published independent survey of retail MK-677 content was found for this review.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
70. Not approved anywhere. In the US it is an investigational drug, in phase 3 as LUM-201 for paediatric growth hormone deficiency, with orphan designations in the US and EU [1,2] (verified).
71. In sport it is named in the WADA Prohibited List under S2 as a growth hormone secretagogue, prohibited at all times [9] (verified). Urinary metabolites are the detection target in anti-doping work.

### Open questions [mixed]
72. Does lean mass gained this way ever become strength or function? The best trial says no at one year in older adults; nobody has tested younger people properly.
73. What is the glucose cost over years? Every trial moved glucose the wrong way, and none ran long enough to show whether that becomes diabetes in susceptible people.
74. How many heart failure cases were there, and in which arm? The answer sits in the full hip fracture paper and the trial's internal data.
75. Will a paediatric approval change access? If LUM-201 is approved, the molecule gets a label, a reference standard and a pharmacovigilance record for the first time, which would change how the rest of the evidence can be read.

# Eloralintide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/eloralintide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: LY3841136
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain
3. Sequence: CNTATCATGKLAEFLVRSSNNFGPKLPPTEVGSNTY (36 amino acids). X (ornithine) shown as K; Amylin-based; N-terminal gGlu cap; alpha-methyl-Phe and N-methyl-Asn swaps; Cys bridge; Lys carries a C20 diacid via gGlu-gGlu; C-terminal amide
4. Legal and approval status: Investigational as of 22 Oct 2026: Phase 3 ENLIGHTEN program recruiting since 2026, results expected around 2028. Not approved anywhere; WADA S0 (non-approved substance) applies (inferred).

## Summary
5. Eloralintide is Lilly's once-weekly amylin analogue, tilted toward the amylin-1 receptor. It is thought to signal fullness and slow stomach emptying, and is being developed for obesity alone or alongside tirzepatide. A 48-week Phase 2 trial showed up to 20.1% weight loss, but it is unapproved and Phase 3 results are expected around 2028.
6. Punch line: Lilly's weekly amylin shot, working through fullness rather than GLP-1. Phase 2 hit about 20% weight loss.
7. Used for: Weight loss

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Appetite & satiety: Fullness via amylin receptors
9. Fat metabolism: Up to 20% weight loss
10. Glucose & insulin: Slows post-meal glucose rise
11. Digestive & gut: Slows stomach emptying
12. Cellular energy (backed only by animal or user reports): Fatigue on higher doses
13. Hair (backed only by animal or user reports): Hair loss at 9 mg
14. Heart & vessels (backed only by animal or user reports): Slow heart rate signal

## How it works
15. Signals fullness to the brainstem · Amylin-1 receptor (CTR + RAMP1) · role Appetite & satiety
   Eloralintide activates the amylin-1 receptor, a calcitonin receptor paired with RAMP1, about 12-fold more than the plain calcitonin receptor. Amylin signalling in the area postrema and brainstem produces a sense of fullness. In the Phase 2 trial this drove up to 20.1% weight loss at 9 mg.
16. Slows stomach emptying · Amylin receptor, vagal · role Digestive & gut
   Amylin receptor signalling, partly through the vagus nerve, slows how fast the stomach empties into the gut. Food stays longer, fullness lasts longer and sugar enters the blood more slowly. It also explains much of the nausea, which was the most common side effect in trials.
17. Blunts glucagon after meals · Amylin receptor, pancreas · role Glucose & insulin
   After meals, amylin action on the pancreas holds back glucagon, the hormone that tells the liver to release sugar. Lower glucagon means a smaller blood sugar rise. HbA1c fell in every active trial arm even though no one had diabetes.
18. Fatty tail rides albumin for weekly dosing · C20 diacid acylation · role Fat metabolism
   A C20 fatty diacid chain on the molecule binds albumin, the main protein in blood. Bound to albumin, it is shielded from breakdown and kidney clearance, so it lasts long enough for weekly dosing. No human half-life has been published.
19. Mechanism overview: Eloralintide is a 36-residue amylin analogue with non-natural residues (ornithine, alpha-methyl-Phe, N-methyl-Asn) for stability and a C20 fatty diacid that binds albumin for weekly dosing. It preferentially activates the amylin-1 receptor, a calcitonin receptor paired with RAMP1, about 12-fold over the plain calcitonin receptor. Amylin signalling in the area postrema and brainstem produces fullness, slows gastric emptying and blunts post-meal glucagon. In rats it caused less conditioned taste aversion than cagrilintide.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
20. Typical: 1–9 mg (trial) · once weekly · cycle Ongoing; 3 → 6 → 9 mg escalation best tolerated · route Sub-Q (verified)
21. Half-life: Not published
22. Most people take: Trial only: weekly Sub-Q 1, 3, 6 or 9 mg; slow 3/6/9 mg escalation had GI rates near placebo. No oral form.

## What people report
23. Almost no genuine first-hand reports; research-chemical listings exist, and interest centres on amylin as a gentler GLP-1 alternative or add-on.
24. Liked / worked: Up to 20.1% weight loss at 48 weeks
25. Liked / worked: 82% lost 10% or more on 9 mg
26. Liked / worked: Low doses near placebo for GI effects
27. Liked / worked: Weight still falling at 48 weeks
28. What worked: Up to 20.1% weight loss at 48 weeks on 9 mg, still falling at trial end; 82% on 9 mg lost at least 10%. Lower doses were close to placebo for GI effects.
29. Went wrong / did not work: Fatigue ~43% on 9 mg
30. Went wrong / did not work: Nausea dose-related
31. Went wrong / did not work: Hair loss 11% on 9 mg
32. Went wrong / did not work: Slow heart rate 11% on 6 mg
33. What went wrong: Dose-related nausea and fatigue (fatigue ~43% on 9 mg), hair loss in 11% on 9 mg and a slow heart rate in 11% on 6 mg in small arms; long-term safety unknown.
34. Most reported: Seen as a gentler GLP-1 alternative
35. Most reported: Interest in stacking with tirzepatide
36. Most reported: Almost no first-hand reports

## What has been tested
37. Fat metabolism: Obesity without diabetes, Phase 2 (human)
38. Glucose & insulin: Obesity with T2D, ENLIGHTEN-2 (human)
39. Appetite & satiety: Taste aversion vs cagrilintide (animal)
40. Phase 1 and a 48-week Phase 2 in 263 adults (The Lancet, 2025); Phase 3 ENLIGHTEN trials began 2026, including type 2 diabetes and tirzepatide combinations.
41. What it helps: A 48-week Phase 2 trial showed up to 20.1% weight loss on 9 mg, with GI effects near placebo on low doses and slow escalation. Fatigue, nausea and small signals for hair loss and slow heart rate need Phase 3 clarity. People look at it as a gentler alternative or add-on to GLP-1 drugs.
42. Trial: active · Phase 3 · obesity · NCT07321886 · Eli Lilly. Lilly's amylin shot moved to Phase 3 in February 2026 and is recruiting across US sites. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (verified)

## Who shouldn't take it
43. Insulin or sulfonylurea users: Amylin analogues add to insulin; severe lows risk. (inferred)
44. Anyone booked for surgery, endoscopy or sedation: Delayed gastric emptying; aspiration risk. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
45. Tirzepatide: Tirzepatide quiets hunger through GLP-1 and GIP receptors, while eloralintide adds fullness through the separate amylin pathway in the brainstem. The two-pathway logic is being tested in a Phase 2 trial in type 2 diabetes, but results are not yet published.
46. Retatrutide: Retatrutide works on GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors to cut hunger and burn liver fat, and eloralintide adds amylin-driven fullness. People eye the pair for maximum weight loss, but the pairing is user logic, not trial data, and both are investigational.

## Where it comes from
47. Lilly's once-weekly amylin analogue, engineered to favour the amylin-1 receptor over the calcitonin receptor, with a C20 fatty tail for weekly dosing.
48. First studied for: Obesity, alone or alongside tirzepatide.
49. Name story: Eli Lilly's weekly amylin drug, coded LY3841136 before it got a real name. The "-lintide" ending is the naming stem for amylin analogues, shared with pramlintide and cagrilintide; amylin is the hormone beta cells release alongside insulin. [S2] (verified)
50. 2024: Phase 1: 2.6–11.3% weight loss at 12 weeks
51. Nov 2025: Phase 2: up to 20.1% at 48 weeks (Lancet)
52. 2026: Phase 3 ENLIGHTEN trials start
53. Today: Hair loss and slow heart rate signals in small arms unexplained

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Why a selective amylin drug, and what that choice is betting on [mixed]
54. Amylin is a hormone released from the same beta cells as insulin. Its receptors are not a single protein: they are the calcitonin receptor paired with one of three accessory proteins called RAMPs, and the calcitonin receptor alone is a separate target again. The first long-acting amylin drug in the current wave, cagrilintide, hits amylin and calcitonin receptors more or less equally. Eloralintide was built to do the opposite, favouring the amylin receptors over the plain calcitonin receptor [1] (verified that selectivity was the design aim).
55. The discovery work tested the molecule in cells carrying rat or human amylin-1, amylin-3 or calcitonin receptors, then in rats and monkeys, before moving to people [1] (verified). The bet behind selectivity is that fullness and slower stomach emptying come mostly from the amylin receptors in the brainstem, while some of the nausea and taste aversion come from broader calcitonin receptor activation (inferred; the rat taste-aversion comparison on the card is the main published support, and nobody has shown the same separation in humans).
56. Whether the bet pays off clinically is still open. Nausea was the single most common adverse event in the phase 2 trial [3], so selectivity did not remove the class's main side effect; what the trial suggests is that it can be managed by dosing speed (see below).

### The human record [people]
57. Phase 1, about 100 people over 12 weeks of weekly multiple ascending doses: weight fell between 2.6% and 11.3% depending on dose, with diarrhoea in about 10% and fewer reporting nausea or vomiting [2,4] (reported). For a 12-week study that is a steep curve, comparable to early data for the incretin drugs.
58. Phase 2, 263 adults with obesity or overweight and no diabetes, 48 weeks, seven arms: placebo, fixed 1, 3, 6 or 9 mg, and two escalation schemes (6 then 9 mg; 3 then 6 then 9 mg). Baseline weight averaged 109 kg and 78% of participants were women [3,5] (verified).
59. Weight change on the efficacy estimand was 9.5% on 1 mg, 12.4% on 3 mg, 17.6% on 6 mg, 20.1% on 9 mg, 19.9% on 6 then 9, and 16.4% on 3 then 6 then 9, against 0.4% on placebo [3,5] (verified). Counting everyone regardless of whether they stayed on treatment, the 9 mg figure falls to 17.5% and placebo rises to 2.3% [3]. At 9 mg, 57% lost at least 20% of body weight and 19% lost at least 30% [3].
60. Body composition was measured: 60 to 70% of the weight lost was fat [3] (reported). HbA1c fell in every active arm against placebo even though nobody had diabetes, and fasting glucose, HDL and triglycerides improved significantly in the 9 mg and escalation arms [3] (reported). The primary endpoint was not adjusted for multiple comparisons across seven arms [5], which is normal for a dose-finding study but means individual arm differences should be read as estimates.

### Safety: the dose-speed finding, and the signals that need checking [people]
61. Overall adverse events were almost identical between drug and placebo, 81% against 79%, and serious adverse events were 5.3% against 5.4% with no deaths [3] (verified). That near-match partly reflects how often placebo groups report symptoms in a year-long trial, so the per-symptom picture is more informative.
62. Nausea (33%) and fatigue (27%) were the most common events across the pooled drug arms [3]. Gastrointestinal events clustered in the 6 mg, 9 mg and 6 then 9 arms; the slow 3 then 6 then 9 escalation had rates close to placebo and still produced 16% weight loss [3,5] (verified). That is the most practically useful finding in the trial: speed of escalation, not final dose, drove most of the stomach trouble.
63. Fatigue is the less familiar signal. It is not a prominent effect of the incretin drugs, it was common here, and all four severe gastrointestinal events were reported alongside fatigue [3] (reported). Why an amylin agonist would cause tiredness has not been explained in anything published.
64. The card's mentions of hair loss at 9 mg and a slower heart rate could not be confirmed in the trial reports accessible for this review; neither appears in the sponsor's release or the conference coverage [3,5]. They may sit in the full paper's supplementary tables, which could not be opened. They are flagged here as unconfirmed rather than repeated.

### What the body does with it [people]
65. The C20 fatty diacid lets it ride on albumin for once-weekly dosing. No human half-life has been published in a source accessible for this review, and the sponsor has not stated one; the phase 1 paper is the place it would appear [2]. Nothing is known publicly about how it is cleared or whether kidney or liver impairment changes exposure.

### Who produced the evidence [people]
66. Every study, from receptor assays to phase 2, was designed and funded by the developer [1,2,3]. The phase 2 paper went through peer review at The Lancet [5]. No independent trial exists, which is the normal state for a drug at this stage and also means the safety picture rests on about 360 treated people in total.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
67. Investigational everywhere. The phase 3 programme, named ENLIGHTEN, opened in 2026: trials in obesity without diabetes, obesity with type 2 diabetes, and obstructive sleep apnoea, the last planning 800 participants for up to 64 weeks of treatment against placebo [6] (verified). A separate phase 2 is testing it alone and with tirzepatide in people with type 2 diabetes [5].
68. In sport it falls under WADA's S0 class for substances with no regulatory approval, prohibited at all times (inferred from the class definition; it is not named on the list).

### Open questions [mixed]
69. Does amylin selectivity matter in humans, or does the escalation schedule explain the tolerability on its own?
70. Why fatigue? It was common, it tracked with the severe events, and no mechanism has been proposed.
71. What do the full safety tables show on heart rate and hair? Phase 3, with thousands of participants, will settle whether those are real signals.
72. How does it combine with an incretin drug? The rationale is two separate fullness pathways; the combination trial is where that gets tested.

Deep read references:
[1] Lilly investigators, 2025, eloralintide (LY3841136), a novel amylin receptor agonist: from discovery to clinical proof of concept, 2025 · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41109426/
