# GHK-Cu + BPC-157
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/ghk-cu-bpc-157
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: GHK-Cu/BPC-157 70 mg, copper peptide + BPC, GLOW without TB-500
2. Origin: Blend of 2 peptides
3. Legal and approval status: US: not approved. Both removed from FDA Category 2 on 15 Apr 2026 (GHK-Cu for injection). BPC-157 won an 8-6-1 PCAC vote in July 2026; GHK-Cu goes to a panel before end of Feb 2027. WADA: BPC-157 banned since 2022 (S0). EU, UK, Australia: no approved product.

## Summary
4. This blend combines GHK-Cu, a copper tripeptide, with BPC-157 in one vial, essentially GLOW without TB-500. People pair them so BPC-157 covers tendon, muscle and gut healing while GHK-Cu covers collagen, skin and scars. Evidence is per component and mostly animal, no study tests the two together, and GHK-Cu makes up most of the vial and its sting.
5. Punch line: GLOW minus TB-500. BPC-157 heals tendon, muscle and gut while the copper peptide rebuilds collagen, skin and scars.
6. Used for: Injury repair with skin and scar support

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Tissue repair: BPC-157 tendon, muscle and wound healing in animals
8. Skin & aesthetics: GHK-Cu collagen and skin repair
9. Digestive & gut: BPC-157 gut lining protection in animals
10. Inflammatory signaling: Both dampen inflammation
11. Hair (backed only by animal or user reports): GHK-Cu used for hair density

## How it works
12. Speeds tendon, muscle and gut healing in animals · Angiogenesis, FAK-paxillin, NO system · role Tissue repair
   BPC-157 drives new vessel growth, moves fibroblasts into the injury through FAK-paxillin, and steadies nitric oxide signalling. That speeds tendon, muscle and gut healing in rodent models. Human data are a small knee report and an unfinished Phase 1.
13. Protects gut lining · Gastric cytoprotection · role Digestive & gut
   BPC-157 protects the gut lining, an effect called gastric cytoprotection, shown against damage such as NSAID injury in rats. It is where the peptide was first studied. The one human trial was a rectal colitis study that regulators judged inadequate.
14. Turns on collagen building in skin · Fibroblast collagen and decorin synthesis · role Skin & aesthetics
   GHK-Cu signals fibroblasts to make more collagen and decorin, a protein that organises collagen fibres. It also shifts the balance of matrix metalloproteinases, the enzymes that remodel tissue. This is shown in cell, animal and small topical human skin studies.
15. Carries copper to healing tissue · Cu(II) bound to Gly-His-Lys · role Tissue repair
   GHK-Cu is Gly-His-Lys holding a copper ion tightly, and it delivers that copper to rebuilding tissue. Copper is needed by enzymes such as lysyl oxidase that cross-link collagen. BPC-157 has no strong copper site, so it does not strip copper from GHK in the vial.
16. Mechanism overview: BPC-157 is a 15-residue fragment of a gastric protein; in rodent injury models it promotes angiogenesis, tendon fibroblast migration (FAK-paxillin) and nitric oxide balance, and protects the gut lining. GHK-Cu is Gly-His-Lys bound to Cu(II); it raises collagen and decorin synthesis and modulates matrix metalloproteinases. BPC-157 has no His and no strong copper site, so it does not strip copper from GHK. The pair targets deep tissue repair plus surface matrix and skin.

## What is inside the blend
17. GHK-Cu: 50 mg · Collagen, skin and scar remodelling; carries copper
18. BPC-157: 20 mg · Tendon, muscle and gut healing
19. Most common ratio: GHK-Cu 50 · BPC-157 10 = 60 mg (1 listing (URL slug only))
20. Version Common retail: GHK-Cu 50 · BPC-157 20 = 70 mg
21. Why GHK-Cu is in it: Skin, scar and hair matrix work that BPC-157 is not used for
22. Why BPC-157 is in it: Deep injury and gut repair; GHK-Cu has little evidence for tendon or gut
23. Mixing chemistry: BPC-157 is most stable around pH 6.5 to 8.5 by its own patent; GHK-Cu keeps its copper above about pH 4. A vial at near-neutral pH suits both reasonably.
24. Mixing chemistry: BPC-157 acetate liquid can sit near pH 3.9; drawn into a copper vial in volume it pushes pH down toward where copper loosens.
25. Mixing chemistry: Blue means the copper complex is intact; green or brown suggests copper has come off.
26. Mixing chemistry: No vitamin C or glutathione in the same vial or syringe: copper plus a reducer drives oxidation.
27. Mixing chemistry: Ask for per-component mg; GLOW certificates show BPC-157 running up to 17% over label.
28. Self-mixing: Mixing separate vials lets you set your own ratio, but each vial carries its own salt and pH, so the combined liquid lands at an unknown pH and overfill errors stack.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
29. Typical: 250–500 mcg BPC-157 equivalent · 1× daily · cycle 4–8 weeks · route Sub-Q (reported)
30. Half-life: per component
31. Most people take: No standard blend dose. 70 mg in 3 mL: 10 units gives about 1.7 mg GHK-Cu and 0.67 mg BPC-157, so many draw 5 to 8 units to land BPC-157 at 330 to 530 mcg.

## What people report
32. Usually Sub-Q once daily. People size it on BPC-157 (250 to 500 mcg), which brings 0.6 to 1.25 mg GHK-Cu, or on GHK-Cu (1 to 2 mg), which brings 0.4 to 0.8 mg BPC-157. Often injected near the injury.
33. Liked / worked: Covers injury repair and skin in one shot
34. Liked / worked: Strong animal repair data for BPC-157
35. Liked / worked: Copper stays bound at near-neutral pH
36. What worked: No blend-specific report pool. Stack users give each peptide a lane: BPC-157 for injury and gut, GHK-Cu for skin, scars and hair. Reports from the related GLOW blend describe faster wound and scar healing and better skin texture.
37. Went wrong / did not work: No trial of the pair
38. Went wrong / did not work: Different pH comfort zones
39. Went wrong / did not work: GHK-Cu sting with every dose
40. What went wrong: GHK-Cu is most of the vial, so its sting, redness and flushing come with every dose. BPC-157 and GHK-Cu prefer different pH ranges, so a shared vial is a compromise. No human efficacy data for injected use of either.
41. Most reported: Sized on BPC-157, 250 to 500 mcg
42. Most reported: Injected near the injury
43. Most reported: Picked for scars and skin after surgery

## What has been tested
44. Never tested as a combination. A stack guide updated 29 Sep 2026 states no controlled human trial has tested BPC-157 with GHK-Cu for any use. BPC-157 has animal injury models and very thin human data; GHK-Cu has cell, animal and small topical human studies.
45. What it helps: Evidence is per component and mostly animal. BPC-157 speeds tendon, ligament, muscle and gut healing in rodents; human data is a 12-patient knee report and an unfinished phase I. GHK-Cu has cell, animal and small topical human skin studies. No study tests the two together.

## Who shouldn't take it
46. Wilson's disease or copper overload: Each dose delivers copper; people who cannot clear copper accumulate it in liver and brain. (inferred)
47. People with active or recent cancer: Raises VEGFR2 signalling and new vessel growth in animal work; tumours use the same pathway. (inferred)
48. People with cholestatic liver disease: Copper leaves the body through bile; PBC, PSC and bile duct blockage raise body copper. (inferred)
49. Drug-tested athletes: Banned since 2022 under S0 (non-approved substances); positives have led to bans. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
50. Thymosin Beta-4: Thymosin beta-4 adds actin-driven cell migration and anti-inflammatory action to the blend's vessel growth and collagen work. Adding it makes the three-part GLOW stack. In the only rat study, BPC-157 plus TB-500 added nothing over either alone.
51. KPV: KPV blocks NF-κB in gut and immune cells, while the blend covers deep repair and skin matrix. People add it for inflamed skin or gut. Adding it gives the KLOW-style stack, but this pairing has not been tested.
52. TB-500 frag 17–23: The fragment carries the actin-binding region of thymosin beta-4 and is used for cell migration into wounds. It fills the same role as full TB-500 in GLOW. Data come mostly from the full 43-mer, and the pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
53. A two-peptide vial: GHK-Cu (50 mg) with BPC-157 (20 mg). It is GLOW without TB-500, with more BPC-157 per vial.
54. First studied for: Sold as a repair and skin blend: BPC-157 for tendon, muscle and gut healing, GHK-Cu for collagen, skin and scars.
55. 1973: GHK-Cu isolated from human plasma
56. 1993: BPC-157 first published by Sikiric's Zagreb group
57. 2020s: GLOW blend spreads; two-peptide GHK-Cu + BPC-157 vials follow
58. Apr 2026: Both removed from FDA Category 2
59. Jul 2026: BPC-157 wins PCAC vote 8 to 6
60. Today: Sold as a repair and skin blend, 50 + 20 mg

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where the pairing came from [mixed]
61. Neither compound was developed with the other in mind. The copper tripeptide comes out of 1970s plasma research and a cosmetic and wound-care programme [1]; the gastric peptide comes out of a Zagreb laboratory's gut and injury work from 1993 onward [2]. The two-peptide vial is a retail descendant of larger multi-peptide repair blends, built by subtraction rather than by any study showing that these two belong together (inferred from the order in which the products appeared; no scientific paper proposes this pair).
62. The rationale offered for it is division of labour: one for deep tissue, one for skin and matrix. That is a reasonable way to describe what each has been studied for. It is not evidence that combining them does more than either alone, and nobody has tested that (verified as absent; no study of the combination in cells, animals or people was found).

### The two halves have different kinds of evidence, by different routes [mixed]
63. The gastric peptide's evidence is almost entirely rodent injury models from one founding group, with one controlled human trial: a 2005 meeting abstract in ulcerative colitis using an enema, whose result regulators judged inadequate [2] (verified). No human pharmacokinetic data exist for injection, and in the rectal studies where plasma was measured, levels were undetectable or below quantification [2].
64. The copper tripeptide's human evidence is topical, small and short, and its one large test failed. Two phase 3 trials in diabetic foot ulcers, 511 patients across 30 centres at 0.5% and 2% against placebo, found it no better than placebo [3,4] (verified). The injected route has never been studied in people.
65. So the blend is injected, while the human data that exist were gathered rectally for one component and on the skin for the other. In route terms, the vial has no human evidence behind either half (inferred from the above, and the most important thing to understand about it).

### What the copper adds that a plain peptide blend does not [lab]
66. The copper tripeptide is roughly 16% copper by mass, from its formula (inferred, calculated). A 50 mg share of copper peptide therefore carries about 8 mg of elemental copper across the whole vial. For scale, the adult dietary requirement is 0.9 mg a day and the upper intake limit is 10 mg a day, a limit set on liver damage [5] (verified).
67. The comparison is imperfect in a way that matters. The body controls copper mainly at the gut, by adjusting how much it absorbs, and at the liver, by excreting it into bile [5] (verified). An injection skips the first of those controls. Whether the copper stays bound to its peptide long enough to be handled differently from free copper, and where it goes once the peptide is broken down, has not been studied for injection (verified as absent).
68. The chemistry of the bound complex is the best-established part of the copper story: held by the tripeptide, copper's ability to drive damaging redox reactions is largely silenced [1] (verified, in vitro). That protection depends on the copper staying bound. Anything in the solution that competes for copper or reduces it works against that, which is the underlying reason the mixing rules on the card exist (inferred).

### Mixing and stability: what is known and what is assumed [lab]
69. For the gastric peptide, regulators recorded that the lyophilised powder should be kept below minus 18 degrees and that reconstituted solution is stable for two to three weeks refrigerated [2] (verified). That is the shortest documented window of the two components and, in a combined vial, it sets the realistic life of the whole solution once mixed (inferred).
70. No stability study of the two together exists. Whether the gastric peptide, which carries two neighbouring aspartates and a lysine, takes up any copper from the complex at the concentrations in a vial has not been measured; the card's statement that it has no strong copper site is a reasonable reading of its sequence, not a tested result (inferred).
71. The quality problems recorded for the gastric peptide on its own, unidentified impurities and no endotoxin, bioburden or aggregate testing on the certificates regulators reviewed [2], carry over unchanged into a blend. Injectable copper tripeptide has had no equivalent public review at all [6] (verified).

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
72. No approved product contains either component, alone or together. In the US the gastric peptide was removed from the do-not-compound category in April 2026 after nominations were withdrawn, then recommended for the 503A bulks list by an advisory committee in July by 8 to 6 with one abstention, against the agency's own staff recommendation [2,7]. That vote is advisory and requires rulemaking that has not begun [8] (verified).
73. Injectable copper tripeptide is in a different position: the topical form was restored to Category 1 in May 2026, the injectable route was left unclassified, and its advisory review is expected before the end of February 2027 [6,8] (verified). So a combined injectable draws on one substance recommended but not yet permitted and one whose injectable form has not been assessed.
74. In sport, the gastric peptide is prohibited at all times under WADA's non-approved substances class [2]; the copper tripeptide is not named, but injected use of an unapproved substance falls under the same catch-all (inferred).

### Open questions [mixed]
75. Does the pair do anything the components do not? Untested.
76. Where does injected copper go, and does repeated dosing shift copper balance? Unstudied for either the single agent or the blend, and it is the larger component by mass.
77. Does the gastric peptide interact with the copper complex in solution? Answerable with routine analytical chemistry, never published.
78. If someone responds, to which half? A fixed-ratio vial makes that impossible to tell.

# Glutathione
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/glutathione
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: GSH, reduced glutathione, L-glutathione, gamma-L-glutamyl-L-cysteinylglycine, philothion (historic)
2. Origin: Made by the body, by enzymes
3. Sequence: ECG (3 amino acids). E is linked through its side chain (gamma bond), not the usual backbone
4. Shown with an FDA approved badge
5. Legal and approval status: NAC is approved; glutathione itself is compounded/supplement-grade, not an approved anti-aging drug.

## Summary
6. Glutathione is the body's main antioxidant, a tripeptide built by two enzymes and present in every cell. It is given IV or by injection to raise antioxidant capacity, support the liver and, popularly, lighten skin. Its precursor NAC is an approved drug, but skin-lightening trials are small and mixed, and oral glutathione is barely absorbed.
7. Punch line: The body's master antioxidant. Given IV or injected for skin brightening and liver support; oral barely absorbs.
8. Used for: Skin brightening, antioxidant support

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
9. Cellular protection: The body's main antioxidant
10. Skin & aesthetics: Brighter skin claims
11. Organ function: Liver detox support
12. Neural protection: Studied in Parkinson's
13. Immunity (backed only by animal or user reports): Immune cell fuel
14. Cellular energy (backed only by animal or user reports): More energy reported

## How it works
15. Neutralises peroxides and free radicals · Glutathione peroxidase · role Cellular protection
   Glutathione peroxidase uses glutathione's cysteine thiol to donate electrons, turning hydrogen peroxide and lipid peroxides into water and harmless alcohols. This is a core antioxidant defence inside nearly every cell. It is textbook biochemistry, though whether glutathione given from outside adds to it in people is still open.
16. Tags toxins for removal · Glutathione S-transferase · role Organ function
   Glutathione S-transferases attach glutathione to toxins and drug breakdown products, making them water soluble so they leave in bile or urine. This conjugation is a main liver detox route. It is why its precursor NAC is the approved antidote for acetaminophen overdose.
17. Tilts melanin toward lighter pigment · Tyrosinase, pheomelanin · role Skin & aesthetics
   In melanocytes, glutathione pushes tyrosinase output away from dark eumelanin toward lighter pheomelanin. That is the basis for skin brightening claims, shown in cell work. Human trials are small and mixed, and any lightening seen faded once dosing stopped.
18. Recycles vitamins C and E · GSH/GSSG redox cycling · role Cellular protection
   After donating electrons, glutathione pairs up as oxidised GSSG, and glutathione reductase converts it back to active GSH. In that cycle it also regenerates vitamin C, which in turn helps restore vitamin E. This keeps the cell's wider antioxidant network running.
19. Main antioxidant pool in brain cells · Neuronal/astrocyte GSH · role Neural protection
   Neurons and astrocytes rely on glutathione as their main antioxidant pool, with astrocytes supplying building blocks to neurons. Low glutathione is found in the brain region that degenerates in Parkinson's disease. IV and nasal trials have not beaten placebo so far.
20. Supports T-cell growth and function · Lymphocyte redox control · role Immunity
   Lymphocytes need a well reduced redox balance to multiply, and glutathione sets that balance. In a six-month human trial, daily oral glutathione raised lymphocyte stores, and natural killer cell activity rose on the high dose as a secondary outcome. Disease outcomes were not measured.
21. Mechanism overview: Glutathione is a tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine and glycine, the glutamate linked by its side chain, so cells build it with two enzymes rather than ribosomes. Its cysteine thiol donates electrons. Glutathione peroxidase uses it to neutralise peroxides, and glutathione S-transferases attach it to toxins for excretion. It recycles vitamins C and E and supports T-cell proliferation. In melanocytes it pushes tyrosinase output toward lighter pheomelanin. It is the main antioxidant pool in neurons and astrocytes.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
22. Typical: 600–1500 mg · 1–3× weekly · cycle Continuous or as courses · route IM, IV (reported)
23. Half-life: ~10 minutes
24. Dose note: 600–1200 mg is an IV clinic dose. A Philippine FDA advisory links high IV doses to serious skin, thyroid and kidney reactions.
25. Most people take: 600-1500mg IV or IM, 1-3x/week · Continuous or as courses.
26. Oral daily: 250–1000 mg · 1–2× daily · 1–6 mo · Oral (incl. liposomal) · for general antioxidant [S1] [S2] (verified)
27. IM/Sub-Q shot: 100–600 mg · 1–3× weekly · 4–12 wk or year-round · IM, Sub-Q · for wellness users self-injecting [S2] [S3] (reported)
28. IV push (skin): 600–1200 mg (to 1400) · 1–2× weekly · courses · IV · for skin-lightening clinics [S4] [S5] (reported)

## What people report
29. IV and SC; reported for skin brightening, energy and recovery.
30. Liked / worked: NAC is an approved antidote
31. Liked / worked: Some signal in Parkinson's and fatty liver
32. What worked: Clear role in detoxification and as an antioxidant; NAC (its precursor) is an approved antidote.
33. Went wrong / did not work: Oral barely absorbed
34. Went wrong / did not work: Injected clears fast
35. Went wrong / did not work: Skin trials small and mixed
36. What went wrong: The skin-lightening and anti-aging IV trend outruns the evidence; injected glutathione clears fast and oral does little.
37. Most reported: Skin brightening
38. Most reported: Energy and recovery

## What has been tested
39. Cellular protection: Acetaminophen overdose, as NAC (human)
40. Neural protection: Parkinson's (trial)
41. Organ function: Fatty liver (trial)
42. Skin & aesthetics: Skin lightening (trial)
43. Oral absorption is poor; IV raises levels briefly. Human trials: used in acetaminophen overdose (as its precursor NAC), some signal in Parkinson's and fatty liver; skin-lightening trials are small and mixed.
44. What it helps: Its precursor NAC is the approved antidote for acetaminophen overdose. Trials show some signal in Parkinson's disease and fatty liver. Skin-lightening trials are small and mixed. Oral glutathione is barely absorbed and injected doses clear fast. Users take it IV or by injection for skin brightening, energy and recovery.
45. Trial: active · Phase 2 · Parkinson's disease (nasal insulin plus glutathione) · NCT05266417 · Gateway Institute for Brain Research. Several glutathione trials are recruiting, including a nasal spray for Parkinson's running to 2027. (checked 2026-10-23) [S6] (verified)

## Who shouldn't take it
46. People with asthma (inhaled form): Nebulised glutathione triggered bronchospasm. (reported)
47. People in chemotherapy or radiation: Antioxidant may shield tumour cells. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
48. Vitamin C: Vitamin C and glutathione recycle each other in the cell's antioxidant network, and both are taken for skin brightening. People pair them to keep both antioxidants topped up. The pair has not been tested together in controlled trials.
49. NAC: NAC supplies cysteine, the slowest building block in the cell's own glutathione production, while glutathione adds the finished molecule from outside. People pair them to raise stores from two directions. NAC alone is the proven route, in acetaminophen overdose, and the pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
50. The body's main antioxidant, a tripeptide whose glutamate is joined by its side chain, a link ribosomes cannot make, so two enzymes build it. Present in every cell.
51. First studied for: Given IV and by injection to raise antioxidant capacity, support the liver, and (popularly) lighten skin.
52. Name story: First spotted in yeast in 1888 and called "philothion", Greek for "love of sulfur". Hopkins renamed it in 1921 (glutamate plus thio, sulfur) believing it a two-amino-acid peptide; in 1929 he corrected himself and added glycine. [S7] (verified)
53. 1920s: Identified as a cellular tripeptide
54. 1970s to 1980s: Precursor NAC becomes the acetaminophen overdose antidote
55. Today: IV skin-brightening and antioxidant trend that outruns its data

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### The core problem: the body makes it inside cells, and it is hard to deliver there [people]
56. Glutathione is made inside nearly every cell from three amino acids, and it does its work there. Blood levels are low by comparison: about 6 micromoles per litre in plasma in one human study [1] (verified), against concentrations inside cells that are orders of magnitude higher. So the question for any supplement is not whether glutathione matters, which is settled, but whether glutathione given from outside reaches the inside of the cells that need it.
57. The gut and liver are built to break it down. They carry an enzyme, gamma-glutamyl transferase, that splits it into its component amino acids [1] (verified). The cells then rebuild glutathione from those parts, and the slowest step in that rebuild is usually the supply of cysteine. That is why the precursor N-acetylcysteine became the approved antidote for paracetamol overdose rather than glutathione itself (inferred from the mechanism; NAC's approval is on the card).

### Oral: a negative result, then a positive one, and how they fit [people]
58. In 1992 a Swiss group gave seven healthy volunteers a single dose of about 3 g by mouth and followed blood for four and a half hours. Plasma glutathione, cysteine and glutamate did not rise significantly, and the authors concluded that oral glutathione's systemic availability was negligible [1] (verified).
59. In 2015 a US group ran a six-month randomised placebo-controlled trial in 54 healthy non-smokers on 250 or 1,000 mg a day. At six months the high dose had raised glutathione in red cells, plasma and lymphocytes by about 30 to 35%, and in cheek cells by about 260%; the low dose raised whole-blood levels 17%. Levels returned to baseline within a month of stopping. Natural killer cell activity more than doubled on the high dose at three months, a secondary outcome measured in a subset [2] (verified).
60. The two are less contradictory than they look. One measured a single dose over hours; the other measured daily dosing over months and found the rise built slowly. The likely reading is that oral glutathione does very little acutely but can shift body stores with sustained use, possibly by supplying its building blocks (inferred). The 2015 trial used a branded ingredient whose maker publicised the result [2], which is worth knowing though it does not undermine a randomised design.

### Skin lightening: what the trials actually tested [people]
61. The pigment mechanism is plausible and comes from cell work: glutathione shifts melanin production from dark eumelanin toward lighter pheomelanin. The human evidence is thinner than the market for it. A 2018 review identified two oral or sublingual studies and one topical trial, which together showed a good safety profile and appreciable but reversible effects on skin tone [3] (verified).
62. For intravenous use, the route most associated with lightening, the same review found a single study, and described its design as dubious and its analysis as apparently flawed, which casts doubt on both the efficacy and the adverse effects it reported [3] (verified). The authors called parenteral use for lightening unjustified. Injectable glutathione's approved uses, where it has them, are in severe liver disorders and in preventing chemotherapy nerve damage, not in skin [3].
63. Reversibility is the practically important word. Every positive result faded once dosing stopped [2,3], so lightening, where it happens, depends on continued use (verified).

### The brain: a reasonable idea that has not cleared a placebo [people]
64. Parkinson's disease involves low glutathione in the brain region that degenerates, which made it an obvious candidate. An open-label 1996 study of nine people reported improvement; a 2009 randomised placebo-controlled pilot in about 20 people found the infusions safe and well tolerated, with a possible symptomatic benefit that did not separate clearly from placebo [4,5] (verified).
65. The intranasal route was then tried, because the nose offers a partial path to the brain. A phase 2b trial randomised 45 people to placebo or two doses three times daily for 12 weeks. The high dose improved scores from baseline, but neither dose beat placebo, because the placebo group improved too, and everyone worsened in the washout. One high-dose participant developed a fast heart rate and cardiomyopathy and withdrew, with causation unclear [6] (verified). The authors concluded the data did not show superiority over placebo.

### Safety: the risk is mostly in the vial, not the molecule [people]
66. Glutathione itself has a long record of tolerability by mouth and on the skin [2,3]. The serious harms in the record come from contaminated injectable product, and they have recurred.
67. In 2019 the FDA reported seven clinic patients who, within minutes of a 1,400 mg infusion of compounded glutathione, developed nausea, vomiting, chills, body aches and in one case low blood pressure and breathing difficulty requiring hospital care; a separate patient was admitted after a 2,400 mg dose. The agency's testing found bacterial endotoxin in every sample, some at five times the appropriate limit, and traced the source to powder labelled for dietary supplement use that had been repackaged for sterile compounding [7] (verified).
68. It happened again in 2026. In August the FDA reported at least 30 patients with fever, chills, pain, dizziness and sepsis-like symptoms after intravenous glutathione, some hospitalised, again traced to supplement-grade powder from a single lot, again consistent with endotoxin, with recalls by two pharmacies [8] (verified). In September a further compounder recalled glutathione and two other IV products shipped to patients' homes, after nine adverse event reports [9] (reported).
69. The pattern is the point. The molecule is cheap and widely sold as a supplement ingredient, the same powder can end up in an injectable, and nothing in a finished vial tells the person receiving it which grade was used. For injectable use, ingredient grade and endotoxin testing matter more than dose (inferred from the two episodes).
70. What has not been studied: long-term high-dose intravenous use, which is how lightening clinics use it, has no controlled safety data at all [3].

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
71. In the US, glutathione is sold legally as an oral dietary supplement. Injectable glutathione is not an FDA-approved drug; it is made by compounding pharmacies, and the agency has twice warned them, in 2019 and August 2026, not to use supplement-grade ingredient for injectables [7,8] (verified). Some countries approve injectable glutathione for liver disease and chemotherapy neurotoxicity; none approves it for skin lightening [3]. A Philippine health authority advisory against off-label IV use for lightening dates from 2011 [3].
72. In sport the substance is not prohibited, but the method can be. WADA prohibits intravenous infusions or injections of more than 100 mL in total per 12 hours outside hospital treatment, surgery or clinical investigation [10] (verified). A typical IV drip exceeds that; a small push may not.

### Open questions [mixed]
73. Does raising blood glutathione by 30% change any outcome that matters to health? The 2015 trial measured stores and immune markers, not disease.
74. Is IV lightening real, and at what cost? One flawed study is the entire controlled record.
75. Would a precursor do the same job more cheaply and safely? Plausible by mechanism, rarely tested head to head.
76. Why did placebo do so well in the Parkinson's trial? The authors flagged it as worth studying in its own right.

# SLU-PP-332
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/slu-pp-332
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: slu pp 332 exercise mimetic, CAS 303760-60-3, 4-hydroxy-N'-(naphthalen-2-ylmethylidene)benzohydrazide
2. Origin: Not a peptide
3. Legal and approval status: Research chemical; no clinical program in humans.

## Summary
4. SLU-PP-332 is a small-molecule research chemical, not a peptide, called an exercise mimetic because it activates the ERR family of receptors that push cells toward an endurance state. It is studied for raising energy expenditure, endurance and fat loss without exercise. All data come from mice, there is no human safety or efficacy data, and first-hand grey-market reports are sparse.
5. Punch line: The exercise mimetic. Flips muscle into an endurance state through ERR receptors; mouse data only, no human safety.
6. Used for: Endurance, fat loss

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Cellular energy: Builds more mitochondria in mice
8. Muscle & performance: Longer running in mice
9. Fat metabolism: Fat loss in mice
10. Drive & mental stamina: Users report more stamina

## How it works
11. Pushes cells into an endurance state · ERR alpha, beta, gamma · role Muscle & performance
   SLU-PP-332 is a synthetic agonist of the estrogen-related receptors ERR alpha, beta and gamma, which are unrelated to estrogen itself. With the coactivator PGC-1 alpha, these receptors switch on endurance genes. In mice, the running effect required muscle ERR alpha.
12. Builds more mitochondria · ERR agonism · role Cellular energy
   Activating ERRs turns on genes that build new mitochondria, a process called mitochondrial biogenesis. Treated mouse muscle showed more mitochondria and more mitochondrial DNA and enzyme proteins. These results come only from mice given injections, with no human data.
13. Shifts muscle to burning fat · Fatty acid oxidation · role Fat metabolism
   The same gene programme shifts muscle toward burning fatty acids for fuel. In obese mice, treatment raised energy expenditure and cut fat gain without changing food intake or movement. No human safety or efficacy data exist.
14. Raised running endurance in mice · Oxidative fibre shift · role Drive & mental stamina
   Muscle fibres shifted toward the oxidative type built for endurance, and the fibres were smaller, the opposite of a muscle-building drug. Treated mice ran about 70% longer before exhaustion. All of this comes from one academic network and has not been replicated independently.
15. Mechanism overview: SLU-PP-332 is a synthetic small molecule agonist of the estrogen-related receptors ERR alpha, beta and gamma, strongest at ERR alpha. Despite the name, these orphan nuclear receptors are unrelated to estrogen signalling. With the coactivator PGC-1 alpha they control mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative metabolism. Activating them switches on genes for mitochondria, fatty acid oxidation and oxidative muscle fibres, mimicking the transcriptional effect of endurance training. In mice that means more mitochondria, more fat burning and longer running capacity.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
16. Typical: 500 mcg–1.5 mg · once daily · cycle 4–8 weeks · route Sub-Q (reported)
17. Half-life: short
18. Most people take: Injectable SC 500 mcg–1.5 mg/day. Oral 30–50 mg/day. No human dose; mouse 25 mg/kg IP.
19. Injected: 0.5–1 mg · 1× daily (some split 2×) · 4–8 wk on, 4–8 off · Sub-Q · for exercise mimetic, fat loss [S1] [S2] (reported)
20. Oral: 25–50 mg · 1× daily · 6–12 wk · Oral · for pill users [S1] [S2] (reported)
21. High: 1.5–2 mg inj or 100 mg oral · 1× daily or split · 4–8 wk · Sub-Q / Oral · for top of community ranges [S3] [S2] (reported)

## What people report
22. Very early grey-market use; reports are sparse.
23. Liked / worked: More mitochondria in mice
24. Liked / worked: Better endurance in mice
25. Liked / worked: Weight loss in mice
26. What worked: In mice, exercise-like metabolic gains and weight loss.
27. Went wrong / did not work: No human safety or efficacy data
28. Went wrong / did not work: BAM-15 pairing also unstudied in people
29. What went wrong: Entirely preclinical; no human safety or efficacy data. The catalog pairs it with BAM-15 as oral tablets, also unstudied in people.
30. Most reported: Few first-hand reports

## What has been tested
31. Cellular energy: Running endurance (mouse)
32. Fat metabolism: Weight and fat loss (mouse)
33. Mouse studies: more mitochondria, better running endurance, fat loss. No human data.
34. What it helps: All data are from mice. Treated mice ran longer, built more muscle mitochondria and lost weight and fat. There is no human safety or efficacy data, and the BAM-15 pairing seen online is also unstudied in people. Grey-market use is very early, and first-hand reports are sparse.
35. Trial: none. No registered human trial; all data are mouse and cell studies. (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
36. Drug-tested athletes: Sold as an "exercise mimetic"; metabolic modulators fall under WADA S4.4. (inferred)
37. People with heart disease: ERR agonism reshapes heart muscle metabolism; no human data at all. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
38. BAM-15: SLU-PP-332 switches on the genes that build mitochondria and burn fat, while BAM-15 lets protons leak across the mitochondrial membrane so cells burn more fuel to keep up. They are sold pre-mixed as SLU-PP-332 + BAM-15 oral. The pairing is unstudied in people.

## Where it comes from
39. A small-molecule 'exercise mimetic' from Saint Louis University that activates the ERR family of receptors, pushing cells toward the metabolic state of endurance exercise.
40. First studied for: Studied to raise energy expenditure and endurance without exercise.
41. Name story: 'SLU' almost certainly marks Saint Louis University, where the Burris and Walker labs built this series (a later sibling is SLU-PP-915). The papers never decode 'PP'. Despite the peptide shelf, it is a small hydrazone molecule. [S5] (inferred)
42. 2020s: Saint Louis University exercise mimetic shows endurance gains in mice
43. Today: Early grey-market oral, often paired with BAM-15; no human data

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where it came from: a tool compound from one academic network [lab]
44. It was designed by medicinal chemists working with Thomas Burris's group, across Saint Louis University, Washington University in St. Louis and later the University of Florida, as a probe for the estrogen-related receptors [1,2]. Those receptors had been studied almost entirely by switching them off genetically; a usable agonist let the group switch them on in a living animal (verified that this was the stated aim).
45. The published record is three papers from that network and its collaborators: an exercise paper in 2023, a metabolic syndrome paper in 2024, and a heart failure paper with a Baylor cardiology group in 2024 [1,2,3] (verified). No independent laboratory has published a replication, and no clinical programme has been announced. The group's own stated next steps were to refine the structure, ideally into something orally usable, and to do more animal safety work before any human trial [4] (reported).

### Mechanism, in the numbers the papers report [cells]
46. Potency depends on the assay. In a chimeric receptor assay the half-maximal concentrations were about 8 nanomolar for ERR alpha, 280 for beta and 770 for gamma; with the full-length receptors they were about 98, 230 and 430 [1] (verified). That is roughly four-fold preference for alpha in the more realistic assay, closer to a pan-agonist than the alpha label suggests.
47. The subtypes appear to carry different jobs. The endurance effect required muscle ERR alpha: in mice lacking it in muscle, treatment no longer improved running, and several target genes stopped responding [1] (verified, animals). In the heart, the protective effect ran mainly through ERR gamma [3] (verified, animals). One molecule is therefore doing two partly separate things in two organs.
48. The heart work also found that, alongside switching on fat-burning and mitochondrial genes, the agonists turned down cell-cycle and developmental gene programmes in heart muscle cells, partly through a regulator called E2F1 [3] (verified, animals and cells). In a failing heart that was presented as part of the benefit. What the same suppression does in tissues that divide normally has not been examined.

### What the animal studies measured [animals]
49. Endurance. Mice given the compound by intraperitoneal injection ran about 70% longer and about 45% further before exhaustion than vehicle-treated mice. Muscle showed stronger succinate dehydrogenase staining, more oxidative type IIa fibres, more mitochondria on electron microscopy, higher mitochondrial DNA relative to nuclear DNA, and more Complex I, Complex V and cytochrome c protein [1] (verified, animals). Myofibres were smaller in diameter, which is the opposite of a muscle-building drug and consistent with an endurance phenotype.
50. Obesity. In diet-induced obese mice, twice-daily treatment for a month produced about 12% weight loss, with roughly ten-fold less fat gained than untreated mice, improved insulin sensitivity and higher energy expenditure. Food intake did not change, and the mice did not move more; the investigator's summary was that they used more energy at rest [2,4] (reported for the numbers, which come from the university's release rather than the paper's abstract).
51. Heart failure. In a mouse pressure-overload model, this compound and a sibling improved ejection fraction, reduced fibrosis and improved survival without changing the degree of cardiac enlargement [3] (verified, animals). This is the strongest outcome in the whole record, and it is in a disease model rather than in healthy animals.

### What the body does with it, and why route matters [animals]
52. Exposure was measured in mice after a single 30 mg per kg intraperitoneal dose: about 0.8 micromolar in muscle and about 0.1 micromolar in plasma at two hours [1] (verified, animals). No plasma half-life, no oral bioavailability figure and no brain exposure were reported in the accessible version of that work, although brain was listed among tissues collected.
53. Every animal result above was produced by injection into the abdominal cavity, twice a day [1,2]. That is a laboratory route, not a human one, and the group's stated goal of making an orally usable version implies this molecule is not it (inferred from their own description [4]). Community oral and subcutaneous use is therefore extrapolating across both species and route from a compound whose oral behaviour has not been published.
54. No human pharmacokinetic data exist, and no established human dose exists.

### Safety: what has been looked at [animals]
55. The only safety assessment in the record is short. At 50 mg per kg twice daily for ten days in mice, the authors reported no overt toxicity, with normal blood counts and electrolytes and no significant change in creatine kinase [1] (verified, animals, ten days).
56. What that leaves untouched: no repeat-dose toxicology beyond those ten days, no genotoxicity, no reproductive or developmental studies, no carcinogenicity work, and no cardiac safety study in healthy animals. The heart results come from animals with induced heart failure, where raising oxidative metabolism helps; nothing tells you what sustained ERR activation does to a healthy heart (inferred).
57. One mechanistic question deserves naming rather than burying. The compound drives mitochondrial biogenesis and fat oxidation in several tissues at once, and in heart cells it suppressed cell-cycle programmes [1,3]. Both of those are broad transcriptional changes rather than narrow effects, and no study has looked for off-target consequences in a healthy animal over months.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
58. A research chemical with no approval anywhere, no investigational new drug programme announced, and no clinical trial registered for this molecule. Material sold for human use is unapproved by definition.
59. In sport it falls under WADA's S0 class, substances with no current approval for human therapeutic use, prohibited at all times (inferred from the class definition; the compound is not named individually on the list). Metabolic modulators are also covered as a class under S4, and anti-doping laboratories have added ERR agonists to screening interest as exercise mimetics (inferred).

### Open questions [mixed]
60. Does anything here happen in a person? Three animal papers from one network, no human data, no replication.
61. Does it work by mouth? The group's own plan to engineer an oral version suggests the published molecule is not well suited to it, and no oral exposure data have been published.
62. What does sustained ERR activation do to a healthy heart, given that the cardiac benefit was shown in failing hearts and came with suppression of cell-cycle genes?
63. Why do the mice burn more energy without moving more, and is that sustainable? The obesity paper reports the result; the thermogenic mechanism in intact animals is not pinned down.
64. Nothing beyond ten days has been examined in any species. That is the single largest gap, given that community use runs in multi-week cycles.

[2] Billon et al., J Pharmacol Exp Ther 2024, a synthetic ERR agonist alleviates metabolic syndrome, 2024 · https://profiles.wustl.edu/en/publications/a-synthetic-err-agonist-alleviates-metabolic-syndrome/

# Cerebrolysin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/cerebrolysin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: brain peptide mixture, FPF-1070, cerebroprotein hydrolysate, CAS 12656-61-0
2. Origin: Not a peptide
3. Shown with an FDA approved badge
4. Legal and approval status: Approved in many countries (not the US) for stroke/dementia. Not FDA-approved.

## Summary
5. Cerebrolysin is not one peptide but a mixture of small peptides and amino acids from pig brain tissue. It is approved in many countries, though not by the FDA, and given by IV or IM courses for stroke, dementia and brain injury. Some trials show modest gains, but a 2023 Cochrane review found no reduction in stroke deaths and a possible rise in serious side effects.
6. Punch line: Pig brain peptide mixture given as IV or IM courses after stroke and brain injury. Approved abroad only.
7. Used for: Stroke, brain injury, cognition

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Cognition: Studied in dementia
9. Neural plasticity: Nerve growth factor-like action
10. Neural protection: Studied after stroke and brain injury
11. Mood: Users report steadier mood
12. Tissue repair (backed only by animal or user reports): Nerve repair after injury
13. Sleep & rhythms (backed only by animal or user reports): Some users report better sleep

## How it works
14. Peptide mix with nerve-growth-like activity · Neurotrophic activity · role Neural protection
   Cerebrolysin is a mix of small peptides and free amino acids from digested pig brain. In cell and animal models it shows neurotrophic activity resembling BDNF and NGF, the brain's own growth factors. That supports neuron survival, though which molecules do this is unknown.
15. Active components undefined · Pig brain peptide mix · role Neural protection
   No active ingredient has been identified, so there is no sequence or reference standard. Batches are released against process controls and activity tests, and some variation between batches is inherent. Research chemical powders sold under the name cannot be assumed to match the approved solution.
16. Supports new connections and neurons · Synaptogenesis, neurogenesis · role Neural plasticity
   In models it supports synaptogenesis, the forming of new connections, and neurogenesis, the birth of new neurons. The aim is to back the brain's own repair after injury and in degenerative disease. This rests on cell and animal work.
17. Limits nerve cell death after injury · Anti-apoptotic · role Neural protection
   After ischaemia or trauma, it limits apoptosis and excitotoxic damage in animal models, so fewer nerve cells die. In human stroke trials this did not translate: a 2023 Cochrane review found no reduction in deaths and more non-fatal serious side effects.
18. Modest memory gains in dementia trials · Cognitive outcomes · role Cognition
   Some dementia trials report modest gains on memory and cognitive scales. A Cochrane review in vascular dementia found benefit but rated the evidence very low quality, with industry funding and risk of bias. Traumatic brain injury trials report small functional gains in limited numbers.
19. Mechanism overview: Cerebrolysin is a mixture of low molecular weight peptides and free amino acids from enzymatically digested pig brain. Its individual active components are undefined. In models it shows neurotrophic activity resembling BDNF and NGF signalling, supporting neuron survival, synapse formation and neurogenesis. It limits apoptosis and excitotoxic damage after ischaemia or trauma. The idea is to support the brain's own repair programme in the window after injury and in degenerative disease.

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### What is actually in the ampoule, and why that is the central question [lab]
55. This is not a peptide, it is a manufacturing process. Purified brain tissue from pigs approved for human food is digested with enzymes under controlled conditions, then ultrafiltered so that what passes through is mostly below 10 kilodaltons [1] (reported). The resulting solution is roughly a quarter low molecular weight peptides and three quarters free amino acids, standardised at about 215 mg per mL of nitrogen-containing substances [1] (reported).
56. No active ingredient has been identified. There is no sequence, no single molecular weight and no reference standard, so batches are released against process controls, composition tests and biological activity assays rather than against a defined molecule [1] (reported). Batch-to-batch variability is inherent to that approach and has been raised by regulators [1] (reported). An independent assessment described it plainly: because it is prepared from brain homogenate, content and concentration can vary between preparations and between manufacturers [2] (verified).
57. Two practical consequences. First, an animal-derived injectable carries contamination risk in a way a synthetic peptide does not, and that risk was explicitly noted in the same assessment [2] (verified). Second, products sold as "cerebrolysin" powder by research chemical suppliers cannot be the same thing as the approved European solution, because the approved product is defined by its manufacturer's process; nothing connects an unrelated powder to the trial evidence (inferred).

### Mechanism, and the gap in it [mixed]
58. The proposal is neurotrophic activity resembling the body's own nerve growth factors, supporting neuron survival, synapse formation and neurogenesis, and limiting cell death after injury. That proposal rests on cell and animal work, and the card covers it.
59. What the mechanism story lacks is a bridge to the dose. With no identified active component, there is no way to say which molecule in the mixture produces which effect, no structure-activity relationship, and no way to measure drug exposure in a patient (inferred from the absence of an identified active substance). Pharmacokinetics in the ordinary sense cannot be done on an undefined mixture, which is why no half-life, distribution or clearance data exist for the product as such.
60. Free amino acids make up most of the mass and are not considered pharmacologically active [1] (reported). If that is right, the active fraction is a minority of what is injected, and its composition is controlled statistically rather than exactly.

### The human record, by indication [people]
61. Acute ischaemic stroke is the best-studied and the least encouraging. A 2023 Cochrane review covering seven randomised trials and 1,773 participants found no effect on all-cause death, with a risk ratio of 0.96 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.41), at moderate certainty [3] (verified). On harms it found the opposite of reassuring: non-fatal serious adverse events were more common on treatment, risk ratio 2.39 (95% CI 1.10 to 5.23) across three trials and 1,335 participants, and 2.87 (95% CI 1.24 to 6.69) in the subgroup given 30 mL for ten days [3] (verified).
62. The same review recorded that the manufacturer supported three of the multicentre studies, by funding them, supplying drug and placebo or randomisation codes, providing grants or supplying statisticians, and noted this may have affected design, conduct and reporting [3] (verified).
63. Vascular dementia reads better but weaker. A 2019 Cochrane review of six trials and 597 participants found benefit on pooled cognitive scales (standardised mean difference 0.36, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.58) and on global clinical response (risk ratio 2.69, 95% CI 1.82 to 3.98), with no difference in adverse events. Every key outcome was rated very low quality, the reviewers flagged high risk of bias and heterogeneity, warned the benefit may be too small to matter clinically, and recorded that all three trials with known funding were industry-supported [4] (verified).
64. Traumatic brain injury has the most favourable published result and the smallest numbers. A prospective meta-analysis of two phase 3b/4 placebo-controlled trials analysed 185 patients with admission Glasgow Coma Scale 6 to 12, given 50 mL a day for ten days then two further ten-day cycles at 10 mL. On a multidimensional ensemble of functional and neuropsychological scales it reported a small-to-medium effect favouring treatment at day 30 (standardised mean difference 0.31, p = 0.0156) and day 90 (0.34, p = 0.0146), with comparable safety [5] (verified). Note the endpoint design: a combined ensemble analysed with pre-ordered hypotheses rather than a single conventional outcome, which is a legitimate but unusual approach and one that makes comparison with other trials difficult (inferred).
65. Alzheimer's disease has meta-analyses reporting benefit on cognition and global change in mild to moderate disease, using 30 mL daily by infusion for four weeks to six months; an independent assessment judged several component trials small, the effects modest, one key Russian trial unreviewable because it was published only in Russian and never replicated, and the overall evidence insufficient to recommend routine use [2] (verified).

### Safety: a rare case where the harm signal is better quantified than the benefit [people]
66. Most sources describe it as well tolerated, with transient headache, dizziness, agitation, feeling hot and weight loss, and adverse event rates similar to placebo over courses up to three years [2] (verified).
67. Against that, the stroke review's finding of roughly 2.4-fold more non-fatal serious adverse events, at moderate certainty, is the single most statistically solid clinical result in the whole record, and it points the wrong way [3] (verified). It was also dose-related: the signal was strongest in the 30 mL arm. The honest summary is that in acute stroke the evidence probably shows no benefit on survival and a possible increase in serious non-fatal harm.
68. Separate from the molecule: it is given intravenously or intramuscularly in multi-week courses, and it is biological material of animal origin, so sterility and viral or bacterial contamination are live concerns rather than theoretical ones [2] (verified).

### Who produced the evidence [people]
69. The product has one manufacturer, and the manufacturer's involvement in the trial base is documented rather than suspected: funding, drug and placebo supply, randomisation codes, grants and statistical support across several multicentre studies, with Cochrane reviewers in two separate reviews noting industry support and its possible effect on reporting [3,4] (verified).
70. The trial network is also concentrated in a small group of investigators across Europe and Asia, with overlapping authorship between the stroke, dementia and brain injury programmes [5] (verified by authorship). That is normal for a single-sponsor drug and it means replication by unrelated groups is largely missing.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
71. Approved and marketed in many European, Asian, Latin American and post-Soviet countries for stroke, traumatic brain injury and dementia; not approved in the United States for anything [2] (verified). It is a prescription parenteral medicine where approved, administered in courses under supervision.
72. In sport, the substance is not named on the WADA Prohibited List. The route matters more than the molecule: intravenous infusions or injections totalling more than 100 mL per 12 hours outside hospital treatment, surgery or clinical investigation are a prohibited method, and clinical courses of 20 to 50 mL sit below that threshold while repeated same-day dosing could approach it (inferred).

### Open questions [mixed]
73. What is the active component? Without it there is no dose-response, no exposure measurement and no way to make a defined synthetic equivalent.
74. Why do the stroke and brain injury results diverge? Different injury type, different timing, different endpoint design and different trial sizes are all candidates, and nobody has reconciled them.
75. What drove the excess non-fatal serious adverse events in the stroke trials, and is it dose-related? The subgroup pattern suggests dose; the mechanism is unknown.
76. Would an independently funded, adequately powered trial reproduce the dementia and brain injury findings? Both Cochrane reviews asked for exactly that, and it has not happened.
77. What is in a non-manufacturer product sold under this name? Nothing links such material to the approved preparation or to any of the evidence above.

# FOXO4-DRI
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/foxo4-dri
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: foxo4 senolytic proxofim, FOXO4 D-retro-inverso peptide, FOXO4-p53 interfering peptide
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: LTLRKEPASEIAQSILEAYSQNGWANRRSGGKRPPPRRRQRRKKRG (46 amino acids). Built from D amino acids in reverse order (retro-inverso), so the body’s enzymes can’t cut it. Sequence reported; verify before release
4. Legal and approval status: Research chemical; no clinical program. Experimental and unproven in humans.

## Summary
5. FOXO4-DRI is a lab-designed peptide built from D-amino acids in reverse order, so enzymes cannot cut it. It is meant to clear aged senescent cells by blocking the FOXO4 and p53 interaction that keeps them alive. In aged mice it restored fur, fitness and kidney function, but there is no human data at all, and the few grey-market users report only anecdotal, inconsistent effects.
6. Punch line: The senolytic peptide. Breaks the FOXO4 and p53 bond keeping aged cells alive; old mice regained fur, fitness.
7. Used for: Senescent cell clearance

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Aging & senescence: Clears senescent cells in old mice
9. Organ function: Restored kidney function in mice
10. Muscle & performance: Better fitness in treated mice

## How it works
11. Frees p53 to kill senescent cells · Blocks FOXO4 and p53 binding · role Aging & senescence
   In senescent cells, the transcription factor FOXO4 holds p53 in the nucleus and keeps the damaged cell alive. FOXO4-DRI is a decoy of the FOXO4 region that grips p53, so it competes for p53 and frees it. p53 then moves to the mitochondria and triggers apoptosis, shown in cell studies and mice.
12. Built so enzymes cannot cut it · Retro-inverso D-peptide · role Aging & senescence
   It is a retro-inverso peptide: mirror-image D-amino acids in reversed order. That keeps the shape that binds p53 while making it unreadable to the protease enzymes that digest normal peptides. A stretch of charged residues helps carry it into cells. No pharmacokinetic study in any species has been published.
13. Restored kidney function in aged mice · Senolysis, renal · role Organ function
   In aged and fast-ageing mice, clearing senescent cells with this peptide restored kidney function in the original 2017 study. Removing these cells also removes the inflammatory signals they secrete into nearby tissue. The effect sizes were not reported in the abstract, and there is no human data at all.
14. Restored fur and fitness in aged mice · Senescent cell clearance · role Muscle & performance
   The same mouse study reported restored fur density and running fitness in naturally aged and fast-ageing mice. A later human cartilage cell study found clearance worked, but the surviving cells did not regain their function. No large independent replication and no human trial exist.
15. Mechanism overview: In senescent cells, the transcription factor FOXO4 binds p53 and holds it in the nucleus, which keeps these damaged cells alive instead of letting them die. FOXO4-DRI is a decoy built from the FOXO4 region that contacts p53. It competes for p53 and frees it, and p53 moves to the mitochondria, where it triggers apoptosis. Healthy cells rely less on FOXO4 and are largely spared. The peptide is retro-inverso: D-amino acids in reversed order, so proteases cannot cut it. Clearing senescent cells removes the inflammatory signals they secrete.

17. Half-life: not established
18. Most people take: No validated human dose. Mouse 5 mg/kg IP; community extrapolates ~3–25 mg/injection on days 1/3/5. Senolytic, caution.
19. Common: 1–3 mg · every other day ×3 · 6 days, 1–3×/yr · Sub-Q · for senolytic course [S1] [S2] (reported)

21. Aggressive: 25–50 mg · 3 doses EOD · 1 course · IV/SC/IM · for self-experimenters [S3] [S4] (reported)

## What has been tested
32. Aging & senescence: Senescent cell clearance (mouse)
33. Hair: Fur regrowth in aged mice (mouse)
34. Organ function: Kidney function (mouse)
35. Cellular energy: Fitness in aged mice (mouse)
36. The original mouse study reported restored fur, fitness and kidney function by killing senescent cells. No human trials.

There is no human data at all. A small number of grey-market users report trying it for general aging, with anecdotal and inconsistent effects.
38. Trial: none. No registered human trial found; evidence is mouse work (Baar 2017) and self experiment reports. (checked 2026-10-23) [S5] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
39. People healing from surgery or injury: Senescent cells help wounds close in mice; clearing them slowed healing. (inferred)

41. Epitalon: FOXO4-DRI aims to clear senescent cells, while Epitalon is claimed to act on telomerase and the pineal rhythm. People pair them as a two-angle anti-aging stack, removing damaged cells and supporting the rest. The pairing is user logic, not trial data, and neither has human outcome proof.

## Where it comes from
42. A designed 'senolytic' peptide: built from D-amino acids in reverse order (retro-inverso) so enzymes cannot cut it. It blocks the FOXO4-p53 interaction that keeps aged 'senescent' cells alive.
43. First studied for: Clearing senescent cells, to reverse aspects of aging; from a 2017 Dutch study.
44. Name story: DRI means D-retro-inverso: a FOXO4 fragment rebuilt from mirror-image D-amino acids in reversed order, so it keeps the original's shape but enzymes can't digest it. Debuted in Cell in 2017 as a decoy that frees p53 to kill senescent cells. [S6] (verified)
45. 2017: Dutch mouse study: senolytic peptide restores aged mice
46. Today: Experimental senolytic; no human trials or clinical program

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### Where it came from, and what the original paper actually claimed [animals]
47. It came out of one 2017 paper from a Dutch group, which identified FOXO4 as what they called a pivot in senescent cell viability, designed a peptide to break the FOXO4 to p53 interaction, and showed that this pushes p53 out of the nucleus in senescent cells and triggers their self-destruction [1] (verified).
48. The paper's three in-vivo claims are worth stating precisely, because they are usually compressed into "it rejuvenated old mice". It neutralised the tissue damage caused by doxorubicin, a chemotherapy drug; and in both fast-ageing XpdTTD mice and naturally aged mice it restored fitness, fur density and kidney function [1] (verified). The abstract reports no effect sizes, and the full paper could not be opened for this review, so the magnitudes behind those three words are not quoted here.
49. The design is the cleverest part. It is a retro-inverso peptide: mirror-image D-amino acids in reversed order, which keeps the shape that binds p53 while making it unreadable to the enzymes that would otherwise digest it, plus a stretch of positively charged residues to carry it into cells [2] (verified from the published sequence). That is why it is injected rather than infused as a protein, and why it is not comparable to ordinary peptides on stability.

### The selectivity argument, and the one study that tested it carefully [cells]
50. The claim that healthy cells are spared rests on them depending less on FOXO4 to keep p53 in check. A 2021 study from a Pittsburgh group is the most careful public test of that in human cells, and it is worth reading because it both supports and limits the claim.
51. Human chondrocytes from eight donors were expanded in culture until over 40% were senescent by beta-galactosidase staining, against under 17% in minimally expanded controls. Treatment at 25 micromolar for five days removed more than half the heavily expanded cells while leaving the minimally expanded population essentially unchanged, with caspase staining confirming apoptosis. Senescent cells fell to under 5%, and p16, p21 and p53 protein dropped [3] (verified, human cells).
52. Then the part that is rarely quoted. The surviving cells did not regain their ability to make cartilage: in three-dimensional pellet culture, pretreatment did not increase matrix deposition or cartilage gene expression, and it reduced SOX9 and COL2, two central cartilage genes. p21 protein rose in pretreated groups, which the authors read as possible stress on the remaining cells. They concluded that removing senescent cells was not enough to restore function and that other strategies would be needed [3] (verified).
53. That is the most informative result in the whole literature for anyone thinking about repair: clearance worked, and clearance alone did not restore the tissue's job.

### What else has been published since [animals]
54. The peptide has been used as a research tool across a scattered set of animal and cell models: senescence in kidney transplantation, Leydig cells and testosterone in aged mice, radiosensitisation and radiation-induced lung fibrosis, bleomycin lung fibrosis, spermatogenesis in aged mice, keloid fibroblasts, and the p53 transactivation domain as a target [2] (verified that these studies exist; their results are not summarised here because the primary texts were not opened).
55. A 2025 study reported that injections suppressed aortic ageing and improved aortic function in naturally aged and progeroid mice, and reduced senescence in endothelial cells deprived of oxygen and glucose, with the proposed chain running from blocked FOXO4 binding to nuclear exclusion of phosphorylated p53 to BAX and caspase-3 activation [4] (reported; dose and route were not stated in the accessible summary).
56. What is missing from this list is a large independent replication of the 2017 ageing result by a group with no connection to the original, and any human study of any kind.

### Safety: what is known, and the structural reason to be careful [animals]
57. The 2017 paper described the peptide as well tolerated in vivo under the conditions tested [1] (verified as stated, with those conditions unspecified in the abstract). That is the extent of the published safety record. No repeat-dose toxicology, genotoxicity, reproductive or carcinogenicity studies have been published, and no pharmacokinetic study in any species was found for this review.
58. The mechanism itself sets the main caution, and it is worth being explicit rather than vague. The peptide works by freeing p53 to kill a cell. p53 is the body's main brake on cancer and also a central damage-response switch in healthy tissue. The selectivity argument is that healthy cells do not need FOXO4 to restrain p53, which the chondrocyte work supports in one cell type at one concentration [3]. Whether that holds across tissues, over repeated courses, and in people with existing damage has not been tested (inferred).
59. The chondrocyte study's incidental finding points the same way: the cells that survived treatment showed raised p21, a stress marker [3] (verified, cells). Not a harm, but not nothing either.
60. There is no established human dose. Figures circulating in self-experimentation circles are extrapolations from a mouse dose, and nothing in the published record supports any of them.

### Who is developing it, and why that has stalled [lab]
61. A company was formed to commercialise the Dutch group's work and is still described as a preclinical operation, with its focus reported as the FOXO4 to p53 interaction more broadly rather than this particular peptide, and candidate indications under selection across chronic diseases, a rare disease and resistant tumours [4,5] (reported).
62. The commentary around it makes an economic point that explains the plateau better than any scientific one: a peptide whose sequence is public and hard to protect struggles to attract the money a proper trial costs, so it stays a tool compound while a patentable successor is sought [4] (reported). Nine years after the original paper, that is still where it sits.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
63. Not approved anywhere, no investigational new drug programme announced, no registered clinical trial found. Material sold under this name is a research chemical.
64. It is not named on the WADA Prohibited List; as a substance with no approval for human therapeutic use it falls under the S0 class, prohibited at all times (inferred from the class definition).

### Open questions [mixed]
65. Does clearance help, if the cells left behind do not work better? The chondrocyte result says removal and restoration are different problems.
66. Does selectivity hold outside a dish and outside one cell type? This is the question the entire safety case depends on, and it has one careful test behind it.
67. What happens with repeated courses? No repeat-dose study in any species has been published, in a mechanism that deliberately promotes cell death.
68. What are the pharmacokinetics? A D-amino acid retro-inverso peptide should be unusually long-lived, which cuts both ways, and nobody has published the numbers.
69. Why has nobody replicated the 2017 ageing result independently? Nine years is a long time for a widely cited finding to stand on one paper.
