# Amycretin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/amycretin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Zenagamtide, NN9487, NNC0487-0111, oral amycretin, GLP-1/amylin unimolecular
2. Origin: Lab-designed: GLP-1 and amylin analogues in one chain
3. Legal and approval status: Investigational, not approved anywhere as of Oct 2026. Phase 3: AMAZE 1 (weekly injection, obesity) recruiting since Feb 2026; AMAZE 2 (obesity with T2D) and HF-POLARIS (heart failure) cleared in Korea Feb 2026; T2D phase 3 planned 2H 2026. Not named on the WADA list.

## Summary
4. Amycretin is Novo Nordisk's single molecule that activates both GLP-1 and amylin receptors, built as one long acylated peptide rather than two drugs in one pen. It is being developed for obesity and type 2 diabetes by suppressing hunger and slowing stomach emptying. Early trials showed 22 to 24% weight loss at 36 weeks by weekly injection, with heavy nausea and vomiting. Community use is near zero.
5. Punch line: Novo's GLP-1 and amylin in one molecule, weekly shot or pill. Early trials reached 24% loss; heavy nausea.
6. Used for: Obesity, type 2 diabetes

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Appetite & satiety: Deep hunger suppression, two pathways
8. Glucose & insulin: Lowers HbA1c in diabetes
9. Fat metabolism: Up to 24% weight loss
10. Digestive & gut: Slows stomach emptying, nausea
11. Heart & vessels (backed only by animal or user reports): Heart failure outcome trial running
12. Reward & urges (backed only by animal or user reports): Amylin may calm food reward

## How it works
13. Quiets hunger in the brain · GLP-1 receptor, hypothalamus/brainstem · role Appetite & satiety
   The GLP-1 segment of amycretin activates GLP-1 receptors in the hypothalamus and brainstem, the brain's hunger centres. That cuts appetite and food intake. Weight loss is shown in early human trials by injection and by mouth.
14. Adds a second fullness signal · Amylin (CTR/RAMP) receptor, area postrema · role Appetite & satiety
   The amylin segment activates calcitonin receptor and RAMP complexes, the amylin receptors, in the area postrema of the hindbrain. This adds a fullness signal separate from GLP-1, so the two together cut intake further. Shown in early human trials.
15. Slows stomach emptying · GLP-1R and amylin receptor · role Digestive & gut
   Both GLP-1 and amylin receptors slow how fast the stomach empties. Food stays longer, so people feel full and eat less. This also drives the nausea and vomiting seen early in human trials.
16. Raises insulin, cuts glucagon · GLP-1R beta/alpha cells; amylin glucagon suppression · role Glucose & insulin
   The GLP-1 part raises insulin and cuts glucagon when glucose is high, and the amylin part also holds glucagon back after meals. Together they lower blood sugar. A phase 2 human trial in type 2 diabetes showed HbA1c falling.
17. Fatty tail rides albumin · C18 diacid, albumin binding · role Fat metabolism
   A C18 fatty acid chain on amycretin binds albumin, the main blood protein. That slows clearance and protects it from breakdown, so a single injection lasts about a week. The oral form uses the SNAC absorption enhancer, as in oral semaglutide.
18. Mechanism overview: Amycretin is a single acylated peptide carrying a GLP-1 receptor agonist segment and an amylin receptor agonist segment joined by a short linker. The GLP-1 part acts in the hypothalamus and brainstem to cut hunger, slows gastric emptying and raises insulin while cutting glucagon when glucose is high. The amylin part acts on calcitonin receptor/RAMP complexes in the area postrema to add a separate satiety and glucagon-suppressing signal. A C18 fatty diacid binds albumin so it lasts a week by injection; the oral form uses the SNAC absorption enhancer, as in Rybelsus.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
19. Typical: 1.25–60 mg injected; up to 100 mg oral · once weekly (Sub-Q) or once daily (oral) · cycle Trial only (20–36 wk) · route Sub-Q; oral tablet with SNAC (verified)
20. Half-life: Long; weekly dosing (not published)
21. Dose note: Phase 3 doses and titration steps are not public. No grey-market dosing guide found.
22. Most people take: Trial doses only: weekly Sub-Q 1.25, 5, 20 or 60 mg after slow escalation, or a daily oral pill up to 2×50 mg. No established community protocol.
23. Trial injectable: 20–60 mg · 1× weekly · 36 wk after escalation · Sub-Q · for phase 1b/2a obesity volunteers [S1] [S2] (verified)
24. Trial low: 1.25–5 mg · 1× weekly · 20–28 wk · Sub-Q · for lower arms; 9.7–16.2% loss [S2] (verified)
25. Trial oral: 50 mg or 2×50 mg · 1× daily · 12 wk · Oral (SNAC tablet) · for phase 1 oral volunteers [S1] [S2] (verified)
26. T2D phase 2: 0.4–40 mg Sub-Q; 6–50 mg oral · weekly / daily · 36 wk · Sub-Q or oral · for type 2 diabetes on metformin [S3] (verified)

## What people report
27. Very little real-world reporting; it is rarely seen outside trials and community dosing data is essentially absent.
28. Liked / worked: 24.3% weight loss at 36 weeks (60 mg)
29. Liked / worked: 13.1% loss in 12 weeks on the pill
30. Liked / worked: HbA1c down up to 1.8 points in T2D
31. Liked / worked: No plateau at higher doses in T2D
32. What worked: Injectable: 22.0% weight loss at 20 mg and 24.3% at 60 mg by week 36 versus about 1–2% on placebo. Oral: 13.1% at 12 weeks. In type 2 diabetes, HbA1c fell up to 1.8 points with up to 14.5% weight loss.
33. Went wrong / did not work: Nausea and vomiting in most people early
34. Went wrong / did not work: About a third left the injectable trial
35. Went wrong / did not work: No long-term safety data
36. What went wrong: Heavy GI load in early trials: nausea about 82%, vomiting 53% in the injectable study (reported); about a third dropped out, mostly for non-side-effect reasons. Long-term safety unknown.
37. Most reported: Barely seen outside trials
38. Most reported: Watched as a successor to CagriSema

## What has been tested
39. Fat metabolism: Obesity, Sub-Q phase 1b/2a and oral phase 1 (human)
40. Glucose & insulin: Type 2 diabetes, phase 2 (human)
41. Heart & vessels: Heart failure outcomes, HF-POLARIS (ongoing) (human)
42. Phase 1b/2a injectable (125 people, Lancet 2025), phase 1 oral (144 people, Lancet 2025) and phase 2 in type 2 diabetes (448 people); phase 3 AMAZE began in 2026.
43. What it helps: Early trials put it near the top of the obesity field: 22–24% weight loss at 36 weeks by weekly injection and 13% in 12 weeks as a daily pill. In type 2 diabetes it cut HbA1c up to 1.8 points with up to 14.5% weight loss. The cost was heavy nausea and vomiting early on. Phase 3 is now testing obesity, diabetes and heart failure; community use is near zero.
44. Trial: active · Phase 3 · obesity and type 2 diabetes · Novo Nordisk. Novo moved both the shot and the pill into Phase 3 in 2026 under the new name zenagamtide. (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
45. Personal or family history of MTC or MEN2: Causes thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents; boxed warning and contraindication on the label. (inferred)
46. Anyone booked for surgery, endoscopy or sedation: Food can stay in the stomach for days and be inhaled into the lungs under anaesthesia. (inferred)
47. Insulin or sulfonylurea users: Amylin plus GLP-1 action stacks low sugar risk. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
48. Semaglutide: Semaglutide acts only on the GLP-1 receptor, which amycretin already covers. Stacking them doubles up GLP-1 action and side effects rather than adding a route. The pair has not been tested together.
49. Cagrilintide: Cagrilintide is a long-acting amylin drug, the same route as amycretin's amylin segment. Adding it doubles up amylin action rather than adding a new one. Amycretin already joins both signals in one molecule, and this stack has not been tested.

## Where it comes from
50. Novo Nordisk's first single molecule that hits both the GLP-1 and amylin receptors, built as one long acylated peptide instead of two drugs in one pen (as in CagriSema).
51. First studied for: Obesity, then type 2 diabetes; one weekly injection and one daily pill of the same molecule.
52. Name story: "Amycretin" blends amylin and incretin, the two hormone families it mimics. The formal INN zenagamtide carries the generic -tide peptide ending and appears in Novo's 2026 releases. [S5] (inferred)
53. Mar 2024: Oral phase 1 results announced
54. Jan 2025: Injectable phase 1b/2a topline: up to 22% loss
55. Jun 2025: Lancet papers; Novo commits both forms to phase 3
56. Nov 2025: Phase 2 in T2D: HbA1c down up to 1.8 points
57. Feb 2026: AMAZE 1 starts; INN zenagamtide in use by mid-2026
58. Today: Phase 3; high early GI rates and dropouts are the watch item

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### One molecule rather than two drugs, and why that is the engineering point [mixed]
59. The competing approach to combining a GLP-1 drug with an amylin drug is to put two separate peptides in one pen. This one instead covalently links a GLP-1 analogue and an amylin analogue into a single molecule, codenamed NN9487 and later given the name zenagamtide [1] (verified).
60. That has practical consequences, which rarely get spelled out. A single molecule has one pharmacokinetic profile instead of two, so the two signals cannot drift apart between doses, and the ratio between them is fixed by chemistry rather than by formulation. It also means the ratio cannot be adjusted if the balance turns out wrong, and that any immunogenicity or impurity question applies to one new chemical entity rather than to two known ones (inferred).
61. The oral form uses salcaprozate sodium, the same absorption enhancer as oral semaglutide, which is why the tablet dose runs in tens of milligrams while the weekly injection runs in single-digit to tens of milligrams [1] (verified). Oral peptide delivery of this kind is inefficient by design: most of the dose does not get absorbed, which is the reason for the gap.

### The human record, and how to read the big weight numbers [people]
62. Injection, phase 1b/2a: 125 people randomised, 101 to drug and 24 to placebo, aged 18 to 55 with BMI in the overweight to mild obesity range, in five parts with single then multiple ascending weekly doses up to 60 mg [2,3] (verified). Weight change against placebo was 24.3% versus 1.1% at 36 weeks on 60 mg, 22.0% versus a 1.9% gain at 36 weeks on 20 mg, 16.2% versus a 2.3% gain at 28 weeks on 5 mg, and 9.7% versus a 2.0% gain at 20 weeks on 1.25 mg [3] (verified).
63. Three things temper those figures. The arms were small and of unequal length, so the headline 24% comes from one part of a dose-finding study rather than a powered comparison. One third of participants withdrew, and the investigators noted that 59% of withdrawals were for reasons unrelated to adverse events, including withdrawn consent and recreational drug use [2] (verified). And the participants were young, with BMI largely in the 25 to 35 range, not the population a phase 3 obesity trial enrols (inferred).
64. Tablet, first-in-human phase 1: 144 people, up to 12 weeks, highest dose two 50 mg tablets daily. Weight fell 13% against 1% on placebo at the top dose, with no sign of plateau [2] (verified).
65. Type 2 diabetes, phase 2: 448 adults on metformin, about 40% also on an SGLT2 inhibitor, randomised to six weekly injected doses from 0.4 to 40 mg, three daily oral doses of 6, 25 or 50 mg, or placebo, for up to 36 weeks. Injected: HbA1c down up to 1.8 points from a baseline of 7.8%, with 89.1% reaching under 7% and 76.2% under 6.5%, and weight down up to 14.5% from 99.2 kg. Oral: HbA1c down up to 1.5 points from 8%, 77.6% under 7%, weight down up to 10.1%. Placebo moved HbA1c 0.2 to 0.4 points and weight about 2.5% [4] (reported, from the sponsor's topline release rather than a paper).
66. Across all of it, the recurring observation is the absence of a plateau at 36 weeks [2,3,4]. That is genuinely unusual for this class and is the strongest argument that the two mechanisms are doing different work rather than overlapping.

### Safety: what the early trials showed, and the honest caveat about rates [people]
67. Oral phase 1: treatment-emergent adverse events in 62% of participants, 364 events in total, of which 180 (49%) were gastrointestinal, mostly nausea, vomiting and reduced appetite. All were mild or moderate, frequency rose with dose, and there were no deaths [2] (verified).
68. Injected phase 1b/2a: in parts B to E, 80 of 83 people on drug reported at least one adverse event (496 events), as did 18 of 18 on placebo (72 events) [2] (verified). The near-universal rate in both arms is why those percentages say little; the investigators themselves attributed part of the gap in event counts to a nocebo effect in a small sample [2]. Gastrointestinal events dominated, were mostly mild to moderate and had resolved by study end.
69. The investigators raised a point worth keeping: rapid weight loss may not deliver the same benefits as gradual loss, and the optimal rate has not been established [2] (verified as their stated caveat). An accompanying editorial argued that the field's question is now cardiovascular and comorbidity risk, and called for head-to-head outcome trials against GLP-1 drugs with proven cardiovascular benefit before judging what these combinations add [2] (verified).
70. What has not been studied: no trial longer than 36 weeks has reported, no cardiovascular outcome trial has read out, and nothing has been published on lean mass, bone or longer-term amylin receptor effects for this molecule. With roughly 700 people treated across all published trials, rare events remain invisible (inferred).

### Who produced the evidence [people]
71. Every study is the developer's own. The two phase 1 trials were peer-reviewed in The Lancet in June 2025 [2]; the diabetes phase 2 result is, as of October 2026, a company release rather than a paper [4]. No independent trial exists.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
72. Investigational everywhere, not approved in any country. The developer announced in June 2025 that both the weekly injection and the daily tablet would go to phase 3 in weight management, after end-of-phase-2 regulatory feedback, with the programme due to start in the first quarter of 2026 [5] (verified). A phase 3 programme in type 2 diabetes followed the November 2025 phase 2 result [4] (reported).
73. In sport, GLP-1 and amylin receptor agonists are not named on the WADA Prohibited List, but an unapproved investigational substance falls under the S0 class, prohibited at all times (inferred from the class definition).

### Open questions [mixed]
74. Is a fused single molecule better than two peptides in one pen? Nothing has compared them head to head, and this is the central bet of the design.
75. Does the absence of a plateau hold past 36 weeks, and at what cost to lean mass? Phase 3 should answer the first; nobody has published on the second for this molecule.
76. What do the tolerability numbers mean when placebo groups report events at the same rate? Larger trials with proper titration schedules are the only way to separate drug effect from expectation.
77. Does it reduce cardiovascular events? The editorial accompanying the phase 1 papers made this the test that matters, and no outcome trial has reported.
78. How much of the oral dose is actually absorbed, and how variable is that between people? Standard for SNAC-based tablets, and not published for this one.

# BAM-15
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/bam-15
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: BAM15, N5,N6-bis(2-fluorophenyl)-[1,2,5]oxadiazolo[3,4-b]pyrazine-5,6-diamine, CAS 210302-17-3
2. Origin: Not a peptide: small molecule
3. Legal and approval status: Preclinical as of 22 Oct 2026: no human trials, not approved anywhere. WADA S0 (non-approved substance) applies (inferred).

## Summary
4. BAM-15 is not a peptide but a small-molecule mitochondrial uncoupler that lets protons leak so cells burn fuel as heat. It was designed to avoid the overheating that made DNP dangerous, and in obese mice it reversed fat gain and insulin resistance. It has never been tested in humans, so dose, safety and effect are unknown.
5. Punch line: Mitochondrial uncoupler built as a safer DNP. Burns fuel as heat; reversed obesity in mice, untested in humans.
6. Used for: Fat loss, insulin sensitivity

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Cellular energy: Burns fuel as heat in mitochondria
8. Fat metabolism: Reversed fat gain in mice
9. Glucose & insulin: Better insulin sensitivity in mice
10. Organ function: Less liver and kidney fat
11. Muscle & performance (backed only by animal or user reports): Muscle benefits in aged mice
12. Inflammatory signaling (backed only by animal or user reports): Calmer inflammation in injury models

## How it works
13. Lets protons leak across the mitochondrial membrane · Protonophore, inner mitochondrial membrane · role Cellular energy
   BAM-15 is a protonophore, a weak acid that carries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane and around ATP synthase. The energy in that proton gradient is lost as heat instead of becoming ATP. Unlike DNP and FCCP, it does not depolarise the outer cell membrane, shown in cell studies.
14. Cells burn more fat to keep up · Raised fatty acid oxidation · role Fat metabolism
   With less ATP made per unit of fuel, cells burn more fuel to keep up, especially fat. In mice a single oral dose raised fat oxidation, and oxygen use rose without more movement or less eating. This is animal work only.
15. Turns on energy-sensing switches · AMPK and PGC-1α activation · role Cellular energy
   The energy shortfall switches on AMPK, the cell's fuel sensor, and PGC-1α, a master regulator of mitochondrial genes. These shift cells toward burning more and building mitochondria. The evidence comes from cell and mouse studies.
16. Better insulin action in muscle and liver · Lower HOMA-IR in mice · role Glucose & insulin
   In obese mice BAM-15 reversed insulin resistance, lowered fasting glucose and insulin, and returned liver fat to normal. Clamp studies showed muscle and fat taking up more glucose. No human data exist on any of this.
17. Mechanism overview: BAM-15 is a lipophilic weak acid that shuttles protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, bypassing ATP synthase. The proton gradient is spent as heat instead of ATP, so cells raise substrate oxidation, especially fat, to keep energy levels up. The resulting energy stress activates AMPK and PGC-1α. Unlike DNP and FCCP it does not depolarise the plasma membrane, which may explain why mice showed no rise in body temperature at effective doses.

18. Typical: No human dose (animal only); 25–50 mg reported · once or twice daily (reported) · cycle 4–8 weeks (reported) · route Oral (reported)
19. Half-life: ~1.7–3 hours (mice)
20. Most people take: No human dose exists. Community: oral 25–50 mg daily with meals, 4–8 weeks; mouse doses do not scale by body weight.

## What people report
21. Sold as a research-chemical powder or capsule; users report oral doses of 25–50 mg a day and watch for warmth, sweating and racing heart.
22. Liked / worked: Reversed obesity in mice
23. Liked / worked: Liver fat down ~75% in mice
24. Liked / worked: No body temperature rise in mice
25. Liked / worked: No food intake drop needed
26. What worked: In obese mice it reversed fat gain and insulin resistance and cut liver fat about 75%, without lowering food intake, lean mass or body temperature.
27. Went wrong / did not work: No human trials
28. Went wrong / did not work: Very short half-life
29. Went wrong / did not work: Uncharacterised heart risk
30. Went wrong / did not work: Mouse doses don't scale to humans
31. What went wrong: Never dosed in humans in a registered trial; short half-life in mice (~2–3 hours); the uncoupler class carries uncharacterised heart and overheating risk.
32. Most reported: Warmth and sweating
33. Most reported: Stacked with GLP-1s for fat loss
34. Most reported: Purity of powders unknown
35. Most reported: Few detailed first-hand reports

## What has been tested
36. Fat metabolism: Diet-induced obesity (animal)
37. Glucose & insulin: Insulin resistance (animal)
38. Organ function: Liver fat and kidney injury (animal)
39. Cellular energy: Cell viability up to 100 µM (cell)
40. Mouse and cell studies only, from several independent labs; no registered human trial.
41. What it helps: Evidence is mouse and cell work. In obese mice, BAM-15 reversed fat gain and insulin resistance, cut liver fat and lowered fasting glucose and insulin without eating less. No human data exist on dose, safety or effect. Users take it orally for fat loss, often beside GLP-1 drugs, and watch for overheating, sweating and racing heart.
42. Trial: none. Still preclinical; mouse studies only, with no human trial registered anywhere. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
43. People exercising or living in heat: Uncouplers like DNP cause fatal overheating. (inferred)
44. People on thyroid hormone or stimulants: Metabolic rate already raised; heat load stacks. (inferred)
45. People with eating disorders: Fast fat-burning drugs of this class have a history of compulsive overdosing. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
46. Semaglutide: Semaglutide cuts how much people eat, while BAM-15 raises how much energy cells burn, so users pair them to attack both sides of energy balance. BAM-15 has no human data, and the pair has not been tested together.
47. Tirzepatide: Tirzepatide lowers intake and improves insulin action through GIP and GLP-1 receptors, and BAM-15 adds raised fuel burning in mitochondria. The logic is complementary, but it is user logic, not trial data, and BAM-15 is untested in people.
48. MOTS-c: MOTS-c mimics exercise through AMPK, and BAM-15 creates an energy shortfall that also switches AMPK on, so both push cells toward burning fat. Both rest on mouse data, and the pair has not been tested together.
49. SLU-PP-332: SLU-PP-332 builds more mitochondria and shifts muscle to fat burning, while BAM-15 makes those mitochondria burn fuel less efficiently, so more is used. They are sold pre-mixed as SLU-PP-332 + BAM-15 oral, but the pair has only been reasoned about, not tested.

## Where it comes from
50. A mitochondrial uncoupler that lets protons leak back across the inner membrane so cells burn fuel as heat, designed to avoid the runaway overheating that made DNP lethal.
51. First studied for: Lab tool, then a candidate for obesity, fatty liver and insulin resistance in mice.
52. 2013: First described as a mitochondria-selective uncoupler
53. 2020: Mouse studies: reverses obesity and insulin resistance (Nat Commun, EMBO Mol Med)
54. 2020s: Kidney and aged-muscle benefits in mice
55. Today: Still no human trial; sold as a research chemical

## Deep read (as of 2026-10)

### The problem it was designed to solve [cells]
56. Uncoupling has an unhappy history. In the 1930s doctors prescribed 2,4-dinitrophenol for weight loss; it worked, and it was abandoned after cataracts appeared in a share of patients and deaths followed. US regulators declared it unfit for human consumption in 1938. The mechanism of the harm is the same as the mechanism of the benefit: energy leaves as heat instead of becoming ATP, so metabolic rate rises, and at higher doses body temperature runs away and death typically follows cardiac arrest [1] (verified).
57. The design brief for this compound was therefore narrow: uncouple mitochondria without the off-target effects that make DNP and the laboratory uncoupler FCCP dangerous. A 2013 screen identified it as a protonophore that carries protons into the mitochondrial matrix bypassing ATP synthase, and the key reported difference was that it does not depolarise the plasma membrane. Against FCCP, described as similarly potent, it produced a higher maximum respiration rate in cultured cells and was less toxic to them [2] (verified, cells). The same paper reported that it was active in living mice and protected them dose-dependently from acute kidney injury caused by interrupted blood flow [2] (verified, animals).
58. That is the whole safety argument in outline, and it is a comparative one: safer than a compound that killed people, in cells and in mice. It is not a demonstration of safety in humans, and no human study exists.

### The main obesity study, in its own numbers [animals]
59. The 2020 paper is the source of nearly everything quoted about this compound, and the details matter because they are often dropped. Male mice, in two designs: prevention, with the compound mixed into a western diet at 0.05, 0.10 or 0.15% by weight for eight days; and reversal, four weeks of western diet to make the mice obese, then five weeks of treatment at 0.10% [3] (verified).
60. Prevention: the lowest dose prevented more than half of fat gain and the two higher doses prevented it entirely, with food intake and lean mass unchanged, glucose tolerance preserved and fasting glucose and insulin lower [3] (verified, animals).
61. Reversal: treated mice ended about 15% lighter than diet controls, the difference almost entirely fat, with lean mass and food intake unchanged. Faecal fat excretion did not change, which rules out the simplest alternative explanation that the compound was blocking fat absorption. Liver triglycerides returned to the level of mice on ordinary chow. Glucose intolerance and high insulin reversed within three weeks, and clamp studies showed more glucose taken up by muscle and fat and better suppression of fatty acid release [3] (verified, animals).
62. On energy use: a single oral dose raised fat oxidation by 51%, and oxygen consumption rose about 15% during the animals' active phase, with the respiratory exchange ratio falling and locomotor activity unchanged [3] (verified). So the weight loss came from burning more, not moving more or eating less, which is what the mechanism predicts.
63. The temperature question, which is the one that matters given DNP: body temperature did not change up to 200 mg per kg by mouth [3] (verified, mice, acute). That is the single most important number in the compound's file.

### What the body does with it, and why mouse doses do not transfer [animals]
64. In mice, oral bioavailability was about 67%, a 10 mg per kg oral dose reached a peak blood concentration of about 8.2 micromolar, the half-life was about 1.7 hours, and distribution was mainly to the liver [3] (verified).
65. Two of those numbers constrain everything. A 1.7-hour half-life means exposure is brief and spiky from a single dose, which is why the mouse studies delivered it continuously in food rather than as discrete doses [3] (inferred from the study design). And liver-weighted distribution means the liver sees far more than other tissues, which fits the liver fat and insulin results and makes the liver the organ to watch (inferred).
66. The authors themselves named the short half-life and low solubility as limitations for development [3] (verified as their stated view). Nothing in the record describes human pharmacokinetics, human bioavailability, or what a human tablet or capsule would need to look like. There is no established human dose, and mouse diet-admixture doses cannot be converted into one.

### The other animal findings [animals]
67. Kidney: protection against acute ischaemia-reperfusion injury in mice, dose-dependent, in the original 2013 paper [2] (verified).
68. Ageing muscle: a 2022 study in aged obese mice, reported in a cachexia and sarcopenia journal, found over 20% fat loss alongside roughly 8% more muscle mass and about 40% more strength, with the animals more physically active; the press account gave no doses or duration, and reduced inflammation and mitochondrial turnover were described without figures [4] (reported). Gaining muscle while losing fat is unusual enough to deserve independent confirmation before it is treated as established.
69. A 2025 preprint reports improved skeletal muscle function and mitochondrial respiration in a sarcopenia model [5] (reported; a preprint has not been peer reviewed, and it is cited here as such).

### Safety: what was measured, and the shape of what was not [animals]
70. The 2020 study ran a reasonable panel for a mouse study: no change in body temperature, ALT, AST, glutamate dehydrogenase, creatine kinase or creatinine; triglycerides fell; blood urea nitrogen rose about 22% but stayed within the normal range; no ketosis. Liver glutathione rose and oxidised lipids and inflammatory eicosanoids fell [3] (verified, mice, up to about five to six weeks).
71. What is absent is everything a drug needs before people take it: no study beyond a few weeks in any species, no genotoxicity, no reproductive or developmental work, no carcinogenicity study, no second species, no eye examinations in a drug class whose predecessor caused cataracts, and no human trial of any kind (verified as absent from the published record).
72. The cataract point is worth stating plainly rather than leaving implied. DNP's human harms included cataracts at doses below the lethal range [1]. No published work on this compound reports lens examination. That is not evidence of a problem; it is an untested question in exactly the place the class's history points (inferred).
73. One structural caution: the therapeutic margin for an uncoupler is the gap between burning more fuel and overheating. In mice that gap looked wide, with no temperature change at twenty times the energy-expenditure dose [3]. Nobody knows what it is in a human, and a short half-life cuts both ways, limiting accumulation but making exposure sensitive to dose and formulation (inferred).

### Who produced the evidence [lab]
74. The compound comes from an academic network spanning Virginia Tech, the University of Virginia, UNSW Sydney, the University of Sydney and the Garvan Institute, with a company among the author affiliations on the 2020 paper [3] (verified). The ageing muscle work came from a separate US group [4], which is the closest thing to independent corroboration in the file.
75. There is no clinical programme. Commentary following the mouse work described progress toward a possible clinical path as slow, with no human data [6] (reported). Six years after the main paper, that is still the position.

### Where the law stands, October 2026 [people]
76. Preclinical. No approval anywhere, no registered human trial found, no investigational new drug programme announced. Material sold under this name is a research chemical, and it is a small molecule rather than a peptide despite where it is usually shelved.
77. In sport it is not named on the WADA Prohibited List; as a substance with no approval for human therapeutic use it falls under S0, prohibited at all times, and metabolic modulators are separately addressed as a class (inferred from the list's wording).

### Open questions [mixed]
78. What is the therapeutic margin in a human? This is the whole question for an uncoupler, and the only data are mouse body temperatures.
79. Does the eye tolerate it? The class's defining human harm has not been looked for in this compound.
80. Can muscle really be gained while fat is lost? One study reports it; it needs replication before it is repeated as fact.
81. What happens past six weeks, and in a second species? Nothing longer or wider has been published.
82. How would a human dose even be set, given 1.7-hour kinetics, poor solubility and liver-weighted distribution? The authors flagged these as development problems, and they have not been solved in public.

# Bromantane
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/bromantane
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: ladasten, bromantan, bromontan, ADK-709, N-(4-bromophenyl)adamantan-2-amine
2. Origin: Not a peptide
3. Legal and approval status: Approved/used in Russia; research chemical elsewhere. WADA-banned (it caused a famous Olympic case).

## Summary
4. Bromantane is a Russian small molecule, not a peptide, classed as an actoprotector that is mildly stimulating and anti-anxiety, partly by boosting dopamine synthesis. It was developed in the Soviet Union for fatigue and anxiety, and users take it orally for energy, motivation and calm that builds over several days. Clinical data are almost only Russian trials, long-term safety is poorly mapped, and it is WADA-banned.
5. Punch line: Soviet oral actoprotector. Builds dopamine for drive and calm that grow over days, with no stimulant crash.
6. Used for: Drive, focus, fatigue

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Drive & mental stamina: Raises dopamine making
8. Cognition: Clearer focus reported
9. Mood: Less anxiety in Russian trials

## How it works
10. Raises the brain's dopamine output · Dopamine synthesis up · role Drive & mental stamina
   Bromantane raises dopamine output by increasing how much the brain makes, rather than forcing stored dopamine out the way amphetamine does. That gives a slower, steadier rise in dopamine tone. The mechanism work comes almost entirely from Russian groups, mostly in animals.
11. Switches on dopamine-making genes · Tyrosine hydroxylase, AADC · role Drive & mental stamina
   It raises expression of tyrosine hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC), the two enzymes that build dopamine from tyrosine. More enzyme means more synthesis capacity over days, which fits its slow onset. This comes from Russian research, with little Western replication.
12. Lifts energy without a classic crash · Claimed, Russian studies · role Mood
   Because it builds dopamine supply instead of draining stores, there is no sudden drop when it wears off. Russian human trials report less fatigue and asthenia with this no-crash profile. Western trials are lacking and long-term safety is poorly mapped.
13. Eases anxiety · Mechanism unclear · role Mood
   Russian trials report lower anxiety alongside the energy lift, an unusual pairing for a stimulating compound. Why this happens has not been worked out. Treat the calming effect as reported in those trials, without a known target behind it.
14. Mechanism overview: Bromantane is an adamantane derivative developed in Russia as an actoprotector. Instead of releasing stored dopamine like amphetamine, it raises expression of tyrosine hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, the enzymes that make dopamine. More synthesis capacity means a gradual, sustained lift in dopaminergic tone, which fits the slow onset and absence of a crash. Its anti-anxiety effect has no clear mechanism. Nearly all mechanistic work comes from Russian groups.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
15. Typical: 50–100 mg · once daily · cycle 2–4 weeks · route Oral (reported)
16. Half-life: ~11 hours
17. Common: 50–100 mg · 1× AM · 28 days, then 4–8 wk off · Oral or sublingual · for asthenia, energy [S1] [S2] (verified)
18. Low / pulse: 25–30 mg · AM, as needed · pulsed · Oral or sublingual · for mood/focus, sensitive users [S2] [S3] (reported)
19. Aggressive: 100–250 mg · daily · unclear · Oral · for heavy users [S3] (reported)

## What people report
20. Oral; reported for energy, motivation and calm; slow onset over days.
21. Liked / worked: Russian trials report less fatigue and anxiety
22. Liked / worked: Energy without the stimulant crash
23. What worked: Russian trials describe energy, mood and anxiety benefit without the crash of classic stimulants.
24. Went wrong / did not work: Evidence is almost all Russian
25. Went wrong / did not work: Long-term safety not well mapped
26. Went wrong / did not work: Mechanism poorly characterised in the West
27. What went wrong: Evidence is Russian; long-term safety and the dopamine-synthesis mechanism are not well characterized in the West.
28. Most reported: Oral
29. Most reported: Reported for energy, motivation and calm
30. Most reported: Slow onset over days

## What has been tested
31. Cellular energy: Fatigue and asthenia (trial)
32. Mood: Anxiety (trial)
33. Drive & mental stamina: Stimulant-without-crash profile (trial)
34. Russian human trials report reduced fatigue and anxiety with a stimulant-without-crash profile; it was a notable sports-doping case. Little Western study.
35. What it helps: Russian trials report less fatigue and asthenia, lower anxiety, and energy without the crash of classic stimulants. These are almost the only clinical data, and long-term safety is poorly mapped. Users take it orally and describe more energy, motivation and calm, building slowly over several days.
36. Trial: none. Approved in Russia as Ladasten for fatigue; no registered trial found in Western registries, and Russian registry checks were not possible. (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
37. Drug-tested athletes: Banned stimulant since the 1996 Olympics; on the WADA list. (verified)
38. People with bipolar disorder or psychosis history: Raises dopamine synthesis; may tip mood or perception. (inferred)

## Where it comes from
39. A Russian 'actoprotector' small molecule (ladasten) that is both mildly stimulating and anti-anxiety, acting partly by boosting dopamine synthesis. Not a peptide.
40. First studied for: Fatigue, asthenia and anxiety; developed in the Soviet Union.
41. Name story: A squashed version of its chemical name, adamantyl-bromphenyl-amine. Built in 1980s Moscow to help Soviet soldiers recover from exertion, it became famous when Russian athletes tested positive at the 1996 Olympics; it is sold in Russia as Ladasten. [S5] (verified)
42. Soviet era: Developed as an 'actoprotector' for fatigue and asthenia
43. 1996: Olympic doping cases put it on the map
44. Today: Used in Russia as ladasten; research chemical elsewhere; WADA-banned

# P21
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/p21
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: P021, CNTF-derived peptide, Ac-DGGL-AdaG-NH2, Peptide 021
2. Origin: Lab-designed from a natural growth factor
3. Sequence: DGGLAG (6 amino acids). Acetylated, with an adamantylated glycine amide at the C-terminus; from CNTF residues 148–151
4. Legal and approval status: Not approved; preclinical; no registered human trial (as of Oct 2026).

## Summary
5. P21 is a short peptide taken from ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF), with an adamantane group added so it can enter the brain. It was developed as an oral neurogenesis lead for Alzheimer's, and people use it for memory and mood. Evidence is mouse work mostly from the inventor's lab, an independent 2024 study did not reproduce the BDNF effect, and no human study exists.
6. Punch line: CNTF fragment with an adamantane key into the brain. Grew new neurons in Alzheimer's mice; no human study.
7. Used for: Memory, neurogenesis

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Neural plasticity: Neurogenesis in aged mice
9. Cognition: Memory in Alzheimer's mice
10. Neural protection: Less tau and amyloid
11. Aging & senescence: Studied in aged animals
12. Mood (backed only by animal or user reports): Mood lift reported

## How it works
13. Copies a nerve growth factor's active spot · CNTF 148–151 mimetic · role Neural plasticity
   P21 is built on a four-residue stretch of ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF), a growth factor for nerve cells. An adamantyl end cap protects it from breakdown and is meant to help it cross into the brain. All of its effects so far come from mouse and rat studies.
14. Raises a brain growth factor in mice · BDNF up, not replicated 2024 · role Neural plasticity
   In mice, P21 raised brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a protein that supports synapse growth and memory. That was proposed as a main route to its memory effects. An independent 2024 study did not reproduce the BDNF increase, so this step is uncertain even in animals.
15. Blocks a signal that holds back new neurons · LIF signalling inhibition · role Neural plasticity
   P21 is reported to block leukaemia inhibitory factor (LIF) signalling, which acts as a brake on forming new neurons. In mice this came with more new neurons in the hippocampus, the memory centre. The authors' own literature is inconsistent here, since LIF blockade would be expected to reduce progenitors.
16. Lowers tau tangles in Alzheimer's mice · GSK-3β down, tau phosphorylation · role Neural protection
   In Alzheimer's model mice, P21 lowered the activity of GSK-3β, the enzyme that adds phosphate groups to tau. Less phosphorylated tau means fewer tangles in neurons. Treated mice also showed less amyloid and better memory, nearly all from the inventor's lab, with no human study.
17. Mechanism overview: P021 is an acetylated peptide built on residues 148–151 of ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF), with an adamantylated glycine at the end to resist breakdown and cross the blood–brain barrier. In mice it is reported to inhibit leukaemia inhibitory factor (LIF) signalling, raise BDNF, lower GSK-3β activity and so reduce tau phosphorylation, and increase hippocampal neurogenesis. Its own literature is partly inconsistent: LIF inhibition would be expected to reduce progenitor formation, not increase it.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
18. Typical: No human dose studied · NA · cycle NA · route Sub-Q or intranasal (community) (reported)
19. Half-life: >3 h (mouse plasma)
20. Most people take: No human dose studied; animal protocols only.

## What people report
21. Used for memory and mood; few detailed first-hand reports.
22. Liked / worked: Memory and pathology gains in Alzheimer's mice
23. What worked: Less tau and amyloid and better memory in Alzheimer's mice.
24. Went wrong / did not work: Core BDNF effect not replicated (Mottolese 2024)
25. Went wrong / did not work: Most positive studies share one inventor
26. Went wrong / did not work: No human data
27. What went wrong: An independent 2024 mouse study did not reproduce the core BDNF effect.
28. Most reported: Memory and mood reported
29. Most reported: Few detailed reports
30. Most reported: Some report nothing

## What has been tested
31. Cognition: Memory in Alzheimer's mice (animal)
32. Neural protection: Tau and amyloid load (animal)
33. Neural plasticity: Hippocampal neurogenesis (animal)
34. Mouse and rat Alzheimer's and aging models; no human studies registered.
35. What it helps: Evidence is mouse and rat work, almost all from the inventor's lab. Alzheimer's mice showed less tau and amyloid and better memory. An independent 2024 study did not reproduce the BDNF increase. There is no human study. People use it for memory and mood, and first-hand reports are few.
36. Trial: none. Only mouse studies; no human trial registered. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
37. People with active or recent cancer: CNTF pathway drives neurotrophic growth; untested. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
38. Semax: Semax is reported to raise BDNF through a melanocortin-derived fragment, while P21 works on the CNTF side and neurogenesis. People pair them to push brain growth factors from two angles. All of this is user logic, not trial data, and the pair has not been tested together.
39. Dihexa: Dihexa boosts HGF and c-Met signalling to build synapses, while P21 targets new neuron formation and tau. Both have only rodent memory data. The stack is user logic for plasticity from two pathways, and it has never been tested together.
40. NA Semax Amidate: NA Semax Amidate is a longer-lasting Semax that is assumed to raise BDNF, while P21 acts on CNTF-linked neurogenesis in mice. People pair them for memory and drive. Neither half has human proof for this use, and the pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
41. A short peptide from ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF), with an adamantane group added for brain entry, from the Iqbal lab in New York.
42. First studied for: An oral neurogenesis drug lead for Alzheimer's disease.
43. Name story: No relation to p21 (CDKN1A), the famous cell-cycle brake protein. P021 is a lab code for a four-residue slice of the nerve growth factor CNTF (residues 148-151), capped with adamantylglycine to survive and reach the brain. [S2] (inferred)
44. 2010s: Iqbal lab derives P021 from CNTF for Alzheimer's
45. 2014–2020: Mouse studies report less tau, less amyloid, more neurons
46. 2024: Independent study fails to reproduce the BDNF effect in live mice
47. Today: Sold as a research nootropic; no human trial

# PTD-DBM
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/ptd-dbm
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: CXXC5-Dvl competitor peptide, CXXC5 inhibitor peptide, protein transduction domain-fused Dishevelled binding motif
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: RRRRRRRRGGGGRKTGHQICKFRKC (25 amino acids). Eight-arginine cell-entry tag (PTD), GGGG linker, then the Dishevelled-binding motif (DBM); free cysteines
4. Legal and approval status: Not approved anywhere and no registered human trial as of Oct 2026; sold in Korea as a cosmetic 'hair booster' ingredient since July 2026 (reported); not named on the WADA list, falls under S0 non-approved substances (inferred).

## Summary
5. PTD-DBM is a lab-designed peptide from Yonsei University that pairs a cell-entry tag with a decoy motif blocking CXXC5, a brake on hair-building Wnt signalling. It was studied for wound healing and hair regrowth, and grew new follicles in bald mice. No human trial exists, and the few detailed forum reports describe no regrowth.
6. Punch line: Korean peptide that releases a brake on Wnt hair signalling. Regrew follicles in bald mice; users saw none.
7. Used for: Hair loss, wound and scar healing

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Hair: New follicles in mice
9. Tissue repair: Faster wound closure in mice
10. Skin & aesthetics: Less scarring in mice

## How it works
11. Arginine tag carries it into cells · Protein transduction domain (R8) · role Skin & aesthetics
   PTD-DBM starts with eight arginines, a protein transduction domain that drags the peptide across cell membranes. That lets it reach its target inside skin and follicle cells when applied to the skin. The delivery has been shown in mouse skin and cell work.
12. Blocks CXXC5 from grabbing Dishevelled · CXXC5-Dvl PDZ interaction · role Hair
   CXXC5 is a brake protein that binds the PDZ domain of Dishevelled (Dvl), a relay in the Wnt pathway. PTD-DBM carries a Dvl-binding motif that competes for that site. In cell studies this pulls CXXC5 off Dvl, and balding human scalp carries more CXXC5.
13. Lets the hair-building signal run again · Wnt/beta-catenin · role Hair
   With the CXXC5 brake released, Wnt/beta-catenin signalling runs again. Beta-catenin rises and switches on genes that build and regenerate hair follicles. In bald mice topical PTD-DBM grew new follicles, but no human trial exists.
14. Speeds skin closure with more collagen · Beta-catenin, alpha-SMA, collagen I · role Tissue repair
   The same Wnt/beta-catenin rise drives wound repair genes, including alpha-SMA and collagen I. In mice, wounds closed faster with more collagen, and scars were smaller with valproic acid alongside. This comes almost entirely from one Korean group.
15. Mechanism overview: PTD-DBM is a 25-residue peptide: eight arginines that carry it across cell membranes, a glycine linker, and a Dishevelled-binding motif. CXXC5 is a feedback brake on Wnt/beta-catenin signalling; it binds the PDZ domain of Dishevelled (Dvl) and stops the signal that builds and regenerates hair follicles and closes wounds. Balding human scalp carries more CXXC5, and DHT raises it in dermal papilla cells. PTD-DBM competes for that Dvl site, releasing the brake rather than forcing the pathway on, so beta-catenin rises and follicle and collagen genes switch back on.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
16. Typical: No human dose (animal only) · Daily in reports · cycle Months in forum reports · route Topical (reported)
17. Half-life: Unknown
18. Most people take: No trial dose. Mice got topical PTD-DBM on bare skin for 28 days. Forum users apply it topically after microneedling, one up to ~20 mg/day for 5 months with no result; oral versions are sold, unsupported.

## What people report
19. Small hair-loss community following since 2017; topical and microneedling use, mostly null results; doubts it penetrates skin at ~3 kDa.
20. Liked / worked: New follicles in bald mice
21. Liked / worked: Stronger with valproic acid or wounding
22. Liked / worked: Faster wound healing in mice
23. What worked: In mice, new follicles and faster regrowth, strongest with valproic acid or wounding; faster, less scarred wound closure.
24. Went wrong / did not work: No human trials
25. Went wrong / did not work: Almost all data from one lab
26. Went wrong / did not work: Forum users report no regrowth
27. What went wrong: No human trial; forum self-experimenters report no regrowth after months of topical use.
28. Most reported: Topical use after microneedling
29. Most reported: No results after ~5 months (one user)
30. Most reported: No side effects reported
31. Most reported: Doubts it crosses skin at ~3 kDa

## What has been tested
32. Hair: Hair regrowth and new follicles (animal)
33. Tissue repair: Skin wound healing (animal)
34. Skin & aesthetics: Scar reduction with valproic acid patch (animal)
35. Hair: CXXC5 high in balding scalp cells (cell)
36. Mouse and cell work only, almost all from the Choi lab; topical on shaved mouse skin for 28 days, alone and with valproic acid.
37. What it helps: Evidence is mouse and cell work from the Yonsei group. Topical PTD-DBM grew new follicles in bald mice and sped wound healing, with stronger effects alongside valproic acid or wounding. No human trial exists. People with pattern hair loss try it topically with microneedling, sometimes with minoxidil-style stacks; the few detailed forum reports describe no regrowth and no side effects.
38. Trial: none. Hair regrowth and wound data are from mice; no human trial registered. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
39. People with basal cell or skin cancer history: Activates Wnt signalling, implicated in skin tumours. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
40. GHK-Cu: GHK-Cu works on collagen, matrix remodelling and dermal papilla cells, while PTD-DBM restarts Wnt/beta-catenin signalling in follicles. People pair them topically, often with microneedling, for hair and scars from two angles. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.
41. AHK-Cu: AHK-Cu targets dermal papilla cells, follicle blood supply and cell survival, while PTD-DBM releases the CXXC5 brake on Wnt. Both aim at thinning hair by different routes. Neither has human regrowth trials, and the pair has not been tested together.
42. Thymulin: Thymulin calms inflammatory cytokines in models, while PTD-DBM pushes follicle regrowth through Wnt. The logic is that a quieter scalp may suit regrowth, used cautiously for inflamed or autoimmune-linked hair loss. There are no data on the pair.

## Where it comes from
43. Designed in Choi Kang-yell's Yonsei University lab: a cell-entry tag fused to a decoy motif that stops CXXC5 from braking Wnt signalling.
44. First studied for: Skin wound healing in mice (2015), then hair regrowth and wound-induced hair neogenesis (2017).
45. Name story: Two parts named in the label: PTD = Protein Transduction Domain (the cell-entry tail) fused to DBM = Dishevelled Binding Motif. From Kang-Yell Choi's lab at Yonsei University. [S2] (verified)
46. 2015: Choi lab shows CXXC5 slows skin wound healing; PTD-DBM speeds it in mice
47. 2017: J Invest Dermatol: hair regrowth and new follicles in mice, best with valproic acid
48. 2020: Forum group buys; users report no regrowth after months
49. 2023: Hydrogel patch with valproic acid reduces scarring in mice
50. July 2026: Korean cosmetic hair booster with PTD-DBM launched (reported)

# Adamax
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/adamax
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Semax derivative, adamantyl Semax, Ac-MEHFPGPAG-NH2 (adamantyl-modified)
2. Origin: Lab-modified Semax
3. Sequence: MEHFPGP (7 amino acids). Semax core; sellers claim an acetylated N-terminus and an adamantane on the C-terminus. Published structures disagree.
4. Legal and approval status: Not approved; no published research; listed by New Zealand's Medsafe in a June 2025 review of unscheduled peptides.

## Summary
5. Adamax is a seller-marketed version of Semax with an adamantane group added, said to make it longer lasting and stronger. Users take it for focus and calm. It is not approved and no published study of Adamax exists, since every cited reference is about Semax, and sellers disagree on what is in the vial.
6. Punch line: Semax with an adamantane group, sold as stronger and longer lasting. Taken for focus, calm; no study exists.
7. Used for: Focus, mood

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Cognition: Focus and clarity reported
9. Neural protection: Borrowed from Semax claims
10. Mood: Less overwhelm reported
11. Drive & mental stamina: Mental energy reported

## How it works
12. Claimed to work like Semax, only longer · ACTH 4–7 core, melanocortin · role Cognition
   Adamax is sold as Semax, a fragment of ACTH, with an adamantane group added to make it last longer. The idea is that it acts on the same melanocortin pathway as Semax. No study has tested this in Adamax itself.
13. Claimed to raise brain growth factors · BDNF up, Semax data · role Neural protection
   Semax raises BDNF, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, a growth factor that supports neuron survival and new connections. Adamax is claimed to do the same. That claim rests entirely on Semax data, mostly from rodents.
14. Adamantane added for stability and brain entry · Adamantyl modification, claimed · role Cognition
   Adamantane is a bulky cage-shaped group, also used in P21, meant to slow breakdown and help the molecule cross into the brain. This is design intent, not a measured result. Published structures of Adamax disagree, and no paper characterises the molecule.
15. Mechanism overview: Adamax is sold as Semax (Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro, from ACTH 4–10) with an adamantane group attached, the same bulky cage used in P21 to slow breakdown and help brain entry. The intended mechanism is Semax's: melanocortin-pathway signalling and raised BDNF. Published structures conflict on chain length, the end groups and where the adamantane sits, and no paper characterises the molecule.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
16. Typical: 100–300 mcg · once daily · cycle 2–4 weeks · route Sub-Q or intranasal (reported)
17. Half-life: unknown
18. Most people take: No study of any dose. Community 100–300 mcg/day, 2–4 week runs.

## What people report
19. Reported for focus, calm and less overwhelm; headaches above about 300 mcg.
20. What worked: No study of Adamax exists.
21. Went wrong / did not work: No studies of Adamax
22. Went wrong / did not work: Structure disputed between sellers
23. What went wrong: Sellers do not agree on its exact molecule.
24. Most reported: Focus and clarity
25. Most reported: Calmer, less overwhelmed
26. Most reported: Headaches above ~300 mcg
27. Most reported: Insomnia or overstimulation

## What has been tested
28. Nothing published on Adamax itself; all cited studies are on Semax.
29. What it helps: There is no published study of Adamax. Every reference sellers cite is about Semax. Users take it for focus and calm, and headaches and overstimulation come up at higher amounts.
30. Trial: none. No human trial in any registry; it exists only as a research chemical derived from Semax. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
31. People with a history of seizures: Semax parent carries convulsion warning; adamantane boosts brain entry. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
32. Semax: Adamax is marketed as a longer-lasting Semax, so pairing them is mostly doubling up on the same claimed pathway, melanocortin signalling and BDNF. Adamax has no published data, and the pair has not been tested together.
33. Selank: Semax-type peptides like Adamax are taken for drive and focus, while Selank is taken for calm through tuftsin and enkephalin effects. People pair them to balance stimulation with calm, but the pairing is user logic, not trial data.
34. P21: Both carry an adamantane group, and both are aimed at brain growth factors, Adamax through Semax-like BDNF claims and P21 through a CNTF mimic. Users stack them for memory and focus, but neither the pair nor Adamax alone has been studied.

## Where it comes from
35. A newer seller-marketed version of Semax with an adamantane group added, borrowing the trick used in P21.
36. First studied for: Marketed as a longer-lasting, stronger Semax.
37. Name story: Semax with an adamantane cage bolted to its tail end; 'Ada' is almost certainly from adamantane, the diamond-shaped hydrocarbon also behind amantadine and bromantane. Described as a designer analogue of Semax, with no published developer. [S2] (inferred)
38. 1980s–1990s: Semax developed in Russia from ACTH 4–10
39. 2020s: Adamax appears in research-peptide catalogs
40. June 2025: Named in New Zealand Medsafe's review of unscheduled peptides
41. Today: No published studies; structure disputed

# Creatine
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/creatine
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: creatine monohydrate, N-methylguanidinoacetic acid
2. Origin: Not a peptide
3. Legal and approval status: Dietary supplement; safe and legal.

## Summary
4. Creatine is an amino-acid-derived compound stored in muscle as a rapid energy buffer; it is not a peptide. People take it orally for strength, power and muscle, because it refills cell energy during short bursts of effort. It is among the best-evidenced supplements here, with smaller newer benefits for the brain, though some people do not respond and early water weight is common.
5. Punch line: The best-proven supplement here. Refills muscle energy for short bursts; more strength, power, some water weight.
6. Used for: Strength, power, brain energy

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Cognition: Some help under sleep loss
8. Cellular energy: Quick energy buffer in muscle
9. Muscle & performance: More strength and power with training

## How it works
10. Refills cell energy in seconds · Phosphocreatine, ATP · role Cellular energy
   Creatine enters muscle and brain through a dedicated transporter and is loaded with phosphate to form phosphocreatine. During hard effort, phosphocreatine hands that phosphate back to ADP and rebuilds ATP within seconds, faster than any other pathway. Supplementing enlarges this reserve, shown repeatedly in human trials.
11. Backs short bursts of power · Creatine kinase · role Muscle & performance
   Creatine kinase is the enzyme that shuttles phosphate between phosphocreatine and ATP. A bigger phosphocreatine pool lets muscle sustain sprints and heavy sets a little longer before fatigue. More training volume then drives more strength and lean mass, one of the most consistent findings in human trials.
12. Draws water into muscle cells · Cell volume · role Muscle & performance
   Creatine pulls water into muscle cells as it is stored, raising cell volume. This explains the early weight gain and fuller look users report in the first weeks. The rise is water inside the muscle, not fat, and it is a known, harmless effect in healthy people.
13. Buffers brain energy under stress · Brain phosphocreatine · role Cognition
   The brain also stores phosphocreatine to buffer its energy supply. Under stress such as sleep loss or mental fatigue, a larger reserve may help keep ATP steady. Human trials show smaller benefits for memory and mental fatigue than for muscle, and brain protection work is still early.
14. Mechanism overview: Creatine is taken into muscle and brain by a dedicated transporter, then creatine kinase loads it with phosphate to make phosphocreatine. During hard, short efforts, phosphocreatine hands that phosphate back to ADP, regenerating ATP within seconds, faster than any other pathway. Supplementing enlarges the phosphocreatine pool, so more repetitions and sprints happen before fatigue. More training volume then drives more muscle growth. Creatine also pulls water into muscle cells, and in the brain it buffers energy supply under stress.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
15. Typical: 3–5 g · once daily · cycle ongoing · route Oral (verified)
16. Half-life: ~3 hours
17. Maintenance: 3–5 g · 1× daily · ongoing · Oral · for almost everyone [S1] (verified)
18. Brain baseline / load: 10 g daily; or 20–25 g (0.3 g/kg) load · daily; load split 4–5× · ongoing; load 5–7 days · Oral · for cognition and fast saturation [S2] [S3] (reported)
19. Acute high (stress): 20 g, up to 0.35 g/kg (~25 g) · single day · sleep loss or high-stress days · Oral · for sleep-deprived; tested in 15 adults [S4] [S2] (verified)

## What people report
20. Oral monohydrate; among the best-evidenced supplements here.
21. Liked / worked: Repeatable gains in strength and power
22. Liked / worked: More muscle with training
23. Liked / worked: Emerging cognitive benefit
24. What worked: Robust, repeatable gains in strength/power and muscle; emerging cognitive benefit.
25. Went wrong / did not work: Non-responders exist
26. Went wrong / did not work: Brain benefits are smaller and newer
27. Went wrong / did not work: Water weight gain
28. What went wrong: Non-responders exist; the brain benefits are smaller and newer; causes water weight.
29. Most reported: Oral monohydrate
30. Most reported: Strength gains, fuller muscles
31. Most reported: Among the best-evidenced here

## What has been tested
32. Muscle & performance: Strength and power in training (trial)
33. Muscle & performance: Lean mass gain (trial)
34. Cognition: Memory and mental fatigue (trial)
35. Neural protection: Brain protection (human)
36. One of the most studied supplements: reliably increases strength, power and muscle in training, with growing evidence for cognition and neuroprotection.
37. What it helps: Among the best-evidenced compounds here. Trials show repeatable gains in strength, power and lean mass alongside resistance training. Newer trials show smaller benefits for memory and mental fatigue, and early human work on brain protection. Users take oral monohydrate and report strength gains and fuller muscles. Some people are non-responders, and water weight rises early.
38. Trial: active · Not applicable · endurance performance with creatine and carbohydrate · NCT07712653 · California Polytechnic State University. One of dozens of open creatine trials, which range from dialysis patients to post concussion symptoms. (checked 2026-10-23) [S5] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
39. People monitoring kidney function by creatinine: Raises blood creatinine, making kidneys look worse on labs. (reported)
40. People with kidney disease or on nephrotoxic drugs: Case reports of kidney injury, mostly with pre-existing disease. (reported)
41. People with bipolar disorder: Case reports of mania during creatine use. (reported)

## Where it comes from
42. An amino-acid-derived compound stored in muscle as a rapid energy buffer, identified in 1832. Not a peptide.
43. First studied for: Athletic performance and muscle; later studied for the brain.
44. Name story: From Greek kreas, meat. French chemist Michel-Eugene Chevreul boiled down meat broth in 1832, found it, and named it after flesh. [S6] (verified)
45. 1832: Identified in muscle; an amino-acid-derived energy buffer
46. 1990s: Supplement boom in sport
47. 2000s to 2020s: Brain and neuroprotection studies grow
48. Today: Among the best-evidenced supplements; safe and legal

# Methylene blue
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/methylene-blue
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: methylthioninium mb, methylthioninium chloride, ProvayBlue, Basic Blue 9, C.I. 52015, Urolene Blue
2. Origin: Not a peptide
3. Legal and approval status: Approved (methemoglobinemia); low-dose wellness use is off-label.

## Summary
4. Methylene blue is a synthetic dye from 1876 and one of the first fully synthetic drugs; it is not a peptide. It is approved as the antidote for methemoglobinemia, and low-dose off-label users take it for focus and energy, based on its role shuttling electrons in mitochondria. Evidence for cognitive and longevity use is thin, and high doses are toxic and dangerous alongside serotonergic drugs.
5. Punch line: The 1876 blue dye and approved blood antidote. Low oral doses for focus and mitochondrial energy; stains urine.
6. Used for: Focus and mitochondrial energy

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Cellular protection: Antidote for blocked blood oxygen
8. Cognition: Small studies on memory
9. Cellular energy: Passes electrons in mitochondria

## How it works
10. Restores blood's oxygen carrying · Methemoglobin reduction · role Cellular protection
   In red cells, an NADPH reductase converts methylene blue to its reduced form, leucomethylene blue. That form reduces methemoglobin back to working haemoglobin, which can carry oxygen again. This is its approved medical use, as the antidote for methemoglobinemia in people.
11. Shuttles electrons in mitochondria · Electron transport chain · role Cellular energy
   Methylene blue can take electrons from NADH and pass them straight to cytochrome c, skipping blocked steps of the electron transport chain. In theory that keeps ATP production going when mitochondria are damaged. This energy claim rests mostly on cell data, with only small human studies.
12. Blocks serotonin breakdown · MAO-A inhibition · role Cognition
   Methylene blue is a potent inhibitor of MAO-A, the enzyme that breaks down serotonin. Less breakdown means more serotonin, which may explain small mood findings in human studies. It also makes the dye dangerous with serotonergic drugs such as SSRIs, due to the risk of serotonin syndrome.
13. Cuts nitric oxide signalling · NOS, guanylate cyclase · role Cellular protection
   It blocks nitric oxide synthase and guanylate cyclase, the enzymes that make and respond to nitric oxide. Nitric oxide relaxes blood vessels, so blocking it raises blood pressure. That is why it is used in some cases of shock, and why high doses carry real toxicity.
14. Mechanism overview: Methylene blue is a redox dye that cycles between oxidised and reduced forms. In red cells, NADPH reductase converts it to leucomethylene blue, which reduces methemoglobin back to working haemoglobin and restores oxygen transport. In mitochondria it can take electrons from NADH and pass them to cytochrome c, bypassing blocked complexes, which is the basis of the energy claims. It is also a potent MAO-A inhibitor, raising serotonin, and it inhibits nitric oxide synthase and guanylate cyclase, which is why it raises blood pressure in shock.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
15. Typical: 5–20 mg · once daily · cycle ongoing or cycled · route Oral (reported)
16. Half-life: ~5–24 hours
17. Common: 5–20 mg · 1× daily, 5 on/2 off · 4–12 wk or ongoing · Oral · for nootropic, energy [S1] [S2] [S3] (reported)
18. Clinic microdose: 0.5–4 mg · 1× daily · ongoing · Oral · for clinic-managed wellness [S4] [S5] (reported)
19. mg/kg / study: 0.5–1 mg/kg (35–70 mg/70 kg) up to 280 mg single · 1× or 2× daily · short · Oral · for weight-based nootropic, research [S6] [S5] (reported)

## What people report
20. Oral low-dose; reported for focus and energy; stains everything blue.
21. Liked / worked: Proven antidote for methemoglobinemia
22. Liked / worked: Small low-dose studies hint at cognitive gains
23. What worked: Proven antidote; low-dose cognitive/energy signals in small studies.
24. Went wrong / did not work: Nootropic and longevity use rests on thin data
25. Went wrong / did not work: Toxic at high doses
26. Went wrong / did not work: Dangerous with serotonergic drugs
27. What went wrong: The nootropic/longevity use rests on thin human evidence; high doses are toxic and it interacts dangerously with serotonergic drugs.
28. Most reported: Taken orally at low dose
29. Most reported: Reported for focus and energy
30. Most reported: Stains urine and everything else blue

## What has been tested
31. Cellular protection: Methemoglobinemia antidote (human)
32. Cognition: Low-dose memory and attention (human)
33. Mood: Low-dose mood support (human)
34. Cellular energy: Mitochondrial support (cell)
35. Approved for methemoglobinemia; studied at low doses for cognition, mood and mitochondrial support, with small and preliminary human data.
36. What it helps: Its proven use is as the antidote for methemoglobinemia. Small low-dose human studies hint at better memory and attention, and some at mood support. Users take low oral doses for focus and energy, and note blue urine. Mitochondrial and longevity claims rest on cell data. High doses are toxic, and the MAO-A effect makes it dangerous with serotonergic drugs.
37. Trial: active · Phase 1 · cytokine storm and neurotoxicity after CAR T immunotherapy · NCT07169487 · Institute of Hematology & Blood Diseases Hospital, China. Approved (ProvayBlue) for methemoglobinemia, and being tested in China against CAR T side effects plus septic shock elsewhere. (checked 2026-10-23) [S7] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
38. People on SSRIs, SNRIs or MAOIs: Strong MAO-A inhibitor; boxed warning for serotonin syndrome. (verified)
39. People with G6PD deficiency: Causes haemolysis; contraindicated on the label. (verified)
40. People relying on a pulse oximeter: The blue dye absorbs the oximeter light, so oxygen readings show falsely low. (verified)
41. Breastfeeding parents: Label says stop breastfeeding for 8 days after a dose. (verified)

## Where it comes from
42. A synthetic dye from 1876, the first fully synthetic drug ever used in medicine, later found to shuttle electrons in mitochondria. Not a peptide.
43. First studied for: A medical dye and antidote (for methemoglobinemia); malaria historically.
44. Name story: Made in 1876 by Heinrich Caro at BASF as a cotton dye. Paul Ehrlich then noticed it stained malaria parasites and used it as a treatment, the first time an infectious disease was cured with a synthetic substance. [S8] (verified)
45. 1876: Synthetic dye; the first fully synthetic drug used in medicine
46. 1890s: Used against malaria
47. 20th century: Became the antidote for methemoglobinemia
48. Today: Approved antidote; low-dose use for focus and energy is off-label

# Tesamorelin + Ipamorelin + CJC-1295 no DAC
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/tesa-ipa-cjc
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Tesa/Ipa/CJC, Tesamorelin/Ipamorelin/CJC 6/3/3, triple GH blend
2. Origin: Blend of 3 peptides
3. Legal and approval status: Tesamorelin: FDA-approved only as Egrifta for HIV lipodystrophy. CJC-1295 and ipamorelin: FDA Category 2, PCAC voted against both in 2024, not removed in April 2026. The blend is not approved anywhere. WADA: all three prohibited (S2).

## Summary
4. This three-part growth hormone blend combines tesamorelin and CJC-1295 no DAC (two GHRH analogues) with ipamorelin, a ghrelin-receptor agonist. It is used for growth hormone release, visceral fat and sleep, since GHRH plus ghrelin routes give a bigger pulse. Evidence belongs to the parts, such as tesamorelin's visceral-fat trials. The triple has no data, and a second GHRH analogue adds cost and side effects without a clear extra mechanism.
5. Punch line: Triple GH stack: two GHRH analogues plus ipamorelin for a bigger pulse. Tesamorelin brings the visceral fat data.
6. Used for: GH release, visceral fat, sleep

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Endocrine & growth: Two GHRH routes plus the ghrelin route
8. Fat metabolism: Tesamorelin's visceral-fat effect
9. Sleep & rhythms: Deeper sleep, from its parts
10. Muscle & performance: Recovery and lean mass, reported for parts
11. Skin & aesthetics (backed only by animal or user reports): Skin quality, reported for parts
12. Tissue repair (backed only by animal or user reports): Recovery, reported for parts

## How it works
13. Full-length GHRH copy with fat-loss trial data · Tesamorelin, GHRH-R · role Fat metabolism
   Tesamorelin is the full 44 amino acid GHRH, the hormone that tells the pituitary to release growth hormone, with a cap that protects it from breakdown. It binds the GHRH receptor and raises cAMP. Phase 3 human trials show it cuts visceral fat in HIV lipodystrophy.
14. Short GHRH copy, lasts about 30 minutes · Mod GRF 1-29, GHRH-R · role Endocrine & growth
   Mod GRF 1-29 is the active first 29 amino acids of GHRH, modified to resist breakdown but still short-acting. It binds the same GHRH receptor and triggers a brief GH pulse. Its own human data are limited; the CJC-1295 trial used the long-acting DAC form.
15. Same receptor as tesamorelin, so overlap not synergy · Shared GHRH-R · role Endocrine & growth
   Tesamorelin and Mod GRF 1-29 both act on the GHRH receptor and raise the same cAMP signal. Two drugs on one receptor add at best and can saturate it, so they do not multiply each other. The second GHRH source brings unknown added benefit.
16. Presses the ghrelin button, selectively · Ipamorelin, GHS-R1a · role Sleep & rhythms
   Ipamorelin activates GHS-R1a, the ghrelin receptor, through a separate phospholipase C and calcium pathway. It releases GH selectively, without the cortisol and prolactin spikes older GHRPs cause. That selectivity is shown in rats and pigs, not in human trials.
17. GHRH plus ghrelin route gives a bigger pulse · GHRH + GHRP synergy · role Muscle & performance
   GHRH drives GH release through cAMP and ghrelin-type drugs through calcium, two independent routes into the same cells. Together they release more GH than either alone. This synergy is shown in a 1990 study in healthy men; the triple itself is untested.
18. Mechanism overview: Tesamorelin (GHRH 1-44 with an N-terminal trans-3-hexenoyl group) and Mod GRF 1-29 both agonise the GHRH receptor and raise cAMP; they differ in length, stability and half-life, but act at the same site, so combining them is additive at best. Ipamorelin acts at GHS-R1a via phospholipase C and calcium, and it is this second route that produces synergy with GHRH. The triple is therefore pharmacologically a GHRH + GHRP blend with two GHRH sources.

## What is inside the blend
19. Tesamorelin: 6 mg · GHRH signal with trial data for visceral fat
20. Ipamorelin: 3 mg · Ghrelin-receptor signal: the synergy partner
21. CJC-1295 no DAC (Mod GRF 1-29): 3 mg · Short GHRH pulse, cheaper and more stable than tesamorelin
22. Most common ratio: Tesamorelin 6 · Ipamorelin 3 · CJC-1295 no DAC 3 = 12 mg (9 of 9 listings (3 state the split, 6 sell 12 mg))
23. Version Common retail: Tesamorelin 6 · Ipamorelin 3 · CJC-1295 no DAC 3 = 12 mg
24. Why Tesamorelin is in it: The visceral-fat trial record
25. Why Ipamorelin is in it: The only part acting on a second receptor; the source of synergy
26. Why CJC-1295 no DAC is in it: Extra GHRH signal at lower cost; same receptor as tesamorelin, so overlap
27. Mixing chemistry: Tesamorelin keeps native Met27 and Asn8 and is the least stable part in solution; its licensed versions are used immediately (SV) or within a week (WR).
28. Mixing chemistry: Mod GRF and ipamorelin are the forgiving parts; the blend's usable life is set by tesamorelin.
29. Mixing chemistry: Two GHRH peptides of different lengths may separate differently on HPLC; ask for per-component mg, not one purity number.
30. Mixing chemistry: No stability data for the reconstituted triple. Discard if cloudy, gelled or particulate.
31. Self-mixing: Mixing three separate vials lets you size tesamorelin to its usual 1 mg without overshooting CJC, but adds needle passes; drawing into one syringe at the time of the shot is better supported than pre-mixing a vial.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
32. Typical: No standard dose · 1× daily, pre-bed · cycle 8–12 weeks, 5 on / 2 off · route Sub-Q (reported)
33. Half-life: per component
34. Most people take: No published dose for the triple. People size it by the components: 100 mcg CJC per shot (the classic CJC/Ipa dose) is 10 units of a 12 mg vial in 3 mL, which also gives 200 mcg tesamorelin and 100 mcg ipamorelin. 20 units brings tesamorelin to 400 mcg, still below the 1 mg most tesamorelin users take.

## What people report

36. Liked / worked: Each part raises GH
37. Liked / worked: Tesamorelin has fat-loss trials
38. Liked / worked: GHRH + GHRP synergy shown

40. Went wrong / did not work: No trial, no protocol, no reports found

42. Went wrong / did not work: Fixed ratio, more side-effect load

44. Most reported: 10 units of 12 mg in 3 mL, nightly
45. Most reported: Schedule borrowed from CJC/Ipa
46. Most reported: Rare; mostly seller-driven
