[S2] EVS Translations: insulin, a word first used 100 years ago · https://evs-translations.com/blog/insulin/
[S3] Insulin (medication) · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin_(medication)


# 5-Amino-1MQ
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/5-amino-1mq
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: methylquinolinium, 5-amino-1-methylquinolinium, 5-amino-1-methylquinolinium iodide, 5-Amino-1-MQ iodide, NNMT inhibitor 5-amino-1MQ
2. Origin: Not a peptide
3. Legal and approval status: Unapproved research chemical everywhere.

## Summary
4. 5-Amino-1MQ is a small molecule, not a peptide, that blocks the enzyme NNMT, which links NAD and methylation metabolism in fat. It is studied to shrink fat cells and raise cellular NAD, and users take it as an oral capsule for fat loss and energy, often stacked with MOTS-c and NAD+. Evidence is mouse-only, and no human trials exist.
5. Punch line: Oral NNMT blocker, not a peptide. Shrinks fat cells and lifts NAD in mice; often stacked with MOTS-c.
6. Used for: Fat loss, metabolic support

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Fat metabolism: Shrinks fat cells in mice
8. Cellular energy: Raises cell NAD in mice
9. Tissue repair: Muscle stem cell support in mice
10. Drive & mental stamina: Users report more energy
11. Muscle & performance (backed only by animal or user reports): Older mouse muscle recovered
12. Aging & senescence (backed only by animal or user reports): Studied for aging metabolism
13. Pain & sensory (backed only by animal or user reports): Some users report less pain

## How it works
14. Blocks a fat-cell enzyme · NNMT inhibition · role Fat metabolism
   5-Amino-1MQ is a small molecule that inhibits nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT). NNMT is highly expressed in the fat tissue of obese animals. Blocking it shifts fat cells toward burning more energy and storing less fat, shown in mouse studies only.
15. Spares NAD and methyl groups · NAD, SAM pools · role Cellular energy
   NNMT normally methylates nicotinamide using SAM, which drains both the NAD salvage pathway and the methyl donor pool. Blocking NNMT keeps nicotinamide available to make NAD+ and preserves SAM. This sparing effect is shown in cell and mouse work.
16. Shrank fat cells in obese mice · Adipocyte NNMT · role Fat metabolism
   In diet-induced obese mice, the inhibitor reduced fat build-up, shrank fat cells and improved metabolic markers. These are the core findings behind its fat loss use. No human trials exist.
17. Claimed to aid aged muscle stem cells · NNMT, satellite cells · role Tissue repair
   One research group claims NNMT inhibition reactivates muscle stem cells, known as satellite cells, in aged animals. That would support muscle repair with age. The claim comes from a single group and has not been tested in people.
18. Mechanism overview: 5-Amino-1MQ is a small molecule, not a peptide, that inhibits nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT). NNMT methylates nicotinamide using SAM, which drains both the NAD salvage pathway and the methyl donor pool. NNMT is highly expressed in the fat tissue of obese animals. Blocking it keeps nicotinamide available for NAD+ synthesis and preserves SAM, shifting fat cells toward higher energy expenditure and less lipid storage. One group also claims it reactivates aged muscle stem cells.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
19. Typical: 50–100 mg · once daily · cycle 8–12 weeks · route Oral (reported)
20. Half-life: ~7 h (rat, oral)
21. Most people take: Oral 50–100 mg/day (up to 150), mornings. Injectable SC rare (~2.5–5 mg). No human PK.
22. Common: 50 mg · 1× daily (morning) · 8–12 wk · Oral · for fat loss, NNMT inhibition [S1] [S2] (reported)
23. Higher: 100 mg · 1× daily or 50 mg 2× · 8–12 wk · Oral · for standard practitioner dose [S3] [S1] (reported)
24. Aggressive: 150 mg · split 2–3× daily · ≤8 wk, ≥6 wk off · Oral · for experienced users [S4] [S2] (reported)

## What people report
25. Oral capsule, reported for fat loss and energy, often stacked with MOTS-c and NAD+.
26. Liked / worked: Less fat accumulation in mice
27. Liked / worked: Better metabolic markers in mice
28. What worked: In mice, less fat accumulation and better energy metabolism. Users report fat loss, drive and energy.
29. Went wrong / did not work: No human trials
30. Went wrong / did not work: NAD and longevity claims extrapolated
31. What went wrong: No human trials; the NAD-raising and longevity claims are extrapolated from animal and cell work.
32. Most reported: Fat loss, drive and energy
33. Most reported: Often stacked with MOTS-c and NAD+

## What has been tested
34. Fat metabolism: Diet-induced fat gain (mouse)
35. Cellular energy: Energy metabolism (mouse)
36. Mouse studies: NNMT inhibition reduced fat mass and improved metabolic markers. Human data are absent.
37. What it helps: Evidence is mouse-only: in diet-induced obese mice it reduced fat accumulation, shrank fat cells and improved metabolic markers. No human trials exist. Users take it as an oral capsule and report fat loss, drive and energy, often stacked with MOTS-c and NAD+.
38. Trial: none. No registered human trial found; evidence is a handful of mouse obesity studies. (checked 2026-10-23) [S5] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
39. People with active or recent cancer: Blocking NNMT raises NAD+ and shifts methylation; tumour effects untested. (inferred)
40. People with liver disease: NNMT is a major liver enzyme; blocking it in damaged livers is untested. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
41. MOTS-c: 5-Amino-1MQ spares NAD and shifts fat cells toward burning energy, while MOTS-c activates AMPK and mimics the metabolic effect of exercise in mice. People stack them for fat loss, and they are sold pre-mixed as NAD+ + MOTS-c + 5-Amino-1MQ. The pair has not been tested together.
42. NAD+: 5-Amino-1MQ slows the NNMT drain on the NAD salvage pathway, while NAD+ adds supply directly. People pair them to fill the pool and close the leak at once, and they come pre-mixed as NAD+ + MOTS-c + 5-Amino-1MQ. The combination has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
43. A small molecule, not a peptide: 5-amino-1-methylquinolinium, an inhibitor of the enzyme NNMT, which sits at a junction of NAD and methylation metabolism in fat.
44. First studied for: Studied to shrink fat cells and raise cellular NAD, mostly for metabolic and body-composition goals.
45. Name story: The name is chemistry shorthand: 5-amino-1-methylquinolinium, a quinoline ring with a methyl on position 1 and an amino group on position 5. It carries a permanent positive charge, so it is sold as a salt, usually the iodide. [S6] (verified)
46. 2010s: Small-molecule NNMT inhibitor studied in mice for fat loss
47. Today: Oral grey-market fat-loss and energy capsule; no human data

# 9-Me-BC
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/9-me-bc
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: 9-methyl-beta-carboline, 9-methyl-β-carboline, 9-methylnorharmane, 9MBC
2. Origin: Not a peptide: beta-carboline
3. Legal and approval status: Not approved anywhere and no registered human trial as of Oct 2026. Sold as a research chemical; not scheduled in most countries. Not named on the WADA list.

## Summary
4. 9-Me-BC is a small beta-carboline molecule, a family found in coffee and tobacco smoke, not a peptide. German researchers found it increased dopamine neurons and growth factors in cell cultures, and online users take it for motivation as a dopamine regenerator. All evidence is from cell cultures and rodents, and no human trial exists. It inhibits MAO-A and can damage DNA under UV light.
5. Punch line: A beta-carboline, not a peptide. Regrew dopamine neurons in cells; taken sublingually in short cycles for drive.
6. Used for: Motivation, mood, dopamine

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Drive & mental stamina: Motivation and drive reported
8. Neural protection: Protects dopamine neurons in lab models
9. Neural plasticity: Raises BDNF and other growth factors in cells

## How it works
10. Increases dopamine neuron numbers in culture · Tyrosine hydroxylase up · role Drive & mental stamina
   In primary midbrain cultures, 9-Me-BC raises tyrosine hydroxylase, the enzyme for the first step of dopamine production, and the number of neurons carrying it. That points to more dopamine making capacity. This is shown in cell cultures only, with no human data.
11. Raises growth factors for neurons · BDNF and other neurotrophins up · role Neural plasticity
   The same cultures show higher expression of BDNF and other neurotrophic genes, signals that help neurons survive and form connections. The effect disappears when PI3K/Akt is blocked and does not need D2/D3 receptors. This is cell and rodent evidence, not human.
12. Blocks dopamine breakdown · MAO-A over MAO-B inhibition · role Drive & mental stamina
   9-Me-BC inhibits monoamine oxidase A more than MAO-B, the enzymes that break down dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline. Slower breakdown leaves more of these signals active, one likely source of the motivation users describe. It also means interaction risk with other drugs that raise monoamines.
13. Protects neurons from toxins · PI3K/Akt dependent · role Neural protection
   Its protective effect runs through PI3K/Akt, a survival pathway that tells stressed cells not to self destruct. In cultures and a rat Parkinson's model it shielded dopamine neurons from toxins and aided recovery. No human trial exists, and photoexcited beta-carbolines damage DNA in vitro.
14. Mechanism overview: 9-Me-BC is a methylated beta-carboline. It is taken up into dopamine neurons via the dopamine transporter, inhibits MAO-A more than MAO-B, and in primary mesencephalic cultures increases tyrosine hydroxylase positive neurons and expression of BDNF and other neurotrophic genes, an effect abolished by blocking PI3K/Akt and independent of D2/D3 receptors. Beta-carbolines absorb UV light and generate reactive oxygen species, and photoexcited 9-methyl-beta-carbolines damage DNA in vitro.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
15. Typical: 5–15 mg/day · once in the morning · cycle 2–4 weeks on, 2–4 weeks off · route Sublingual, oral (reported)
16. Half-life: Unknown in humans
17. Most people take: No human dose exists. Community use is 5 to 15 mg once in the morning, held under the tongue.
18. Users run 2 to 4 week cycles with equal time off and avoid sun exposure while taking it.

## What people report
19. Discussed heavily on nootropic forums, mostly at 5 to 15 mg a day under the tongue in 2 to 4 week cycles. Users report better motivation, mood and ability to start tasks, sometimes lasting after stopping, and some use it after stimulant burnout. Complaints are insomnia, headache, anxiety and sunburn sensitivity; users avoid sun and MAO or serotonin drugs. No aggregator counts located.

24. Went wrong / did not work: MAO-A inhibitor; interaction risk

# Acetic Acid Water
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/acetic-acid-water
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: HAC
2. Origin: Sterile mixing water, not a peptide
3. Class: water
4. Legal and approval status: Sold as a mixing liquid for freeze-dried peptides. Not taken on its own.

## Summary
5. Punch line: Sterile water with a little acetic acid, usually 0.6%. Dissolves peptides that clump or gel in plain water.

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
6. Mixing water: Sterile water containing a small amount of acetic acid, most commonly sold at 0.6%. The mild acidity helps certain peptides that clump or gel in neutral water dissolve cleanly.

## How it works

## Water
7. Made of: Sterile water, about 99.4%
8. Made of: Acetic acid, commonly 0.6% (retail range about 0.6 to 1%; confirm on certificate of analysis)
9. pH: About 2.9 for 0.6% acetic acid (about 0.1 mol/L), calculated from acetic acid's pKa of 4.76. Not stated on most labels.
10. When used: AOD-9604 and HGH fragment 176-191, which are commonly reported to gel or clump in bacteriostatic water and dissolve more cleanly in dilute acid.
11. When used: Other positively charged (basic) peptides that do not dissolve in water. Peptide manufacturers' solubility guides recommend trying acetic acid for basic peptides when water fails.
12. When used: Sometimes used as a first step: the peptide is dissolved in a small amount of acid, then diluted with water or bacteriostatic water.
13. not_for: Peptides that dissolve fine in bacteriostatic water. Acid adds sting without benefit.
14. not_for: Acid-sensitive peptides, or peptides the supplier says to keep at neutral pH.
15. not_for: Repeated draws over weeks if the product has no preservative. Most acetic acid waters list none.
16. not_for: Mixing with strongly buffered or alkaline liquids in the same vial, which can neutralize the acid and cause the peptide to fall out of solution.
17. storage: Unopened: cool place away from light, within the printed expiry date. Refrigeration (2 to 8°C) is a reasonable default if no instructions are given.
18. storage: After first puncture: treat as preservative-free unless the label says otherwise. Refrigerate and use within a short period. The USP 28-day multi-dose limit is meant for preserved vials and should be treated as an upper bound, not a target.
19. storage: Once a peptide is dissolved in it, follow that peptide's storage rules, usually refrigerated at 2 to 8°C.
20. storage: Do not freeze unless the label allows it.
21. how: Check the label, concentration, expiry date and clarity. Write the date of first puncture on the vial.
22. how: Wipe the stopper with an alcohol swab and let it dry. Use a new sterile needle and syringe each time.
23. how: Add the liquid slowly down the inside wall of the peptide vial.
24. how: Swirl gently until clear. Do not shake.
25. how: If the solution gels or stays cloudy, do not use it; a different solvent or lower concentration may be needed.
26. watch: Cloudiness, haze or particles in the plain liquid: discard.
27. watch: A light vinegar smell is expected. Any other odor is not.
28. watch: Stinging or burning on injection is common with acidic liquids; worsening redness, swelling, heat or pain at the site is a warning sign.
29. watch: Gel, strands or white flakes after mixing indicate the peptide has aggregated.
30. facts: 'HAc' is a standard chemistry shorthand for acetic acid, where Ac stands for the acetate group (AcOH and HOAc are also used). The retail label is almost certainly this abbreviation.
31. facts: AOD-9604 is a 16 amino acid piece of human growth hormone with two arginines and a ring formed by two cysteines. In acid, the molecules carry a stronger positive charge and repel each other, which is the likely reason they stop clumping.
32. facts: 0.6% acetic acid is roughly seven to twelve times more dilute than table vinegar (4 to 7%), yet still several hundred times more acidic than bacteriostatic water (pH about 2.9 versus 5.7).
33. tile: 0.6% acetic acid
34. tile: pH about 2.9 · no preservative
35. cells: In it, 0.6% acetic acid
36. cells: pH, about 2.9
37. cells: Opened, short, fridge
38. cells: Route, Mixing only

# Adipotide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/adipotide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: ftpp prohibitin, FTPP (fat-targeted proapoptotic peptide), prohibitin-TP01, prohibitin-targeting peptide 1, CKGGRAKDC-GG-D(KLAKLAK)2
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: CKGGRAKDCGGKLAKLAKKLAKLAK (25 amino acids). Ring closed between the two C at the start; the KLAKLAK half is made of D amino acids
4. Legal and approval status: Never approved; no active clinical program known. Research chemical only.

## Summary
5. Adipotide is a lab-designed pro-apoptotic peptide that targets prohibitin on the blood vessels feeding fat tissue. It was designed at MD Anderson to starve fat by cutting its supply rather than suppress appetite. It produced fast fat loss in obese mice and monkeys, but kidney toxicity stalled development, no human results were published, and it remains a research chemical.
6. Punch line: Kills the blood vessels feeding fat rather than curbing appetite. Rapid monkey fat loss; kidney risk widely cited.
7. Used for: fat loss, insulin sensitivity

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Fat metabolism: Starves fat of its blood supply
9. Glucose & insulin: Better insulin response in monkeys

## How it works
10. Homes to blood vessels feeding white fat · Prohibitin, ANXA2 · role Fat metabolism
   One end of adipotide is a homing sequence that binds prohibitin and annexin A2, proteins on the cells lining the blood vessels that feed white fat. This lets it gather on those vessels rather than on vessels elsewhere. The targeting was shown in mouse and monkey studies.
11. Triggers death of those vessel cells · Pro-apoptotic KLAKLAK · role Fat metabolism
   The other end, a KLAKLAK sequence, is taken into the cell and disrupts mitochondrial membranes. Damaged mitochondria trigger apoptosis, programmed cell death, so the vessel cells die. This is shown in animal studies.
12. Fat shrinks once its supply is cut · Adipose vessel pruning · role Fat metabolism
   With their blood supply pruned, fat cells lose oxygen and nutrients and the tissue shrinks. Obese mice and monkeys lost fat fast. A human Phase 1 began but never published results.
13. Improves insulin response in obese monkeys · Insulin sensitivity · role Glucose & insulin
   In obese monkeys insulin worked better after treatment, so blood sugar was handled with less insulin. Whether this is a direct effect or a result of the fat loss is not clear. It has not been shown in people.
14. Injures kidney tubules at higher doses · Renal proximal tubule · role Organ function
   The same death payload injures cells in the kidney's proximal tubules, the part that reabsorbs filtered fluid and nutrients. In monkeys this damage appeared at higher exposure and stalled development. It is the main reason grey-market use is rare and cautious.
15. Mechanism overview: Adipotide is a two-part peptide. One end homes to prohibitin and annexin A2 on the endothelial cells lining vessels that feed white fat. The other end, a KLAKLAK sequence, disrupts mitochondrial membranes once inside and triggers apoptosis. Killing the vessels starves the fat tissue, which shrinks. The same apoptotic payload injures kidney proximal tubule cells at higher doses, which is its main toxicity.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
16. Typical: 0.1–0.5 mg/kg · Every 2-3 days · cycle Short cycles only · route Sub-Q (reported)
17. Half-life: Unknown
18. Most people take: 0.1-0.5mg/kg every few days (animal dosing, human unknown) · Short cycles only.

## What people report
19. Grey-market use is rare and cautious; the kidney signal is widely cited.
20. Liked / worked: Fast fat loss in obese monkeys
21. Liked / worked: Better insulin sensitivity in monkeys
22. What worked: In obese monkeys, fast fat loss and improved insulin sensitivity.
23. Went wrong / did not work: Kidney toxicity in monkeys
24. Went wrong / did not work: No published human data
25. What went wrong: Kidney toxicity appeared in the monkey work, which stalled development. No published human efficacy or safety data.
26. Most reported: Rare, cautious grey-market use
27. Most reported: Kidney risk widely cited

## What has been tested
28. Fat metabolism: Obesity (mouse)
29. Fat metabolism: Obesity (monkey)
30. Glucose & insulin: Insulin sensitivity (monkey)
31. Fat metabolism: Obese men with prostate cancer (trial)
32. Mouse and monkey studies showed rapid fat loss. A first human Phase 1 started in 2012 in obese men with prostate cancer; no results were ever published.
33. What it helps: In obese mice and monkeys it produced fast fat loss and better insulin sensitivity. A human Phase 1 in obese men with prostate cancer began, but no results were published. Kidney toxicity in monkeys stalled development. Grey-market use is rare and cautious, with the kidney signal widely cited.
34. Trial: none · Phase 1 · obese men with prostate cancer · NCT01262664 · Arrowhead Research. Its only human trial started in 2011 in obese prostate cancer patients and was dropped by Arrowhead after kidney toxicity seen in monkeys. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
35. People with kidney disease or on NSAIDs: Caused kidney tubule damage and dehydration in monkeys. (reported)
36. People prone to dehydration: Dehydration was a key toxicity in primate work. (reported)

## Where it comes from
37. A pro-apoptotic peptide (FTPP) that targets prohibitin on the blood vessels feeding fat tissue, designed by a team at MD Anderson to starve fat rather than suppress appetite.
38. First studied for: Obesity, by killing the vasculature of white fat.
39. Name story: Adipose + peptide. Its front half (CKGGRAKDC) is a vascular 'ZIP code' that homes to prohibitin on blood vessels feeding fat; the back half, KLAKLAK repeats, punches holes in mitochondria. Starve the vessel, starve the fat. Tested in obese monkeys at MD Anderson, 2011. [S2] (verified)
40. 2000s: Designed at MD Anderson to starve fat of its blood supply
41. 2011: Obese monkeys lose fat fast
42. 2012: Phase 1 in obese men with prostate cancer; never published
43. Today: Stalled fat-killer known for its kidney signal

# AHK-Cu
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/ahk-cu
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: L-alanyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine copper(II), Ala-His-Lys-Cu, copper tripeptide AHK
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: AHK (3 amino acids). Bound to one copper ion; weight shown is AHK alone
4. Legal and approval status: Cosmetic ingredient; not an approved drug.

## Summary
5. AHK-Cu is a lab-made copper tripeptide (Ala-His-Lys plus copper), a cousin of GHK-Cu studied mostly for hair follicles. People apply it topically for thinning hair, and it is thought to stimulate follicle cells and new blood vessels. The real data are cell studies, human use is small and cosmetic, and first-hand reports are few.
6. Punch line: GHK-Cu's hair-focused cousin, a copper tripeptide for the scalp. Studied to wake follicle cells; few user reports.
7. Used for: Thinning hair

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Hair: Stimulates hair follicle cells
9. Skin & aesthetics: Collagen support
10. Cellular protection: Copper delivery

## How it works
11. Stimulates hair-follicle cells · Dermal papilla cells · role Hair
   AHK-Cu acts on dermal papilla cells, the signalling hub at the base of each hair follicle that steers how the hair grows. In cell work it stimulates these cells to grow and multiply. Human use is small and cosmetic, with no serious trials.
12. Feeds follicles with new vessels · VEGF, vascularization · role Hair
   It raises VEGF, a growth factor that tells small blood vessels to sprout. More vessels around the follicle means more blood supply to feed hair growth. This is shown in cell studies.
13. Slows follicle cell death · Bcl-2 up, Bax down · role Cellular protection
   It tips the balance between Bcl-2, which keeps cells alive, and Bax, which pushes them to self-destruct, toward survival. Follicle cells then die off more slowly. This is cell data only.
14. Delivers copper for collagen cross-linking · Lysyl oxidase · role Skin & aesthetics
   The copper it carries supports lysyl oxidase, an enzyme that cross-links collagen and elastin into a firm network. That strengthens the skin around the follicle. This is textbook copper biology, not shown for AHK-Cu in people.
15. Mechanism overview: AHK-Cu is a copper tripeptide built for hair. In cell work it stimulates dermal papilla cells, the signalling hub at the base of each follicle, and raises VEGF to grow the small vessels that feed it. It shifts the Bcl-2 to Bax balance toward survival, slowing follicle cell death. The copper also supports lysyl oxidase, which cross-links collagen in the surrounding skin.

27. Hair: Small cosmetic use (human)

# Amylin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/amylin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: iapp reference, IAPP, islet amyloid polypeptide, diabetes-associated peptide (DAP), insulinoma amyloid peptide
2. Origin: Made by the body (reference)
3. Sequence: KCNTATCATQRLANFLVHSSNNFGAILSSTNVGSNTY (37 amino acids). Ring closed between the two C; amide end
4. Legal and approval status: Reference molecule (pramlintide is the approved analogue).

## Summary
5. Amylin is a natural hormone released with insulin that slows the stomach and curbs how much is eaten. It is the template behind cagrilintide and the approved add-on pramlintide, which carry its fullness pathway. The native hormone is too unstable to use as a drug, so this is a reference entry with no user reports.
6. Punch line: The pancreas's second fullness hormone, released with insulin; slows the stomach. Template for cagrilintide.
7. Used for: Pramlintide analog: mealtime glucose

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Appetite & satiety: Fullness signal from the pancreas
9. Glucose & insulin: Slows sugar after meals
10. Digestive & gut: Slows the stomach

## How it works
11. Released with insulin after a meal · Beta cells, co-secreted · role Glucose & insulin
   Amylin is made in pancreatic beta cells and released together with insulin after a meal. The two work as a pair: insulin moves glucose into tissue, while amylin slows how fast new glucose arrives. Human amylin clumps into amyloid fibrils, so drugs use stable analogues.
12. Slows the stomach, curbs intake · Amylin receptor, hindbrain · role Appetite & satiety
   Amylin receptors, built from the calcitonin receptor plus a RAMP partner protein, sit mostly in the hindbrain. Activating them slows stomach emptying and reduces how much is eaten. Analogues carry the human evidence: cagrilintide produces weight loss in obesity trials.
13. Holds back glucagon after meals · Amylin receptor · role Glucose & insulin
   Through amylin receptor signalling, it suppresses the glucagon surge that normally follows a meal. The liver releases less sugar while food is absorbed, so the post-meal glucose rise is gentler. Pramlintide, an analogue, is approved as a mealtime add-on in diabetes on this basis.
14. Signals fullness to the brainstem · Area postrema · role Digestive & gut
   The area postrema, a brainstem region outside the blood-brain barrier, is amylin's main site of action. Signalling there registers fullness, so meals end sooner and are smaller. This is the central mechanism behind the amylin analogue drugs.
15. Mechanism overview: Amylin is a 37 amino acid hormone co-secreted with insulin from pancreatic beta cells after meals. It binds amylin receptors, built from the calcitonin receptor plus a RAMP partner, mostly in the area postrema of the brainstem. There it signals fullness, slows gastric emptying and suppresses post-meal glucagon. The result is smaller meals and a gentler post-meal glucose rise. Human amylin clumps into amyloid fibrils, so it cannot be used directly; pramlintide and cagrilintide are stable analogues.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
16. Typical: 15–120 mcg · before major meals · cycle ongoing · route Sub-Q (verified)
17. Half-life: ~48 min
18. Type 1 (pramlintide): 15–60 mcg · before each major meal · ongoing; +15 mcg steps · Sub-Q · for type 1 diabetes with mealtime insulin cut 50% [S1] (verified)
19. Type 2 (pramlintide): 60–120 mcg · before each major meal · ongoing · Sub-Q · for insulin-using type 2 diabetes [S1] (verified)
20. Obesity trial: 120–360 mcg · 2–3× daily before meals · 16 wk · Sub-Q · for non-diabetic obesity (trial only) [S2] [S3] (reported)

## What people report
21. A reference entry.
22. Liked / worked: Defines the amylin pathway now used for weight loss
23. Liked / worked: Pramlintide approved for diabetes
24. What worked: Defines the amylin pathway now used for weight loss.
25. Went wrong / did not work: Native amylin clumps; too unstable to use directly
26. What went wrong: Native amylin aggregates and is too unstable to use directly.
27. Most reported: A reference entry; no user reports here

## What has been tested
28. Glucose & insulin: Pramlintide in diabetes (trial)
29. Appetite & satiety: Cagrilintide for weight (trial)

31. What it helps: Native amylin is too unstable to use. Its analogues carry the pathway: pramlintide is approved as an add-on in diabetes, and cagrilintide produces weight loss in obesity trials, alone and with semaglutide. This is a reference entry defining the mechanism behind those drugs, with no user reports.

## Who shouldn't take it

## Where it comes from
36. Found in 1987 in the amyloid clumps of a diabetic pancreas, released with insulin to slow the stomach and curb intake.
37. First studied for: The natural hormone behind cagrilintide and pramlintide.
38. Name story: First published in 1987 as 'diabetes-associated peptide', pulled from the amyloid plaques clogging pancreases of type 2 diabetics. It was renamed amylin, from amyloid, and is also called IAPP: islet amyloid polypeptide. [S5] (verified)

# AOD-9604
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/aod-9604
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: AOD9604, Tyr-hGH(177-191), hGH fragment 176-191 (Tyr-modified), CAS 221231-10-3
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain
3. Sequence: YLRIVQCRSVEGSCGF (16 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: Never approved as a drug; the obesity program failed. Grey-market and supplement use only.

## Summary
5. AOD-9604 is a modified fragment of human growth hormone (residues 176-191 with a tyrosine added), built to keep the fat-burning part without the growth or blood sugar effects. People use it for fat loss and joint relief, and it is thought to boost fat breakdown. Its human obesity trial failed to beat placebo, so it was never approved, and users describe mild effects.
6. Punch line: Growth hormone's fat-burning tail plus a tyrosine, without growth or blood sugar effects. Used for fat and joints.
7. Used for: Fat loss and joint support

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Fat metabolism: GH's fat-burning tail
9. Bone & cartilage: Cartilage repair studied
10. Pain & sensory: Joint relief reported

## How it works
11. Claimed to boost fat breakdown · hGH 177-191 + Tyr · role Fat metabolism
   AOD-9604 copies residues 177 to 191 of growth hormone, the tail linked to GH's fat effects, plus an added tyrosine. In rodents it increases lipolysis, the breakdown of stored fat. In human obesity trials up to Phase 2b it did not beat placebo on weight.
12. Spares growth and blood sugar · No GH receptor action · role Fat metabolism
   Because it does not activate the GH receptor, it does not raise IGF-1 or blood sugar the way full growth hormone can. That keeps the fragment free of GH's growth and glucose effects. The trade-off is that its fat-loss effect in people has not been shown.
13. Blocks new fat storage in fat cells (rodents) · Lipogenesis inhibition · role Fat metabolism
   In rodent fat cells, AOD-9604 inhibits lipogenesis, the building of new fat from sugars and other fuels. Less new storage alongside more breakdown should shrink fat stores. This held in animals but did not translate into weight loss in human trials.
14. Claimed to aid cartilage repair (rabbit data) · Chondrocyte proliferation · role Bone & cartilage
   Rabbit studies suggest AOD-9604 encourages chondrocytes, the cells that build cartilage, to multiply, supporting cartilage repair. That led to its repositioning toward joint use. This is animal data only, with no human cartilage trials.
15. Mechanism overview: AOD-9604 is growth hormone residues 177 to 191 with an added tyrosine, built to keep GH's fat-burning tail. It does not activate the GH receptor, so it does not raise IGF-1 or blood sugar. Rodent studies show it boosts lipolysis and blocks new fat storage in fat cells. Rabbit data suggest it supports chondrocyte proliferation and cartilage repair. Its human fat-loss effect is claimed rather than shown.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
16. Typical: 250–500 mcg · daily · cycle 4-12 weeks on, 4 weeks off · route Sub-Q (reported)
17. Half-life: Very short
18. Most people take: 250-500mcg/day · 4-12 weeks on, 4 weeks off.
19. Common: 300 mcg · 1× daily, fasted · 8–12 wk, 4 wk off · Sub-Q · for fat loss, joint stacks [S1] [S2] (reported)

21. Aggressive: 1 mg · 1× daily · short · Sub-Q · for users pushing past 500 mcg [S1] (reported)

## What has been tested

34. What it helps: Animal studies show fat breakdown. Human obesity trials ran to Phase 2b, which failed to beat placebo on weight and ended the drug programme. Rabbit work led to interest in cartilage repair. Users report it for fat loss and joint relief, and describe the effects as mild.

## Who shouldn't take it
36. Drug-tested athletes: WADA has stated AOD-9604 is banned (S0). (verified)
37. People with prediabetes or poorly controlled diabetes: GH fragment; glucose effects in long-term use unclear. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
38. Tirzepatide: Tirzepatide drives weight loss through GIP and GLP-1 receptors, cutting hunger and improving how fat tissue handles fuel, with strong trial data. AOD-9604 is added for fat breakdown and joint support without touching blood sugar. The add-on is user logic, not trial data.
39. Semaglutide: Semaglutide does the heavy lifting on weight through GLP-1 effects on appetite and the stomach, proven in human trials. People add AOD-9604 hoping for extra fat breakdown and joint relief, though it failed alone in obesity trials. The pair has not been tested together.
40. Retatrutide: Retatrutide adds glucagon receptor action to GLP-1 and GIP, raising energy use and cutting liver fat. AOD-9604 is stacked on for fat breakdown and joints. The combination is user logic, and AOD-9604 did not beat placebo for weight on its own.

## Where it comes from
41. A modified fragment of growth hormone (residues 176-191 with a tyrosine added) built by Metabolic Pharmaceuticals in Australia to keep GH's fat-burning tail without its growth or blood-sugar effects.
42. First studied for: Obesity, as a fat-burning agent without GH's downsides.
43. Name story: AOD reportedly stands for 'Anti-Obesity Drug'; 9604 is a project number with no published meaning. It is the tail end of human growth hormone (residues 176 to 191) with a tyrosine added to the front. [S5] (reported)
44. 1990s to 2000s: GH fragment 176-191 built in Australia to burn fat without GH effects

# ARA-290
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/ara-290
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: cibinetide (INN/USAN), ARA290, pHBSP, pyroglutamate helix B surface peptide
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: EQLERALNSS (10 amino acids). Starts with pyroglutamate, shown as E
4. Legal and approval status: Investigational; no approval. Research chemical on the grey market.

## Summary
5. ARA-290 (cibinetide) is an 11-amino-acid peptide that copies the tissue-protective part of erythropoietin (EPO) without its blood-making effect. It was studied for neuropathic pain and nerve damage, where it is thought to calm inflammation and protect small nerve fibres. Phase 2 trials showed modest benefit, no Phase 3 followed, and it remains unapproved.
6. Punch line: EPO's tissue-protective piece, minus the blood-making. Phase 2 showed small nerve fibre regrowth and less pain.
7. Used for: Small fibre nerve pain

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Neural protection: Repairs small nerve fibres
9. Tissue repair: Tissue protection from EPO
10. Inflammatory signaling: Calms inflammation
11. Pain & sensory: Less nerve pain in trials

## How it works
12. Protects tissue without making blood · Innate repair receptor · role Tissue repair
   ARA-290 binds the innate repair receptor, the tissue-protective receptor that erythropoietin also uses, but not the EPO receptor pair that drives red cell production. So it carries EPO's protective signal without making blood. Phase 2 trials found no rise in red cells.
13. Calms inflammation around nerves · EPOR/CD131 complex · role Inflammatory signaling
   The innate repair receptor is a complex of the EPO receptor with CD131, and activating it dampens inflammatory signalling around injured nerves. Calmer surroundings give damaged nerve fibres a better chance to recover. This is the proposed route to its effects in neuropathy.
14. Regrows small nerve fibres in cornea (trials) · Corneal nerve fibre density · role Neural protection
   Small nerve fibres in the cornea can be counted under a microscope and serve as a window on small-fibre nerve health elsewhere. In Phase 2 trials in sarcoidosis and diabetic neuropathy, ARA-290 increased corneal nerve fibre density, a sign of nerve regrowth.
15. Eases neuropathic pain in small trials · IRR-mediated analgesia · role Pain & sensory
   Through the innate repair receptor, ARA-290 reduces neuropathic pain signalling from damaged small fibres. In Phase 2 trials in sarcoidosis and diabetic neuropathy, people reported less pain. Benefits were modest, and no confirmatory Phase 3 followed.
16. Mechanism overview: ARA-290, or cibinetide, is an 11-amino-acid peptide copying the tissue-protective face of erythropoietin. It binds the innate repair receptor, a complex of the EPO receptor with CD131, rather than the EPO receptor dimer that drives red cell production. So it protects tissue without making blood. Activation dampens inflammation around injured nerves, supports regrowth of small nerve fibres, and reduces neuropathic pain signalling.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
17. Typical: 2–4 mg · daily · cycle 28-day cycles · route Sub-Q (reported)
18. Half-life: ~11 minutes
19. Dose note: In the trial, 8 mg a day did no better than 4 mg.
20. Most people take: 2-4mg/day SC · 28-day cycles.
21. Trial standard: 4 mg · 1× daily · 28 days · Sub-Q · for small-fiber neuropathy, sarcoidosis [S1] [S2] (reported)
22. Low: 1–2 mg · 1× daily · 4–8 wk · Sub-Q · for general neuroprotection [S3] [S2] (reported)
23. Trial high: 8 mg · 1× daily · 28 days · Sub-Q · for dose-ranging arm only [S2] (reported)

## What people report
24. Reported for nerve pain and recovery; small user base.
25. Liked / worked: Less neuropathic pain in Phase 2
26. Liked / worked: Signs of nerve fibre recovery
27. Liked / worked: No rise in red cells
28. What worked: Phase 2 signals for neuropathic pain relief and nerve repair, with a clean blood-count profile.
29. Went wrong / did not work: No confirmatory Phase 3
30. Went wrong / did not work: Benefits modest
31. What went wrong: Development stalled before a confirmatory Phase 3; benefits are modest and unconfirmed at scale.
32. Most reported: Nerve pain and recovery
33. Most reported: Small user base

## What has been tested
34. Pain & sensory: Sarcoidosis small-fibre neuropathy (trial)
35. Pain & sensory: Diabetic neuropathy (trial)

Benefits were modest and no confirmatory Phase 3 followed. A small user base reports it for nerve pain and recovery.
39. Trial: none · Phase 2 · diabetic macular oedema · ISRCTN16962255 · Belfast Health and Social Care Trust. Its last trial, for diabetic eye swelling in Belfast, was terminated; earlier Phase 2s in sarcoidosis nerve pain finished around 2016. (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
40. People with active or recent cancer: EPO-derived; EPO raises tumour progression risk, though ARA-290 does not raise red cells. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)
41. BPC-157: ARA-290 works on nerve inflammation and small-fibre regrowth through the innate repair receptor, while BPC-157 grows blood vessels and draws repair cells into injured tissue. People pair them for nerve and tissue injury recovery, but the pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
42. Also called cibinetide, an 11-amino-acid peptide copying the tissue-protective part of erythropoietin (EPO) without the blood-making part, developed by Araim.
43. First studied for: Neuropathic pain and tissue protection, especially diabetic neuropathy and sarcoidosis-related small-fibre neuropathy.
44. Name story: ARA-290 is a code from its developer, Araim Pharmaceuticals; the official name is cibinetide. It copies the outward-facing 'helix B' of erythropoietin, which protects tissue without raising red blood cells, hence its lab name pHBSP: pyroglutamate helix B surface peptide. [S5] (verified)

# Bacteriostatic Water
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/bacteriostatic-water
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: BAC
2. Origin: Sterile mixing water, not a peptide
3. Class: water
4. Legal and approval status: Sold as a mixing liquid for freeze-dried peptides. Not taken on its own.

## Summary
5. Punch line: Sterile water with 0.9% benzyl alcohol. The preservative slows bacteria, so one vial takes many draws over weeks.

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
6. Mixing water: Sterile water with 0.9% benzyl alcohol added as a preservative. The benzyl alcohol slows bacterial growth, so the vial can be punctured many times over several weeks.

## How it works

## Water
7. Made of: Water for injection, about 99.1%
8. Made of: Benzyl alcohol, 0.9% (9 mg per mL)
9. pH: About 5.7 (allowed range 4.5 to 7.0), per the US prescribing label for bacteriostatic water for injection.
10. When used: The default liquid for most lyophilized (freeze-dried) peptides that dissolve readily in water near neutral pH, such as BPC-157, TB-500, ipamorelin, CJC-1295 and the GLP-1 class.
11. When used: Used when one vial will be drawn from over days or weeks, because the preservative protects against contamination from repeated needle entries.
12. When used: Available in 3 mL (small vials, few draws) and 10 mL (larger or multiple vials).
13. not_for: Newborns and premature infants. The label reads 'Not for use in neonates' because benzyl alcohol has caused fatal toxicity in this group.
14. not_for: Anyone with a known allergy or hypersensitivity to benzyl alcohol, which is listed as a contraindication on regulatory product information.
15. not_for: Peptides that do not dissolve at its near neutral pH and need an acidic liquid (for example AOD-9604 or HGH fragment 176-191). Use acetic acid water for these.
16. not_for: Large volume use, IV fluid replacement, or spinal and epidural use. The label excludes these.
17. not_for: Pregnancy and breastfeeding call for caution: benzyl alcohol crosses the placenta, and product information advises counting total daily intake from all sources.
18. storage: Unopened: room temperature, 20 to 25°C, until the printed expiry date.
19. storage: After first puncture: the USP rule for multi-dose vials is to date the vial and discard it 28 days after first entry unless the manufacturer states otherwise.
20. storage: Once a peptide has been dissolved in it, the mixed vial follows the peptide's own storage rules, usually refrigerated at 2 to 8°C.
21. storage: Do not freeze the plain water. Keep away from heat and direct sunlight.
22. how: Check the expiry date, seal and clarity before first use. Write the date of first puncture on the vial.
23. how: Wipe the rubber stopper with an alcohol swab and let it dry before every entry.
24. how: Use a new sterile needle and syringe every time you draw from the vial.
25. how: Add the water slowly down the inside wall of the peptide vial instead of spraying it directly onto the powder.
26. how: Swirl gently or let the vial sit until the powder dissolves. Do not shake hard.
27. watch: Cloudiness, haze or color change in the plain water: discard.
28. watch: Floating particles, fibers or residue: discard.
29. watch: Cracked vial, missing or broken seal, or a stopper that has been punctured many times and leaks.
30. watch: A faint sweet, almond-like smell is normal (benzyl alcohol). A sour or unusual smell is not.
31. watch: Rash, itching or swelling after use may indicate benzyl alcohol sensitivity.
32. facts: In 1982 the US CDC and FDA reported 16 deaths in premature infants linked to benzyl alcohol in flush solutions and diluents, a condition later named 'gasping syndrome'. Since then the label carries a neonatal warning.
33. facts: Benzyl alcohol is a mild local anesthetic. A 1994 double-blind trial found lidocaine containing benzyl alcohol was 27% less painful to inject than plain lidocaine.
34. facts: Bacteriostatic means it stops bacteria from multiplying, not that it kills them. It is not a substitute for clean technique.
35. tile: 0.9% benzyl alcohol
36. tile: pH about 5.7 · 28 days once opened
37. cells: In it, 0.9% benzyl alcohol
38. cells: pH, about 5.7
39. cells: Opened, 28 days
40. cells: Route, Mixing only

# Brenipatide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/brenipatide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: LY3537031, LY-3537031, 'brinipatide' (common misspelling), Lilly addiction GLP-1
2. Origin: Lab-designed: dual GIP and GLP-1 agonist peptide with a fatty acid tail
3. Legal and approval status: Investigational, not approved anywhere as of Oct 2026. Phase 3 for alcohol use disorder, recurrent depression and bipolar disorder; alcohol results expected by mid-2028. Not named on the WADA list (falls under S0, inferred).

## Summary
4. Brenipatide is Eli Lilly's long-acting GIP and GLP-1 dual agonist, a cousin of tirzepatide. It is aimed at alcohol use, depression relapse and inflammatory lung disease rather than weight, and is thought to quiet the brain's reward pathway. There is no efficacy data yet, and the addiction case rests on the wider GLP-1 class. Phase 1 showed it is tolerable, though abnormal skin sensations occurred in 15.2% on drug.
5. Punch line: Lilly's tirzepatide cousin aimed at cravings, not weight. In Phase 3 for heavy drinking; not on grey market.
6. Used for: Alcohol use disorder, depression, investigational

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Reward & urges: Aims to cut heavy drinking and cravings
8. Mood: Tested for preventing relapse of depression
9. Inflammatory signaling: Aimed at inflammatory pathways in asthma and COPD
10. Appetite & satiety: Shares tirzepatide's appetite pathway

## How it works
11. Turns on GLP-1 and GIP receptors together · GLP-1R and GIPR agonist · role Reward & urges
   Brenipatide activates GIP and GLP-1 receptors together, like tirzepatide, but Lilly designed it to reach these receptors in the central nervous system. The goal is brain and reward effects rather than weight. Phase 1 in people shows only that it is tolerated; no efficacy data exist yet.
12. Thought to quiet the brain's reward pathway · Mesolimbic signalling (inferred from GLP-1 class) · role Reward & urges
   GLP-1 drugs are thought to quiet the mesolimbic reward pathway, the dopamine circuit behind craving. Brenipatide is meant to do the same for alcohol and other addictions. This is inferred from the GLP-1 class, where semaglutide reduced heavy drinking in a small trial.
13. Stays in the body for over a week · C20 diacid, alpha-methyl residues · role Appetite & satiety
   A C20 fatty acid tail grips albumin, and alpha-methyl residues plus a D-tyrosine at the start resist enzyme breakdown. Together they give a half-life of over a week in Phase 1. Levels stay fairly flat between weekly doses.
14. Mechanism overview: Brenipatide is a synthetic GIP and GLP-1 receptor dual agonist from Eli Lilly. A single C20 diacid tail binds albumin, and alpha-methylated residues plus an N-terminal D-tyrosine resist enzyme breakdown, giving a half-life of about 9 to 12.5 days in Phase 1 with a low peak-to-trough ratio. Lilly describes it as designed to reach GIP and GLP-1 receptors in the central nervous system and in inflammatory pathways, including reward circuits.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
15. Typical: 0.3 to 4.5 mg tested in Phase 1; Phase 3 dose not public · Once weekly in Lilly's trials (some databases list monthly) · cycle Trial only (56 weeks in alcohol use disorder) · route Sub-Q (trial)
16. Half-life: 9 to 12.5 days (Phase 1)
17. Most people take: No approved dose. Phase 1 tested 0.3, 0.75, 1.5, 3 and 4.5 mg; Lilly's poster says the data support weekly maintenance doses across a broad range of body weights.

## What people report
18. Heavily discussed online after Lilly's Phase 3 alcohol trials opened in 2025 and 2026, often under the misspelling 'brinipatide'. No credible first-hand user reports; it is not on the grey market in any verified form.
19. Liked / worked: Well tolerated in Phase 1
20. Liked / worked: Long half-life suits weekly dosing
21. What worked: Phase 1: no deaths or serious adverse events, half-life of 9 to 12.5 days, and stomach side effects no more common than placebo (25% in both groups). No efficacy data for any addiction has been released yet.
22. Went wrong / did not work: No efficacy results released yet
23. Went wrong / did not work: Skin sensation side effect in Phase 1
24. What went wrong: Abnormal skin sensations (dysesthesia) in 15.2% on drug versus none on placebo in Phase 1; 2.2% stopped for side effects.
25. Most reported: Mostly news and forum speculation, no verified use

## What has been tested
26. Reward & urges: Alcohol use disorder, Phase 3 (trial)
27. Mood: Recurrent depression and bipolar disorder, Phase 3 (trial)
28. Reward & urges: Smoking and opioid use disorder, Phase 2 (trial)
29. Phase 1 in more than 200 people (NCT06606106) at 0.3 to 4.5 mg weekly. Phase 3 in alcohol use disorder (RENEW-ALC-1 and 2, about 2,200 people, 56 weeks), relapse prevention in depression (RENEW-MDD-1, about 1,000 people) and bipolar disorder; Phase 2 in smoking, opioid use disorder, schizophrenia, asthma, COPD and IBS.
30. What it helps: No efficacy data yet. Phase 1 in more than 200 people showed it is tolerable at up to 4.5 mg. The case for addiction rests on the wider GLP-1 class, where semaglutide reduced heavy drinking in a small 2025 trial.
31. Trial: active · Phase 3 · NCT07219966. Two 56-week Phase 3 trials in alcohol use disorder with about 2,200 people are running, with results expected by mid-2028. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1]

## Synergies (paired with)
32. Tirzepatide: Tirzepatide hits the same GIP and GLP-1 receptors but is built for weight and glucose, while brenipatide is aimed at the brain. They are related molecules, not a stack. Combining them has not been tested.
33. Semaglutide: Semaglutide's small alcohol trial is the main reason brenipatide exists, and both act on GLP-1 reward signalling. They overlap rather than complement. The pair has not been tested together.
34. GLP-1: Native GLP-1 is the hormone both GLP-1 arms of brenipatide copy, but it is broken down in about two minutes. It is a reference point, not a practical partner. The pairing has no trial data.

## Where it comes from
35. Made by Eli Lilly as a cousin of tirzepatide: the same GIP plus GLP-1 double action, but built to last longer and aimed at the brain and inflammation rather than at weight.
36. First studied for: Alcohol use disorder and recurrent depression, both taken straight into Phase 3 without a Phase 2.
37. 2024: Phase 1 dose-finding study (NCT06606106) in people with and without obesity
38. Late 2025: Two Phase 3 alcohol use disorder trials registered, RENEW-ALC-1 and 2
39. Dec 2025: Name brenipatide appears; listed in Phase 3 for alcohol use disorder and bipolar disorder
40. Jun 2026: UW Medicine and about 30 US sites enrolling for the alcohol trial
41. Sep 2026: Phase 1 data and Phase 3 designs shown at Psych Congress
42. Mid 2028: Alcohol use disorder results expected

# Bronchogen

Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity

# Carnosine
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/carnosine
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: l-carnosine beta-alanyl histidine, beta-alanyl-L-histidine, L-carnosine
2. Origin: Made by the body, by enzymes
3. Sequence: AH (2 amino acids). First link is β-alanine, not regular alanine, shown as A
4. Legal and approval status: Supplement; not an approved drug.

## Summary
5. Carnosine is a small compound made from beta-alanine and histidine by an enzyme, stored mostly in muscle, where it buffers acid and acts as an antioxidant. People use it for muscle endurance and anti-aging, since it also blocks sugar damage to proteins. The human benefit comes mainly through beta-alanine loading, oral carnosine is broken down before reaching muscle, and the anti-aging claims remain preclinical.
6. Punch line: Muscle's acid buffer, made from beta-alanine and histidine. Also blocks sugar damage to proteins, hence anti-aging.
7. Used for: Antiglycation, healthy aging

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Aging & senescence: Blocks sugar damage to proteins
9. Cellular protection: Antioxidant in muscle and brain
10. Muscle & performance: Buffers acid in hard efforts

## How it works
11. Soaks up acid in working muscle · pH buffer · role Muscle & performance
   Carnosine's imidazole ring has a pKa close to muscle pH, so it absorbs hydrogen ions as acid builds during intense effort. That delays the acidosis that shuts down contraction. Raising muscle carnosine through beta-alanine gives modest gains in short, hard efforts in human trials.
12. Mops up reactive sugars and oxidants · Antiglycation, antioxidant · role Aging & senescence
   Carnosine quenches reactive carbonyls, the sticky sugar breakdown products that glycate proteins and stiffen tissue. It also scavenges oxidants. These anti-aging effects are shown in cell and animal work, not in human outcome trials.
13. Muscle levels set by its building block · Beta-alanine limits supply · role Muscle & performance
   Muscle builds carnosine from beta-alanine and histidine, and beta-alanine supply is the limiting step. Oral carnosine is largely broken down by the enzyme carnosinase before it reaches muscle. That is why beta-alanine, not carnosine itself, is the practical way to raise stores.
14. Binds metals that drive oxidation · Copper and zinc chelation · role Cellular protection
   Carnosine binds copper and zinc, metals that can drive oxidation reactions when free. Holding them reduces that source of oxidative damage in tissue. This chelation is shown in lab chemistry and animal work, and its human relevance is not established.
15. Mechanism overview: Carnosine is a dipeptide of beta-alanine and histidine, concentrated in skeletal muscle and brain. Its imidazole ring has a pKa close to muscle pH, so it soaks up hydrogen ions during intense effort and delays the acidosis that shuts down contraction. It also quenches reactive carbonyls that would otherwise glycate proteins, scavenges oxidants, and chelates copper and zinc. Muscle levels are limited by beta-alanine supply, and oral carnosine is largely broken down by carnosinase before reaching muscle, which is why beta-alanine is the practical way to raise stores.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
16. Typical: 500–2000 mg · 1–2x daily · cycle ongoing · route Oral (reported)
17. Half-life: Minutes (serum)
18. Common: 500–1000 mg · 1–2× daily · ongoing · Oral · for anti-aging, general [S1] [S2] [S3] (reported)
19. Higher (glycation): 1–2 g · split 2× daily · ongoing; trials to 15 wk · Oral · for anti-glycation, metabolic [S1] [S4] (reported)

## What people report
20. Reported for endurance and anti-aging; the injectable form is niche.
21. Liked / worked: Beta-alanine reliably raises muscle carnosine
22. Liked / worked: Modest help in short, hard efforts
23. What worked: Beta-alanine loading reliably raises muscle carnosine and helps short high-intensity efforts.
24. Went wrong / did not work: Oral carnosine is broken down before muscle
25. Went wrong / did not work: Anti-aging claims are preclinical
26. What went wrong: Oral carnosine is broken down before it reaches muscle; the anti-aging claims are preclinical.
27. Most reported: Reported for endurance
28. Most reported: Reported for anti-aging
29. Most reported: Injectable use is niche

## What has been tested
30. Muscle & performance: High-intensity output, via beta-alanine (trial)
31. Aging & senescence: Anti-aging effects (animal)
32. Human trials mostly use beta-alanine (its rate-limiting precursor), which raises muscle carnosine and modestly improves high-intensity performance. Carnosine itself is poorly absorbed orally.
33. What it helps: The human benefit comes through beta-alanine loading, which reliably raises muscle carnosine and gives modest gains in short, high-intensity efforts. Anti-aging effects are animal-only. Users report it for endurance and anti-aging; injectable carnosine is a niche use with few detailed reports.
34. Trial: active · Phase 1/2 · peripheral arterial disease · NCT06480760 · Shahid Baba (University of Louisville). Six months of 2 g daily carnosine is being tested in leg artery disease, running to 2028. (checked 2026-10-23) [S5] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
35. People on blood pressure medicines: Carnosine may lower blood pressure slightly; effects could add up. (inferred)

## Where it comes from
36. Found in 1900 in meat extract (the name is from Latin for flesh). Made by an enzyme, not a gene, and stored mostly in muscle, where it buffers acid.
37. First studied for: A muscle buffer and antioxidant; studied for performance and aging.
38. Name story: From Latin carnis, flesh: Russian chemist Vladimir Gulevich found it around 1900 in meat extract. It shares the root with carnitine and carnivore. Chemically it is just beta-alanine joined to histidine. [S6] (verified)
39. 1900: Found in meat extract; named from Latin for flesh
40. Decades: Known as a muscle acid buffer, made by an enzyme, not a gene
41. 2000s to 2010s: Beta-alanine loading shown to raise muscle carnosine
42. Today: A supplement for performance and aging; injectable form is niche

# cGP
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/cgp
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: cyclic glycine-proline, cyclo(Gly-Pro), cyclo-prolylglycine, cycloprolylglycine, CPG
2. Origin: Fragment of a natural protein: cyclised breakdown product of IGF-1
3. Sequence: GP (2 amino acids). Cyclic dipeptide (2,5-diketopiperazine) of glycine and proline; formed from GPE, IGF-1's first three residues
4. Legal and approval status: Not an approved drug. Sold in New Zealand and online as a dietary supplement ingredient and blackcurrant extract. Not named on the WADA list.

## Summary
5. cGP (cyclo-prolylglycine) is a tiny ring of two amino acids the body makes when IGF-1 is broken down. It is also the main active metabolite of Noopept and appears in blackcurrants. It is studied for brain ageing, thought to compete with IGF-1 for its carrier protein and so steady IGF-1 activity. Higher levels link to better memory and stroke recovery in observational data. Whether taking it helps anything is untested.
6. Punch line: A tiny ring the body makes from IGF-1; also Noopept's active metabolite. Found in blackcurrants; tied to memory.
7. Used for: Brain ageing, memory

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Cognition: Higher levels track with better memory in older adults
9. Neural protection: Linked to better stroke recovery
10. Endocrine & growth: Steadies IGF-1 activity

## How it works
11. Competes with IGF-1 for its carrier protein · IGFBP-3 binding · role Endocrine & growth
   cGP binds IGFBP-3, the main carrier protein that holds IGF-1 in blood, at the same site IGF-1 uses. By taking that seat it changes how much IGF-1 is free to reach its receptor. This binding is shown in lab studies.
12. Raises IGF-1 activity when low, damps it when high · IGF-1 normalisation · role Endocrine & growth
   Because it competes for the carrier, cGP acts as a buffer: in vitro it raised IGF-1 activity when IGF-1 was low and inhibited it when IGF-1 was high. In older adults a higher cGP to IGF-1 ratio tracked with better memory, but that is observational, not proof.
13. Boosts fast excitatory signalling · AMPA positive modulation · role Cognition
   cGP positively modulates AMPA receptors, the glutamate receptors that carry fast excitatory signals and underpin learning. Stronger AMPA signalling fits its links to memory. Human memory data are observational, so whether taking cGP improves cognition is untested.
14. Raises BDNF · TrkB dependent neuroprotection · role Neural protection
   cGP raises BDNF, which acts through TrkB receptors to keep neurons alive and adaptable. This fits the observational finding that higher plasma cGP went with better stroke recovery in 34 patients. The neuroprotective mechanism comes from lab work, not supplement trials.
15. Mechanism overview: IGF-1 is cleaved to des-N-(1-3)-IGF-1 and the tripeptide glycine-proline-glutamate (GPE), which is further processed to cyclo(Gly-Pro). cGP binds IGFBP-3 at the site IGF-1 uses, so it shifts how much IGF-1 is free: in vitro it raises IGF-1 activity when IGF-1 is low and inhibits it when IGF-1 is high. It also positively modulates AMPA receptors and increases BDNF. The trofinetide and NNZ-2591 drug programmes grew out of the same GPE and cGP chemistry.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
16. Typical: Unknown as pure cGP; blackcurrant anthocyanins 300 mg 2× daily studied · Daily · cycle Continuous · route Oral (trial)
17. Half-life: Unknown in humans
18. Most people take: No established dose of pure cGP. The only human supplement study used blackcurrant capsules, 300 mg (35% anthocyanins) twice daily for 28 days, to raise the body's own cGP.
19. Supplements are taken daily without cycling.

## What people report
20. A niche but growing brain health supplement, sold as standardised cGP or blackcurrant extract, mainly to people over 50 and to Noopept users who want the metabolite directly. Reports are sparse and mostly subtle: clearer thinking for some, nothing noticed for many. No consistent side effect pattern reported. No aggregator counts located.
21. Liked / worked: Blackcurrant raises cGP in spinal fluid
22. Liked / worked: Higher levels linked to better stroke recovery and memory
23. What worked: Blackcurrant supplementation raises cGP in blood and spinal fluid; cGP crosses into the brain. Animal and cell work shows it steadies IGF-1 activity, raising it when low and damping it when high.
24. Went wrong / did not work: No outcome trial of cGP itself
25. Went wrong / did not work: Human data mostly associations
26. What went wrong: No trial shows that taking cGP improves memory or any outcome in people. Most human data are associations.
27. Most reported: Taken by over 50s for brain health
28. Most reported: Noopept users take it directly
29. Most reported: Subtle or no effect for many

## What has been tested
30. Neural protection: Stroke recovery, 34 patients, observational (human)
31. Cognition: Memory in older adults, observational (human)
32. Neural protection: Blackcurrant in Parkinson's, 11 patients (human)
33. Human data are observational plus one supplement study. In 34 stroke patients, higher plasma cGP went with better recovery at three months. In older adults, higher cGP and cGP to IGF-1 ratio tracked with better memory. In 11 Parkinson's patients, blackcurrant anthocyanin capsules (300 mg twice daily for 28 days) raised spinal fluid cGP by 74%.
34. What it helps: Observational human data link higher cGP to better stroke recovery and memory in older age, and blackcurrant anthocyanins raise cGP in blood and spinal fluid. Whether supplementing it improves any outcome is untested. Users report subtle effects at most.
35. Trial: none. No registered trial of cGP itself confirmed; past studies used blackcurrant extract to raise it. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1]

## Synergies (paired with)
36. IGF-1 LR3: IGF-1 LR3 drives growth directly and is built to escape carrier proteins, while cGP works on the carrier side, buffering how much natural IGF-1 is free. Since LR3 barely binds IGFBP-3, cGP likely does little to it, and the pair has not been tested together.
37. Somatropin (HGH): Somatropin raises liver IGF-1, and cGP is proposed to buffer IGF-1 availability by competing for IGFBP-3. People pair them to keep a raised IGF-1 axis in range, which is user logic, not trial data.
38. MK-677: MK-677 lifts GH and IGF-1 through the ghrelin receptor and deepens sleep, while cGP is proposed to normalise IGF-1 activity and supports AMPA and BDNF signalling. The pairing aims at the IGF-1 axis plus brain ageing, but has not been tested together.
39. Semax: Both raise BDNF, cGP through TrkB dependent signalling and Semax as reported in rodents, and both have links to stroke recovery. People stack them for brain ageing and memory, but the pair has not been tested together.
40. Dihexa: Dihexa boosts HGF and c-Met signalling that builds synapses in rats, while cGP modulates AMPA receptors, BDNF and IGF-1 availability. Users pair them for memory from separate growth factor routes, and the pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
41. A tiny ring of two amino acids that the body makes when IGF-1 is broken down: IGF-1 sheds the tripeptide GPE, which closes into cGP. It is also the main active metabolite of Noopept, and is found in blackcurrants and some cooked or fermented foods.
42. First studied for: Studied in New Zealand (Jian Guan's group) as a natural regulator of IGF-1 in the ageing brain, stroke and Parkinson's disease.
43. Name story: cGP is short for cyclic glycine-proline: two amino acids joined head to tail into a ring. [S2] (verified)
44. 1990s: Russian researchers describe cGP as a brain peptide; later shown to be Noopept's main metabolite
45. 2010s: Guan's group links cGP to IGF-1 regulation, ageing and stroke
46. 2020: Blackcurrant capsules raise spinal fluid cGP 74% in Parkinson's patients
47. 2023: Review: cGP normalises IGF-1 function
48. Today: Sold as a brain health supplement; no outcome trial

   The group claims it turns down inflammatory genes in the bronchial lining. Less inflammatory signalling would mean calmer, less reactive airways. This has not been confirmed outside Russian studies, and user reports are very few.

# CJC-1295 with DAC
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/cjc-1295-with-dac
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: DAC:GRF, CJC-1295 DAC
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain
3. Sequence: YADAIFTQSYRKVLAQLSARKLLQDILSRK (30 amino acids). Position 2 is D-Ala; the last K carries the DAC (maleimide) linker that binds albumin; amide end
4. Legal and approval status: Unapproved research chemical. WADA-banned.

## Summary
5. CJC-1295 with DAC is a lab-modified GHRH analogue that prompts the pituitary to release growth hormone. A Drug Affinity Complex binds albumin and extends its action to about a week, so people use it for infrequent dosing aimed at recovery and body composition. Small studies show raised GH and IGF-1 for days, but there are no outcome results and users note water retention.
6. Punch line: The once-weekly GHRH analogue. An albumin-binding DAC keeps GH and IGF-1 raised for days; more bloat than no-DAC.
7. Used for: Higher GH and IGF-1 for recovery, body comp

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Endocrine & growth: Keeps GH and IGF-1 raised for days
9. Sleep & rhythms: Deeper sleep reported

## How it works
10. Prompts the pituitary to release GH · GHRH receptor · role Endocrine & growth
   CJC-1295 binds the GHRH receptor on the growth hormone cells of the pituitary, the same switch the brain's own GHRH flips. That raises cAMP inside the cell and releases stored growth hormone. Small human studies confirmed GH rises after a single dose.
11. Raises IGF-1 for up to two weeks · Hepatic IGF-1 · role Endocrine & growth
   Growth hormone travels to the liver and tells it to make IGF-1, the hormone that carries much of GH's growth and repair signal to muscle, bone and other tissue. In small human studies IGF-1 stayed raised for days after one dose, but there are no outcome data on recovery or body composition.
12. Binds albumin for about a week · Drug Affinity Complex · role Endocrine & growth
   The Drug Affinity Complex is a reactive chemical tag that bonds the peptide to albumin, the most common protein in blood. Bound to albumin, it escapes fast breakdown and kidney clearance, so it acts for about a week instead of minutes. Small human studies confirm the long action.
13. Raises baseline GH while pulses persist · Trough GH levels · role Endocrine & growth
   Because the peptide keeps the receptor engaged around the clock, GH between natural pulses stays higher than usual while the pulses still happen on top. The result is a steadier GH signal than the body normally produces, seen in small human studies. Users also report more water retention than with the no-DAC version.
14. GHRH tone deepens slow-wave sleep · Hypothalamic GHRH · role Sleep & rhythms
   In the hypothalamus GHRH does more than release GH. It also promotes slow-wave sleep, the deepest stage of non-REM sleep, so raising GHRH tone is expected to deepen it. Sleep has not been measured in the CJC-1295 studies themselves.
15. Mechanism overview: CJC-1295 is a GHRH analogue that binds the GHRH receptor on pituitary somatotrophs, raising cAMP and prompting growth hormone release. The Drug Affinity Complex lets it bond covalently to circulating albumin, stretching its life to about a week. GH then drives the liver to make IGF-1, which stays raised for up to two weeks. Natural GH pulses continue, but baseline GH between them rises, giving a more constant signal than the body normally produces. Hypothalamic GHRH tone also deepens slow-wave sleep.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
16. Typical: 2 mg · once weekly · cycle 8-12 weeks · route Sub-Q (reported)
17. Half-life: ~8 days
18. Most people take: 2mg once weekly SC · 8-12 weeks.
19. Common: 2 mg · 1× weekly · 12–16 wk · Sub-Q · for standard [S1] [S2] (reported)
20. Split: 1 mg · 2× weekly · 12–16 wk · Sub-Q · for steadier levels [S1] (reported)
21. Low: 0.5–1 mg · 1× weekly · 8–16 wk, or 3 mo on/1 off · Sub-Q · for conservative, anti-aging [S2] [S1] (reported)

## What people report
22. Reported for recovery and body composition; longer action but more water retention reported than no-DAC.
23. Liked / worked: GH and IGF-1 stay raised for days
24. Liked / worked: Infrequent dosing
25. What worked: Sustained GH and IGF-1 elevation from infrequent dosing.
26. Went wrong / did not work: Constant, non-pulsatile rise
27. Went wrong / did not work: No outcome data
28. What went wrong: The continuous (non-pulsatile) elevation is less physiological than the no-DAC version, which some argue blunts benefit; no outcome data.
29. Most reported: Recovery and body composition
30. Most reported: More water retention than no-DAC

## What has been tested
31. Endocrine & growth: GH and IGF-1 after one dose (human)
32. Fat metabolism: HIV lipodystrophy (trial)
33. Small human studies in 2006 confirmed GH and IGF-1 stay raised for days after one dose. A Phase 2 in HIV lipodystrophy was halted (reported). No efficacy results.
34. What it helps: Small human studies confirmed that a single dose keeps GH and IGF-1 elevated for days, allowing infrequent dosing. A trial in HIV lipodystrophy was reportedly halted, and there are no outcome results. Users report it for recovery and body composition, noting more water retention than the no-DAC version.
35. Trial: none · Phase 2 · HIV fat redistribution and growth hormone deficiency · ConjuChem. Last trials were around 2006; ConjuChem halted development after a participant death, and it never returned to the clinic. (checked 2026-10-23) [S3] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
36. People with active or recent cancer: Raises GH and IGF-1 for weeks per dose; cannot be switched off quickly. (inferred)
37. People with prediabetes or poorly controlled diabetes: Sustained GH raises insulin resistance. (inferred)
38. People with heart disease: A phase 2 trial was halted after a participant death (judged unrelated). (reported)
39. Drug-tested athletes: GHRH analogues are banned under WADA S2. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
40. Ipamorelin: CJC-1295 raises the GHRH signal while ipamorelin works the ghrelin receptor, a second route to the same GH release, and together they give a bigger pulse than either alone. Ipamorelin is picked because it spares cortisol, prolactin and hunger. The pair has not been tested together in a trial.
41. GHRP-2: GHRP-2 drives GH through the ghrelin receptor and amplifies the brain's own GHRH pulses, so a long-acting GHRH analogue gives it more signal to amplify. The cost is GHRP-2's rise in hunger, prolactin and cortisol. This pairing is user logic, not trial data.
42. GHRP-6: GHRP-6 triggers a GH pulse through the ghrelin receptor and blunts somatostatin, the brake on GH, while CJC-1295 keeps the GHRH side raised. People choose it for bulking because it brings strong hunger. The pair itself has not been tested together.
43. Hexarelin: Hexarelin is the strongest GH releaser of the ghrelin-receptor group and also acts on heart tissue through CD36, while CJC-1295 supplies a steady GHRH signal. Its GH response fades with repeated use and it lifts cortisol and prolactin more. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
44. The same GHRH analogue with a Drug Affinity Complex added, which binds albumin and extends its action to about a week.
45. First studied for: A longer-acting GH-raising agent, for less frequent dosing.
46. Name story: CJC is reportedly the in-house prefix of its Canadian developer ConjuChem. DAC means Drug Affinity Complex: a chemical hook on an extra lysine that latches onto albumin in blood, stretching its life from minutes to days. [S4] (reported)
47. 2006: Small human studies: GH and IGF-1 raised for days per dose
48. Late 2000s: HIV lipodystrophy Phase 2 halted (reported)
49. Today: Weekly grey-market GH raiser; WADA-banned

13. Claimed to shift gene activity in brain cortex · Cortex gene expression · role Neural protection
   The group reports that Cortagen shifts gene activity in cells of the brain cortex, the outer layer that handles thinking and memory. Russian human reports describe effects on brain function. None of this has been independently confirmed.

   In rat injury models, the group reports that Cortagen helped damaged nerves regrow and recover. That is the basis for its use in brain and nerve recovery. These are Russian animal findings, not independently repeated.
