## Identity
1. Also called: XW003, ecno, Sciwind GLP-1, biased GLP-1
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain: cAMP-biased GLP-1 analogue
3. Legal and approval status: Approved in China: type 2 diabetes in January 2026 and chronic weight management in March 2026 (NMPA). Not approved by the FDA or EMA. Not on the WADA list (inferred).

## Summary
4. Ecnoglutide is a GLP-1 receptor drug from Sciwind Biosciences in China, tuned to favour the cAMP signal over beta-arrestin, which the company says slows receptor wearing out. It is used for type 2 diabetes and weight loss, cutting appetite like other GLP-1 drugs. In Chinese adults it gave semaglutide-range weight loss, up to about 15% at 48 weeks. It is approved in China only.
5. Punch line: China's homegrown biased GLP-1, sold by Pfizer China. Weekly shot; up to 15% weight loss in company data.
6. Used for: Weight loss, type 2 diabetes

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Appetite & satiety: Cuts appetite like other GLP-1 drugs
8. Glucose & insulin: Approved in China for type 2 diabetes
9. Fat metabolism: Up to 15% weight loss in 48 weeks
10. Organ function: Halved liver fat in Phase 3

## How it works
11. Activates the GLP-1 receptor · GLP-1R agonist · role Appetite & satiety
   Ecnoglutide activates the GLP-1 receptor in the brain's appetite centres and gut. Hunger falls and the stomach slows. In the SLIMMER Phase 3 human trial in Chinese adults, weight loss was in the range of semaglutide.
12. Favours cAMP over beta-arrestin · Biased agonism · role Glucose & insulin
   When the GLP-1 receptor is switched on it sends signals through cAMP and also recruits beta-arrestin, which pulls the receptor inside the cell. Ecnoglutide is a biased agonist that favours the cAMP route. The aim is stronger insulin and appetite signalling per dose.
13. Less receptor shutdown over time (company claim) · Reduced desensitisation · role Appetite & satiety
   Less beta-arrestin recruitment should mean fewer receptors pulled off the cell surface, so the response fades less over time. The company claims this reduced desensitisation. It has not been shown to give a clinical edge over standard GLP-1 drugs.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
14. Typical: 1.2, 1.8 or 2.4 mg · Once weekly · cycle Ongoing · route Sub-Q (trial)
15. Most people take: Phase 3 doses were 1.2, 1.8 and 2.4 mg once a week; 2.4 mg gave the most weight loss. Chinese label dosing not found in the sources checked.

## What people report
16. Discussed as China's first homegrown 'biased' GLP-1 and as a cheaper rival to semaglutide; Pfizer China sells it. Little first-hand use reported outside China.
17. Liked / worked: Up to 13.2% weight loss at 40 weeks
18. Liked / worked: Liver fat down 53%
19. What worked: SLIMMER: 9.1%, 10.9% and 13.2% weight loss at 40 weeks by dose versus 0.1% gain on placebo; 15.4% at 48 weeks on 2.4 mg in company data, still falling. Liver fat down 53% at 40 weeks on 2.4 mg. Adolescents: BMI down 11 to 13% at 20 weeks.
20. Went wrong / did not work: Common mild GI effects
21. Went wrong / did not work: China-only data
22. What went wrong: Stomach side effects are common (adverse events in 93% on drug versus 84% on placebo, mostly mild GI). Data are from Chinese patients only so far.
23. Most reported: China's first biased GLP-1
24. Most reported: Cheaper semaglutide rival

## What has been tested
25. Fat metabolism: Obesity, SLIMMER Phase 3, China (trial)
26. Glucose & insulin: Type 2 diabetes, Phase 3 (trial)
27. Fat metabolism: Adolescents with obesity, Phase 1b (trial)
28. Phase 3 SLIMMER in 664 Chinese adults at 1.2, 1.8 and 2.4 mg weekly; type 2 diabetes Phase 3; a 20-week Phase 1b in 48 adolescents, with a larger adolescent Phase 3 underway.
29. What it helps: In Chinese adults it gives weight loss in the range of semaglutide: 13.2% at 40 weeks on 2.4 mg, and 15.4% at 48 weeks in company data, with a large drop in liver fat. It is approved in China only.
30. Trial: active · Phase 3 (adolescents). After approval in Chinese adults, a Phase 3 in adolescents with obesity is underway. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1]

## Synergies (paired with)
31. Semaglutide: Semaglutide and ecnoglutide both activate the GLP-1 receptor, with ecnoglutide biased toward cAMP signalling. They are alternatives giving similar weight loss. Stacking them has not been tested.
32. Liraglutide: Liraglutide is an older daily GLP-1 drug on the same receptor. The two are alternatives, not complementary. The pair has not been tested together.
33. GLP-1: Native GLP-1 is the hormone ecnoglutide is modelled on, but it lasts about two minutes. It is a reference point for the mechanism, not a working partner. There is no trial data on the pair.
34. Mazdutide: Mazdutide adds a glucagon arm for liver fat and energy use, while ecnoglutide is GLP-1 only. Both act on GLP-1, so combining them doubles that side. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
35. Made by Sciwind Biosciences in Hangzhou, China. It is a GLP-1 drug tuned to favour one signal inside the cell (cAMP) and avoid another (beta-arrestin), which the company says slows the receptor wearing out.
36. First studied for: Weight loss and type 2 diabetes in China.
37. Jun 2025: SLIMMER Phase 3 in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology: up to 13.2% at 40 weeks
38. Jan 2026: Approved in China for type 2 diabetes
39. Feb 2026: Pfizer China takes commercial rights, deal up to 495 million dollars
40. Mar 2026: Approved in China for weight management
41. Sep 2026: Adolescent Phase 1b shown at EASD
42. Today: Adolescent Phase 3 underway

# Exenatide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/exenatide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: exendin-4 gila monster reference, exendin-4, AC2993, Byetta, Bydureon, Bydureon BCise, exenatide LAR
2. Origin: Made by a body: the Gila monster’s
3. Sequence: HGEGTFTSDLSKQMEEEAVRLFIEWLKNGGPSSGAPPPS (39 amino acids). Amide end
4. Legal and approval status: Approved. Byetta and Bydureon were discontinued in the US in 2024; a generic exenatide was approved in November 2024. Reference molecule here.

## Summary
5. Exenatide is a GLP-1 drug based on a lizard version of the hormone, which lasts far longer in the body than the human one. It was the first GLP-1 drug, approved in 2005 for type 2 diabetes, giving better glucose control and modest weight loss. It is weaker and shorter acting than modern agents, causes typical GI side effects, and is largely superseded.
6. Punch line: The first GLP-1 drug, approved 2005, copied from Gila monster saliva. Proved the hormone could be a medicine.
7. Used for: Type 2 diabetes glucose control

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Appetite & satiety: Longer fullness signal
9. Glucose & insulin: Releases insulin after meals
10. Heart & vessels: Studied for heart outcomes

## How it works
11. Boosts insulin when sugar is high · GLP-1 receptor, pancreas · role Glucose & insulin
   Exenatide activates the same GLP-1 receptor on pancreatic beta cells as the native hormone. Insulin release rises only when glucose is high, which limits low blood sugar when used alone. Phase 3 trials in type 2 diabetes confirmed better glucose control and led to approval.
12. Slows the stomach · GLP-1 receptor, gut · role Appetite & satiety
   Acting on GLP-1 receptors in the gut and its nerve signalling, exenatide slows stomach emptying. Food and sugar reach the blood more slowly, and fullness lasts longer. This also drives the nausea and GI side effects typical of the class.
13. Quiets hunger in the brain · GLP-1 receptor · role Appetite & satiety
   GLP-1 receptors in the brain's appetite centres turn down hunger when activated. In diabetes trials this showed up as modest weight loss alongside glucose control. It is weaker on appetite than modern agents such as semaglutide.
14. Holds back glucagon after meals · Alpha cell suppression · role Glucose & insulin
   Exenatide suppresses glucagon from pancreatic alpha cells after meals. With less glucagon, the liver releases less sugar while a meal is absorbed. This adds to the insulin effect to lower post-meal glucose in people with type 2 diabetes.
15. Resists breakdown, unlike GLP-1 · DPP-4 resistant · role Glucose & insulin
   A glycine at position 2, where human GLP-1 has alanine, stops the enzyme DPP-4 from cutting it. Its half-life stretches from minutes to a few hours. That change made exenatide, a copy of a Gila monster peptide, the first working GLP-1 drug.
16. Mechanism overview: Exenatide is a synthetic copy of exendin-4, a peptide from Gila monster saliva that shares about half its sequence with human GLP-1. It activates the same GLP-1 receptor, boosting glucose-dependent insulin release, suppressing glucagon, slowing gastric emptying and reducing hunger. The key difference is a glycine at position 2 instead of alanine, which makes it resistant to DPP-4. That stretches its half-life from minutes to a few hours, enough to make the first GLP-1 drug.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
17. Typical: 5–10 mcg · twice daily · cycle ongoing · route Sub-Q (verified)
18. Half-life: ~2.4 hours
19. Start (Byetta): 5 mcg · 2× daily, ≤60 min before AM and PM meals · first month · Sub-Q · for type 2 diabetes [S1] (verified)
20. Maintenance (Byetta): 10 mcg · 2× daily before meals · ongoing · Sub-Q · for type 2 diabetes [S1] [S2] (verified)
21. Weekly (Bydureon BCise): 2 mg · 1× weekly · ongoing · Sub-Q · for type 2 diabetes, weekly preference [S3] (reported)

## What people report

24. Liked / worked: Proved a GLP-1 analogue could be a drug
25. What worked: Approved diabetes therapy; the class pioneer.
26. Went wrong / did not work: Weaker and shorter acting than modern agents
27. Went wrong / did not work: GI side effects
28. Went wrong / did not work: Largely superseded
29. What went wrong: Weaker and shorter than modern agents; GI side effects; largely superseded.
30. Most reported: A reference entry, historically important

## What has been tested
31. Glucose & insulin: Type 2 diabetes, Phase 3 (trial)
32. Appetite & satiety: Weight change in diabetes trials (trial)
33. Phase 3 diabetes trials; the original proof that a GLP-1 analogue could work as a drug.
34. What it helps: Phase 3 trials in type 2 diabetes led to approval, with modest weight loss alongside better glucose control. It proved a GLP-1 analogue could work as a drug. It is weaker and shorter acting than modern agents, causes the typical GI side effects, and is largely superseded. This is a reference entry kept for its history.
35. Trial: active · Phase 3 · brain satiety responses in children with obesity · NCT04520490 · University of Washington. Approved diabetes drug derived from Gila monster venom; its big Parkinson's Phase 3 failed in 2025. (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
36. People with severe kidney disease: Cleared by the kidneys; label advises against use below CrCl 30. (verified)
37. People with a history of low platelets: Label warns of drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia. (verified)
38. Personal or family history of MTC or MEN2: Extended-release form carries the boxed C-cell tumour warning. (verified)
39. Anyone booked for surgery, endoscopy or sedation: Slowed stomach emptying; aspiration risk under anaesthesia. (verified)

## Where it comes from
40. Found in 1992 by John Eng in Gila monster saliva; the lizard's version of GLP-1 lasts far longer than ours. The first GLP-1 drug, 2005.
41. First studied for: Type 2 diabetes (Byetta/Bydureon).
42. Name story: A synthetic copy of exendin-4, isolated from Gila monster venom in 1992. "Exendin" fuses exocrine and endocrine: secreted by a venom gland, yet acting like a gut hormone. It became the first GLP-1 drug, Byetta, in 2005. [S5] (verified)
43. 1992: Found by John Eng in Gila monster saliva; a long-lasting GLP-1 cousin
44. 2005: Approved for type 2 diabetes; the first GLP-1 drug
45. 2024: Brand versions discontinued in the US; a generic approved in November
46. Today: The class pioneer; a reference molecule, largely superseded

# GHK (no Cu)
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/ghk-no-cu
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: ghk copper free, glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine, Gly-His-Lys, tripeptide-1 (INCI)
2. Origin: Fragment of a natural protein
3. Sequence: GHK (3 amino acids). Same chain as GHK-Cu, without the copper
4. Legal and approval status: Cosmetic-ingredient status (as copper tripeptide's parent); not an approved drug.

## Summary
5. GHK (no Cu) is the glycyl-histidyl-lysine tripeptide of GHK-Cu without the copper, so it is clear instead of blue. It is used topically or by injection for skin repair and collagen, and it is thought to pick up copper from the body and boost collagen building. Most of its evidence is borrowed from GHK-Cu, and the copper-free form has few trials of its own.
6. Punch line: Copper-free GHK, clear instead of blue. Thought to borrow the body's copper for collagen; topical or injected.
7. Used for: Skin and general repair

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Skin & aesthetics: Collagen support
9. Organ function: Tissue repair signals
10. Tissue repair: Wound healing
11. Cognition: Studied for the brain
12. Neural protection (backed only by animal or user reports): Nerve protection studied
13. Inflammatory signaling (backed only by animal or user reports): Calms inflammation
14. Cellular protection (backed only by animal or user reports): Picks up the body's copper

## How it works
15. Picks up the body's own copper · Copper chelation · role Tissue repair
   GHK has a strong grip on copper ions, so the copper-free form binds copper already circulating in the body and carries it into cells. That copper feeds copper-dependent enzymes such as lysyl oxidase and superoxide dismutase. Most of this evidence comes from GHK-Cu research.
16. Boosts collagen building · Fibroblast signalling · role Skin & aesthetics
   GHK signals fibroblasts, the cells that make skin's structural proteins, to build more collagen. Cell and cosmetic studies of GHK-Cu show collagen and firmness gains. Data for the copper-free form on its own are sparse.
17. Claimed to reset repair genes · Gene-expression data · role Organ function
   Gene-expression studies claim GHK shifts large sets of genes toward repair and away from damage patterns. These come from gene-expression data in cells, not from outcome studies. Whether it resets genes in the body is unproven.
18. Calms inflammatory signals · IL-6, TNF-alpha down · role Inflammatory signaling
   GHK lowers IL-6 and TNF-alpha, two signalling proteins that drive inflammation. Less of these signals gives tissue a calmer setting to repair in. This is shown in cell studies, largely with GHK-Cu.
19. Curbs oxidative damage · Antioxidant genes · role Cellular protection
   By supplying copper to superoxide dismutase and turning up antioxidant genes, GHK is said to curb oxidative damage, the harm done by reactive oxygen molecules. This rests on cell and gene-expression work. There is no human proof for the copper-free form.
20. Claimed to protect nerve cells · Gene-expression data · role Neural protection
   The same gene-expression data claim GHK turns up genes linked to nerve cell survival and growth. That points to a protective role for nerve cells. It is a claim from cell data, not shown in people.
21. Mechanism overview: GHK is a tripeptide found in plasma, saliva and urine that declines with age. Its core trick is chelating copper and ferrying it into cells, so even the copper-free form picks up the body's own copper. That supply feeds copper-dependent enzymes like lysyl oxidase and superoxide dismutase, and GHK signals fibroblasts to build collagen. It lowers IL-6 and TNF-alpha. Gene-expression studies claim it resets large sets of repair and antioxidant genes and protects nerve cells.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
22. Typical: 1–2 mg · Daily · cycle 4–8 weeks · route Sub-Q, Topical (reported)
23. Half-life: Unknown

## What people report
24. Topical and injected; reported for skin and general repair.
25. Liked / worked: Skin firmness and repair reported, like GHK-Cu
26. What worked: Reported skin firmness and repair similar to GHK-Cu; may chelate the body's own copper.
27. Went wrong / did not work: Few trials on the copper-free form
28. Went wrong / did not work: Evidence mostly borrowed from GHK-Cu
29. What went wrong: Without pre-bound copper, the copper-delivery mechanism depends on the body; evidence is mostly extrapolated from GHK-Cu.
30. Most reported: Topical and injected
31. Most reported: Used for skin and general repair

## What has been tested
32. Skin & aesthetics: Collagen and repair, via GHK-Cu data (cell)
33. Skin & aesthetics: Topical cosmetic use (users)
34. Shares GHK-Cu's mechanism literature (collagen, gene-expression 'resetting'); copper-free topical use is common in cosmetics. Human trials specific to the copper-free form are sparse.
35. What it helps: Most evidence is borrowed from GHK-Cu, which has cell and cosmetic data on collagen, firmness and repair. The copper-free form has few trials of its own. Users apply it topically or inject it, reporting skin firmness and general repair similar to GHK-Cu.
36. Trial: none. No trial of copper free GHK found, though its copper bound form GHK-Cu is in a recruiting Phase 2 wound healing gel trial (NCT07437586). (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
37. People with low copper (post-bariatric, high zinc): Copper-free GHK binds the body’s own copper. (inferred)

## Where it comes from
38. The same glycyl-histidyl-lysine tripeptide as GHK-Cu but without the copper, so clear instead of blue. In the body it picks up copper on its own.
39. First studied for: A skin-regenerating and wound-healing signal; the copper-free form for formulations where added copper is unwanted.
40. Name story: GHK is one-letter code for Gly-His-Lys. Loren Pickart pulled it from human plasma in 1973 after noticing young people's blood made old liver cells behave younger. The copper-bound form gets the fame; this is the bare peptide. [S2] (verified)
41. 1970s: GHK found in human plasma; copper complex studied
42. Today: Copper-free cosmetic ingredient; not an approved drug

# GHRP-2
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/ghrp-2
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: pralmorelin, pralmorelin hydrochloride, pralmorelin dihydrochloride, KP-102, GPA-748, WAY-GPA-748, GHRP Kaken 100
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: AAAWFK (6 amino acids). D-Ala and D-2-naphthylalanine shown as A, D-Phe shown as F; amide end
4. Legal and approval status: Approved in Japan as a diagnostic test for growth hormone deficiency (pralmorelin). Unapproved elsewhere. WADA-banned.

## Summary
5. GHRP-2 is a synthetic hexapeptide that mimics ghrelin and triggers a strong pulse of growth hormone. People use it for the GH effect, lean mass and sleep, and it also raises hunger. It is approved in Japan only as a diagnostic test, it also raises prolactin and cortisol, and many users prefer ipamorelin for that reason.
6. Punch line: Ghrelin mimic with a strong growth hormone pulse. Taken for lean mass and sleep; less hunger than GHRP-6.
7. Used for: GH release, appetite, recovery

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Endocrine & growth: Strong GH release
9. Muscle & performance: Lean mass reported
10. Appetite & satiety: Raises hunger
11. Sleep & rhythms: Better sleep reported

## How it works
12. Mimics ghrelin to drive a strong GH pulse · Ghrelin receptor, GHSR-1a · role Endocrine & growth
   GHRP-2 binds the ghrelin receptor, GHSR-1a, on pituitary and hypothalamic cells, the same switch the hunger hormone ghrelin uses. That sets off a strong pulse of growth hormone from the pituitary. Human studies confirm the release, and it has been used to test for GH deficiency.
13. Also lifts hunger, prolactin and cortisol · Less selective GHS · role Appetite & satiety
   It is a less selective secretagogue than ipamorelin, so the same receptor activity also spills over into other hormone systems. Hunger rises through ghrelin signalling in the brain, and prolactin and cortisol climb as well. These side effects are shown in human studies and are why many users switch to ipamorelin.
14. Amplifies the brain's own GHRH pulses · Synergy with GHRH · role Endocrine & growth
   GHRH from the hypothalamus and GHRP-2 act on different receptors in the pituitary, and together they release more GH than either alone. GHRP-2 amplifies each natural GHRH pulse rather than replacing it. This synergy is well established in human hormone studies.
15. GH pulse lifts IGF-1, aiding muscle and recovery · GH/IGF-1 axis · role Muscle & performance
   Each GH pulse travels to the liver and other tissues, which respond by making IGF-1, the main messenger of growth hormone. IGF-1 drives protein building and tissue repair in muscle. The GH rise is shown in people, while lasting muscle or recovery outcomes have not been trialled.
16. May deepen slow-wave sleep (ghrelin data) · Ghrelin, sleep EEG · role Sleep & rhythms
   Ghrelin receptor signalling has been linked to changes in the sleep EEG, including more slow-wave or deep sleep. This idea comes from ghrelin research, not from sleep trials of GHRP-2 itself. Treat it as a plausible extra, not a shown effect.
17. Mechanism overview: GHRP-2 is a synthetic hexapeptide that activates the ghrelin receptor, GHSR-1a, on pituitary and hypothalamic cells. That triggers a strong growth hormone pulse and amplifies the brain's own GHRH pulses, so the two work synergistically. It is less selective than ipamorelin, so it also raises prolactin, cortisol and hunger. The GH pulse lifts IGF-1, aiding muscle and recovery, and ghrelin data suggest effects on slow-wave sleep.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
18. Typical: 100–300 mcg · 2–3× daily · cycle 8-12 weeks on, 4 weeks off · route Sub-Q (reported)
19. Half-life: ~25 minutes
20. Most people take: 100-300mcg 2-3x/day SC · 8-12 weeks on, 4 weeks off.
21. Common: 100 mcg · 2–3× daily, fasted · 8–12 wk · Sub-Q · for saturation dose, often + Mod GRF [S1] [S2] [S3] (reported)
22. Pre-bed: 200 mcg · 1× nightly · 8–12 wk · Sub-Q · for convenience [S1] [S4] (reported)
23. Higher: 200–300 mcg · 2–3× daily · 8–16 wk · Sub-Q · for advanced [S4] [S2] (reported)

## What people report
24. Reported for GH effect and hunger (useful for bulking); less favored than ipamorelin for side effects.
25. Liked / worked: Potent GH release
26. Liked / worked: Strong appetite stimulation
27. What worked: Strong GH release and appetite stimulation.
28. Went wrong / did not work: Raises prolactin and cortisol
29. Went wrong / did not work: Hunger spike unwanted by many
30. What went wrong: Less selective: raises prolactin and cortisol; appetite spike is unwanted for some.
31. Most reported: Used for GH effect and hunger when bulking
32. Most reported: Less favored than ipamorelin for side effects

## What has been tested
33. Endocrine & growth: GH release (human)
34. Endocrine & growth: GH deficiency diagnosis (human)
35. Appetite & satiety: Hunger rise (human)
36. Human studies confirm potent GH release; raises appetite, prolactin and cortisol more than ipamorelin.
37. What it helps: Human studies show potent GH release, use in diagnosing GH deficiency and a clear rise in hunger. Users take it for the GH effect and for hunger when bulking. Raised prolactin and cortisol and the hunger spike lead many to prefer ipamorelin.
38. Trial: none · growth hormone deficiency diagnosis · Kaken. Approved in Japan since 2004 as a one time diagnostic test for growth hormone deficiency, but no registered trials in recent years. (checked 2026-10-23) [S5] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
39. People with Cushing’s or high cortisol: Raises cortisol and ACTH alongside GH. (reported)
40. People with prolactinoma or high prolactin: GHRPs push prolactin up alongside GH, worsening prolactin problems. (reported)
41. People with active or recent cancer: It raises GH and IGF-1, growth signals that tumour cells also respond to. (inferred)
42. Drug-tested athletes: GH-releasing peptides are named on the WADA banned list. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
43. CJC-1295 no DAC: CJC-1295 no DAC works on the GHRH receptor while GHRP-2 works on the ghrelin receptor, so together they release more GH than either alone. It is a classic pairing built on established GHRH and GHRP synergy, but this exact pair has not been trialled.
44. CJC-1295 with DAC: The DAC version keeps GHRH signalling switched on for about a week, and GHRP-2 adds sharp pulses on top. People pair them for higher GH and IGF-1 over time, but the pairing is user logic, not trial data.
45. Sermorelin: Sermorelin supplies a short GHRH signal that keeps the pituitary's natural feedback intact, and GHRP-2 amplifies the pulse it starts. The two receptors work together in principle, but the pair itself has not been tested together.
46. Tesamorelin: Tesamorelin is a stabilised GHRH with trial data for cutting visceral and liver fat, while GHRP-2 boosts GH through the ghrelin receptor. Users combine them to push GH higher, but no study has tested the pair, and GHRP-2 adds hunger and cortisol.

## Where it comes from
47. A synthetic GH-releasing hexapeptide, a ghrelin-receptor agonist that drives a strong GH pulse.
48. First studied for: A GH-releasing agent and a probe of the ghrelin system; studied as a diagnostic.
49. Name story: Growth Hormone Releasing Peptide 2, from a series descended from opioid enkephalin analogues. Officially it's pralmorelin, and Japan sells it as a one-shot diagnostic for growth hormone deficiency, the first secretagogue used clinically. [S6] (verified)
50. 1990s: Built as a potent GH-releasing hexapeptide; human studies follow
51. 2000s: Approved in Japan as pralmorelin, a GH deficiency test
52. Today: Strong but less selective GH releaser; unapproved outside Japan, WADA-banned

# GHRP-6
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/ghrp-6
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: SK&F 110679, His-D-Trp-Ala-Trp-D-Phe-Lys-NH2, growth hormone releasing hexapeptide
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: HWAWFK (6 amino acids). D-Trp and D-Phe shown as W and F; amide end
4. Legal and approval status: Unapproved research chemical. WADA-banned.

## Summary
5. GHRP-6 is an early synthetic hexapeptide that acts like ghrelin to trigger a growth hormone pulse. People use it mainly for appetite stimulation and GH release, and it was studied in hunger and cachexia. The hunger is extreme for many users, it mildly raises cortisol and prolactin, and there are no outcome trials.
6. Punch line: The original hunger peptide. Ghrelin mimic with a reliable GH pulse and fierce appetite; a bulking favourite.
7. Used for: GH release and appetite for bulking

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Endocrine & growth: GH release
9. Appetite & satiety: Strong hunger
10. Sleep & rhythms: Better sleep reported

## How it works
11. Mimics ghrelin to trigger a GH pulse · Ghrelin receptor, GHSR-1a · role Endocrine & growth
   GHRP-6 binds the ghrelin receptor, GHSR-1a, on cells of the pituitary, the gland that stores growth hormone. Activation releases a pulse of GH into the blood. Human studies confirm a reliable GH rise.
12. Switches on strong hunger · Hypothalamic ghrelin signal · role Appetite & satiety
   In the hypothalamus, the brain's appetite centre, the same ghrelin receptor carries the body's main hunger signal. GHRP-6 switches it on hard, giving the strongest hunger effect of the GHRPs. This is shown in people and has been studied for cachexia, the wasting seen in serious illness.
13. Amplifies GHRH pulses, blunts somatostatin · GHRH synergy · role Endocrine & growth
   GHRP-6 boosts each pulse of GHRH, the hypothalamic hormone that tells the pituitary to release GH. It also blunts somatostatin, the hormone that holds GH back. The result is a bigger GH pulse than GHRH alone would give.
14. Mildly raises cortisol and prolactin · ACTH, prolactin release · role Endocrine & growth
   The ghrelin receptor also nudges the pituitary to release ACTH, which raises cortisol from the adrenal glands, and some prolactin. With GHRP-6 these rises are mild. They are part of why it is less selective than ipamorelin.
15. May deepen slow-wave sleep (ghrelin data) · Ghrelin, sleep EEG · role Sleep & rhythms
   Ghrelin signalling has been tied to deeper slow-wave sleep in sleep EEG research. That link comes from ghrelin data, not from sleep trials of GHRP-6. It is a possibility, not a shown effect.
16. Mechanism overview: GHRP-6 is a hexapeptide that activates the ghrelin receptor, GHSR-1a. In the pituitary that triggers a GH pulse, amplifying GHRH and blunting somatostatin. In the hypothalamus the same ghrelin signal switches on strong hunger. It mildly raises ACTH, so cortisol, and prolactin. Animal work shows cardioprotective effects, and ghrelin data suggest it may deepen slow-wave sleep. Its hunger effect is the strongest of the GHRPs.

18. Half-life: ~20 minutes

## Who shouldn't take it
39. People with Cushing’s or high cortisol: Raises cortisol and ACTH alongside GH. (reported)
40. People with prolactinoma or high prolactin: GHRPs push prolactin up alongside GH, worsening prolactin problems. (reported)
41. People with active or recent cancer: It raises GH and IGF-1, growth signals that tumour cells also respond to. (inferred)
42. People with binge eating: It mimics the hunger hormone ghrelin and drives intense appetite. (reported)

## Synergies (paired with)
43. CJC-1295 no DAC: CJC-1295 no DAC drives the GHRH receptor and GHRP-6 drives the ghrelin receptor, so the pituitary releases more GH than with either alone. The synergy between the two receptor types is established, but this exact pair has not been trialled, and GHRP-6 brings strong hunger.
44. CJC-1295 with DAC: The DAC version keeps GHRH tone raised for about a week while GHRP-6 adds pulses and appetite. People stack them for bulking, with more GH and more food intake, but the pairing is user logic, not trial data.
45. Sermorelin: Sermorelin starts a natural GHRH pulse and GHRP-6 amplifies it while blunting somatostatin. The mechanisms fit together, but the pair itself has not been tested together.
46. Tesamorelin: Tesamorelin is a stabilised GHRH with trial data for visceral fat, and GHRP-6 adds GH release through a second receptor. The strong hunger from GHRP-6 works against a fat-loss goal, and the pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
47. An earlier GH-releasing hexapeptide, strongly ghrelin-like, with marked appetite stimulation.
48. First studied for: A GH-releasing agent; its intense hunger effect became its signature.
49. Name story: Built by Cyril Bowers and Frank Momany in the early 1980s by reworking met-enkephalin, an opioid peptide. It hit a receptor nobody knew existed; ghrelin, the body's own key for that lock, wasn't found until 1999. [S5] (verified)
50. 1980s: One of the first GH-releasing hexapeptides, strongly ghrelin-like
51. 1990s to 2000s: Studied for cachexia and heart protection
52. Today: Known mainly for intense hunger; unapproved, WADA-banned

# GLP-1
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/glp-1
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: glucagon-like peptide reference, glucagon-like peptide-1, GLP-1(7-36) amide, GLP-1(7-37), proglucagon 78-107
2. Origin: Made by the body (reference)
3. Sequence: HAEGTFTSDVSSYLEGQAAKEFIAWLVKGR (30 amino acids). GLP-1 (7–36); the body also makes a 37 version
4. Legal and approval status: Reference molecule.

## Summary
5. GLP-1 is the gut's own fullness hormone, released minutes after a meal and gone in about two. The whole weight-loss drug class, including exenatide, semaglutide, tirzepatide and retatrutide, is an attempt to imitate or extend its signal for appetite and blood sugar control. The native hormone is not used as a drug because it lasts only minutes, so this is a reference entry with no user reports.
6. Punch line: The gut's fullness hormone, gone in about two minutes. Semaglutide and its class are built to outlast it.

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Appetite & satiety: The gut's fullness signal
8. Glucose & insulin: Releases insulin after meals
9. Heart & vessels: The class protects the heart

## How it works
10. Boosts insulin after meals · GLP-1 receptor, pancreas · role Glucose & insulin
   GLP-1 binds the GLP-1 receptor on pancreatic beta cells, which raises cAMP inside the cell. This amplifies insulin release only when glucose is already high, so on its own it rarely pushes blood sugar too low. This glucose dependence is well established in human physiology.
11. Quiets hunger in the brain · GLP-1 receptor · role Appetite & satiety
   GLP-1 receptors in the hypothalamus and brainstem, the brain's appetite centres, turn down hunger signalling when activated. People eat less and feel full sooner. The native hormone is too short-lived to use this way; the long-acting drugs built on it carry the human trial evidence.
12. Slows stomach emptying · GLP-1 receptor, vagal · role Appetite & satiety
   Through vagal nerve signalling from the gut, GLP-1 slows how fast the stomach passes food into the intestine. Sugar from a meal enters the blood more gradually and fullness lasts longer. This also explains the nausea seen with the drugs in this class.
13. Holds back glucagon · Alpha cell suppression · role Glucose & insulin
   GLP-1 suppresses glucagon release from pancreatic alpha cells after meals. Less glucagon means the liver puts out less sugar while food is being absorbed, so post-meal glucose stays lower. It works alongside the insulin boost to flatten the glucose curve.
14. Gone in about two minutes · Cut by DPP-4 · role Glucose & insulin
   The enzyme DPP-4 (dipeptidyl peptidase-4) cuts native GLP-1 within about two minutes of release. That is why the hormone itself is not used as a drug. Every medicine in this class, from exenatide to semaglutide, is engineered to resist this cut.
15. Mechanism overview: GLP-1 is a gut hormone released by intestinal L-cells after a meal. It binds GLP-1 receptors, which raise cAMP. On pancreatic beta cells this amplifies insulin release only when glucose is high, which is why it rarely causes hypoglycemia alone. It suppresses glucagon from alpha cells, slows stomach emptying through vagal signalling, and acts on the hypothalamus and brainstem to cut hunger. Native GLP-1 is cleaved by DPP-4 within about two minutes, so every drug in this class is engineered to resist that.

18. Liked / worked: Defines the pathway the drugs use
19. What worked: As a reference, it defines the pathway.
20. Went wrong / did not work: Too short-lived to be a drug itself
21. What went wrong: The native hormone is too short-lived to be a drug itself.
22. Most reported: Reference entry, not a product

## What has been tested
23. Appetite & satiety: Template for appetite drugs (human)
24. Glucose & insulin: Template for glucose drugs (human)
25. Studied as the template; the drugs (semaglutide, etc.) carry the trial evidence.
26. What it helps: Native GLP-1 is not used as a drug because it lasts only minutes. Its value is as the template: the appetite and glucose drugs in this class, from exenatide to semaglutide, tirzepatide and retatrutide, copy or extend its signal. This is a reference entry with no user reports.
27. Trial: active · Not applicable · GLP-1 infusion effects on organ glucose uptake · NCT07398300 · Rigshospitalet. Native GLP-1 lasts about 2 minutes in blood, so it is used only as an IV research tool, here with total body PET in Copenhagen. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
28. Personal or family history of MTC or MEN2: Causes thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents; boxed warning and contraindication on the label. (verified)
29. Anyone booked for surgery, endoscopy or sedation: Food can stay in the stomach for days and be inhaled into the lungs under anaesthesia. (verified)
30. People with gastroparesis or severe slow digestion: GLP-1 drugs slow the stomach further; labels advise against use in severe GI disease. (verified)

## Where it comes from
31. The gut's own fullness signal, released minutes after a meal and gone in about two. Every GLP-1 drug is an attempt to make it last.
32. First studied for: The natural hormone the whole weight-loss drug class imitates.
33. Name story: "Glucagon-like" because it's cut from the same precursor as glucagon (proglucagon) and resembles it. The active hormone carries odd labels, GLP-1(7-36) amide or (7-37), because it's a trimmed version of a longer 1-37 peptide first read off the gene. [S2] (verified)
34. 1980s: Identified as a gut hormone released after meals
35. 2005 to 2021: Long-acting drugs follow, from exenatide to semaglutide
36. Today: The template the whole weight-loss drug class imitates

# Glucagon
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/glucagon
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: reference, GlucaGen, Gvoke, Baqsimi, hyperglycemic-glycogenolytic factor (HGF, historic)
2. Origin: Made by the body (reference)
3. Sequence: HSQGTFTSDYSKYLDSRRAQDFVQWLMNT (29 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: Approved (emergency kits). Reference molecule here.

## Summary
5. Glucagon is a pancreatic hormone that raises blood sugar, acting as insulin's opposite. It is the approved emergency rescue for severe hypoglycemia, and in combination drugs like retatrutide its arm adds energy expenditure and liver fat loss. On its own it raises blood sugar and is not a weight drug. This is a reference entry with no user reports.
6. Punch line: Insulin's opposite: frees stored fuel to raise blood sugar. Emergency hypo rescue; retatrutide's fat-burning arm.
7. Used for: Severe low blood sugar rescue

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Glucose & insulin: Raises blood sugar
9. Cellular energy: Releases stored fuel
10. Fat metabolism: Burns fat between meals

## How it works
11. Tells the liver to release stored sugar · Glucagon receptor, liver · role Glucose & insulin
   Glucagon binds the glucagon receptor, found mainly on liver cells, when blood sugar falls. The liver responds by releasing glucose into the blood within minutes. This is why it is the approved emergency rescue for severe hypoglycemia, backed by long clinical use.
12. Breaks down glycogen, makes new glucose · cAMP, PKA · role Glucose & insulin
   The receptor raises cAMP, which switches on the enzyme PKA (protein kinase A). PKA turns on glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis, the making of new glucose from non-sugar sources. Together these give a fast release of stored sugar and a slower ongoing supply.
13. Raises fat burning and energy spend · Glucagon receptor · role Fat metabolism
   Glucagon receptor signalling raises whole-body energy expenditure and fat burning. On its own it also raises blood sugar, so it is not a weight drug. In combination agonists such as retatrutide, this arm adds energy spend while the GLP-1 arm offsets the glucose rise.
14. Drives liver fat burning and ketones · Hepatic beta-oxidation · role Cellular energy
   In the liver, glucagon increases fatty acid oxidation (hepatic beta-oxidation), burning fat for fuel and producing ketones. This is the basis for the liver fat loss attributed to the glucagon arm of newer combination drugs, which carry the trial evidence.
15. Mechanism overview: Glucagon is a 29 amino acid hormone from pancreatic alpha cells, released when glucose falls. It binds the glucagon receptor, mainly on liver cells, raising cAMP and activating PKA. PKA switches on glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis, so the liver releases glucose within minutes. It also increases liver fatty acid oxidation and ketone production, and raises whole-body energy expenditure. In combination agonists the glucagon arm adds that energy spend and liver fat burning, while the GLP-1 arm offsets its glucose-raising effect.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
16. Typical: 1 mg · once, may repeat · cycle rescue only · route IM, Sub-Q, IV, Nasal (verified)
17. Half-life: ~8–18 min

## What people report
18. A reference entry.
19. Liked / worked: Approved emergency hypoglycemia rescue
20. Liked / worked: Adds energy spend to combination agonists
21. What worked: Approved hypoglycemia rescue; adds fat-burning/energy-expenditure to combination agonists.
22. Went wrong / did not work: Raises blood sugar alone; not a weight drug by itself
23. What went wrong: On its own it raises blood sugar, so it is a reference, not a weight drug alone.
24. Most reported: A reference entry; no user reports here

## What has been tested
25. Glucose & insulin: Severe hypoglycemia rescue (human)
26. Cellular energy: Glucagon arm in combination agonists (trial)
27. Long clinical use as emergency hypoglycemia treatment; the glucagon arm is now built into multi-agonist weight drugs.
28. What it helps: Glucagon is the approved emergency rescue for severe hypoglycemia. In newer combination drugs such as retatrutide, its arm adds energy expenditure and liver fat loss. On its own it raises blood sugar and is not a weight drug. This is a reference entry with no user reports.
29. Trial: active · Phase 4 · preventing exercise low blood sugar in type 1 diabetes · 2025-523996-45-00 · Steno Diabetes Center Copenhagen. Approved rescue drug, now being tested in tiny doses to prevent rather than treat lows; recruiting in Denmark since April 2026. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (verified)

## Who shouldn't take it
30. People with pheochromocytoma: Glucagon can release a surge of adrenaline and spike blood pressure; label contraindication. (verified)
31. People with insulinoma: An initial rise is followed by rebound low blood sugar; label contraindication. (verified)
32. People starving, with adrenal insufficiency or chronic lows: No liver glycogen to release, so it may not work in an emergency. (verified)

## Where it comes from
33. Named in 1923 from 'glucose agonist': the hormone that raises blood sugar, insulin's opposite, from the same pancreas.
34. First studied for: Rescuing severe hypoglycemia.
35. Name story: Coined in the early 1920s by Charles Kimball and John Murlin from "glucose agonist", for a pancreatic factor that pushed blood sugar up while everyone else was chasing the one that brought it down. [S2] (verified)
36. 1923: Named from 'glucose agonist'; the pancreas hormone that raises blood sugar
37. Decades: Standard emergency rescue for severe low blood sugar
38. 2020s: Its receptor arm built into multi-agonist weight drugs
39. Today: Approved rescue kit; a reference molecule for the glucagon arm

# Glycerin Acetic Acid Water
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/glycerin-acetic-acid-water
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: GAC
2. Origin: Sterile mixing water, not a peptide
3. Class: water
4. Legal and approval status: Sold as a mixing liquid for freeze-dried peptides. Not taken on its own.

## Summary
5. Punch line: Sterile water with acetic acid and glycerin. The acid dissolves stubborn peptides; the glycerin stabilizes the mix.

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
6. Mixing water: A sterile water based liquid containing a small amount of acetic acid and glycerin. The acid helps certain peptides dissolve and the glycerin is added as a stabilizing and thickening agent.

## How it works

## Water
7. Made of: Sterile water, balance
8. Made of: Acetic acid, not stated on label; dilute, likely in the 0.5 to 1% range (unverified)
9. Made of: Glycerin (glycerol), not stated on label (unverified)
10. pH: Not published. If the acetic acid content is around 0.6%, the pH would be roughly 2.9 to 3, calculated from acetic acid's pKa of 4.76. Glycerin is neutral and does not change pH meaningfully.
11. When used: Peptides that dissolve poorly or clump in plain or bacteriostatic water and do better in mild acid, the same group as acetic acid water (for example AOD-9604 and HGH fragment 176-191).
12. When used: Glycerin is used in protein and peptide formulation as a co-solvent that can reduce clumping (aggregation) of hydrophobic molecules, which is the likely reason it is included.
13. When used: Only when the peptide's own instructions or supplier call for an acidic diluent. It is not a general purpose replacement for bacteriostatic water.
14. not_for: Peptides that are acid sensitive or that the supplier says to dissolve in neutral water or bacteriostatic water.
15. not_for: Situations requiring a preservative for many punctures over weeks, unless the product's certificate of analysis states a preservative is present.
16. not_for: Anyone sensitive to acidic injections, since low pH liquids are more likely to sting.
17. not_for: Any use where the exact composition matters and the certificate of analysis is unavailable. The concentrations are not standardized across makers.
18. storage: Unopened: cool, dry place away from light, within the printed expiry date. Refrigeration (2 to 8°C) is a reasonable default if no instructions are given.
19. storage: After first puncture: no published standard exists for this liquid. Treat as preservative-free unless stated otherwise: refrigerate and use within a short period. The USP 28-day multi-dose limit applies only to vials with a preservative and should be treated as an upper bound.
20. storage: Once a peptide is dissolved in it, follow the peptide's own storage rules, usually refrigerated at 2 to 8°C.
21. storage: Do not freeze unless the label allows it.
22. how: Confirm the label, expiry date and clarity. Write the date of first puncture on the vial.
23. how: Wipe the stopper with an alcohol swab and let it dry before every entry. Use a new sterile needle and syringe each time.
24. how: Draw slowly. The glycerin makes the liquid slightly thicker than water, so it may draw and push a little more slowly.
25. how: Add it gently down the inside wall of the peptide vial and swirl, do not shake.
26. how: If the peptide does not fully dissolve, let it rest in the refrigerator before deciding it has failed.
27. watch: Cloudiness, haze or color change: discard.
28. watch: Floating particles or strands: discard.
29. watch: A noticeable vinegar smell is expected. Any other odor is not.
30. watch: Stinging or burning at the injection site is more likely with acidic liquids; persistent redness, swelling or heat is a warning sign.
31. watch: A gel or clumps forming after mixing suggests the peptide has aggregated.
32. facts: Glycerin (glycerol, C3H8O3) is one of the oldest protein stabilizers in biochemistry labs. Research on plant proteins showed it prevents acid-induced clumping in proportion to how much it shields water-repelling surfaces.
33. facts: Acetic acid is the same acid in vinegar. Glacial acetic acid is the pure, water-free form, named for the ice-like crystals it forms just below room temperature (16.6°C).
34. facts: Unlike bacteriostatic water, there is no official pharmacopeia monograph for a 'glycerin plus acetic acid' reconstitution water, so composition varies by maker.
35. tile: Acetic acid + glycerin
36. tile: pH about 3 · recipe varies
37. cells: In it, acid + glycerin
38. cells: pH, about 3
39. cells: Opened, short, fridge
40. cells: Route, Mixing only

# Gonadorelin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/gonadorelin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: gnrh lhrh, Factrel, Lutrepulse, Hoe 471, AY 24031, RU 19847, Abbott 41070, LH-RH, gonadorelin acetate, gonadorelin hydrochloride
2. Origin: Made by the body
3. Sequence: QHWSYGLRPG (10 amino acids). First link is pyroglutamate, a curled ring, shown as Q; amide end
4. Legal and approval status: Was FDA-approved (Factrel/Lutrepulse); now mostly compounded. Not a controlled substance.

## Summary
5. Gonadorelin is synthetic GnRH, the brain's ten-amino-acid signal to the reproductive system, once FDA-approved and now mostly compounded. Pulsed delivery switches on LH and FSH release, and men on testosterone therapy use it in place of HCG to keep testicular size, natural testosterone and fertility. Its very short half-life demands frequent injections, and steady exposure paradoxically switches the system off.
6. Punch line: Synthetic GnRH, the brain's LH and FSH trigger. An HCG swap on TRT; needs frequent, pulsed dosing.
7. Used for: Keep testes working on TRT

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Connection & desire: Supports natural testosterone
9. Endocrine & growth: Pulses switch on the reproductive axis

## How it works
10. Pulses switch on LH and FSH release · GnRH receptor, pituitary · role Endocrine & growth
   Gonadorelin is synthetic GnRH. It binds GnRH receptors on pituitary gonadotroph cells, which then release LH and FSH. Its half-life is minutes, so it acts as a brief pulse, like the natural hormone. Pulsed delivery restores fertility in people whose hypothalamus fails to make GnRH.
11. Steady exposure switches the axis off · Receptor desensitization · role Endocrine & growth
   Steady exposure to GnRH desensitises its receptors, and the pituitary stops releasing LH and FSH. Long-acting GnRH drugs use this on purpose to suppress hormones. The timing of doses decides whether gonadorelin switches the axis on or off.
12. LH keeps testes making testosterone · Leydig cell stimulation · role Connection & desire
   LH drives Leydig cells in the testes to make testosterone. On testosterone therapy the body's own LH falls, so these cells go quiet. Gonadorelin aims to keep them active, a use supported by user reports rather than formal trials in men on TRT.
13. Helps keep testes size and function on TRT · FSH, spermatogenesis · role Reproductive
   FSH supports Sertoli cells, which nurse sperm production. Keeping LH and FSH active helps preserve testicular size and fertility while on testosterone. Men use gonadorelin in place of HCG for this, and user reports describe it as effective but demanding to dose.
14. Mechanism overview: Gonadorelin is synthetic GnRH, the ten amino acid hypothalamic hormone. It binds GnRH receptors on pituitary gonadotroph cells, which release LH and FSH. LH drives Leydig cells in the testes to make testosterone; FSH supports Sertoli cells and sperm production. The pattern matters: pulses keep the receptors responsive, while steady exposure desensitises them and shuts the axis down. Long-acting GnRH agonists exploit exactly that to suppress hormones. Gonadorelin's half-life is minutes, so frequent dosing is needed to keep pulses meaningful.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
15. Typical: 50–100 mcg · twice weekly · cycle Continuous alongside TRT · route Sub-Q (reported)
16. Half-life: ~2-4 hours
17. Most people take: 50-100mcg 2x/week SC · Continuous alongside TRT.
18. Common: 100–200 mcg · 2–3×/wk · ongoing with TRT · Sub-Q · for TRT fertility/testes support [S1] [S2] (reported)
19. Low: 50–100 mcg · 2–3×/wk · ongoing · Sub-Q · for conservative [S1] (reported)

# Hexarelin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/hexarelin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: examorelin, EP-23905, MF-6003
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: HWAWFK (6 amino acids). 2-methyl-D-Trp and D-Phe shown as W and F; amide end
4. Legal and approval status: Unapproved research chemical. WADA-banned.

## Summary
5. Hexarelin is a synthetic hexapeptide that mimics ghrelin and is the most potent of the classic growth hormone releasers. People use it for the GH effect, and it also acts directly on heart tissue, which draws separate interest. Its GH response fades with repeated use, it raises cortisol and prolactin, and it has no outcome trials.
6. Punch line: The most potent classic GH releaser. Also acts directly on heart tissue; the response fades with steady use.
7. Used for: Strong GH release, cardiac interest

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Endocrine & growth: The strongest GH release
9. Heart & vessels: Direct heart protection
10. Muscle & performance: Lean mass reported

## How it works
11. Mimics ghrelin to trigger a strong GH pulse · Ghrelin receptor, GHSR-1a · role Endocrine & growth
   Hexarelin binds the ghrelin receptor, GHSR-1a, in the pituitary and hypothalamus. It produces one of the strongest GH pulses of any GHRP. Human studies confirm the size of the release.
12. Acts directly on heart tissue · CD36 receptor · role Heart & vessels
   Separately from GH, hexarelin binds CD36, a receptor found on heart muscle and blood vessel cells. This gives it a direct route into heart tissue that other GHRPs mostly lack. The effect works even without GH, shown in animal and early human work.
13. Protects heart muscle in injury models · CD36 cardioprotection · role Heart & vessels
   Through CD36, hexarelin protected heart muscle in injury models, such as reduced blood flow followed by reflow. Small human studies have looked at heart function, but there are no outcome trials. The cardiac interest rests mainly on animal work.
14. GH response fades with repeated use · Receptor desensitization · role Endocrine & growth
   With repeated use, the ghrelin receptor becomes less responsive, a process called receptor desensitisation. The GH pulse shrinks, and it fades faster with hexarelin than with other GHRPs. This is widely noted in studies and by users.
15. Raises cortisol and prolactin more than ipamorelin · ACTH, prolactin release · role Endocrine & growth
   The ghrelin receptor also prompts the pituitary to release ACTH, which raises cortisol, and prolactin. Hexarelin raises both more than ipamorelin does. Human studies show these hormone rises.
16. GH pulse lifts IGF-1, aiding muscle · GH/IGF-1 axis · role Muscle & performance
   Each GH pulse prompts the liver and tissues to make IGF-1, the main growth messenger of GH. IGF-1 drives protein building in muscle. The GH rise is shown in people, while long-term muscle outcomes are not.
17. Mechanism overview: Hexarelin activates the ghrelin receptor, GHSR-1a, and produces one of the strongest GH pulses of any GHRP, lifting IGF-1. It also binds CD36 directly on heart tissue, a route separate from GH, which protects heart muscle in injury models. It raises cortisol and prolactin more than ipamorelin. With repeated use the GH response fades through receptor desensitisation, faster than with other GHRPs.

# HGH frag 176–191
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/hgh-frag-176-191
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: hGH fragment 176-191, GH(176-191), somatotropin (176-191), Fragment 176-191
2. Origin: Fragment of a natural protein
3. Sequence: YLRIVQCRSVEGSCGF (16 amino acids). Same chain as AOD-9604
4. Legal and approval status: Unapproved research chemical.

## Summary
5. HGH frag 176-191 is the last stretch of the growth hormone molecule, the part linked to fat metabolism, isolated to keep fat breakdown without GH's growth effects. People use it for fat loss, sometimes injected locally, and animal work shows it raises fat burning. Human weight loss has not been shown, and it is an unapproved research chemical with mild reported effects.
6. Punch line: The fat-burning end of growth hormone, cut free of its growth effects. Often injected into stubborn fat; mild.

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)

9. Endocrine & growth: Cut from growth hormone
10. Bone & cartilage: Cartilage studied

## How it works
11. Keeps GH's fat-burning, drops growth effects · GH C-terminal fragment · role Fat metabolism
   The fragment is the C-terminal tail of growth hormone, residues 176 to 191, the stretch linked to fat metabolism. It does not switch on the GH receptor in the usual way, so the growth signals that build tissue are left out. What remains is a fat-focused piece, studied mainly in animals.
12. Spares blood sugar · No IGF-1 rise · role Endocrine & growth
   Because it skips normal GH receptor activation, it does not raise IGF-1, the liver hormone behind most of GH's growth effects. Full GH can push blood sugar up and blunt insulin action, and this fragment avoids that. That is the reasoning behind its design, with human data coming mostly from its relative AOD-9604.
13. Raises fat breakdown and burning in obese mice · β3-adrenergic upregulation · role Fat metabolism
   In obese mice it raises the number of beta-3 adrenergic receptors on fat cells, the receptors that tell fat cells to release stored fat. More receptors meant more lipolysis and more fat burned for energy. This is animal work, and human weight loss has not been shown.
14. Mechanism overview: This is the C-terminal 176 to 191 region of growth hormone, the part linked to fat metabolism. It does not activate the GH receptor in the usual way, so it does not raise IGF-1 or disturb blood sugar. In obese mice it upregulates beta-3 adrenergic receptors on fat cells, increasing lipolysis and fat oxidation. Its human data come mostly from its close relative AOD-9604.

# IGF-1 LR3
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/igf-1-lr3
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: igf1 lr3 long r3, Long R3 IGF-1, LR3-IGF-1, Long arginine 3-IGF-1, IGF-1 Long R3
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain
3. Sequence: MFPAMPLSSLFVNGPRTLCGAELVDALQFVCGDRGFYFNKPTGYGSSSRRAPQTGIVDECCFRSCDLRRLEMYCAPLKPAKSA (83 amino acids). IGF-1 with position 3 swapped (E to R) and a 13 amino acid tail added; three internal bridges between C pairs
4. Legal and approval status: Unapproved research chemical (native IGF-1 is approved for a rare deficiency). WADA-banned (S2).

## Summary
5. IGF-1 LR3 is a lab-modified insulin-like growth factor 1 with an extra N-terminal extension and an arginine swap, so it avoids carrier proteins and lasts far longer. It was a cell-culture reagent that was adopted for muscle growth, acting through the IGF-1 receptor to drive protein building. It has no human safety data, and users flag hypoglycaemia as a real risk.
6. Punch line: IGF-1 tweaked to dodge carrier proteins and last longer. Users report fuller muscles; hypoglycemia is the risk.
7. Used for: Muscle growth and recovery

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Endocrine & growth: Long-lasting growth factor
9. Muscle & performance: Fuller, bigger muscle reported
10. Tissue repair: Cell growth and repair

## How it works
11. Drives cell growth and protein building · IGF-1R, PI3K/Akt/mTOR · role Muscle & performance
   IGF-1 LR3 binds IGF-1R, a receptor tyrosine kinase on the cell surface, and switches on the PI3K, Akt and mTOR chain. That chain tells the cell to build protein and grow. It is a strong growth driver in cell culture, but LR3 itself has no human trials.
12. Dodges carrier proteins, so lasts far longer · Low IGFBP binding · role Endocrine & growth
   Most natural IGF-1 in blood is held by IGF-binding proteins, which limit how much reaches tissue. The arginine swap and added tail in LR3 stop most of that binding, so far more stays free and active, and for much longer. This is shown in biochemistry and cell work.
13. Pulls sugar into cells, can drop blood sugar · Insulin-like signalling · role Glucose & insulin
   IGF-1R is a close relative of the insulin receptor and shares much of its signalling, so cells pull more glucose out of the blood. That can drop blood sugar. Hypoglycaemia is a known effect of native IGF-1 as a drug, and LR3 users flag it as a real risk.
14. Spurs muscle stem cells to multiply · Satellite cells, MAPK · role Tissue repair
   Through the MAPK branch of IGF-1R signalling it pushes satellite cells, the stem cells parked along muscle fibres, to divide. Those new cells can fuse into damaged fibres during repair. This is shown in cell culture, while muscle gains in people rest on user reports.
15. Suppresses the body's own GH release · Pituitary feedback · role Endocrine & growth
   The pituitary reads high IGF-1 as a sign that GH is already high and releases less of its own, a negative feedback loop. This is textbook endocrinology for IGF-1 in general. In practice the body's own GH output drops while LR3 is in use.
16. Mechanism overview: IGF-1 LR3 is IGF-1 with an arginine swap at position 3 and a 13-amino-acid extension. Those changes stop most binding to IGF-binding proteins, so far more stays free and active for far longer. It binds IGF-1R, a tyrosine kinase that fires PI3K/Akt/mTOR to build protein and MAPK to drive proliferation, including muscle satellite cells. Its insulin-like signalling pulls glucose into cells and can drop blood sugar. High IGF-1 also feeds back on the pituitary and suppresses the body's own GH.

# Larazotide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/larazotide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: at-1001 larazotide acetate, INN-202
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: GGVLVQPG (8 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: Not approved; Phase 3 stopped for futility in 2022.

## Summary
5. Larazotide is a lab-designed eight-amino-acid peptide that tightens the junctions between gut-lining cells, blocking the zonulin pathway behind so-called leaky gut. It was developed for celiac disease to reduce symptoms from gluten exposure despite a gluten-free diet. Earlier trials showed symptom relief, but the Phase 3 trial was stopped for futility in 2022, and grey-market users report variable results.
6. Punch line: Oral gut-barrier peptide that blocks zonulin to reseal leaky gut lining. Earlier trials eased celiac symptoms.
7. Used for: Celiac and leaky gut symptoms

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Inflammatory signaling: Calms gut reaction to gluten
9. Digestive & gut: Tightens the gut lining

## How it works
10. Tightens seals between gut-lining cells · Tight junctions · role Digestive & gut
   Larazotide acts on tight junctions, the protein seals between gut-lining cells. It helps the junction proteins and the actin skeleton beneath them reassemble, closing gaps in the barrier. It acts locally in the gut rather than through the bloodstream.
11. Blocks the 'leaky gut' signal · Zonulin pathway · role Digestive & gut
   In celiac disease, gliadin from gluten triggers release of zonulin, which loosens tight junctions. Larazotide blocks this zonulin-driven opening. Earlier human trials reduced symptoms in celiac patients still affected despite a gluten-free diet, but the Phase 3 trial was stopped for futility in 2022.
12. Less gluten leaking in, less inflammation · Reduced antigen uptake · role Inflammatory signaling
   With the barrier tighter, fewer gluten fragments cross into the gut wall and reach immune cells. Less immune activation means less inflammation in the lining. This chain is well described in celiac biology, though the clinical benefit was never confirmed at scale.
13. Mechanism overview: Larazotide is an eight amino acid peptide that acts on the tight junctions sealing the gaps between gut-lining cells. In celiac disease, gliadin triggers release of zonulin, which loosens these junctions so gluten fragments slip through and activate immune cells. Larazotide blocks this zonulin-driven opening and helps tight junction proteins and the actin cytoskeleton reassemble. Fewer gluten fragments cross the barrier, so less immune activation and inflammation follow. It acts locally in the gut rather than systemically.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
14. Typical: 0.5 mg · 3x daily · cycle ongoing · route Oral (verified)
15. Half-life: Unknown

## What people report
16. Grey-market use for leaky gut/celiac; reported variable.
17. Liked / worked: Earlier trials cut celiac symptoms
18. Liked / worked: A genuinely new gut-barrier mechanism
19. What worked: Earlier trials showed symptom reduction; a genuinely novel tight-junction mechanism.
20. Went wrong / did not work: Phase 3 stopped for futility in 2022
21. Went wrong / did not work: Benefit never confirmed at scale
22. What went wrong: The Phase 3 stop ended the main development program; benefit was never confirmed at scale.
23. Most reported: Grey-market use for leaky gut and celiac
24. Most reported: Reported results vary

## What has been tested
25. Digestive & gut: Celiac symptoms despite gluten-free diet (trial)
26. Digestive & gut: Celiac disease, Phase 3 (trial)
27. Reached Phase 3 in celiac disease, further than any celiac drug before it, but the trial was stopped in 2022 after an interim analysis showed it was unlikely to succeed.
28. What it helps: Earlier trials reduced symptoms in celiac patients who still had symptoms despite a gluten-free diet. The Phase 3 trial was stopped for futility in 2022, so the benefit was never confirmed at scale. Grey-market users take it for leaky gut and celiac symptoms, with variable reported results.
29. Trial: recent · Phase 2 · long COVID · NCT05747534 · Massachusetts General Hospital. Celiac Phase 3 was dropped in 2022, but the drug lived on in pediatric post COVID studies; the long COVID trial completed June 2026. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
30. People with coeliac disease planning to eat gluten: Phase 3 stopped for futility in 2022; it does not protect against gluten. (reported)

## Synergies (paired with)
31. KPV: Larazotide works on the gut barrier, tightening the seals between lining cells, while KPV calms inflammation inside gut and immune cells by turning down NF-κB. People pair them for leaky gut and gut inflammation from two angles. The pair itself has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
32. Larazotide acetate (AT-1001), a synthetic octapeptide that tightens the junctions between gut-lining cells, reversing the 'leaky gut' zonulin pathway.
33. First studied for: Celiac disease, to reduce symptoms from gluten exposure despite a gluten-free diet.
34. Name story: Built from a sliver of cholera biology: Zot (zonula occludens toxin) from Vibrio cholerae loosens gut tight junctions, and an eight-residue stretch it shares with human zonulin became this blocker. The "-zot-" in the name appears to nod to it. [S2] (verified)
35. 2000s: Synthetic 8-amino-acid peptide (AT-1001) built to tighten the gut lining
36. 2010s: Celiac trials show symptom reduction

## Identity

## Summary
5. Livagen is a lab-made peptide Khavinson bioregulator aimed at the liver, related to Vilon. It is used for liver function and tissue support, and it is claimed to loosen chromatin and wake silenced genes in old cells. Evidence is Russian animal work and cell studies with no independent trials, and user reports are very few.

9. Tissue repair: Liver tissue claims
10. DNA & telomeres: Claimed to loosen packed DNA

## How it works
11. Claimed to loosen chromatin, shift genes · Khavinson group · role DNA & telomeres
   Livagen is claimed to loosen chromatin, the packed DNA and protein inside the nucleus, so more genes can be read. That would shift gene activity in the cells it reaches. This is from the Khavinson group's cell studies and is not independently replicated.
12. Claimed to wake silenced genes in old cells · Heterochromatin opening · role DNA & telomeres
   With age, stretches of DNA pack tightly into heterochromatin and the genes there go silent. Livagen is claimed to open these regions and switch those genes back on in old cells. This rests on cell work from one group.
13. Claimed to support liver and gut tissue · Tissue gene expression · role Organ function
   The group also claims it shifts gene expression in liver and gut tissue, supporting their function. Russian animal work reports liver support. There are no independent trials and very few user reports.
14. Mechanism overview: Livagen is a short Khavinson bioregulator peptide. The group claims it decondenses heterochromatin, reopening genes silenced in aging cells, and shifts gene expression in liver and gut tissue. These chromatin effects come from one research group and are not independently replicated.

# Melanotan 1
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/melanotan-1
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: afamelanotide, Scenesse, CUV1647, EPT1647, NDP-MSH, NDP-α-MSH, [Nle4,D-Phe7]-α-MSH, Melanotan I
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: SYSLEHFRWGKPV (13 amino acids). Nle shown as L, D-Phe shown as F; acetylated start, amide end
4. Shown with an FDA approved badge
5. Legal and approval status: FDA- and EMA-approved (Scenesse) for EPP. Cosmetic tanning use is off-label/grey-market.

## Summary
6. Melanotan 1 (afamelanotide, Scenesse) is a lab-made, stabilized version of alpha-MSH that tells skin cells to make dark melanin. It is approved for erythropoietic protoporphyria, a painful sunlight sensitivity disorder, and is used off label for tanning. Users report fewer side effects than Melanotan 2, with little nausea and no spontaneous erections.
7. Punch line: Afamelanotide, approved as Scenesse for sun sensitivity in EPP. Tans skin with less nausea than Melanotan 2.
8. Used for: EPP light tolerance; tanning

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
9. Tanning: Darkens skin, protects from light
10. Skin & aesthetics: Approved for light sensitivity

## How it works
11. Tells skin cells to make melanin · MC1R · role Tanning
   Melanotan 1, or afamelanotide, binds MC1R, the melanocortin 1 receptor on melanocytes, the skin's pigment cells. This raises cAMP inside the cell and turns up melanin production. Skin darkening is shown in human studies.
12. Shifts pigment to dark eumelanin · Eumelanin synthesis · role Tanning
   MC1R signalling shifts pigment output from pale, reddish pheomelanin toward dark eumelanin. Eumelanin absorbs UV light better and gives deeper, more protective colour. This is textbook MC1R biology and fits the darkening seen in people.
13. Little sexual effect, unlike MT-2 · MC1R-selective vs MT-2 · role Tanning
   It is largely selective for MC1R and barely touches MC3R and MC4R in the brain, the receptors Melanotan II also hits. Those central receptors drive sexual arousal and appetite changes. So users report little nausea and no spontaneous erections, unlike MT-2.
14. Raises sunlight tolerance in EPP (approved) · Photoprotection · role Skin & aesthetics
   In erythropoietic protoporphyria, sunlight causes severe pain in the skin. Phase 3 trials showed people on afamelanotide had longer pain-free time in sunlight. This led to approval as Scenesse, given as a slow-release implant.
15. Calms UV-driven skin inflammation · MC1R anti-inflammatory · role Skin & aesthetics
   MC1R activation also dampens inflammation in the skin after UV exposure. This adds to the protection from the extra pigment itself. It is part of the established melanocortin pharmacology behind its EPP use.
16. Mechanism overview: Afamelanotide is a stabilised alpha-MSH analogue that is largely selective for MC1R on melanocytes. Activation raises cAMP and shifts pigment output toward dark eumelanin, darkening skin and adding photoprotection. MC1R signalling also calms UV-driven inflammation in the skin. Because it barely touches the central MC3R and MC4R that Melanotan II hits, it has little sexual or appetite effect. It is delivered as a slow-release implant in its approved form.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
17. Typical: 0.5–1 mg · daily load, weekly maint · cycle load 10 days, then maintenance · route Sub-Q (reported)
18. Half-life: not stated
19. Most people take: Loading 0.5–1 mg/day ×10 days, then 1–2 mg/week. Afamelanotide implant (16 mg) is a separate product.
20. Standard load: 0.5–1 mg · 1× daily · 10 days · Sub-Q · for most tanning users [S1] (reported)
21. Conservative: 250–500 mcg · 1× daily · 2–3 wk · Sub-Q · for first-timers [S2] [S1] (reported)
22. Weekly maintenance: 1–2 mg · 1× weekly · sun season · Sub-Q · for post-load [S1] [S2] (reported)

## What people report
23. Reported for tanning with fewer side effects than MT-2 (no strong nausea or erections).
24. Liked / worked: Longer pain-free light exposure in EPP
25. Liked / worked: Reliably darkens skin
26. What worked: Approved, proven protection for EPP; reliably darkens skin.
27. Went wrong / did not work: None of MT-2's libido or appetite effects
28. Went wrong / did not work: Tanning outside EPP is off-label
29. What went wrong: Does not have MT-2's libido/appetite effects; the tanning use outside EPP is off-label.
30. Most reported: Tanning with fewer side effects than MT-2
31. Most reported: Little nausea, no erections

## What has been tested
32. Cellular protection: Light tolerance in EPP (trial)
33. Tanning: Skin darkening (human)
34. Phase 3 trials in EPP showed longer pain-free light exposure; approved for EPP as Scenesse (an implant).
35. What it helps: Phase 3 trials in erythropoietic protoporphyria, a painful light-sensitivity disorder, showed longer pain-free time in sunlight, leading to approval for EPP. It reliably darkens skin. Users take it for tanning and report fewer side effects than MT-2, with little nausea and no spontaneous erections.
36. Trial: active · Phase 3 · vitiligo · Clinuvel. Approved as Scenesse for EPP; the 210 patient Phase 3 vitiligo study CUV105 reports topline results in December 2026, and a second pivotal vitiligo trial (CUV107) is planned to start November 2026. (checked 2026-10-23) [S3] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
37. People with many moles or melanoma history: Label requires skin checks; increases pigmentation of moles. (verified)
38. People with liver or kidney impairment: SmPC lists severe hepatic disease and impairment. (verified)

## Where it comes from
39. Afamelanotide, a stabilized analogue of alpha-MSH that drives melanin production, built at the University of Arizona.
40. First studied for: Protecting skin in people with the painful light-sensitivity disorder erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP).
41. Name story: Melanotan is literally melano + tan: a 1980s University of Arizona project to tan skin with minimal sun. The tanning dream became afamelanotide (Scenesse), now an approved implant for people with a rare light-sensitivity disorder (EPP). [S4] (verified)
42. 1980s: Built at the University of Arizona as a stable alpha-MSH
43. 2014: Approved in the EU as Scenesse for EPP
44. 2019: FDA approval as Scenesse implant
45. Today: Approved EPP drug; tanning use off-label and grey-market
