# Modafinil
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/modafinil
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Provigil, Modiodal, Modalert, Modvigil, CRL 40476, moda; armodafinil (Nuvigil, Waklert, R-modafinil)
2. Origin: Not a peptide: wakefulness promoting agent (dopamine reuptake inhibitor)
3. Shown with an FDA approved badge
4. Legal and approval status: FDA approved: Provigil (modafinil) 1998, Nuvigil (armodafinil) June 2007, for narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnoea and shift work disorder. US Schedule IV. In the EU limited to narcolepsy since 2010. Cognitive enhancement in healthy people is off label. WADA prohibited in competition (stimulant).

## Summary
5. Modafinil is a wakefulness drug from Lafon Laboratories in France, not a peptide, and the successor to adrafinil. It is approved for sleepiness in narcolepsy, sleep apnoea and shift work, and used for long focus days, thought to work by keeping dopamine around and raising wake-centre activity. In rested healthy adults it gives modest gains on complex tasks only. Lost sleep is the most common complaint.
6. Punch line: The classic smart drug, not a peptide. Approved for narcolepsy; used off label for long workdays with Semax.
7. Used for: Focus, wakefulness, long work days

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Drive & mental stamina: Hours of alert, motivated focus
9. Cognition: Small gains on complex tasks
10. Sleep & rhythms: Pushes back sleepiness

## How it works
11. Keeps more dopamine around · Dopamine transporter blocked · role Drive & mental stamina
   Modafinil weakly blocks the dopamine transporter, the pump that clears dopamine from the synapse. More dopamine stays active in the striatum and prefrontal cortex. This is its best understood action and underlies the alertness seen in human trials.
12. Switches on the brain's wake centres · Orexin and histamine activity up · role Sleep & rhythms
   Downstream it raises activity in the orexin and histamine systems, the brain's main wake-promoting centres. This keeps people awake without the jittery push of classic stimulants. It is approved and effective for sleepiness in narcolepsy, sleep apnoea and shift work.
13. Sharpens planning and decisions · Prefrontal catecholamines up · role Cognition
   It raises catecholamines such as dopamine and noradrenaline in the prefrontal cortex, the region for planning and decisions. In rested healthy adults, a review of human studies found gains on long, complex tasks. Simple tasks and working memory changed little.
14. Mechanism overview: Modafinil's best understood action is weak blockade of the dopamine transporter, raising dopamine in the striatum and prefrontal cortex. Downstream it increases activity in orexin and histamine wake systems and raises noradrenaline and glutamate while lowering GABA in some regions. It is a racemate: armodafinil is the R enantiomer, which clears more slowly, so it holds higher levels late in the day. The serious but rare risks on the label are severe rashes, including Stevens Johnson syndrome, and psychiatric reactions.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
15. Typical: 50–200 mg (armodafinil 50–150 mg) · once in the morning · cycle As needed; many limit to a few days a week · route Oral (reported)
16. Half-life: ~12–15 hours (armodafinil longer late levels)
17. Most people take: Off label users commonly take 100 mg, ranging 50 to 200 mg, early in the morning. Label dose is 200 mg once each morning (or before a shift); armodafinil 150 to 250 mg.
18. Usually taken on demand rather than daily to limit tolerance and sleep loss. Taking it after midday commonly wrecks sleep.

## What people report
19. One of the most used off label 'smart drugs', taken for long work or study days, often stacked with Semax or caffeine. A 2020 Reddit survey (Teodorini) had 219 of 404 respondents report using it. Users describe hours of locked in focus and motivation; insomnia is the top complaint, then headache, diarrhoea, low appetite, mood changes, and less often palpitations and tremor. Some report tolerance and a flat or irritable feel with daily use. No aggregator counts located.
20. Liked / worked: Approved wakefulness drug
21. Liked / worked: Holds performance during sleep loss
22. Liked / worked: Modest gains on complex tasks in rested people
23. What worked: Reliably reduces sleepiness in narcolepsy and shift work and props up performance during sleep loss. In rested people, modest gains in attention and executive function on demanding tasks.
24. Went wrong / did not work: Little effect on working memory
25. Went wrong / did not work: EU restricted it to narcolepsy
26. Went wrong / did not work: Insomnia and headache common
27. What went wrong: Little benefit on simple tasks and working memory in rested people, and a few studies saw worse divergent creative thinking. The EMA judged risks outweighed benefits outside narcolepsy and removed the sleep apnoea and shift work uses in Europe in 2010.
28. Most reported: 100 mg mornings for long focus days
29. Most reported: Insomnia the top complaint
30. Most reported: Headache, low appetite, diarrhoea
31. Most reported: Tolerance with daily use

## What has been tested
32. Sleep & rhythms: Narcolepsy, sleep apnoea, shift work (trial)
33. Cognition: Rested healthy adults, 24 studies (human)
34. Drive & mental stamina: Sleep deprived military personnel (trial)
35. Many trials in narcolepsy, sleep apnoea, shift work and sleep deprived soldiers and pilots. In rested healthy people, a 2015 Oxford and Harvard review of 24 studies (Battleday and Brem) found consistent gains on longer, complex tasks such as planning and decision making, but not on working memory or flexible thinking.
36. What it helps: Approved and effective for sleepiness in narcolepsy, sleep apnoea and shift work. In rested healthy adults the evidence shows modest gains on long, complex tasks, little change on simple ones. Users take it for long focus days and most often complain of lost sleep.
37. Trial: recent · NCT07830056. A US Army study of modafinil in cold stressed, sleep deprived personnel is registered; current status was not confirmed. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1]

## Synergies (paired with)
38. Bromantane: Bromantane raises dopamine production, while modafinil keeps existing dopamine around longer. People stack them for drive and focus from two directions. Both lean on dopamine, and the pair has not been tested together.
39. Semax: Semax is reported to raise brain growth factors and monoamine turnover, while modafinil drives wakefulness and focus. The pairing aims at alertness plus longer-term brain support. It is user logic, not trial data.
40. Selank: Selank is used to calm anxiety without sedation, which can offset the edginess some feel on modafinil. People pair them for focus with calm. The pair has not been tested together.
41. Methylene blue: Methylene blue acts on mitochondrial energy and blocks MAO-A, while modafinil works on dopamine and wake systems. Users stack them for focus and mental energy. The MAO-A effect is a reason for caution, and the pair has not been tested together.
42. NA Semax Amidate: NA Semax Amidate is a longer-lasting Semax form assumed to raise BDNF and monoamine turnover, adding to modafinil's wake and focus effect. People stack them for long work days. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
43. A French wakefulness drug from Lafon Laboratories, the successor to adrafinil, which keeps people alert without the jittery rush of amphetamine. Armodafinil is its longer lasting R half, sold separately as Nuvigil and covered here in the same entry.
44. First studied for: Narcolepsy, then excessive sleepiness from obstructive sleep apnoea and shift work sleep disorder.
45. Name story: 'Moda' plus 'finil' from its parent adrafinil; CRL stands for Centre de Recherche Lafon, the French lab that made it. Armodafinil is the R (rectus) mirror form. [S2] (reported)
46. 1970s: Lafon Laboratories in France develops adrafinil, then its active metabolite modafinil
47. 1994: Launched in France as Modiodal
48. 1998: FDA approves Provigil for narcolepsy
49. 2007: Armodafinil (Nuvigil) approved in the US
50. 2010: EMA restricts EU use to narcolepsy
51. 2015: Oxford and Harvard review finds benefit on complex tasks in rested people
52. Today: Generic worldwide; a staple off label focus drug

# NA Selank Amidate
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/na-selank-amidate
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: N-acetyl Selank amide, Ac-TKPRPGP-NH2, TP-7 (vendor label)
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: TKPRPGP (7 amino acids). Same residues as Selank; acetylated start, amide end
4. Legal and approval status: Research chemical; not approved.

## Summary
5. NA Selank Amidate is Selank capped at both ends with an N-acetyl and a C-amide so it resists breakdown and lasts longer. It is used nasally for calm and focus, and it is assumed to act like Selank. The capped form has never been trialled itself and rests on Selank's Russian data and stability logic. It is one ingredient of the IllumiNeuro blend.
6. Punch line: Selank capped at both ends to resist breakdown. A nasal calm reported as longer and slightly stronger.
7. Used for: Calm and focus without sedation

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Mood: Calm without sedation
9. Immunity: Built from an immune peptide
10. Cognition: Clearer focus reported
11. Sleep & rhythms: Better sleep reported

## How it works
12. Selank capped at both ends to last longer · N-acetyl, C-amide · role Mood
   An N-acetyl group on one end and an amide on the other block the peptidase enzymes that normally trim short peptides from their ends. The intent is a longer working life in the body than plain Selank. This is stability logic. The capped form has no mechanism or absorption data of its own.
13. Assumed to act like Selank · Tuftsin analogue · role Mood
   Selank is a synthetic analogue of tuftsin, a natural immune peptide, extended to make it more stable. The capped form is assumed to hit the same targets, so everything below comes from Selank studies. Whether the caps change how it binds has not been tested.
14. Claimed to boost GABA calming signal, as Selank · GABA-A allosteric modulation · role Mood
   Selank is reported to act as an allosteric modulator at GABA-A receptors, the brain's main calming channel, changing how strongly they respond to GABA rather than opening them directly. That fits the calm without sedation described in Russian human anxiety studies of Selank. The capped form is untested here.
15. Slows breakdown of calming enkephalins (Selank) · Enkephalinase inhibition · role Mood
   Selank inhibits enkephalinase, the enzymes that break down enkephalins, the body's own opioid-like calming peptides. With slower breakdown, enkephalins stay active at their receptors for longer. This comes from Selank lab work and is assumed, not shown, for the amidated form.
16. Shifts immune signalling (Selank data) · IL-6, interferon genes · role Immunity
   In Selank studies, it changes expression of immune genes including IL-6 and interferon-related genes, a link back to its tuftsin origin. That points to a shift in immune signalling alongside its brain effects. This is Selank data from lab and animal work, not measured for this form.
17. Raises BDNF in rat brain (Selank data) · BDNF expression · role Cognition
   Selank raised BDNF, a growth factor that supports neuron survival and new connections, in rat brain. Higher BDNF is linked to learning and resilience to stress. This is animal data for Selank only, and the capped form has not been measured.
18. Mechanism overview: This is Selank with an N-acetyl cap and a C-terminal amide, changes meant to resist peptidases and extend its life. It is assumed to act like Selank, a tuftsin analogue. From Selank data: it modulates GABA-A receptors allosterically for a calming effect, inhibits enkephalinase so natural enkephalins last longer, shifts immune genes such as IL-6 and interferon, and raises BDNF in rat brain. The modified form has no mechanism data of its own.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
19. Typical: 100–200 mcg · daily · cycle Same as Selank · route Intranasal (reported)
20. Half-life: Longer than regular
21. Most people take: 100-200mcg/day intranasal · Same as Selank.

# NA Semax Amidate
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/na-semax-amidate
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: N-acetyl Semax amide, Ac-MEHFPGP-NH2
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: MEHFPGP (7 amino acids). Same residues as Semax; acetylated start, amide end
4. Legal and approval status: Research chemical; not approved.

## Summary
5. NA Semax Amidate is Semax capped at both ends with an N-acetyl and a C-amide for longer action than plain Semax. It is used nasally for focus and drive, and it is assumed to act like Semax on BDNF and monoamines. The modified form has not been trialled itself, its case rests on stability logic, and it is one ingredient of the IllumiNeuro blend.
6. Punch line: Semax capped at both ends for longer action. A nasal focus spray users report as stronger than Semax.
7. Used for: Focus, drive and mental stamina

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Cognition: Focus and attention
9. Neural plasticity: Nerve growth signal
10. Neural protection: Neuron protection
11. Drive & mental stamina: More motivation reported
12. Mood (backed only by animal or user reports): Brighter mood reported

## How it works
13. Semax capped at both ends to last longer · N-acetyl, C-amide · role Cognition
   An N-acetyl cap on one end and an amide on the other shield the peptide from enzymes that trim short peptides from their ends. The aim is a longer working life than plain Semax, which users describe as stronger and longer lasting. That is stability logic and user report, not trial data for this form.
14. Assumed to act like Semax · ACTH(4-7) analogue · role Cognition
   Semax is the ACTH(4-7) fragment of the stress hormone ACTH, extended with Pro-Gly-Pro so it resists breakdown and lacks ACTH's hormonal action on the adrenals. The capped form is assumed to act the same way. Everything below comes from Semax studies.
15. Raises BDNF and TrkB in brain (Semax data) · BDNF/TrkB expression · role Neural plasticity
   Semax raises BDNF and its receptor TrkB in the brain, the growth factor signal that helps neurons survive and form new connections. That is the basis for its plasticity and cognition claims. It is shown in animal studies of Semax, not measured for the capped form.
16. Lifts dopamine and serotonin turnover (Semax data) · Monoamine release · role Drive & mental stamina
   Semax increases turnover of dopamine and serotonin, the monoamine messengers behind motivation, drive and mood. More turnover means these signals are released and recycled more actively. This comes from Semax animal work and fits user reports of drive, but is not measured for this form.
17. Shields neurons after stroke in models (Semax) · Anti-ischemic gene response · role Neural protection
   In stroke models, Semax switches on an anti-ischaemic gene response, a set of genes that help neurons survive when blood and oxygen supply is cut. That protects brain tissue around the injury. Semax has Russian human data in stroke, while the capped form has not been trialled.
18. Mechanism overview: This is Semax with an N-acetyl cap and C-terminal amide to slow breakdown. Semax is a fragment of ACTH(4-7) extended with Pro-Gly-Pro, and the capped form is assumed to act the same way. Semax data show it raises BDNF and its receptor TrkB in the brain, lifting plasticity, increases dopamine and serotonin turnover, and in stroke models triggers an anti-ischaemic gene response that protects neurons.

# Noopept
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/noopept
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: omberacetam, GVS-111, DVD-111, N-phenylacetyl-L-prolylglycine ethyl ester, Ноопепт
2. Origin: Lab-designed: dipeptide prodrug of cyclo-prolylglycine
3. Sequence: PG (2 amino acids). Pro-Gly dipeptide capped with an N-phenylacetyl group and an ethyl ester; converts to cyclo(Pro-Gly)
4. Shown with an FDA approved badge
5. Legal and approval status: Registered medicine in Russia, sold over the counter (since about 2006). In the US an unapproved new drug: FDA has sent warning letters (2019) and treats it as needing a drug application, yet it is widely sold online. Prescription only in Australia, controlled in Hungary since 2020, sale for human use banned in the UK. Not named on the WADA list.

## Summary
6. Noopept is a lab-designed dipeptide related to piracetam, not a natural peptide. It is used for memory and focus, and acts as a prodrug of cyclo-prolylglycine (cGP), a compound the body also makes, which boosts excitatory signalling and growth factors in rodents. Russian open studies report memory gains but had no placebo arm. About half of users notice nothing.
7. Punch line: Piracetam's tiny Russian cousin, a prodrug of cGP. A nootropic staple for recall and fluency, stacked with choline.
8. Used for: Memory, focus, verbal fluency

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
9. Cognition: Better memory scores in Russian studies
10. Neural plasticity: Raises BDNF and NGF in rodents
11. Neural protection: Shields neurons from glutamate damage in lab work

## How it works
12. Turns into cGP, the brain's own small cyclic peptide · Prodrug of cyclo(Pro-Gly) · role Cognition
   After absorption Noopept is cleaved and closed into a ring to form cyclo-prolylglycine, or cGP, a small cyclic peptide the brain already makes from IGF-1. cGP is thought to carry most of its effects. Human pharmacokinetics are poorly described, so how much cGP forms in people is uncertain.
13. Boosts fast excitatory signalling · AMPA positive modulation (cGP) · role Cognition
   cGP positively modulates AMPA receptors, the glutamate receptors behind fast excitatory signalling between neurons. Stronger AMPA signalling supports learning and memory formation. Its protective effects depend on AMPA and TrkB activation in lab work.
14. Raises growth factors for neurons · BDNF, NGF up (rodent) · role Neural plasticity
   In rodents it raised BDNF and NGF, growth factors that keep neurons healthy and support new connections. In cell culture cGP also raised BDNF. These effects have not been measured in people.
15. Blunts calcium and glutamate toxicity · Antioxidant, anti-excitotoxic · role Neural protection
   Rodent work shows it reduces damage from excess glutamate and calcium, which kill neurons when they flood in after injury. It also showed antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. This protection is shown in animals and cells, not in human trials.
16. Mechanism overview: Noopept is N-phenylacetyl-L-prolylglycine ethyl ester. After absorption it is cleaved and cyclised to cyclo-L-prolylglycine (cGP), an endogenous diketopiperazine also produced from IGF-1. cGP positively modulates AMPA receptors and its neuroprotective effects depend on AMPA and TrkB activation; in cell culture it raises BDNF. Rodent work also reports antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, reduced glutamate and calcium toxicity, and HIF-1 activation. Human pharmacokinetics are poorly described.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
17. Typical: 10–30 mg/day · 10 mg 2–3× daily · cycle 1.5–3 months, then 1 month off (Russian label) · route Oral, sublingual (label)
18. Half-life: Short; metabolite cGP lasts longer (rat)
19. Most people take: 10 mg twice daily (20 mg/day) is the Russian labelled dose, with a 30 mg/day ceiling. Users take 10 to 30 mg a day split into two or three doses; occasional reports of 40 to 60 mg.
20. Russian label: 1.5 to 3 months on, then about a month off. Longest human study lasted 56 days.

## What people report
21. A long running r/Nootropics staple taken 10 to 30 mg a day, often with a choline source and sometimes alongside Semax or Selank. Positive reports describe quicker recall, verbal fluency and clarity within an hour; many feel nothing. Headache is the most common complaint, then irritability, poor sleep with late doses, and in some a flat mood, low motivation or low libido. No aggregator counts located.
22. Liked / worked: Better memory scores in Russian open studies
23. Liked / worked: Low dose, well tolerated
24. What worked: Russian open studies report better memory scores in mild cognitive impairment and after stroke, with good tolerance.
25. Went wrong / did not work: No placebo controlled trials
26. Went wrong / did not work: Many users feel nothing
27. Went wrong / did not work: Blood pressure rise in a quarter of one record
28. What went wrong: No placebo controlled, Western or healthy adult trials. Roughly half of users report noticing nothing. Blood pressure rose in about a quarter of people in one tolerability record. Products tested often hold the wrong amount (9 of 12 off label).
29. Most reported: 10 to 30 mg a day, often with choline
30. Most reported: Quick clarity for some
31. Most reported: Headache most common
32. Most reported: Flat mood or low libido in some

## What has been tested
33. Cognition: Mild cognitive disorders vs piracetam (human)
34. Cognition: Post stroke cognition, 60 patients (human)
35. Neural plasticity: BDNF and NGF expression (rat)
36. Few human studies, none placebo controlled. Neznamov and Teleshova 2009 compared it with piracetam over 56 days in vascular and traumatic mild cognitive disorders. Amelin 2011 gave 20 mg daily for two months to 60 stroke patients in an open study. Rodent work shows BDNF and NGF increases.
37. What it helps: Russian open studies in mild cognitive impairment and after stroke report memory gains at 20 mg a day with good tolerance, but none had a placebo arm. Users take it for recall and verbal fluency; responses split, and headache is the usual complaint.
38. Trial: none. No registered human trial found. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1]

## Synergies (paired with)
39. Semax: Semax is reported to raise BDNF and monoamine turnover, while Noopept works through AMPA signalling and growth factors. Users pair them for memory and focus from overlapping angles. The pair has not been tested together.
40. Selank: Selank is used for calm and anxiety, which can balance the stimulating side of a focus stack with Noopept. People pair them for clear thinking without edge. It is user logic, not trial data.
41. Semax + Selank: The Semax and Selank blend adds BDNF support, alertness and calm on top of Noopept's AMPA and growth factor effects. Users stack all three for focus with calm. The combination has not been tested.
42. Dihexa: Dihexa boosts HGF and c-Met signalling to build synapses, while Noopept works through AMPA and BDNF. Both aim at memory through different growth pathways. The pair has not been tested together, and c-Met's link to cancer is a reason for caution.
43. Cerebrolysin: Cerebrolysin is a pig brain peptide mix with nerve growth activity, used for stroke and brain injury, and Noopept has been studied open label after stroke. People pair them for recovery and cognition. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
44. Designed in Moscow in the 1990s by Gudasheva, Seredenin and colleagues as a dipeptide relative of piracetam. Its main metabolite is cyclo-prolylglycine (cGP), a compound the body also makes.
45. First studied for: Mild cognitive problems after stroke, head injury and vascular disease in Russia.
46. Name story: 'Noo' from the Greek nous, mind, plus 'pept' for peptide. The INN name omberacetam files it with the racetams. [S2] (reported)
47. 1996: Synthesis reported by the Zakusov Institute group in Moscow
48. Early 2000s: Registered in Russia as Noopept
49. 2009: Open comparison with piracetam in mild cognitive disorders
50. 2011: Open study in 60 stroke patients
51. 2019: FDA warning letter to a US seller
52. Today: OTC in Russia, grey market online elsewhere

   The group claims it shields hepatocytes, the main working cells of the liver, from toxic damage. Protected hepatocytes keep up their work of detoxifying and making proteins. This is reported only in Russian animal work.

33. Trial: none. Khavinson bioregulator studied only in unregistered Russian clinical reports; no registry trial found in ClinicalTrials.gov, EU CTR, ISRCTN or ChiCTR, Russian registry unverifiable. (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
34. People with active or recent cancer: Marketed as gene-regulating; no human tumour safety data. (inferred)
35. Insulin or sulfonylurea users: Claimed to act on pancreatic cells; additive lows untested. (inferred)

## Synergies (paired with)

37. Thymalin: Thymalin rebalances immune cells, while Pancragen is aimed at pancreatic function. People add both to bioregulator courses to cover immune and metabolic aging at once. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
38. A tetrapeptide Khavinson bioregulator aimed at the pancreas.
39. First studied for: Pancreatic function and glucose-metabolism support.
40. Name story: Khavinson's organ-naming at work: Pancragen = pancreas. The tetrapeptide Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp was studied by his St. Petersburg group on aging pancreatic cells. [S5] (inferred)

# PEG-MGF
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/peg-mgf
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: mgf mechano growth factor, PEGylated MGF, IGF-1Ec, IGF-IEc E-peptide
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain
3. Sequence: YQPPSTNKNTKSQRRKGSTFEEHK (24 amino acids). MGF E-domain peptide with a PEG chain attached, not shown
4. Legal and approval status: Unapproved research chemical. WADA-banned. On the FDA compounding advisory agenda for a meeting due before end of February 2027.

## Summary
5. PEG-MGF is a pegylated form of Mechano Growth Factor, an IGF-1 splice variant that muscle releases after mechanical load. It is studied as the local signal that wakes muscle stem cells after damage, and the PEG tag extends its short natural life. Evidence is cell and animal only, and a small user base reports it for recovery, though the pegylated form has never been studied in people.
6. Punch line: Muscle's own post-load repair signal, PEG-tagged to last longer. Wakes muscle stem cells; dosed around workouts.
7. Used for: Muscle recovery after training

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Muscle & performance: Wakes muscle stem cells
9. Tissue repair: Muscle repair after damage

## How it works
10. Wakes muscle stem cells after damage · Satellite cells · role Muscle & performance
   MGF is a version of IGF-1 that muscle makes after mechanical damage, and it switches on satellite cells, the resting stem cells beside muscle fibres. Once active they divide and fuse into damaged fibres. This has been shown in cell and animal studies, not in people.
11. Claimed to act through its own E-peptide tail · MGF E-domain · role Tissue repair
   MGF carries its own C-terminal tail, the E-peptide, which is claimed to signal separately from the main IGF-1 receptor. That would let it start repair through a route distinct from IGF-1. The idea comes from cell work and is not settled.
12. PEG tag stretches a short natural life · Pegylation · role Tissue repair
   Native MGF is cleared within minutes. Attaching a polyethylene glycol chain makes the molecule bigger and slower to clear, a standard drug-design method. The pegylated form has never been studied in people.
13. Shields stressed heart and nerve cells in animals · Anti-apoptotic signalling · role Tissue repair
   In animal studies MGF switches on anti-apoptotic signalling, which stops stressed cells from self-destructing. This protected heart and nerve cells in injury models. No human work has tested it.
14. Mechanism overview: Mechano growth factor is a splice variant of IGF-1 produced in muscle after mechanical damage. Its distinct C-terminal E-peptide is claimed to act separately from IGF-1R, activating satellite cells, the muscle stem cells that fuse into damaged fibres. Native MGF lasts minutes, so the pegylated version adds a polyethylene glycol chain to slow clearance. Animal work also shows anti-apoptotic signalling that protects stressed heart and nerve cells.

16. Half-life: ~Several hours
17. Most people take: 200mcg/day SC · 4-6 weeks.

19. Higher: 200–400 mcg · 2–3×/wk, bilateral · 6–8 wk · IM · for targeted muscle [S1] [S2] (reported)
20. Top / injury: 200–500 mcg · daily 5–7 d, then 2–3×/wk · 4–6 wk · Sub-Q or IM · for injury loading [S1] [S3] (reported)

## What people report
21. Reported for muscle recovery, often timed around training; small user base.
22. Liked / worked: Muscle stem-cell activation in models
23. Liked / worked: Muscle repair in models
24. What worked: In models, muscle-stem-cell activation and repair; users report recovery.
25. Went wrong / did not work: No human trials
26. Went wrong / did not work: Pegylated form unstudied in people
27. What went wrong: No human data; the pegylated grey-market form is unstudied in people.
28. Most reported: Muscle recovery, timed around training
29. Most reported: Small user base

## What has been tested
30. Muscle & performance: Satellite-cell activation (cell)
31. Tissue repair: Muscle repair (animal)
32. Animal and cell work supports a role in muscle repair and satellite-cell activation; no human trials of the grey-market peptide.
33. What it helps: Evidence is cell and animal only: satellite-cell activation and better muscle repair in models. There are no human trials, and the pegylated form has never been studied in people. A small user base reports it for muscle recovery, timed around training.
34. Trial: none. No human trial of MGF or its pegylated form has ever been registered; all data come from cell and animal work. (checked 2026-10-23) [S4] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
35. People with active or recent cancer: An IGF-1 splice variant that drives cell growth. (inferred)
36. Drug-tested athletes: Mechano growth factors are named on the WADA banned list. (verified)

## Synergies (paired with)
37. IGF-1 LR3: PEG-MGF is used for the local repair signal that wakes satellite cells, while IGF-1 LR3 drives protein building and growth through IGF-1R across the body. Users time them around training as a repair then growth stack. The pair has no combination data in cells, animals or people.

## Where it comes from
38. A pegylated version of Mechano Growth Factor, a splice variant of IGF-1 released by muscle after mechanical load; the PEG tag extends its short natural life.
39. First studied for: Studied as the local signal that activates muscle stem (satellite) cells after damage.
40. Name story: Geoff Goldspink's group named it Mechano Growth Factor because muscle makes this IGF-1 splice variant in response to mechanical stretch and load. PEG is the polyethylene glycol chain bolted on to make it last longer. [S5] (verified)
41. 1990s: MGF found as an IGF-1 splice variant released by loaded muscle
42. 2000s: Studied as the signal that wakes muscle stem cells
43. Today: Pegylated grey-market form, unstudied in people; WADA-banned; on FDA compounding agenda

# Petrelintide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/petrelintide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: ZP8396, petre, Zealand amylin, Roche amylin
2. Origin: Lab-modified natural chain: long-acting amylin analogue
3. Legal and approval status: Investigational, not approved anywhere as of Oct 2026. Phase 3 ZUPREME program started in 2026 with Roche. Not named on the WADA list (falls under S0, inferred).

## Summary
4. Petrelintide is Zealand Pharma's once-weekly copy of amylin, the fullness hormone released with insulin. It is developed for weight loss through earlier fullness and slower stomach emptying, as a gentler route and a partner to GLP-1 drugs. Phase 2 showed up to 10.7% weight loss at 42 weeks with good tolerance. That is well below tirzepatide or semaglutide, and some investors called the trial disappointing.
5. Punch line: Zealand's weekly amylin shot, the gentle fullness route. Up to 10.7% weight loss; built to pair with GLP-1s.
6. Used for: Obesity, type 2 diabetes, investigational

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Appetite & satiety: Makes you feel full sooner
8. Fat metabolism: Up to 10.7% weight loss at 42 weeks
9. Glucose & insulin: Lowers HbA1c in type 2 diabetes
10. Digestive & gut: Slows stomach emptying, milder nausea

## How it works
11. Activates amylin and calcitonin receptors in the brainstem · Amylin receptor agonist · role Appetite & satiety
   Petrelintide activates amylin and calcitonin receptors in the brainstem, the area that signals fullness after a meal. People feel satisfied with less food. In Phase 2 human trials this gave modest, steady weight loss with good stomach tolerance.
12. Slows stomach emptying · Gastric emptying · role Digestive & gut
   Amylin receptor signalling slows how fast the stomach empties into the intestine. Food stays longer, adding to fullness and flattening sugar rises after meals. This is textbook amylin pharmacology, shared with pramlintide.
13. Blunts glucagon after meals · Glucagon suppression · role Glucose & insulin
   After a meal it holds back glucagon, the hormone that tells the liver to release sugar. Less glucagon means a smaller post-meal glucose rise. This fits the improvements seen in the type 2 diabetes trial.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
14. Typical: Trial doses not disclosed in the sources checked (Phase 1b started at 0.6 and 1.2 mg) · Once weekly · cycle Trial only (28 to 42 weeks in Phase 2) · route Sub-Q (trial)
15. Most people take: No approved dose. Weekly injection with the dose raised every four weeks for up to 16 weeks, then held.

## What people report
16. Discussed online as the 'gentle' amylin shot and a possible partner for GLP-1 drugs; Roche plans a combination with its GLP-1/GIP drug CT-388. Little verified first-hand use.
17. Liked / worked: Up to 10.7% weight loss at 42 weeks
18. Liked / worked: Few stomach-related dropouts
19. What worked: Up to 10.7% weight loss at 42 weeks versus 1.7% on placebo in ZUPREME-1, with no vomiting and no stomach-related dropouts in the most effective arm. Up to 9.2% weight loss and HbA1c down 0.61 to 0.88 points in type 2 diabetes.
20. Went wrong / did not work: Less weight loss than GLP-1 drugs
21. Went wrong / did not work: Nausea during dose increases
22. What went wrong: Weight loss is well below tirzepatide, semaglutide and CagriSema; some investors called ZUPREME-1 disappointing. Nausea still occurs, mostly mild and during dose increases.
23. Most reported: Talked about as a gentler amylin option
24. Most reported: Possible GLP-1 partner

## What has been tested
25. Fat metabolism: Obesity, ZUPREME-1, 42 weeks (trial)
26. Glucose & insulin: Obesity with type 2 diabetes, ZUPREME-2 (trial)
27. Phase 1b over 16 weeks in 48 people; Phase 2 ZUPREME-1 in 493 people with obesity over 42 weeks; Phase 2 ZUPREME-2 in 220 people with type 2 diabetes over 28 weeks. Phase 3 (ZUPREME-3, 4 and 5, about 7,000 people) has started.
28. What it helps: Phase 2 shows modest, steady weight loss with good stomach tolerance: up to 10.7% at 42 weeks in obesity and up to 9.2% at 28 weeks in type 2 diabetes. Its main pitch is tolerability and use as a partner to GLP-1 drugs.
29. Trial: active · Phase 3. Zealand and Roche have started the ZUPREME-3, 4 and 5 Phase 3 trials with about 7,000 people. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1]

## Synergies (paired with)
30. Cagrilintide: Cagrilintide is another long-acting amylin analogue on the same receptors, so the two are alternatives. Stacking them duplicates the mechanism. It has not been tested together.
31. Amylin: Amylin is the natural hormone petrelintide copies, and pramlintide is its short-acting drug form. They overlap completely, so this is a reference point, not a stack. The pair has no trial data.
32. Eloralintide: Eloralintide is a competing weekly amylin drug on the same receptors. They are rivals in one class, not complementary partners. Combining them has not been tested.
33. Amycretin: Amycretin already combines GLP-1 and amylin activity in one molecule, so adding petrelintide doubles the amylin side. That overlap gives little reason to stack. The pair has not been tested together.
34. Semaglutide: Semaglutide cuts appetite through GLP-1 receptors while petrelintide adds amylin fullness signalling, two separate routes to eating less. Pairing with GLP-1 drugs is petrelintide's main pitch. The specific combination has not yet been tested in published trials.

## Where it comes from
35. Designed by Zealand Pharma in Copenhagen as a once-weekly copy of amylin, the fullness hormone released with insulin. Roche bought half the rights in March 2025 for 1.65 billion dollars upfront.
36. First studied for: Weight loss as a gentler alternative to GLP-1 drugs, aiming for fullness with less nausea.
37. Jun 2024: Phase 1b: 8.6% weight loss in 16 weeks
38. Dec 2024: ZUPREME-1 Phase 2 starts
39. Mar 2025: Roche deal worth up to 5.3 billion dollars
40. Mar 2026: ZUPREME-1: up to 10.7% at 42 weeks
41. Oct 2026: ZUPREME-2: up to 9.2% in type 2 diabetes
42. Today: Phase 3 ZUPREME program with about 7,000 people

# Phenylpiracetam
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/phenylpiracetam
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Phenotropil, fonturacetam, carphedon, 4-phenylpiracetam
2. Origin: Not a peptide: racetam stimulant
3. Shown with an FDA approved badge
4. Legal and approval status: Prescription medicine in Russia (Phenotropil). Not approved in the US and not a legal dietary supplement there, though sold online. WADA prohibited in competition as a stimulant (listed as carphedon).

## Summary
5. Phenylpiracetam is piracetam with a phenyl ring added, made in Russia and sold there as Phenotropil. It is used for energy, focus and motivation, working as a dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor with a stimulant edge. Russian studies report less fatigue after stroke and in asthenia, without modern placebo-controlled confirmation. Tolerance builds within days of daily use, and it is banned in sport.
6. Punch line: Piracetam plus a phenyl ring, sold in Russia as Phenotropil. A stimulant lift kept for hard days.
7. Used for: Energy, focus, motivation

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Drive & mental stamina: Stimulant lift, energy and motivation
9. Cognition: Sharper focus reported

## How it works
10. Blocks dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake · DAT and NET inhibition (R enantiomer) · role Drive & mental stamina
   The R enantiomer binds the dopamine transporter (DAT) and noradrenaline transporter (NET) and slows how fast those signals are cleared from the synapse. More dopamine and noradrenaline linger, which fits the quick stimulant feel and the fast tolerance users describe. Human data are older Russian clinical studies without modern placebo controls.
11. Racetam style support of signalling · AMPA and acetylcholine links (proposed) · role Cognition
   Like piracetam, it is proposed to tune AMPA receptors, which carry fast excitatory signals, and acetylcholine signalling, both central to learning and attention. This racetam side is much less well supported than the transporter action. Russian clinical reports of better cognition after stroke have not been confirmed in modern placebo controlled trials.
12. Mechanism overview: Phenylpiracetam adds a phenyl group to piracetam's pyrrolidone ring, which raises brain entry and adds stimulant activity. The R enantiomer inhibits dopamine and noradrenaline transporters, which fits the quick stimulant feel and fast tolerance. The racetam claims of AMPA and cholinergic modulation are less well supported. Human data are mostly Russian.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
13. Typical: 100–200 mg · once in the morning · cycle Occasional use, days off between doses · route Oral (reported)
14. Half-life: ~3–5 hours (reported)
15. Most people take: Users take 100 to 200 mg once in the morning. The Russian label covers similar 100 to 200 mg daily doses.
16. Mostly used as needed with days off, since tolerance shows within a few consecutive days.

## What people report
17. Taken 100 to 200 mg in the morning, mostly as an occasional boost for hard days, exams or cold training rather than daily. Users describe energy, motivation and sharper focus that fade noticeably after a few consecutive days. Insomnia, overstimulation, irritability and headache appear mainly at high or late doses. No aggregator counts located.
18. Liked / worked: Russian studies report less fatigue
19. Liked / worked: Clear stimulant effect on first use
20. What worked: Russian studies report less fatigue and better cognition in patients. Users feel a clear stimulant lift on first doses.
21. Went wrong / did not work: Tolerance within days
22. Went wrong / did not work: No Western controlled trials
23. Went wrong / did not work: WADA banned
24. What went wrong: Tolerance builds within days of daily use, so effects fade fast. No modern controlled trials. Banned in sport.
25. Most reported: 100 to 200 mg mornings, as needed
26. Most reported: Energy and focus for hard days
27. Most reported: Insomnia and irritability at high doses

## What has been tested
28. Drive & mental stamina: Asthenia and fatigue (human)
29. Cognition: Stroke and cognitive decline (human)
30. Human evidence is older Russian clinical work in stroke, epilepsy, asthenia and stress, with limited independent replication. No Western placebo controlled trials.
31. What it helps: Russian clinical studies report less fatigue and better cognition in asthenia and after stroke, without modern placebo controlled confirmation. Users take it occasionally for energy and focus and note that the effect drops within days of repeated use.
32. Trial: none. No registered human trial found. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1]

## Synergies (paired with)
33. Bromantane: Phenylpiracetam slows dopamine clearance, while bromantane raises how much dopamine neurons make by switching on tyrosine hydroxylase. People pair them to work on drive from both the supply and the clearance side, but the pair has not been tested together.
34. Semax: Phenylpiracetam gives a fast stimulant lift through dopamine and noradrenaline transporters, while Semax is reported to raise BDNF and monoamine turnover in rodents. Users stack them for focus with a growth factor angle on top, which is user logic, not trial data.
35. Methylene blue: Methylene blue feeds electrons through the mitochondrial chain for cellular energy, while phenylpiracetam adds catecholamine drive. Methylene blue also blocks MAO-A, so the stack raises monoamines from two sides, a known interaction concern, and the pair has not been tested together.
36. NA Semax Amidate: NA Semax Amidate is a longer lasting Semax analogue assumed to share its BDNF and monoamine effects, while phenylpiracetam adds direct dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake block. People pair them for mental stamina, but the pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
37. Piracetam with a phenyl ring added, made in Russia and sold there on prescription as Phenotropil. The ring makes it far more stimulating than piracetam.
38. First studied for: Asthenia, fatigue and cognitive decline in Russia; it is said to have been developed for cosmonauts.
39. Name story: Piracetam with a phenyl ring bolted on; WADA lists it as carphedon, and fonturacetam is its INN. [S2] (reported)
40. 1980s: Developed in the Soviet Union from piracetam
41. 2000s: Registered in Russia as Phenotropil
42. Today: Russian prescription drug; grey market elsewhere; banned in sport

   The group claims it calms chronic inflammation in the prostate, the kind behind long-running prostatitis. Less inflammation would mean less swelling and pain. There is no Western validation and first-hand reports are few.

# SNAP-8
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/snap-8
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: acetyl octapeptide, Acetyl Octapeptide-3, Acetyl Glutamyl Heptapeptide-3
2. Origin: Lab-designed
3. Sequence: EEMQRRAD (8 amino acids). Acetylated start, amide end (acetyl octapeptide-3)
4. Legal and approval status: Cosmetic ingredient; not a drug.

## Summary
5. SNAP-8 is acetyl octapeptide-3, an eight-amino-acid lab-made peptide and a longer relative of Argireline. It is used in cosmetic serums as a Botox-like wrinkle agent, and it interferes with the SNARE complex that muscles use to release their contraction signal. Studies show only a modest drop in wrinkle depth, often come from the maker, and penetration is poor.
6. Punch line: Argireline's longer cousin, a Botox-like serum peptide. It quiets the muscle signal behind lines; modest results.
7. Used for: Expression lines, forehead and eyes

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Skin & aesthetics: Softens expression lines

## How it works
9. Blunts the signal that contracts face muscles · SNARE complex · role Skin & aesthetics
   SNAP-8 interferes with the SNARE complex, the protein machinery that fuses acetylcholine-filled vesicles with the nerve ending. With that machinery less stable, the nerve's signal to contract reaches facial muscle more weakly. Topical cosmetic studies show a modest drop in wrinkle depth.
10. Mimics SNAP-25 and competes for its place · SNAP-25 N-terminus · role Skin & aesthetics
   Its eight amino acids copy the start of SNAP-25, one of the three core SNARE proteins. It competes with the real SNAP-25 for its place, so fewer working complexes form. The competition is mild, unlike botulinum toxin, which cuts SNAP-25 outright.
11. Less nerve-to-muscle release; fades when stopped · Reduced ACh exocytosis · role Skin & aesthetics
   Less acetylcholine release means expression lines around the eyes and forehead soften a little. Because nothing is cut, the effect fades once use stops. Studies are often manufacturer-run, skin penetration is poor and results fall far short of injected toxin.
12. Mechanism overview: SNAP-8 is an octapeptide copying the N-terminal end of SNAP-25, one of the SNARE proteins that fuse acetylcholine vesicles with the nerve membrane. By competing for SNAP-25's place, it destabilises SNARE assembly, so less acetylcholine reaches facial muscle and contraction softens. It works on the same machinery botulinum toxin cuts, but by mild competition, not cleavage, so the effect is small and fades when use stops.

## Synergies (paired with)

34. Argireline: Argireline is a shorter peptide from the same SNAP-25 mimic family, so it works on the same SNARE machinery. Pairing them stacks a mild anti-wrinkle effect, but they overlap rather than complement, and the pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
35. Acetyl octapeptide-3, a longer relative of Argireline, an eight-amino-acid peptide that interferes with the SNARE complex muscles use to release the signal that contracts them.
36. First studied for: A topical cosmetic 'Botox-like' wrinkle agent, to soften expression lines.

# Somatropin (HGH)
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/somatropin-hgh
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: hgh growth hormone somatropin gh, somatotropin, rhGH, Genotropin, Norditropin, Humatrope, Nutropin, Omnitrope, Saizen, Zomacton
2. Origin: Made by the body
3. Sequence: FPTIPLSRLFDNAMLRAHRLHQLAFDTYQEFEEAYIPKEQKYSFLQNPQTSLCFSESIPTPSNREETQQKSNLELLRISLLLIQSWLEPVQFLRSVFANSLVYGASDSNVYDLLKDLEEGIQTLMGRLEDGSPRTGQIFKQTYSKFDTNSHNDDALLKNYGLLYCFRKDMDKVETFLRIVQCRSVEGSCGF (191 amino acids). Two bridges between C pairs hold the fold; not shown
4. Legal and approval status: FDA-approved for specific deficiencies; anti-aging/athletic use is off-label and illegal to distribute for that purpose. WADA-banned (S2).

## Summary
5. Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone, the full 191-amino-acid protein the pituitary makes, now produced by engineered bacteria. It is approved for growth hormone deficiency and wasting, where it restores growth and raises lean mass while cutting fat, working through the GH receptor and IGF-1. Anti-aging and physique use is off-label and WADA-banned, and water retention, carpal tunnel and rising blood sugar are common.
6. Punch line: The real pituitary hormone, not a secretagogue. What GH peptides chase: more lean mass, less fat, water retention.
7. Used for: Adult GH deficiency, body composition

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Tissue repair: Supports tissue and bone repair
9. Fat metabolism: Breaks down stored fat
10. Endocrine & growth: Replaces growth hormone
11. Muscle & performance: Adds lean mass

## How it works
12. Signals growth and fat breakdown · GH receptor, JAK2/STAT5 · role Endocrine & growth
   Somatropin binds the GH receptor, which activates the JAK2 enzyme, which then switches on STAT5 to change gene activity. That signal drives growth in children and shifts metabolism toward fat breakdown in adults. It is identical to the body's own growth hormone, with decades of human trials.
13. Drives IGF-1 from the liver · IGF-1 axis · role Endocrine & growth
   In the liver, STAT5 drives production of IGF-1, which carries most of growth hormone's growth and building effects. IGF-1 acts on bone, muscle and connective tissue throughout the body. Raised IGF-1 is the main marker clinicians track during treatment.
14. Releases fat from fat cells · Lipolysis · role Fat metabolism
   Growth hormone acts directly on fat cells to trigger lipolysis, the release of stored fat for fuel. This is part of why trials show less fat mass in adults with deficiency and HIV wasting. GH also opposes insulin, which raises blood sugar.
15. Builds lean mass and protein · Protein synthesis · role Muscle & performance
   Through IGF-1, growth hormone raises protein synthesis and lean mass. Trials show clear gains in true GH deficiency and HIV wasting. In older adults without deficiency, anti-aging trials found the risks outweighed the gains, and some of the added mass is retained fluid.
16. Supports collagen and tissue repair · IGF-1, collagen synthesis · role Tissue repair
   IGF-1 drives collagen formation in tendon, ligament, bone and skin. That is the basis of the recovery reputation among users. Clear human evidence exists for growth and body composition in deficiency, while repair claims in healthy adults rest mostly on user reports.
17. Mechanism overview: Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone, identical to the 191 amino acid pituitary hormone. It binds the GH receptor, which activates JAK2, which phosphorylates STAT5. In the liver, STAT5 drives IGF-1 production, and IGF-1 carries most of the growth and anabolic effects: protein synthesis, bone growth and collagen formation. GH also acts directly on fat cells to trigger lipolysis, and it opposes insulin, raising blood glucose. That anti-insulin action, plus sodium retention, explains the common side effects of high blood sugar and fluid retention.

# Tadalafil
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/tadalafil
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Cialis, Adcirca, Alyq, Tadliq, Entadfi (with finasteride), IC351, LY450190, daily Cialis
2. Origin: Not a peptide: PDE5 inhibitor
3. Shown with an FDA approved badge
4. Legal and approval status: FDA approved (Cialis 2003; once daily ED 2008; BPH 2011; Adcirca for pulmonary arterial hypertension; Entadfi with finasteride 2021). Generic worldwide. Daily use for pumps, performance or longevity is off label. Not on the WADA Prohibited List.

## Summary
5. Tadalafil is a small-molecule drug from ICOS and Eli Lilly, not a peptide, that blocks the enzyme PDE5 and so keeps nitric oxide signalling on in blood vessel walls. It is approved for erectile dysfunction, enlarged prostate symptoms and pulmonary arterial hypertension, and lifters use it for fuller pumps. The gym claims rest on user reports, and the heart benefit is observational. It is dangerous with nitrates.
6. Punch line: Daily Cialis, not a peptide. The most stacked prescription in peptide circles, for blood flow, pumps and erections.
7. Used for: Blood flow, pump, BPH, erections

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Heart & vessels: Widens blood vessels via nitric oxide
9. Reproductive: Treats erectile dysfunction
10. Organ function: Eases urinary symptoms of an enlarged prostate
11. Muscle & performance: Fuller pumps reported by lifters

## How it works
12. Keeps the blood vessel relaxing signal switched on · PDE5 inhibition, cGMP up · role Heart & vessels
   Tadalafil blocks phosphodiesterase type 5, or PDE5, the enzyme that breaks down cGMP in smooth muscle. Nitric oxide from the vessel lining raises cGMP and relaxes the muscle, so with PDE5 blocked the relaxation lasts longer. Its long half-life keeps a steady effect on daily low dosing.
13. Lets penile blood vessels fill · Corpus cavernosum smooth muscle relaxation · role Reproductive
   In the erectile tissue, nitric oxide released during arousal relaxes the smooth muscle and lets the vessels fill. Tadalafil prolongs that signal, so it still needs arousal to work. This is proven in large human trials, on demand and daily.
14. Relaxes prostate and bladder neck muscle · PDE5 in lower urinary tract · role Organ function
   PDE5 is also present in the prostate and bladder neck, and blocking it relaxes that muscle. Urine flows more easily. Large human trials showed improved urinary symptoms in men with BPH.
15. Lowers lung artery pressure at high dose · Pulmonary vasodilation · role Heart & vessels
   At higher doses it relaxes the smooth muscle of the lung arteries, lowering their pressure. This is the basis of its approval for pulmonary arterial hypertension in human trials. It works the same way as in other vessels, through cGMP.
16. Mechanism overview: Tadalafil blocks phosphodiesterase type 5, the enzyme that breaks down cGMP in smooth muscle. Nitric oxide from the vessel lining raises cGMP and relaxes the muscle; with PDE5 blocked, that relaxation lasts longer wherever nitric oxide is being released. That is why it needs arousal to work for erections, why it relaxes prostate and bladder neck muscle, and why it lowers pressure in the lung arteries. Its half life of about 17.5 hours is far longer than sildenafil's, so a small daily dose keeps a steady level. Some PDE11 cross reactivity explains the back and muscle ache.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
17. Typical: 2.5–5 mg · once daily · cycle Continuous · route Oral (reported)
18. Half-life: ~17.5 hours (label)
19. Most people take: Off label users take 2.5 to 5 mg once a day, every day. Label doses: 5 to 20 mg before sex for ED, 2.5 to 5 mg daily for ED, 5 mg daily for BPH, 40 mg daily for pulmonary hypertension.
20. Taken continuously rather than cycled; many start at 2.5 mg for two to four weeks to let headaches settle. Never combined with nitrates or other PDE5 inhibitors.

## What people report
21. The most stacked prescription drug in peptide and enhanced lifting circles: 2.5 to 5 mg every day for blood flow, fuller pumps, morning erections and easier urination, often next to TRT, PT-141 or citrulline. Users describe pumps and vascularity as noticeable but modest. Headache and flushing in the first one to two weeks, nasal congestion and lower back or muscle ache are the usual complaints, and some drop to 2.5 mg for that reason. No aggregator counts located.
22. Liked / worked: Approved for ED, BPH and pulmonary hypertension
23. Liked / worked: Daily 5 mg improves vessel lining markers
24. Liked / worked: Observational link to fewer heart events
25. What worked: Reliable for erections and for BPH urinary symptoms. Daily dosing improves vessel lining markers in men with ED or cardiovascular risk. Observational studies tie PDE5 inhibitor use to fewer cardiovascular events and deaths, with a meta analysis estimating about 22% fewer major events.
26. Went wrong / did not work: Heart and longevity data are observational
27. Went wrong / did not work: No trials of pumps or strength in healthy lifters
28. Went wrong / did not work: Headache, flushing, back ache common
29. What went wrong: The heart and longevity signal is observational and may reflect healthier men getting prescriptions. Gym claims of bigger pumps and better performance rest on user reports, not trials in healthy lifters. Headache, flushing, back pain and indigestion are common; it can drop blood pressure dangerously with nitrates.
30. Most reported: Daily 2.5 to 5 mg for blood flow and pumps

## What has been tested

## Synergies (paired with)
42. PT-141: PT-141 raises desire through melanocortin receptors in the brain, while tadalafil handles blood flow. People pair them to cover desire and erection from two ends. Both can affect blood pressure, and the pair has not been tested together.

45. L-Carnitine: L-carnitine moves fatty acids into mitochondria, and tadalafil improves blood flow to muscle. Users pair them for training energy and pump. The pairing is user logic, not trial data.

## Where it comes from
46. A small molecule from ICOS and Eli Lilly that blocks PDE5, the enzyme that switches off nitric oxide signalling in blood vessel walls. Its long half life (about 17.5 hours) is why it became the daily option among erection drugs.

# TB-500 frag 1–4
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/tb-500-frag-1-4
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Ac-SDKP, Goralatide, seraspenide, AcSDKP, Thymosin β4 (1-4), N-acetyl-Ser-Asp-Lys-Pro
2. Origin: Fragment of a natural protein
3. Sequence: SDKP (4 amino acids). Acetylated start (Ac-SDKP), not shown
4. Legal and approval status: Unapproved research chemical. (Identity note: confirm your vial is 1-4, not 17-23.)

## Summary
5. TB-500 frag 1-4 is Ac-SDKP, the four-amino-acid N-terminal piece of thymosin beta-4 that an enzyme cuts off naturally. It is studied as the body's own anti-scarring and blood-vessel-growth signal, working by turning down TGF-beta signalling. Animal studies show anti-fibrotic effects in heart and kidney, but there is no human efficacy data, and it is often confused with the 17-23 fragment sold as TB-500.
6. Punch line: Ac-SDKP, the anti-scarring tip cut from thymosin beta-4. Protects heart and kidney in models; TB-500 does not.

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Heart & vessels: Protects heart from scarring in animals
8. Inflammatory signaling: Lowers inflammation
9. Tissue repair: Anti-scarring signal
10. Pain & sensory: Less pain reported

## How it works
11. Turns down scarring signals · TGF-beta, Smad · role Heart & vessels
   Ac-SDKP inhibits TGF-beta signalling through the Smad proteins, the main relay that tells fibroblasts to activate and lay down collagen. With that relay turned down, less scar tissue builds up after injury. Animal studies show protection against fibrosis in the heart and kidney.
12. Grows new blood vessels · Angiogenesis · role Tissue repair
   Ac-SDKP promotes angiogenesis, the sprouting of new blood vessels from existing ones. More vessels can bring oxygen and repair cells into damaged tissue. This has been shown in cell work and has not been tested as a treatment in people.
13. Broken down by ACE; rises on ACE inhibitors · ACE substrate · role Heart & vessels
   Angiotensin-converting enzyme, the same enzyme that ACE inhibitor blood pressure drugs block, is the main enzyme that breaks Ac-SDKP down. When ACE is blocked, Ac-SDKP levels rise. That is why it serves as a marker in ACE inhibitor research and may contribute to those drugs' anti-fibrotic effect.
14. Calms immune cell influx into damaged tissue · Macrophage infiltration · role Inflammatory signaling
   Ac-SDKP limits macrophage infiltration, the influx of immune cells that pile into injured tissue and release inflammatory and scar-promoting signals. Fewer of these cells means less ongoing inflammation feeding fibrosis. This has been shown in animal models of heart and kidney injury.
15. Keeps blood stem cells resting · Haematopoietic stem cells · role Immunity
   Ac-SDKP keeps haematopoietic stem cells, the bone marrow cells that make all blood cells, in a resting, quiescent state. It acts as a natural brake that holds them back from dividing. This comes from lab and animal work, with no human efficacy data.
16. Mechanism overview: This is Ac-SDKP, the N-terminal tetrapeptide of thymosin beta-4, a separate molecule from the 17 to 23 fragment. It inhibits TGF-beta signalling through Smad proteins, which turns down the fibroblast activation and collagen deposition behind scarring. It promotes new vessel growth and limits macrophage influx into injured tissue. It also keeps haematopoietic stem cells quiescent. ACE breaks it down, so levels rise in people taking ACE inhibitors, which may contribute to their anti-fibrotic effect.

## What has been tested

30. Tissue repair: New vessel growth (cell)
31. Animal and cell work: Ac-SDKP reduces fibrosis by turning down TGF-beta, protects the heart and kidney, and promotes new vessels. It is also a marker used in ACE-inhibitor research. No grey-market human trials.
32. What it helps: Animal studies show clear anti-fibrotic effects in the heart and kidney, with protection against fibrosis and organ damage, and cell work shows new vessel growth. There is no human efficacy data for injected Ac-SDKP. A small user base takes it for recovery and anti-scarring, and vial identity is often confused with the 17 to 23 fragment.
33. Trial: none · Phase 1/2 · protecting bone marrow during chemotherapy · Ipsen. As goralatide it reached early chemotherapy trials in the 1990s, then was abandoned; nothing since. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
34. People on ACE inhibitors: ACE breaks down Ac-SDKP; ACE inhibitors already raise levels 4- to 5-fold. (reported)
35. People with active or recent cancer: Ac-SDKP promotes new blood vessel growth, which tumours exploit. (reported)

## Where it comes from
36. Ac-SDKP, the N-terminal four-amino-acid piece of thymosin beta-4, cut off naturally by an enzyme. A different molecule from TB-500 (the 17-23 fragment).
37. First studied for: Studied as the body's own anti-fibrotic and blood-vessel-growth signal.
38. Name story: Ac-SDKP is one-letter code for acetyl-Ser-Asp-Lys-Pro (INN goralatide): thymosin beta-4's first four residues, which the body snips off naturally. Sellers file it under 'TB-500' because that became the trade label for anything from Tβ4, though it shares nothing with the 17–23 'TB-500' heptapeptide. [S2] (verified)
39. 1980s: Ac-SDKP found as a natural blood-cell regulator
40. 1990s to 2000s: Studied as the body's own anti-scarring and vessel signal
41. Today: Research chemical; distinct from TB-500 (17 to 23)

# Teriparatide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/teriparatide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Forteo, Forsteo, rhPTH(1-34), PTH(1-34), LY333334, Bonsity, Terrosa, Movymia
2. Origin: Fragment of a natural protein
3. Sequence: SVSEIQLMHNLGKHLNSMERVEWLRKKLQDVHNF (34 amino acids). PTH 1–34
4. Shown with an FDA approved badge
5. Legal and approval status: FDA-approved (Forteo, plus follow-on versions) for osteoporosis. Catalog vials are not the approved product.

## Summary
6. Teriparatide (Forteo) is the first 34 amino acids of parathyroid hormone. Given as a daily pulse it switches on bone building, and it is an FDA-approved treatment for severe osteoporosis that cuts spine fractures. It needs daily injection, the gains are lost unless another bone drug follows, and grey-market catalog vials are not the approved product.
7. Punch line: Forteo, the active front of parathyroid hormone. A daily pulse builds new bone and cuts spine fractures.
8. Used for: Osteoporosis with high fracture risk

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
9. Bone & cartilage: Builds new bone
10. Endocrine & growth: Parathyroid hormone piece
11. Pain & sensory: Less back pain after fractures

## How it works
12. Mimics parathyroid hormone's first 34 amino acids · PTH(1-34) · role Endocrine & growth
   Teriparatide is the first 34 amino acids of parathyroid hormone, the part that does the hormone's work. This piece carries full activity at the PTH1 receptor. It is a well-established approved drug.
13. Daily pulses switch bone building on · PTH1 receptor · role Bone & cartilage
   Given as a short daily pulse, PTH1 receptor activation switches on osteoblasts, the cells that lay down new bone. Constant PTH does the opposite and breaks bone down. Timing decides the outcome, and this is shown in large human trials.
14. Bone formation outpaces bone loss · Osteoblast activation · role Bone & cartilage
   Bone is constantly built by osteoblasts and removed by osteoclasts. Pulsed teriparatide tips the balance so formation outpaces removal, giving a net gain of new bone. Phase 3 trials show rising bone density.
15. Lowers the bone-building brake sclerostin · Sclerostin suppression · role Bone & cartilage
   Sclerostin is a protein from bone cells that acts as a brake on bone building. Teriparatide lowers it, freeing osteoblasts to work. This is part of how the pulse turns into new bone.
16. Briefly raises blood calcium · Renal Ca reabsorption, vit D · role Endocrine & growth
   Like natural PTH, it raises blood calcium for a few hours by helping the kidneys hold on to calcium and by activating vitamin D. The rise is brief because the drug is a short pulse. It is a known, monitored effect.
17. Cuts spine fractures and back pain · Fracture risk reduction · role Pain & sensory
   In large Phase 3 trials in severe osteoporosis, it cut new spine fractures and reduced back pain. It is one of the few drugs that builds bone rather than only slowing loss. The gains fade unless another bone drug follows.
18. Mechanism overview: Teriparatide is the first 34 amino acids of parathyroid hormone, the part that activates the PTH1 receptor. Constant PTH breaks bone down, but a daily pulse switches osteoblasts on and suppresses sclerostin, the brake on bone building. Formation then outpaces resorption, adding new bone. It also briefly raises blood calcium by increasing kidney reabsorption and vitamin D activation. The pulse matters: timing, not total dose, decides whether bone is built or lost.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
19. Typical: 20 mcg · 1× daily · cycle Up to 2 years (usual) · route Sub-Q (verified)
20. Half-life: ~1 h
21. Dose note: The 40 mcg trial arm had twice the side-effect dropouts and healed fractures no faster. 20 mcg is the real top.
22. Label: 20 mcg · 1× daily · up to 2 yr · Sub-Q · for osteoporosis; off-label fracture healing [S1] [S2] (verified)
23. Weekly (Japan): 56.5 mcg · 1× weekly · up to 72 wk · Sub-Q · for Japan, Teribone [S3] (verified)
24. High trial arm: 40 mcg · 1× daily · ~18 mo; 8 wk fracture trial · Sub-Q · for trial only [S1] [S4] (verified)

## What people report
25. Grey-market use is rare and usually for genuine bone issues; it is a real approved drug.
26. Liked / worked: Builds bone density
27. Liked / worked: Cuts fractures
28. Liked / worked: One of few bone-building osteoporosis drugs
29. What worked: Proven bone building and fewer fractures; one of a few bone-building osteoporosis drugs, alongside abaloparatide and romosozumab.
30. Went wrong / did not work: Daily injection
31. Went wrong / did not work: Gains lost if no bone drug follows
32. What went wrong: Daily injection; an old rat bone-cancer boxed warning was removed in 2020; stopping loses the gains unless another bone drug follows.
33. Most reported: Rare grey-market use
34. Most reported: Mostly for genuine bone problems

## What has been tested
35. Bone & cartilage: Bone density, Phase 3 (trial)
36. Bone & cartilage: Fracture reduction, Phase 3 (trial)
37. Large Phase 3 trials showed it builds bone density and cuts fractures; a well-established approved osteoporosis drug.
38. What it helps: Large Phase 3 trials showed it builds bone density and cuts spine fractures in severe osteoporosis, with less back pain. It is one of few bone-building osteoporosis drugs. It needs daily injection, and gains are lost unless another bone drug follows. Grey-market use is rare and mostly for genuine bone problems.
39. Trial: active · Phase 4 · postmenopausal osteoporosis · NCT06558188. Approved since 2002; still recruiting in osteoporosis and fracture studies, and an oral tablet version (EB613) is heading to Phase 3. (checked 2026-10-23) [S5] (reported)

## Who shouldn't take it
40. Paget's disease, unexplained high ALP, prior bone radiation: Higher baseline osteosarcoma risk; label warns. (verified)
41. People on digoxin: Transient high calcium can trigger digoxin toxicity. (verified)
42. People with kidney stones or high urine calcium: It raises urine and blood calcium, which can grow new stones. (verified)
43. People prone to dizziness on standing: Orthostatic hypotension at first doses. (verified)

## Where it comes from
44. The active 1-34 fragment of parathyroid hormone (Forteo), which, given in once-daily pulses, builds bone instead of breaking it down.
45. First studied for: Severe osteoporosis at high fracture risk.
46. Name story: The name hides a plain recipe: residues 1–34 of the 84-amino-acid parathyroid hormone, made recombinantly. Lilly's Forteo (Forsteo in Europe) carried a rat bone-cancer warning that human data never confirmed. [S6] (verified)
47. 2002: FDA approves PTH(1-34) as Forteo for severe osteoporosis
48. 2020: Old rat bone-cancer boxed warning removed
49. Today: An established bone-building drug, with follow-on versions

   Lys-Glu-Asp-Gly is aimed at the testis, where Leydig cells make testosterone. The group claims it supports that hormone output in aging men. Russian human reports describe this, but no independent Western trial has tested it.

# Thymogen

## Identity

## Summary

It is registered as a medicine in Russia, including a nasal form, and is used for respiratory and immune conditions and faster recovery from infection. It is claimed to help T-cells mature, but independent data are thin and there is no Western validation.

## How it works
13. Claimed to stimulate immune cells · Khavinson group · role Immunity
   Thymogen, the dipeptide Glu-Trp, is claimed by the Khavinson tradition to activate immune cells and rebalance their responses. That is the basis for its Russian clinical use, including a nasal form, in respiratory and immune conditions. Independent data are thin.
14. Claimed to help T-cells mature · Glu-Trp dipeptide, thymus · role Immunity
   Glu-Trp comes from research on the thymus, the organ where T-cells mature, and is claimed to help T-cell precursors finish that maturation. Better maturation would mean more working T-cells during infection. This rests on Russian studies with no Western validation.
15. Claimed to speed wound and tissue healing · Regenerative response · role Tissue repair
   The group also claims Thymogen speeds wound and tissue healing, framed as a knock-on effect of its immune action on the repair response. Russian clinical reports describe faster recovery from infection. Independent controlled trials of this are lacking.

The group claims it stimulates immune cells, helps T-cells mature and speeds wound and tissue healing. These claims rest largely on one research tradition with little outside data. Like other bioregulators, it is a short peptide said to act directly on DNA rather than through a surface receptor.

# Thymulin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/thymulin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: facteur thymique sérique, FTS, serum thymic factor, zinc-thymulin
2. Origin: Made by the body
3. Sequence: EAKSQGGSN (9 amino acids). Starts with pyroglutamate, shown as E; carries zinc
4. Legal and approval status: Research chemical; no approval.

## Summary
5. Thymulin is a natural nonapeptide hormone made by the thymus that matures T cells and only works with a zinc atom attached. It is studied as a regulator of immune balance and inflammation, and in animal models it lowers inflammatory signals and reduces pain hypersensitivity. Evidence is animal work, there are no modern human efficacy trials, and it has no approval.
6. Punch line: The thymus hormone that matures T cells, active only with zinc bound. Calms inflammation and pain in animals.
7. Used for: Immune support and inflammation

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Immunity: Matures T cells, needs zinc
9. Endocrine & growth: Thymus hormone
10. Inflammatory signaling: Calms inflammation
11. Cellular protection: Cell protection
12. Pain & sensory (backed only by animal or user reports): Pain relief in animals
13. Neural protection (backed only by animal or user reports): Nerve protection studied
14. Skin & aesthetics (backed only by animal or user reports): Hair and skin studied

## How it works
15. Matures T-cells · Thymic hormone · role Immunity
   Thymulin is a hormone made by thymic epithelial cells that signals T-cell precursors to mature and specialise. That keeps up the supply of working T-cells, which falls as the thymus shrinks with age. Its role is shown in animal work, with no modern human efficacy trials.
16. Only active with bound zinc · Zinc-dependent · role Immunity
   Thymulin only works when bound to a zinc ion, which locks the peptide into its active shape. Without zinc it is present but inactive, so zinc status shapes its effect. This dependence complicates practical use of the peptide on its own.
17. Lowers inflammatory cytokines in models · TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6 · role Inflammatory signaling
   In animal models, thymulin lowers TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta and IL-6, three main signals that drive inflammation. Less of these signals means a calmer immune response in tissue. These results come from animals, not human trials.
18. Cuts pain hypersensitivity in animal models · Anti-hyperalgesia · role Pain & sensory
   In animal pain models, thymulin reduces hyperalgesia, the state where nerves overreact to normal or mild stimuli. This fits with its lowering of the inflammatory cytokines that sensitise nerves. It has not been tested for pain in people.
19. Two-way link with pituitary hormones · Neuroendocrine-thymus axis · role Endocrine & growth
   Pituitary hormones regulate how much thymulin the thymus releases, and thymulin in turn affects pituitary output. This two-way neuroendocrine loop ties the immune and hormone systems together. It is described from animal and some human work.
20. Mechanism overview: Thymulin is a nine-amino-acid hormone secreted by thymic epithelial cells. It is only active when bound to zinc, which locks it into its working shape. It drives T-cell maturation and differentiation. In animal models it lowers TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta and IL-6 and reduces pain hypersensitivity. It sits in a two-way loop with the pituitary: pituitary hormones regulate its secretion and thymulin in turn affects pituitary output.

22. Half-life: ~10 min
23. Dose note: Guides span 1 mcg to 5 mg. The mg figures likely come from Thymalin or from vial sizes.
24. Most people take: Zinc-bound nonapeptide (FTS), active only with bound zinc; dosed in the low microgram range. NOTE: Thymalin is a different compound (calf-thymus peptide extract, 5–10 mg/day IM, 5–10 day course) and is not this entry.
25. Research (mcg): 1–10 mcg · 1× daily · varies · Sub-Q · for research protocols [S1] (reported)
26. Community cycle: 1–2 mg · 1× daily, PM · 20 days, ~3×/yr · Sub-Q · for vial users, often with 15–30 mg zinc [S2] [S3] (reported)

## What people report
27. Thin grey-market use; reported for immune support.
28. Liked / worked: Immune modulation in models
29. Liked / worked: Anti-inflammatory and pain relief in models
30. What worked: In models, immune modulation and anti-inflammatory/analgesic effects.
31. Went wrong / did not work: Zinc dependence complicates use
32. Went wrong / did not work: No modern human efficacy trials
33. What went wrong: Zinc-dependence complicates use; no modern human efficacy trials.
34. Most reported: Few first-hand reports
35. Most reported: Used for immune support

## What has been tested
36. Immunity: Immune modulation (animal)
37. Inflammatory signaling: Anti-inflammatory effect (animal)
38. Pain & sensory: Pain relief (animal)
39. Animal and some human work: zinc-thymulin influences immune and neuroendocrine signaling and has anti-inflammatory and pain effects in models.
40. What it helps: Evidence is animal work showing immune modulation, anti-inflammatory effects and pain relief. There are no modern human efficacy trials, and the zinc dependence complicates practical use. First-hand reports are few, mostly from people using it for immune support. Pain models show reduced hypersensitivity.

## Who shouldn't take it
42. Transplant recipients on anti-rejection drugs: Thymic hormone that matures T cells. (inferred)
43. People with autoimmune disease: Turning up immune activity can flare an autoimmune condition. (inferred)

## Where it comes from
44. A natural zinc-dependent thymus hormone (nonapeptide) that matures T-cells; its activity depends on bound zinc.
45. First studied for: A marker and modulator of thymic/immune function, studied in immune deficiency and inflammation.
46. Name story: Discovered by Jean-François Bach's group in 1977 as 'facteur thymique sérique' (FTS), a thymus factor found in blood serum. It only works with a zinc atom bound. Easily confused with Thymalin, a whole-gland extract. [S5] (verified)

48. Today: Research chemical; no approval
