# Trofinetide
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/trofinetide
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: Daybue, Daybue Stix, Daybu (EU), NNZ-2566, G-2MePE, glycyl-L-2-methylprolyl-L-glutamic acid
2. Origin: Lab-modified fragment of a natural protein: IGF-1's first three amino acids
3. Shown with an FDA approved badge
4. Legal and approval status: FDA approved March 2023 for Rett syndrome from age 2; Daybue Stix powder approved December 2025. EU authorised as Daybu on 20 August 2026 from age 5. Also approved in Canada (reported).

## Summary
5. Trofinetide is a tiny three-amino-acid fragment of IGF-1 (GPE) with one methyl added so it survives in the body. It became the first drug approved for Rett syndrome in 2023, thought to support synapse maturation and calm brain inflammation. A 12-week Phase 3 showed modest but real gains in caregiver and clinician ratings. Diarrhea affected 82% versus 20% on placebo, and how it works is officially unknown.
6. Punch line: Daybue, a stabilised IGF-1 fragment and the first approved Rett drug. Taken twice daily; diarrhea is the hurdle.
7. Used for: Rett syndrome

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Neural plasticity: Thought to help synapses form and mature
9. Neural protection: Calms brain cell stress in Rett models
10. Cognition: Small gains in communication and alertness
11. Inflammatory signaling: Reduces brain inflammation (proposed)

## How it works
12. Mimics GPE, a natural IGF-1 fragment in the brain · IGF-1 N-terminal tripeptide analogue · role Neural plasticity
   Trofinetide is a modified copy of GPE, the three amino acid piece cut from the start of IGF-1 in the brain. The change makes it last longer than natural GPE. It is approved for Rett syndrome on human trial data, though how GPE acts is still being worked out.
13. Proposed to support synapse maturation · Synaptic function · role Neural plasticity
   It is proposed to help synapses, the connections between neurons, mature and work properly, which is impaired in Rett syndrome. That would fit the modest gains in caregiver and clinician ratings. The synapse mechanism comes from preclinical work, not human measurements.
14. Proposed to dampen microglial inflammation · Neuroinflammation · role Inflammatory signaling
   It is also proposed to calm microglia, the brain's immune cells, and the inflammation they drive. Lower neuroinflammation may protect neurons in Rett syndrome. This is a proposed mechanism from preclinical studies, not shown in patients.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
15. Typical: 5 to 12 g by body weight (12 g at 50 kg and up) · Twice daily · cycle Ongoing · route Oral, or by G-tube (label)
16. Half-life: About 1.5 hours
17. Most people take: Weight-based, twice daily by mouth or G-tube: 5 g (9 to 12 kg), 6 g (12 to 20 kg), 8 g (20 to 35 kg), 10 g (35 to 50 kg), 12 g (50 kg and up).

## What people report
18. Caregivers describe better eye contact, hand use and alertness in some children, against hard-to-manage diarrhea and weight loss; dose reductions and stopping laxatives are common advice.
19. Liked / worked: First approved Rett syndrome drug
20. Liked / worked: Caregiver and clinician scores improved
21. What worked: LAVENDER: caregiver-rated Rett symptoms (RSBQ) improved by 4.9 points versus 1.7 on placebo, and clinicians rated overall change slightly better (CGI-I 3.5 versus 3.8). Communication also improved, and gains tended to keep growing in extensions.
22. Went wrong / did not work: Diarrhea in 82%
23. Went wrong / did not work: Modest effect size
24. What went wrong: The effect is modest. Diarrhea in 82% versus 20% on placebo and vomiting in 29% versus 12%, so many families struggle to stay on it. How it works is officially unknown.
25. Most reported: Better eye contact and hand use for some
26. Most reported: Diarrhea and weight loss hard to manage

## What has been tested
27. Neural plasticity: Rett syndrome, ages 5 to 20, LAVENDER Phase 3 (trial)
28. Neural plasticity: Rett syndrome, ages 2 to 4, DAFFODIL (trial)
29. Phase 3 LAVENDER in 187 girls and women aged 5 to 20 over 12 weeks, with LILAC open-label extensions over several years, and DAFFODIL in 15 children aged 2 to 4.
30. What it helps: Approved for Rett syndrome on a 12-week Phase 3 with modest but real gains in caregiver and clinician ratings, which tended to grow in multi-year extensions. Diarrhea and vomiting are the main limit.
31. Trial: none · Approved; pivotal Phase 3 complete · NCT04181723. Its pivotal Phase 3 LAVENDER trial led to approval; no new major trial was found in the sources checked. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1]

## Synergies (paired with)
32. IGF-1 LR3: IGF-1 LR3 is a long-acting full IGF-1 analogue aimed at muscle growth, while trofinetide copies only the small brain fragment. They share a parent molecule but have different targets. The pairing is user logic and has not been tested.
33. Cerebrolysin: Cerebrolysin is a pig brain peptide mix with nerve growth activity, and trofinetide targets synapse function and brain inflammation. Both are used for brain support from different angles. The pair has not been tested together.

## Where it comes from
34. Developed by Neuren Pharmaceuticals in New Zealand from GPE, a tiny piece cut from IGF-1 in the brain, then licensed to Acadia Pharmaceuticals.
35. First studied for: Rett syndrome, a genetic disorder in girls that takes away speech and hand use. It is the first approved treatment for it.
36. 2000s: Neuren develops NNZ-2566 from the IGF-1 fragment GPE
37. 2015: EU orphan designation for Rett syndrome
38. Mar 2023: FDA approves Daybue, first Rett syndrome drug
39. Dec 2025: FDA approves Daybue Stix powder
40. Aug 2026: EU authorises it as Daybu
41. Today: Standard Rett treatment in the US; GI side effects limit use

# Ubiquitin
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/ubiquitin
Checked against Library v68, exported 2026-10-25

## Identity
1. Also called: protein reference, UBIP, polypeptide beta-1, APF-1
2. Origin: Made by the body (reference)
3. Sequence: MQIFVKTLTGKTITLEVEPSDTIENVKAKIQDKEGIPPDQQRLIFAGKQLEDGRTLSDYNIQKESTLHLVLRLRGG (76 amino acids)
4. Legal and approval status: Reference molecule.

## Summary
5. Ubiquitin is a small protein made by nearly every cell, almost unchanged across species, that tags other proteins for recycling, work that won the 2004 Nobel Prize. It is a fundamental cell signalling molecule rather than a therapeutic and is not used as an injectable. Its clinical relevance is indirect, through drug targets such as proteasome blockers. This is a reference entry with no user reports.
6. Punch line: The cell's recycling tag, nearly identical in every species. Marks damaged proteins for disposal; Nobel Prize 2004.

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
7. Cellular protection: Tags damaged proteins for recycling
8. Organ function: Keeps every cell clean
9. DNA & telomeres: Directs DNA repair
10. Immunity: Runs immune signalling

## How it works
11. Tags worn proteins for shredding · Ubiquitin-proteasome system · role Cellular protection
   Ubiquitin is attached to worn or unneeded proteins, and K48-linked chains of it send them to the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder. This keeps damaged and misfolded proteins from building up. It is one of the best-mapped systems in cell biology, though not a drug itself.
12. Chains of tags route proteins to fates · E1, E2, E3 ligases · role Cellular protection
   An enzyme cascade attaches ubiquitin: E1 activates it, E2 carries it, and one of hundreds of E3 ligases picks the target protein. The linkage type of the chain sets the fate, destruction or signalling. This fine control is shown across a vast cell and biochemistry literature.
13. Marks DNA damage sites for repair · Histone ubiquitination · role DNA & telomeres
   Ubiquitin added to histones, the proteins DNA wraps around, flags sites of DNA damage. The mark recruits repair proteins to the break. This is established in cell studies and is part of how cells keep their genome intact.
14. Switches on immune alarm signalling · K63 chains, NF-kB · role Immunity
   K63-linked ubiquitin chains do not trigger destruction; they act as scaffolds that assemble signalling complexes. One key output is activation of NF-kB, the master switch for immune and inflammatory genes. This is mapped in cell studies.
15. Clears damaged organelles · Mitophagy, PINK1/Parkin · role Organ function
   When mitochondria are damaged, PINK1 builds up on their surface and recruits Parkin, which coats them with ubiquitin. The tag marks the organelle for mitophagy, its removal and recycling. This quality-control pathway is well shown in cell studies.
16. Mechanism overview: Ubiquitin is a 76 amino acid protein found in every eukaryotic cell. An enzyme cascade of E1 activators, E2 conjugators and E3 ligases attaches it to lysines on target proteins. The chain type sets the fate: K48-linked chains send proteins to the proteasome for destruction, while K63-linked chains act as scaffolds for NF-kB immune signalling and DNA repair. Ubiquitin on histones marks DNA damage sites. PINK1 and Parkin use it to tag damaged mitochondria for removal. Hundreds of E3 ligases give fine control over which proteins survive.

## What people report
18. A reference entry, included to show the scale of peptide/protein signaling.
19. Liked / worked: Central to how cells clear proteins
20. Liked / worked: Drug targets sit around it, like proteasome blockers
21. What worked: Central to how cells dispose of proteins; drug targets sit around it.
22. Went wrong / did not work: Not used as an injectable therapeutic
23. What went wrong: Not used as an injectable therapeutic.
24. Most reported: A reference entry; shows the scale of protein signalling

## What has been tested
25. DNA & telomeres: Protein disposal and cell signalling (cell)
26. Vast basic-science literature on the ubiquitin-proteasome system; not a drug.
27. What it helps: Ubiquitin is not used as an injectable therapeutic. Its clinical weight comes indirectly: drug targets sit around the system, such as the proteasome blockers. It is a reference entry that shows the scale of protein signalling inside cells, and it has no user reports.
28. Trial: none. No human trial uses ubiquitin as a treatment; it is studied as a biomarker and drug target only. (checked 2026-10-23) [S1] (inferred)

## Where it comes from
29. Named for being everywhere: nearly every cell makes it, almost unchanged. Tagging proteins for recycling won the 2004 Nobel Prize.
30. First studied for: A fundamental cellular protein, not a therapeutic.
31. Name story: Named in 1975 as 'ubiquitous immunopoietic polypeptide' because it turned up in every cell. It was first fished out of calf-thymus extracts as thymosin 'polypeptide beta-1'; its real job, tagging proteins for destruction, won the 2004 Nobel. [S2] (verified)
32. 1970s: Named for being everywhere; nearly unchanged across life
33. 2004: Nobel Prize for showing it tags proteins for disposal
34. Today: A core cell protein and reference molecule; not a drug

# VIP
Page: https://baresignals.co/library/#/p/vip

## Identity
1. Also called: vasoactive intestinal polypeptide, aviptadil

4. Legal and approval status: Aviptadil (synthetic VIP) with phentolamine is approved for erectile dysfunction in the UK and some European countries; not FDA-approved. Other uses are research or compounded.

## Summary
5. VIP (vasoactive intestinal polypeptide) is a 28-amino-acid hormone made in the gut, lung, nerves and immune cells that widens blood vessels and calms inflammation. It has been studied in pulmonary hypertension and sarcoidosis, and aviptadil is approved for erectile dysfunction in some countries. Nasal VIP is popular in mold-illness circles, but formal evidence is thin.
6. Punch line: Gut, lung and nerve hormone that widens vessels and calms inflammation. A nasal staple in mold illness protocols.
7. Used for: Mold illness (CIRS), inflammation

## Roles (what it is used for, strongest first)
8. Organ function: Lung and gut signalling
9. Inflammatory signaling: Calms inflammation
10. Connection & desire: Erection treatment abroad
11. Neural protection: Nerve protection studied
12. Immunity (backed only by animal or user reports): Immune balance
13. Digestive & gut (backed only by animal or user reports): Gut movement and secretion
14. Sleep & rhythms (backed only by animal or user reports): Body clock signalling

## How it works
15. Widens blood vessels · VPAC1, VPAC2 · role Organ function
   VIP binds VPAC1 and VPAC2, receptors that raise cAMP inside the smooth muscle around blood vessels. That relaxes the muscle and widens the vessels. Small human studies show vascular benefit in pulmonary hypertension.
16. Dampens immune inflammation, boosts Tregs · VPAC on immune cells · role Inflammatory signaling
   On immune cells, VPAC signalling lowers inflammatory cytokines and favours regulatory T cells, which calm immune responses. This shifts the immune system away from inflammation. Small human studies show anti-inflammatory signals in sarcoidosis.
17. Relaxes airway and gut smooth muscle · VPAC receptors · role Digestive & gut
   The same cAMP rise through VPAC receptors relaxes smooth muscle in the airways and gut. This is why VIP was studied in lung conditions. It is well-established receptor pharmacology, though human outcome trials are limited.
18. Relaxes erectile tissue, used for ED · Cavernosal VPAC, cAMP · role Connection & desire
   In erectile tissue, VPAC activation raises cAMP and relaxes the smooth muscle, letting blood fill the tissue. Aviptadil, a form of VIP, has been trialled with phentolamine for erectile dysfunction. Those trials used the combination, not VIP alone.
19. Shields neurons via glial protective factors · ADNP release · role Neural protection
   VIP prompts glial cells, the brain's support cells, to release protective factors such as ADNP. These factors shield neurons from damage. This is shown in cell and animal studies, not in people.
20. Syncs the body clock in the brain · SCN VPAC2 signalling · role Sleep & rhythms
   In the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the brain's master clock, VPAC2 signalling keeps clock neurons in step with each other. This keeps the body's daily rhythms synchronised. It is well established in animal research.
21. Mechanism overview: Vasoactive intestinal peptide is a 28-amino-acid neuropeptide acting on VPAC1 and VPAC2, Gs-coupled receptors that raise cAMP. In smooth muscle that relaxes blood vessels, airways, gut and erectile tissue. On immune cells it dampens inflammatory cytokines and favours regulatory T cells. It prompts glia to release protective factors such as ADNP that shield neurons, and VPAC2 signalling in the suprachiasmatic nucleus synchronises the body clock. Its half-life is very short.

## Dosage (community reported unless tagged)
22. Typical: 50–100 mcg · daily · cycle 4-8 weeks · route Sub-Q, Intranasal (reported)
23. Half-life: ~2 minutes IV
24. Most people take: 50-100mcg/day intranasal or SC · 4-8 weeks.
25. Sub-Q standard: 50–100 mcg · 1–2× daily · ongoing · Sub-Q · for research-vial users [S1] (reported)
26. Shoemaker nasal: 200–400 mcg/day (50 mcg x4–8 sprays) · split 2–4× daily · months; trial 18+ mo · Intranasal · for CIRS/mold patients, clinic-prescribed [S2] [S3] [S4] (reported)
27. Sub-Q advanced: 200 mcg · 1–2× daily or 5×/wk · ongoing · Sub-Q · for experienced users, clinic-style [S1] (reported)

## What has been tested
40. Heart & vessels: Pulmonary hypertension (human)
41. Inflammatory signaling: Sarcoidosis (human)
42. Inflammatory signaling: CIRS, nasal spray (users)
43. Reproductive: Erectile dysfunction, aviptadil (trial)
44. Small human studies in pulmonary hypertension and sarcoidosis; nasal VIP has a following in chronic inflammatory response syndrome with limited formal evidence.
45. What it helps: Small human studies show vascular benefit in pulmonary hypertension and anti-inflammatory signals in sarcoidosis. Aviptadil combined with phentolamine has been trialled for erectile dysfunction. Nasal VIP is popular in mold-illness circles, where users report relief from CIRS symptoms including inflammation, sinus problems and low energy, though formal evidence is thin.
46. Trial: none · Phase 2/3 · severe COVID 19 lung failure · NCT04843761 · NIAID (ACTIV-3b/TESICO). Aviptadil was tested in COVID trials during 2020 to 2022 without a clear win; a planned German sarcoidosis trial never visibly reported and no active trial was found. (checked 2026-10-23) [S5] (inferred)

## Who shouldn't take it
47. People with low blood pressure or on BP drugs: VIP dilates vessels; hypotension and flushing in trials. (reported)
48. People prone to dehydration or low potassium: VIP drives water and potassium into the gut; tumours making it cause severe diarrhoea. (reported)

## Where it comes from
49. Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide, a 28-amino-acid signaling hormone in gut, lung, nerves and immune cells, with broad anti-inflammatory and vasodilating action.
50. First studied for: Studied in pulmonary hypertension, sarcoidosis, and in the CIRS/mold-illness community (as a nasal spray) for immune and inflammatory dysregulation.
51. Name story: Vasoactive intestinal peptide: Said and Mutt pulled it from pig intestine in 1970 and named it for widening blood vessels. It later proved to be a brain and nerve messenger too. The drug version's INN is aviptadil. [S6] (verified)
52. 1970: Discovered in the gut as a vasoactive peptide
53. 2000s: Small human studies in pulmonary hypertension and sarcoidosis
54. 2010s: Nasal VIP adopted in CIRS and mold-illness protocols
55. Today: Aviptadil approved for ED in the UK and parts of Europe; not in the US
